events.title: Hong Kong business leaders examine investment opportunities under city’s first Five-Year plan
events.summary: More than 30 senior business leaders from sectors across banking and finance, healthcare and life sciences, real estate and infrastructure, and AI and technology, gathered yesterday to examine how Hong Kong’s first five-year plan could translate regional and national policy priorities into tangible investment and business opportunities. Co-organised by the South China Morning Post and the Hong Kong Investment Corporation (HKIC), the closed-door SCMP C-Suite roundtable welcomed Financial Secretary Paul Chan Mo-po as guest of honour, alongside HKIC CEO Clara Chan as guest speaker. Held under the theme “From APEC Consensus to Action: Hong Kong’s Five-Year Plan and Strategic Role in China’s Next Phase of Growth”, the discussion explored how the city’s development strategy aligns with China’s 15th Five-Year Plan and its implications for businesses and investors. Following October’s APEC Finance Ministers’ Meeting in Hong Kong, where digital infrastructure financing and financial inclusion were among the key priorities, participants examined how long-term development objectives could be translated into commercially viable investment opportunities. The Financial Secretary outlined Hong Kong’s economic priorities and reaffirmed its role as an international financial centre and a hub for innovation and talent connecting mainland China with global markets. The discussion examined how these strengths could support emerging industries and mainland enterprises expanding overseas. The Northern Metropolis was a key focus, with participants exploring opportunities for cross-boundary collaboration in technology and healthcare, alongside the infrastructure, financing and regulatory coordination needed to advance its development. The financial secretary encouraged business leaders to visit the area to appreciate the scale of the development first-hand. Attention also turned to HKIC’s use of patient capital to attract private investment and support technology companies, while pursuing financial returns and longer-term economic benefits for Hong Kong. Taken altogether, the discussion offered a picture of Hong Kong’s next phase of economic development, with strategic public investment, private capital and cross-border collaboration helping to turn policy ambitions into commercial opportunities. Part of the SCMP C-Suite roundtable series, the event reinforced the value of bringing together senior business leaders, investors and policymakers for candid dialogue, informed perspectives and meaningful connections on issues shaping Hong Kong’s future.

events.title: What smart people in business and tech are saying about the Nvidia board potentially ousting Jensen Huang
events.summary: Jensen Huang's potential ouster as Nvidia CEO has got people in tech talking. Tomohiro Ohsumi/Getty Images Nvidia stock fell 8% following a Wall Street Journal report that the company's board plans to oust CEO Jensen Huang. The New York Times reported on Wednesday that Huang had a second extramarital affair, this time with an Nvidia employee. This is what smart people in business and tech are saying about Huang's potential exit from Nvidia . Speculation over what Nvidia's future could look like without its high-profile chief executive ramped up on Wednesday. The chipmaker's stock fell 8% in after-hours trading Wednesday after The Wall Street Journal reported that its board was preparing to remove CEO Jensen Huang . The New York Times also reported Wednesday that Huang had an affair with an Nvidia executive who reported to him, citing five people who worked at the company. The report came days after Huang said in a memo to employees that he had an extramarital affair , and after Nvidia's board launched an investigation into whether Huang had been targeted by a foreign intelligence operation. The New York Times previously reported US officials believed Huang had grown close to a tech executive, Alice Huang , who had been recruited to gather information for the Chinese government. As the chip giant's succession plans remain unknown, here is what smart people in business and tech are saying about Huang's potential exit from Nvidia . Ross Gerber, CEO of Gerber Kawasaki Wealth & Investment Management Ross Gerber has been bearish on Tesla. Emma McIntyre/Getty Images Ross Gerber said Huang's departure would be a disappointment for Nvidia shareholders but said the company could move forward without him. "Looks like Jensen is done. What a disappointment. Sad day for Nvidia shareholders and looks like another tough day for the stock. Never would have guessed he'd go down this way," Gerber wrote in one of several posts on X on Wednesday. "Jensen will be replaced and Nvidia is still Nvidia. That's business. He must go and Nvidia needs to focus on selling chips!" Gerber added. Eric Wallerstein, chief macro strategist at Clocktower Group Eric Wallerstein wrote on X on Wednesday that Huang's likely ousting could shake investor confidence in the broader AI trade , given Nvidia's role in financing the industry. "Jensen has helped foster a complex web of circular financing relationships, and ultimately backstopped the AI trade, with Nvidia's balance sheet," Wallerstein said. "Removing that Put, or even placing uncertainty on its availability, will cause investors to increase the risk premium on AI-related assets," Wallerstein added. Ed Zitron, CEO of EZ Primary Research Carlos Rodrigues/Sportsfile for Web Summit via Getty Images Ed Zitron said in a post on X that he questions what else Nvidia might be withholding from investors, pointing to the company's past regulatory troubles. "Oh so NVIDIA knew about this affair already, huh? What else is this company not telling us?" Zitron wrote on Wednesday. Zitron also cited two previous SEC cases involving Nvidia, one in 2002 over accounting practices and one in 2022 over disclosures related to cryptocurrency mining and gaming revenue. Jason Calacanis, co-host and executive producer of the All-In Podcast Jason Calacanis said that the ban was "smart" because of the risk of terrorism. Bloomberg/Getty Images Jason Calacanis said the company shouldn't be so quick to remove Huang. "A much better solution for NVIDIA's board, shareholders, customers and employees (and America) would be to (a) finish their investigation and (b) make @JensenHuang the chairman if it comes to that," Calacanis wrote on X on Wednesday. "China doesn't need NVIDIA's chips. America needs NVIDIA to win. Act accordingly," Calacanis added, alongside a screenshot of his new Nvidia share purchases. Keith Urbahn, president of Javelin Keith Urbahn, president of Javelin, a literary and creative agency that has repped prominent figures like James Comey and Tucker Carlson, said Wednesday in an X post that the situation was "a generational case study in how not to manage a crisis." He outlined several lessons to take away from the ordeal, including: "Never let a CEO's personal crisis take precedence over the interests of the company and its shareholders." "The board must speak with its own voice. It cannot outsource its institutional credibility to the CEO," he added. Byrne Hobart, venture capitalist and founder of The Diff Byrne Hobart, general partner at Anomaly Fund and founder of The Diff, a finance and tech newsletter, suggested ousting Huang could lead to new competition for Nvidia. "On one hand, boards have to do what they have to do. On the other hand, he's a guy who's worth $150bn, knows everyone in hardware, named his company after the Latin word for "spite," and he lives in a state where you can't enforce noncompetes," he wrote in a post on X. Anthony Pompliano, crypto investor and entrepreneur Slaven Vlasic/Getty Images for Anthony Pompliano Anthony Pompliano, a crypto investor and entrepreneur, wrote on X: "Jensen's yet-to-be-launched Nvidia competitor is going to do numbers in the seed round." Gene Munster, managing partner at Deepwater Asset Management Peter Foley/Bloomberg via Getty Images Gene Munster, a tech analyst and managing partner at Deepwater Asset Management, said in an X post that Nvidia will go on, with or without its famous CEO. "Remember: AI infrastructure customers will act in their best interest," he said. "That means they'll keep buying just as many $NVDA chips with or without Jensen." He also said he guesses the stock will open on Thursday at $150, or about 20% lower than the close at the end of last week, but that he expects it to "quickly rally back." Jim Cramer, host of CNBC's Mad Money Jim Cramer said Apple's new filing was "gloves off." John Nacion/Variety via Getty Images Jim Cramer, who has interviewed Huang on several occasions, questioned how investors should value Nvidia if Huang were suddenly gone. "As I said this morning, there is a bench. As Mike from Coreweave said, there is a company," Cramer said on X on Wednesday. "What is it worth when a key man is just erased?" "Let me think about how sickening this is and then i will come back to you," Cramer added. "I want to throw up." Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Who is Kimberly Powell, the Nvidia exec alleged to have a relationship with CEO Jensen Huang?
events.summary: Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's VP of healthcare HLTH Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's VP of healthcare, reportedly had a relationship with CEO Jensen Huang. Powell joined Nvidia in 2008 and has risen through the ranks. Huang wrote in a memo to staff earlier this week that he was "unfaithful" to his wife. Kimberly Powell , Nvidia's vice president of healthcare, had an extramarital relationship with CEO Jensen Huang , according to a New York Times report on Wednesday that cited five company sources. Powell, 48, reports to Huang, 63. The Times reported that the duo was "captured on video being affectionate" at an Nvidia conference hotel in San Jose in March, and that Powell is also married. Huang is already under investigation at Nvidia on whether he was the target of a "foreign intelligence effort." The Times had reported that US officials believed another woman he grew close with, tech executive Alice Huang , may have been recruited by the Chinese government to spy on the chip giant. The Nvidia CEO admitted to being "unfaithful" to his wife in a note to staff on Sunday. Here's what to know about Powell. Powell steered Nvidia's healthcare efforts Powell joined Nvidia as a director in 2008 and has steadily risen through the ranks. According to her corporate profile, she was originally responsible for promoting the use of Nvidia's AI chips for medical imaging. She'd previously worked as an engineer and then in product at an electronics startup and ended up getting ahold of Nvidia to talk about their computing chips. Once the company realized its technology would have healthcare applications, it got back in touch to hire her, she said on an episode of the Lifers podcast published this August. Powell called the job a "dream come true" on the podcast. Her LinkedIn says she was promoted to senior director in 2016, and she led a business development team focused on AI. Powell's authority was growing — in 2017, she became vice president of healthcare, her profile says. Her corporate profile now says she is responsible for both the hardware and software sides of the company's healthcare business, including technology for medical imaging, life sciences, and drug discovery. "I pretty much live and breathe healthcare. So I'm talking about it all the time," Powell told Business Insider in 2025. Kimberly Powell's ties to Jensen Huang Huang, one of the entire tech industry's best-known representatives, has led Nvidia since he founded the company in 1993, so he and Powell have worked together for over 18 years. In the August interview with Lifers, Powell credited Huang's healthcare ambitions. "Jensen has been passionate about the healthcare industry going back 20-plus years, and that was really fueled by seeing just researchers who had dreams and aspirations to do something very, very meaningful and impactful in the healthcare domain and us potentially having the tools to do it, to achieve that goal," she said. Nvidia's code of conduct, which begins with a letter from Huang, includes personal relationships among the activities that can create a conflict of interest. It also says, "We promptly investigate reports of misconduct." Neither Powell nor Nvidia responded to requests for comment from Business Insider. CNN reporter Meg Tirrell posted on X that she'd been planning to moderate a conference panel featuring Powell on Thursday morning, but that Powell had cancelled. Have a tip? events.title: Outgoing Trump foe Massie forces new Epstein files showdown
events.summary: Outgoing Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) secured the 218 signatures needed to force another House showdown over the Jeffrey Epstein files Wednesday, just one day after fellow Republicans blocked his attempt to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Why it matters: Congress overwhelmingly voted last year to force the release of the Epstein files, but survivors and lawmakers say the Trump administration has still withheld records. The new bill would give them the power to sue the DOJ and help state prosecutors pursue investigations. Driving the news: Massie announced Wednesday afternoon that his discharge petition for the Epstein Files Transparency Act II had reached the required 218 signatures. Rep. John Garamendi (D-Calif.) provided the final signature Wednesday, according to the House clerk's records . Just four Republicans signed the petition: Massie, Nancy Mace of South Carolina, Ralph Norman of South Carolina and Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania. The other 214 signatures came from Democrats. What he's saying: "I'm working closely with @RepJayapal, @RepTeresaLF and @RepRoKhanna to get this to the floor for a vote soon," Massie wrote on X . The White House and Speaker Mike Johnson's offices have not yet provided comment. The intrigue: President Trump helped drive Massie out of Congress by backing a primary challenger, but the Kentucky Republican is using his final weeks in office to challenge the administration on some of its most politically sensitive topics. This latest effort could force Republicans to revisit a scandal that dogged the Trump administration for more than a year, even after Congress overwhelmingly voted to require the release of Epstein's files. This time, Massie wants to give Epstein survivors, state prosecutors and lawmakers the power to sue the Justice Department over records they believe it has unlawfully withheld. Catch up quick: Massie and Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) led the original push to force the release of the Epstein files. Their first bill passed the House 427-1 in November 2025 after they secured enough signatures to bypass Speaker Mike Johnson. Trump ultimately signed it into law. The law required DOJ to release its Epstein-related investigative records by Dec. 19, 2025, with limited exceptions to protect victims, ongoing investigations and other sensitive information. The department missed that deadline but announced in January that it had released nearly 3.5 million pages. The controversy: Epstein survivors and lawmakers have accused DOJ of withholding too much information while simultaneously exposing victims through inadequate redactions. A report released Tuesday by the Republican-led House Oversight Committee faulted the Trump administration's handling of the disclosures, including failures to protect victims and excessive redactions concealing alleged co-conspirators. The committee also said its investigation found no evidence implicating Trump in Epstein's crimes. What's next: Massie's petition is expected to become eligible for a floor vote by early December, with more than enough legislative days remaining under the House's current schedule. But passage is not guaranteed, and Senate Republican leaders could still decline to consider the measure before the new Congress takes office in January.

events.title: What could Chinese intelligence have learned from Nvidia CEO’s affair?
events.summary: Nvidia says no secrets were compromised, but experts question what sensitive information may have been exposed. United States lawmakers are pushing for answers from Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang amid growing concerns over whether an affair he had compromised national security. Huang, 63, has admitted to having extramarital relations during his time leading Nvidia, a major US tech firm. Media reports indicate the woman involved was Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based tech company Megaspeed who is accused of working for Chinese intelligence. list 1 of 3 Trump says FBI probing Nvidia CEO Huang’s affair with alleged spy list 2 of 3 Nvidia spy scandal fuels debate over chip exports to China list 3 of 3 Anthropic targets $1.4 trillion valuation in massive stock market debut As the scandal continues to grip Washington, Republican leaders of three committees in the House of Representatives have asked Huang to appear at a closed-door briefing to testify about the relationship. House Foreign Affairs Committee Chair Brian Mast said he was prepared to subpoena Huang if he did not respond by the end of Wednesday. According to The New York Times, US intelligence officials believe Alice Huang was recruited by Chinese intelligence to gather information about the Nvidia CEO and influence him to push for looser restrictions on chip sales to China. In a statement on Sunday, Jensen Huang apologised to his family and Nvidia employees about the affair. His company also launched an independent investigation, saying it had no reason to believe that “either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised”. Still, by Wednesday, media reports emerged that Nvidia was preparing to part ways with Huang over the controversy. US President Donald Trump confirmed on Monday that the Federal Bureau of Investigation was looking into the matter, but he has stood by Huang, calling him an “honourable guy”. But the pressure on Huang intensified on Tuesday when Republican Senator Kevin Cramer called for him to resign. “The potential for extortion is so tremendous that something as sensitive as Nvidia chips, I just think he’s got to go,” Cramer said in an interview with Politico. But Huang, who co-founded Nvidia more than 30 years ago, has shown no signs of heeding that call. Despite the company’s assurances, experts say the affair raises concerns about what information Alice Huang may have been privy to and what role the relationship may have played in the Nvidia CEO’s decisions. What are the national security concerns surrounding Nvidia? Nvidia’s advanced chips, which power much of today’s artificial intelligence, have put the company at the centre of the race for tech dominance between China and the US. Since 2022, Washington has restricted sales of some of the most advanced chips to China over concerns that they could be used by the country’s military or intelligence agencies. According to US intelligence officials cited by The New York Times, Alice Huang was tasked with getting Jensen Huang to lobby for looser restrictions on chip exports. The Nvidia CEO had already been pushing for an easing of the rules, arguing that China’s domestic chip industry would get stronger without better access to US products. But some experts say it is worth looking at how Alice Huang may have influenced decisions Nvidia made specifically about her former employer Megaspeed, which bought more than $4.8bn worth of Nvidia chips over the span of about two years. Megaspeed has also been investigated over allegations that it helped Chinese companies get access to restricted chips. Megaspeed denies the allegation. Ryan Fedasiuk, a fellow at the Foundation for American Innovation who studies Chinese technology and intelligence activities, pointed to reports from Bloomberg and The New York Times that Nvidia contacted the US Commerce Department about its investigation into Megaspeed. events.title: The biggest winner from the downfall of Jensen Huang is China
events.summary: Nvidia's Jensen Huang speaking at a conference in San Francisco Alistair Barr/Business Insider Nvidia's market value drops more than $300 billion on concerns that the board will oust Jensen Huang. Analysts warn removing Huang weakens America's AI lead as China tries to catch up. Huang had a romantic relationship with a woman who may be a Chinese spy. How valuable is a CEO? Often, it's hard to say. Sometimes, though, a series of unusual events provides a crystal-clear answer. On Wednesday afternoon, the New York Times reported that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with a subordinate, following revelations earlier this week that he had a romantic relationship with a possible Chinese spy . Right after that, The Wall Street Journal reported that Nvidia's board was preparing to oust Huang. That one-two punch knocked Nvidia shares down about 8% in after-hours trading, wiping more than $300 billion off the company's market value. The Chinese spy allegations were already known days ago. The new news today is that Jensen Huang is likely to be ousted as CEO. So we have our answer: Huang is worth at least $300 billion. That's more than Morgan Stanley and Goldman Sachs, the world's most important investment banks. And quite right, too. Huang is "the architect of the US AI trajectory," Stacy Rasgon, a top chip analyst from Bernstein Research, wrote in a note to investors earlier this week. This is the most powerful new technology to emerge since the dawn of the internet 30 years ago. And the US is in the lead — well ahead of China in second place. Now, with Huang likely out, and no obvious successor, America's AI lead looks shakier. "We can't even begin to speculate as to who they might find to fill Jensen's shoes," Rasgon wrote in a note to investors Wednesday evening. He slashed Nvidia's price target to $200 from $400. Earlier in the week, Rasgon warned of the geopolitical risks if Huang was forced to step down. "The primary beneficiary of Jensen's removal as Nvidia's CEO would clearly be China; we hope cooler heads prevail," he wrote. On Wednesday night, other analysts shared similar concerns. "This would be a setback for the US, particularly as China continues aggressively investing in its own AI capabilities," Brad Gastwirth, global head of research at Circular Technology, told me. "Removing Jensen would be a tremendous mistake," he added. "Nvidia is central to America's AI leadership, and losing Jensen at this stage could create unnecessary disruption." Nvidia's board has serious questions to answer about Huang's conduct, especially his relationship with a possible Chinese spy. If they do nothing, the directors expose themselves to legal risk as representatives of the company's shareholders. One of the few real powers a public company board holds is the ability to hire and fire executives, so actions often involve tough decisions like this. But the board also has to weigh the enormous cost of losing the man who built Nvidia into the engine of the AI boom. Tonight, that cost is at least $300 billion. "The board obviously needs to take the allegations seriously, particularly anything involving national security," Gastwirth said. "Unless the investigation uncovers something that makes his position untenable, I believe the board would be making a major strategic mistake by removing him." events.title: Nvidia stock falls 8% after report board is preparing to oust Jensen Huang after second affair
events.summary: Jensen Huang, chief executive of Nvidia. Joel Saget / AFP via Getty Images Nvidia stock fell 8% after hours after two major reports dropped about CEO Jensen Huang. The WSJ reported the board was preparing to oust him days after announcing an investigation. The NYT reported Huang had an affair with an Nvidia executive who reported to him. Nvidia's stock was down 8% after hours on Wednesday after new reports dropped concerning CEO Jensen Huang. The Wall Street Journal reported the Nvidia board was preparing to remove Huang. Days earlier, the board said it was investigating whether Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort after the CEO acknowledged having an extramarital affair. The New York Times also reported new allegations on Wednesday, saying Huang had a second extramarital affair with an executive at Nvidia who reports to him, citing five unnamed sources who worked at the company. The Times said the executive was Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of health care. Nvidia declined to provide a statement to The New York Times. Other stocks with direct ties to Nvidia also seemed to move in response to Wednesday's news. CoreWeave, a cloud computing company that uses Nvidia chips and counts Nvidia as an investor, saw its stock drop over 4% after hours. Micron, which supplies memory used alongside Nvidia's chips, was down nearly 3% after hours while Supermicro, which builds servers, was down nearly 5%. TSMC, which manufactures the chips Nvidia designs, was down over 2%. Later on Wednesday, Bernstein, a global equity research and brokerage firm, downgraded Nvidia's stock and slashed its price target in half to $200. "We admit to struggling mightily with this call, and can sympathize with the case to buy the dip," researchers at the firm wrote in their report. "But our gut tells us that we probably haven't yet fully probed the depths of what might be found here; we've had enough, and prefer to watch from the sidelines." On Sunday, Huang admitted to having an affair in a memo to employees and said he was cooperating with the board's investigation. He did not name his affair partner. The New York Times had previously reported that US intelligence officials believed Alice Huang, a tech executive who had grown close to the CEO, was recruited to gather information for Beijing. Days before disclosing his affair, Huang told Bloomberg his interactions with Alice Huang were related to their business dealings and "all completely normal and not unusual." A photo shows NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang with a woman confirmed by a Reuters source to be Alice Huang in Taipei, Taiwan released on June 7, 2024. Obtained by Reuters/via REUTERS Alice Huang , a Chinese national who is not related to the Nvidia CEO, has worked as an executive at Megaspeed, a cloud computing company in Singapore that was also an Nvidia customer. Nvidia's board hired Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz, an elite Wall Street law firm, to carry out the investigation, with partner Joon H. Kim , a former US attorney, tapped to lead it. Lawmakers last week also sent a letter to Huang requesting he testify about his relationship with Alice Huang, citing "significant national security concerns." Nvidia succession plans Nvidia's CEO has become nearly synonymous with the company he cofounded, but the question of succession at one of the world's most valuable companies has gotten major attention this week. Nvidia has not publicly shared a succession plan . On Sunday, the board told Business Insider that "Jensen is committed to continuing to lead Nvidia as CEO without interruption." Analysts and former employees said there were several potential successors, including vice president Ian Buck and chief financial officer Colette Kress. Huang's two adult children, Madison and Spencer , also work at Nvidia. This is a developing story. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: How India is marketing its skilled workforce to Australian businesses
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Qantas the latest in list of companies to outsource jobs to India Qantas is cutting 850 local jobs with some roles to be outsourced to Accenture workers in India. ( ABC News: ABC News: Adriane Reardon ) Qantas's announcement to shift 850 local jobs to India is the latest in a wave of white-collar jobs moving offshore. Some of Australia's biggest companies are outsourcing jobs to India. India has marketed its large, mostly English-speaking workforce to businesses for decades, but the nature of the jobs has changed. From clothing to credit cards, some of Australia's largest companies are shifting hundreds of jobs overseas, and the trend is not slowing down. NAB, Westpac, Telstra, Bank of Queensland, Coles, Officeworks and Qantas are among companies that have announced plans to cut Australian jobs and move roles to Asia in recent years — most under so-called global capacity centres (GCCs). Qantas announces cuts to 850 corporate jobs Qantas announces it will slash 850 roles in the coming years, with the first changes expected to be in place by mid-2027. GCCs are subsidiaries of foreign companies that allow them to maintain full control of their business rather than contracting a third party. Bunnings announced plans for a GCC in India in 2020, but has not yet announced job cuts. Kmart opened one in 2018. The companies said roles needed to move to cope with rising costs and the rapid adoption of artificial intelligence (AI). The Finance Sector Union has called the cuts "callous" and "ruthless" in the face of soaring corporate profits. From call centres to corporate hubs India is home to about 50 per cent of the world's GCCs, the latest evolution of offshoring, which began with contracting out call centre work decades ago. Global Capacity Centres take up a huge footprint in the city of Bengaluru in India's south. ( Reuters: Vivek Prakash ) In 2024, Australia's high commissioner to India, Philip Green, estimated Australian companies directly employed about 30,000 people in Indian GCCs. "In very simple terms, a GCC is setting up another office for a company. Instead of hiring contractors, you're hiring employees," said Lalit Ahuja, the chief executive of ANSR, which helps companies establish GCCs in India. Mr Ahuja said tighter immigration restrictions were accelerating the trend. Rather than waiting for skilled workers to migrate to Australia, he said, companies were moving operations to where the talent was. The shift could eventually extend to senior executives. "It's quite conceivable that one day for a large Australian company, they may have some key leaders sitting in Bangalore or Hyderabad," Mr Ahuja said. Arya Roy Bardhan, a junior fellow at the Observer Research Foundation in Kolkata, said that while India did offer skilled workers, it was the cost savings that attracted foreign companies. "If you're comparing India with Australia, the average wage is one third of what you have to pay in Australia," he said. "The only incentive for opening a GCC in India is cost savings. It's lower tax rates and major savings in wages." Dr Kanupriya, an assistant professor in the Department of Economics and Trade Policy at the Indian Institute of Foreign Trade, said it was a combination of both. "It's a cost-saving measure, and it taps into the diverse talent pool that India has to offer." A big part of that is the sheer number of potential employees available. India has marketed its large, mostly English-speaking workforce to foreign businesses since the 1990s, offering cheap wages and tax breaks to offshore companies. India has a huge number of tech graduates to offer Australian companies amid a domestic skills shortage. ( Reuters: Rishika Sadam ) By the early 2000s, more technical jobs shifted to the country as India prioritised tech and engineering graduates. With the world's largest youth population and about 830,000 engineering and technology graduates annually, according to India's Ministry of Education, creating jobs is a major priority. "Post-COVID, people realise this workforce has the skill and technical expertise needed to work with new products and even innovate," Mr Bardhan said. Time zones also did not matter when the work was not customer service. "Now you want us for tasks which can be done overnight, we don't have to operate at the same hours," he said. Before COVID, Mr Ahuja said his pitch to foreign companies was "anyone, any work, anytime, anywhere". With remote work normalised, companies became more comfortable running operations across borders. "You can run the company from India and have stores in Australia," Mr Ahuja said.

events.title: Former Italian Red Brigades member escapes house arrest in Argentina
events.summary: Bertulazzi used a rope and harness to climb down from a fifth-floor apartment and evade authorities in Argentina. A 74-year-old former member of Italy’s far-left Red Brigades has escaped from house arrest in Argentina by climbing down from a fifth-floor apartment using a harness and rope, prompting a nationwide search. Leonardo Bertulazzi, who faces extradition to Italy to serve a 27-year prison sentence, escaped on Tuesday and was still on the run on Wednesday, Argentine police officials told The Associated Press news agency. list 1 of 3 Iran designates Argentinian navy, air force as ‘terrorist organisations’ list 2 of 3 President Milei welcomes Pope Leo during historic visit to Argentina list 3 of 3 Photos: Crowds greet Pope Leo in Argentina after 40-year wait Bertulazzi was convicted in absentia by a court in his home country for his role in the kidnapping and death of a former Italian prime minister by the left-wing armed group, and his refugee status in Argentina was revoked under right-wing President Javier Milei. Police said he descended onto the second-floor terrace of a neighbouring house, climbed down to a first-floor terrace, crossed a vacant lot and got onto the street by climbing over a gate. Authorities did not immediately notice Bertulazzi was gone as he had tampered with his electronic ankle monitor, the officials said. They said he placed it inside a device containing a thermal blanket to maintain its temperature, along with grease or animal fat, apparently to keep moisture in. Explosives specialists examined the device, which had been made to resemble an explosive. Argentina’s Security Ministry has offered a reward of 20 million pesos (about $13,000) for information leading to his capture. The Red Brigades were a far-left armed group responsible for a wave of kidnappings and killings in Italy in the 1970s and 1980s, a period known as the “Years of Lead”. The group kidnapped and killed former Prime Minister Aldo Moro in 1978. Argentine authorities have said Bertulazzi, who belonged to the group’s Genoa branch, was involved in the logistics of Moro’s kidnapping. Italian courts convicted him in the 1980s of “terrorism-related” crimes, resulting in a combined 27-year sentence, according to Argentine court records. He was first arrested in Buenos Aires in November 2002, but an Argentine judge rejected Italy’s extradition request in 2003 because Italian law did not guarantee him a new trial after a conviction in absentia. He was granted refugee status in 2004. Argentina revoked it in 2024, under Milei, and re-arrested him that August. Its Supreme Court approved his extradition last year. Wanda Ferro, an undersecretary in Italy’s Interior Ministry, said Argentine police were responsible for ensuring he was handed over. “I am certain that every effort will be made,” she told local television, adding that she hoped the extradition could take place “very quickly” if Bertulazzi is recaptured.

events.title: Hardware-Based Location Checks Target AI Chip Smuggling (Texas A&M)
events.summary: Manufacturing, Packaging & Materials Technical Papers Home '; AI/ML/DL Architectures Automotive/ Aerospace Communication/Data Movement Design & Verification Lithography Manufacturing Materials Memory Optoelectronics / Photonics Packaging Power & Performance Quantum Security Test, Measurement, Analytics tech papers Transistors Z-End Applications Videos & Research Videos Industry Research Newsletters & Store Newsletters Store MENU Home Special Reports Systems & Design Low Power-High Performance Manufacturing, Packaging & Materials Test, Measurement & Analytics Auto, Security and AI Knowledge Center Videos Startup Corner Business & Startups Jobs Technical Papers Events Webinars Industry Research Newsletters Store Special Reports Researchers at Texas A&M University published “5G CATS: 5G-Based Cryptographic Authorization Against Trafficking of Semiconductor Devices.” Abstract : “Enforcing export controls on AI accelerators requires verifying where a chip operates after deployment. Round-trip time measurements can bound a chip’s distance from a trusted landmark, but any jitter in honest replies forces the verifier to loosen its timeout, giving an attacker slack to relay traffic over fiber from a restricted region. Prior approaches either cross the untrusted host stack or rely on noisy power-line channels that inflate this slack. We present 5G CATS, a location certification system that pairs a co-packaged 5G radio, cryptographic engine, and hardware interlock on the GPU package with 5G Ultra-Reliable Low-Latency Communication (URLLC) base stations. Terminating the radio link inside the package removes the host software, PCIe fabric, and baseboard management controller from the verification path. We map an authenticated challenge-response protocol onto 5G’s slot structure, replace permanent key erasure with short-lived execution leases, and specify a cross-check of the chip’s reported serving cell against the carrier’s own attachment records. In ns-3 and 5G-LENA simulations of an unloaded cell, our URLLC-based radio profile narrows the 99.9th percentile round-trip spread to 2.60 ms, more than ten times narrower than default 5G. A tracer rejects every round of a fiber relay from 300 km, against 2,000 km for default 5G. Against a 3,000 km attacker, a tracer stays safe at up to 1,410 km from the chip, against at most 619 km for PowerCATS’s published model, while default 5G is never safe.” Find the technical paper here . events.title: Poundland set for more time to secure a rescue deal as emergency talks continue
events.summary: Poundland looks set to avoid immediate collapse after its US owners told MPs on Wednesday they were in favour of extending a deadline to find a rescue deal. The discount chain, which has 11,000 employees, has been edging towards administration after being blocked by Gordon Borthers from accessing cash in its bank accounts. A deadline to secure a buyer for the business is set to expire at midnight, but sources close to the situation told the BBC they expect more time will be given, thanks to the release funding in recent days. A committee of MPs questioned Gordon Brothers following accusations that the investment firm hopes to profit from selling off Poundland's 600 stores and stock piecemeal. Gordon Brothers - which bought the chain for just £1 last year - is accused of forcing that outcome by restricting Poundland's access to available cash needed to restock stores and pay wages and rent, ahead of the crucial Christmas trading period. The investment firm, which specialises in buying and restructuring distressed companies, has denied the claims. But pressure remains on Poundland's owners after a takeover bid was rejected. The decision prompted calls for answers from politicians, including Prime Minister Andy Burnham. About £50m had been frozen by Gordon Brothers, the BBC understands, meaning Poundland bosses were unable to restock shelves across its 600 shops. The BBC understands that Gordon Brothers agreed to release a further £9m from Poundland's accounts, on top of £10m announced earlier. This will grant the company an additional 10 days to find a new buyer. There are three bids currently on the table for Poundland, all of which have so far been rejected by the Gordon Brothers, who stand to profit from selling the company and its stock piecemeal. Following the meeting between MPs on the business and trade committee and representatives of Gordon Brothers, chairman Liam Byrne told the BBC he was "deeply concerned" and described the firm's behaviour as "much like a wolf on Wall Street, on the British High Street". "They refused to prioritise, protecting jobs and stores over and above their own financial returns," he added. "It's clear that they've taken millions out of Poundland at a time when they themselves said the business was on a knife edge." Byrne said the committee's message to Gordon Brothers was to ensure Poundland had "access to the funds that it needs to trade at what should be one of the busiest periods in the year". He urged Gordon Brothers to "do what is right to save jobs and stores and do that now". "It's a good business, it's a much-loved business, and particularly in the middle of the cost of living crisis, communities up and down the country rely on access to the kind of stores that it operates," Byrne added. Following the private meeting with MPs, Poundland's chief executive Barry Williams told the BBC the chain's board would hold an urgent meeting on Wednesday night. Views on Poundland performance differ Views on the chain's performance differ between those running operations and the owners. Poundland boss Williams told staff last week that like-for-like sales, which exclude new store openings, were up 11.4%. The sales period included Halloween, but Williams said this was £1.5m ahead of budget. He added the business made a profit of £18.1m in the year to September, which was a "strong recovery" from the previous year where there were losses of £68m. However, Gordon Brothers has painted a different picture, saying the chain remains "challenged and vulnerable to any potential downturn in future trading". It has argued the best way of securing jobs may be to split up the business and sell chunks of its 600 sites to other retailers. There has been interest from the likes of Poundstretcher, Tesco and B&M in picking up Poundland stores which could mean continuing employment for workers in the event the chain is broken up. The main issue is whether a piecemeal sale would protect more jobs than a buyer willing to keep Poundland as a national chain. Are you affected by issues discussed in this story? events.title: Meta head of infrastructure will leave and be succeeded by former AWS cloud exec
events.summary: Meta's head of infrastructure and co-head of engineering Santosh Janardhan will leave in 2027. Janardhan's successor, former AWS senior vice president David Brown, will lead Meta's infrastructure efforts of the Meta Compute initiative, spearheaded by Dina Powell McCormick and Daniel Gross. The executive move underscores Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg's efforts to expand the company's data center operations under newer leaders at a time of increasing investor scrutiny on capital expenditure spending by the social media giant and its hyperscaler rivals. Meta's long-time infrastructure leader will leave the company in the new year, setting the stage for a recently hired former Amazon Web Services executive to oversee its massive data center technical operations. Santosh Janardhan, Meta's head of infrastructure and co-head of engineering, revealed his upcoming departure on Wednesday in an internal memo obtained by CNBC. Janardhan, who has worked at Meta since 2009, said "it's time to pass the baton" to former AWS senior vice president David Brown, who joined Meta in July from AWS. Brown will now formally lead Meta's infrastructure efforts as part of the Meta Compute initiative, which is spearheaded by the company's president and vice chairman Dina Powell McCormick and technical leader Daniel Gross. Zuckerberg is relying on these new executives to continue developing cutting-edge data centers and related infrastructure needed to support its AI ambitions. The company said during its recent third-quarter earnings report that it expects full-year capex to fall in the range of $135 billion to $145 billion. Meta also logged negative free cash flow of $2.12 billion, which S&P Global Ratings noted as part of its decision in late October to revise Meta's credit rating from AA- stable to AA- negative. Janardhan said in the memo that he will help support Brown through the first quarter of 2027 as part of "the transition." "As we make the next set of choices about our priorities, this is the right time for Dave to take the lead in shaping that work," Janardhan said in the memo. "Dave has spent his career building and operating dependable infrastructure for a wide range of demanding workloads. He has the instincts, depth and judgment this moment requires." Bloomberg News first reported on the executive transition. WATCH : AI challenge is lack of compute in the marketplace .

events.title: Nvidia shares plunge amid reports board to discuss CEO Huang’s future
events.summary: Chip giants stock price falls more than 8 percent amid speculation over co-founder’s position. Chip giant Nvidia’s stock price has tumbled amid reports that its board of directors is meeting to consider the future of CEO Jensen Huang. Nvidia shares fell 8.6 percent in after-hours trading on Wednesday as questions swirled over Huang’s position at the top of the $4.2 trillion company. list 1 of 4 Cameroon: Who is really calling the shots? list 2 of 4 Why the US, Mexico and Guatemala may lose their measles-free status list 3 of 4 Hegseth entourage reprimanded by guard at Tomb of the Unknown Soldier list 4 of 4 Nvidia shares plunge amid reports board to discuss CEO Huang’s future The plunge comes after The New York Times, The Wall Street Journal and the Financial Times reported that Nvidia’s board of directors would discuss Huang’s position amid revelations he engaged in an extramarital relationship with an Nvidia employee, in addition to an affair with a woman accused of working with Chinese intelligence services. Nvidia, which launched an investigation into Huang’s conduct on Sunday, did not immediately respond to Al Jazeera’s requests for comment. Huang, who co-founded Nvidia in 1993, is one of the most visible faces of the AI boom, spearheading the development of high-end graphics processing units (GPUs) used to used to train and run frontier models. The leather jacket-sporting tech executive’s position has also placed him at the centre of the geopolitical rivalry between United States and China, which are locked in a battle for supremacy in AI. As a confidante of US President Donald Trump, Huang has lobbied for the easing of restrictions on exports of high-end chips to China, putting him at odds with national security hawks in Washington who argue that Beijing must be blocked from access to cutting-edge US tech. If Nvidia’s board were to oust Huang, 63, it would mark a seismic moment for the chip giant. Viewed as integral to Nvidia’s meteoric rise to the ranks of the world’s most valuable companies, Huang is known for a centralised leadership style that places him at the centre of the company’s day-to-day operations and strategic decisions. “Jensen is Nvidia, without him the company loses it central, animating spirit,” Jay Goldberg, a senior analyst at Seaport Research Partners in San Francisco, told Al Jazeera. “The organization is built around him and replacing him will be very painful organizationally, and impossible to do personality wise.” It is unclear whether Nvidia has a succession plan and analysts see few obvious candidates to take Huang’s place. Dan Ives, senior managing director at Yorkville Ives, said Huang had been the “hearts and lungs” of Nvidia and that investors would closely scrutinise the executive’s possible replacement. “We believe Nvidia’s value is $300 per share with Jensen as CEO and $225 per share without Jensen as CEO. The stock will clearly be under pressure with this fluid news but the reality is its a dark day for Nvidia, but the company will navigate this turmoil and get through to the other side and remain a core foundational piece of the AI Revolution,” Ives said in a note to clients. “Jensen is not replaceable by another CEO or group of interim executives, but Nvidia likely now has to move on without Jensen at the helm which seemed like a Twilight Zone episode narrative before Sunday afternoon when the news broke.

events.title: Hegseth entourage reprimanded by guard at Tomb of the Unknown Soldier
events.summary: Can Trump find a way to work with Democrats? Guard at memorial site can be heard yelling at group to ‘maintain an atmosphere of silence and respect at all times’. Hegseth scolded by security at Tomb of the Unknown Soldier A video has spread online showing a military guard scolding a group accompanying United States Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth during a visit to the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier. On Wednesday, Hegseth and members of his staff visited the memorial site at Arlington National Cemetery. list 1 of 3 House Republicans block Pete Hegseth impeachment effort list 2 of 3 Did Democrats save Hegseth from impeachment? list 3 of 3 US congressman files resolution to impeach Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth But as they paused to take group photos, they could be heard laughing. The video shows an Army sentinel turning to loudly reprimand them. “All visitors will maintain an atmosphere of silence and respect at all times,” the guard yelled. The tomb, seen as a sombre memorial to those who have died in war, marks the resting place of unidentified US soldiers from World War I and later conflicts. A member of the 3rd Infantry Regiment – known as the “Old Guard” – watches over the site 24 hours a day. The incident, which took place on Veterans Day, comes amid speculation over whether Hegseth will be able to maintain his cabinet-level position in the administration of US President Donald Trump. Hegseth narrowly avoided a vote on articles of impeachment brought against him in the US House of Representatives on Tuesday, with Republican lawmakers banding together to derail the effort. Critics have accused Hegseth of overseeing several unlawful actions while in his post, including spearheading the US-Israel war on Iran without seeking congressional authorisation first. The war became a central topic in the November 3 midterm elections, in which Trump’s Republican Party suffered a bruising setback, losing both chambers of Congress. Hegseth has also championed a campaign of deadly strikes targeting alleged drug-trafficking boats in the Caribbean Sea and eastern Pacific Ocean. Legal scholars have called that campaign a series of extrajudicial killings. During his time as defence secretary, Hegseth has been criticised for weakening rules meant to diminish civilian casualties in US strikes. In addition, his tenure has been marked by right-wing culture war issues: he has sought to ban transgender service members from the armed forces and instituted testosterone testing for male soldiers. In response to Wednesday’s interaction at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier, chief Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell said in a statement that the sentinel had responded “correctly”. He also underscored Hegseth’s commitment to respecting US soldiers. “The Secretary and the entire Department have always honored – and will always honor – the sacrifices our military men and women have made to keep America safe,” Parnell said.

events.title: Mississippi elects first Democratic senator in 44 years as Dems finally find a winning strategy: Spend nothing and let the other candidate talk beef
events.summary: For four decades, the typical plan the national Democratic Party had for Mississippi was to leave it alone. Seems like they finally found their winning strategy: Democrat Scott Colom has narrowly eked out a razor-thin win over incumbent Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, and arguably, it was because he let her do the talking. Colom is the first Democrat Mississippi sent to the Senate since noted segregationist John Stennis won his last term in 1982. Mississippi, which up until last week’s elections was nearly unanimously rated as a solid Republican state, is the only state in the country that doesn’t allow automatic recounts, meaning the loser has to go to court to get the votes reexamined. What’s notable about the race is the sheer lack of attention it has garnered (at least, up until recently) and how Colom even became a viable contender in the first place. In 2022, President Joe Biden nominated Colom, a district attorney, to the federal bench in northern Mississippi. Mississippi’s senior senator, Republican Roger Wicker, supported him. Hyde-Smith blocked the nomination in 2023, citing his “opposition to legislation to protect female athletes” and past support from a PAC funded by George Soros. Had she let it through, Colom might be a federal judge today instead of her successor. Two years later, he announced his campaign against her. Likely Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer saw an opening. He told the New York Times in 2025 he wanted to help elect a Democrat in Mississippi and find other winning tickets in states that would be relatively cheap to compete in. While he referenced Colom at the time, Colom said Schumer isn’t why he ran: in his launch video, he referenced his two daughters and Hyde-Smith’s vote for a law he said would cut more than 100,000 Mississippians from their health care. Kitchen table economics That kitchen table economic sentiment may be why Colom won in a state represented, for now, by a cattle rancher. In February, a reporter asked Hyde-Smith, who also married a fifth-generation cattle rancher, what Republicans were doing about rising beef prices. “You know, you have so many proteins to choose from,” she said . Ground beef had risen from $5.55 a pound when President Donald Trump returned to office to $6.79 in September, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. Colom’s campaign turned her answer into an ad of Mississippians reacting to it, a move widely regarded to have tipped the scale in his favor . The ad’s release was also when the national Democratic Party started showing up. Former President Bill Clinton rallied for him in Tupelo on Oct. 30. “Scott is the correction,” Clinton told the crowd. Still, the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee put just $500,000 into the race in its final week, while Hyde-Smith raised about $6.3 million for her campaign. Colom wasn’t alone, though: counting outside groups, money spent backing him outpaced money backing Hyde-Smith roughly three to one, according to FEC data . The win was mostly Colom: he held events in all 82 Mississippi counties, the Washington Post reported , while Hyde-Smith hadn’t held a town hall in six years. Local organizers did the rest. When Holmes County, home to about 15,000 people, reported its votes near midnight on election night, its surge in turnout put Colom ahead by 28 votes. Colom also flipped Forrest County, named for the Ku Klux Klan’s first grand wizard, 12,064 to 9,749, and won Jefferson Davis County, named for the president of the Confederacy, 2,943 to 1,534. He would also be Mississippi’s first Black senator since Blanche K. Bruce, who was born into slavery and left office in 1881, and the first Black senator the state’s voters have ever chosen directly. Mississippi’s first, Hiram Revels, was also the nation’s first Black senator, appointed by the state legislature in 1870. Colom held events in all 82 Mississippi counties while Hyde-Smith hadn’t held a town hall in six years. Brad Vest/Getty Images Democrats with 56 seats Democrats entered Election Day with 47 Senate seats and were projected to flip at least seven. Now already with control of both chambers , Colom makes it 55. If Democrat Mary Peltola holds her narrow lead in Alaska, where counting continues, it’s 56. The difference between 54 and 56 shows up in the filibuster. Most legislation needs 60 votes to end debate and pass the Senate. At 54 seats, Democrats would need six Republicans to cross over, but at 56, they need four. A bigger majority also gives Schumer room on his own side. With 51 seats, a single Democratic defection can sink a nominee or a party-line vote. With 56, he can lose several and still confirm judges and officials, which takes only a simple majority. That matters for Trump’s picks as well: a Democratic Senate can now block his nominees to the federal bench, the kind of seat Colom was once denied. The lesson of Mississippi isn’t only for Democrats. Voters named the cost of living and government corruption as their top two issues in AP exit polls. Two years earlier, voters who were worried about the economy broke for Trump by 2 to 1 . The issue that won Republicans the White House helped cost them the Senate. Some Republicans saw it coming. But Trump called affordability “a con job” by Democrats, even as nearly three-quarters of his own voters rated the cost of living bad or the worst ever. Vice President JD Vance warned his party not to blame young people for socialism’s growing appeal when they couldn’t afford homes, then answered one young voter’s affordability question with a joke . “We used to own the affordability issue just two years ago,” Republican Rep. Elise Stefanik of New York said . “We let that slip away.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Why the US, Mexico and Guatemala may lose their measles-free status
events.summary: A independent commission is meeting to review whether countries in the Americas still meet its measles elimination criteria. International health experts are meeting in Washington, DC, this week to determine which countries in the Americas have endemic measles transmission. The outcome could decide whether the United States, Mexico and Guatemala retain their “measles elimination status”: a designation that the virus has not spread uncontrolled domestically for at least 12 months. list 1 of 3 CDC reports third measles death in the United States this year list 2 of 3 Why a measles outbreak in Pennsylvania poses risks beyond US borders list 3 of 3 CDC reports more than 5,000 measles cases, highest number in 35 years The Pan American Health Organization’s (PAHO) Regional Monitoring and Re-Verification Commission (RVC) began its annual conference on Tuesday to assess the countries’ status. The conference will adjourn on Friday. The review comes as a sharp resurgence of the virus has spread across the Americas, with the US experiencing its largest and deadliest measles outbreak in nearly 30 years. The US has held its elimination status since 2000, but it risks losing it this year. The commission will review reports submitted by all 35 PAHO member states, with particular attention to countries experiencing prolonged outbreaks. How does the process work? Al Jazeera breaks down what happens in this explainer. Who decides whether a country has eliminated measles? The RVC is an independent panel of international experts in epidemiology, public health and virology. The group advises PAHO, which is part of the World Health Organization, on which countries have maintained the elimination of measles and rubella. The Americas became the first region in the world to eliminate endemic measles transmission in 2016, following decades of vaccination campaigns. For this year’s review, the commission is examining epidemiological data from 2025 and the first half of 2026. Which countries could lose their elimination status this year? The US, Mexico, Guatemala, Peru and Bolivia are at risk. Canada lost its status last November. The US, which eliminated endemic measles transmission in 2000, has experienced sustained outbreaks since January 2025. Mexico has also reported prolonged transmission. PAHO reported 57,666 confirmed measles cases across 17 countries and territories in the Americas between January and October 2026. How does a country lose its status? Experts at the conference evaluate whether infections result from separate introductions of the virus or whether the same strain has circulated locally. Reported measles cases or deaths alone do not determine whether a country loses its elimination status. Some cases, for instance, come from exposure to measles during travel. A limited outbreak due to such exposure would not result in the loss of a country’s measles elimination status. Under PAHO’s criteria, a country loses its elimination status if the same measles virus strain continues to spread uninterrupted for at least 12 months in a country or defined geographical area. Investigators use genetic sequencing to determine whether infections are linked to the same virus strain. They also examine epidemiological data to establish how the virus has spread and whether transmission has been interrupted. In addition, the commission considers vaccination coverage, how healthcare systems monitor measles cases, and the speed of outbreak responses in its decisions. When will the decision be announced? The commission’s deliberations in Washington run until Friday. It will assess the evidence and make recommendations on the status of individual countries to PAHO Director Jarbas Barbosa, who will make the final determination. The official announcement is expected early next week following the conclusion of the conference. What happens if the US loses its status? Experts agree that the US will likely lose its measles elimination status, marking a reversal of a major public-health achievement. “It would be a disappointment, not a shock,” Matt Ferrari, the director of Pennsylvania State University’s Center for Infectious Disease Dynamics, told Al Jazeera. “This is moving backwards from a great public health achievement, and to see that backslide is just heart-wrenching.” Although the loss of status would not trigger any immediate consequences, those working in the field say it would be an embarrassment. “It’s a stain on your health programme,” Edwin Asturias, a professor of infectious disease and epidemiology at the University of Colorado, told Al Jazeera. The long-term effects include greater pressure on public-health systems, which must devote resources to identifying infections, tracing contacts, conducting laboratory tests, isolating patients and organising vaccination campaigns.

events.title: Cameroon: Who is really calling the shots?
events.summary: Biya’s absences raise questions about who holds power and what comes next in Cameroon. Yaounde, Cameroon – A dispute over roadworks in Yaounde in March, ahead of Pope Leo XIV’s visit to Cameroon the following month, highlighted tensions between central government and municipal authorities. The disagreement involved Housing and Urban Development Minister Celestine Ketcha Courtes and Yaounde City Mayor Luc Messi Atangana over the rehabilitation of a road along the papal visit route, according to local media reports. The episode raised a broader question about competing centres of authority in Cameroon: Who exercises power when President Paul Biya is absent? Biya, 93, has governed Cameroon since 1982. His prolonged absences from public view have intensified scrutiny on how decisions are made, who has access to him and how much authority is exercised by those around him. Biya returned to Yaounde on August 20 after more than 10 weeks abroad, following a stay in Europe that began on June 7 . His return did little to dispel questions about the management of power. The issue is not simply whether the state continues to function. It is whether the institutions and informal networks built around one president can manage power coherently when he is not visibly directing government. Cameroon’s constitution gives the president extensive executive authority. He defines national policy, appoints the prime minister and, based on the latter’s proposal, other members of government. He is also commander-in-chief of the armed forces. The prime minister heads the government and directs its activities within the framework of the president’s policy. Under Section 10 of the constitution, the president may delegate some of his powers to the prime minister, other members of government and senior administrative officials, within the scope of their respective responsibilities. Where the president is temporarily unable to perform his duties, he must expressly delegate some of his functions to the prime minister or, if the prime minister is also unavailable, another member of government. An absence abroad does not, in itself, establish that the president is temporarily unable to perform his duties or automatically transfer his constitutional powers to the prime minister. The government has not provided a detailed public account of whether a clear delegation of presidential functions is in effect during Biya’s prolonged absences. Research by the Organised Crime and Corruption Reporting Project (OCCRP) found that Biya spent at least four and a half years abroad on private visits over a period of more than three decades. The investigation, which examined records of his travels from 1982 onwards, renewed questions about how much government business depends on his direct involvement. One figure central to that debate is Ferdinand Ngoh Ngoh, the secretary-general at the presidency. According to the official biography published by the Prime Minister’s Office, his responsibilities include receiving the president’s instructions, monitoring the implementation of presidential decisions and coordinating administrations attached to the presidency. On February 5, 2019, Biya signed Decree No. 2019/043, granting Ngoh Ngoh a permanent delegation of signature. The measure gave him authority to sign certain official documents on the president’s behalf. A delegation of signature, however, is not a transfer of presidential powers. Ngoh Ngoh is not constitutionally the president’s successor, and his formal responsibilities should not be confused with the informal political influence attributed to him. Other figures regularly mentioned in discussions about the presidency include First Lady Chantal Biya and the president’s son, Franck Biya. Neither holds a constitutional executive office. Claims about their influence and about rival networks around the president are difficult to establish independently. Ryan Cummings, an Africa-focused security analyst, has argued that individuals close to the president may be playing increasingly tangible roles as questions grow about the management of power. His assessment points to the importance of the presidential circle but does not establish who makes particular decisions or on whose authority. Access to the president does not, in itself, establish that those around him exercise executive powers. The succession question has become more pressing following a constitutional amendment approved on April 14 this year. The amendment reintroduced the office of vice president, with the president given the authority to appoint and dismiss its holder. Under the revised Article 6, the vice president would assume the presidency if the office became vacant through the president’s death, resignation or permanent incapacity established by the Constitutional Council. The vice president would complete the remainder of the presidential term.

events.title: Nvidia prepares to oust Jensen Huang, WSJ reports — stock sinks
events.summary: The New York Times reported that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had an extramarital affair with an employee named Kimberly Powell. The report comes days after Huang admitted to an affair with a woman who is believed by U.S. intelligence of being a Chinese spy. Powell is vice president of health care at Nvidia, and joined the company in 2008. The news landed minutes after The New York Times reported that Huang had an extramarital relationship with another executive at the company. Nvidia's board is preparing to meet as soon as Wednesday to determine Huang's future at the company, according to the Journal. The alleged relationship was with Kimberly Powell, vice president of health care at Nvidia, according to the Times' report. Powell's bio on the Nvidia website says she's "responsible for the company's worldwide healthcare business, including hardware and software platforms for accelerated computing, AI, and visualization that power the ecosystem of medical imaging, life sciences, drug discovery, and healthcare analytics." Huang and Powell were reportedly captured on camera being affectionate with one another at a hotel in San Jose, California in March, according to the Times. Nvidia and Powell did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment. Heller, the crisis PR firm Huang reportedly hired as early as last year, did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment. The report comes days after Huang admitted to an affair with a woman who is believed by U.S. intelligence of being a Chinese spy. The CEO was romantically involved with Alice Huang, according to The Financial Times , who U.S. intelligence officials believe is a spy for China's Ministry of State Security, The New York Times reported. Nvidia's board of directors has opened an independent investigation and hired the law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to look into the spying allegations. "I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did," Huang wrote in the message to Nvidia staff on Sunday. "I am deeply sorry." Most of Huang's Nvidia shares are co-owned with his wife, Lori Huang, and are held in trusts. About 800 million shares are held by those trusts. Huang holds about 70 million shares on his own and has limited economic control over the company. Rumors of an affair between Huang and Powell have circulated for years, in part because Powell lacks a background in health or science, according to a former employee who asked not to be named because of the sensitivity of the matter. Healthcare is a smaller business at Nvidia. The company makes chips for medical devices and MRI machines, but they are a minor in comparison to the revenue generated from its advanced AI systems and graphics processing units, or GPUs. In recent appearances, including at the company's annual GTC conference, Powell has spoken about how Nvidia's AI technology can help accelerate drug discovery, assist providers and improve clinical efficiency. Powell has been leading the group since 2017. Nvidia's stock was down 7% this week prior to the after-hours drop on Wednesday and is on pace for its sixth straight weekly slide, reflecting broad concern on the sustainability of the artificial intelligence buildout. The AI infrastructure trade was hit particularly hard last week after the midterm elections, as Democrats won sweeping majorities in both houses of Congress, and dozens of ballot measures past that could make building data centers more difficult. Huang has become synonymous with the AI industry, and he is often referred to by his first name ,"Jensen," by customers and rivals. Nvidia has been one of the primary beneficiaries of the AI boom since its chips are used to train models and run large AI workloads. —CNBC's Lora Kolodny and Kif Leswing contributed to this report Is Nvidia too big to fail? events.title: US election results could be positive for Lebanon, Hezbollah chief says
events.summary: Naim Qassem says Republican losses and Israel’s election result could help Lebanon maintain sovereignty. Hezbollah Secretary-General Naim Qassem has welcomed Republican setbacks in US midterm elections last week and a lacklustre showing for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in Israeli polls, calling them a boon for Lebanon. During a speech on Wednesday honouring members of the group killed by Israel, along with their families, Qassem described the elections in the US as an “earthquake” and the Israeli elections as a “defeat”. The bloc of Netanyahu, an arch-nemesis of the group, fell short of the 61 seats it needed to stay in power after the October 27 vote. list 1 of 3 Lebanon’s lost olive season: harvesting olives under drones and warplanes list 2 of 3 Iran and US explore diplomacy amid rising threats of war list 3 of 3 Israel is ‘disrupting entire ecosystems’, including Lebanon’s wheat crop Qassem said the results were good for Lebanon and a signal that the country should resist the Trump administration’s push to disarm the group. “Come, let us rebuild our country together, save it from the darkness of failure, and protect it from the empty rhetoric of those who sow discord and those who rely on American tutelage,” he said in a video-link address. “Lebanon belongs to all of us. We are partners in building it and sharing the cost of protecting its sovereignty.” Iran-backed Hezbollah is locked in a standoff with US-backed Lebanese President Joseph Aoun over whether it will relinquish its arms, in a move Washington seeks but the group says would be a surrender to Israel. The Hezbollah leader insisted it would not hand over its weapons and cited a continued Israeli military occupation over parts of the country’s south. “There will be no state monopoly on the resistance’s weapons, no regulation, no prohibition, and no disarmament under Israeli occupation,” Qassem said. The secretary-general assumed the role after Israel assassinated former Secretary-General Hassan Nasrallah and his successor Hashem Safieddine in 2024. Sparking months of ongoing war, the US and Israel launched surprise attacks on Iran in February, assassinating Iranian Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei. Hezbollah’s retaliation by firing missiles and drones into Israel led to weeks of intense Israeli strikes on south Lebanon, in which more than 4,300 people were killed, Lebanese authorities say, and around a million were displaced, according to the United Nations. Qassem praised Iran’s closure of the Strait of Hormuz for causing a spike in global oil prices and suspending shipping routes, saying it would weaken American and Israeli influence in the region. US President Donald Trump has also acknowledged the role of the Iran war and the rise in fuel prices it stoked in last week’s electoral drubbing for Republicans, as did US Vice President and likely 2028 electoral hopeful JD Vance. “The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so,” Vance said last week. Qassem also warned against Lebanese authorities making commitments and deals that serve Israeli goals and urged them to focus on domestic issues. “Why are you binding yourselves before the world to positions that serve the Israeli project?” he asked. Israel continues to occupy large swathes of southern Lebanon and has decimated dozens of the roughly 60 villages and towns it occupies. events.title: From Paris to DC - why offices are being turned into apartments
events.summary: Le Diamant office building is to close and be converted into apartments When Roland Cubin walks you round what will eventually be a new Parisian apartment you have to use your imagination. "Here you will be in the kitchen, and here is the bathroom," says the deputy CEO of French real estate company Groupama Immobilier. It all sounds appealing, an upmarket flat in the west of Paris, but presently the space doesn't look like one at all. That's because it's currently a corner of one floor of a nine-storey office building called Le Diamant, where 1,800 people work. Groupama Immobilier intends to convert the entire building into apartments. It should be the first of many such office-to-apartments conversions in the surrounding area. We are in La Défense, the purpose-built, business district of the French capital, where the city has congregated its modern skyscrapers. Mirroring a similar trend in places such as New York, Washington DC and London; Paris La Défense, the public development authority that runs the area, has unveiled plans to turn up to a fifth of the office buildings into housing. Cubin leads us into what is currently a conference room in the centre of the building. It has no windows, which is indicative of a big challenge when turning offices into apartments – what to do with the large amount of space in the middle of every floor that doesn't get any natural light. "There won't be any rooms there. Just access," says Roland Cubin, in reference to lifts and stairs. Other issues include the need for more plumbing, and ceilings that can be too low. Despite these challenges, there is a simple reason why there are plans for so many conversions – demand for offices in La Défense and across Paris has plummeted since the Covid-19 pandemic and the growth of homeworking. Authorities want La Défense to become an area were people also live and play "La Défense has a vacancy rate of 14-15% which is higher than it used to be," says Pierre-Yves Guice, CEO of Paris La Défense. He adds that another reason for the conversion programme is the need to transform the business district from a place where the only thing people do is work. "To retain companies in France and in Western Europe we need to diversify these office landscapes of the last century, because no-one wants to work in such an environment any longer," says Guice. Ludovic Delaisse, CEO of the French arm of the Canadian real estate business Colliers, says that demand for office space in Paris has fallen by almost a third over the past five to six years. He adds that office high rises will continue to be needed, but that cities need to make sure that leisure time can be enjoyed around them, such as having restaurants, bars, cinemas and gyms on their doorstep. "People like the idea of grouping together in a centre of expertise [for work] - in tech hubs, for example. The challenge for La Défense is to be a place where you want to be, that you want to see when you leave work in the evening." The Geneva building is the biggest office to apartments conversion in Washington DC Inspiration for La Défense can come from Washington DC and New York City, where tax cuts for property developers are fuelling the largest amount of office to apartment conversions in the US. Like in Paris, this is in response to falling demand for office space since the pandemic. A report last year , external found that 8,310 converted flats were in the pipeline in New York, and 6,533 in Washington. In third place was Los Angeles on 4,322, followed by Chicago on 3,606. "We set a goal of introducing 15,000 new residents downtown by 2028 and we are now on track to doing that," says Washington DC's deputy mayor for planning and development Nina Albert. She says that while "there may be one or two pretty significant building demolitions… the majority are office conversions". As in Paris, they've faced technical challenges. They've sometimes solved the natural light problem in the middle of office buildings by creating atriums – light sinks in other words – in the middle of them. Albert adds that about "hundreds of millions of dollars of private investment" has flooded into the sector. In addition to tax cuts, the DC Department of Buildings, part of the Council of the District of Columbia, has eased planning restrictions to make it easier for office conversion schemes to gain official approval in the US capital. It's a similar case in New York City. In the UK, there are also tax cuts and eased planning rules , external for converting offices into apartments. This has led to a continuing boom in conversions. A report last year by property firm Knight Frank said that the number of such projects in London were 60% higher , external than pre-Covid levels. Back in Paris, Cubin hopes that French authorities follow these examples and reduce both taxes and rules regarding conversions.
