events.title: JetBlue unveils new first-class seats to bring back profits
events.summary: JetBlue's CEO, Joanna Geraghty, has said the airline is focused on its turnaround plan that includes more upmarket products to return to profitability. Geraghty said the airline has met with bondholders in recent weeks and made it clear it doesn't need to reorganize. The carrier on Wednesday unveiled its new domestic first-class seats called BlueFirst. JetBlue Airways unveiled its new domestic first-class seats Wednesday as more of the country's carriers bet on the premium travel boom to make them profitable again. JetBlue announced it would offer a domestic first class — BlueFirst — in December 2024 and plans to start flying aircraft with the new seats and full on-board product next month. The carrier showed off the new cabin at its home hub at John F. Kennedy International Airport on Wednesday. Retrofits will continue during 2027, CEO Joanna Geraghty told CNBC late last month. JetBlue will have 12 of the seats on its Airbus A320 fleet and 30 extra-legroom seats, down from 42 of those options previously. Because the airplanes don't have ovens, JetBlue said it is offering an array of cold food options like sesame noodles, pastrami sandwiches and tortellini salad, though they vary by route. The rollout comes as the New York airline tries to stabilize after last posting a profit in 2019. Last month, JetBlue executives sought to calm investors after shares in the airline hit a record low following a report that bondholders had contracted restructuring advisors. "We have no intention, no plans to file for bankruptcy. We are not engaged with any restructuring company," Geraghty told CNBC in an interview on Oct. 27. Geraghty told CNBC's Phil LeBeau on Wednesday that JetBlue has "met with a few of the creditors over the last couple of weeks as part of ... normal investor engagement." She said the company made it clear to bondholders that JetBlue doesn't need to reorganize. JetBlue stock surges as company outlook calms investors JetBlue overhauls fare options, from basic first to flexible economy. Here’s what to know JetBlue bets big on Fort Lauderdale, from a new airport lounge to an international gateway JetBlue to bring ‘junior Mint’ first class to domestic flights in 2026 The airline's shares are up more than 40% this month, more than other passenger carriers, as of midday Wednesday, though they are still off about 11% so far this year. JetBlue is betting that resilient travel demand, especially for roomier seats will help fuel its turnaround plan, which aims to get the carrier to an operating profit next year and $1 in adjusted earnings per share in 2028. Airline executives have said they expect fares to stay elevated next year as they grapple with higher costs, including but not limited to fuel, such as labor and airport fees. Geraghty said Wednesday that even if fuel prices moderate next year, "I don't think fares are going to fall as much as people expect." Airlines large and small are racing to outfit their cabins with roomier, more expensive seating options to help cover ever-higher costs, from jet fuel to labor to airport operation fees. For example, a ticket in the new recliner first-class seats between Kennedy airport and Fort Lauderdale-Hollywood International Airport in Florida is going for $847 roundtrip in the first week of March while standard economy is $446. On Tuesday, budget carrier Frontier Airlines unveiled its new first-class seats, which will take up the first two rows, and said it would outfit its Airbus fleet with premium seating that has extra legroom and in-seat power through row eight. The airline will take out a row of seating on its planes to make the pricier ones fit, Chief Marketing Officer Bobby Schroeter told CNBC in an interview Monday. JetBlue last month reported that it ended the third quarter with $2.2 billion in liquidity and that its unencumbered asset base is now $7 billion, including $2.8 billion in aircraft and engines. JetBlue had total debt of $8.4 billion as of Sept. 30, the carrier said in its earnings filing. Geraghty told CNBC last month there is a "fundamental disconnect between the narrative in the bond market and what our financial results actually demonstrate." When asked whether JetBlue's eye on keeping costs down includes furloughs, layoffs or buyouts, Geraghty last month said "absolutely not." events.title: Judge rules Trump’s $10bn BBC defamation suit can proceed
events.summary: Can Trump find a way to work with Democrats? The BBC denies defamation charge as Trump celebrates “huge victory” in court decision. A United States judge has allowed President Donald Trump’s $10bn defamation lawsuit against the BBC to move forward in a blow to the state broadcaster. The US president’s civil case alleges that the United Kingdom broadcaster deceptively edited a January 6 documentary, claiming the broadcaster acted with malice to damage his reputation. list 1 of 4 Trump threatens to report journalist Kristen Welker to broadcast regulator list 2 of 4 Can Trump ban CNN, news outlets he doesn’t like from the White House? list 3 of 4 Trump ordered to sit for deposition in BBC defamation lawsuit list 4 of 4 Trump ordered to testify in $10bn BBC lawsuit discovery: What happens now? Jeffrey T Kuntz, a Trump-appointed federal district judge in the Southern District of Florida, issued a 40-page ruling on Tuesday partially rejecting the United Kingdom broadcaster’s motion to dismiss the case. He ruled that Trump’s claim that the broadcaster damaged his reputation and knew or should have known the clip was misleading was “plausibly alleged”, or credible. While Kuntz’s decision moves the case forward, it did not establish whether Trump has proven those claims. The president’s case against the BBC centres on an October 2024 documentary titled Trump: A Second Chance? It features clips of a speech Trump made on January 6, 2021, to his supporters, allegedly directing attendees to storm the US Capitol , the seat of the US Congress, as lawmakers voted to certify former President Joe Biden’s win. The president alleged that the documentary was selectively edited, with incorrect sequencing of two separate video and audio clips of the same speech – nearly 55 minutes apart – as well as editing the footage to make it appear that he was directly calling for violence. The two curated clips included one section in which he told supporters to march on the Capitol, and another where he said, “Fight like hell”. Trump has maintained that he never told his supporters to commit violence in a bid to prevent the peaceful transition of power, though he has long falsely claimed that vote-rigging cost him the 2020 race. Trump had also said the edited sections of his speech omitted his calls for peaceful protest. The BBC admitted the edit was misleading and apologised to Trump on November 13, 2025, a month before he filed the lawsuit. In seeking to have the case dismissed, it contended that its edits condensed a 70-minute speech, which the judge rejected. However, the broadcaster continues to deny it defamed the president. Following the ruling, a BBC spokesperson said, “We are surprised by this decision but respect the Court’s authority and note the case will now proceed to the next stage. We remain confident in our position and will continue to respond through the proper legal process.” In a Truth Social post on Tuesday, Trump called the latest ruling a “huge victory against Fake News BBC”. After skipping his scheduled October deposition to hit the midterm campaign trail , the president faces a court-ordered December 11 deadline to testify under oath or risk having his defamation lawsuit against the BBC thrown out. The original lawsuit, filed in federal court in Miami in December 2025, sought a minimum of $5bn in damages each for alleged defamation and violation of the Florida Deceptive and Unfair Trade Practices Act. The judge threw out the second claim on Tuesday. The dispute over the edited speech, featured on the BBC’s Panorama show shortly before the 2024 presidential election, prompted a public relations crisis for the broadcaster, leading to the resignations of its two most senior executives. The BBC case is one of several that Trump has privately filed against the press, as part of a wider pressure campaign targeting coverage he dislikes. Across multiple jurisdictions, his attorneys have pursued staggering financial penalties against major news organisations and publishers. The president is currently enmeshed in another $10bn defamation lawsuit against The Wall Street Journal that he refiled in May after it was previously dismissed. A judge dismissed the refiled suit on October 31, and Trump is appealing. Another defamation case seeks $15bn in damages from The New York Times and Penguin Random House, a book publisher. In September, the president also moved to bar CNN, MS Now and Politico from the White House and its press pool – a blanket ban a federal judge later blocked , though the outlets have continued fighting ongoing exclusions from Air Force One and the Oval Office.

events.title: Clashes erupt in Barcelona after thousands join Spain general strike
events.summary: Watch: Protesters and police clash in Barcelona Clashes have broken out between groups of masked men and police in Barcelona after tens of thousands of people took part in Spain's first general strike for 14 years, called by the country's main unions over housing and the high cost of living. Some 120,000 people joined a demonstration in the capital Madrid and more than 50,000 turned out in Barcelona, where footage showed masked men setting fire to rubbish bins and smashing shop windows as police fired tear gas. Transport and other public services across Spain faced serious disruption. Spaniards are due to vote in parliamentary elections on 29 November. The head of the big UGT labour union, Pepe Álvarez, said the strike was a success with "massive" participation, while Unai Sordo of the CC OO union said turnout was "very significant." There was a heavy police presence in the centre of Barcelona on Wednesday evening, with officers wearing helmets and riot shields. Some of the disturbances took place in the Passeig de Gràcia, close to the iconic Plaça de Catalunya in the centre of the city. Small fires burned in the middle of the streets as bins were set alight. Local media reported that a group of people fired fireworks towards police and looted shops including the Lego store. Protesters were also seen trying to enter the Apple Store. The BBC spoke to a woman who attended the protests in Barcelona who said it was mostly very peaceful and "joyful". She said she was there to protest about the housing costs and that "there were a lot of children and old people there." She was in the area of Las Ramblas in the evening and saw fires in the streets. "The fires were everywhere, it was very intense," she said. Earlier in the day there was major disruption around Madrid and Barcelona, with traffic halted on several main roads. The interior ministry said dozens of people were arrested for a variety of incidents and Spanish reports said estate agencies had seen attacks on their offices. Police said they had made dozens of arrests "We've completely brought the city to a standstill," a protester in Madrid told Reuters news agency, adding there was widespread support for the general strike. "Everyone's out there, despite the rainy weather; everyone's out on the streets." Another protester, 37-year-old teacher Olga Domingo, said she was protesting because "the housing situation is outrageous. The current cost of living compared to wages is completely unsustainable". The strike was triggered by widespread protests over affordable housing and rising living costs, after the eviction of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal from a flat in Madrid where she had lived for seven decades. She died in hospital weeks later. Rental prices in the capital have risen in recent years. The monthly cost of a 50 sq m apartment in Madrid was an average of €1,170 ($1,300; £1,000) in October, according to property portal Idealista, while Spain's average gross monthly salary is about €2,460. That amounts to nearly half the average gross salary, well above the 30% level of affordability often recommended by housing experts and public institutions. Watch: Protesters gather across Spain for first general strike in 14 years Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez called snap elections last month after parliament failed to approve his plan for housing reform. Not since 2012, under the conservative government of Mariano Rajoy, has Spain held general strikes. And while previous strikes have been problematic for the government in power, this one is different. Sánchez and his ministers have even encouraged workers to down tools and demand affordable housing. "Your eight-hour day. Your pension. Your public healthcare… These were collective conquests," he wrote on social media, praising those who took part in previous strikes. Tyres were set on fire in the city of Gijon in northern Spain The conservative People's Party (PP), by contrast, has accused the government of attempting to weaponise the strike for electoral gain. PP leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo called the general strike "nonsense", calling the unions "mafia" and "trash". Feijoo's party is leading in the polls and party spokesman Miguel Tellado accused the government of exploiting the strike to warn voters against allowing a right-wing government to be formed, which looks the most likely outcome of the 29 November election. Sánchez told Spanish TV this week: "What is nonsense is to question the rights of workers to strike." Among those taking part in the general strike was Gonzalo Álvarez, 27, who was visiting different picket lines in central Madrid. Although he works in sales, he has been volunteering for a housing union that tries to protect tenants and makes them aware of their rights. The eviction of Maricarmen Abascal at the end of September "was the little fire" that sparked this protest, he told the BBC.

events.title: A day after Anthropic’s office push, Databricks jumps in with AI agents that never sleep
events.summary: The AI industry’s battle for the knowledge worker is heating up.  On Wednesday, San Francisco startup Databricks launched a new set of agentic AI tools that continuously analyze and organize the reams of data scattered throughout a business—a capability Databricks says will transform the way office workers do their jobs.  “The agents are running in the background all the time. So it’s always on,” Databricks CEO and cofounder Ali Ghodsi told Fortune ahead of the announcement. “I personally use it every day. Every hour of the day. It’s basically made me a 10x better CEO than I was a year ago,” Ghodsi said.  The product introduction comes a day after Anthropic, the maker of the Claude AI models, released its own set of AI productivity tools aimed at corporate users. Those tools include a new AI-powered spreadsheet application that competes with Microsoft Excel and Google Sheets, as well as a feature that lets Claude join video calls, allowing the AI to listen to the conversation and “start on the work while people are still talking.” Databricks’ updated version of its Genie assistant, launched Wednesday, also operates in the background, shadowing an office worker throughout the day, proactively making suggestions and retrieving information based on whatever is happening. A separate “Ontology” feature essentially scans all the data within an organization—from management reporting lines to projects in various departments—so that an individual can quickly access information or run analyses. “Lots of companies, both big and small, will use this,” said Ghodsi. The AI industry is stepping up efforts to make inroads into corporations and to broaden the base of paying customers. While AI has transformed the way that software programmers do their jobs, becoming an indispensable tool in the profession, the technology is still in the experimental phase for other business functions where the return on investment is not as clear-cut. With the advent of AI agents that autonomously perform tasks on a user’s behalf, as well as recent advances in AI model capabilities, some believe the technology may be ready to capture a broader swath of the market.  “We believe the work that knowledge workers perform represented more than $40 trillion in economic value globally in 2025, and with frontier AI’s potential to make them meaningfully more productive, our near-term opportunity is to expand this value and accelerate economic growth,” Anthropic says in the prospectus for its initial public offering, expected next week. The IPO, which could value Anthropic at $1.4 trillion , is being closely watched, with many in the industry hoping a strong debut on Wall Street will serve as a positive signal for the prospects of the broader AI industry. Databricks, which is still a privately held company, raised $5 billion at a $190 billion valuation in August. The industry has also been shaken by the recent revelation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s extramarital affair with a woman that U.S. officials believe to be a spy for China. Given the importance of Nvidia’s chips, and its financing, across the AI industry, there are fears of a ripple effect if he is forced to step down . Databricks’ Ghodsi brushed off the notion however. “I think that Jensen is an amazing CEO. He’s built that company for the last many decades. I think he should continue to be the CEO of that company,” he added. “I think we will weather through this storm,” he added, noting that the AI revolution is too big to be impacted by the revelations of the Nvidia CEO’s affair. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Developer says gigantic WA data centre will not use fracked gas
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Gingerah says it will not use fracked gas to power proposed WA data centre Gingerah Energy's proposed data centre project includes a local micro-grid powered by a 5,200-megawatt solar farm and 250 wind turbines. ( Supplied: Jop van Hattum ) The company behind a proposed data centre has sought to ease fears it will power the facility with fracked gas. Gingerah Energy says the centre will be mostly powered by renewables, with gas sourced from "the domestic gas market" as backup supply. The company intends to refer its project to the WA Environmental Protection Authority for review within weeks. The company proposing to build a massive data centre in northern Western Australia has sought to ease concerns the facility will be powered by gas sourced through fracking. Gingerah Energy referred its plan to build a 1,000-megawatt data centre and renewable energy hub to the Commonwealth's environmental agency last month. The site proposed is on Karajarri country, near Broome, about 2,000 kilometres north of Perth. Jop van Hattum says Project Meridien will be mostly renewables-powered. ( Supplied: Energy Club WA ) Chief executive Jop van Hattum said Project Meridien, which Gingerah hopes to be delivered by 2030, would initially be powered by solar, batteries, gas, and later also by wind. He said renewables would initially provide more than 85 per cent of the facility's total energy demand, with that figure rising as it expanded towards its full one-gigawatt capacity. The gas used would most likely come from Karratha, Mr van Hattum said. "We target for that renewable energy capacity to increase to 94 per cent," he said. Environmentalists have suggested Gingerah might source the gas it needs for the centre through fracking in the Kimberley. While there is no ban on fracking in the region's Canning basin, no projects have received the required approvals to proceed. Critics of fracking, or hydraulic fracturing, say it is harmful due to risks involving water contamination and long-term climate impacts. Mr van Hattum said the project's gas would be sourced from "the domestic gas market". "As energy storage systems and technology improve and costs reduce, our preference would obviously be to be free of the gas and use those technologies to make the project fully carbon-free if we can," he added. Environs Kimberley director Martin Pritchard called for greater clarity on where the gas would come from. "Could it come from another company that is planning to do fracking in the Kimberley? Could it come from a new conventional well that Buru Energy is working on at the moment? Could it come from Theia Energy, and are they going to want to start fracking to supply gas to this AI data centre?" Meridien is proposed to be developed on the KTLA-held Frazier Downs pastoral lease, about 100 kilometres south of Broome in WA's west Kimberley. ( Supplied: Jop van Hattum ) Gingerah is a joint venture between Karajarri Traditional Lands Association (KTLA), Dutch geodata company Fugro and Australian geoscience firm Longreach Capital Investment, which owns Theia Energy — a company that previously applied to drill and frack exploration wells in the Kimberley. Grattan Institute energy expert Alison Reeve estimated the Meridien data centre would need about eight terajoules of gas a day in its initial 240-megawatt phase and about 32 terajoules at full capacity. "All of WA consumes about 1,100 terajoules a day," she said. Ms Reeve said the project was not large enough to lead to more gas exploration or fracking in the Kimberley because the state already had enough gas to cover it. Traditional owner confident no fracked gas will be used KTLA director Justin King Senior said the gas needed for Meridien would "absolutely not" come from fracking. KTLA director Justin King signed the Gingerah Energy Indigenous Land Use Agreement in 2024. ( Supplied: Jop van Hattum ) "I say with conviction and reassure the people, our members, and the public [fracking] would never be part of the project make-up of energy," he said. Among KTLA members, Mr King said "a small minority" were opposed to the project for several reasons, including the increase in negative sentiment towards data centres online. "Social media plays a big part in giving out information," he said. The Raging Grannies protest data centres and power hikes in North Carolina, US. ( ABC News: Bec Symons ) This month's US midterm elections put data centres in the spotlight , with voters overwhelmingly rejecting their development. Ms Reeve said this resistance was also prevalent in Australia.

events.title: Commonwealth Bank allegedly overcharged business customers
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts ASIC accuses Commonwealth Bank of overcharging tens of thousands of business customers The CBA faces allegations it failed to report cash transactions made through intelligent deposit machines. ( ABC News: Margaret Burin ) Commonwealth Bank allegedly overcharged millions of dollars in fees to tens of thousands of business customers, many of them small businesses, according to the corporate regulator. ASIC has started civil penalty proceedings against Australia's biggest bank, alleging customers have been overcharged fees they were never told about. ASIC alleged CBA's CommBiz terms and conditions were misleading because they failed to clearly and accurately disclose all the fees business customers would be charged for direct debit and direct credit payments. Business customers were told they would be charged a fee for a payment to or from a third-party account. If you have more information about this story, please contact Nassim Khadem at khadem.nassim@abc.net.au or nassimkhadem@protonmail.com However, ASIC alleges CBA also charged an additional, undisclosed fee for the corresponding movement of money into or out of the customer's CommBiz account. ASIC alleges that between November 2020 and May 31, 2025, about 42,000 CommBiz customers were overcharged about $8.5 million in fees. ASIC alleges that in one example a small business paying the fortnightly wages of 10 employees from two CommBiz accounts was charged 12 fees: 10 for the payments to its employees and another two undisclosed fees for the money being withdrawn from its own accounts. "We allege Commonwealth Bank broke a basic promise to its business customers," ASIC commissioner Alan Kirkland said. "Small businesses are busy enough. They should not have to scrutinise every transaction to make sure that their bank is charging them the right fees." ASIC says customers were overcharged for years ASIC alleges business customers were overcharged for about 19 years, with the allegedly misleading terms and conditions in place from the launch of CommBiz in 2006. ASIC further alleges CBA received customer complaints about the issue from at least 2015, while a 2016 internal audit identified overcharging of direct debit fees and required corrective action. ASIC also alleges governance failings at CBA meant the alleged misleading statements were not identified and corrected, and that CBA allegedly failed to act efficiently, honestly and fairly. "What makes this particularly concerning is how long the alleged conduct went on, despite customer complaints to Commonwealth Bank pointing to a problem years earlier," Mr Kirkland said. ASIC commissioner Alan Kirkland says "Commonwealth Bank broke a basic promise to its business customers". ( ABC ) CBA temporarily ceased charging the relevant fees in June 2025 and amended the CommBiz terms in August 2025. Since February 2026, the bank has waived the "contra leg" fees for processing direct debits and direct credits. CBA has completed a remediation program covering December 1, 2006, to present for past and current CommBiz customers. This has resulted in more than $26.4 million in remediation payments to about 93,000 CommBiz customers, including about 40,000 small businesses. The case was filed in the Federal Court on late Wednesday afternoon. However, the court has not yet listed the matter for a case management hearing. It is the second legal action ASIC has taken against a big bank in as many days, with Macquarie Bank on Monday admitting to failures in the promotion of its "welcome" interest rate for new savings account customers, which could result in a $14 million penalty. CBA apologises but says it will defend aspects of litigation The Commonwealth Bank said in a statement to the ASX that it intended to defend aspects of the litigation. "While CBA charged the fee consistently over time, the issue arose from changes made to certain Terms and Conditions intended to simplify them, which did not accurately reflect the fee charging method," the CBA statement said. "The relevant fee was 25 cents (plus GST). "CBA self-identified this matter, reported it to ASIC, and has cooperated fully with ASIC throughout its investigation. "CBA has taken additional rectification steps to reduce the risk of similar incidents." It said up to October 20, the median payment made to affected CommBiz customers was about $85, and the mean payment was about $442, inclusive of interest.

events.title: Singapore’s first Moxy hotel to open at former Novotel building in Clarke Quay in 2027
events.summary: Guests at Moxy Singapore Clarke Quay will be able to enjoy a view of the Singapore River once the hotel is complete. Singapore’s first Moxy hotel will open by end-March 2027 at the former Novotel site in Clarke Quay. The 21-storey, 475-room hotel is part of CanningHill Piers. CDL Hospitality Trusts will buy the hotel for $474.6 million. The deal should lift its Singapore room count by 19% and its global room count by 10%. CDLHT will fund the purchase with a $148.8 million preferential offering and debt. It will also raise payouts from 90% to 100% of distributable income. SINGAPORE – Marriott’s first Moxy hotel in Singapore is expected to open by the end of March 2027 on the site of the former Novotel Singapore Clarke Quay. The 21-storey, 475-room Moxy Singapore Clarke Quay is part of the CanningHill Piers development, a mixed-use project currently being developed on the former Liang Court site. CDL Hospitality Trusts (CDLHT) expects to complete its $474.6 million acquisition of the hotel when it opens, it said in a stock exchange filing on Nov 10. In a separate announcement on the same day, CDLHT also said it would raise its dividend payouts from 90% to 100% of distributable income, starting with the six months from July 1 to Dec 31. CanningHill Piers is being developed by CapitaLand Development and City Developments Limited (CDL), in partnership with CapitaLand Ascott Trust. CDLHT in 2019 sold the Novotel, which was part of Liang Court, while agreeing to buy the new hotel once it was built. The Moxy hotel is expected to have more than 93 years left on its 99-year lease when the deal is completed. Moxy is Marriott International’s lifestyle hotel brand, known for its compact rooms and lively communal spaces where guests can work, drink and socialise. The hotel will have a rooftop pool and restaurant overlooking Marina Bay, while guests can choose rooms from about 17 sq m to 27 sq m in size, with views of the Singapore River, Fort Canning Park or the city skyline. Guests will also have access to shops and dining outlets in the development, which will be linked to Fort Canning MRT station by an underground walkway. The deal will increase CDLHT’s Singapore room count by about 19% to 3,030 and lift its global hotel room count by about 10% to 5,399, it said. Singapore is expected to account for about 67% of the trust’s portfolio value after the deal, up from about 62% as at the end of 2025. CDLHT’s managers said the Clarke Quay location would help the hotel draw both leisure and business travellers, while Marriott’s global booking network and Bonvoy loyalty programme could help it build occupancy after opening. They also expect limited growth in local hotel supply, with Singapore’s room inventory projected to rise by just around 1.3% a year from end-2026 to end-2029. The acquisition is expected to increase the cash payout investors receive for each CDLHT security they hold once the hotel’s operations stabilise. The estimated purchase price for the hotel, excluding fees, is $468.8 million, or 5.7% below Knight Frank’s Oct 30 valuation of $497 million. At that price, CDLHT’s managers estimate that annual net property income could reach about 4.8% of the purchase price once operations stabilise. The hotel received its temporary occupation permit on Oct 30, and CDLHT made its first payment of $23.4 million on Nov 4. A further $421.9 million is due when the deal is completed. The acquisition will be partially funded through a preferential offering to raise about $148.8 million from existing investors, CDLHT said. Under the preferential offering, eligible investors can subscribe for 18 new stapled securities for every 100 they hold. The issue price of 64.3 cents is 9.9% below CDLHT’s volume-weighted average traded price of 71.35 cents on Nov 10. The offer opens on Nov 23 at 9am and closes on Dec 1 at 5.30pm, with a later deadline of 9.30pm for applications through participating banks’ ATMs. The new securities are expected to begin trading on Dec 9. CDLHT plans to use about $145.6 million in net proceeds raised through the offering and about $324.7 million in debt to finance the acquisition. Gearing, a measure of debt relative to assets, is expected to rise from 35.6% as at Sept 30 to 39.5% after the deal. The managers expect the hotel’s income to cover its associated interest costs from 2028. They estimate it will take about two to 2½ years for occupancy at the hotel to stabilise, with 2030 expected to be its first full year of stabilised operations. In a separate announcement, CDLHT’s managers added that they will raise the trust’s payout ratio to 100% after reviewing its portfolio’s performance, financial position and cash needs. It has paid out 90% of its distributable income since July 2009.

events.title: Nvidia hires leading US law firm to investigate Jensen Huang’s relationship
events.summary: Move comes as chipmaker reels from reports its CEO was having an affair with an alleged Chinese spy Nvidia has appointed a leading US law firm to conduct a “thorough and independent” investigation into the relationship between its chief executive, Jensen Huang, and an alleged Chinese spy . The $4.1tn (£3tn) chipmaker’s board has hired New York-based Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz for the investigation, which will be led by the Wachtell partner Joon Kim. The firm’s website describes Kim, a former government prosecutor in New York, as a specialist in areas including internal investigations, white-collar criminal and regulatory defence, and crisis management. Nvidia did not give a timeframe for the investigation but the company has said Huang will continue to lead the business he co-founded “without interruption”. A committee of independent board directors, assisted by Kim and Wachtell, will oversee the investigation. The company is reeling from an espionage scandal after reports that its chief executive had been having an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, Alice Huang, who was also an Nvidia customer. The US ambassador to China , David Perdue, said: “The situation with Nvidia is another reminder that we have to stay diligent. “National security is part of this economic conversation because economic security is national security. And so, what we’re doing with China is bumpy right now,” he told Bloomberg Television. Nvidia had at first denied an improper relationship with the Chinese citizen, who is no relation to the Nvidia boss, but Huang then admitted on Sunday he had been unfaithful to his wife – without referring directly to Ms Huang. On the same day Nvidia announced an investigation into reports that Huang “has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort”. The Wall Street Journal and the New York Times yesterday reported Huang had had another affair with an executive who reports to him, which led Nvidia stocks to fall by more than 8% in extended trading. Wachtell is one of the most prestigious corporate law firms in the US. Its founding partner Martin Lipton invented the “poison pill defence” in the 1980s, a corporate gambit that helps companies ward off hostile takeovers. Technically called the “shareholder rights plan”, the poison pill allowed investors to buy more shares at a discount if one shareholder acquired a certain percentage of the company’s stock. This made it harder for corporate raiders to acquire a company without the board’s approval. The firm was closely involved in the takeover of Getty Oil by Texaco. This was the largest corporate takeover in history at the time, although it turned sour when the thwarted suitor Pennzoil sued Texaco and won. In 2008, a team of Wachtell lawyers advised the US Treasury department on the takeover of Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac during the financial crisis. The company was founded in the 1960s and is said to be the most profitable law firm in the US. It pulled in revenues of $5.1m per lawyer last year and made profits of $12m per partner, the highest profits per partner ever, according to the Am Law 100 rankings . Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning From 2017 to 2018, Kim was the acting US attorney for the southern district of New York, where he ran a team of lawyers investigating securities and commodities fraud, mail and wire fraud, public and private corruption, money laundering, cybercrime and tax offences. That included the case of the former US representative Anthony Weiner , who was sentenced to 21 months in prison for sending obscene material to a minor. He also oversaw the prosecution of the banker Mehmet Hakan Atilla, who was convicted in 2017 of helping to evade US sanctions on Iran . Another high-profile assignment landed on Kim’s desk in 2021, when he investigated multiple allegations of sexual harassment by the then New York governor, Andrew Cuomo. One analyst has put Huang’s chances of leaving Nvidia at 15%. “Right now the Street and investor chatter is assigning roughly a 15% chance he is removed as CEO of Nvidia with a high probability (85%) he stays on as CEO after the board investigation is completed,” wrote the tech analyst Dan Ives in a note to investors. “We would expect a board investigation that could take four weeks to six weeks and will create a clear overhang on the stock until more news emerges from Nvidia.” However after reports of the second extramarital affair, the WSJ last night reported that the board was preparing to oust Huang. Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, the senior associate dean for leadership studies at the Yale School of Management and the founder of the Chief Executive Leadership Institute, has put Huang’s survival chances at “about 50-50”.

events.title: US stocks end higher as CoreWeave results ease AI spending worries
events.summary: Traders working on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange in New York City on Nov 10. NEW YORK - US stocks closed higher on Nov 11, with the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq each rallying more than 1% as earnings from neocloud firm CoreWeave cooled investor concerns about the durability of the AI trade, while Nvidia stabilised after two straight sessions of sharp declines. Battered CoreWeave shares surged 24.7%, their biggest daily percentage jump in more than three months, to close at the highest level in two weeks. The company said it would become profitable in the first half of 2028 on an adjusted basis, seeking to reassure investors that strong demand and customer commitments could support its debt-fuelled expansion. Sentiment improvedacross AI infrastructure stocks, as Nebius Group surged 15.4% and Applied Digital shot up 7.4%. Nvidia advanced after shedding about US$430 billion (S$550 billion) of market capitalisation in the previous two sessions as investors worried ​about chief executive officer Jensen Huang’s relationship with a businesswoman alleged to be a Chinese spy. Equities have been volatile in recent days. Investors have expressed concerns about more regulation in the AI space after sweeping Democratic victories in the US midterm elections last week. That, and worries about Nvidia’s leadership, pressured one of the biggest pillars of the current bull market. Contributing to choppy stock trading, investors have been encouraged by cooling oil prices but concerned by hot inflation data that pushed Treasury yields sharply higher. “Everybody’s looking for a canary in a coal mine every single day, every minute of every day, and then they’re reacting every single day,” said Thomas Martin, senior portfolio manager at Globalt in Atlanta. “What we’ve seen is that you’ve gone back and forth, back and forth, back and forth between AI is good, AI is not so good. We’re worried about it, then oh, it’s great.” The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 254.60 points, or 0.49%, to 52,486.49, the S&P 500 gained 98.45 points, or 1.31%, to 7,619.38, and the Nasdaq Composite gained 400.31 points, or 1.60%, to 25,466.19. The Philadelphia SE Semiconductor index jumped 5.7% to close at its highest since November 3. Every component of the index advanced. Recent pronounced selling pressure prompted some investors to buy the dip, but early indicators show it is too soon to sound the all-clear. Investors bought equities even during last week’s selloff, with all net inflows coming through ETFs and institutional clients leading the purchases, Bank of America Global Research analysts said in a note. The S&P 500 technology index, up 2.7%, was the best-performing of the 11 major S&P sectors and has risen in three of the past four sessions. The CBOE Volatility Index fell for the fourth straight session to close at a one-week low of 17.49. Last week, Wall Street’s fear gauge hit its highest in more than seven months. Investors also examined the terms set by Anthropic on Nov 10 for its blockbuster initial public offering. The Claude chatbot creator is aiming for a valuation of up to US$1.4 trillion in the share sale. Vanda Research said in a note that the IPO could attract record buying by retail investors, with the potential to surpass SpaceX as one of the biggest single-day retail purchases ever. Hotter-than-expected inflation data on Nov 10 cemented market expectations the US Federal Reserve would raise interest rates in December, with traders now fully pricing in a hike of at least 25 basis points and a 10.4% chance of an increase of 50 basis points, according to CME FedWatch. Comments from multiple Fed officials also suggested the US central bank was open to a more aggressive path of rate hikes as price pressures worsen. The US bond market was shut on Nov 11 for Veterans Day. Advancing issues outnumbered decliners by a 1.48-to-1 ratio on the NYSE and by a 1.77-to-1 ratio on the Nasdaq. The S&P 500 posted 17 new 52-week highs and no new lows, while the Nasdaq Composite recorded 77 new highs and 159 new lows. Volume on US exchanges was 14.74 billion shares, compared with the 18.68 billion average for the full session over the last 20 trading days. REUTERS

events.title: 'Not the answer': Labour MPs speak out against Rosebank as decision looms
events.summary: If production is approved, oil and gas will be pumped up through a large ship 80 miles north west of Shetland Some Labour MPs have called on the government to reject the Rosebank oil field, saying it is "incompatible" with the UK's climate commitments. There is a growing expectation among senior Labour figures that drilling in the oil field off the north-west coast of Shetland will be given the go-ahead. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on Wednesday that a decision would be "taken in due course" while Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh stressed that affordability of energy bills was her "overriding objective". But in a sign of the division within the party, more than a dozen Labour MPs expressed concerns in Parliament about approving it. Others expressed support, pointing to economic benefits. Supportive Labour MPs said some other parts of the world emitted far more greenhouse gases than the UK and warned of relying on imports. Reports have suggested that Chancellor John Healey is in favour of approval. Separately, it is understood some Labour backbenchers have organised a letter opposing Rosebank - intended for Burnham, but not yet sent - which more than 60 out of about 400 Labour MPs have indicated they support. One signatory told the BBC that approving Rosebank "would not create new jobs, would bring minimal money into the Treasury and be bad for the climate". "The government's central aim is to tackle the cost of living crisis, and drilling for more oil at Rosebank isn't the answer," the MP said. Wednesday's Westminster Hall - a type of parliamentary debate where backbench MPs raise topical issues but do not vote - was organised by Green MP Carla Denyer. Labour MP for Sheffield Central Abtisam Mohamed told the debate: "Rosebank fails on every test. "It will not benefit taxpayers who will shoulder the vast majority of the development costs, it will not strengthen our energy security because most of the oil will be sold on international markets, and it will not reduce energy bills for our constituents, who will remain exposed to volatile fossil fuel prices." Richard Burgon, a former frontbencher on the left of the party, said: "Rosebank is not compatible with our climate targets - it's dangerous to pretend otherwise." The UK is committed to reaching net zero by 2050 and wants to limit global warming to no more than 1.5C above the pre-industrial period. The UK government has always insisted that Rosebank is a quasi-judicial decision, formally resting with Fahnbulleh . She green-lit production in the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea last month, but Rosebank hangs in the balance. Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh will formally announce the Rosebank decision, expected in the coming weeks Labour's manifesto upon entering power in 2024 pledged not to "issue new licences to explore new fields". Licences for both Jackdaw and Rosebank were granted by the then Conservative UK government in 2022 and 2023 respectively. But the Court of Session in Edinburgh ruled last year that the government had made the approvals unlawfully, leaving the current Labour government to make a fresh decision on whether to give the go-ahead. Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch sought to tease at Labour divisions on the issue during Prime Minister's Questions on Wednesday. During the debate, Labour MP Anna Gelderd said: "We live in an unprecedented era where our energy security is more vital than ever, in which jobs and wealth must be protected and economic opportunities seized - on both of these points, Rosebank fails." Labour MP Julia Buckley said she had received opposition to Rosebank from her constituents in "regularly flooded Shrewsbury" and said fossil fuels "belong in the past, not the future". She urged Fahnbulleh to "reject the oil licence in favour of renewables", adding: "Please don't add further to our climate emergency." Other Labour MPs expressed their support, including recently departed veterans minister Al Carns, who warned that Britain would continue to need fossil fuels for decades and importing more would be a mistake. "Refusing to produce it here does nothing on its own to eliminate that demand - it simply increases our reliance on imports which can carry their own environmental cost," he added. Those representing communities with ties to the oil and gas industry, including Jonathan Brash, the Labour MP for Hartlepool, stressed the benefits of approving Rosebank for British jobs. Speaking to BBC Radio 5 Live, Labour MP Bill Esterson, chair of Energy Security and Net Zero Committee, said "the economics of it (Rosebank) are that you should carry on with it" and "there's an element of energy security" by approving it. Energy minister Michael Shanks told the debate the government would take a "pragmatic approach" to a clean energy transition, stressing it was "not a turn off the taps government, but nor can we justifiably be a drill every last drop government either".

events.title: What it takes to bring an AI research assistant to thousands of medical experts
events.summary: From custom infrastructure to hosted agents What we learned rebuilding Novo’s clinical trials data agent on Microsoft Foundry: a simpler operating model, a stronger session isolation, and a direct path from tracing to evaluation and optimization. Clinical research rarely ends with the questions defined in a trial protocol. Medical experts also explore the data from new angles: testing a hypothesis, comparing patient populations, visualizing a trend, or identifying a promising direction for further research. As part of a forward-deployed engineering engagement, a joint Microsoft and Novo Nordisk development team built an agent that helps medical experts perform this kind of secondary analysis of clinical trial data. We described the original project in a Microsoft customer story . More recently, we reimplemented the solution as a hosted agent in Microsoft Foundry . The move gave us a simpler operating model, stronger session isolation, and a direct path into Foundry’s tracing, evaluation, experimentation, optimization, and governance capabilities. It also taught us practical lessons about infrastructure planning, observability, and preserving the learning loop that already made the agent better over time. Here’s what changed, what we measured, and what we would recommend to teams making a similar move. An agent for questions that don’t have a fixed workflow Secondary analysis of clinical data is a great task for an agent because the execution path depends heavily on the question. The agent interprets the request, inspects the available data, writes and executes analysis code, examines the result, and often revises its approach before returning a summary and visualization. This isn’t just attaching a chat interface to a single API. The agent needs a reasoning loop, access to domain-specific skills, and tools for working with data. In our implementation, code execution is the central tool. The agent can generate analysis code and visualizations inside a controlled environment while the surrounding application manages the conversation and presents the result to the user. Our first production architecture ran the agent in Azure Container Apps . We used PostgreSQL for conversation storage and Azure Container Apps dynamic sessions for sandboxed code execution. That architecture gave us explicit control over every component, and it proved the value of the use case. It also meant that our team owned much of the platform around the agent: container scaling, session lifecycle, conversation persistence, execution isolation, networking, telemetry, and the integration among them. Foundry hosted agents offered a simpler division of responsibility. Moving the runtime boundary into Foundry A hosted agent is our code, packaged as a container, running on infrastructure managed by Foundry Agent Service . We retain control of the orchestration logic, models, tools, and runtime behavior. Foundry manages the endpoint, agent identity, session compute, state persistence, scaling, and lifecycle around it. At runtime, each session gets its own VM-isolated sandbox. Foundry provisions compute on demand, keeps it active while the session is in use, and de-provisions it after the configured idle period. Session files can persist and be restored when the session resumes. Scaling follows active sessions rather than a replica count that we have to predict and configure. For Novo’s workload, that model aligned well with the unit of work we were building for: one expert conducting one analysis session. It also changed the architecture in four important ways: Scaling became session-native. We no longer needed to connect application-level session creation to a separately scaled pool of execution environments. The platform owns that lifecycle. Isolation became the default unit of execution. Each session runs in a VM-isolated sandbox rather than sharing a process or general-purpose application container with other sessions. That matters when the workload includes model-generated code operating on sensitive clinical data. Network isolation became part of the service architecture. Foundry Agent Service supports private networking, including virtual network integration and private access to dependent Azure resources. This lets us design controls for both ingress and egress around the agent environment. Those controls are especially important for data that must remain inside an approved network boundary. The agent joined a broader development lifecycle. Traces, evaluations, experiments, monitoring, and optimization can now be connected through the same platform. Microsoft Agent 365 integration also provides a path to enterprise inventory, identity, access control, and lifecycle governance. Using Foundry hosted agents didn’tt remove our responsibility for security or quality. We still had to define access controls, minimize and protect telemetry, test the agent for our use case, and review every system it can call. What changed is that several controls we previously assembled ourselves are now platform capabilities we can configure and operate consistently. Here are the top lessons we learned during this project—and some practical advice for your own hosted agents projects in Foundry: Lesson 1: Treat infrastructure choices as product decisions Private networking should be an early architecture decision, not a production hardening task left until the end. Hosted agents consume network capacity according to sessions. The Foundry account, its projects, hosted agents, concurrent sessions, and agent revisions all contribute to IP usage. Because the assigned subnet is an immutable reference at the account level, an undersized range can turn a capacity adjustment into a broader infrastructure migration. Our advice is to estimate peak concurrent sessions across the account, include headroom for deployments and growth, and involve the network team before creating the Foundry resource. The current networking guidance recommends a /24 subnet for production hosted agent deployments and documents /27 as the supported minimum for smaller deployments. We used Azure Verified Modules as the foundation for repeatable environments. That gave us a strong starting point, but infrastructure as code doesn’t remove the need to inspect generated dependencies. Throughput for resources like Azure Cosmos DB should reflect expected concurrency and data access patterns. Where a setting requires an operational adjustment, capture it in the deployment process or operator runbook rather than leaving it as unwritten production knowledge. Subnet sizing, database throughput, private endpoints, DNS, and concurrency aren’t separate infrastructure details. Together, they shape the scale ceiling and reliability of the product. Lesson 2: Make traces easy to navigate Foundry tracing uses OpenTelemetry and stores telemetry in Azure Monitor Application Insights.

events.title: Is she a spy, or just out of your league? How to avoid getting honeypotted
events.summary: Jensen Huang, chief executive of Nvidia. Bloomberg/Getty Images Nvidia is investigating whether CEO Jensen Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort. The episode raises questions about the company's future, Huang's future, and the AI trade. It also raises a pressing question for execs with access to company secrets: How do you avoid dating a spy? It often starts with a beautiful stranger, a "chance" encounter, and a powerful man who thinks he simply got lucky. As Nvidia's board investigates whether CEO Jensen Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort and Huang has admitted to having an affair , an old spycraft tactic has been thrust into the modern world of AI chips, corporate access, and national security. "The Chinese MSS and PLA are very aggressive and play the long game," Fred Burton, a former US Diplomatic Security Service special agent, told Business Insider, referring to China's Ministry of State Security and People's Liberation Army. For executives with access to company secrets, the episode raises a pressing question: How do you avoid dating someone who just may be a spy? A sticky business Will Geddes, the founder of London-based corporate threat-management firm International Corporate Protection Group, said the most effective operations rarely begin with an obvious proposition at a hotel bar. Instead, operatives may spend months studying a target's "pattern of life" — their travel, routines, hobbies, and vulnerabilities like isolation, marital difficulty, or separation — before engineering a meeting at a conference, work event, or through someone the executive already trusts, he said. In this case, the woman linked to Huang is Alice Huang, a former executive at Nvidia customer Megaspeed. The New York Times reported that US officials believe she was an asset of China's Ministry of State Security who had been recruited to collect intelligence on Huang . China's foreign ministry has repeatedly said the "Chinese spy" allegation is unsubstantiated. Jensen and Alice Huang, who aren't related, can be seen together in photos dating back to June 2024 at an after-party following Computex 2024, Taiwan's annual computer and tech trade show. Since then, they've been pictured together in Taipei in May 2025, on the sidelines of Computex 2025, and in a series of photos shared by Alice Huang on WeChat, the Chinese social media platform. The warning signs and the key questions There are several key questions executives should ask themselves if they start to suspect someone in their lives, said Eric O'Neill, a former FBI counterintelligence operative. O'Neill helped capture Robert Hanssen, the FBI agent who spied on the US for Moscow for over two decades. Among those questions: Who initiated contact? How quickly did it develop? What does the person know about their business, finances, travel, and personal life? And have they sought introductions, access, or unusual favors? "A skilled intelligence officer rarely arrives wearing a trench coat and introducing herself as a spy," O'Neill said. "The best ones look and behave exactly like the person you want to meet." O'Neill said executives should verify a new partner's identity and background before allowing them into their home, private life, or professional orbit. They should also separate personal and corporate devices and accounts, and use multifactor authentication. Yet Burton said background checks on people close to a CEO are "rarely done unless they are requested." And when they do happen, he said, they often focus on criminal or financial checks for household staff rather than a boss's friends or romantic partners. The most dangerous spy in your life If you suspect something is amiss, seek help before embarrassment becomes leverage. "The most dangerous spy in your life may be the person you've stopped questioning," O'Neill said. Geddes said executives should be alert if a new partner seems unusually attractive, initiates contact, or accelerates intimacy faster than expected. They should also pay attention to someone who repeatedly controls where and when they meet — choosing the restaurant, bar, or hotel and steering the timing. None of those signs alone proves malicious intent. But together, Geddes said, they can warrant a closer look. "Even sharp, experienced decision-makers can lose their judgement in the presence of someone attractive," Geddes said. A slim track record Documented cases involving major corporate leaders falling for foreign operatives are rare, Burton said, but the tactics used are well established. In March 2024, authorities charged ex-Army officer David Slater with sharing classified information through a dating site with someone claiming to be a Ukrainian woman. He pleaded guilty and received a 70-month sentence in October 2025. And in December 2020, Axios reported that US officials believed Chinese national Christine Fang cultivated politicians, including sexual or romantic relationships with two Midwestern mayors, in an alleged intelligence-gathering operation. Fang left the US in 2015 amid an FBI-led investigation and has not faced public charges. While the Huang matter is still under investigation and Huang has not disclosed with whom he had the affair, the news has roiled markets and led to widespread speculation about whether Huang will have to step down as CEO . It's also, Burton said, a reminder to companies at the cutting edge of the tech sector to be wary of threats from hostile agencies and threat actors. "The oldest tricks in the espionage playbook still work," O'Neill said. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Developer 'pauses' AI data centre proposal after it 'misread' community feeling
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Quantum DC halts approval process of Adelaide Hills AI data centre A community protest event held in Mannum against the Tungkillo data centre last month. ( ABC News: James Wakelin ) Quantum DC has delayed its planned hyper-scale AI data centre at Tungkillo following "deep frustration" in the Adelaide Hills community. The technology developer says it will not apply for development approval this year but has not ruled out progressing the data centre in the future. The company says it will now convene a panel of independent experts to review specialist studies and make their findings public. A developer says it has paused its plans to build a 1200-megawatt AI data centre in the Adelaide Hills, saying it "misread" community feeling about the proposal. Quantum DC chief executive Alby Tomassi said the company would not seek development approval this year and would instead undertake a "longer-term and more comprehensive engagement programme" to address community concerns. "We misread the strength of feeling about this proposal and acknowledge the first weeks of our early engagement created more questions than answers," he said in a statement. "We sincerely apologise for this, and we understand the disappointment and frustration it has caused. That is why we are pausing and intend to take a fresh approach to how we engage and how this proposal is tested." Quantum DC is proposing a hyper-scale data centre along with energy infrastructure on Collins Road in Tungkillo, about 41 kilometres directly east of the Adelaide CBD. Mr Tomassi said the company has been contacted by more than 350 people about the proposal and the community had submitted a consolidated list of 432 questions. He said the issues raised related to water, energy, noise, lighting and the night sky, traffic, bushfire, farming land, location and the local environment. "There is such deep frustration amongst the community, which was not our intent at all, and I admit we misread these responses and the only responsible thing to do now is to pause and reset," he told 891 ABC Adelaide. The company had scheduled two community consultation sessions last month but postponed them to later this month amid safety concerns. In their absence, locals instead convened their own protest meetings where a few hundred attended . Mr Tomassi said those November community sessions were now cancelled because "it wouldn't be effective to meet 500 people and answer 432 questions in an emotive open forum". Magdalene Lippett looking over the proposed site for the hyperscale data centre and energy hub. ( Supplied: Magdalene Lippett ) Tungkillo resident Magdalene Lippett opposed the data centre and welcomed the pause. "I think that Quantum DC need to get the hint that no means no," she told 891 ABC Adelaide. "Our community have done the research, we've spoken to the experts, we've had a look at the issues … and this just isn't the right place, the hills is not the right place for their data centre." Quantum DC said it would now convene a panel of independent experts to review specialist studies and make their findings public. Mr Tomassi emphasised the development application would not proceed until "we set up these groups to scrutinise this project appropriately", but has not ruled out progressing the Tungkillo data centre in the future. "It's a global issue in regards to social acceptance [of data centres] and I think South Australia is appropriately poised to take this opportunity if the framework is right," he said. The proposed site of the Tungkillo data centre. ( Supplied: Magdalene Lippett ) Mid Murray Council Mayor Simone Bailey said the council had received one briefing from Quantum DC and further information provided since would be discussed at an upcoming meeting. She said the council has "big concerns" about the location of the proposed data centre, its proximity to a dark sky reserve , distance from an SA Country Fire Service station, limited access on unsealed roads and how the centre might affect noise pollution and the water table. But about a two-hour drive north of Tungkillo, an elected member at a different regional council expressed his support for the project to relocate to his patch. Northern Areas councillor Hank Langes said he would put a question without notice to the chamber to see if the council will support the data centre in their area, which covers Jamestown and Spalding. "We are a pro-development council so we'd love to have the data centre up our way," Cr Langes said. "It gives us a bit more employment and so forth, and widens the employment structure.

events.title: CoreWeave soars more than 24% for best day since April 2025 after strong Q3 report
events.summary: CoreWeave posted quarterly revenue that beat estimates and raised its full-year guidance. Neoclouds such as CoreWeave, Nebius and IREN have come under scrutiny this month as investors assessed the sustainability of the AI trade. CoreWeave has done well to allay concerns by moving away from unsecured bond financing, Zacks Chief Equity Strategist John Blank told CNBC. CoreWeave shares jumped 24.71% Wednesday for its best day since April 2025 after the neocloud posted quarterly earnings that beat estimates and raised its guidance for the year. "Demand for the infrastructure is and remains overwhelming." CEO Michael Intrator told CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" Wednesday. "I think I said that we are 10x oversubscribed to the existing capacity that we have left in 2027, and we are multiples ... oversubscribed on the capacity we have out in 2028," he said. Neoclouds such as CoreWeave, Nebius and IREN have come under scrutiny this month as investors assessed the sustainability of the AI trade. CoreWeave, in particular, sparked alarm when spreads on its CDS widened past 11% , generally viewed as a distress level, as investors have to pay up for protection against default. With the price of its high-yield debt climbing, CoreWeave highlighted additional routes to finance its data center build-out with less alarming yields, quelling investor concerns for the time being. "Our asset level debt has basically been rock solid through this entire thing," Intrator told CNBC. "There is an enormous demand for that product. We're about to launch another asset-level debt in the next week or two that has already been rated high investment grade." Intrator added that he expects it "will be underwritten in the market at 7% to 7.5% interest," which will bring down the average weighted cost of capital for the company. The three months to Sept. 30 marked a "breakout quarter" for CoreWeave, Intrator said on the conference call, adding that growth was supported by multiple sources of funding, including financing backed by customer contracts and around $9 billion in customer prepayments and deposits. Revenue jumped 168% to $3.7 billion in the third quarter, the company said in a Tuesday statement . Other neclouds also rose on CoreWeave's strong results, with Nebius rising 15.44%, Applied Digital 7.37% and Iren 5.63% Wednesday. Despite fears that a "blue wave" in last week's midterm elections could restrict data center capacity, Intrator reiterated that data center growth looks poised to continue as expected for CoreWeave. "We don't see any impact on our ability to deliver the data centers within the U.S. that are required for us to deliver on our backlog," Intrator told CNBC on Wednesday. "In Texas, Governor-elect [Gina Hinojosa], said that facilities that are permitted and under construction will continue, and we've been really, really thoughtful about the broad distribution." CoreWeave expects $1.275 billion to $1.375 billion in adjusted operating income on $13 billion to $13.3 billion in revenue. Analysts surveyed by Visible Alpha were looking for $1.07 billion in adjusted operating income, and analysts polled by LSEG had expected $12.86 billion in 2026 revenue. The neocloud has done well to allay concerns about financing by moving away from unsecured bond financing, Zacks Chief Equity Strategist John Blank told CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe." "It might be the bottom for CoreWeave," Blank said Wednesday. "But the shares are so beaten up, you have to believe at this point there's more value on the upside than the down." events.title: A timeline of Meghan Markle's relationship with her father, Thomas Markle
events.summary: Thomas Markle was arrested in November 2026. MEGA/Getty Images/Jonathan Brady/AP Thomas Markle was arrested and charged with one count of possession of child pornography. Meghan Markle's relationship with her father has been publicly strained since 2018. A judge ruled Thomas Markle must be detained as his case proceeds after first granting him home detention. Thomas Markle was arrested and charged with one count of possession of child pornography, the Department of Justice confirmed on Friday . The news comes less than a month after Thomas Markle Jr., Meghan Markle's half-brother, told The Sun he had reported finding child sex abuse images at their father's home in the Philippines to the Philippine police and the FBI. Markle Sr., 82, denied the allegations to the Daily Mail on October 23 before his arrest, describing them as the "worst thing anyone could accuse" him of. Markle Sr. and Markle Jr. did not respond to requests for comment. Meghan said she was "deeply distressed" by the allegations against her father in a statement made before his arrest. The Duchess of Sussex, 45, has had a publicly strained relationship with her father since 2018, when he posed for paparazzi photos for money ahead of her wedding to Prince Harry. Here's a timeline of their relationship. Meghan Markle has said she and her father had a close relationship in her childhood. Meghan Markle in Melbourne, Australia, in April 2026. Jonathan Brady/AP Meghan's mother, Doria Ragland, and her dad divorced in 1987 when she was 6 years old. In her December 2022 Netflix series, "Harry & Meghan," the Duchess of Sussex said she was with her mom during the week and her dad on the weekends after their split. She said her parents "co-parented well" and that she was close with her dad, describing herself as a "daddy's girl my whole life." She also said in the series that she would spend time with her dad after school, joining him on sets when he worked as a lighting director on shows like "Married…With Children." He also helped with lighting at her school plays, as a friend of Meghan's shared in "Harry & Meghan." May 2018: Markle accepted money for paparazzi photos and didn't attend his daughter's wedding. Prince Harry, King Charles, and Meghan Markle at their wedding in May 2018. Jonathan Brady - WPA Pool/Getty Images Days before Meghan's wedding on May 19, 2018, tabloids including TMZ and the Daily Mail reported that Markle had sat for staged paparazzi photos — which showed him preparing for the event, reading articles about it, and looking at a book about England — in exchange for money.  The Daily Mail's reporting included a video that appeared to show the photo shoot. TMZ also reported Markle's back-and-forth decisions on whether he would attend his daughter's wedding ahead of the event. He ultimately said he would not be there because he needed urgent heart surgery. On May 17, 2018, Meghan confirmed in a statement shared by the royal family that her father wouldn't be in attendance. "Sadly, my father will not be attending our wedding," the statement said. "I have always cared for my father and hope he can be given the space he needs to focus on his health." In episode three of their Netflix series, Meghan said her dad did not return her phone calls after the story broke, even though she called him over 20 times. She also said she learned he wasn't attending the wedding from the tabloids. Harry's father, then known as Prince Charles, walked Meghan down the aisle in her dad's absence. Summer of 2018: Markle began doing public interviews about Meghan and the royal family. Meghan Markle in July 2018. Anwar Hussein/Getty Images After he didn't attend her wedding , Markle began speaking to the British press about Meghan more frequently, including making an appearance on "Good Morning Britain" in June 2018. He said in the interview that making a deal  with the paparazzi was "a serious mistake," though he hoped it would change his image, as other paparazzi photos showed him in ways he found unflattering. He also said that he regretted not being able to walk Meghan down the aisle. On July 15, 2018, he told The Sun that Meghan wasn't speaking to him. He said the same thing to the Daily Mail about two weeks later. He also took aim at Harry in an August 2018 interview with the Mail on Sunday, saying he hung up on the prince when he called about the paparazzi incident and that Harry was "rude" to speak to him about the matter after his heart attack. Kensington Palace declined to comment on the phone call at the time. February 2019: The Mail on Sunday published excerpts from a letter Meghan wrote Markle. Meghan Markle in February 2019. Gotham/Getty Images In February 2019, Markle gave the Mail on Sunday a letter Meghan wrote to him in August 2018, three months after her wedding. The Mail on Sunday published excerpts of the letter , in which the Duchess of Sussex said her father had "broken my heart into a million pieces" by speaking to tabloids about her and Harry. She also contradicted his claims that she did not reach out to him about his heart attack in May 2018, saying he ignored her calls and texts in the lead-up to her wedding. She beseeched him in the letter to stop speaking to the press, a request he ignored by sharing the letter with the Mail on Sunday. In 2019, Meghan sued Associated Newspapers , which owns the Mail on Sunday, for publishing the excerpt, alleging breach of the Data Protection Act 2018, copyright infringement, and misuse of private information. "The Mail on Sunday stands by the story it published and will be defending this case vigorously," a spokesperson for the newspaper told Business Insider at the time. "Specifically, we categorically deny that the Duchess's letter was edited in any way that changed its meaning." Meghan won her case in December 2021, and the Mail on Sunday had to publish a statement acknowledging that it had infringed her copyright and had to pay her £1. March 2021: Meghan opens up about her fractured relationship with Markle in her interview with Oprah Winfrey. The Duke and Duchess of Sussex speak to Oprah Winfrey for their March 2021 CBS interview. CBS During the interview , Winfrey asked Meghan "if it felt like betrayal" when she discovered her father had accepted money for paparazzi photos. Meghan responded that her father had lied to her when she confronted him about the photos. She said she had learned that a story would be coming out about the pictures from the royals' "comms team," and she and Harry then called her dad to ask him about it. Meghan said her father denied the story, even after she and Harry offered to try to prevent its publication. "I look at Archie, and I think about this child, and I go, 'I genuinely can't imagine doing anything to intentionally cause pain to my child,'" she said, referring to her son and daughter Lilibet, whom she was pregnant with at the time. events.title: Hormuz Strait will ‘never return’ to pre-war status, Iran’s Ghalibaf says
events.summary: Iran’s parliament speaker and top negotiator says Tehran is waiting for an official US response to its seven conditions for ending war. Iran’s Ghalibaf tells Al Jazeera the ball is in US’s court on talks to end war Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, Iran’s parliament speaker and top negotiator, has told Al Jazeera that the Strait of Hormuz will “never return” to its status prior to the US-Israel war on Iran. In an exclusive interview published on Wednesday, Ghalibaf said Iran and Oman reached an understanding to oversee the critical waterway as part of Tehran’s seven-point proposal to end the eight-month conflict. list 1 of 4 Iran backs nuclear treaty even as hardliners raise prospect of bomb list 2 of 4 Rubio says no need for major combat operations against Iran list 3 of 4 Iran denies talks with US, says Hormuz will stay shut until demands are met list 4 of 4 Can Tehran survive a ‘zero oil’ budget, if US blockade on Iran persists? “There are no ‘free waters’ [international waters] there, and the 1982 [UN Convention on the Law of the Sea] does not apply to the strait … The regulations within the Strait of Hormuz are governed by the laws of the two littoral states that border it,” he said. Ghalibaf said Tehran provided a clear response to the US through a Qatari mediator that included its seven conditions for peace talks, adding that Iran is waiting for an official response. “The ball is now in the American court,” he said. Iran’s conditions, as outlined by the chief negotiator, include lifting the US-imposed naval blockade and sanctions, the release of Iranian frozen funds, ending fighting on all fronts, and an explicit announcement of an end to the war. He said these demands were part of the Islamabad memorandum of understanding signed in June and their implementation was necessary before entering negotiations with the US. “If America limits itself to what has been agreed upon without making excessive demands or engaging in behaviour that breeds distrust, then, naturally, reaching an agreement is possible,” he said. “What stands in the way of an agreement is our lack of trust in the United States.” Ghalibaf said US officials asked Russian President Vladimir Putin to mediate direct negotiations with Tehran during a visit to Moscow. He warned against new US attacks against Iran, saying that US President Donald Trump will face another defeat and political pressure from the new Congress that takes office in January. Iran is determined to move beyond a state of “no war and no peace”, he said, urging a sustainable deterrent capability, including military capabilities. On the ongoing fighting in Yemen between the Saudi-backed internationally recognised government forces and the Houthis, an armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for “Supporters of God”), Ghalibaf said that “no one should interfere” in it. “If both the government in Yemen and Saudi Arabia were to ask for our help, we would certainly offer our assistance to help resolve their conflict,” he said. Iran has previously offered to facilitate talks between Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Houthi group in October following a series of deadly attacks on the kingdom.
