events.title: Local media startup City Cast reshuffles leadership
events.summary: The locally-focused media startup City Cast has named Andi McDaniel, the company’s chief creative officer, its new CEO, replacing David Plotz. City Cast launched in 2021 as a local podcast and newsletter venture aimed at serving cities where local news was shifting from old newspapers and radio to screens. The company has since expanded to 13 cities, including Austin, Las Vegas, and Philadelphia, among others. “This next chapter for us is about expanding audiences. It’s about adapting to AI, and it’s about making the business successful,” McDaniel, a veteran public radio executive and co-founder of City Cast , told Semafor. City Cast has gained greater visibility in recent months, primarily for its expansion in its hometown. As Semafor first noted last year, in response to what the company saw as an opportunity created by the turbulence at The Washington Post, City Cast scaled up its newsroom and business in Washington. City Cast is backed by Graham Holdings, which owned the Post before selling to Jeff Bezos. City Cast DC now has 20 people on staff, and said it has found some success attracting a younger audience to its content, tripling the size of people it reaches regularly from roughly 100,000 at the beginning of the year to around 300,000. Not every bet has paid off. The company shuttered two arms, in Boise and Houston. In a telephone interview, Plotz said Houston was too large and sprawling an area to cover with the company’s resources — most cities operate with a staff of just 5 or 6 employees — while he said the company didn’t understand Boise enough when City Cast launched there. The company learned that their podcasts were not a replacement for radio, and that the City Cast model seemed to resonate best within mid-sized cities with concentrated downtowns that orient residents’ perspectives. Plotz said that revenue was up 40% this year, but the company was still not profitable. In the six years since the company’s launch, the company’s founder told Semafor he’d grown to better understand habits in the local media landscape. He noted that many people under the age of 60 largely got their information from social media, neighborhood listservs, local newsletters, and Reddit. “People do not want local news,” Plotz said. “They want to know about things to do in their city. They want to know what’s going on in their city. But if you ask them about local news, they do not express an interest. “Local news as a concept does not really have a lot of valence. It’s more like learning about my city.” He also noted that national media narratives and big political fights were not as animating to local audiences, who seek out information to be connected to their local communities. “The need that people are finding met in local media has almost nothing to do with the highly partisan, cortisol-driven conversations that drive national media and national news media,” he said.

events.title: Scoop: Lutnick stalled curbing Nvidia chip sales to China — again — after Oval Office showdown
events.summary: President Trump on Thursday authorized a crack down on companies suspected of diverting Nvidia's advanced AI chips to China for the third time this year — even consulting Elon Musk before giving the go-ahead. One administration official has repeatedly stood in the way: Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. Why it matters: This standoff illustrates a breakdown in efforts to keep American technology out of China's hands as the world wonders why the Trump administration has not taken action against the company at the center of suspected chip smuggling — and an espionage scandal. This report was assembled from interviews with six high-level sources who were briefed on or, in some cases, heard the discussions. Inside the room: On Thursday, as the spy scandal rocked the administration, Lutnick met in the Situation Room with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer and National Security Adviser and Secretary of State Marco Rubio. During the meeting, Bessent confronted Lutnick about why his department has resisted implementing the export controls, particularly on Megaspeed, the company at the center of the spy scandal. The group sided with Bessent. Lutnick appeared to agree, but then muttered under his breath, "I need to check with the president." Friction point: Lutnick's seemingly innocuous comment raised concerns, the sources said, because officials have repeatedly believed the Commerce Department would impose the export controls, only to have nothing happen. "He's stalling it out," said one official, describing how Lutnick had previously met privately with the president to change his mind about the export limit. "This is an ongoing concern with Howard and this issue," said another. This time, one person in the room called his bluff by saying: "Great. Why don't we do it today?" Around 5pm, the group headed to the Oval Office. Trump called tech advisor Elon Musk and agreed to move forward. Musk supported Rubio, Bessent, Greer and Hegseth's case to impose the controls while Lutnick warned it "will start a trade war with China." "Everyone argued back that China is already doing to us what Lutnick warned would happen," a source said. Behind the scenes: With Lutnick the lone holdout, Trump made his decision: "Let's get it done." But once everyone was outside of the Oval Office, Lutnick proposed a new delay tactic. "I'll develop some options and come back," he said. "Everyone was like: 'No, no, the decision's been made. Go fucking execute,'" one source said. "Well, it still hasn't happened." The other side: Commerce Department spokesperson Kristen Eichamer denied that Bessent confronted Lutnick and would not immediately comment on the other allegations. Flashback: On at least three separate occasions — in May, August, and Nov. 5 — Trump approved taking action against suspected diversions of Nvidia chips to China. But Lutnick and Commerce Undersecretary Jeffrey Kessler resisted pressure from Bessent and others to move forward. In May, a highly classified memo warning about Jensen Huang's relationship with Alice Huang, a Megaspeed employee suspected by U.S. intelligence of being a Chinese agent, was shared with the president and other officials. In a subsequent meeting, Bessent, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, Hegseth and White House officials pressed Lutnick and Kessler to act, the source said, "and they were refusing." Catch up quick: The Trump administration last year announced it would loosen export controls on Nvidia H200 chip sales to China — something Nvidia has lobbied hard for. Trump has taken a more lax approach to export controls on China, agreeing to allow sales of Nvidia's H200 chips, which are older but still powerful, in exchange for a 25% tariff. Long before the affair with Alice Huang, Jensen Huang has pushed for tapping into the Chinese market. The CEO at the center of an AI boom Trump is dead set on winning has largely been successful at convincing Trump and Lutnick that selling less powerful chips to China is good for national security because it prevents China from developing its own alternatives and keeps the adversary dependent on the U.S. The bottom line: While Lutnick oversees the department squarely at the center of export control policy, Trump is the ultimate decider.

events.title: Amanda Seyfried has no regrets about sparring with Elizabeth Holmes' partner Billy Evans in that jaw-dropping scene
events.summary: Amanda Seyfried and Billy Evans. Getty Images Amanda Seyfried gave her first detailed account of starring in "You Can See Everything." Seyfried spoke to Rolling Stone about sparring with Billy Evans in one of the movie's climactic scenes. "There was no reason for him to get that aggressive," Seyfried said, referring to Evans, who is Elizabeth Holmes' partner. The wait is over: Amanda Seyfried has finally spoken out about appearing in " You Can See Everything ." In an interview with Rolling Stone released on Wednesday, Seyfried, along with directors Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, spoke about how "The Dropout" star got involved in the hit Elizabeth Holmes documentary. It began harmlessly enough, when Seyfried's friend Emma Stone connected her with Fielder, who asked if she'd look over the interview footage they'd shot with Elizabeth Holmes . After sharing her thoughts, Seyfried's involvement eventually expanded to include her filming reenactments playing Holmes, and, in one shocking moment, traveling with Fielder to have dinner at the home of Holmes' partner, Billy Evans . The scene is one of the doc's most climactic and surreal moments, as Seyfried ends up sparring with Evans at the dinner table. Seyfried admits in the Rolling Stone interview that she already had "negative feelings" toward Evans after seeing Fielder's footage. But she said things "only got worse" after meeting him. "I am sitting there with her children and cuddling with her dog! While she's in prison!" Seyfried said of being in Evans' home while Holmes is in prison. Holmes even calls from prison while Seyfried and Fielder are there. Billy Evans and Elizabeth Holmes in "You Can See Everything." A24 "Someone asked me if that was real, if that was really her on the phone. And I'm like, 'It's a documentary. Who else would it be?'" she said. Things quickly went downhill during dinner when Evans insulted Seyfried's acting and the two sparred over Seyfried's comments about Charlie Kirk. Seyfried told Rolling Stone the moment really was as intense as it's portrayed onscreen. "There was no reason for him to get that aggressive," Seyfried recalled. "That's the word I'm going to use, as it's more diplomatic. If my jaw wasn't obviously on the floor, you could tell, like, it had come unhinged. I don't want to provoke him, but at this point, it's kind of like, the gloves are off. Because this guy has disrespected me in such a way that I was like, 'Oh, I don't think so, buddy.'" Seyfried said she has no regrets about how she handled the argument. "I was in the frame of mind where I'm like, 'OK, this guy is disrespectful, and I'm here in his home, I'm gonna argue this because I actually have a pretty solid stance on things. I don't like the way he's using this human being, his wife — the person he says he's "building monuments of love' to — as a tool. Maybe he does respect her, but he's behaving like he does not respect her. And not only am I protective of myself, I'm just trying to set the record straight in a way where I'm trying to defend myself, too, while maintaining some kind of rapport with him, so I can stay and he doesn't kick us out, you know?" Billy Evans did not respond to a request for comment. "You Can See Everything" is in theaters now. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: David Ellison’s Skydance replaces DC Studios bosses James Gunn and Peter Safran with a Marvel veteran
events.summary: Skydance has removed James Gunn and Peter Safran as co-chairmen and co-CEOs of DC Studios, ending a four-year run that began with a hit Superman and was expected to survive the company’s takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery. Their replacement is Jeremy Latcham, a former Marvel Studios executive who helped launch the Marvel Cinematic Universe. Skydance Motion Picture Group announced the change on Nov. 9 . Latcham starts Dec. 1 as president and chief creative officer of DC Studios, overseeing its film, television, and animation slate. The move puts Batman, Superman, Wonder Woman, and the rest of the DC Comics roster under new creative control barely a month after Skydance closed its deal. It also resets a franchise strategy that Warner Bros. has now restarted twice in 13 years. A reprieve that lasted a month Paramount completed its takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery on Oct. 6 and renamed the combined company Skydance . Early reports said Gunn and Safran would keep their jobs , even as Warner Bros. film chiefs Michael De Luca and Pamela Abdy were expected to give way to Paramount’s Dana Goldberg and Josh Greenstein. That assurance did not hold. According to The Hollywood Reporter , Skydance chairman and CEO David Ellison and co-CEO Ynon Kreiz visited Gunn and Safran’s office on Nov. 6 to deliver the news in person. Gunn and Safran will still produce DC projects, and they are finishing post-production on Man of Tomorrow , the Superman sequel slated for July 2027. Latcham reports to Goldberg and Greenstein, now co-chairs of Skydance Motion Picture Group. “I’ve had the privilege to help bring some of the most celebrated superhero stories to life on the big screen, and I’m excited and honored for the opportunity to now lead DC Studios into its next era,” Latcham said in a statement. A $618 million start, then a flop Gunn and Safran took over DC Studios on Nov. 1, 2022, hired to reboot the DC characters as a single connected universe. The deal came months after Discovery merged with WarnerMedia to form Warner Bros. Discovery. Gunn arrived as a proven voice in the genre. He wrote and directed all three Guardians of the Galaxy films for Marvel, then made his DC debut with The Suicide Squad in 2021. Safran produced that film, other DC adaptations of the 2010s, and the Conjuring films for Warner Bros.’ New Line Cinema. Their first release, Gunn’s Superman , opened to $217 million globally in July 2025 and finished with $618.7 million worldwide. It introduced David Corenswet as the Man of Steel and set up a wider universe of familiar DC characters. The second did not soar. Supergirl cost a reported $170 million and became one of DC Studios’ worst opening-weekend flops this summer, grossing $126 million worldwide amid weak reviews. The third paid off. Clayface , an R-rated body-horror film made for a reported $44 million, opened at No. 1 and had grossed $109 million worldwide as of Nov. 8. On television, the pair delivered a second season of Peacemaker , the animated Creature Commandos , and HBO’s Lanterns , a hit when it debuted in August. Marvel’s playbook, 18 years later Latcham was part of the founding team at Marvel Studios under Kevin Feige. He worked on Iron Man , The Avengers , and Tom Holland’s Spider-Man films, and he collaborated with Gunn on Guardians of the Galaxy . He left Marvel in 2017 to found Latcham Pictures, whose films include Dungeons & Dragons: Honor Among Thieves and Bad Times at the El Royale . DC is his return to superheroes. The task he inherits has defeated Warner Bros. before. The studio’s first attempt at a Marvel-style connected universe, the DC Extended Universe, began with Zack Snyder’s Man of Steel in 2013 and ended with Aquaman and the Lost Kingdom in 2023, after Gunn and Safran had already been hired to start over. In between came a decade of uneven results, from Batman v Superman: Dawn of Justice and Wonder Woman to The Flash and Black Adam . Unlike Marvel’s tightly linked films, the DCEU fractured. Suicide Squad and The Suicide Squad are entirely separate movies released five years apart. Troubled productions and turnover behind the camera made it worse. Fans campaigned for years after the 2017 theatrical Justice League until Warner Bros. released Snyder’s original vision as Zack Snyder’s Justice League in 2021. Warner Bros. also kept DC stories outside the main universe. The CW’s Arrowverse, including Arrow , The Flash , Supergirl , and Black Lightning , built its own connected TV world. On the big screen, 2019’s Joker and 2022’s The Batman stood apart from the DCEU. The split continued under Gunn and Safran. Joker: Folie à Deux arrived in 2024, while Matt Reeves’ Batman films and HBO’s The Penguin remain in their own world. John Cena’s Peacemaker, meanwhile, carried over from the old universe into the new one. What Latcham inherits The near-term slate is set. Man of Tomorrow remains on the calendar, and Reeves’ The Batman: Part II is still in production, with Steven Soderbergh recently brought in to shoot the remaining scenes . The series The People v. Gorilla Grodd is also in the works. Beyond that, little is settled. It is not yet clear whether Corenswet’s Superman continues after Man of Tomorrow , whether Lanterns gets a second season, or whether Latcham starts over from scratch and hands fans another round of whiplash. Whether the universe Gunn and Safran built survives is a Riddler-worthy mystery. Latcham helped build Hollywood’s most successful franchise once. Nearly two decades after Iron Man , he will find out whether that origin story can be repeated, or whether the superhero universe no longer comes with a reliable playbook. events.title: Why the data center you dread might never even be built
events.summary: The data center boom is running into serious real-world obstacles, from widespread local opposition and permitting delays to a scramble for electricity . Before those challenges even come into play, though, there’s a more basic problem: A lot of the projects being announced may never get built in the first place. With billions of dollars in AI infrastructure investment at stake, separating realistic projects from speculative ones is becoming increasingly important. On this episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast, hosts Rebecca Bellan and Tim De Chant are joined by Brent Nelson , senior managing director of markets and strategy at Ascend Analytics , to separate the data center projects that are likely to get built from the ones that may never get off the ground. Before joining TechCrunch in 2022, she was one of 2 producers at a four-station conglomerate where she wrote, recorded, voiced and edited content, and engineered live performances and interviews from guests like lovelytheband. events.title: Meta is losing its longtime head of infrastructure
events.summary: A key figure in Meta’s growth into a social media and tech industry powerhouse is leaving the company. Santosh Janardhan, the company’s longtime head of infrastructure and co-head of engineering, will be stepping down, Meta told TechCrunch. He will be replaced by Dave Brown, who joined the company as vice president of infrastructure earlier this year, the company added. Previous to coming aboard at Meta, Brown spent 19 years at Amazon, where he focused on compute, cloud, and AI, his LinkedIn shows . It sounds like Janardhan will remain at Meta for a little bit, although he is expected to leave next year. “Santosh will stay on for transition and he is moving into an advisory role on Meta Compute,” said a Meta representative. Janardhan, who originally joined the company in 2009, helped the firm grow into the massive internet presence that it is today. Bloomberg originally reported Janardhan’s departure, citing an internal memo that had recently been circulated. It’s unclear why Janardhan is stepping down from the role. The memo did not specify the reasons for his departure and Meta didn’t immediately respond to a request for clarity on the issue. However, Janardhan’s memo apparently cited the need to “pass the baton.” In recent years, the company’s investment in infrastructure has exploded , as it seeks to keep up with its competitors in the AI race. Earlier this year, Janardhan was tasked with leading Meta Compute , the company initiative to scale its data center investments and strategy. events.title: Olaf Sakkers is betting he can beat the emerging-manager squeeze
events.summary: Entering into the world of venture capital has never been easy, especially as a first-time fund manager. But it’s especially daunting right now. According to PitchBook data, firms raising their fourth fund “or later” captured a whopping 88.2% of U.S. VC fundraising dollars through the first three quarters of this year, while first-time funds captured a measly 4.5% . Just 81 first-time funds closed in the first nine months of 2026. That puts the year on track to be the worst for first-time managers in at least a decade, according to PitchBook’s estimate. Olaf Sakkers has spent the past five years proving that difficult doesn’t mean impossible. He founded his firm RedBlue Capital in 2021 and closed its first fund with roughly $5 million in capital commitments in 2023. He has now held a first close on a second fund that he says will total at least $50 million. Raised in South Africa, he studied anthropology at Princeton, focusing on global health and health policy, and wrote his thesis on HIV in his home country. He moved to Israel after graduating and was drafted into the Israel Defense Forces, where he says he had a desk job liaising with the U.S. military, and where he became interested in autonomous vehicles. An introduction led to Michael Granoff, founder of the venture firm Maniv Mobility and an early backer of electric-vehicle startup Better Place. Granoff, who had money to invest, hired him on the spot, Sakkers says. Neither had been a venture investor at that point, so they built a fund “almost by accident,” learning as they went. Sakkers says he ran the investment process day to day, backing Israeli founders who were bringing cybersecurity skills into the automotive world, and later expanding to the U.S. and other markets. By 2021, Sakkers says, he was an equal partner in Maniv’s economics, but he wanted something different — more formal and scalable — so struck out on his own. Today, RedBlue backs what he calls the “real economy,” including robotics, logistics, manufacturing and energy. Getting to this point has been a test of endurance as much as salesmanship, seemingly. Sakkers says that institutional limited partners, outfits like endowments and pension funds, have been the toughest to win over because his checks are small (and theirs are comparatively huge) but also because their risk model is built to “avoid getting a zero,” which is why they tend to gravitate toward established brands. Says Sakkers, it’s akin to founders who come to be seen as “inevitable,” after they’ve previously founded another company. Meanwhile first-time founders often battle against the “gravity of perception,” meaning a more dominant brand can bend how people perceive a newer one. His answer has been to let the results speak, but it takes time. “It’s a long-term game of building trust, demonstrating performance over time,” Sakkers says. The first fund was a proof of concept, backed by LPs he had known for a while, including family offices. The second draws on family offices and institutions. RedBlue writes small checks, $50,000 to $100,000, mostly joining deals led by other investors rather than leading them. That lets it do more deals and be “the last investor that they take” on by promising practical help, including introductions to lead investors like Andreessen Horowitz and Thrive Capital, and to customers. Founders expect little from VCs, in Sakker’s view, so RedBlue tries to overdeliver on the support part. By his account, the results are strong. Of 28 investments, he says that 15 have been marked up, and he cites a net internal rate of return of “significantly above 50%.” There has been just one exit — an acqui-hire — so most gains from the tiny fund remain on paper and unrealized. Public records support part of Sakker’s story. HappyRobot, which RedBlue backed early, raised a $150 million Series C at a $1.2 billion valuation in August. Westmag, which makes motors for drones and robots and which Sakkers backed at pre-seed alongside Nat Friedman, emerged in June with an $11 million seed led by Andreessen Horowitz. Flai, an AI startup for car dealerships, followed its 2025 seed with a $27 million Series A. And Humble Robotics, a driverless-truck startup in whose $24 million seed round RedBlue participated, announced a $51 million Series A led by Obvious Ventures earlier this month. Sakkers argues that discipline is his edge. RedBlue publishes thesis essays, such as one on robotics, and runs on a custom database that he built with Claude Code to log relationships, meeting notes and introductions. That lets him and his lone full-time principal, based in New York, work asynchronously. AI agents, he says, are “useless if they just have to guess,” so everything gets written down. He contrasts that with Benchmark’s more artisanal model, which he says suits a firm with a record he lacks.

events.title: Scoop: U.S. asks Russia to propose new security agreement with Europe
events.summary: The U.S. has asked Russia to submit a new proposal for a future security agreement with Europe that includes Russian steps to ease tension with the continent, two sources with knowledge of the matter said. Why it matters: For years, Russia has sought a European security deal that limits NATO expansion and scales back its military presence in Eastern Europe. The U.S. has rejected those demands in the past, but now appears open to them in some form as part of a broader agreement to end the war in Ukraine. But many European governments are deeply suspicious of the administration's approach. State of play: President Trump's envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff will meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow on Thursday to reiterate the request. They also want Putin to allow European representatives to join the next round of Russia-Ukraine peace talks, a U.S. official said. From Moscow, Kushner and Witkoff are expected to travel to Dublin to meet with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky on Thursday night. Catch up quick: The talks on Tuesday and Wednesday were the first time Ukrainian and Russian officials met with U.S. mediators present since February, when they were suspended due to the war in Iran. In recent weeks, Witkoff and Kushner met with both Putin and Zelensky, creating a bit of momentum. Putin agreed to resume peace talks and release U.S. citizen Stephen Hubbard, who was detained by Russia in 2022 . Together with First Lady Melania Trump and her team, Witkoff and Kushner also brokered a humanitarian ceasefire in the city of Oleshky. Driving the news: The talks in Abu Dhabi started on Tuesday with Witkoff, Kushner and commander of the U.S. European Command Gen. Alexus Grynkewich mediating between the Russians and the Ukrainians. The parties agreed to a prisoner exchange deal that Kushner and Ukrainian negotiator David Arakhamia said could be the biggest since the war began. U.S. and Ukrainian officials said the exact number of prisoners to be released will be decided during meetings with Putin and Zelensky on Thursday. Before and after the talks, the U.S. and Ukrainian negotiating teams briefed a delegation of senior diplomats from Germany, the UK, France, Italy, the EU and NATO. Behind the scenes: The meetings between the Russians and the Ukrainians on Tuesday were tense and at times emotional, with both sides airing grievances after nine months of not talking directly, according to a source in the room. Kushner and Witkoff tried to lower the temperature, telling Russian and Ukrainian negotiators that the goal is to end this round of talks with options for the leaders on both sides. Eventually, after each party made its case, the discussion became more constructive, the source said. "We had pretty tough discussions," Kushner said at a press conference after the talks concluded on Wednesday. "The Russians came with strict directives. It was very hard to soften it, but it ended productively," Arakhamia said. Zoom in: The U.S. proposal to secure a deal on a new Europe-Russia security architecture as part of an agreement to end the war in Ukraine was a key focus of the Abu Dhabi talks. Russian negotiators said Putin launched the invasion of Ukraine because then-President Biden did not reply to his 2021 letter laying out his security concerns, two sources with knowledge of the talks said. According to one of the sources, Kushner and Witkoff told the Russians that the world has changed a lot since 2021. They proposed that Russia draft a new proposal that includes its security concerns and demands, but also lays out what "symmetrical steps" it's willing to take to de-escalate and reassure Europe that it will not attack in the future. Kushner and Witkoff also told the Russians that in order to seriously discuss security issues in Europe, they need to agree to allow European representatives to participate in future peace talks. "We told the Russians, they have their desires and fears, but they have to provide different de-escalation and different proposals as well, if they want Europe to be able to receive those proposals in a good way," Kushner said at the press conference. The other side: So far, Russia has been unwilling to allow Europeans to be part of peace talks with Ukraine. "As for the leadership of a number of European countries, they are essentially engaged in a collective deception of the Ukrainian people and contributing to the mass deaths of civilians," Putin adviser Vladimir Medinsky, who headed the Russian delegation, said at a press conference after the talks. "Therefore, I don't understand what can be discussed with them." Still, Medinsky said that Russia wants to reach a broader security deal with Europe as part of an agreement to end the war. "In Ukraine, an abscess has simply burst. The entire body needs to be treated — a Band-Aid won't do the trick," he said. What to watch: The Trump administration wants to negotiate a new Europe-Russia security architecture and a Russia-Ukraine peace deal simultaneously. But the implementation of a security arrangement would only happen after a deal to end the war is reached, according to a source familiar with the White House's thinking. The president of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen, said before the talks in Abu Dhabi that Europe will discuss a new security architecture only after the war in Ukraine ends. But two sources with knowledge said European officials who were in Abu Dhabi this week agreed to engage on both tracks simultaneously, while stressing that final decisions on European security architecture would be made only after the war in Ukraine ends. The U.S. hopes giving European representatives a seat at the peace talks will make their governments more willing to discuss and agree on a broader security agreement before the war ends. "Zelensky won't agree to a deal until he knows what happens next regarding security guarantees and Putin wants to know this, too. This is why the security issue is so important," the source said. The source added that the U.S. made it clear to European countries that it would not agree to a security deal with Russia unless Europe and Ukraine are on board. The U.S. also wouldn't give Russia a veto over Europe's security considerations, the source said. The bottom line: Security will be a key issue at a summit of European leaders in Dublin later this week. European diplomats said the idea of a Russia-Europe security arrangement still faces a lot of resistance and unanswered questions.

events.title: Niche work if you can get it
events.summary: Legal tech has its own Davos, and it’s got much better weather. The LegalTech Fund Summit , which enters its fifth year in Scottsdale, Arizona, next week, brings together the industry’s founders, funders, and power brokers for a few days of five-star schmoozing. I’ll be there in my cowboy boots. Come say hi and tell me what you’re building. Mentioned in this edition: Crosby, Rami Karabibar, EvenUp, Harvey, Legora, Latham & Watkins, Lerer Hippeau, Blackletter, Cohere, Blue J, Herbert Smith Freehills Kramer, Stanford, Ilona Logvinova, and Adam Sterling. EvenUp reminds us there are riches in niches What I’m reading and writing Inside a Big Law firm’s executive retreat J Studios/Getty Images Is legal AI in a bubble? Tech stocks got clobbered last week as AI doomsayers declared a bubble burst. Our little corner of the tech world has its own bubble to worry about. Investors are plowing money into legal tech. Valuations are soaring. “AI-native law firms” seem to be sprouting from the ground, each with a pitch about how it’s different from Crosby . It’s a good time to ask which of these businesses are built to last. Last week, I spoke with Rami Karabibar , CEO of EvenUp , which sells software to personal injury law firms. It’s a niche market, but a lucrative one. EvenUp has surpassed $150 million in recurring revenue under contract and now serves more than 2,000 firms.  Karabibar has a theory about what separates legal-tech startups with staying power from those that could get swept away when the tide goes out. It comes down to how deeply they embed themselves in their customers’ business. EvenUp started out as something of a one-trick pony, helping plaintiff-side lawyers draft demand letters. Over the past 18 months, the company has expanded into software that helps lawyers manage their cases from start to finish. While its product line has broadened, its target market hasn’t. Other players like Harvey and Legora build applications that serve everyone from Big Law to multinational corporations. EvenUp has never strayed from personal injury. And Karabibar thinks that focus keeps his company bubble-proof. Quick links Young money. Harvey held early talks with lawyers at Latham & Watkins about an IPO.  A neofirm is born. Early-stage venture firm Lerer Hippeau is backing Blackletter , a new law firm started by former executives at Cohere and Blue J . Campus life. My colleague Aditi Bharade profiled two college students who are helping law firms figure out technology.  Big Law goes back to school David Madison/Getty Images How do you teach an old law firm new tricks? Herbert Smith Freehills Kramer went to Stanford to find out. The law firm retreat, which took place over three days before the start of school, was designed to get the firm’s top brass out of their offices, said Ilona Logvinova , HSF Kramer’s chief AI officer . She wanted them to think less like lawyers and more like founders. Thirty-one firm members traveled to Palo Alto, where they stayed together and took a bus to campus each morning. Logvinova encouraged them to pack hoodies. Only a few obliged. The first day gave them a crash course in the state of AI. Executives heard from legal-tech founders, OpenAI representatives, Stanford researchers, and general counsels about where the tech is heading and what clients increasingly expect from their outside counsel. On day two, the executives got their hands on AI developed at Stanford. One tool helped them turn the expertise rattling around in their heads into instructions that autonomous agents could potentially follow. The exercises were meant to close what Logvinova calls the “imagination gap” — the distance between knowing what the tech can do and actually applying it. The lawyers weren’t the only ones learning. For Stanford, the program doubled as a dry run for its new bootcamp, Legal Engineering Academy, which launches next summer. Adam Sterling , an associate dean at Stanford Law, said the university wanted to see how the lawyers engaged with the technology in practice, not just in theory. Just as importantly, Sterling said, working with practitioners helps the faculty better understand the profession its students are entering and how to prepare them for the future. The experiment suggests that preparing the next generation of lawyers may start with retraining the current one. Please let me know what you think of the newsletter and send along your story ideas. events.title: Trump administration to pursue public land sales and a decrease in federal ownership
events.summary: President Donald Trump’s administration wants to sell public lands to states, tribes and local governments as part of an effort to “decrease the size of the federal estate.” BILLINGS, Mont. -- President Donald Trump's administration wants to sell public lands to states, tribes and local governments as part of an effort to “decrease the size of the federal estate," according to a new five-year plan presented by the Interior Department. Agency officials said the sale of federal property would allow the government to focus resources on “nationally significant" lands. They offered no details on what lands could be sold, nor the scope or location of potential sales. The proposal drew quick objections from some lawmakers, including Republican Rep. Ryan Zinke of Montana, who was Interior Secretary in Trump's first term. The plan also calls for strategic land transfers and exchanges to support greater energy production, a centerpiece of the administration's pro-fossil fuel policies. It reflects the Trump administration’s view of most public lands as assets to be used, rather than to be set aside for preservation . The Interior Department oversees more than 750,000 square miles (1.9 million square kilometers) of land — an area greater than Texas and California combined — along with vast underground mineral reserves. That puts the agency at the center of a contentious, decades-long debate over whether the government controls too much land. The Associated Press sent emails to Interior officials Wednesday requesting comment and further details. Most public lands are in Western states. In some, the government controls the vast majority of land, protecting it from potential exploitation but also hindering growth. Nevada, for example, is almost 80% under federal control. Interior officials said that under the plan a portion of any land sale proceeds would go back to the buyer for conservation purposes elsewhere. Yet it’s uncertain if Interior Secretary Doug Burgum can achieve the administration’s goals without cooperation from Congress. Zinke’s office said in a statement that he “remains firmly opposed to the sale or transfer of public lands." He will vote against any legislation on the issue if it happens before the lawmaker leaves Congress at the end of this term, the statement said. The ranking member of the Senate Natural Resources Committee also pledged to fight any federal land sales or privatization efforts. Public lands belong in public hands,” said Sen. Martin Heinrich, a New Mexico Democrat. Some Western lawmakers last year sought to sell vast tracts of land in Utah and Nevada, saying that could generate revenue and ease growth pressures in booming cities. Among the proposals, Utah Republican Sen. Mike Lee suggested selling more than 2 million acres (8,000 square kilometers) to states or other entities. Those efforts failed amid bipartisan opposition. The plan sets out a road map for the Interior Department's priorities and actions between 2026 and 2030. Future administrations would not be bound by it. The department regulates mining, drilling, grazing, recreation and other activities that many state and local officials want greater control over. Interior includes the Bureau of Land Management, National Park Service, Fish and Wildlife Service and Bureau of Indian Affairs. The agency's strategic plan was last updated four years ago under former Democratic President Joe Biden. events.title: Nostalgia is paying off big for video game makers
events.summary: US gamers can start playing "Grand Theft Auto VI" on November 19. Vernon Yuen/Nexpher Images via Getty Images Nostalgia is proving lucrative for video game makers. "The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time" and "World of Warcraft: Forever" debuted this month. Take-Two's CEO said preorder sales of "Grand Theft Auto VI" have exceeded his expectations. Gen X and millennial gamers might be feeling a heavy dose of deja vú right now. Major developers are leaning into nostalgia, releasing new  video games this month from beloved, decades-old franchises. So far, it seems to be paying off. Blizzard Entertainment, owned by Microsoft, kicked it off on November 4 when it debuted "World of Warcraft: Forever." The original "World of Warcraft" came out 22 years ago. Two days later, the company said the "World of Warcraft: Forever" launch made franchise history. Blizzard said the video game has been the largest launch in "World of Warcraft" history in terms of peak concurrent players and the highest number of returning players. Nintendo then released "The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time" for Nintendo Switch 2 on November 5. This game is a full remake of the company's original 1998 version developed for the Nintendo 64. On Wednesday, Nintendo said the game set a record by selling more than 5.2 million units worldwide in the first four days. And who could forget "Grand Theft Auto VI," the highly anticipated game by Rockstar Games, a subsidiary of Take-Two Interactive? Although the latest "Grand Theft Auto VI" doesn't hit shelves until November 19, fans have been clamoring for a copy since at least 2022, when a hacker leaked footage of the game, which was still in development at the time. Rockstar Games formally announced "Grand Theft Auto VI" in 2023. The last iteration of "GTA" was released in 2013, and the original came out in 1997. Despite the production delays , Take-Two Interactive CEO Strauss Zelnick told CNBC on Tuesday that preorder sales have "vastly exceeded" their expectations. "The good news is it's our second biggest release in the history of the franchise," Zelnick said. "And we expect it's going to be immensely successful and profitable." While Zelnick declined to share the official sales numbers, Sensor Tower, a market intelligence and data analytics platform, estimated that "Grand Theft Auto VI" has already raked in over $1 billion in revenue. The success around the three games comes at a time when the video game industry is trying to win over customers even as rising hardware costs and semiconductor competition drive up prices. events.title: I Saw the Future of Robotics in a Virtual Duck That Chases My Cat
events.summary: Allow me to introduce you to the robot cat butler I’m developing with help from AI. Using OpenAI’s GPT-6 Sol , I taught a virtual version of Microduck —a cute robot from Pollen Robotics and Hugging Face—to walk around a room and identify any bengal cats in its vicinity. (The clip above shows the robot waddling toward a target feline; its eye view is shown top right.) I’m still waiting patiently for a physical Microduck— please hurry up and ship it, guys —but simulated behavior is relatively simple, so it should transfer over to the real thing. I plan to have the robot automatically dispense a treat for my pet bengal, Leona, perhaps by bowing its head to release one from a 3D-printed, head-mounted storage chamber. I was able to code and train the virtual robot in just a few hours, which is, quite frankly, incredible. Previously, this kind of thing might have taken me weeks to figure out. It was possible because OpenAI’s latest models are remarkably good at understanding and manipulating 3D representations of the physical world and then translating that into useful code, agentic actions, and robot training. Real roboticists are using the latest models to do some amazing stuff. When OpenAI released Astra this past September, University of California, Berkeley professor Ken Goldberg and his students saw demos that showcased its ability to render 3D images. They wondered if it could help with the simulations required to train different kinds of robots. These simulations need to be incredibly detailed and extremely accurate to ensure that sophisticated behavior—a humanoid that can dance or a robot hand that can grasp—will transfer faithfully to the real world. One member of Goldberg’s lab gave Astra access to an Nvidia tool called Newton , showed it a video clip of a real robot in action, and asked if it could create a simulation of the scene. “What blew us all away was that within an hour it had produced a full 3D simulation with all the parameters set—the position of the camera, the lighting, the background, all the materials,” Goldberg tells me. Astra is also able to automate much of the drudgery involved with training a robot in simulation, Goldberg says, by running experiments and examining the results. This is precisely what I found while training the virtual Microduck. Along with GPT-6 Sol, I used an agentic harness from Nous Research called Hermes and a Nvidia DGX Spark, a personal computer that contains a powerful AI chip. I’ve previously written about using agents and coding models to configure, program, and debug physical robots. Normally, this kind of work requires significant expertise; modern coding models make it a cinch. But OpenAI’s newest model went far beyond just writing code. It used a piece of Nvidia software called Isaac Sim to feed instructions to a model that controlled the virtual robot, watch videos of it in action to assess how well things were working, and suggest tweaks to its training regime. This process allowed me to train the Microduck to walk around without toppling over. I initially tried getting GPT-6 Sol to teach the robot to moonwalk—I fed it a GIF of Michael Jackson sliding across the stage, which it tried to copy—but after hours of effort, it only resulted in a very jaunty backward jog. (The robots don’t have us totally beat quite yet.) Jim Fan, a researcher at Nvidia who has collaborated with Goldberg, says the way AI can now control robots mirrors how software agents function. LLMS can use models trained to control physical actions—visual language action (VLA) models—just as they access different software on a computer. This week, Fan, Goldberg, and others open sourced an agentic framework for robots called Aspire , which allows a robot to discover and use new skills. One example: GPT-6 Astra figured out how to use a pair of robot arms to solve a Rubik’s cube. “It picks it up, tries to twist it, but has the wrong angle,” Fan says. “Then it reasons for a very, very long time, but it eventually is able to solve it because it learns the skills over time.” At the Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL), held in Austin, Texas, this week, Fan gave a keynote speech in which he talked about the incredible realization that AI models can automate a lot of the work needed to have a robot do sophisticated things. Fan showed off a demo in which Astra was put in control of a robot arm and told to paint a picture of the Golden Gate Bridge. Using some paint and brushes nearby, it duly completed the task . Of course, getting robots to work reliably and efficiently is still extremely difficult, requiring significant engineering expertise. The vision system on my robot duck does not work well enough to be deployed in a real product. Still, the ease and speed of training robots with AI could soon have an enormous impact on manufacturing and e-commerce, and Goldberg says a number of industrial robotics and automation firms have shown an interest in the approach.

events.title: Mississippi Senate: Scott Colom lead over Hyde-Smith pops to more than 4,400 votes
events.summary: Democratic nominee Scott Colom extended his lead over incumbent Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in the Mississippi Senate election by more than 4,400. If Colom is elected, he would be the first Black senator from Mississippi since the Reconstruction Era after the Civil War. In Alaska, Democratic nominee Mary Peltola holds a narrow lead over Sen. Dan Sullivan, a Republican, in a Senate race that could come down to ranked-choice ballots. Democratic nominee Scott Colom on Wednesday significantly expanded his lead over incumbent Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in the Mississippi Senate election to more than 4,400 votes as the ballot count continued. When the day began, Colom had a 2,990-vote lead over Hyde-Smith. That spread ticked upward slowly until just after 2 p.m. ET when a surge of newly counted ballots boosted his tally by 607 votes, and then soon after by another 621 votes. As of 2:30 p.m., Colom was ahead of Hyde-Smith by 4,404 votes, according to the Associated Press. With an estimated 99% of the votes in, Colom led Hyde-Smith by 49.18% to 48.72%. Independent candidate Ty Pinkins had 2.1% of the vote. Colom has steadily expanded his lead over Hyde-Smith for days as he has won a higher share of so-called affidavit ballots than he received in ballots counted on Election Day night. Affidavit ballots are cast by voters on a provisional basis if there is a question about the voter's eligibility. The AP estimates that fewer than 15,000 ballots are left to be processed. Colom was boosted by newly counted votes from Hinds County, the second-most populous county in Mississippi, which encompasses the capital of Jackson. Most of the county's residents are, like Colom, Black. In 2024, Democratic presidential nominee Kamala Harris defeated President Donald Trump by 46 percentage points in Hinds County. As of Wednesday morning, Colom was winning 80% of the vote in the county, with just 19% for Hyde-Smith. Mississippi, which has not elected a Democratic senator since the segregationist John Stennis in 1982, was on the radar of few, if any, political analysts as a possible pickup for Democrats. Tuesday was the deadline for resolving affidavit ballots. It is also the deadline for the receipt of mail-in absentee ballots that are postmarked by Election Day, Nov. 3. Mississippi is one of just two states whose Senate election has not been called. Alaska is the other. Democrats so far have flipped seven Senate seats held by Republicans going into the election. That gives Democrats a new majority in the Senate of at least 54 seats in the 100-member chamber come January. Alaska before Election Day was viewed as possibly key to the question of whether Republicans would retain their narrow majority in the Senate. In Alaska, Democratic nominee Mary Peltola's lead extended to 4,250 votes over incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan, with 84% of the total votes counted, a margin of 1.8 percentage points. If neither she nor Sullivan gets more than 50% of the total vote, the race will go to a ranked-choice round, in which the two other candidates, Gerald Heikes and another candidate named Dan Sullivan, will be eliminated, and the second choices of voters who made them their first choice will be allocated between Peltola and the incumbent.

events.title: Social Security could pay full benefits until 2059 if taxable payroll kept pace with GDP: AARP report
events.summary: Social Security's taxable payroll has fallen as a share of gross domestic product over the past four decades, according to a new AARP Public Policy Institute report. Had payroll taxes kept up with GDP, the program would be able to pay full benefits until 2059 — an additional 25 years versus current projections, according to the research. "The fix for Social Security isn't cutting earned benefits; it's rebuilding the revenue behind them," said Richard Johnson, vice president of financial security at the AARP Public Policy Institute. Social Security 's taxable payroll, which provides most of the revenue for the program that pays monthly benefits to millions of Americans, has fallen as a share of gross domestic product over the past four decades, according to a new report from the AARP Public Policy Institute. Had payroll tax revenue kept up with GDP, the program could pay full benefits until 2059, according to the research — an additional 25 years beyond the latest projected depletion date of 2034 for the program's combined funds. The AARP Public Policy Institute provides policy research, analysis and development at AARP, a nonprofit, nonpartisan organization that represents Americans ages 50 and over. "Social Security's finances have weakened not simply because America has grown older, but because the economy has changed, while the program's revenue system has not," Richard Johnson, vice president of financial security at the AARP Public Policy Institute, said during a Tuesday press briefing on the research. "America's economy is larger and more productive than it was four decades ago, but Social Security is receiving support from a smaller share of that economy," Johnson said. How Social Security has fallen behind Social Security's trustees projected in June that the program's combined retirement and disability trust funds may be depleted in the third quarter of 2034. Unless Congress takes action, 83% of scheduled benefits will be payable at that time, according to the trustees' projections. The trustees' report also included an earlier projected depletion date for Social Security's retirement trust fund — the fourth quarter of 2032, when 78% of benefits would be payable. However, the AARP said it based its analysis on the later 2034 date because Congress has shifted money between the funds in the past. Market sell-off hits hard: Advisors say 'stay the course with an eye on buying' IRS announces new federal income tax brackets for 2027 These states are offering extra ACA premium subsidies in 2027 CNBC's Financial Advisor 100: Best financial advisors, top firms for 2026 ranked CNBC Elite Advisors: Top ultra-high net worth wealth management firms for 2026 The program's current shortfall is worse than lawmakers had anticipated in 1983, when the last major Social Security reforms were enacted. Rising income inequality means the payroll tax cap no longer covers 90% of earnings — a percentage lawmakers expected to remain constant when they made the 1983 reforms, according to research from the Roosevelt Institute, a New York-based liberal think tank. The share of earnings covered by Social Security payroll taxes fell to around 83% in 2000 and has mostly stabilized there, according to the institute. AARP points to an aging population as another reason for Social Security's funding challenges. The worker-to-beneficiary ratio will fall from 3.4 to 2.4 between 2000 and 2030. Falling fertility rates are also shrinking the worker-to-beneficiary ratio. Shifting income patterns have also meant that a smaller share of U.S. GDP is subject to the Social Security payroll tax. Taxable payroll has fallen from 41% of GDP in 1983 to 34% as of 2025, a level Social Security's trustees project will remain, according to the AARP. AARP attributes the decline to a shift from wages toward business and investment income, which generally isn't subject to payroll taxes. Automation has reduced demand for workers, and pass-through businesses allow some owners to report compensation as profits rather than wages, according to the report. Social Security would have collected $10.8 trillion in additional funding between 1984 and 2034 if taxable payroll had stayed at 41% of GDP, according to the AARP. That figure is in inflation-adjusted 2025 dollars. In 2026, up to $184,500 in wages are subject to the Social Security payroll tax. Payroll taxes accounted for 91% of Social Security's revenues in 2025, according to AARP's research, while 5% came from interest income and 4% was through federal income taxes paid by high-income beneficiaries on their benefits. To increase Social Security's revenues, lawmakers may consider changes that make high-income taxpayers contribute more to the program while sparing low- to moderate-income taxpayers, according to the AARP report. "The fix for Social Security isn't cutting earned benefits; it's rebuilding the revenue behind them," Johnson said.

events.title: CoreWeave turns to customer prepayments, shorter contracts to fund AI growth
events.summary: CoreWeave is rewriting how it pays for the AI boom, according to the company’s third-quarter earnings , reported on Tuesday. CoreWeave, a neocloud that rents out the computing power behind AI, said it’s increasingly asking customers to pay up front, borrowing against specific contracts, and even pursuing short-term deals that could lead to higher prices. The new strategies could help CoreWeave finance its growth more efficiently while squeezing more cash from existing infrastructure. But these bets only hold if today’s demand and pricing power continue. CoreWeave reported $3.66 billion in revenue, up 168% from the year prior, but it also posted a $709 million net loss and $846 million in quarterly interest expense. “We will not use the unsecured debt market to fund our business at current yields, nor do we need to,” CoreWeave CEO Michael Intrator said during Tuesday’s earnings call. Instead, CoreWeave’s plan is to rely on loans backed by specific customer contracts, drawing on funds as needed to finance most of the infrastructure it still has to build to deliver on its significant backlog of $132.5 billion. CoreWeave also said it expects about $9 billion in customer prepayments and deposits over the next three months, including more than $3 billion tied to signing new customer contracts for capacity it has already built, which requires no additional spending on hardware. Rivals Nebius and IREN have also relied on hefty Microsoft prepayments to pay for computing capacity, signaling that the industry is moving toward asking Big Tech to pay up for their buildouts. Upfront payments could alleviate CoreWeave’s immediate borrowing needs, but they also commit the company to providing services at a price that might be less attractive down the road if compute demand continues to surge. CoreWeave is also looking to capitalize on that growing demand by signing more shorter-term contracts that can command much higher prices. The company raised prices across its offerings by about 25% in July and by another 10% later in the quarter. Prices are still climbing this quarter, in a way that “more than offset[s] cost increases,” said Intrator. “We are also allocating more capacity to short-term opportunities, where the pricing justifies it, selling capacity at more than $40 million per megawatt annually, while pricing for new infrastructure on four- and five-year contracts is moving to $20 million to $25 million per megawatt,” the chief executive said. CoreWeave’s financing strategy now revolves around those opportunities. In August, the company closed a $2.6 billion loan, its first designed specifically for shorter-term customer contracts. Known as DDTL 5.5, it lets CoreWeave borrow in installments as it needs the money. While short-term deals let CoreWeave charge higher prices and change them more frequently, it’s a trade-off. Lenders give more weight to longer-term contracts, even if they’re priced lower, because they value predictable cash flow and consistency to repay the loan above all. Even though Wall Street reacted positively to CoreWeave’s earnings, bond investors are much less sanguine. Last month, yields on some of the company’s bonds hit above 15%, highlighting that investors are concerned about the debt needed to fund data center buildouts before those investments see a return. In short, CoreWeave is finding new ways to expand without relying on unsecured debt. The strategy it has chosen could boost profits, but it also carries greater risk around contract renewals and pricing — and it just goes to show how dependent the AI infrastructure boom is on sustained, and as yet unproven, demand. events.summary: Hello . Welcome to the first edition of VC Insider! We’re excited to land in your inbox every Thursday.  We’ve been covering venture capital for a long time, but we’ve never seen a pace of dealmaking like this, with such eye-popping valuations. Each week, we’ll make sense of the biggest stories in VC and get beyond the chatter to reveal what Silicon Valley’s sharpest minds are actually thinking, not just what they’re posting on X or LinkedIn. -Ben and Katie This week is SF Tech Week here in San Francisco, aka Andreessen Horowitz marketing week. The free flood and drinks are flowing, and for some reason, there are two blimps floating over the Bay.  It turns out that AI hasn’t replaced human networking…yet. Topics du jour include: Is SaaS making a comeback? Why is there so much drama between Factory AI and Cognition? How do I get into Claude Founder House? With some 2,000 events, there is always a better one you’re hearing about around the corner. The FOMO is real.  We’re biased, but we think the best event was our Tech Insider: Growth Mode town hall, where one of Anthropic’s biggest investors weighed in on the upcoming IPO.  FARR Summit Somehow, I ended up with two sisters of famous tech founders. My tweet this week about “Zuck’s sister” DJing in a rooftop penthouse at the FARR Summit went viral, with many people adding she does have a name of her own and is a successful VC in her own right. Sorry, Arielle Zuckerberg! (Arielle later chimed in to add she has been DJing since 2018 at Burning Man and small festivals.) Tuesday, I interviewed Ginger Luckey Gaetz, the sister of Anduril founder Palmer Luckey, who is an advisor to the government of El Salvador. Interestingly, when I asked what company she wished she had invested in, she said it was Anduril. She said she was prohibited from investing because her husband, Matt Gaetz, was a US congressman.  If startup investing isn’t a gamble enough for you, I’m co-hosting a poker tournament with $10,000 at stake tonight at the Foundry. I will donate any winnings to charity, so wish me luck! -Ben Business Insider Major Anthropic investor says he’s not concerned about losses or competition Last night, Ben sat down with Menlo Ventures partner Matt Murphy , an early investor in Anthropic. If the listing goes well, Menlo will be one of the biggest winners, turning an estimated $1 billion investment into around $25 billion at a $2 trillion valuation. The firm has invested in every round since 2023. Not surprisingly, Murphy remains extremely bullish. He shrugged off leaked financials obtained by Reuters showing Anthropic racked up an eye-watering $8 billion in operating losses last year, saying investors should wait for the company’s S-1 before judging the business. “If I could buy more, I would,” Murphy said. He also pushed back on the idea that Chinese open-weight models are poised to commoditize the biggest AI labs. His argument is that the market has moved beyond experimentation and into optimization, with companies increasingly focused on cutting costs, post-training models, and routing work to the right system. Menlo is betting heavily on that infrastructure layer — compute, inference, routing, and optimization — which Murphy said has accounted for roughly 60% to 70% of the firm’s AI investments. As for finding the next Anthropic, Murphy was blunt: “I don’t think there’s going to be another Anthropic.” That doesn’t mean he sees no froth. Murphy called neo-labs and robotics “super interesting,” but warned that some startups are raising $100 million or even billion-dollar rounds before showing much real traction.  And in a lightning round, he took a swipe at Anthropic’s biggest rival. Asked which company was most overhyped right now, Murphy didn’t hesitate: “Definitely OpenAI,” he said with a grin. The Tech Insider audience of investors and founders was less bullish on Anthropic. When Ben asked how many people would invest in Anthropic at a $3 trillion valuation, the response was tepid , with most in the audience saying they would not buy Anthropic stock at that price.  The head of Washington University’s endowment, in comments last month, sided more with the audience. Yet early OpenAI investor Vinod Khosla told Ben he strongly disagrees with Wilson, saying OpenAI and Anthropic have a huge cost advantage in chips and data centers.  I have found that most investors remain highly bullish on American AI, particularly the largest players like Anthropic and OpenAI, but many privately voice skepticism about ballooning valuations in the broader ecosystem. -Katie  Read more The Buzz Katie Roof I was at Munich’s Bits & Pretzels last week, where even the robots were dressed for Oktoberfest.  I chatted with Legora CEO Max Junestrand, who made the case for building legal AI in Stockholm. events.title: AI’s dealmaking frenzy
events.summary: Hi! Katie here. I’m excited to lead my first edition of VC Insider (taking turns with Ben!) This week, I’m digging into the extraordinary boom in startup acquisitions and why the deals keep getting bigger. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang Bloomberg/Getty Images I’ve been covering venture-backed deals for 13 years, and we’re in an M&A environment unlike I’ve ever experienced. We’re seeing some of the biggest deals on record, including SpaceX’s $60 billion acquisition of Cursor. (OK, technically, the $250 billion Elon-Elon SpaceX/xAI deal was bigger.) And billion-dollar venture-backed acquisitions are at their highest level since 2021, according to Crunchbase . The year kicked off with Capital One’s $5 billion-plus deal for Brex, but the real frenzy began after SpaceX’s Cursor acquisition in June. Most of the action since has been in AI. We were first to report that Hugging Face was attracting takeover interest, followed by our scoop on Nvidia’s acquisition talks. Nvidia has since agreed to buy the company for $12.9 billion. Stripe struck an $8 billion deal for OpenRouter, while AMD agreed to buy World Labs for $8.2 billion. And the deals keep coming.  This week, there was a WSJ report that Amazon is in talks to buy Decart for $7 billion, while according to the FT, Nvidia is eyeing Reflection AI, which has been seeking a $25 billion valuation. We also reported that Decagon hired a bank to explore M&A interest. And we scooped Salesforce’s $2 billion deal to buy Listen Labs, as well as Google’s $1.5 billion deal with Mechanize. So what’s driving all this activity? First, there is clearly a frenzy to acquire AI talent.  Some of these are like giant acqui-hires, bringing in skilled AI teams that work well together. But they are also gaining advanced technology that is improving at a rapid clip. Missing out on new technology can be a lot more costly in the long run than the purchase price of a deal. There are also a number of trillion-dollar technology companies now that can easily afford to make a multibillion-dollar purchase.  Sometimes the market even rewards strategic acquirers for making AI-related deals. If the stock jumps on the deal announcement, it reduces the cost, or sometimes makes the acquisitions “free.” SpaceX, for instance, surged 10% after its $60 billion Cursor announcement (although it was shortly after the IPO, so that might not have been the sole reason). Regardless, AI acquisitions are making venture capitalists a lot of money right now, even if they missed out on IPO-bound behemoths like Anthropic and OpenAI. Deedy Das, partner at Menlo Ventures, recently posted on X that “it is absolutely possible to return a multibillion dollar venture fund with phenomenal IRR, even if you aren’t in big AI! This is one of the hottest liquidity markets ever.” In an interview at the 2026 M&A Summit in San Francisco this week, John Chambers shared with me that he made 180 acquisitions while CEO of Cisco, including the $3.2 billion deal for WebEx. He touted what he viewed as a 70% success rate, saying he wished it were lower because it meant he hadn't taken enough risk. Chambers said in the conversation the best acquisitions are so transformative that they offset failures, and predicted that the uptick in venture-backed M&A will continue, with cybersecurity deals a particularly strong point.  What’s clear is that the M&A industry now takes venture-backed deals a lot more seriously. For many years, some in the industry scoffed that this genre of deals was too small. I regularly told bankers, lawyers, PR people, and fellow journalists to keep an eye on VC because the price of these deals would rise someday.  How did I know? There was a significant increase in capital flow in the startup ecosystem and ballooning valuations. Even if a small percentage of today's 1900+ unicorns are valued correctly, that leads to a number of large liquidity events, including acquisitions. The economics of the startup ecosystem also attract some of the best and brightest employees, talent that strategic acquirers might want in-house. - Katie The Buzz Ben here. I was standing at a happy hour for Tinder and Wonder Ventures at a Venice Beach golf course Tuesday afternoon when an eager twenty-something founder walked up and asked, “What are you building?” He seemed crestfallen when I told him I wasn’t building anything. After SF Tech Week last week, the action has shifted to LA for Tech Week. Many of the attendees, desperate to land any funding for their nascent idea, attend both.  The problem is that there are few VCs at these events, so founders (or mostly wannabe founders) end up pitching to each other. As others have suggested, founders would have much better luck finding VCs if they went to the South Park Blue Bottle in San Francisco on any day of the week.  People love to talk about how many Tech Week events they got into or how many connections they made, but it's not clear to what end. I was also at SF Tech Week, where there were almost twice as many events, and the mood was more technical and serious. With the exception of defense tech, LA’s tech scene has taken a noticeable step back since Andreessen Horowitz hosted its first LA Tech Week here in 2022. AI is all the rage, and San Francisco is the undisputed epicenter of the AI revolution.  Continuing the theme from last year, wellness is a big focus, with a daily 6 am lifting club and surf lessons in Manhattan Beach. Elizabeth Holmes is back  Back up North, the Valley is abuzz with excitement for You Can See Everything, Nathan Fielder’s fly-on-the-wall documentary about Elizabeth Holmes that opens Friday. VC firms are renting out theaters for the occasion. One Menlo Park firm, Felicis, is hosting a screening next week for tech reporters and PR people, which is a curious choice given that Theranos was probably the biggest black eye in Silicon Valley history. "The group chat needed a field trip," the invitation reads. "Black turtlenecks optional, but encouraged. Leave your crisis plan at home." It would be like Wall Street hedge funds hosting screenings of a documentary about Bernie Madoff.  Around the Cap Table Unlike its 2010 predecessor,  the Social Reckoning has been a flop at the box office. I think the movie is worth watching for one scene alone, in which a monstrous Mark Zuckerberg, played by Jeremy Strong, sits robotically in his bulletproof glass-enclosed office and rejects safety proposals because they would put a small dent in engagement. The movie also effectively shows how hard it is to cultivate a source. One less realistic part is that writer and director Aaron Sorkin seems to relish the fact that the protagonist, Wall Street Journal reporter Jeff Horowitz, is bad with tech and barely knows how to use his GPS to find the bureau.  In reality, just because you’re a tech reporter does not mean you are good with tech. events.title: VCs are questioning the neolab math
events.summary: Hello. It’s Ben Bergman in Venice Beach. I’ll be in New York next week for The Long Play: Stories of Reinvention, where I’ll interview Nadia Carlson, who is trying to turn Allbirds into an AI infra company. But first, I’ll dive into the neolab debate, and Katie has the deets from Menlo Venture’s black-tie 50th-anniversary soiree. Mentioned in this edition: Jeff Dean, Ilya Sutskever, Mira Murati, Thinking Machines Lab, Matt Murphy, Menlo Ventures, Deedy Das, Aaron Rosenberg, Radical Ventures, Andrew Schoen, NEA, Jeffrey Katzenberg, Venky Ganesan, and Michael Grimes. VCs are questioning the neolab math  Ben here. Up until recently, it was a great time to be the founder of a neolab, the lavishly funded, research-first AI startups founded by top talent who defected from the likes of OpenAI or Google DeepMind. We reported last month that Jeff Dean, Google’s former chief scientist, is seeking a valuation as high as $50 billion for his new AI science startup. OpenAI cofounder Ilya Sutskever’s Safe Superintelligence is worth $32 billion. Another OpenAI alum, Mira Murati, is raising a round for Thinking Machines Lab at a valuation of around $40 billion.  But lately, in conversations with multiple VCs around Silicon Valley, there is a growing divide about whether neolabs can make the economics work with their multibillion-dollar price tags and formidable competition from frontier labs.  Menlo Ventures' Matt Murphy speaking to Ben Bergman at Tech Insider: Growth Mode. JY Studio One VC at a top firm, who asked that I not use his name, told me neolabs are the most hotly debated type of investment right now. “Some would say you shouldn't invest in any, and others would say this is basically all you should be investing in because software's dead, and you either have to own models or hardware, and even if you enter at a billion, the company could be worth a trillion,” he said.  Business Insider; Randy Yeip When I recently asked Menlo Ventures partner Matt Murphy at Business Insider’s Growth Mode conference which sector he thought was most overhyped, he immediately cited neolabs, which was noteworthy, given that Menlo invested in some of them . Murphy pointed to an example from his time as an early board advisor at Google, which he said did so well because it “was like a match thrown into a bonfire.” “The opposite thing you want to do is start a match with a bonfire,” Murphy told me. “That's the risk of what's going on now with companies raising such large rounds.” Another Menlo partner, Deedy Das, posted last month about the “difficult game” of making neolab math work.  Das seemed a bit taken aback by the reaction to his post and later texted me: “Like all startups, many will fail, some will work.” Picking which ones will work is why VCs get paid the big bucks.  Neolabs are a power-law bet taken to an extreme, Radical Ventures’ Aaron Rosenberg told me.  Investors know most will likely burn enormous sums on compute and talent without ever becoming profitable. But the rare winner could become a foundational AI company worth hundreds of billions or more. “We're confident that the best neolabs will attract ongoing support,” Rosenberg said. “Talent continues to transition out of the incumbents and academia into founder roles, and we see no signs of that slowing.” Like Radical, New Enterprise Associates wrote a bullish view in June . One of the authors, Andrew Schoen, told me his views have not changed. "There are neolabs I know of that are finalizing billion-plus-dollar rounds of equity financing, and those processes are moving very smoothly and quickly," he said. The Buzz Menlo Ventures' partners Shawn Carolan, Matt Murphy, and Venky Ganesan. Will Mackie Productions Katie here. Many of tech’s biggest names gathered at the Ritz-Carlton in San Francisco on Saturday, at a black-tie event in the name of Menlo Ventures' 50th anniversary.  Hollywood titan turned venture capitalist Jeffrey Katzenberg of Dreamworks fame asked the audience to join a prayer “for the blockbuster IPO of Anthropic,” a joking reference to Menlo’s early investment in the company.  I also spotted Morgan Stanley’s storied technology banker Michael Grimes, who is undoubtedly holding his own AI IPO prayers. Other attendees included an array of public company and startup CEOs, including those from Snowflake, Zscaler, Legora, and OpenRouter. As Menlo partner Venky Ganesan quipped, there was more AUM (assets under management) in the room than in many countries, given the attendees' net worth and the investment capital they manage.  Menlo isn’t the first venture firm to host a splashy anniversary party; Index Ventures recently went big for its 30th anniversary . A person at a rival venture shop expressed disappointment that their firm doesn’t host such celebrations. Menlo’s night ended with concerts from two super confidential Grammy Award winners trying to rake in those AI bucks! Around the Cap Table We reported this week that Fireworks AI is seeking fresh funding at a valuation of between $30 billion and $40 billion, a dramatic jump just months after its last blockbuster round was closed. "You Can See Everything" has everyone talking . Ben thought it was absolute genius, if a bit long. It will make  this year's Oscars race exciting. See it in theaters before the experience is lessened by spoilers. Our colleague Rya Jetha explored the excitement and pitfalls of investing in robotics startups. Like neolabs, robotics companies are commanding big valuations with little to show for it, yet.  Foursquare’s $0 acquisition ended with no payout for employees or investors, according to founder Dennis Crowley . Post of The Week There are only 130 US tech companies, public or private, valued at $10B or more (decacorns). That’s roughly 20 to 30 new companies per decade, for the last five decades. This year alone, with a quarter to go, there have been 42 decacorns minted privately.
