events.title: Anthropic mints record gains in record time
events.summary: Katie here. The Anthropic S-1 is here, and it confirms what VCs have been whispering for months: this is a company moving at warp speed. Just over three years after its first major VC round, Anthropic is poised to break IPO records and deliver historic wins to its earliest backers. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei Finn Gomez/Getty Images Anthropic mints record gains in record time It happened! After a fall full of delays, Anthropic’s S-1 finally dropped.  What stood out to me was how incredibly fast Anthropic has scaled. Spark Capital was the first firm to lead a round into the AI giant in spring 2023 – just three and a half years ago. They own more than 1% of the company, an investment that could be worth tens of billions of dollars in short order. It was just months ago that SpaceX set the record for the  largest ever IPO , but that timeline was remarkably different: the first venture capitalists invested in 2002! "There's no company that's gone from zero to where they are today in this period of time,” said Byron Deeter, partner at Bessemer Venture Partners. The firm has spent $800 million investing in Anthropic since 2024, the largest bet in its history, netting Bessemer an almost 1% stake. Andy Kiersz/BI At the time Bessemer first invested, many in the industry considered the $18 billion price tag to be steep for a startup that wasn’t the industry leader. Some dismissed Anthropic as a “FOMO bet,” that investors were just disappointed that they missed out on OpenAI.  Deeter knew that was the perception, but said he had conviction that Anthropic could take the lead or come close, believing that “even if they didn't fully get there, they were going to be a hell of a challenger.” They not only challenged OpenAI, but they also beat them to the IPO. The ChatGPT-maker expects to go public next year. Although Anthropic’s numbers quieted some (but not all) financial critics, other AI-related issues are still expected to be controversial at the ballot box next week. Right now, the tech industry wants more compute, and the populists are against data centers... The Buzz jirigeorge/Getty Images Ben Bergman here in New York. I’m in town for The Long Play , featuring media mogul Barry Diller, Take-Two’s Strauss Zelnick, Ro’s Zach Reitano, and many more. I hope to see some of you there today, or tonight at the Eniac Ventures Halloween party. Costumes are required, so I’ll be curious to see what VCs are choosing this year. I’m tempted to go as filmmaker Nathan Fielder. I went on a walk this week with a VC at a large firm on a sunny fall day in the West Village. Even though they are based here, they said they spend nearly all their time in San Francisco these days because it’s the epicenter of the AI boom and home to the startups they care about. Separately, I asked New York-based VC Jesse Middleton, a general partner at Flybridge, for his read on New York these days, and he texted me: “It’s true that SF is where most of the models have been trained, and the dollars are certainly there for the big guys, but New York is where founders turn them into products for the rest of the world (not just developers). The app layer here is booming, including Clay, Hebbia, Rogo, and ElevenLabs. Every industry that actually has to buy this stuff sits within a few subway stops of our office.” By the way, New York is still the more expensive city to rent an apartment, but San Francisco is rapidly closing the gap. Median asking rent for a one-bedroom is about $4,580 per month in New York City, versus roughly $4,400 in San Francisco, a difference of only $180, according to Zumper. Who wants to bet San Francisco will be more expensive next year?  Post of The Week The craziest reveal in You Can See Everything is actually the fact that she never sold secondary — Olivia Moore (@omooretweets) October 25, 2026 Around the Cap Table We tallied the founders and  many of the VC stakeholders in Anthropic ahead of the company’s expected IPO.  Spark Capital was mentioned more than 50 times in Anthropic’s IPO paperwork.  Here’s why . A scoop from Katie: AI coding startup Cognition has received  fresh offers valuing it between $70 and 80 billion. Software business Guidewire  announced that it was acquiring UK-based agentic insurance startup Hyperexponential for $1.7B. Canada’s fintech Wealthsimple  said that it raised financing at a $13.8B CAD valuation. Ferring agreed to acquire fertility startup Gameto in a deal worth up to $1.4B. Elizabeth Holmes’ husband Billy Evans’ blood-testing startup  has the support of Palantir board member Lauren Friedman Stat, who co-founded it with him. Intel  acquired Israeli quantum startup Classiq for $2.3B. Andreessen Horowitz  expanded its crypto fund to include other emerging technologies and rebranded as a16z Frontier. The US Department of Justice is  asking questions about whether Nvidia’s deal to buy Hugging Face for nearly $13 billion would hurt competition in AI. events.title: Celebrity deaths in 2026: Remembering the famous people we lost this year
events.summary: Patrick Stewart. Neilson Barnard/Getty Images Actors James Van Der Beek, Hayden Panettiere, Robert Duvall, Chuck Norris, Patrick Stewart, and Eva Marie Saint died in 2026. So did musicians Dolly Parton and Duncan Sheik. Civil rights leader Rev. Jesse Jackson, activist Gloria Steinem, and NFL Hall of Famer Mike Ditka also died this year. Below, we look back at the celebrities we lost in 2026, listed in alphabetical order. Scott Adams, 68 Scott Adams. Michael Macor/Getty Images Scott Adams worked at a telephone company in the 1980s. The experience inspired his beloved comic strip, "Dilbert." By the end of the decade, the character and his satirical office humor began appearing in comic strips. At its peak, "Dilbert" was syndicated in over 2,000 newspapers. A cartoon series debuted in 1999, running for two seasons. Adams gained notoriety when he began writing blog posts praising Donald Trump during his 2016 presidential run. In 2023, "Dilbert" was pulled from newspapers across the US following racist comments made by Adams. Adams died on January 13 from metastatic prostate cancer . Brad Arnold, 47 Brad Arnold. Scott Gries/ImageDirect/Getty Images The lead singer of 3 Doors Down, Brad Arnold launched the group into fame with the 2000 rock anthem "Kryptonite," which peaked at No. 3 on the Billboard Hot 100 that year. The success led to other hits like "Loser," "Here Without You," and "When I'm Gone." Arnold's vocal range and lyrics focused on love and love lost, which fueled the group to stardom. Arnold died on February 7 from a type of kidney cancer. Afrika Bambaataa, 68 Afrika Bambaataa. Paul Natkin/WireImage/Getty A hip-hop pioneer during the 1970s and 1980s, Lance Taylor, known professionally as Afrika Bambaataa, first gained attention as a DJ in the Bronx. He signed with Tommy Boy Records in 1981 and released landmark songs like "Jazzy Sensation" and "Planet Rock." He would go on to influence the likes of Queen Latifah and A Tribe Called Quest throughout his career. Bambaataa founded the hip-hop awareness group, Universal Zulu Nation, in the 1970s to steer kids away from gang life. Bambaataa stepped down as the head of the organization in 2016 after accusations of sexual abuse . Bambaataa denied all claims. He died on April 9 due to prostate cancer . Rob Bass, 59 Rob Bass. Al Pereira/Michael Osche Archives/Getty Images One of the icons responsible for bringing hip-hop to the mainstream, Rob Bass crafted the iconic track "It Takes Two" alongside DJ E-Z Rock. The track, released in 1988, reached No. 3 on the Billboard Hot Dance/Club Songs chart and later went certified platinum. In 1989, it was voted the greatest single of all time by Spin magazine. Bass died on May 22 following cancer . Nicholas Brendon, 54 Nicholas Brendon. Getty Images Nicholas Brendon was a television actor, best known for playing Xander Harris in all seven seasons of "Buffy the Vampire Slayer." He also starred in "Criminal Minds" and "Kitchen Confidential." Brendon died in his sleep on March 20 due to natural causes, according to his family's statement. In 2023, Brendon suffered a heart attack and was diagnosed with a congenital heart defect. He also had cauda equina syndrome, which led to several spinal surgeries. "While it's no secret that Nicholas had struggles in the past, he was on medications and treatment to manage his diagnosis, and he was optimistic about the future at the time of his passing," the statement to The Hollywood Reporter read. "Our family asks for privacy during this time as we grieve his loss and celebrate the life of a man who lived with intensity, imagination, and heart." Peabo Bryson, 75 Peabo Bryson. ABC Photo Archives/Getty Images Two-time Grammy winner Peabo Bryson is best known for his classic love ballads. Bryson began releasing music in the late 1970s, but one of his first major hits was opposite Roberta Flack on the 1983 duet, "Tonight, I Celebrate My Love." He continued hit-making a year later with the smash "If Ever You're in My Arms Again," and in 1991, he topped the R&B charts with "Can You Stop the Rain." Bryson found global stardom with his renditions of two Disney classics. In 1991, he released the pop version of "Beauty and the Beast," alongside Céline Dion, and a year later, he duetted with Regina Belle on "A Whole New World" from the 1992 release of "Aladdin." Bryson died on June 2. No cause was given. James Burrows, 85 James Burrows. Aaron Rapoport/Corbis/Getty Images An 11-time Emmy winner and co-creator of "Cheers," director James Burrows helped shape modern TV comedy through his work on iconic sitcoms including "Will & Grace," "Friends," and "Frasier." Known for his comedic timing and elaborate blocking, Burrows got his start directing episodes of "The Mary Tyler Moore Show." Throughout his career, he directed episodes of "Frasier" (winning an Emmy for the pilot episode), "Will & Grace," "Friends," and "The Big Bang Theory." He directed over 50 pilot episodes. Burrows died on June 19. No cause was given. Kyle Busch, 41 Kyle Busch. Sean Gardner/Getty Images Two-time NASCAR Cup Series champion Busch was considered one of the greatest racers of all time. Busch was hospitalized on May 21, before two upcoming races. Hours later, he was pronounced dead. Busch died from severe pneumonia that progressed into sepsis. Robert Carradine, 71 Robert Carradine. Bobby Bank/WireImage/Getty Robert Carradine was best known for his roles as Lizzie McGuire's dad and as the iconic geek Lewis Skolnick in the 1980s franchise "Revenge of the Nerds." As a member of Hollywood's famed Carradine family, Robert was destined for an onscreen career. He received one of his first screen credits starring in his brother David Carradine's popular 1970s TV series "Kung Fu" and went on to land roles in everything from Samuel Fuller's World War II classic "The Big Red One" to the "Lizzie McGuire" series. Carradine's family shared statements with Deadline that emphasized being open about his struggles with mental illness. "We are bereft at the loss of this beautiful soul and want to acknowledge Bobby's valiant struggle against his nearly two-decade battle with Bipolar Disorder," Carradine's family said. "We hope his journey can shine a light and encourage addressing the stigma that attaches to mental illness." Carradine died by suicide on February 23. If you or someone you know is experiencing depression or has had thoughts of harming themself or taking their own life, get help. In the US, call or text 988 to reach the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline . Help is also available through the Crisis Text Line — just text "HOME" to 741741. The International Association for Suicide Prevention offers resources for those outside the US. Bud Cort, 77 Bud Cort. events.title: With $720M round, Britain’s Fractile gets a leg up in the race for AI chips
events.summary: Fractile , a British startup developing AI chips, has raised a $720 million Series C backed by Britain’s Sovereign AI Fund with hopes of “ensuring the U.K. has a greater stake in the hardware that will underpin its future economy,” its government stated . Alongside the likes of Axelera , Etched , and OLIX , this makes Fractile one of the top-funded startup players in the race for purpose-built AI chips. Such chips are one of several avenues being explored to reduce the cost of inference — aka using increasingly demanding AI models in production. However, Fractile seeks to go beyond hardware with a full-stack approach that also includes a machine learning compiler to maximize the speed at which LLMs will get executed on its chips. As a result, the company frames itself as a frontier AI company, and its latest round led by Thrive Capital, Founders Fund, Lightspeed Venture Partners, and Redpoint was priced accordingly. According to the British government, the valuation was “over £5 billion” — quite possibly $7 billion, a figure reported both by the Financial Times and a Reuters source . Still, Fractile’s main differentiator will arguably be its hardware design. After a pivot , its approach now revolves on DRAM, the most common type of RAM, but stacked on top of each chip in such a way that it is hoping will bypass the usual trade-off between memory and capacity. This trade-off has become more problematic with the rise of agentic AI, as companies seek to perform longer chains of tasks with large models without compromising on speed. As compute struggles to keep up, hopes are high for AI chips, despite their limited availability to date. In a LinkedIn post , Fractile CEO Walter Goodwin wrote that “there is still a lot of work ahead” for the company, and that the new funding will enable the startup to “ship [its] first chips and systems next year.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . events.title: 10 famous women who served in the military
events.summary: Queen Elizabeth II served as a military truck driver during World War II. Central Press/Getty Images Women have been serving in the military, officially or unofficially, since the Revolutionary War. Queen Elizabeth II was a military truck driver during World War II. "Golden Girl" Bea Arthur was one of the first members of the Marine Corps Women's Reserve. Women have been an important part of the armed services since the beginning, with icons like Harriet Tubman participating in the Civil War. While being female in a traditionally male-dominated space hasn't always been easy, these women still served their countries. In 2024, the US Department of Defense reported that the percentage of women serving in active-duty roles grew between 2022 and 2023 — 17.7% of active-duty roles were held by women in 2023, it reported, citing the 2023 Demographics Profile of the Military Community. That trend has continued. Per a DoD report released in August 2025, 24,000 women entered basic training that year, up from 16,700 in 2024. These 10 famous women served in the military around the world, including Bea Arthur, Queen Elizabeth, and more. Harriet Tubman was a military leader and Union spy during the Civil War. MPI/Getty Images Most know Harriet Tubman for her groundbreaking work with the Underground Railroad and, later, as an abolitionist, but as National Geographic wrote, Tubman was also an integral part of the Civil War. In 1863, Tubman and Colonel James Montgomery led a group of soldiers to free enslaved people from plantations in South Carolina, making Tubman the first woman in US history to lead a military expedition, according to National Geographic. Her work continued as a spy and recruiter for the Union Army. This operation was so covert that only President Lincoln knew about it. Tubman received compensation for her military contributions decades later, in 1899.  Thomas B. Allen , the author of "Harriet Tubman, Secret Agent," called Tubman "one of the great heroines of the Civil War." Queen Elizabeth was a military truck driver during World War II. Keystone/Getty Images Queen Elizabeth was only 18 years old when she begged her father, King George VI, to help during World War II.  She joined the Women's Auxiliary Territorial Service in England that same year and was known as "Second Subaltern Elizabeth Windsor," according to the National Archives. While serving, the young queen drove military trucks and trained as a mechanic, making her, to this day, the only female member of the Royal Family to have served in the armed forces.  NASA's Eileen Collins was one of the first female pilots in the Air Force and in space. NASA Eileen Collins broke several barriers during her career: Not only was she NASA's first female shuttle commander, but at 23, she became the Air Force's first female flight instructor, according to the agency. She joined the Air Force in 1978, becoming one of the first four women to go through pilot training at Vance Air Force Base in Enid, Oklahoma.  She wrote in Time , "The Air Force was testing whether women could succeed as military pilots. We obviously were living in a fishbowl — everyone knew who we were, our personal business, our test scores and our flight performance. My philosophy was to be the best pilot I could be." Her military training directly led her to test pilot school, where she "knew" she would become the first female space shuttle pilot — and she succeeded.   "Golden Girl" Bea Arthur was one of the first members of the Marine Corps Women's Reserve. Lennox McLendon/AP Photo Before she was Dorothy Zbornak on "The Golden Girls," Emmy Award-winning actor Bea Arthur was a Marine. As reported by The Daily Beast,  Arthur enlisted in the Women's Reserve at age 21. She first served as a typist and truck driver. She worked her way up to the rank of staff sergeant and was honorably discharged in 1945.  Official documents show that Arthur's supervisors thought she was "argumentative," which is not a far cry from the feisty persona she became known for on both "The Golden Girls" and "Maude." "Stranger Things" actor Jennifer Marshall served in the US Navy for five years. Netflix Before Jennifer Marshall scored the role of Susan Hargrove on Netflix's hit show "Stranger Things," she served in the United States Navy from ages 17 to 22.  According to Marshall's website, during her service, she was a forklift operator, aircraft handler, and logistics specialist. She also worked for the USS Theodore Roosevelt's Sexual Assault Victim Intervention (SAVI) program.  Marshall was awarded many honors and medals for her time in the Navy. Now, in addition to acting, she works with Pin-Ups For Vets, a nonprofit organization that aids hospitalized veterans and deployed troops. Food Network star Sunny Anderson was in the Air Force. NEW YORK, NY - NOVEMBER 12: Cook Sunny Anderson attends the 2nd Annual Variety Salute to Service at Cipriani Downtown on November 12, 2018 in New York City. Jim Spellman/Getty Images Anderson, who hosts "The Kitchen," "Cooking for Real," and "Home Made in America," grew up around the military because of her parents. As an adult, she enlisted in the US Air Force as a radio broadcaster and journalist, working in Seoul, South Korea, and in San Antonio.  "I knew that there were radio stations, television stations, newspapers, and magazines, for the military, by the military, and I wanted to be a part of that," Anderson told ABC News  in 2013. She also wanted to train in something that would be useful when she left the military. "My transition from the Air Force started before I even got in the Air Force," she said. Radio talk show host Robin Quivers was a captain in the Air Force. Walter McBride/WireImage via Getty Images Robin Quivers has co-hosted "The Howard Stern Show" for over 30 years, but before that, she served as a captain in the US Air Force. Quivers earned her nursing degree from the University of Maryland and put it to use by joining the military as a second lieutenant after college. She quickly climbed the ranks, and when she was discharged in 1978, her official title was captain, according to Biography.com. She served as a reserve in the Air Force until 1990, per military records , after which she pivoted fully to her radio career. But Howard Stern hired her for his show in 1981, which means that Quivers — though she was "inactive" — was still technically serving while she was on the air. Actor Zulay Henao served in the US Army for three years. JB Lacroix/ Getty Images Colombian-American actor Zulay Henao has appeared on the show "Army Wives," but few know that she herself served in the US Army before becoming an actor. Henao enlisted after completing high school and, after three years of serving, went on to enroll at the New York Conservatory for Dramatic Arts. events.title: The top 10 US states set to build the most housing in the coming years
events.summary: Idaho and the Carolinas are leading in housing growth. Jeremy Erickson/Bloomberg via Getty Images An October report shows some states are approving housing permits at double the national average. The Carolinas and Idaho are approving the most permits per 1,000 residents. New supply could ease prices and cost burdens as housing comes online in 2028 and 2029. America needs to build more housing — and some states are outperforming. Housing permits were "essentially flat" nationwide from January to August 2026 compared to the same months a year earlier, according to an October research report from the Lied Center for Real Estate at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas. Yet, some states are ahead of the curve, issuing permits for new homes at rates above the national average of 2.83 units per 1,000 residents, according to the report. States like Idaho, South Carolina, and North Carolina all had permit rates more than double the national average. Nicholas Irwin, coauthor of the report and research director at the Lied Center for Real Estate, said prospective homebuyers in states issuing more permits and building more housing will benefit, as more supply could put downward pressure on prices . "That means hopefully, as wages continue to grow year over year, and the amount of building you're doing is putting downward pressure on housing prices, housing naturally becomes more affordable," he said. Here are the top 10 states that issued the most permits per 1,000 residents from January to August 2026. These show the new housing supply that may come online throughout 2028 and 2029. Overall, America is doing a "terrible job" building housing , Irwin said. Yet, some of the states that came out on top were unsurprising, especially those with abundant land and population growth. "South Carolina, Idaho, North Carolina, Kansas, Nebraska — what a lot of these states have in common is they have a lot of land, and that is a key input into building," he said. "Developers, they don't build it in without some indication that demand is rising." Idaho had the most permits issued per 1,000 residents during this period, with 12,994 housing units approved from January through August 2026. That is 126% above the US rate, according to the report. Idaho is also ranked first in the country for the number of units permitted per 1,000 cost-burdened households, a measure that accounts for those who pay 30% or more of their income on housing, said the report. Yet, while increased housing supply could help ease prices, that does not mean housing will immediately be more affordable for residents in Idaho . The report said that in the state, households would need to earn 47% more income to afford a typical home at the same affordability level as in 2018. Eight years ago, a median-priced home cost 28.7% of a median income — today, the median home costs 42.1% of a median income in the state. Although these 10 states with high permit approval rates are seeing higher permitting rates, each state is unique with its own factors. Irwin said the rate of permits issued cannot be viewed in a vacuum — states must be analyzed holistically. "There's no one state that is sort of the perfect example, and there's no one state that is perfectly problematic," Irwin said. "It's how much are these states growing, and what's the rate of household formation in these states? How many folks in these states are cost-burdened?" Meanwhile, South Carolina was the top-ranked state in the report's overall housing supply pipeline rankings — performing well across four metrics, including the permit rate per 1,000 residents. The state with the second-largest number of permits in the country per resident issued 33,822 across the first eight months of 2026, 114% above the US rate — up 5% from the same period in 2025 and up 15% from 2023. Residents in the state need around 35% more income to return to 2018 housing affordability levels, less than in Idaho. "Your Carolinas and Idaho are sort of leading the way," Irwin said. "Some states clearly have prioritized it and have made meaningful changes when it came to encouraging more housing to be built." Tennessee rounded out the top 10. While it still finds itself approving permits above the national average, at 3.88 permits per 1,000 residents, it was ranked 18th overall across the report's four measurement pillars. Although the state is permitting at a higher rate than 40 other states, its overall permitting is declining over time within the state. The report shows a loss of momentum, with Tennessee experiencing a 4.9% decrease in permits per resident from 2025 to 2026 and an 18.5% decrease from 2023 to 2026. There are many approaches to "building this cake of housing," Irwin said. "Every state's different. Every state's needs are different." Read the original article on Business Insider

events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Labor announces $420m regional rail boost and attacks Liberal leader's surplus claim Topic: State and Territory Elections Labor is promising to increase the number of regional train services if elected. ( Supplied: Thomas Hobley ) Labor will commit $420 million to boost Victoria's regional rail services if it wins the election. The plan would mean an extra 550 extra weekly V/Line services to regional centres. Labor is also attacking the Liberal leader's pledge to reach a budget surplus by 2032. Regional and outer suburban commuters would get an extra 550 weekly V/Line train trips if Labor is re-elected, as the party costs Jess Wilson's commitment to reduce the public service to claim she cannot reach her promised cash surplus. Premier Ben Carroll will today commit $420 million to increase the regional train network by 24 per cent, targeting voters in regional and outer-fringe seats where Labor is under pressure from both the Coalition and One Nation. Victoria election 2026 live updates: For all the latest news from the campaign trail, read our blog. Transport in the outer-west and south-west has been especially painful for the government. Melton and Wyndham Vale still rely on V/Line, two elections after Daniel Andrews promised to electrify the tracks. Under Labor's announcement today, Melton would get an extra 162 weekly trips from 2027 so that services run every 20 minutes. Longer nine-car trains previously announced will also run from next year. The plan to increase regional rail services has been costed by Labor at $420 million. ( ABC News: Ethan Seiderman ) Wyndham Vale would get a dedicated new service with 249 weekly trips, to minimise crowding. Geelong would get more express services as a result, cutting 10 minutes from the journey with double the number of total services. An extra two services would also run on Sundays to Geelong and Waurn Ponds. Government attacks Liberal surplus claim Labor has separately turned to the Parliamentary Budget Office (PBO) in an attempt to undercut the opposition leader's commitment to reach a cash surplus by 2032, a key plank of Ms Wilson's election platform. Ms Wilson has largely relied on her announcement that she would reduce the Victorian Public Service through attrition to save $22 billion over a decade to reach the cash surplus. But analysis by the PBO, requested by Labor, found the majority of the savings would not be realised until after 2032. The budget office estimated the Coalition policy would save $8.5 billion by 2032, billions short of what would be necessary. Treasurer Colin Brooks used the findings to claim Ms Wilson would need to cut essential services, in particular health, to meet their commitment. Labor is challenging Liberal leader Jess Wilson's pledge to reach a budget surplus. ( ABC News Melbourne ) In a statement, Ms Wilson said she would not take lectures on costings from Labor. "Only our Liberal and Nationals team has a costed and credible plan to repair the budget, underpinned by more than $26 billion in responsible and disciplined savings," she said. Ms Wilson has not released the full copy of her version of the PBO's analysis, and has been under pressure to explain how she can scrap taxes, make a suite of spending commitments while also bringing down debt — on track to reach almost $200 billion by 2029-2030. PBO analysis can vary depending on the assumptions put to them. More express trains from regional centres Under Labor's transport announcement, the Seymour line to the outer-north through Wallan and Donnybrook would get an extra 29 services from 2028. Another 101 weekly services would also run through the Bendigo line from 2028; 21 to Bendigo and 80 to Kyneton, allowing most off-peak trains to run express from Bendigo. The Warrnambool line would also get an extra eight weekend services from next year, while the Traralgon line would wait until 2028 for an additional Sunday service. V/Line services have been plagued by overcrowding as demand increases. ( Supplied: Kate Young ) Most weekday off-peak trains from Ballarat would also run express to Melbourne from next year, shaving up to 10 minutes off the journey, Labor said. The Coalition has previously promised $1.7 billion to run hybrid trains to Melton and Wyndham Vale, though the government disputed this was feasible with the rest of the network. After delaying electrification, the government now says the new Sunshine station hub must be built first to separate the V/Line and Metro tracks.

events.title: Photos show what life is like on the International Space Station, from haircuts to sleeping arrangements
events.summary: Six of the seven Expedition 74 crew members in the International Space Station. Their mission ended in July 2026. NASA/Jessica Meir Life on board the International Space Station takes some getting used to. Being weightless affects everything from the way food tastes to getting a good night's sleep. Photos show what it's like to spend months in space. Ask any astronaut who has spent extended periods in the International Space Station what the most challenging part was, and they will probably say missing friends and family . While it's a unique experience, life in space comes with other little challenges, too — try getting your hair to stay flat without gravity or wearing the same outfit for days on end. NASA and other space agencies are trying to learn all they can about how humans cope with difficulties , big and small, while traveling at 17,500 miles an hour around the Earth. They work hard to bring some of the comforts of home to space. Films, TV shows, and books have attempted to shed light on humans' experience of going to space, from Samantha Harvey's "Orbital" to Taylor Jenkins Reid 's "Atmosphere," and the Ryan Gosling-led "Project Hail Mary," signaling our obsession with imagining life off Earth. However, real photos taken aboard the International Space Station show what it really looks like to spend months in space. Since 1998, the International Space Station has had nearly 300 visitors. The International Space Station as seen by astronauts from NASA's space shuttle Endeavour on February 19, 2010. NASA Astronauts and cosmonauts from 26 countries have been on board, according to NASA. It's a floating lab where researchers conduct experiments related to space travel. Astronauts typically stay for six months to a year. Almost everything they do revolves around discovering more about life in space, and they keep meticulous track of how their bodies respond to the weightless environment. Some of what they've learned has led to developments in drugs and medical technology that benefit humans on Earth, too. There's not a lot of room on the ISS. Astronaut Peggy Whitson in the doorway of the Temporary Sleep Station (TSS) on the International Space Station in 2002. NASA It's more like a not-a-lot-of-space station. It's a six-bedroom house packed into an area that's shorter than a football field , according to NASA. Five agencies share the station, which has six sleeping quarters, a gym, and two bathrooms. Astronaut Frank Rubio described it as a building made of hallways, with no large space like a living room to gather. "You almost have to block the fact that it is so small," he told "Houston: We Have a Podcast" in 2024. The food isn't all freeze-dried. NASA Space food needs to meet a few requirements. It can't crumble to bits and clog machinery; it has to stay fresh for months, and it should taste good. Several newer methods for preserving food for long-distance travel have given astronauts more meal options, and ISS astronauts can make everything from spicy shrimp to chocolate pudding cake. "A lot of it was really tasty," retired astronaut Leland Melvin told Business Insider in 2023. Lots of astronauts like spicier options because the lack of gravity causes fluid to float into their sinuses, leaving them stuffed up and affecting how food tastes. Astronauts and cosmonauts will often bring snacks that remind them of home. For example, one of Rubio's crewmates brought items for a charcuterie board. Daily exercise helps prevent bone loss. NASA astronaut Steve Swanson exercises on a special ISS treadmill in 2014. NASA Early in space travel, doctors realized that astronauts were losing bone density after spending long periods in a weightless environment. Now, ISS residents do a couple of hours of exercise every day to help prevent that. It's a mix of cardio and load-bearing workouts, Rubio said. They do so many squats that "every day is leg day in space," he added. There's a special lifting machine. NASA The advanced Resistive Exercise Device (ARED) enables astronauts to perform exercises such as bench presses and squats. Using vacuum cylinders, it can simulate weightlifting up to 270 kg. And a cycling machine. NASA The Cycle Ergometer with Vibration Isolation and Stabilization System (CEVIS) enables astronauts to cycle. In fact, NASA astronaut Jessica Meir recently joined a Peloton class live using satellite for a special 20-minute "Space Ride." There's a technique for brushing your teeth without running water. Astronaut Scott Altman holds a drink container on the International Space Station in 2000. NASA In 2013, retired astronaut Chris Hadfield demonstrated how he brushed his teeth in space on the Canadian Space Agency's YouTube channel. First, he used a resealable water container to wet the toothbrush. Then he slurped the water off the brush and applied regular toothpaste. When he was done, he swallowed the toothpaste and filled his mouth with water to clean the toothbrush. Showers are actually sponge baths with washcloths, per NASA . Astronauts use shampoo that they don't have to rinse out. Suction takes care of extra water, which then goes to a waste tank. The toilets on the ISS rely on airflow. A team member at Johnson Space Flight Center lifts the urine hose of a space toilet. NASA Hoses, funnels, and suction are all crucial components when it's time to go in space. In 2020, NASA redesigned its toilets for more comfort and durability. Astronauts dispose of toilet paper in watertight bags, and the  solid waste  is burned up on reentry into Earth's atmosphere. Urine is another story. Most of the water on board is reused. Astronaut Satoshi Furukawa processes samples from the JEM Water Recovery System (JWRS) on the International Space Station in 2023. NASA Water is a precious and heavy commodity. Humans generate a lot of it, including through sweat, urine, and the droplets in their breath. Most of it doesn't go to waste on the ISS. "We have hardware on station that helps take that output and turn it back into clean, drinkable water," NASA aerospace engineer Brendan Lutes told "Houston: We Have a Podcast" in 2024. In 2023, NASA said it attained its goal of recycling 98% of the water astronauts bring along the journey. There's no laundromat on the ISS. Astronaut John Phillips holds a wet/dry vacuum cleaner on the International Space Station in 2005. NASA Astronauts only get to bring a small amount of clothes with them, and they have to make them last. They might wear the same outfit for a week, according to NASA. Washing clothes would be too water-intensive, so their well-worn garments get burned up like other waste. That doesn't mean there are no chores on the ISS. Astronauts have to use vacuums — like the one pictured above — to make sure there are no crumbs or debris floating around that could damage instruments. The astronauts are on the ISS to work. events.title: Prediction markets tied to clinical trials and drug approvals draw lawmakers' ire
events.summary: Democratic Sens. Angela Alsobrooks and Ron Wyden are pressing the Department of Health and Human Services to mitigate risks from prediction markets related to clinical trials and Food and Drug Administration approvals. In a letter obtained first by CNBC, the senators raise concerns about the markets affecting patients who are deciding whether to participate in a trial, and express worry over potential insider trading. Kalshi, which offers such event contracts in the U.S., says it has put in place guardrails to maintain the integrity of markets. Prediction market event contracts on both clinical drug trials and Food and Drug Administration regulatory approvals are drawing attention from two Democratic senators, according to a letter obtained first by CNBC. Sen. Angela Alsobrooks , D-Md., and Sen. Ron Wyden , D-Ore., expressed concern over the related event contracts in a Wednesday letter to Department of Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr . The senators asked what measures HHS has taken to mitigate any risks that may arise from the markets. "Allowing individuals to bet on the success of these trials and drugs undermines the scientific process, creates perverse incentives for researchers, harms trial participants, and could lead to dangerous medical outcomes for untold numbers of Americans," the senators wrote. Alsobrooks and Wyden repeated concerns raised by some healthcare professionals that the markets could alter patient thinking when considering whether to participate in a trial and expressed concern over potential insider trading risks from researchers and regulators who may have access to nonpublic information. The senators requested HHS provide all internal communication regarding staff participation in prediction markets tied to matters governed by the department. They also requested all communication between the department and the prediction market platforms themselves, the Commodity Futures Trading Commission — which regulates event contracts — and any internal analyses that have been done regarding the potential impact of the markets. "HHS, FDA, and [the National Institutes of Health ] must uphold the integrity of the drug development process and maintain public trust in the public health by putting essential guardrails in place to prevent individuals profiting on the success and approval of drugs that the American people depend on," Alsobrooks and Wyden said in the letter. Both leading prediction market platforms, Kalshi and Polymarket , offer the contracts, although in Polymarket's case the markets can only be found on its international exchange, which isn't regulated in the U.S. When Kalshi launched its related markets in July , the company said it put in place the guardrails, such as only allowing markets related to late-stage trials, in order to limit the risk of trading. Kalshi also vowed to list contracts only after a trial had completed enrollment and to use employee verification technology for all traders participating in the markets. "Drug development is one of the most important and most information-constrained industries on earth," Kalshi CEO Tarek Mansour said in July. "The data that determines which drugs advance and which don't is largely locked away from the people who need it most. Surfacing information is what Kalshi is for, and we are committed to doing it right." Kalshi noted that investors also buy shares in companies in fields including biotechnology and pharmaceuticals that are awaiting regulatory approvals. "The hypothetical concerns of the Senators apply equally to the equities market, which appears to be left out of their letter.," Kalshi spokesperson Jack Such told CNBC. "The only difference is that the size — and incentive for bad activity — is significantly higher in the equities market than it is on Kalshi." Polymarket and the Department of Health and Human Services didn't immediately respond to CNBC's requests for comment. Disclosure: CNBC and Kalshi have a commercial relationship that includes customer acquisition and a minority investment.

events.title: Poundland owner extracted millions when chain was on ‘knife-edge’, MPs say
events.summary: Retailer’s management to seek two-week extension of legal protection from creditors in high court MPs have accused the owner of Poundland of extracting millions of pounds from the budget retailer when it was on a “knife-edge” as it seeks extra time to secure a rescue deal. The management of Poundland, which employs 12,000 people and operates 600 stores in the UK and Ireland, will seek a two-week extension of legal protection from creditors from the high court on Thursday morning. The budget chain’s owner, Gordon Brothers, is under pressure to accept a bid for the company that would save retail jobs and protect thousands of suppliers. Poundland filed a notice of intention to appoint administrators two weeks ago. The legal measure protects Poundland from the demands of creditors until Thursday morning while a solution to its problems is sought. Directors of Poundland are now seeking a further 10 working days’ grace, which must be approved by the high court. That comes after Gordon Brothers, which is understood to be supportive of the extension, released £10m more in funds to help Poundland secure new stock and keep trading. Without the legal protection in place, Poundland is likely to have to call in administrators; the advisory firm Alix Partners is already lined up. The European head of Gordon Brothers, Mark Newton-Jones, gave evidence in private for almost two hours to the Commons business select committee on Wednesday afternoon after MPs called on the government to protect Poundland and other high street stores from “predatory capitalism” and asset-stripping last week. Liam Byrne, the chair of the committee, said that after questioning Newton-Jones he was “deeply concerned that Gordon Brothers’ behaviour may have jeopardised thousands of jobs on Britain’s high streets”. He said: “Over the last 17 months, they have taken millions out of Poundland when the business was on a ‘knife-edge’. “Now Poundland appears to be on the rebound, there’s concerning signs it’s been strangled of access to its own funds in what should be its busiest trading period in the run-up to Christmas. “Worse, Gordon Brothers refused to say it will prioritise saving jobs over and above its own financial returns.” The committee separately heard from Poundland’s management team, led by Barry Williams, who had been fighting to save the business. Sources said Poundland continued to trade well, with sales up year on year, despite its problems, but it has only enough cash to support the business for a short period. Gordon Brothers has said Poundland remains “challenged and vulnerable to any potential downturn in future trading”. Gordon Brothers is understood to remain in talks with three potential bidders for the entire chain but has indicated it can raise more from a break-up of Poundland, selling off stock and parcels of stores to rival retailers. The bids are understood to be worth less than the £30m in debts taken on by shareholders when Gordon Brothers bought the chain. It bought Poundland for a nominal £1 from its previous owner, the European retail group Pepco, in June 2025. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Pepco still holds £7.5m of the £30m shareholder debt. It is prepared to wait for repayment in the hope of saving the business. Gordon Brothers is still in talks with Martin Property Group, the Northern Irish family-owned firm supporting a management-backed rescue bid for the discount chain, which includes the Dealz chain in Ireland. Martin Property Group’s first bid had been rejected by Gordon Brothers as it amounted to no more than half the £30m it wants for Poundland with less than £7m up front. A little-known finance company, Xyra Group, is thought to have offered about £12m up front and close to £30m in total. However, Xyra has not been involved with retail businesses previously. Gordon Brothers has been approached for comment.

events.title: Rising costs hurt South Australia's regional high streets
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Rising costs and online shopping hurt Mount Gambier's historic Commercial Street Kathy Gandolfi says there have been some tough periods for Mount Gambier businesses. ( ABC South East SA: Sam Bradbrook ) Businesses operating on Mount Gambier's main street say increasing costs and changing consumer habits are hurting retail. The city's chamber of commerce says large shop fronts are becoming increasingly unsustainable. The city is planning upgrades to the street, and some small retailers are setting up shop. Empty shops and "for lease" signs line Mount Gambier's main retail strip as high costs and online shopping drive customers away. The city, in South Australia's South East, is home to about 30,000 people. It also serves as the commercial hub for the wider Limestone Coast region. Mount Gambier's economic heart has always been based around Commercial Street, but that is rapidly changing. A historic photo of Commercial Street shows the heritage-listed town hall. ( ABC South East SA: Josh Brine ) A walk down the 1.2-kilometre retail strip between Wehl and Crouch streets reveals retailers are few and far between. Country Attitude co-director Kathy Gandolfi, who has been in business on the main street for 22 years, said having fewer shops hurt everyone. Kathy Gandolfi has been in business on Mount Gambier's main street for 22 years. ( ABC South East SA: Sam Bradbrook ) "It's good to have a vibrant main street," she said. As high interest rates and inflation hurt consumers' pockets, increased overheads are putting added pressure on businesses. Businesses are finding it hard to maintain large shop fronts. ( ABC South East SA: Sam Bradbrook ) Mount Gambier Chamber of Commerce chair Samuel Taylor said having a large shopfront on the main street was increasingly unviable. He said bigger shops required more stock to display, but those items just racked up costs for the business every day they were not sold. Mount Gambier's Commercial Street in 1964, from the Life in Australia film series. ( Supplied: National Film and Sound Archive ) "We're seeing a big shift away from large-scale businesses and you're moving into a more cost-effective model which is a smaller shopfront," he said. For larger retailers, a move away from the main street made more sense in terms of rental and operating costs, he said. Like bricks-and-mortar shops everywhere, Mount Gambier's retail sector has also been hit by the online shopping boom. Commercial Street during SA's COVID-19 lockdowns. ( ABC South East SA: Bec Whetham ) Ms Gandolfi said more food and service businesses, like health clinics and hairdressers, were now opening on the main street "because you can't buy a job by a physio or something online". Retailers like Keiran Hein, however, are hopeful for the future of Commercial Street. Ms Hein opened her ice cream and confectionary shop, Lollies & Scoops, just two weeks ago. She believed her business would succeed. Two previously empty buildings have also now been leased. Keiran Hein hopes her new shop can fill a gap in the market. ( ABC South East SA: Sam Bradbrook ) "I would have loved to have spent so much money in decorating this place and doing it up into a wonderland, but the reality is that I can't," she said. "So it's basic, it's bright, it's clean. We've got good food and produce and that's all that matters at the moment." As some businesses move out, others are taking a chance on Commercial Street. ( ABC South East SA: Sam Bradbrook ) Mount Gambier Mayor Lynette Martin described the movement of businesses along the street as "cyclical", and said the council was working on a master plan for the CBD which was set to include updates to the main street. Lynette Martin says Commercial Street is a "survivor". ( ABC News: Isadora Bogle ) "It's been there for over 100 years, shops have come and gone, businesses have come and gone, but it always seems to come back to be fully or almost fully occupied," she said.

events.title: Elon Musk says Tesla will extend Cybertruck production through end of summer
events.summary: Tesla's Cybertruck production will extend a few months longer, Musk said on X. Finn Gomez/Getty Images, Reginald Mathalone/NurPhoto via Getty Images The Cybertruck has a new lease on life (for a few months) because of an "order backlog." Elon Musk previously said the truck would end production by around mid-2027. Now, he says production will continue through the summer. The Cybertruck is getting a last-minute extension. Maybe call it Cyber luck ? On Wednesday, CEO Elon Musk posted on X saying the angular electric truck's production would be "extended through the end of summer 2027," as Tesla works "through more of the Cybertruck order backlog." In order to work through more of the Cybertruck order backlog, production will be extended through the end of summer 2027 — Elon Musk (@elonmusk) November 11, 2026 It comes five days after Musk said the Cybertruck was getting chopped from the Tesla lineup around the middle of 2027 to focus more assembly power toward Cybercab, its steering wheel-less robotaxi. Musk said that the Cybertruck was still profitable — but the company had to kill the truck because of manufacturing "complexity." Wednesday's production update also comes after Musk said that Tesla would have to " return deposits for a lot of people." After the Cybertruck's 2019 unveiling, Tesla said it received more than 1 million reservations, costing $100 a pop. Musk said at the time that he expected to sell 150,000 to 250,000 units of the truck each year. Instead, like nearly every electric pickup that has hit the US market, the Cybertruck underperformed sales expectations. Per Cox Automotive data shared with Business Insider, Tesla sold just 76,000 Cybertrucks over the past three years. That includes the $131 million worth of Cybertruck sales to another Musk company, SpaceX, in 2025. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: How Democrats could snarl Trump administration stakes in private sector companies
events.summary: The Trump administration's unprecedented interventions in private sector companies could be on Democrats' investigation list when they take control of the House and Senate. That could affect how President Donald Trump interacts with those companies, after spending two years forging equity agreements or, in the case of U.S. Steel, acquiring a "golden share." The next Congress could try to ensure the government takes stakes that are "forwarding genuine national security priorities" without giving "special favors to political and family connections," said professor Sarah Bauerle Danzman. With Republicans in charge of the White House and Congress , President Donald Trump has embedded the federal government in private sector companies' affairs in unprecedented ways. That could change once Trump's Democratic adversaries take over the House and Senate following the blue wave midterm . Democrats, planning to root out alleged corruption involving Trump, his family and their business associates, have signaled they will closely scrutinize companies that have curried the president's favor. Their investigations may extend to Intel and the dozens of other companies that have clinched equity stakes with the government during Trump's second term. Democratic lawmakers in July asked law firm Skadden Arps for details about its involvement in the Intel deal. The dynamic could affect how Trump approaches relationships with private sector companies, after spending two years involving the government in their affairs through stock agreements or, in the case of U.S. Steel, acquiring a "golden share" when the company was acquired by Nippon Steel . Trump's successors already fighting over who to blame for GOP midterm wipeout China panel chair demands answers on Huang's alleged affair with a Chinese spy Pete Hegseth decries impeachment push, defends Iran war handling The golden share , which allows a holder to outvote other shareholders, was negotiated as part of the June 2025 deal. The highly unusual arrangement gives Trump veto power over several key areas of the steelmaker's business, including those related to employee salaries, capital investment and even the company name. In a unique twist, the company's amended charter specifies that after Trump leaves office, the veto power passes not to his successor, but to the Treasury and Commerce departments as representatives of the U.S. government. U.S. Steel CEO David Burritt said Wednesday that the government's representative on its board, Commerce Department official David Shapiro, typically abstains from voting but has access to company discussions. "He gets to hear everything we're doing," Burritt told CNBC's Megan Cassella at the U.S. Chamber of Commerce's B20 summit in Washington, adding that the arrangement has not constrained the company's operations. "The government has not stepped in and said 'you can't do this or can't do that,' but we know what the rules are," Burritt said. The U.S. Steel intervention turned out to be just the beginning of the U.S. government taking stakes in companies, a highly unusual move stateside. A month after acquiring the golden share, the Trump administration agreed to a $400 million stock deal with rare earths company MP Materials . The month after that, Trump announced the U.S. would take a 10% stake in chipmaker Intel . By January, one year into Trump's second term as president, the administration had established some form of equity position in 14 companies, according to the CATO Institute's tracker . That number skyrocketed to 41 by November, including nine such announcements in May alone, the tracker shows. The holdings include both publicly traded and privately held companies, and CATO tracks deals that are closed as well as others that have been made public but are still being negotiated. Following Republicans' decisive defeat in the Nov. 3 midterm election , the federal government has not revealed any new stock positions. But Trump, entering lame-duck status and on the verge of losing political power over Congress, could keep trying to steer his government to forge more equity deals with companies, said Indiana University associate professor Sarah Bauerle Danzman, who researches the intersection of national security and investment policy. "He might feel he has less to lose," Bauerle Danzman, who is also a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council , told CNBC. White House spokesman Matthew Middleton told CNBC in a statement, "Through voluntary equity investments in willing companies, the Trump Administration has partnered with the private sector to rebuild America's industrial base and bring critical production back home." "Moving forward, the President is willing to work with anyone to advance solutions that strengthen our economy and put more money back in the pockets of American workers," Middleton said. But Trump's so-far unimpeded efforts may face sudden resistance once Democrats take majority control of the House and Senate in January.

events.title: Companies laying off staff this year include Meta, Amazon, and Dropbox — see the list
events.summary: Boeing is trimming its commercial airplanes workforce after coming up short on its 737 delivery targets. Jason Redmond / AFP via Getty Images Companies including Meta, Amazon, and Visa have said they're trimming staff this year. Many firms, like Wix and Block, have cited the rise of AI as a reason they need fewer staff. See the list of companies letting workers go in 2026. Big companies are still cutting jobs in 2026. So far this year, dozens of major brands have laid off employees, continuing a trend of significant workforce reductions across a broad range of industries, including tech, media, finance, and retail. While prominent brands continue to announce cuts, the broader economy shows that unemployment hasn't spiked. Economists frequently describe the environment as low-fire, low-hire. The big change is AI. Several companies, including Block , Coinbase, and Standard Chartered, have cited the impact of artificial intelligence as a key reason for the layoffs. A World Economic Forum survey last year found that some 41% of companies worldwide expected to reduce their workforces in the next five years because of the rise of artificial intelligence. The survey also found that jobs in big data, fintech, and AI are expected to double by 2030. Last year, Business Insider tracked layoffs at around 65 major companies, including Amazon, Meta, Paramount, and Starbucks. In 2026, we'll continue to track additional job cuts based on company announcements, WARN notices, and our own reporting. Here are the companies with job cuts underway in 2026, listed in alphabetical order. Amazon is laying off thousands of employees Matthias Balk/picture alliance via Getty Images Amazon said in January that it would eliminate around 16,000 corporate roles globally. Beth Galetti, senior vice president of people experience and technology, described the January move in a company memo as part of broader efforts to cut back on bureaucracy inside the company. The cuts followed mass layoffs from October 2025, when the tech and retail giant shed 14,000 roles. In May, Amazon's Selling Partner Services team slashed additional jobs as it continued to reshape its organization. "Following a recent review, we've made the difficult decision to eliminate a relatively small number of roles in our Selling Partner Services team," a spokesperson told Business Insider. American Express is cutting 5% of its workforce Amex is planning cuts as it prepares for AI to help run its internal systems. Alex Tai/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images American Express took a $336 million restructuring charge as it plans to cut around 5% of its workforce, the company announced during its third-quarter earnings call. It employed around 77,000 people by the end of 2025, meaning the layoffs could impact between 3,000 and 4,000 employees. On the earnings call, the company also highlighted how AI has changed its internal structure. "There's been a lot of talk about how companies are using AI to increase productivity, automate processes, and generally make their organizations more efficient," Stephen Squeri, Amex's CEO, said during an October earnings call. "We're using AI to do all of those things too." Angi is cutting 350 jobs Donald King/AP Angi, the popular contractor listing site once known as Angie's List, said in January that it was cutting around 350 jobs "to reduce operating expenses and optimize the organizational structure in support of long-term growth." The company also said it's making the cuts "in light of AI-driven efficiency improvements." In a January 7 SEC filing, Angi said that the cuts would save between $70 million and $80 million in annual spending. The layoffs will cost the company between $22 million and $30 million, according to the filing. In Angi's November 3 earnings report, the company said it is cutting another 300 roles globally, "mostly in middle management and support functions, to increase focus and organizational velocity." Angi added in the report that it expects the layoff to accrue between $50.0 million and $60.0 million in annual run-rate savings. Atlassian is cutting 1,600 employees Atlassian Thomas Fuller/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images Atlassian, the enterprise software company and maker of Confluence, said on March 11 that it will be cutting about 10% of its workforce as it invests in AI to reshape its organization. CEO Mike Cannon-Brookes said in a statement that about 1,600 employees will be affected by the cuts. "We fundamentally believe people and AI create the best outcomes. Our approach is not 'AI replaces people,'" Cannon-Brookes said. "But it would be disingenuous to pretend AI doesn't change the mix of skills we need or the number of roles required in certain areas. It does." The company expects to incur $225 million and $236 million in restructuring charges, according to an SEC filing. Barclays cuts 5,000 jobs KHemaz/GVN via Getty Images Barclays, the British financial institution , disclosed plans to cut around 5% of its workforce. Anna Cross, the Group Finance Director of Barclays, said on an October 22 earnings call that the company expects more than GBP 1 billion in efficiency savings in 2027, which will involve reducing its head count by 5,000 full-time employees. Cross said that 60% of affected workers are related to "support functions, including fewer developers as AI makes our people more productive." The company reported Q3 pretax profit of GBP 2.3 billion — about $3 billion — up 12% from the same quarter a year earlier. Barclays CEO, C.S. Venkatakrishnan, said that the company is moving to "drive even greater cost efficiency through deep technological transformation, reducing the unit cost of product, manufacturing, service and innovation." events.title: Plug-in solar push sparks house fire warning from electricians
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Plug-in solar and batteries risk causing house fires, warn electrical trade groups Germany has plug-in solar and few safety issues, but "Australians aren't Germans" and may not follow the rules. ( Getty: Stefan Sauer/dpa ) Advocates are calling on the federal government to legalise plug-in solar and batteries by mid-2027. Industry groups say the devices could cause house fires and a "rushed process" could repeat the mistakes of the 2009 "pink batts" scheme. Australia's energy ministers have agreed to explore pathways for "safe deployment" of plug-in solar across the country and will report back in December. Solar panels and batteries that can be plugged into regular power outlets could cause house fires due to rushed implementation and lack of safety oversight, according to electrical trade groups. Advocates want the devices to be legalised in Australia by mid-2027, saying it would allow renters, apartment dwellers and low-income households to benefit from lower energy bills. The federal government is working with states and territories to develop a safety framework, with Minister for Climate Change and Energy Chris Bowen telling a webinar last week he had asked Standards Australia to fast-track the project, which would be completed "very quickly". Australia readies to lift a ban on plug-in solar, unlocking access to the technology for millions of apartment dwellers and renters for the first time. Western Australia has struck out on its own, releasing a draft technical standard that would bypass this national process and aiming to be the first state or territory to legalise the technology. But industry groups and unions are warning of safety risks, saying a rushed process could result in deaths. The organisations include the peak body for electricians, Master Electricians Australia (MEA); the peak body for electrical contractors, National Electrical and Communications Association (NECA); and the Electrical Trades Union (ETU). The solar panels and batteries can be plugged into regular power outlets They feed power into the home's network to help offset electricity used by appliances Overseas, plug-in panels are commonly attached to apartment balconies or mounted in backyards MEA CEO Kate Raymond said the current proposed safety measures, including those in WA's draft standard, could cause house fires, the release of toxic battery gases, and other dangerous outcomes. "We understand the cost of living; we understand people want and need to reduce their energy bills," Ms Raymond told the ABC. "But what's the cost of a house fire? What's the cost of someone losing their life?" Could plug-in solar and batteries cause fires? Power pushed into a circuit by a plug-in solar panel or battery bypasses circuit breakers that protect wiring in walls and switchboards from overheating. Germany, which has added more than 1 million plug-in solar systems in two years without disaster, limits the output of such devices so extra current cannot overload wiring. Plug-in solar, or "balcony solar", has also been legalised in the UK and some US states. ( Supplied: Holger's Pictures ) The same approach is being proposed by plug-in advocates and the WA government, which permits one plug-in system per household in its draft standards. But "Australians aren't Germans", MEA national technical manager Matthew Duncan said. "Households either won't read the safety instructions or they'll ignore them. Multiple solar panels or batteries can overload a circuit, and the risk is higher in houses with faulty wiring. Plug-in batteries may also be riskier than panels because they can push power into a circuit for longer. NECA director of safety Neil Roberts said misuse was inevitable. "You're trusting the competency of the general public to install these," he said. This is a small plug-in battery, but stacked systems can exceed 15 kilowatt-hours, which is about the size of an average home battery. ( Supplied: Fuse ) Carl Copeland, the CEO of the Electrotechnology Training Institute (ETI), which represents hundreds of electrical contractors and trains thousands of apprentices in WA, warned of a repeat of mistakes from the 2009 home insulation program. The pink batts scheme's rushed rollout and a lack of safety oversight contributed to the deaths of four installers , according to a later royal commission. "We're going to end up with a situation like we did with the pink batts insulation where we'll have home owners plug in three or four of these things into the system, overloading their system, and causing house fires," Mr Copeland said.

events.title: Verizon’s CEO turned down the job several times before leaving retirement on his ranch: ‘I came in with a little bit of a bad attitude’
events.summary: Dan Schulman thought he had traded the corner office for cowboy boots for good. After nearly a decade running digital payments giant PayPal , he was enjoying retirement on a Montana ranch with his wife, Summerly, and roughly 900 head of cattle. He was happy, in love, and had no desire to return to the grueling CEO schedule. So when his fellow Verizon board members came calling for him to step in as CEO, he said no. Several times. But the telecommunications giant was losing market share, falling behind competitors, and struggling with a bureaucracy . Eventually, a sense of obligation—and some convincing from his wife—brought him out of retirement to take the top job in October 2025. “I came in with a little bit of a bad attitude,” Schulman told Fortune Editor-in-Chief Alyson Shontell in the latest episode of Fortune 500: Titans and Disruptors of Industry . A year later, he said, he’s “absolutely loving it and pretty hopeful about our future.” The reluctant hire is now one year into a three-year turnaround plan for Verizon, a Fortune 500 company with $138 billion in revenue last year. The early numbers are moving his way. A reluctant return to the corner office The former PayPal chief had stepped down in 2023 and retirement gave him plenty of time to embrace his inner cowboy. The New Jersey native had been wearing cowboy boots since eighth grade, long before he had a ranch—or cattle—to go with them. “I really didn’t want to come back into the CEO job,” he said. “These jobs are all-consuming. You’re putting in 10 to 14 hours a day.” Verizon, as it turns out, knows a thing or two about making repeat calls. Although Schulman may have been ready to hang up on corporate life, it wasn’t ready to part ways with him just yet.  He had sat on Verizon’s board since 2018 and had been its lead independent director since December 2024. He knew the management team, understood the business, and had watched the company struggle to compete. He was already the board’s backup plan. “I was the hit-by-the-bus scenario,” he said. If anything had happened to then-CEO Hans Vestberg, “I would go in temporarily.” Verizon had been losing market share for roughly five years, Schulman said. Once first in its industry by market capitalization, it had fallen to last, and its longtime reputation for having a superior wireless network was no longer enough to keep customers from looking elsewhere. “We had the lowest P/E, which is what the Street thinks of our future growth potential,” he said. Schulman acknowledged the board probably should have acted sooner. It had developed a plan to address the company’s struggles, but the strategy didn’t deliver. Quoting his father, he put it this way: “People plan, God laughs.” “We had a plan. It didn’t work out, so we had to go to Plan B, which was me, not Plan A,” he said. Despite his reservations, Schulman believed Verizon still had the assets to turn things around, including what he estimated at 150 million customer lines. The board kept asking. In the end, it was Summerly who convinced him, reminding her husband that he could still make a difference. “I felt an obligation,” he said. Verizon’s CEO cut 35-signature approvals and 13,000 jobs Once he accepted, Schulman wasn’t interested in easing into the job. At his first all-employee meeting, he delivered a blunt assessment of the company’s problems without notes or slides. Verizon had become a “big, lumbering giant that had fallen behind,” he said, with a hierarchical culture, slow decision-making, and processes that required something like 35 signatures to move forward. He also warned employees that layoffs were likely. That warning became reality in November 2025, just weeks after he took over, when Verizon began cutting more than 13,000 jobs , the largest round of layoffs in its history. Verizon had cut 2,000 or 3,000 people, often through voluntary buyouts, every year, Schulman said. He wanted the cuts to free up money to reinvest in the business, and to show employees this turnaround was different. “I needed to show this was different, that I was very serious about the change that was going to happen,” he said. “Playing to win is not just a slogan for me or a nice marketing thing.” His strategy centers on replacing Verizon’s risk-averse culture with one willing to experiment, make decisions faster, and put customers ahead of internal processes. That means rethinking what Verizon has long put first. The network is “foundational to everything we do,” Schulman said, but “it can’t be about the network. It has to be about the customer.” Verizon’s early results are promising, with two years to go The overhaul is beginning to show up in the numbers. In the third quarter of 2026 , Verizon added a net 406,000 postpaid phone lines, up from 44,000 a year earlier. Its promotional costs to acquire customers fell 41%, and free cash flow rose 12% to $7.8 billion. Part of the shift came from breaking an industry habit of luring customers with free phones and promotional offers. “A free line is not really a net add from my perspective,” Schulman said. Still, he knows the turnaround is far from over. He expects it to take three years, and the company has extended his contract through December 2028 to see it through. The ranch will have to wait. Asked how he’ll judge his tenure when he eventually hands Verizon to a successor, Schulman pointed first to customer trust, then to pride inside a company many had written off as too big and too bureaucratic to change. “We’re surprising a lot of people right now,” he said, “and it feels good when that happens.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Bouncing Wynn Shares might be primed for the 'wheel strategy'
events.summary: From a valuation standpoint, Wynn is trading very close to its five-year historical averages across key metrics. With the next earnings report not scheduled until February, the stock has a clear runway free of binary fundamental catalysts, yet implied volatility remains surprisingly high. This environment makes buying options expensive and short premium strategies more attractive. In Barry Levinson's classic film Rain Man , Dustin Hoffman's character leans over to his brother in the middle of a blackjack hand with a simple piece of advice: bet two for good, one for bad. In the case of Wynn Resorts shares, it might be time to bet two for good. Steve Wynn hasn't exactly been on a winning streak. No longer running his namesake company, he finally sold his 50 Central Park South penthouse after years on the market. WYNN shares haven't really been on a winning streak either. The stock is down more than 27% year-to-date as I write this. It was down more than 46% from the 2025 highs within the past couple of weeks. But it has bounced a bit since then, and perhaps the tables are turning. Fundamentally, the business is demonstrating exceptional strength, particularly in the United States. Wynn's Las Vegas EBITDA margin has actually surpassed that of its Macau resorts. Recognizing this, management has accelerated capital spending in Las Vegas, where the company's profit has doubled from pre-pandemic levels. Meanwhile, the Asian market is also showing signs of life. Strategic property upgrades in Macau are successfully drawing lucrative premium mass play, which is directly supporting the company's ambitious expansion plans for the Enclave at Wynn Palace. From a valuation standpoint, WYNN is trading very close to its five-year historical averages across key metrics, including P/E, EV/EBITDA (currently around 9x to 10x), and Price-to-Book Value. Although this represents a slight premium compared to the broader gaming industry mean, Wynn's justifies a premium. (The Encore, the newer of the two adjacent Las Vegas properties, is one of my preferred hotels on "The Strip"). Technically, the stock has admittedly been in a downtrend, but this recent sharp bounce off the late October lows may indicate the run is over. Several technical indicators—specifically the MACD, Fear & Greed Index, Commodity Channel Index (CCI), and several key Moving Averages—are now aligned, suggesting it may be time to go long. So, how should traders play this setup? With the next earnings report not scheduled until February, the stock has a clear runway free of binary fundamental catalysts, yet implied volatility remains surprisingly high. This environment makes buying options expensive and short premium strategies more attractive. Rather than betting on the roulette wheel, traders should look once again to "the wheel" strategy. Something I discussed earlier this week on United Rentals. The strategy? Step one, sell cash-covered puts below the current market price to collect that inflated premium. If WYNN stays above your strike price through expiration, you keep the cash and repeat the process. If the stock dips and you are assigned, you acquire shares at a discount. Once assigned, you move to step two: selling covered calls against your new stock position to generate continuous income until the shares are eventually called away, after which you revert back to step one and play again. A methodical, high-probability way to get long a world-class operator while getting paid to wait. Disclosures: Tidal owns/holds all the securities mentioned in the article.
