events.title: ITV to cut show budgets as UK TV and film production spend drops by more than £2bn
events.summary: Broadcaster plans to make £30m in ‘temporary’ savings before inquiry into takeover by Sky ITV plans to slash its programming budget as new figures showed that spend on the production of films and prestige TV shows in the UK was down more than £2bn over the last year. The broadcaster plans to make £30m in “temporary” savings, including £25m in content and £5m elsewhere in the business. The announcement by ITV, which has agreed to sell its television and streaming business to Sky, came amid a backdrop of ditched commissions , falling advertising sales and job reductions in the TV and streaming industry . The Love Island and I’m a Celebrity … Get Me Out of Here! broadcaster said it expected ad revenues to fall between 5% and 10% in the crucial final quarter of the year, despite the typically busy Christmas season. Ad sales are expected to drop between 2% and 3% over the course of the full year, ITV said. ITV’s programming cuts will mostly affect small external commissions, pushing them into 2027, it is understood. Separately, the latest update from the British Film Institute (BFI) showed that spending in the UK on making film and high-end TV shows – those that cost at least £1m an episode – had plunged by £2.08bn year on year. The figures showed that £5.2bn was spent by domestic and international broadcasters, Hollywood studios and streamers in the year to the end of September. This was a 28% decrease on the £7.26bn spent in the same period in 2025, a record year that included productions such as Avengers: Doomsday, Spider-Man: Brand New Day and the first instalment of the Harry Potter TV series. A spokesperson for the BFI said: “The figures are the result of a complex picture, ranging from significant shifts in the global industrial context through to increased competitiveness [for productions] from other international territories, and set against a backdrop of a strong [2025]. This is obviously something we and the British Film Commission are looking at very closely.” The latest figures are classified as “first reported”, with the BFI typically significantly revising up spending levels as it receives more information over the coming months. The BFI said the final figures for 2025 was revised up £900m from their “first reported” level. However, with the latest provisional figures showing a more than £2bn plunge in investment, 2026 is on track to be a dismal year for the UK production industry. Carolyn McCall, ITV’s chief executive, said demand for ads had weakened because of “continuing broader macroeconomic uncertainty” and “increased digital advertising on global streaming platforms”. She also cited new rules this year that imposed a 9pm watershed on TV advertising for less healthy food. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning The business has struggled in recent years to keep up with deep-pocketed streaming companies such as Netflix and YouTube, which have muscled in on traditional media’s audiences and commercial revenue. Other mainstream broadcasters are also struggling, with the BBC intending to shed as many as 2,000 jobs and Channel 4 planning layoffs . ITV indicated the proposed cost savings would not involve staff cuts. McCall has argued that the £1.6bn sale of its TV and streaming business to Sky is ITV’s route to survival. However, last week, the culture secretary, Lisa Nandy , issued a public interest intervention notice, triggering an investigation by the media regulator Ofcom and the Competition and Markets Authority. Nandy raised concerns that the combined broadcasters would account for about 86% of linear news and current affairs viewing in Britain, as well as concerns over potential US political influence on editorial independence. Sky is owned by the US broadcaster Comcast. ITV said on Wednesday that the deal was “progressing as planned” and it was still expected to complete in the second half of 2027. The sale will leave ITV with its studios business, which makes shows for ITV and other broadcasters and streamers. The company told investors that studios revenue was down 1% in the first nine months of the year, but it had made five of the UK’s top 10 most-watched dramas in the third quarter of 2026, including The Gentlemen for Netflix and The Blame for ITV.

events.title: Lithium Americas raises Thacker Pass cost estimate by 31% to $3.83bn
events.summary: Lithium Americas on Wednesday increased its cost estimate for its flagship Thacker Pass lithium project to $3.83 billion, an increase of 31 per cent, the company said, giving higher labour, ⁠construction and logistics costs as reasons. The company said the revised budget adds $895 million in capital costs and raises the Nevada-based project's funding requirements by about $995 million. It said it expects the additional funds to be met through company contributions and available loan reserves from the US Energy Department. The company's shares plunged more 12 per cent during Wednesday trading. Lithium Americas chief executive Jonathan Evans said Phase 1 construction on the project is planned for late 2027, increasing throughout 2028. “Despite external and internal factors impacting the project’s capital cost estimate, the anticipated capital cost for Thacker Pass is expected to remain funded as we continue to deliver on our execution plan and bring the project safely into production,” Mr Evans said in a statement. The Canada-based company said labour installation rates for piping, steel and equipment accounted for $245 million of the increase, with tariffs and logistics adding a further $100 million. Logistics costs have been heavily affected by rising fuel prices, challenges to global and national shipping conditions and reduction in the availability of US fabrication. The Thacker Pass mine, a joint venture with General Motors, is one of the largest known lithium deposits in the US. Lithium Americas said it expects Thacker Pass to produce 40,000 tonnes a year of battery-quality lithium carbonate when at full capacity. Lithium carbonate is critical for electric vehicles. Total global demand for rechargeable chemical batteries is expected to more than quadruple from 2023 levels by 2030, according to an analysis from the Centre for Strategic and International Studies. The Silver Peak Lithium Mine is the only active, commercial-producing lithium mine in the US and generates about 1 per cent of global production. “Thacker Pass is essential to America's economic and national security, and we are committed to delivering it,” Mr Evans said. However, the project's rising estimated costs expose the challenges of establishing a US supply chain. Mining is mainly concentrated in Australia, Chile and China , which together account for 90 per cent of production, according to an analysis from Columbia's Centre on Global Energy Policy. And about 65 per cent of global lithium processing is done in China, making it the dominant player. In September 2025, the Energy Department took a 5 per cent equity stake in Lithium Americas and another 5 per cent ownership in the form of warrants in the Thacker Pass joint venture, restructuring a multibillion-dollar loan that the department said would help to solidify the launch of the only US-based source of lithium carbonate. Mr Evans said on a panel at Future Initiative Investment's Miami summit in March that Lithium Americas is "very fortunate to have the us government as a big backstop", adding the US has been losing the critical minerals race "for a long time". US President Donald Trump's administration has taken equity stakes in other mining companies including MP Materials , USA Rare Earth , Vulcan Elements and Trilogy Metals as part of its multibillion-dollar push for self-reliance on critical minerals. The administration is also backing a project from Korea Zinc in Tennessee. It has also been looking to diversify the critical minerals supply chain through diplomatic channels, including through the Quad and G7 memberships. The US and Saudi Arabia last year announced a framework for co-operation on securing uranium, metals, permanent magnets and the critical minerals supply chain during Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman's visit to Washington. The mining agreement is intended to help support two-way investment in minerals. And the Defence Department, through its partnership with MP Materials, announced that it would finance a 49 per cent equity stake in a new rare earth refinery in the kingdom through a joint venture with Maaden.

events.title: KKR and RWE are rich firms. Why do they need a UK state loan for their windfarms? | Nils Pratley
events.summary: Deep-pocketed windfarm developers shouldn’t need a £1bn state loan National wealth fund is to lend £1bn towards the Vanguard projects – but whether the private equity giant needed help is debatable “This major investment in UK renewables is a vote of confidence for building in Britain,” declared the prime minister. Andy Burnham is obviously correct that the two Vanguard windfarms off the coast of Norfolk are huge investments . Together, they require almost £13bn of debt financing. But he can’t claim they represent a fresh expression of confidence. The project has been on the runway since the German utility RWE, the developer, was awarded a contract to build the windfarms in January’s renewables auction. Instead, the new news on Wednesday was how the project will be financed, which is where the story becomes interesting. On the equity front, RWE said it had sold a 50% share in the Vanguard schemes to KKR, the giant US private equity and infrastructure investor. On the debt side, £12.8bn has come from “a consortium of 35 international banks”, including £1bn from the UK’s own national wealth fund (NWF). It is fair enough, one might say, for the NWF to get involved – directing capital to energy transition projects is, in part, what it was set up to do. But here’s another key aspect of its role: the state-backed body is not meant to be a substitute for private capital; instead, its funding is supposed to be “additional”, in the terminology, to ensure infrastructure is built that might not otherwise be. Here is how the NWF describes the process: “For each investment we are considering, we test and assess the extent to which impact would not have materialised without us, so we are confident we are delivering financial and non-financial value that would not otherwise be achieved.” So how does that work with the Vanguard windfarms? Would they have been scrapped if the NWF had not chipped in its £1bn? That seems highly unlikely. Consider that RWE is one of Europe’s biggest electricity generators and that KKR is a giant among private equity houses. These rich firms are experienced at raising capital. Consider, too, that the main way in which offshore wind projects are de-risked for developers is the auction process that sets a guaranteed inflation-linked price for their electricity for 20 years. In this case, the price is £91.20 a megawatt hour (in 2024 money), or high by historic standards. If the cost of borrowing has risen post-auction – and it has – that’s unfortunate for RWE and KKR. They might have to pay a bit more for their debt, or pony up more equity, both of which would depress their returns. But that is an everyday risk of commercial life. Why did the NWF, having stayed away from fixed offshore wind until now, think it had to join a lending syndicate on a project where it is a stretch to think its contribution was the make-or-break element? The NWF’s argument is that its involvement “widens the pool of capital available to offshore wind developers and helps to meet unprecedented liquidity requirements after the success of AR7 [the last auction round]”. In other words, the sector will need so much capital over coming years that the state-backed lender needs to be on standby. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning It’s a defence, but it will sound very appealing from the point of view of developers. They can bid for an index-linked contract that guarantees revenues for 20 years; then, if borrowing conditions are tight, they are invited to think that the state will lend a hand to try to ease funding pressures. No wonder KKR wanted in. The NWF, note, says it is lending at market rates. Even so, its definition of how it adds “additional” value seems to have become very stretched. Many of the NWF’s other big loans, such as billions for Sizewell C and £599m for Rolls-Royce’s development of small modular reactors , are far easier to understand. Those projects genuinely might not have happened without state backing. The same applies to the myriad of its smaller investments in battery technology and so forth. Offshore wind generation, by contrast, is an established market with an effective mechanism – the contract-for-difference – for incentivising developers. The NWF’s pot of capital is not bottomless. Better targets for loans right now might be anything to do with electrification, meaning the take-up of heat pumps and electric vehicles, or storage solutions. As half the energy world is pointing out, it is where the big decarbonisation gains are available. A bit of state activism to accelerate energy transition is a good thing, many of us would say. But, as argued here previously , more scrutiny of that “additionality” principle is overdue. There is little point replicating what the private sector would do anyway.

events.title: Airwallex’s CEO isn't worried about AI
events.summary: Jack Zhang isn’t worried about AI taking over global finance, but he is concerned about cybersecurity. Zhang co-founded Australian fintech unicorn Airwallex, which allows businesses to make cross-border payments and manage finances in dozens of countries, and is now morphing into an agentic finance company. Zhang joined Future Proof to discuss how his company is using AI to build systems to help companies handle their finances — essentially building an AI-managed CFO office. The company currently relies mainly on ChatGPT and Claude, but Zhang also said it’s looking at developing proprietary models using open-weight solutions. Zhang doesn’t think AI will get so good that it can entirely replace humans, at least not in his field. “The laws still require you to have somebody sign off as auditor, and how the auditor does that sign-off can be assisted by agents,” he said. “I don’t think we can completely get rid of the human in the loop.” What Zhang is “very, very, very, very worried” about is cybersecurity. With news about cyber breaches emerging almost daily, the company is tackling the issue by using behavioral monitoring and hiring experts from the Australian Department of Defence and Palantir, among other strategies. “We’re moving hundreds of billions of dollars today ... We’re constantly paranoid about how good our defense [is] against this type of threat,” he said. — Reed Albergotti

events.title: Who Runs the Ransomware Group Qilin?
events.summary: The cybercrime group Qilin has emerged as the world’s most active ransomware affiliate program, claiming at least 365 victim organizations in the past three months alone. But even top Russian hackers make operational security mistakes, and the administrator of Qilin has made a few key missteps over the last decade that all point to a 36-year-old man living in St. Petersburg, Russia. Operating since September 2022, the Russia-based ransomware group Qilin is the currently the most industrious ransomware-as-a-service gang, according to a report (PDF) this month by the cybersecurity firm NCC Group (KrebsOnSecurity profiled the administrator of the second most active ransomware group — The Gentlemen — in June). The Qilin ransomware administrator “Haise” advertising his affiliate program on the cybercrime forum RAMP. Image: Ke-la.com. Qilin attracts affiliates to hack into companies and deploy ransomware by offering them at least 80 percent of any extortion amount paid by victims. Its members practice the “double extortion” model, stealing sensitive data before encrypting systems and threatening to publish the files online. Unlike most ransomware partnerships based out of Russia, Qilin is happy to team with English-speaking affiliates, and its leader has shared on Telegram that they’ve worked with cybercrime groups like Scattered Spider and RansomHub . The head of Qilin goes by the handle “ Haise ,” but they weren’t always known by this nickname. It is not uncommon for cybercriminals to change their handle periodically as an operational security (opsec) measure. Doing so is generally a smart move, because it helps to sever one’s ties to older identities that may not have been as careful on basic opsec, such as separating their real life identity from their cybercrime activities. But even those cautious criminals will sometimes have to reference their past monikers when applying for membership at a new forum. And forums eventually get hacked or seized. That is precisely what happened with Haise. The cyber intelligence platform Intel 471 records that in June 2022, Haise applied for membership to RAMP , a closely-guarded Russian cybercrime forum that was created as a haven for ransomware affiliate programs. Intel 471 has indexed direct messages from RAMP (the forum was seized by the FBI in January 2026), and those missives show the RAMP administrator approved Haise’s application, referring to this user as Haise and by their Telegram username: Alexbigboss44 . Searching Intel 471 for Alexbigboss44 reveals this was the Telegram account name shared by the user Rjun on the Russian cybercrime forums Exploit and XSS two years earlier in 2020. The cyber intelligence platform Flashpoint finds Alexbigboss44 is a prolific participant in cybercriminal forums and Telegram channels, primarily focused on the illicit trade of traffic, logs, and corporate access [full disclosure: Flashpoint is an advertiser on this blog]. The Qilin administrator once used the nickname “Rjun” on several forums, and shared their Telegram handle as “Alexbigboss44.” Image: Ke-la.com. Flashpoint says this user was engaged in high-volume acquisition of Facebook logs and Google Ads accounts to facilitate fraudulent advertising and gambling schemes, and that they functioned as a broker and operator — managing a network of traffickers and purchasing compromised data to fuel their operations. The link between the Qilin administrator Haise and the much older Rjun and Alexbigboss44 accounts was shared privately earlier this month by IntelHawk , which describes itself as an AI-based platform capable of de-anonymizing threat actors based on historical usernames, stylometry and other signals. IntelHawk founder and chief technology officer Leo Bogod said an analysis of these identities shows a progression from novice arbitrageur and credit card fraudster in 2018–2019 to a more experienced participant and organizer of complex cybercrime-related activities in 2020–2023, with increasing attention to malware, botnets, and payment infrastructure. Where does this connection between these threat actor identities lead? Intel 471 finds that by the time Alexbigboss44 was applying for membership to RAMP, Rjun was already a longtime member of several other Russian crime forums, including Darkmarket , Verified , and Zloy . Intel 471 says Rjun signed up at all of these sites with the email address mail-30a@mail.ru . The identity threat protection firm Spycloud found the email address mail-30a@mail.ru at one time used the password “Rjun132” [Spycloud is also an advertiser on this blog]. A search for that email at the breach tracking service Constella Intelligence shows that it appeared in records maintained by gosuslugi.ru , the official digital platform for state and municipal services in the Russian Federation. Gosuslugi was breached in late 2025, reportedly exposing more than 20 million records with full names, birth dates, and mobile numbers. According to the leaked Gosuslugi records (via Constella), the address mail-30a@mail.ru belongs to 36-year-old Aleksey Mikhailovich Yakovtsev from St. Petersburg, Russia. Flashpoint finds Haise has long used a Telegram account with the user ID 118329521 , recording more than 5,000 messages from this user since 2018. Records from Russia’s education watchdog Rosobrnadzor reveal that Mr. Yakovtsev went to grade school in Murmansk and that he holds a master’s degree in computing and information systems. A search on this Telegram ID in Constella shows it is linked to the Russian phone number + 79602347275 . Pivoting on that phone number in Constella reveals it is connected to the email addresses aleksey1990yakov@mail.ru and rjun123321@mail.ru . IntelHawk finds that +79602347275 belongs to Yakovtsev’s biological sister, and that Aleksey often used his sister’s email address when registering at different websites. That phone number appears on several airline flight records at Russian travel agencies that have experienced a data breach in recent years, and those records show Aleksey Yakovtsev, born August 18, 1990, flew between St. Petersburg and Murmansk at least three times between 2013 and 2014. More recent flight records show that while Mr. Yakovtsev has not traveled by plane outside of Russia, he does fly frequently between Saint Petersburg and Sochi. Often called the “Russian Riviera,” Sochi is Russia’s largest resort city, situated along the coast of the Black Sea and about 1,200 miles south of Saint Petersburg by plane. Attempts to reach Mr. Yakovtsev via email and phone were unsuccessful. Further reading: Gang Exposed , an anonymous Twitter/X account that has a history of successfully deanonymizing suspected ransomware actors, reached similar conclusions about Haise’s real-life identity, crediting IntelHawk’s platform for help

events.title: Scoop: Inside Bessent's Situation Room confrontation with Lutnick over China chip security
events.summary: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent confronted Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick over a failure to place Nvidia customer Megaspeed on a list of companies that pose national security concerns, sources familiar told Axios. Why it matters: The Commerce Department oversees the export of sensitive U.S. technologies and Lutnick's actions — or lack thereof — are increasingly under scrutiny following revelations that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huan g had an affair with Megaspeed employee and suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang. Driving the news: At a White House Situation Room meeting on Thursday after the midterm elections, Bessent pressed Lutnick on why Megaspeed had not been added to the Commerce Department's entity list, to which Lutnick responded he would "look into it." Commerce Undersecretary Jeff Kessler also was repeatedly warned about Megaspeed in deputy meetings. But Kessler deferred to Lutnick, saying "That's a decision for the secretary." Sources told Axios that Lutnick has spent the last year "undoing" efforts by other administration officials to hold Megaspeed — a company accused of illegally diverting U.S. chips to China — accountable because of concerns it would escalate the trade war with China. Spokespeople for Treasury couldn't be immediately reached for comment. The other side: The Commerce Department denied the Situation Room confrontation occurred. "This is false. Secretary Bessent and Secretary Lutnick had no such conversation," spokesperson Kristen Eichamer said. Catch up quick: The Commerce Department is increasingly at the center of scrutiny over the broader Trump administration's handling of an intelligence memo overseen by State Department head Marco Rubio. Lutnick was among the officials who received the report in May, ahead of a trip to China, Axios first reported. On Tuesday, the New York Times reported Commerce Undersecretary Kessler abruptly stopped an investigation into Megaspeed after Nvidia intervened. The Financial Times reported the department was delaying efforts to blacklist Megaspeed despite several U.S. government agencies pushing it to do so. Inside the room: White House and intelligence officials have pressed Lutnick and his top advisers to take action against Megaspeed since the fall of 2025, sources tell Axios. But they refused, so Bessent spoke up Thursday. "How come Megaspeed isn't on the entities list?" Bessent asked Lutnick, according to a source briefed on the meeting. Lutnick initially stammered, sources said, and then replied: ""I don't know. I'll look into it." One source, who has extensive experience concerning the chip controversy, said the reply was "bullshit" because Lutnick had resisted action ever since he was personally handed a memo, drafted by National Security Adviser and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, that outlined the problems with Megaspeed. The big picture: Nvidia's AI chips provide the computing power needed to develop cutting-edge artificial intelligence, including systems that could transform warfare and cyberattacks. Editor's note: This is a breaking news story and will be updated.

events.title: General strikes to paralyze Spain as protestors clash with police ahead of election campaign
events.summary: Millions of workers are expected to join Spain’s first general strike in 14 years, with transport and businesses facing widespread disruption. Soaring rents and living costs are driving the unrest, as unions demand stronger government action on housing and wages. The strike comes less than three weeks before Spain’s Nov. 29 election, with polls suggesting the Popular Party and Vox could secure a parliamentary majority. Spanish workers are expected to turn out in the millions on Wednesday for the country's first general strike in 14 years, as anger over soaring rents and living costs intensifies less than three weeks before a general election. Demonstrators clashed with police at a wholesale market in Madrid in the early hours of the strike, while roadblocks were also reported in the early hours of Wednesday. The 24-hour labor walkout is expected to disrupt public transport and flights, as well as bring some businesses, shops and factories to a standstill. Spain's biggest unions call strike action Housing costs are a particular source of frustration among demonstrators. Rents have almost doubled over the past decade, squeezing household budgets as many workers feel homeownership is beyond their reach. The Bank of Spain estimates that the country faces a shortage of 750,000 homes, potentially rising to 1 million over the next two years. Spain's two largest trade unions, CCOO and UGT, which called the strike, are calling for greater government intervention in the housing market. Housing activists demand an end to tourist rentals and automatic lease renewals, while unions are seeking greater housing intervention and a new minimum-wage agreement. UGT Secretary-General Pepe Álvarez urged members to join the protests, saying "there is no salary that can cope with the price of housing in this country," in comments translated by CNBC. He added that it was time for the government to listen to citizens' demands. The strike follows weeks of social unrest. The eviction of an 87-year-old woman from her Madrid home, followed by her death around two weeks later, sparked national outrage. The left-wing government's attempts to pass measures to help tenants were blocked by the opposition. Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez's coalition responded by calling an election for Nov. 29, hoping to bolster his support and secure another four years in power. But a high-speed train collision that killed 69 people, the second such disaster this year, shifted the debate toward public safety and accusations of government mismanagement. The government has not officially endorsed the strike, whose slogan is "Salaries. Housing. Prices." But the protests are widely seen as an opportunity for left-wing parties, including Sánchez's Spanish Socialist Workers' Party, to put housing at the center of the election campaign. Political scientist Oriol Bartomeus of the Autonomous University of Barcelona told The Associated Press that a strong, peaceful turnout could help the left return the campaign to a focus on housing. Sánchez took to social media earlier this week to voice support for existing policies including national health insurance and a 40-hour workweek, warning that a right-wing government would introduce austerity measures and cuts to social services. "Your eight-hour working day. Your pensions. Your public healthcare. None of this fell from the sky. They were collective achievements," he told voters on Monday. The conservative Popular Party and far-right Vox, which already govern in some parts of Spain, accuse the unions of organizing the protests to keep the current government in power. "The strike is not a general strike, it's an election strike," Miguel Tellado, a spokesperson for the Popular Party, said Tuesday. Both parties oppose intervention in the housing market. Polls point to a right-wing majority Opinion polls suggest a shift to the right, with the Popular Party leading and potentially able to form a government with Vox. Such a coalition would bring the far right into Spain's national government for the first time since Francisco Franco's 36-year dictatorship ended in 1975. A poll for El País and Cadena SER, published Nov. 9, put the Popular Party at 31.9%, Sánchez's Partido Socialista Obrero Español at 29.9% and Vox at 18%. The survey, conducted Nov. 2-4, projected a combined 190 seats for the Popular Party and Vox, above the 176 needed for a majority in the 350-seat lower house. A strong turnout at Wednesday's protests could prove crucial for the government, whose handling of the migration crisis in Ceuta drew widespread criticism. Sánchez's family has also been plagued by corruption scandals. What’s making Europe so angry? The frustration behind the protests The prime minister's personal standing has suffered. Some 58% of respondents had a "bad" or "very bad" opinion of him, compared with 41% who had a good or very good opinion, according to a poll for elDiario.es conducted Nov. 2-5.

events.title: Nvidia is more than a chip company
events.summary: Reed’s view Nvidia has been battered over the past couple of days, but it could get worse. That is, if founder and CEO Jensen Huang is forced or chooses to step down, or if investigations pin him down for doing something illegal. In most sectors of the economy, CEOs are expected to run businesses well, but they are generally interchangeable parts — albeit expensive ones. Google and Apple show that founder CEOs, which are harder to replicate, can be replaced. But even among founder CEOs, Huang stands apart for bold bets that helped him endure short-term suffering in return for long-term gain. Most people know Nvidia for the climbing stock in their portfolios, or the GPUs on every tech company’s Christmas list. But his creation of the CUDA platform in 2006 is perhaps the best example of how he’s been able to step ahead of the industry for decades. Nvidia’s computing platform and programming model, the software that essentially underpins the modern AI industry, created one of the most valuable moats in business history. A half dozen years later, seeing the progress in neural networks, he pivoted to AI. Huang realized AI would require massive data centers with interconnected chips, and concluded that networking would become the bottleneck. He bet billions on the development of NVLink, a nervous system that allows discrete GPUs to act as one massive supercomputer, and the $6.9 billion acquisition of Mellanox Technologies, the Israeli networking company, in 2019. He funded neoclouds so he wouldn’t be reliant on a few customers and acquired Hugging Face to stay ahead of the game on open source. Huang is 63, and while he has said he could run the company for decades to come, the current investigations raise questions about the future of one of the world’s most consequential companies. Even if he does ride out the turmoil, will he still have the same bold personality that got him here? Nvidia may still mint money, as demand for the company’s products shows no signs of slowing down. But it’s difficult to imagine anyone stepping into the role with the strategic vision and gravitas to match Huang’s. The next handful of years are going to be even trickier. China is ascendant. Once it gains independence on semiconductors, it will be able to scale faster than the US. There won’t be any data-center red tape and China will have abundant energy compared to the US. Because Moore’s law is dead, AI chipmakers are no longer making exponentially better chips every year. Now, they must design entire systems with compute and cooling crammed into server racks like the world’s highest-stakes game of . They involve immensely complex supply chains colored by geopolitics, big personalities, and vast sums of money. Nvidia will be a crucial player in the effort to stay ahead of China. Without Huang, it will be fundamentally weakened. It may be already. Notable Semafor analyzed how Huang’s rhetoric on China has evolved in the past few years.

events.title: Royalty, fashion firsts and elephants. The highs and lows of David Jones's family history
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts David Jones's descendants hope for a revival as retailer prepares to close half its stores In the early 60s, Charles Lloyd Jones and his sisters were front and centre at opening ceremonies as David Jones exploded into Sydney's suburbs and interstate. ( ABC News: Shaun Kingma ) More than 60 years ago, two young siblings were front and centre at a jam-packed opening ceremony in Sydney's west, as the department store founded by their great-great-grandfather, David Jones, expanded into Sydney's suburbs. An estimated 4,000 people gathered outside the building in Parramatta, trying to catch a glimpse of seven-year-old Susanna de Vienne cutting the ribbon inside. Looking back, Ms de Vienne recalls being "overwhelmed" seeing the crowd. Susanna de Vienne was seven when David Jones opened its Parramatta store. ( ABC News: Jerry Rickard ) "I remember coming in … and people were just glued to the door," she told 7.30. A photo of the historic moment shows the little girl and her younger brother Charles E Lloyd Jones surrounded by eager faces peering through the glass doors. A young Susanna, with her brother Charles, opens the David Jones Parramatta store. ( Supplied ) Decades on, a receiver for David Jones has confirmed the Parramatta store is one of 19 on the chopping block amid a restructure. Administrator McGrath Nicol is now racing to find a buyer and hoping the "urgent restructure" will save the iconic 188-year-old brand. Speaking before the restructure was announced, Ms de Vienne told 7.30 she felt sad for David Jones staff after the company entered voluntary administration last week. David Jones hosted the first Christian Dior fashion parade outside Paris. Now, concession store shelves have been stripped of stock. ( AAP: Eleanor Wilson ) But she hoped the retailer — which was owned or run by her family for more than 140 years — would be rebuilt as "David Jones 2.0". Her brother, Mr Lloyd Jones, also believed the department store would survive but said if it did not, he would still feel "fortunate to have been part of its history". As children, the siblings were too young to understand the significant role their family had played in shaping Australia's then-skyrocketing retail landscape. Their great-great-grandfather started the first store in Sydney in 1838, more than six decades before Australia became a nation. It started as a drapery business on the corner of Barrack and George streets, before their grandfather, Sir Charles Lloyd Jones, expanded it to new buildings in Market and Elizabeth Streets in the 1920s. David Jones's first Sydney store opposite the General Post Office. ( Supplied: David Jones ) Mr Lloyd Jones said his grandfather's time as chairman was a new era of innovation for the department store. "The store had the first escalators in the Southern Hemisphere," he told 7.30. "They did aeroplane parcel deliveries to country customers. They did a lot of things that no one was doing." In the 1940s, David Jones hosted the first-ever Christian Dior fashion parade outside of Paris. In 1954, Sir Charles and his wife held a royal banquet for Queen Elizabeth and Prince Philip, as the couple became the first serving British monarchs to visit Australia. Queen Elizabeth and Prince Philip arrive at David Jones in Elizabeth Street, Sydney. ( Supplied: State Library of NSW ) One of Ms de Vienne's earliest memories was seeing an exhibition of circus animals inside the Elizabeth Street store in the 1950s. "I was just blown away by that as a child." A circus visited the flagship David Jones store and its star elephant, Eddie, made an appearance. ( Supplied ) As a teenager, Mr Lloyd Jones worked in the David Jones toy department as a Christmas casual. He would later go on to manage multiple stores, as the fifth and final generation of his family to work for the firm. Charles Lloyd Jones was the fifth and final generation to work for the company his family founded. ( ABC News: Shaun Kingma ) Mr Lloyd Jones feared he would lose his job at David Jones after a hostile takeover by Adelaide Steamship in 1980. "I thought having the name 'Lloyd Jones' might not be good," he said. Charles Lloyd Jones went on to manage multiple David Jones stores. ( ABC News: Shaun Kingma ) "But the managing director at the time … said to me, 'If you perform and you do the job, your name is not a hindrance to your career here.'" The company has since changed hands multiple times, and has been owned by private equity firm Anchorage Capital for the past three years.

events.title: The giant gas project and the billion-dollar funding question
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Woodside's $30b gas project could struggle to find financial backers Woodside wants to pipe gas from the Browse Basin to the North West Shelf processing operation on the Burrup Peninsula. ( ABC News: Chris Lewis ) Questions have been raised about whether the Woodside Browse project, which stands to become Australia's most expensive resource development, will be able to secure financial backing. A climate finance expert says banks are increasingly turning away from financing fossil fuel projects. The gas project off WA's northern coast has been given fresh momentum in the wake of rising gas prices. Australia's biggest untapped gas resource would involve building one of the world's longest subsea pipelines and would be among the more expensive projects ever developed in this country. The $30 billion Browse gas project, off Western Australia's Kimberley coast, lends itself to superlatives. But for all its scale and ambition, some critics say Browse could face a basic problem. They suggest its backers, led by Australian oil and gas giant Woodside, may struggle to borrow the huge sums of money needed to build it. "I think it's really important again to stress how high the project cost has become," said Elisa Leys, the acting Tokyo office director of advocacy group Solutions for Climate. Plans for a national gas reservation scheme are before parliament but experts say the player to blame for high prices may get off the hook. "As the project cost continues to increase, we just see that the pool of financing is drying up." Amid a renewed push by Woodside and its partners, which include BP and Japanese firms Mitsui and Mitsubishi, Browse is firmly back on Australia's development radar. Last year, the federal government paved the way for the project by giving the green light to a 50-year extension of the North West Shelf, an enormous gas plant that would process Browse gas. Western Australia Premier Roger Cook has described a "Browse-sized hole" in the state's gas supplies from next decade without it, despite most of its gas being earmarked for export. Just last week, the Australian arm of the United Arab Emirates' (UAE) oil and gas behemoth placed a $2.1 billion bet on Browse when it bought Shell's stake in the North West Shelf. But Ms Leys said none of this would matter if banks and other financiers were unable or unwilling to lend the project or its proponents the necessary funding. Elisa Leys focuses on Japan's public financing of fossil fuels and alternatives. ( Supplied ) "A really fair question here is to see if the financing pool really fully dries up; companies like Woodside will have to start reaching into their own pockets," she said. The heat on oil and gas companies from lenders was turned up this week after ANZ revealed it would not directly finance "new or expanded upstream gas projects". In its annual report, the bank said these projects included "LNG liquefaction plants, floating production storage and dedicated offloading infrastructure". It also included "new midstream infrastructure dedicated solely to new upstream gas projects … such as new transmission pipelines". How super could help fund renewables Australian super funds manage $4.5 trillion in retirement savings, but directing some of that war chest towards the clean energy transition could be more difficult than it seems. The move adds to pressure from other Big Four Australian banks, including the biggest of them all: Commonwealth Bank (CBA). Under its environment and social lending policy, CBA said it would "provide no project finance to new or expanded oil and/or gas extraction" developments. Meanwhile, NAB said it would not "directly" lend money to developments "where these assets are dedicated solely to greenfield oil and gas extraction projects". Saul Kavonic, an oil and gas analyst at MST Financial, said it was almost a moot point whether Australian banks were willing to lend to a project such as Browse. Mr Kavonic said every participant in the project was a serious player on the global stage and could access money from much deeper overseas funding pools. For starters, he said Japan in particular was willing to lend to oil and gas projects in which its homegrown champions were investing. Meanwhile, he said, the entry of the UAE's Abu Dhabi National Oil Company (ADNOC) on the scene, through its purchase of Shell's 16.7 per cent share of the North West Shelf, was a big deal in Australia. events.title: Kurdish minister rebuts 'nonsense' claims over Khor Mor gasfield attack
events.summary: A Kurdish minister has dismissed claims that a Kurdish group could have attacked the gasfield at Khor Mor, and warned against speculation while an investigation is under way. Ahmed Mufti, Deputy Minister for Natural Resources of the Kurdistan Region of Iraq, said he had confidence in the investigation launched by Prime Minister Ali Al Zaidi in the aftermath of Sunday's attack. “We are open to giving all the related data to the related party for the investigation,” he said, speaking at the foreign affairs think tank Chatham House. Earlier on Wednesday, Basim Al Badri, the head of Iraq’s National Security Department, said the Iraqi government had not ruled out the possibility of an internal attack by feuding Kurdish groups on the facility. “Perhaps a Kurdish party made use of these attacks. We cannot definitely attribute it to a specific faction - it could even be a foreign entity. Therefore the Iraqi government must exercise great precision in handling this important matter,” Mr Al Badri said. Mr Mufti told The National the claims were “nonsense”. “I’m surprised that within 24 hours [of the investigation’s launch] a bold statement like this can be made. I believe this is emotional. Let’s wait for a conclusion,” he told a Chatham House panel. “My advice to all and everyone is to refrain from making any statements right now until the final investigation is out,” he said. Around 10 million people in Iraq were left without electricity and cooking fuel as a result of the attack, according to estimates by Crescent Petroleum, which had operations at the gasfield. The price of electricity more than doubled. Mr Al Badri’s comments come as Iraq's government is struggling to disarm Iran-backed Shiite militias in the country, which have attacked energy facilities in the Gulf in response to the US war in Iran. Oil and gas insiders in Iraqi Kurdistan told The National that Khor Mor oil and gas operators would be able to know which direction the drone came from, with one describing Mr Al Badri’s comments as “really insulting, it’s like saying the sky is green”. Majid Jafar, Crescent Petroleum’s chief executive, said that although it was the 12th attack on the facility, it had been among the worst. “This last one really was a shock, especially at a time when the wider war seems to be de-escalating. We saw significant damage to the production facilities. We’re still assessing the scale. There will be lots of repairs,” Mr Jafar said. But he praised the Iraqi government’s response. “The attack was an attack on the people of Iraq and on Iraq’s sovereignty. We welcome Prime Minister Al Zaidi taking quick action, sending an investigation committee,” he said. Mr Al Zaidi had met oil and gas companies in June, promising to protect the companies and ensure their compensation in case of attack, he said. This was followed up with an official letter from the Iraqi government reiterating those assurances. “This time we hope to see, unlike previous attacks, concrete steps for protection and for identifying and holding accountable the perpetrators,” Mr Jafar said.

AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Operators face longer connection waits and a growing need to bring their own electricity OpenAI builds a kill switch for its research models 19 hours ago Australia may make knowingly selling unsafe AI a crime 22 hours ago Anthropic tiptoes into MS Office territory 1 day ago To thwart reverse engineering by agents, dev proposes blinding them 1 day ago 14-year-old creates tool for AI agents to band together like a team 1 day ago Datacenter power consumption in the US is growing roughly ten times faster than grid capacity, meaning facilities may soon need to find a large chunk of their own electricity from other sources. Surging demand for AI infrastructure is driving a wave of new server farms across America, but it is exposing long-term underinvestment in the grid networks required to deliver power where it's needed. Insurance broker Howden calculates that datacenters would need to source up to 58 percent of their power off the grid by 2030 just to keep their share of grid capacity from growing. Gartner warned in June that the energy consumed by AI datacenters is on track to grow 26 percent this year, and grid supply may be unable to keep pace with demand by the end of this decade. Howden's analysis of data from the US Energy Information Administration (EIA) and S&P Global found that since the year 2000, power being fed to data campuses has risen 19 percent a year on average, while the electricity grid expanded capacity by just 2 percent per annum over the same period. Datacenters' share of US grid capacity was circa five percent in 2025, up from 0.1 percent in 2000 – a 50-fold increase. Management consultancy Bain & Company issued a report two years ago warning that energy companies must switch gear and invest in building out grid capacity faster , as energy draw by server farms is expected to more than double by 2030. This doesn't mean that datacenters are in danger of eating all of America's electricity, at least not in the immediate future. The graph makes it appear that the two lines are about to cross, but the chart uses different scales: 1,400 gigawatts on the left axis for grid capacity, versus just 80 on the right for datacenters. Keeping datacenters at five percent of grid capacity requires 110 gigawatts of behind-the-meter capacity by 2030, Howden estimates – an expansion it considers unlikely. Instead, it expects a combination of greater reliance on the grid, slower development at power-constrained sites, and alternative supplies. For the largest, most power-constrained projects, Howden warns that grid delays of two to six years could mean $800 million to $2.4 billion in forgone revenue. "Power availability is becoming one of the defining challenges of the datacenter boom," says Howden head of Natural Resources Stuart Adam. "As demand for AI infrastructure accelerates, developers are increasingly looking beyond traditional grid connections to secure the electricity they need." events.title: J. Crew debuts new AI shopping tool that’s designed to think like a stylist
events.summary: Over the course of four decades, J. Crew’s style has woven cashmere cardigans, tweed jackets, and other preppy staples that have attracted high-profile fans including Michelle Obama, Demi Moore, and Meghan Markle. Throughout the apparel brand’s history—beginning as a catalog, then growing to become a physical and omnichannel retailer—those styling decisions were made by humans. But beginning today, there’s artificial intelligence at work too. On Wednesday, J. Crew announced a new consumer-facing, AI-enabled tool called Style Advisor, which runs on a collection of Anthropic’s models. Style Advisor is trained on data from thousands of outfit pairings from the company’s photo shoots and J. Crew’s styling principles, outfit and accessories pairings. “It’s not just about the piece that you’re looking for, but how to style it,” says Danielle Schmelkin, chief information officer at J. Crew. “What those stylists bring to the table—and really recommend more than just the item that you may have picked up when you walked into the store—we are really looking to create that online.” As more shoppers gravitate to agentic shopping, with more than 50% of global consumers using AI to buy goods within the past three months, new tools have proliferated ranging from Meta Platforms’ Muse agent and Alexa for Shopping from Amazon to AI shopping assistants created by retailers including Lowe’s, Ulta Beauty , and Macy’s. But while 56% of consumers say they use AI chat or search tools including Anthropic’s Claude or OpenAI’s ChatGPT, only 27% are gravitating to retailer-created AI shopping assistants, according to consulting firm McKinsey. “I think the visual piece is really important,” says Schmelkin of the distinctive edge that she promises Style Advisor will offer. In the future, the tool will also pull in data from a consumer’s past purchase history, allowing Style Advisor to make even more personalized recommendations, replicating that’s already possible during the omnichannel shopping experience. She says Style Advisor is also grounded in contextual details, asking questions to better understand a shopper’s intent. If a J. Crew customer were to tell it that they were looking for an outfit to attend a wedding—in, say, Miami, but not too formal—the tool will make recommendations based on these nuances. Style Advisor will debut on J. Crew’s desktop website and is expected to later be added to the retailer’s mobile app. J. Crew’s Style Advisor runs on a variety of Claude’s models, including Fable 5.1, which is leveraged to handle the more complex and ambiguous judgment that allows the tool to think and respond like a stylist. Claude’s Sonnet 5.5 and Haiku 4.5 support the speed and efficiency of the back-and-forth responses between consumers and the AI stylist, while Claude Opus 5.5 was utilized by J. Crew’s team to build a working prototype.  “What is the actual experience that we want the shopper to have, and then, how do we think about making sure that we’re mapping the right models to be able to deliver that,” says Lauren Collett, Anthropic’s enterprise go-to-market leader.  Schmelkin says J. Crew built in a back-end observation layer that allows the retailer to closely monitor the costs. “We want to make sure we are constantly refining and using these models in the right way, both in terms of the outputs for our customers, but also the efficiency we want to see to make this scalable,” says Schmelkin. Internally at J. Crew, to bolster AI adoption, the retailer has created an AI fluency program that begins with the basics and advances up through vibe coding. An internal AI lab, called “Second Thread,” began with just the tech team but has broadened to incorporate all corporate employees to discuss AI use cases and propose other technology solutions. For four years, J. Crew has also run a two-day tech summit that features workshops, hackathons, guest speakers, and vendor presentations. Initially, this programming was only available to the tech team, but J. Crew has more recently democratized access. Employees are also encouraged to use AI enterprise tools from Anthropic and OpenAI. The Style Advisor was conceptualized by a J. Crew digital product designer, who developed a working prototype before engineers were pulled into the project. The fact that the tool wasn’t mandated from the top of J. Crew’s C-suite reflects Schmelkin’s efforts to encourage employees to chart their own path on AI.  “I’ve been screaming to anyone who will listen for years now to get in there and build a habit,” says Schmelkin. “You have to find your a-ha moment and then all of a sudden…this could really change the way you think about your own life, work, and team productivity.” John Kell This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Progressives try to have it both ways on Medicare for All
events.summary: The News Progressive Democrats are trying a tricky feat as their party takes power : endorsing Medicare for All while quietly pushing for smaller steps toward it. Their dilemma began with the party’s remarkable midterm success. Democrats are united in attributing their electoral triumph in part to voter backlash against GOP healthcare moves — and this year, even purple-district candidates won while backing Medicare for All. But now, the left is split on how to make it happen. Without a filibuster or veto-proof majority in Congress next year, Democrats are calibrating their expectations for change based on what can potentially pass through the maneuver known as reconciliation, which requires only a simple majority. Some progressives are calling for a unified drive to lower the Medicare eligibility age, add guaranteed coverage up to age 19, and add dental and vision coverage. That could offer a middle ground for party leaders who are looking to stave off fights over bills likely to be vetoed by President Donald Trump. Embracing a big step toward pure Medicare for All could also hand a victory to progressives who have long pushed for legislative action — if they can settle for something less than the litmus test they set up. “It’s the perfect way for us to get ready for the next trifecta if we pass those three bills, and then if we mark up the entire Medicare for All bill,” said Rep. Pramila Jayapal, D-Wash., the lead sponsor of the House’s Medicare for All bill. Others on the left may not be content with pushing off action on the marquee policy until later. An incoming cohort of progressives want to push their party to vote on the full government-run healthcare package now. Rep.-elect Melat Kiros, D-Colo., said the program was “one of our number one priorities.” “I’ll never let perfect be the enemy of the good,” she added. “But if we’re not fighting like hell to actually get healthcare to every single American, then I don’t know what we’re doing here.” Centrists wanted the party to work towards consensus — a tall order for Democrats. Quite a few in the caucus want the party to focus on the underlying drivers of healthcare costs before considering a system where taxpayers pay for all healthcare. “I think we should talk more about cost and less about coverage,” said Rep. Jake Auchincloss, D-Mass. Democratic leaders have said they would need to have a “family conversation” on their path forward; a working group led by Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., and Terri Sewell, D-Ala., laid out a menu of options that included Medicare for All alongside many other proposals. “Are we messaging or are we getting something done?” said Rep. Adam Gray, D-Calif., a member of the moderate Blue Dogs. “We know that we have broad agreement that we want healthcare to be affordable, that we want it to be accessible … and that every American should have it, and so what are the solutions we can get agreement on to do that?” The Plan Democrats across the ideological spectrum have coalesced around their healthcare agenda in the near term. After relentlessly campaigning on reversing GOP-enacted Medicaid cuts and restoring lapsed health care subsidies, Democrats plan to put those up for a vote. They may even use the issues as leverage in the looming December government funding fight. “I think everything should be on the table,” said Rep. Glenn Ivey, D-Md. “It’s important for us to make sure we listen to and respond to the message of the voters, and I think they want to really get relief.” Rep. Kim Schrier, D-Wash., said that she wants both of those priorities to advance, but cautioned that “we still have the same president in the White House.” The View From The Senate Across the Capitol, Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., is pushing to use reconciliation to immediately advance his bill to lower the Medicare eligibility age to 55, add dental, vision and hearing coverage to the federal health insurance program for seniors, and ensure universal coverage for children through age 19. Sanders already has one powerful ally: Sen. Ron Wyden, D-Ore., the expected chair of the Senate Finance Committee, said he wants “to push for the boldest, best bill possible.” “I’m not taking anything off the table,” Wyden said, when asked about whether he supported using reconciliation to advance the legislation. Other senators are already calling for a more moderate approach. On Tuesday, Sen. Tammy Baldwin, D-Wis., introduced a bill that would lower the Medicare eligibility age to 50 and allow adults to buy into traditional Medicare or Medicare Advantage plans. The legislation would allow adults eligible for Affordable Care Act cost-sharing subsidies and premium tax credits to continue to use such assistance to help make Medicare plans more affordable. But it would not give adults taxpayer-funded Medicare before they turn 65. Nicholas and David’s View Democrats are going to eventually grapple with what exactly “Medicare for All” means to the disparate factions in their caucus. While Republicans will be quick to paint any effort as a first step toward implementing a single-payer healthcare system that replaces private insurance, the truth is more complicated. The reality is that very few Democrats on the campaign trail explicitly called for the enactment of a single government-run insurance plan. But with dozens of Democrats expected to launch presidential campaigns over the coming year, supporting universal healthcare coverage may quickly become, yet again, an up-or-down question for primary voters.

events.title: Revenge of the China hawks: Jensen Huang’s enemies take a victory lap
events.summary: The News In the fall of 2025, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was riding high on the wave of the AI boom. He also landed at the center of an ideological war over chip exports that the $4 trillion company and its allies now think played a pivotal role in his undoing. On one side were the China hawks inside the Trump administration — and circling outsiders — who worried Huang’s chips were helping fuel China’s AI ambitions. On the other side were Huang, David Sacks, and other technologists that argued for spreading US tech around the globe to ensure American-backed AI became the world standard. Huang’s long-held, pro-trade views were already unpopular with many of the think tankers, academics, national security staffers, and US government officials that make up a loosely held group of anti-China ideologues. But in a podcast interview with influential venture capitalists Bill Gurley and Brad Gerstner, Huang took things further, arguing the term “China hawk” is a badge of “shame” and that those who wear it are not “patriotic.” The slight did not go unnoticed, drawing the ire of anti-technology voices like far-right podcast host Steve Bannon and other critics who had railed against Huang’s lobbying against strict China export controls. “Let’s just say this — China hawks are patient and have long memories,” wrote Eric Sayers, a former Congressional defense staffer and current managing director of lobbyist Beacon Global Strategies, a firm that has done work on China policy, according to people familiar with the matter. Sayers re-upped his year-old X post again on Nov. 2, days before Huang admitted to having an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, on the back of weeks of media coverage digging into Megaspeed, an AI data center company based in Singapore that US government officials allege might be smuggling Nvidia chips into China. The implication was clear: Huang’s fate was not simply a result of the Nvidia CEO’s own personal failings or bad judgment. He had also made powerful enemies at the highest echelons of government that Nvidia now believes has all but stopped the company’s ability to lobby for the export of chips to China, according to a person briefed on the matter. Although there’s no evidence to suggest they are connected to any leaks, among the most prominent of the China hawks that have been mentioned, these people say, are Sayers’ former colleague, Ivan Kanapathy, who serves as senior director for Asia at the National Security Council, and Tarun Chhabra, who served as deputy assistant to the president and coordinator for technology and national security on the National Security Council, and Landon Heid, an NSC staffer who nearly became assistant secretary of commerce for export administration at the Bureau of Industry and Security. Chhabra now works for Anthropic, another vocal critic of chip sales to China, with CEO Dario Amodei comparing the practice to selling nuclear weapons to North Korea. Anthropic has also accused Chinese AI companies of stealing its intellectual property in order to train open weight AI models. Spokespeople for Nvidia, the White House, Commerce Department, State Department, NSC, Marco Rubio, and Beacon Global didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment. It’s unclear who was responsible for leaking national security documents that were used to discredit Huang. And whether the Nvidia CEO was the target of an espionage plot, or if there was any wrongdoing on his or Nvidia’s part, will be determined by investigators in the months ahead. But the damage has already shaved about $280 billion off the market value of the $4.2 trillion company. Huang’s now facing a board probe, shareholder lawsuits, Congressional questioning, and the near-certain prospect of details leaking out in drips and drabs. Several people familiar with their China policy agenda say the group of hawks wield considerable power and influence in DC, and the elimination of Huang from the other side of the debate will make the upcoming fight over export controls being added to the National Defense Authorization Act significantly easier. Reed’s view Huang obviously walked into a scandal, but the US government bears some responsibility for clearing up whether or not it’s investigating the founder of the country’s most successful company, potentially harming a company with massive strategic value and shaving off billions of dollars of a stock that’s in most people’s investment accounts. Nvidia’s success and failure has direct and indirect impacts on almost everybody in the US, and many around the world. We should get a full accounting of the impacts of an extrajudicial action against a US citizen by the government with enormous economic implications, positive and negative. Either something is classified or it’s not. Now that it’s been leaked, the rest of the information should be made public. Room for Disagreement From James Czerniawski, head of emerging technology policy at the Consumer Choice Center. “The government shouldn’t be able to weaponize a surveillance file against an American and their business. It should concern every American whenever intelligence is selectively surfaced and leveraged to advance certain policies, whether that means tighter chip export controls or building support for reauthorizing a deeply flawed surveillance program. When the government wields this kind of power, it isn’t just disrupting an individual’s life; it can put a target on an American company and create economic uncertainty in the marketplace. That kind of power demands real limitations and accountability. Protecting our national security is important, but giving the government carte blanche to use its surveillance capabilities is a recipe for disaster that will ultimately leave everyone worse off.”

events.title: A Tool Built by Election Deniers Said These Voters Were Dead. We Found Them Alive.
events.summary: A voter departs after casting a ballot at a polling location in Atlanta on Nov. 3. Elijah Nouvelage/Bloomberg via Getty Image Ahead of the midterms, conservative election activists discussed plans to wield a powerful new weapon in the war against fraud: a data tool built by one of their own that could identify suspicious voters and help with contesting their ballots. The system was put to the test this week in Forsyth County, Georgia, where a member of the county’s election board provided other officials with what he suggested was evidence of wrongdoing: four allegedly dead voters. But it turns out all four are alive and well, ProPublica determined. The board rejected the attempt to challenge their ballots. The effort, though, shows that even after last week’s blue wave, those who believe the 2020 election was stolen have continued to relentlessly search for ways to contest Republican losses. In Georgia, Democrats swept statewide offices . The board member who initiated the Forsyth County challenge, Max Clavijo, is a member of the Election Integrity Network, a group led by conservative lawyer Cleta Mitchell that works to restrict voting and tighten election laws and rules. Mitchell worked closely with Donald Trump in his attempt to overturn his defeat in the 2020 election and, since he retook the presidency, has been central to his push to assert greater federal control over voting . In the run-up to the midterms, on right-wing media and on private organizing calls, EIN participants outlined plans to search voter rolls with a software tool known as ELLY’s Election Monitor and contest ballots the tool deemed suspicious. ELLY was developed by EIN member Rick Richards. It aggregates public data from state voter files, federal change-of-address records, tax documents, obituaries, property websites like Zillow and other sources. In Georgia, State Election Board members and top staffers have urged counties to use the tool to search their voter rolls for signs of fraud. Richards talked about ELLY’s national potential on a podcast in late September, on which right-wing media personalities and activists touted its capacity to help GOP candidates contest their defeats. “We can prove the fraud that’s gone on in every state,” one commentator said. “This data will be able to set up challenges to those who lose.” The following month, on a private call with EIN members and other conservative activists, Richards promised to provide data from more than 3,000 counties to “citizen monitors” and GOP candidates to try to prove fraud, according to a recording reviewed by ProPublica. Read More How Cleta Mitchell Turned Trump’s “Big Lie” Into a Movement In an interview, Richards told ProPublica that he gave Clavijo data on Forsyth County at Clavijo’s request. He said in a subsequent email that their actions were meant to inform the board and remain confidential. Clavijo didn’t respond to questions from ProPublica. Richards refused to answer questions about whether Clavijo’s effort was part of a wider EIN campaign to contest votes cast in the midterms. “That’s irrelevant,” he said. “The data is the data. People can use it for what they want to.” Mitchell, EIN’s leader, didn’t respond to questions about the group’s plans related to ELLY, either in Georgia or nationally. In the months since some on Georgia’s State Election Board started promoting ELLY’s use, its accuracy has been much debated. The tool doesn’t have access to personal identifiers such as voters’ Social Security or driver’s license numbers or full dates of birth, which increases the potential for mismatches involving people with the same names. Voting rights groups have called ELLY error-prone . The Cherokee County election director complained to the state board after the tool falsely flagged a county board member’s spouse as dead . State Election Board members and Richards have defended ELLY. Accusations that the data is unreliable were “horse hockey,” Richards told ProPublica, explaining this was “a Southern colloquialism for B.S.” Late last week, according to several people familiar with the matter, Clavijo circulated documents to board members and Forsyth County’s election director. Based on data from ELLY, Clavijo questioned whether the names of more than 22,000 people on the county’s voter roll were correct and disputed the eligibility of 69 voters. In addition to four he claimed were deceased, he alleged others had moved out of the county or state, had voter ID irregularities or had registered under fictitious names, giving an initial as their first name. During the meeting, Clavijo claimed that he was not trying to disrupt the election’s certification or formally challenge the voters, a process outlined in statutes that can lead to ballots being tossed or voters removed from the rolls. (Richards also said they had not formally challenged ballots.) Clavijo said he was merely seeking “to clean the voter rolls” and inform the board so officials could investigate further. But other board members accused him of doing an end run around the formal challenge process. Barbara Luth, the board chair, said she felt “sorry for” Clavijo because activists were bypassing the challenge procedure “by coming to you and having you submit it.” Under fire from fellow board members, Clavijo admitted he could not vouch for the data’s accuracy. “I did not make any explicit accusation that the information was 100% correct,” he said. The cover letter Clavijo submitted with the challenges said that they had not been verified with any “human review,” according to sources familiar with the matter. Richards and Clavijo submitted obituaries for the voters they claimed were dead, but there were discrepancies between the information in them and the voters’ records. All of the obituaries said or suggested the deceased lived outside of Forsyth County, which would have made it impossible to vote there. One said the person lived in Arizona . ProPublica confirmed that all four are actually alive. Alexis Ramirez, a night-shift nurse, told ProPublica that she cast her ballot during early voting. She was surprised to hear her vote had been contested — and why. “It’s kind of crazy that they attempted to do that without trying to prove it first,” she said. Saramma George, another voter Richards and Clavijo claimed was dead, said she was “really angry” to have the validity of her ballot questioned. In the third case, ProPublica spoke with a voter’s son, who said she was alive but didn’t want to talk to ProPublica. Her “ballot is valid,” he said. The fourth voter, Chris Strickland, said, “I don’t know where they’re getting their information from, but it’s false. I’m alive. I’m here.” The majority of the challenges — 38 of them, according to people familiar with the matter — involved voters who’d registered using an initial. events.title: CFTC investigates if Kalshi improperly self-certified event contracts
events.summary: Kalshi called it a minor issue in how the contracts were filed and said it is working with the CFTC to address the matter. Prediction market platforms are allowed to self-certify event contracts without the federal agency's approval, as long as they comply with the Commodity Exchange Act. The Commodity Futures Trading Commission is investigating whether prediction market platform Kalshi failed to properly inform the agency of proposed event contracts, Kalshi confirmed to CNBC. Kalshi called it a minor issue in how the contracts were filed and said it is working with the CFTC to address the matter. The CFTC flagged weather-related contracts, Kalshi said. The leading prediction market platform didn't say when the agency began investigating Kalshi. The CFTC didn't immediately respond to a request for comment. Politico first reported on the probe on Tuesday, noting charges could happen soon, based on the CFTC's private notification to Kalshi. The platform declined to comment on any possible charges. Prediction market platforms are allowed to self-certify event contracts without the federal agency's prior approval, as long as they comply with the Commodity Exchange Act. The self-certification allows for faster introduction of new contracts. "The notice is about a procedural error involving the submission of a handful of contracts, many of which weren't live," said Elisabeth Diana, head of communications at Kalshi. "We are already addressing the issue." The move is the latest by the CFTC as it seeks to rein in prediction markets, which face growing scrutiny in Washington from regulators and members of Congress . In August, the CFTC ordered Kalshi to take down sports-related " mention markets " — where speculators can trade on what individuals will say in a broadcast or speech — while it looked into the event contract type. The agency is also conducting a broad probe into competitor Polymarket , which includes reviewing if the company violated a 2022 settlement with the CFTC to prohibit U.S. traders from accessing its international trading platform. Polymarket's domestic exchange operates separately from the global platform. Prediction markets are also expected to face heightened scrutiny once the Democratic Congress is sworn into office in January. Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., in a Tuesday social media post on X , called for a ban on sports prediction markets — which account for the overwhelming majority of volume on leading platforms. Disclosure: CNBC and Kalshi have a commercial relationship that includes customer acquisition and a minority investment.

events.title: Dubai's Parkin posts record profit as fines outpace fees for first time
events.summary: Dubai's public parking operator Parkin reported a 27 per cent annual jump in third-quarter profit, with income from fines and seasonal permits outpacing parking fees for the first time. Net profit after tax was at Dh199.2 million ($54.2 million), as revenue grew 21 per cent year-on-year to a record Dh415.2 million, the company said in a filing to the Dubai Financial Market. Its enforcement category – which groups fines and seasonal parking passes – contributed Dh136.4 million, surpassing parking fees that added Dh127.8 million, which was a 5 per cent annual drop. Earlier this year, Parkin introduced micro cameras on kerbsides to catch motorists who avoid tickets. Cars with automatic cameras to scan entire streets have been operating for several years. Earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation – a key metric for profitability – for the three-month period jumped 28 per cent to a record Dh255 million. For the third quarter, Parkin sold a record 110,600 seasonal passes, which was a 37 per cent annual jump, while total fines issued jumped 34 per cent to about 916,100. For the first nine months of 2026, Parkin's profit grew by a quarter to Dh550.6 million, as revenue through September climbed 24 per cent to more than Dh1.16 billion. Ebitda for the period also grew by 24 per cent to Dh703.4 million. During the period, seasonal permits grew 58 per cent to about 308,600, while fines rose 24 per cent to more than 2.36 million. The company added about 53,500 parking spaces over the past 12 months to lift its total to a record 272,500, it said. Parkin's results demonstrate “the strength of our diversified business, with growth across developer parking, seasonal cards and our other revenue streams more than offsetting softer public parking revenues during the quarter”, chief executive Mohamed Al Ali said in a statement. “We continued to execute our growth strategy with discipline,” he added. Parkin has been playing a major role in Dubai 's strategy of expanding its paid public parking network to curb illegal parking and better manage available spaces. Last week, paid parking was extended to certain areas of the emirate's Jebel Ali Industrial area and Al Furjan. Last month, Parkin partnered with Q Mobility to manage smart parking facilities across Etihad Rail’s passenger station network .
