There was one problem: there was a slim chance the depiction might be wrong. This week, a small team of four Australian researchers have published their work confirming the result based on a new machine learning algorithm using the same base data. The 2019 Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) image came from hundreds of scientists working together to capture the first direct view of a black hole's shadow. The measurements were taken at eight telescopes around the world, at locations including Chile, the US, and Antarctica. Reconstructing the image from the data so geographically distant meant instrument and environment errors could influence the accuracy of the resulting image. Potentially, alternative analyses of the data could have reconstructed an image without the iconic ring shape. Samuel Lai – a postdoctoral fellow at the Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organisation (CSIRO) in Western Australia – and his team created an independent imaging algorithm to process the historic dataset to validate the result. The new approach used closed triplets (using three telescopes for error correction) rather than station pairs in an effort to reduce error. To the relief of the EHT team, the new image recreated the iconic ring-like image seen in the original, according to a paper published in Nature today . In a prepared statement, Lai said taking pictures of black holes was not easy. "It is like standing in your backyard and trying to take a photo of a doughnut on the Moon," he said. He explained that when his team applied new advanced machine learning and artificial intelligence techniques to the original Event Horizon Telescope dataset, they found a black hole almost identical in size and shape to the historic EHT image. "Importantly, our model had no idea what a black hole looked like when we applied it to the M87 data. This is the first truly independent validation of the EHT image, an important step in the scientific process," he said. Event Horizon Telescope director Laurent Loinard welcomed the new study. "It is extremely gratifying to see that an elegant, entirely independent method recovers the ring structure of M87 across several years, in excellent agreement with the EHT Collaboration's published results," he said. ® Russian cloud Yandex says drone attacks on its datacenters caused data loss Now enables backup by default and hints a little on-prem infra never hurt anyone US bit barn boom sees energy needs grow 10x as fast as grid capacity Operators face longer connection waits and a growing need to bring their own electricity From expertise to intelligence: NISCO deploys world's first swarm-intelligence steel model at scale PARTNER CONTENT: 300+ AI applications delivering surges in core metrics and annual cost reduction of over CNY100m AI echo chambers and sanity in tech leadership: Three case studies Altman, Torvalds, Yen. events.title: What to know about this year’s UN climate talks
events.summary: It’s that time of year again: Thousands of delegates, lobbyists, and journalists are gathered for the annual UN climate talks, taking place this time in Antalya, Turkey. COP31 officially kicked off on November 8, marking the beginning of negotiations on one of the biggest stages of the climate world. Turkey and Australia are cohosting this year’s talks, which are scheduled to wrap up on November 20. This annual gathering can often serve as an indicator of where the world stands on addressing and adapting to the climate crisis. And this year’s talks are sure to be a doozy—expect a lot of back and forth on fossil fuels and climate finance in particular. Here’s what you should know about COP31.   In recent years, the tension always feels high when COP rolls around. (COP stands for “Conference of the Parties.”) But this year feels especially charged: The world is still grappling with the ongoing war in Iran, which has disrupted the Middle East and sent economic shock waves around the world as energy prices have spiked. This year’s COP will be the second without a formal delegation from the US. President Trump formally withdrew the country from the Paris Agreement earlier this year and is in the process of withdrawing from the UN Framework Committee on Climate Change. That’s the treaty that allows formal participation in negotiations.  Meanwhile, things aren’t looking good for the Paris Agreement, which was established at UN climate talks 11 years ago, setting a goal of limiting warming to 1.5 °C over preindustrial levels. In a report published in September, the UN Environment Program acknowledged that global warming is set to exceed that 1.5 °C goal, “likely within the next few years.” So as climate talks kick off, there’s an obvious, urgent question looming about how to quickly cut emissions to limit warming. There’s also the major issue of how to pay for efforts to address emissions and to help a warming world endure the inevitable damage.  Two years ago, talks ended in a goal of mobilizing $300 billion per year by 2035 to help pay to reduce emissions and adapt to climate change. (Rich nations provided $136.7 billion in 2024, according to the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development. ) And last year, the COP30 agreement included a goal of tripling the money for adaptation over that period. (Such funding has been quite flat over the past few years.) The world got a tragic reminder of just how high the stakes are earlier this year, when a glacier collapse caused devastating flooding in the Himalayas. The flood killed approximately 1,500 people, left over 5,000 missing, and caused nearly $5 billion in damage. The UN loss and damages fund committed $20 million to helping Nepal recover (less than 1% of the total estimated cost to the country). Another key trend to watch is how the formal negotiations engage with the topic of fossil fuels. Three years ago, the final agreement text explicitly called for a transition away from them. But it felt as if things took a step back last year, when the final agreement didn’t even mention the phrase “fossil fuels” once. This will be an interesting conversation, especially because cohosts Turkey and Australia have both faced criticism over their relationships with these fuels—Australia is a major exporter of coal and natural gas, and Turkey’s grid relies heavily on fossil fuels, including coal. Outside the formal negotiations, COP31 president Murat Kurum, Turkey’s environment minister, is spearheading a side agenda, including two informal initiatives that will be worth watching. These wouldn’t be part of the official agreement text, but countries could sign on to signal support.   One is a pledge to make AI more sustainable; this is almost comically squishy, even as voluntary COP pledges go. The text includes explicit wording that it creates no new obligations for countries, so don’t expect anything resembling enforcement there. The COP leadership is also pushing to make electricity a larger part of member countries’ energy use. Today, only about 23% of global energy is used in the form of electricity. Fossil fuels, like gasoline in vehicles or natural gas for heating, make up the bulk of the rest. Shifting to more electricity use, and relying on cleaner sources for that electricity, could help drive down emissions. The new pledge’s target is for electricity to make up 35% of total energy consumption by 2035.  With leadership billing this as an “implementation COP,” it would be great to see some real, tangible progress on the global challenge of addressing climate change. I’m not expecting anything groundbreaking, but we’ll be tuned in to see what the final agreement shapes up to be.  This article is from The Spark, MIT Technology Review ’s weekly climate newsletter. To receive it in your inbox every Wednesday, sign up here .

events.title: Chris Kempczinski's new value menu for McDonald's
events.summary: The Signal Interview An 11-item menu board from the 1950s still hangs in McDonald’s Chicago headquarters, recalling the era when Ray Kroc struck his franchise agreement with the McDonald brothers and began building the world’s best known fast-food chain. The 10-cent root beers are long gone, but Chris Kempczinski, who marked his seventh anniversary as CEO this week, is having to pay new attention to its value proposition. The business is facing a “challenging” US consumer environment, he told investors this week, with comparable sales falling 0.2% in the three months to September. Kempczinski’s assurance that the company had started to turn things around in the last month of the quarter helped revive a stock that had fallen a jarring 32% between February and October. But to reverse the drop in customer visits, he has had to put more marketing dollars behind potentially slimmer-margin deals, like a $2 breakfast sandwich with free fries for loyalty program members. “Our goal is straightforward,” Kempczinski told Wall Street: “Customers should see a clear and compelling value proposition every time they consider McDonald’s.” Few companies see as many consumers each week as McDonald’s does, and it has seen growing numbers of lower-income Americans staying home for breakfast or skipping it altogether, Kempczinski says in an interview for . “Housing, medical care, childcare, utilities, transport — all of those things are putting, I think, a lot of pressure on people’s disposable income,” he says. McDonald’s sometimes benefits in tough economic times, as higher-earning households trade down from pricier restaurants. But the US economy’s current “K-shaped” nature means that wealthier households are still eating out in pricier restaurants, rather than trading down to eat burgers and fries. Reserving the right to get smarter in a franchised system Kempczinski’s $8.5 billion game plan, announced in June and dubbed “McDonald’s > NEXT,” is the second strategic overhaul of his tenure. Designed to update the group’s menu and modernize restaurants, he expects it to lift sales and margins by making McDonald’s “more customers’ first choice more often.” The complication is that about 95% of the world’s 46,000 McDonald’s restaurants are owned and operated by franchisees — and some have pushed back against a proposal that could require $650,000 to $800,000 of investment per store. There is tension in any business where customers want better value, franchisees want healthier returns, and shareholders want faster growth. McDonald’s relies on its 5,000 independent partners to execute its strategy, Kempczinski notes, which means he must operate “through influence, not through direct control.” A clear focus on growth can unite his disparate stakeholders, he believes. “If you have growth and the pie is expanding, it’s amazing how harmonious everything is,” he says. “When the pie isn’t growing, then everybody starts to think about their share … and then a system can turn on itself.” Restaurant upgrades are essential for driving that growth, he says, because “you can’t sell a $5 burger in a $1 lobby.” But he knows he can’t influence franchisees who think he’s not listening to them, and he says the headline number McDonald’s put on its proposals “for sure is going to get knocked down” in response to their feedback. He won’t be so “dogmatic” about the details of his strategy that he won’t learn from their feedback, he says. “We have a saying here at McDonald’s: We reserve the right to get smarter.” This week, he told analysts he feels “overall, good” about franchisees’ willingness to roll out the upgrades his strategic plan requires. Changing a risk-averse culture through ‘positive shaming’ Kempczinski, who grew up in a Catholic household in Cincinnati and would visit McDonald’s after Friday night football games, admits to some Midwestern conservatism. When he was invited to pick art for his office from the McDonald’s archive, he chose an all-American Norman Rockwell painting. But the former Procter & Gamble brand executive says he balances those instincts with a restlessness that he is trying to bring to McDonald’s. “The company is never going to go faster than the pace that the CEO sets,” he says, and he is pushing people to take more risks and make faster decisions. McDonald’s is “awesome” at testing new offerings and ideas, Kempczinski says, by way of example. With thousands of restaurants, “we can do A/B testing forever … but you can also test for too long.” The danger in a collaborative culture like at McDonald’s is that “everybody owns it and nobody owns it,” he observes. “Yes, we all need to work together, but at the end of the day, there needs to be a person or a group who’s actually held accountable for the results.” A CEO can do that by appointing people to senior positions who model the behavior they want others to adopt, he says. And, instead of shaming people for their mistakes, he believes “positive shaming” — praising top performers who set the right example — gets better results. The lessons of a Big Arch and a little bite McDonald’s menu now ranges from Cookie Butter Iced Coffee to the Red Bull Dragonberry Energizer drink, and includes far more chicken than it once did. Demand for chicken has been surging for several years, and the home of the Big Mac already sells more of it than KFC or Chick-fil-A. But Kempczinski sees “a lot of headroom” to sell more still, he says, with a push to add KFC-style breaded chicken to the menu. McDonald’s already commands more than 40% of the beef business in its 10 biggest markets, amounting to about $50 billion, he explains — but it has only 20% of the $130 billion chicken market. His strategy is about more than building on the power of McNuggets and McCrispy Strips, he says. “It’s just simple math.” Consumers have higher expectations than before about the taste and quality of their fast food, Kempczinski says, even as they also want it at affordable prices. “And the reality is, today, we don’t have enough customers saying that McDonald’s is the best place to go, if I want to get a great tasting chicken sandwich, or if I want to get a great cup of coffee.” In an hour-long interview, Kempczinski doesn’t refer to any of his menu items as “the product” — the sterile marketing term he used to describe a new Big Arch burger he introduced in March. The awkwardly small bite he took during one of his regular “Chris K” LinkedIn videos prompted days of mockery, as gleeful rivals recorded themselves sinking their molars into their own burgers. Kempczinski says he and his team debated whether and how to respond before deciding to “just let the internet run wild.” Jumping in and trying to control the conversation would have been “the biggest mistake” they could have made, he concluded. “The internet’s undefeated. events.title: How the MAGA map cracked
events.summary: The News It’s easy to understand why Republicans couldn’t imagine the Trump coalition cracking. The MAGA electoral map, first built in 2016, stayed mostly intact for eight years and five elections. Rural areas stayed red or got redder. Non-white, working class areas drifted away from Democrats. The party of the New Deal was reduced to an urban and suburban archipelago, blue smudges on a red map that the president liked to show off to White House visitors. One good thing about America’s languid vote count is that a more interesting picture fills in after the big story is over. We knew last week that the Trump coalition came apart, and we’re learning now that Democrats won the country by 14 points, in the average House vote. Republicans couldn’t imagine that shift before Tuesday. Obviously, they didn’t plan for it when they heeded the president, in deep red states, and re-drew congressional maps. They planned for at least another decade of the Trump coalition, with rural America locked up, suburban America still competitive, and non-white voters alienated from the “woke” opposition party. Gerrymander hubris The story of North Carolina this year is the shattered GOP gerrymander — seven seats that backed Trump by double digits in 2024, then elected Democrats. The stories in Indiana, South Carolina, and Utah are that Republicans tried to re-draw their maps, failed, and were saved from electoral disaster. Had Republicans built the districts they wanted, most of them, across those three states, would have voted for Democrats. Why were Republicans so hubristic? Look closely at what happened from 2016 to last week. The Trump electoral map was the most solid either party had built in generations. It kept the upper Midwest competitive, which George W. Bush hadn’t been able to do. It made Appalachia nearly uninhabitable for Democrats, which Ronald Reagan couldn’t do. Richard Nixon couldn’t carry a GOP Congress on his coattails. Trump did several times — both chambers in 2016 and 2024, the Senate in 2018, the House in 2022. Every political coalition falls apart eventually, unless you’re running the Liberal Democratic Party of Japan or something. Barack Obama’s 2008 win led Democrats into some dizzy daydreams about a “permanent” majority that Republicans could only temporarily defeat. “Obama doesn’t need right-leaning whites anymore,” Ron Brownstein wrote in 2013, after Democrats won a second presidential election with a minority of white voters but a supermajority of non-whites. For a long time, both parties wondered if Trump had built something sturdier than that. He wasn’t counting on demographic change to keep Republicans in power. He’d ditched the GOP’s commitment to entitlement reform, which alienated working class voters, and its support for free trade, which was one of the Democrats’ best arguments when those voters got queasy about their cultural views. Not only did he do it, but Republicans who campaigned like him were able to keep those gains. In 2016, Trump carried 206 counties that had supported Barack Obama twice. Democrats believed this was a fluke, that more populist politics could win them back — not asking “if we broke up the big banks, would that end racism?” In 2020 they campaigned like eastern Iowa, northeast Ohio, and southeast Pennsylvania had gotten their anti-establishment votes out of their system and could be won again.But when he won back the White House in 2024, Trump carried 181 of those counties. And nearly every Republican walked the same map. The GOP’s disastrous midterm strategy was premised on voters who had become comfortable supporting Republicans after 2016 and nodded when Mike Johnson said “this isn’t your grandfather’s Democrat Party” — always “Democrat,” never “Democratic.” Democrats changed Republicans didn’t plan for Democrats to change, and offer a less culturally left-wing package to these voters. In much of the country, Democrats were able to reintroduce themselves and slice up the Trump map. The Rio Grande Valley and South Florida were disasters for Republicans, who treated Latino voters like new members of the MAGA movement, not as the swing voters they are. But the drop-off with rural white voters was more damaging in more of the country. Republican gerrymandering followed a simple formula: Carve up Democratic cities and overwhelm them with rural voters. This worked because they had a good idea of how Republican those rural voters were. It stopped working because Democrats competed for so many of them. That explains the disaster in North Carolina, where 47% of white voters backed Sen.-elect Roy Cooper, and Republicans did historically poorly with those voters down-ballot. Rep. Tim Moore, who had helped draw the state’s gerrymander, had given himself a seat where liberal Mecklenburg County voters were outnumbered by rural conservatives to the west. Lakesha Womack beat him by doubling the Democratic margin in Mecklenburg and by losing by less elsewhere, cutting his margins in rural counties by 15 to 20 points. “Rural voters are not necessarily all the way MAGA voters,” North Carolina Democratic Party chair Anderson Clayton told me last week. “They’re not necessarily bought into Republican politics. It’s just that the Republicans were the only party that’s been communicating to them and aggressively trying to be in their communities, and running candidates in them.” Clayton had been trying to make this change for years. Lots of Democrats had, with little success. This gave Republicans the confidence that, while Trump voters were harder to motivate without him on the ballot, they had ruled out supporting Democrats and could be convinced to come out to protect their guns, kids, and religion from them.If that’s not true, the electoral map stops looking so solid. Seats built to withstand a +13 swing to Democrats couldn’t be saved on a +14 swing. But Republicans believed that Trump’s nationalism and populism were locking in voters; Democrats were relying on their messy coalition and old issues, like protecting Social Security, losing their most loyal voters to the grave. It was a good strategy for a decade. It lasted longer than Karl Rove’s “permanent majority,” which was less appealing to rural voters and more appealing in the suburbs. But neither theory of the electorate worked without voters who believed their vote was protecting their way of life – culture and costs. What’s next What implications does this have for the electoral map, which both parties are still empowered to re-draw next year? It’s definitely changed the risk assessment. Republicans learned that black voter turnout will increase, against them, if their party draws maps to reduce their power — and that they don’t get a commensurate thank-you turnout from white voters. That will probably cost them a Senate seat in Mississippi, nearly cost them another in Louisiana, and almost blocked Marsha Blackburn’s wide path to the governor’s mansion in Tennessee. events.title: Is Jensen Huang’s bad behavior more commonplace than it seems?
events.summary: The AI industry is still reeling from Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s honeypot scandal, but some in the industry see it as an issue that’s much larger than one man. The Chinese government has been active in economic espionage for decades, and with semiconductors at the center of the AI boom, there’s intense pressure to infiltrate any company involved. At the same time, many of the executives getting rich off that boom have made themselves easy targets. As CEO of investment intel firm Heron Intelligence, Nate Singer has a unique view into the problem. His firm works on corporate due diligence: Essentially, making sure companies know the relevant dirt before making a major acquisition or executive hire. And while the Nvidia case is particularly severe, Singer says there are lots of similar cases in the semiconductor industry that have stayed under the radar. “We’ve got former employees talking about behavior at senior executive levels,” Singer told TechCrunch, saying executives are “really crossing lines that should not be crossed.” In a widely circulated LinkedIn post , Singer detailed one case in which a CEO’s wife made an unexpected board room appearance, “screaming about her husband and another company exec flying around in the corporate jet with a couple young ladies (who also turned out to be state-sponsored actors).” It’s an alarming story, but an unfortunately common one. Singer says he’s seen at least three reports of similar cases, and suspects many more have gone unreported. “There’s a lot more than this one woman,” Singer said. “They are embedded in these companies.” Semiconductor companies are already big targets for international trade secret theft. There have been dozens of prosecutions for similar cases in recent years, including a case involving the fabrication powerhouse TSMC in 2007. In 2017, four executives at an unnamed “Bay Area semiconductor equipment manufacturer” were charged with stealing trade secrets for use at a competing company in China. According to the indictment, the technology in question “related to the high-volume manufacturing of semiconductor wafers to be used in lighting and electronic devices, such as flat screen televisions and smart phones.“ Any sexual elements in such cases rarely become public, in part because of the severe consequences for executives and their companies. But according to Singer, the ongoing threat has become a kind of open secret in the industry. “There are a lot of senior people in the industry that know this is happening, and are effectively condoning it,” he told TechCrunch. events.title: OpenAI’s quarterly revenue reportedly crosses $10B for the first time
events.summary: OpenAI is bouncing back from the doldrums it experienced earlier this year. The company’s quarterly revenue crossed $10 billion for the first time, thanks to strong demand for its recent AI models, Bloomberg reported , citing anonymous sources. If true, that would represent an almost 50% jump from the $6.7 billion in sales the company reportedly recorded in the second quarter. That would also mark a sizable increase in its revenue growth rate, which was previously said to be about 18% between the first and second quarters of the year. OpenAI’s profitability picture also appears to have improved, with its adjusted operating margin narrowing from -150% in the second quarter to -109% in the third quarter, the report said. OpenAI, one of the first to commercialize AI models, wasn’t exactly struggling to continue growing its top-line expansion — 18% growth on top of $5.7 billion in quarterly revenue is massive by any measure, especially compared to most software businesses. But it was seeing those gains be trumped by its archrival Anthropic, which has taken the lead in capturing the enterprise market for AI models and recently reported Q3 revenue of $17 billion . OpenAI’s broader focus helped it attract a large user base and gain popularity early on, and it says it has over a billion users , but it’s reasonable to assume most of those are free users or subscribers to its cheapest plans. Still, the company lagged Anthropic in catering to enterprises, a market where the Claude maker has pulled ahead, at least in terms of revenue growth. OpenAI has recently benefited from a combination of tighter pricing, discounts, improving models, and a greater focus on building more enterprise-focused products and AI agents that can help people complete tasks. OpenAI has now reached an annual revenue run rate of $50 billion, according to Bloomberg. Meanwhile, Anthropic, which is seeking a $1.4 trillion valuation in an IPO likely to happen soon , said yesterday that its annual revenue run rate had increased by $10 billion within a month to $81 billion as of the end of October. (Note that OpenAI and Anthropic calculate their annualized revenue differently: Anthropic counts sales made by its cloud partners, while OpenAI only reports its share of some sales through its partners.) None of those figures are small, of course, but the companies are also competing with models from Meta, Amazon, Microsoft, and Google, as well as a plethora of cheaper but still highly capable models from open source AI labs, especially those from China. events.title: Tired of spending time fixing other people's AI slop at work? How to talk to them about it
events.summary: Work AI is making a mess of how humans interact at work Work Forcing workers to use AI can be counterproductive—3 tips for a better approach Work IBM chief talent officer: Top 2 skills entry-level workers need to succeed now Work Your AI interviewer will see you now—what experts think job seekers should know Work 3 signs work is consuming your life—and what to do about it: ‘Catch it now,' says expert You open slides you got from a teammate for a joint project presentation you're giving. Within minutes you suspect that it's largely AI-generated. The stats are incorrect and the writing is littered with generic phrases that sound plausible at a glance but, upon inspection, say nothing of substance. AI was supposed to make work faster and easier, and sometimes it does. Eighty-five percent of surveyed workers, all of whom were active AI users, said the technology saved them between one and seven hours per week, according to a Workday study of 3,200 full-time employees published in January. But as the author of " Managing Up " and an executive coach to high performers at companies like Google, Amazon and JPMorgan, I've seen a new problem emerge. You may regularly find yourself on the receiving end of what looks like finished work that still needs hours of editing. The Workday survey found that nearly 40% of the time "saved" from using AI was then lost to "rework" like verifying, correcting and rewriting. Calling that extra work out to your colleagues and bosses can feel awkward. You might use AI too; 40.5% of employed U.S. adults ages 18 to 64 reported using AI for work in Q3 2026, according to data from the Real-Time Population Survey. So you don't want to sound hypocritical. Plus, you can't always be 100% sure someone used AI, even if it seems obvious to you. So how do you address the extra work landing on your plate without the conversation becoming confrontational? Begin by showing that you're not trying to embarrass anyone or prove them wrong. You're on the same side. Frame your feedback in terms of working toward an outcome that preserves the quality of the work and the team's reputation. That way, your intentions are clear, which makes the discussion less adversarial from the outset. "We both want the executive team to be happy with this." "Since both of our names are on this, I hope you'll agree it needs to hold up to scrutiny from the client." "The goal is for the final version to have the most accurate and up-to-date numbers." Avoid saying, "this whole thing looks AI-generated," especially if you can't prove that. A blanket accusation takes the focus off of what needs to change and puts the other person on the defensive. Instead, point to concrete issues such as vague wording, missing context, hallucinated examples or off-brand visuals. "A few things jumped out to me that we need to fix before this goes to leadership." "There are two sections where the data could better match what we had previously discussed." "The formatting is different throughout, so I think that needs another quick pass." This is particularly important when speaking with your boss or someone senior, since you don't want to suggest that you're judging their choices . It can help to acknowledge if you use AI too, which makes it clear that the extra work and the impression the report or presentation could make are the problems, not the tool itself. "I could be wrong, but some of this reads like AI was involved. I use it too, so that's not the issue. I'm more concerned about making sure we have enough time to edit it before the meeting." "Some of the phrasing and design choices in a couple sections have an AI-generated feel that people are getting more sensitive to. Since I also use ChatGPT and Claude in my work, I'm pretty familiar with some of the 'tells,' and I'd rather remove those so no one makes false assumptions." "People are getting quicker to label certain things AI-generated even when they're not and I'd hate for that to distract from the quality of the work." Be specific about how much time it's already required or will involve to clean up the work and whether it's taken away from other priorities. The other person may not realize the cost unless you explicitly say it. Depending on the relationship, you might ask them to review AI-generated content before sending it over, limit when AI is used or simply flag it up front so you can plan accordingly. "I've spent time redoing this, which meant pushing back a project for my boss. I hope you understand that's not sustainable. So going forward, can you give AI drafts a quick glance before sending them my way? That'll help me focus my time on core changes." "One thing that would help is knowing when AI was used. That gives me a better sense of how much verification and editing may be needed before it's ready to go so that we don't miss any deadlines.

events.title: Labour MPs warn against weakening electric vehicle targets ahead of crunch talks
events.summary: Exclusive: Cutting 2030 goal would be a ‘step backwards’, say MPs, as ministers clash over proposed reductions Labour MPs are urging the government not to weaken its electric vehicle targets as divided cabinet ministers prepare for a crunch meeting on Thursday to thrash out a compromise. Members of the climate and nature crisis caucus (CNCC) say ministers must not water down a legal requirement for carmakers to ensure that 80% of the vehicles they sell in 2030 are electric, saying doing so would be a backward step and “shortsighted”. The intervention comes as Louise Haigh, the de facto deputy prime minister, prepares to meet the energy, business and transport secretaries to decide whether to change the target. A meeting planned for Wednesday has been pushed back to Thursday, according to government sources. Jonathan Reynolds, the business secretary, wants to slash the target to 50%, while Heidi Alexander, the transport secretary, wants to cut it to about 60%. Miatta Fahnbulleh , the energy secretary, is pushing for it to remain as close to 80% as possible. Sources say Haigh, who is standing in for Andy Burnham after the prime minister recused himself over a potential conflict of interest, is likely to support a middle route and agree a new target of between 60% and 65%. With a final announcement likely this month, Labour MPs are making a final push for ministers not to reduce the target, which many see as emblematic of the government’s approach to the green agenda. Chris Hinchliff, the chair of the CCNC, wrote to Alexander on Tuesday saying that a decision to cut the 2030 target would be a “step backwards”. “This would undermine the government’s wider net zero ambitions and our credibility as a climate leader on the world stage,” he added. Arguing that reducing the target would undermine Burnham’s push to reindustrialise Britain, he said: “Diluting the mandate would be a backward-looking distraction from the urgent need for a coordinated industrial strategy.” The Department for Transport has been contacted for comment. Hinchliff is being backed by several other Labour members of the caucus. Clive Lewis, the MP for Norwich South, said: “We need more ambitious targets, not less ambitious ones. What this will say to the country is that we set these targets and then drop [them]. We need to show some consistency and ambition.” Nadia Whittome, the MP for Nottingham East, said: “This is the government’s biggest decarbonisation policy. Watering it down would carry serious environmental consequences and it wouldn’t help the cost of living.” Some Labour MPs from industrial areas are backing cuts to the target. Antonia Bance, the MP for Tipton and Wednesbury, said: “A 50% ZEV target by 2030 would give manufacturers a more realistic pathway while still keeping us on track for net zero. “We can cut emissions and create the cars of the future – but we also need to protect good jobs, investment and supply chains here in the UK.” Others in the party, however, are concerned that decisions such as weakening the EV policy and approving the Jackdaw gasfield are undermining the government’s green credentials and could risk boosting the Green party. “Climate is not something that seems to be close to Andy [Burnham]’s heart,” said one MP. “Decisions like the EV mandate and Jackdaw develop a sense, which the public pick up, that we are not very progressive.” Electric, hybrid and low-emission cars

events.title: At COP31, Turkey pushes zero-waste plan to curb climate change
events.summary: As world leaders arrive at United Nations climate talks in the Turkish resort town of Antalya, calling for urgent climate action, co-host Turkey also wants to halve the amount of global waste in the next decade ANTALYA, Turkey -- As world leaders gathered for United Nations climate talks in the Turkish resort town of Antalya on Wednesday, host Turkey urged countries to commit to a zero-waste initiative aimed at reducing emissions and helping get global efforts to curb climate change back on track. Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan touted his country's progress on recycling, saying its rate had risen from about 13% in 2017, when the zero waste movement began, to about 40% by the end of 2025. "Some 90 million tons of waste have been brought back into our economy,” Erdogan told the leaders' summit. “We’ll not stop here and we will continue working and making every effort until we achieve the goal of zero waste." Turkey has outlined 10 priorities for this year’s climate talks, known as COP31 , with a pledge to accelerate electrification and the zero-waste initiatives emerging as major talking points during the opening days of the conference. Turkish first lady Emine Erdogan, who attended Wednesday's talks, has been a driving force behind the zero-waste initiative, which aims to reduce methane emissions, cut food waste and promote a circular economy in which materials are reused and recycled. “Recovered materials can be cheaper when reliable supplies, efficient processing and nearby demand outweigh the costs of collection, sorting and transport,” said Samed Agirbas, president of the nonprofit Zero Waste Foundation and a COP31 high-level climate champion. If implemented, energy experts say the initiatives could slow global warming and reduce the environmental footprint of renewable energy technologies, like solar panels and batteries. But there is still a risk these climate ambitions may fall flat. Conference agreements are often nonbinding and past hosts have been criticized for failing to follow through on promises. Turkey also faces scrutiny over its own climate record. “The Zero Waste target is a good target. It definitely needs to be supported with concrete measures and further action,” said Berk Butan, who heads the waste campaign for Greenpeace Turkey. “But fundamentally, we also need to recognize its shortcomings.” As the second biggest cause of climate change after carbon dioxide, the reduction of methane emissions could significantly slow global warming, according to the U.N. During the first three days of the climate talks, leaders repeatedly called for urgent climate action. The U.N. recently had to readjust a decades-old goal of limiting the rise of global temperatures because the world was blowing past previous thresholds. While Turkey wants countries to commit to reducing methane emissions, it has not signed the Global Methane Pledge. Launched at the 2021 climate talks in Glasgow, the initiative aims to reduce methane emissions by at least 30% from 2020 levels by 2030. Turkey is also the world’s fifth-biggest emitter of methane from solid waste, according to nonprofit emissions tracker Climate TRACE. “Methane emissions from waste disposal are an important challenge,” said Agirbas, with the Zero Waste Foundation. Ke Wang, an energy expert at the WRI's Polsky Center for the Global Energy Transition, said that this is “a vital strategy for cutting greenhouse gas emissions." But recycling food waste is difficult because it decomposes quickly, making separation and processing expensive. Collecting and transporting wet, smelly food waste also requires specialized logistics and infrastructure that many countries lack. “Waste and food loss account for almost 10% of total emissions, so we need to integrate these actions,” Adalberto Maluf, a top official in Brazil’s environment ministry, told The Associated Press. The recycling of already-mined materials is key to reducing the reliance on mining, according to experts, which will only become more important as the world relies more on critical mineral-dependent renewable technologies. The International Energy Agency estimates that scaling up recycling could lower the need for new mining by between 25% and 40% by 2050. Most countries don’t recycle critical materials because it’s cheaper to mine them. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Easy lid swaps earn praise from iFixit, but panel removal ends in cracks and USB-C repairs require logic board surgery Apple tells its Support Community to STFU 11 hours ago Huawei says it’s made a 100 percent Chinese PC 2 days ago Mac lookalikes multiply as Linux raids Apple's wardrobe 5 days ago Safari's Autofill feature may be distorting time 5 days ago Apple turns iCloud into spy cloud, will start looking at public share links 7 days ago Apple's first touchscreen MacBook got a mixed reception from iFixit's teardown specialists, who praised its easily replaced lid but found fans and USB-C ports buried beneath the logic board. The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR display was unveiled at the end of October. It features a tandem OLED screen that stacks two layers of organic light-emitting pixels, eliminating the need for a backlight, and adds touch capability to the MacBook line for the first time. Although the vendor was patted on the back in recent years for improving the repairability of its famously locked-down products, this machine shows Apple still has some way to go. The good? The entire lid comes off relatively easily. Its three-screw hinges closely resemble those on the M6 14-inch MacBook Pro, while streamlined display cable brackets simplify removal. Apple's Repair Assistant tool also handled a full system board swap well. Despite concerns about Touch ID fingerprint authentication, everything went relatively smoothly when iFixit paired a touchscreen from one machine with a logic board from another. On the first boot, Repair Assistant recognized the battery, display, and Touch ID sensor, and touch control needed no separate calibration. The bad? Replacing the panel alone is not possible. When iFixit tried to separate it from the lid, the glass delaminated, cracking the OLED and touch-sensitive layers beneath. That could make for a costlier repair than bargained for. Under the bottom cover, the PROLED has a similar internal layout to the last few models of MacBook Pros, with the fans, board, speakers, and trackpad all in the same places. That means the same annoyances persist. The MagSafe power connector can be removed via two screws and a bracket, yet the USB-C ports can't be extracted the same way because the logic board is in the way. The headphone jack and the fans also require removing the system board first, and the HDMI port and SDXC card reader are soldered to the board itself, as is the storage and memory. Another gripe is that this MacBook's battery pack is hard to remove, though at least it is removable, unlike in many thin-and-light laptops. The tested Pro weighs 1.38 kg or about 3 pounds. For these reasons, the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR display earns a 5 out of 10 repairability score from iFixit , but this is actually a one point increase over the score it gave the M5 MacBook Pro. The Apple logo has its own lighting. Older MacBooks with illuminated logos borrowed light from the LCD backlight shining through an apple-shaped window in the lid. This model uses a strip of LEDs along one edge of the logo, passing through a diffuser for an even glow. Because it sits behind the display panel, it would be nearly impossible to repair if it failed, especially if the panel is destroyed during removal. Under a microscope, the PROLED XDR display looks very different from earlier MacBooks: the blue subpixel is significantly larger than the green and red ones. The reason, we're told, is that blue OLED materials wear out faster, so a larger subpixel can emit the same amount of light while putting less strain on the material.

events.title: China’s Nvidia Honeypot Isn’t Surprising. Jensen Huang Fell for It Anyway
events.summary: There’s a specific mantra drilled into government workers, military officers, and intelligence personnel during counterintelligence briefings: “If she’s a 10 and you’re a 5, she’s a spy!” Or, as the US Army’s Counterintelligence Command posted on Valentine’s Day: “It doesn’t take a mathematician to figure out ‘10 + 5 = honeytrap.’” The very beautiful woman who is suddenly interested in your very ordinary existence probably has ulterior motives , is the message. Jensen Huang surely doesn’t live a typical life—he’s a centibillionaire, the swashbuckling CEO of Nvidia, one of the hottest and most geopolitically consequential companies of the 21st century. Surely he’s aware of the possibility that he’d cross paths with intelligence assets. In fact, it’s hard to think of many companies in the world that would be a higher priority target for foreign intelligence agencies. All of that makes the stock-shaking news this week all the more surprising. How did Huang get embroiled in a spy scandal that mixes infidelity, international espionage, the Trump administration, and the economic behemoth of the multitrillion-dollar AI industry? The story kicked off just before Halloween, with a six-byline story in The New York Times reporting that Huang was the target of a Chinese spy plot. Starting somewhere between 2024 and 2025, Huang allegedly had an affair with Alice Huang (no relation), a one-time executive at a Singapore-based cloud provider known as Megaspeed. US intelligence agencies warned top US officials that they believed she was a Chinese intelligence asset. So far, Nvidia’s board, which has launched its own investigation, says it has “no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised,” but that’s far from the only concern. As one would expect, China has denied any nefarious plot centered on Jensen Huang. A Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson on Monday said , “The narrative about so-called Chinese spies is entirely based on groundless speculation—it’s nothing more than slander and smearing.” But according to reporting by The New York Times and the Financial Times , US intelligence officials also claim that Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, was reporting to China’s Ministry of State Security intelligence agency. On Monday, Megaspeed said on LinkedIn that US authorities found “no evidence of any violations concerning the illicit transfer of chips or any illegal activities." (There’s no indication so far that Alice Huang, a one-time Chinese state journalist, is an employee or “officer” of Chinese intelligence; she’s believed to be an “asset,” an outsider who aids an intelligence agency, sometimes for pay, sometimes not.) China, though, has elevated economic espionage to a core pillar of its economic and military development, stealing the designs for everything from US fighter jets to solar panels and commercial paint recipes . “Honeypots” or “honey traps”—positioning an alluring operative to seduce or develop a relationship with a key target—are one of intelligence’s most infamous and well-established strategies. French officials have warned specifically about Chinese honeypots since at least 2011, when intelligence reports cited a pharmaceutical researcher who was seduced and then blackmailed by a Chinese spy operation. Over the past quarter of a century, as Silicon Valley emerged as a center of political and economic power, it has become a key focus of Chinese intelligence. In one plot, a Chinese national named Fang Fang spent years trying to cozy up to Bay Area politicians , including then US Representative Eric Swalwell. (While intelligence officials at the time reportedly believed Fang to be an operative, law enforcement officials never brought any charges against her). When traveling to China, US business executives have become accustomed to leaving their regular phones and computers at home and using burner devices to prevent the installation of spyware or malware (as I did, when I traveled to China for WIRED in 2019 to report on Huawei ). In 2012, when Leon Panetta was making his first trip to China as defense secretary, he and his team were advised to bathe and shower in the dark in the event his hotel room was bugged. Last year, the threat of honeypots prompted the US government to explicitly ban personnel working in China and Hong Kong from engaging in romantic or sexual relationships with Chinese citizens. More recently, US officials joined with allies to warn about China’s increasingly sophisticated “ LinkedIn espionage ”: using the business-focused social networking site to recruit and build relationships with unwitting executives. Alice Huang’s Megaspeed, for its part, is a major Pacific region player in cloud services focused on the advanced computer chips that are the heart of Nvidia’s business.

events.title: Nvidia handed downgrade on Jensen Huang and AI uncertainty
events.summary: Baird gave Nvidia a rare downgrade on Wednesday, as chief executive Jensen Huang 's alleged affair with a Chinese spy casts doubt over his tenure. In a note, Baird analyst Tristan Gerra more than halved the chip maker's target from $500 to $200. Mr Gerra delayed his forecasts for data centres in 2027, saying supply issues are “mostly behind a potential slowdown, alongside potential demand softening”. AI hyperscaler capital expense could also slow to 40 per cent growth or slightly less for 2027, he said. Baird downgraded Nvidia stock to neutral, while a separate analysis from Morgan Stanley removed it as a top pick. Nvidia was trying to rally after a difficult period for tech-related stocks. Shares in the chip bellwether rebounded on Wednesday as CoreWeave's better-than-expected quarterly results lifted other chip stocks. Nvidia closed 2.92 per cent higher on Wednesday at $173.73 a share, after ending 5 per cent lower in the previous session. However, shares in Nvidia are on track for a sixth consecutive losing week. The company's stock is down about 8 per cent for the year. Mr Huang admitted to an extramarital affair in a letter to employees on Sunday. “To my colleagues at Nvidia, including those I have worked alongside for decades, and to our board, partners and shareholders around the world: you deserve better from me. Leading Nvidia is the privilege of my life. My responsibility is to serve you and be worthy of your trust. I have fallen short of that responsibility. I am fully committed to Nvidia and will work to earn back your confidence,” he wrote. Nvidia's board of directors has launched an investigation into the affair, adding that Mr Huang fully supports the review and is committed to co-operating with it. “While the board has no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, the board's inquiry will examine all available information … The board has confidence in Jensen and his leadership team and will provide further updates as appropriate,” it said. The explosive allegations come at a time when traders were already scrutinising AI tech stocks after recent earnings reports stoked fears over data centres and the financing behind them. Mr Huang's affair has also rocked Washington, with some legislators calling for investigations . The House foreign affairs committee has requested US President Donald Trump to appear for a closed-door briefing with Mr Huang on his interactions with the alleged spy. US Representatives Brian Mast, John Moolenaar and House permanent select committee on intelligence chairman Rick Crawford requested in a letter to Mr Huang that he brief their committees by November 18. “The issue of PRC infiltration and access to cutting-edge US technology is core to the investigative work of our three committees this Congress. It is vital that Congress determines the extent to which US national security has been placed at risk,” they wrote, referring to the “People's Republic of China”. Analysts are also considering Mr Huang's future as they assess the direction of Nvidia, one of the key nodes in the broader AI nexus. Morgan Stanley analyst Joseph Moore wrote that Mr Huang's leadership is “crucial to the company's direction”. On Tuesday, tech analyst Dan Ives said he estimates there is a 15 per cent chance Mr Huang is removed as chief executive. We believe if Jensen was removed as CEO, Nvidia is worth a lot less (25%-30%) as a company/stock and would change the future direction of the company and create a dramatically different competitive environment around AI GPUs globally especially for China. ~15% chance he removed… — Dan Ives (@DivesTech) November 10, 2026 “We believe if Jensen was removed as CEO, Nvidia is worth a lot less (25 per cent to 30 per cent) as a company/stock and would change the future direction of the company and create a dramatically different competitive environment around AI GPUs globally especially for China ,” Mr Ives wrote. The next test for Nvidia will be on November 16, when it is due to report its third-quarter results.

events.title: Is AIIB's complaint mechanism failing affected communities?
events.summary: The AIIB has a grievance redress mechanism for people affected by projects it finances. But those seeking to file a complaint face significant hurdles. Critics say reforms and greater transparency are needed. For members of the Indigenous Sasak community on the Indonesian island of Lombok, the conflict over their land is not over. For them, a tourism and infrastructure project co-financed by the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (AIIB) is a source of frustration, as they believe it has led to the expropriation of their land and destruction of their livelihoods. In late September, they officially filed a complaint with the bank. It remains unclear whether this complaint will lead to an independent investigation. The AIIB, which finances major infrastructure projects across Asia, has a mechanism in place to deal with such complaints. Individuals who suffer adverse effects from the bank-financed projects may, under certain conditions, file a complaint with the institution. However, access to this process — known as the Project Complaints Mechanism (PPM) — remains controversial. According to a report by The Diplomat , a magazine that covers political and economic developments in Asia, none of the 45 complaints listed on the AIIB's website had been deemed admissible as of mid-September. The bank acknowledged that "no cases have passed the PPM's eligibility assessment," but it stressed that this is "only part of the story." South Asia projects boost China's presence in India's sphere The AIIB emphasized that not every issue needs to be resolved through this mechanism. The PPM is "only one part of AIIB's grievance redress ecosystem," the Beijing-based bank said in response to a query from DW. Those affected should first attempt to resolve concerns directly with the project team at the local level, it said. According to the bank, "twelve complaints were in fact resolved at the project level — as a direct result of AIIB's follow-up and intervention — and one was resolved through domestic courts." But critics see this as a major weakness. "The mechanism must be easily accessible," said Arntraud Hartmann, a development economist at the Johns Hopkins University School of Advanced International Studies (SAIS Europe) in Bologna, Italy. She argued that people affected by the projects, for instance, are required to document potential violations of environmental and social standards from the start. "How is the affected party supposed to know which standards might have been violated?" she questioned. The AIIB disputes this claim. "In terms of accessibility, we have made the submission form simpler and translated it into 12 languages," it said, adding that complaints can be submitted online, by phone, or by email. Urgewald, a German environmental NGO, cites another problem with AIIB-financed projects. For many of them, information on environmental impacts and resettlements is either missing or published late, it noted. For 2024, the NGO found that 11 of the 16 projects it examined lacked complete environmental and social impact assessments. In many cases, information on the potential number of displaced residents was also missing, it added. "The information published on the bank's website is often insufficient and inconsistent. Particularly important documents, such as environmental impact assessments or resettlement plans, vary widely or are missing entirely," said Nora Sausmikat, a China expert at Urgewald. The lack of information makes it difficult for those affected to respond in a timely manner and report violations early on, she underscored, adding that the situation is particularly difficult for people without formal land titles. Christoph Steinert, a political scientist at the University of Konstanz, said the mere existence of such grievance redressal mechanisms "is not enough." Particularly vulnerable groups often know little about their rights, he said, adding that information should be available in local languages and targeted outreach directed at affected communities. Criticism of the AIIB's procedures is not new. A 2023 report by international aid organizations, including Recourse, Accountability Counsel, and Inclusive Development International, revealed that the AIIB's grievance mechanism had failed to accept a single complaint since its 2019 inception. The study highlighted that 101 of the 219 AIIB-financed projects, or 46% of of the total projects at the time, were ineligible for review due to co-financing exemptions. The AIIB typically provides funding without leading projects, a standard practice in development finance. When complaints arise, it directs complainants to the lead lender. As a result, nine of the 45 complaints fell outside its jurisdiction. For Sausmikat, this is part of the problem. "The AIIB, however, decided against revising this requirement and established a mechanism that is very difficult to access," she said.

events.title: Siri co-founder backs Helix for its voice ID tech
events.summary: For years, websites have relied on technology like CAPTCHA to prove that the user on the other end is human. More recently, social media platforms have turned to photos or videos to verify users’ identities. Now, a startup called Helix is betting that voice technology can do the same job, without requiring users to hand over sensitive personal information. The voice technology, which can run directly on a user’s device, has attracted backing from Siri co-founder Dag Kittlaus, who will also act as an adviser. The company raised $6.2 million in funding in a round led by Chicago Ventures, with participation from BAM Ventures, Aglaé Ventures, Corazon Capital, Press On Ventures, Tusk Ventures, Yonder Ventures, Rule 30, and Brown Angel Group. The startup was founded by Alex Oberg, Anna Dorofiyenko, and Mike Hall in 2025. Oberg previously worked at Ticketmaster, which acquired his startup; Dorofiyenko led data science teams at Live Nation and Zillow; and Hall has worked at Nike and Tinder, where he helped develop the initial matching algorithm. At Ticketmaster, Oberg played a role in creating Verified Fan, which is designed to keep bots out of the platform. As AI advanced, he started thinking along the same lines for a new solution. “As AI started to come up in the last two years, I was realizing that it’s going to make it increasingly difficult to determine who’s human and who’s not on the internet. Identity on the internet’s always been about proxies for identity, right? It’s your email, it’s your phone, it’s your IP address, it’s your device fingerprint, it’s your device ID,” Oberg said. He noted that with the rise of AI agents like Instinct and Muse, the industry needs to rethink human identity on the internet and rely on biometric signals like voice, which is where Helix comes in. Its core technology can run directly on a device to determine whether someone is human and estimate their age. The company is also running pilots to explore whether voice can be used as a biomarker to detect conditions such as drunkenness or distress. The company can deploy its technology to replace or supplement CAPTCHA and help block bot attacks. Helix said that because its model can run locally even on an iPhone 13, the cost of deploying the technology is minimal. The startup said one of its customers is Zeel, an in-home healthcare provider that uses Helix’s tech to verify the identities of providers visiting customers’ homes. Oberg said verifying workers, such as cabdrivers, is another use case the startup is exploring. He also said that age-verification regulations for social media platforms around the world are forcing users to trade privacy for access. Helix’s voice technology, he said, could offer an alternative. “There’s like an avalanche of regulation coming down because essentially society has decided children should not be able to use the internet as adults. That has created a bit of a strawman argument that everyone needs to trade their privacy for the sake of security and child safety. We are that company that’s saying, nope, don’t agree. It’s a four-second voice challenge,” he said. The CEO also emphasized the limitations of Helix’s technology, noting that it cannot reliably detect whether someone is lying. He added that its voice technology doesn’t identify individual speakers — while verifying them being unique humans — and claimed that even if the company stores a voiceprint, it cannot be used to reconstruct a person’s voice. AI-powered fraud is also a growing problem in phone calls. But Helix believes its technology isn’t yet capable of reliably detecting AI agents during live calls. Siri co-founder Kittlaus said that voice-identification technology has finally reached a point where it works reliably, positioning Helix to scale as AI-powered fraud increases. He also said that Helix’s work to compress its models gives the startup a cost advantage. “What folks at Helix are doing is, instead of teaching computers how to understand speech, these guys are understanding what the speech of the speaker actually means, what’s going on with them, if they are lying, are they impaired? That side of it is fascinating to me within the larger picture that I just described,” he told TechCrunch. When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . events.title: Databricks’ new AI agent tells CEO Ali Ghodsi the unvarnished truth
events.summary: Databricks on Wednesday unveiled an updated version of its AI agent Genie, which can now perform multistep jobs that take extended work to finish. It does this through an ontology that Databricks built to give Genie the context it needs from the information that customers store on the Databricks platform. Corporate leaders can now assign the agent a wide range of tasks, and it will complete them unsupervised, the company says. To prove the point, Databricks CEO Ali Ghodsi showed me how he uses it internally. Instead of a product demo, he fired up his actual agent and walked me through his most recent chats and charts. He showed me how it analyzed the parts of an employee satisfaction survey where the company didn’t score well, and how it helped him rate (and discard) fixes for those low scores that some executives suggested. He showed me how it summarized a big sales pitch to a prospect that went poorly — including the features the prospect said it needed before buying. It also prepped him for a podcast interview by reviewing his previous appearances and developing likely questions. While we talked, he even had it tell him what he should say to me. (And its advice on that wasn’t bad.) The fascinating part was that Ghodsi was using Genie to find the stuff that he’s now unlikely to hear as the big boss. It was a source of unvarnished truth about what wasn’t going well that he needed to address. “Have you heard of Dunbar’s number? The magic number is 150,” he said when I pointed this out. Named for British anthropologist Robin Dunbar, it’s theoretically the maximum number of people with whom humans can maintain stable relationships. In a small startup, a CEO knows everyone, has direct relationships with them, and they feel safe to tell him negative info straight up. With 12,000 employees, Ghodsi is the first to admit he can’t know everyone. At that size, a salesperson isn’t likely to confess a disastrous sales call to the CEO. An HR manager isn’t likely to confess that their idea for increasing employee satisfaction will probably fail. “Anyone who has more than 150 employees, which is a lot of companies, a lot of people can get value out of this,” he said of AI agents generally and his product, Genie, specifically. Ghodsi’s own use of Genie (often called dogfooding, from the phrase “eating your own dogfood”) is one reason why Databricks is now pitching it as an always-on agent for business leaders. He says he also uses it in his personal life, rather than a security-questionable alternative like OpenClaw or Instinct or Muse. He believes Genie can do for the business side what AI, agents, and harnesses (the software that wraps around an AI model and lets it use tools) are doing for programmers. As for the risk that agents will ratchet up corporate AI costs, Ghodsi has an answer for that, too. He said costs can be controlled through Databricks’ Unity Gateway product. Patch Tuesday contained a truckload of fixes for Microsoft products . However, for some users, installing the update, KB5132061, is proving challenging. In the hours after the patch was released, multiple complaints began to surface that the download and installation were failing, with some customers reporting a 0x800F0993 error code. Others say they received a 0x800F0989 error. Microsoft does not currently list any known issues with the update and is yet to make a statement or provide explanation for the glitch. In addition to the security fixes, this patch resolves a number of known issues from previous updates, including a problem where USB Audio 1.0 devices might fail to start and display an error code 10 in Device Manager. In the absence of a statement from Microsoft, several users have taken to sleuthing. One, with the handle of Forceflow on the ElevenForum site, suggested the bug might be related to Windows Sandbox, and said that after disabling the feature and rebooting, the patch installed successfully. However, others reported problems regardless of Windows Sandbox status, and alternative solutions included using DISM (Deployment Image Servicing and Management) to check the package or downloading the update manually. It's an important patch to install, since it addresses 726 vulnerabilities in Windows alone, and the difficulties affected users face are less than ideal. Microsoft patches have lately displayed more gremlins than usual. Out-of-band releases are depressingly regular after updates break functionality. A September Out-of-band release, for example, was hurriedly pushed out after the September 2026 Windows security update caused trouble for Remote Desktop Services. The October Patch Tuesday for Windows Server sent Exchange Servers toppling , with a registry edit workaround suggested. There was no out-of-band update - Microsoft said the problem had been resolved in the November update. At least this latest release appears to be failing before users get a chance to see what is broken this time. events.title: CDL flags ‘significantly weaker’ performance for H2 2026
events.summary: CDL says its anticipated weaker performance in H2 is “compounded by adverse foreign exchange movements”. CDL expects a “significantly weaker” H2 2026, as some capital-recycling deals slip into 2027 and foreign exchange losses, especially the Korean won, hurt results. The group is reviewing its property portfolio and may book impairment losses. Its China office assets still face market challenges, while it pushes divestments and asset optimisation. CDL says its balance sheet is still sound, with $2.1 billion cash and no near-term debt worries. Sales, occupancy and hotel revenue stayed strong despite a tough market. SINGAPORE – Fresh from announcing the roll-out of a comprehensive strategic review , City Developments Limited (CDL) flagged that it expects to post a “significantly weaker” financial performance for its second half ending Dec 31. Certain capital-recycling deals that the Kwek-controlled group had earlier expected to materialise in the rest of the 2026 financial year are now expected to be completed in the 2027 financial year , it said in a third-quarter business update on Nov 11. This comes “in contrast to” the second half of 2025, when the group reported a capital-recycling gain of $473.1 million from the divestment of South Beach Consortium . CDL added that the anticipated weaker H2 performance is “compounded by adverse foreign exchange movements, particularly the appreciation of the Korean won against the Singapore dollar since July”. The group is also currently undertaking valuations of its property portfolio, which it noted “may give rise to impairment losses”. As at Sep 30, its China office portfolio “continued to face market challenges”. The group said that it is “actively pursuing divestment initiatives and optimisation opportunities in line with its capital-recycling priorities”. The property giant had at end-September unveiled a plan focused on capital recycling and deleveraging, targeting $6 billion in divestments by FY2029 to recycle capital from mature, non-core or underperforming assets. It aims to achieve a gearing of 55% by FY2029, representing an estimated 20-percentage-point reduction in net gearing. CDL’s net gearing ratio was 75% as at Sept 30, largely due to the acquisition of two government land sale sites in Tanjong Rhu Road and Peck Hay Road in H1. The group partnered Hong Realty to buy the prime Peck Hay Road parcel for $542.4 million, and tied up with Woh Hup to pick up the Tanjong Rhu plot for $709 million. CDL said its interest cover now stands at 2.7 times and that its debt expiry profile remains healthy, with cash reserves of $2.1 billion and a “robust liquidity position, supported by $4.8 billion in cash and available committed credit facilities”. “There are no material concerns over the group’s ability to fulfil its near-term debt obligations,” it added. In the third quarter, CDL and its joint-venture associates sold 124 units in Singapore with a total sales value of $322.6 million. This compares with 88 units worth $313.2 million a year earlier. With no new launches during the quarter, sales were primarily from existing projects such as Norwood Grand and The Myst, the group said. Both properties, which are 96% and 99% sold, respectively, have obtained their Temporary Occupation Permits. For the nine months ended Sep 30, the group and its joint-venture associates sold 476 units totalling $1.2 billion, largely driven by the 246-unit freehold Newport Residences. The group’s Singapore office portfolio had a committed occupancy of 97.4%, sustaining positive rental reversions for three quarters in 2026. Two new Grade A office developments, Newport Tower and Union Square Central, are on track for completion in 2027 and 2028, respectively. CDL expects an anticipated supply crunch to “provide a supportive backdrop for leasing activities”. CDL’s retail assets had an overall 97.1% committed occupancy, with Palais Renaissance reaching 100%. Global hotel operations had higher revenue per available room, up 6.4% to $175.20 for the first nine months of the 2026 financial year, from $164.60 the year before. Revenue per available room grew in Australasia (11.8%), Singapore (3%), Europe (4.7%) and New York (8.9%), CDL said. “The global operating environment remains challenging, characterised by heightened geopolitical uncertainties, financial market volatility and evolving macroeconomic conditions,” the group noted. Against this backdrop, it “remains focused on sustaining operational momentum across its core businesses while navigating these headwinds”.

events.title: UAE's biggest bank FAB to raise $4.08bn to boost next phase of growth strategy
events.summary: First Abu Dhabi Bank plans to raise Dh15 billion ($4.08 billion) through a rights issue as it prepares for “the next phase” of its growth strategy across the UAE and its global portfolio. The UAE's biggest bank will be offering 1,109,467,456 new shares, with each to be offered at Dh13.52, a 30 per cent discount on its closing share price on Tuesday, a FAB statement on Wednesday said. Mubadala Investment Company, FAB’s largest shareholder, plans to subscribe for its full pro-rata entitlement, which is a reflection of its “continued confidence” in FAB’s strategy and long-term growth prospects, the bank said. “The UAE continues to advance an ambitious long-term economic agenda, underpinned by diversification, investment, innovation and a growing role in global trade and capital flows,” said Sheikh Tahnoon bin Zayed, chairman of FAB. “FAB is at the centre of this growth, enabling strategic investment across the UAE and internationally. The proposed rights issue will further strengthen FAB’s ability to support the UAE’s ambitions and capture the opportunities ahead.” The rights issue is also meant to capture “significant opportunities” in the UAE and across FAB's international network, group chief executive Hana Al Rostamani said. Aside from the Gulf, FAB also maintains a presence in the Middle East, Africa, Asia, Europe and the Americas. “The strength of our home market, combined with the reach and connectivity of our international network, gives us a strong platform for growth,” Ms Al Rostamani said. Capital markets in the UAE continue to sustain their momentum despite the fallout from the war in Iran, prompting companies to tap into equity markets for additional funds through secondary shares sales and rights issues. Other notable companies to have done so include Adnoc, Abu Dhabi Commercial Bank, artificial intelligence company G42 and Mamoura Diversified Global Holding, an investor in Dubai telecom firm du. “We will deploy capital with discipline and focus, pursuing opportunities that deepen our competitive position, expand the scale and reach of our franchise, and deliver superior, sustainable returns for our shareholders,” Ms Al Rostamani said. Last month, FAB reported a 6 per cent annual jump in third-quarter profit , as net interest income, and fee and commission income grew on the back of strong business activity. Net profit attributable to shareholders for three months to the end of September climbed to Dh5.73 billion. Nine-month profit grew 3 per cent to Dh16.4 billion.

events.title: SIA’s first-half profit falls 43.9% as fuel costs bite
events.summary: SIA had a strong second quarter, with operating profit up 16.3% year on year to $463 million and net profit quadrupling to $210 million over the same period. SINGAPORE – High fuel costs continued to weigh on Singapore Airlines’ earnings, as the airline reported on Nov 11 a 43.9% slump in net profit to $134 million for the first half of its 2027 financial year. This was despite a 16.8% rise in revenue for the first half to $11.3 billion, driven by stronger demand for both passenger travel and air cargo. The group noted strong seasonal travel demand and said cargo demand remained firm, supported by shipments linked to semiconductors and cloud computing. Geopolitical and weather-related disruptions to sea freight also prompted some shippers to switch to air freight. This came on the back of a 14.3% year on year increase in total revenue to $5.6 billion. Still, the carrier’s total expenditure rose by 14.1% to a hefty $5.1 billion over the same period. This was mainly due to a surge in fuel prices as a result of the war in the Middle East, with the group’s fuel costs before hedging rising 63.3% to $2.1 billion during the quarter. The group declared a total dividend of seven cents per share for the first half, comprising an interim two- cent ordinary dividend and five- cent special dividend. While it has adjusted air fares and cargo rates to overcome complexities in its operations and supply chains, these measures do not fully offset the impact of sustained high fuel prices, SIA said. It added that an extended Middle East conflict “could also have spillover effects on broader macroeconomic conditions, potentially leading to further inflationary cost pressure and affecting demand for passenger travel and air freight”. Nevertheless, the group remains in a strong position to navigate this volatility, with a diversified global network and broad mix of traffic flows helping to cushion shifts in demand. Additionally, the complementary positioning of SIA and its low-cost carrier Scoot enables the group to serve different markets and customer segments, and adjust capacity and schedules where needed. Despite the global airline industry facing headwinds from the conflict, the company reported a 4.9% increase in passenger capacity for the first half of its financial year. It cited Scoot’s network expansion in fast-growing Asia-Pacific markets, exclusively operating routes to 58 of the 84 destinations that it serves. With uncertainty still looming over the Middle East, both SIA and Scoot will continue to suspend their flights to the region. SIA’s services to Saudi Arabia’s capital Riyadh, which was supposed to launch in June, have now been deferred to March 2027. SIA said its first-half net profit was also partially cushioned by a lower share of losses from Air India and other associated companies. It added that Air India, whose substantial financial losses over the years have weighed on SIA’s performance, has made “tangible progress in its multi-year transformation, including enhancements to customer experience and operational performance”. SIA has a 25.1% stake in the Air India Group, and noted that a large-scale transformation of the airline would take time. It said it will work with majority partner Tata Sons “to support Air India’s journey towards profitable growth, including strengthening structural cost efficiencies, unlocking greater synergies between Air India and Air India Express, sharpening its commercial strategy to navigate current external challenges elevating its customer proposition”. Following the signing of a commercial cooperation agreement in January, Air India and SIA in October launched additional flight options between Singapore and eight Indian cities through the airlines’ respective booking channels, greater flexibility and a more seamless booking experience, the carrier said. It reiterated its commitment to its investment in Air India, which remains a key part of its multi-hub strategy. SIA’s shares closed at $7.17 on Nov 11, up 0.8%, before it announced its earnings.

events.title: MSF urges global health officials to widen Ebola vaccine access
events.summary: Global health officials have been urged to widen the use of an existing Ebola vaccine in DR Congo following reports it may provide protection against a strain it was not designed to target. The Bundibugyo strain — for which there is currently no vaccine — has killed more than 5,300 people in the country’s largest-ever outbreak. Medical charity Doctors Without Borders said restrictions on using Ervebo, developed by Merck for use against a prior Ebola strain, should be lifted so more people at risk, including young children, can be vaccinated. The charity said DR Congo requested 500,000 doses of Ervebo, but only 70,000 were released. The World Health Organization recommends limiting its use against Bundibugyo to research studies because its effects remain unproven. Doctors Without Borders said early observations of fewer infections and deaths among previously vaccinated people justified wider use. A larger release from the global stockpile requires backing from the WHO’s vaccine advisers, who meet next week. — Ruben Nyanguila
