events.title: Africa calls on COP31 to boost adaptation finance
events.summary: African countries want the COP31 climate talks, now underway in Türkiye, to set out how the world will deliver on last year’s pledge to triple adaptation finance designed to help cope with the growing impact of extreme weather events. A large share of the money has previously come from aid budgets, which have fallen to their lowest level since 2014 , and most wealthier countries have pledged little-to-no new climate finance from this year . The African Group of Negotiators says addressing this issue is vital to a successful outcome in Antalya as support for the continent’s vulnerabilities has been “dwindling,” according to its chairperson. But even a tripling in financing will not close the gap: In 2024, the amount available for developing economies reached around $30 billion — that pales against the $305 billion the UN estimates they need annually to 2035. Plans have been announced at COP31 to scale up successful adaptation projects and attract larger investments. But these cannot be “entirely dependent on voluntary contributions,” Kenya’s climate envoy told Semafor. — Chloé Farand

events.summary: South Africa’s unemployment crisis deepened in the third quarter, official data showed, with anger over the lack of jobs spilling into the country’s politics and its debate over migration. The official unemployment rate reached 33.7%, slightly higher than the previous three months, with 8 million-plus people looking for work and more than four in five of them unemployed for at least a year, Statistics South Africa said in Tuesday’s update. The data deepens questions about the economic record of President Cyril Ramaphosa, who made job creation a central priority after taking office in 2018. It also risks compounding voter fury that has battered Ramaphosa’s African National Congress at the polls , and feeds into a combustible political environment in which migrants are blamed for competition over jobs and public services. — Tiisetso Motsoeneng

events.title: Botswana to double stake in diamond miner De Beers
events.summary: Botswana said it will double its stake in diamond miner De Beers to 30% to increase its strategic influence on the gemstone giant, backing a buyout that would allow majority owner Anglo American to exit the business. Africa’s largest diamond producer by volume is grappling with falling prices and competition from cheaper lab-grown stones. A larger share would give it more say over how De Beers sells and markets its diamonds. President Duma Boko told lawmakers that Angola and Namibia would also take stakes in De Beers. Botswana is backing joint marketing campaigns with other producers in an attempt to rebuild demand for natural gems. The country relies on diamond sales for around three-quarters of its foreign exchange earnings. Anglo American has sought to sell its 85% stake in De Beers since 2024 to refocus on copper and iron ore. — Ruben Nyanguila

events.title: Plurai wants to help AI agents work better using the same approach that helped get self-driving cars to roads
events.summary: AI agents are all the rage, but they’re not quite as capable as their purveyors would have you believe. Efforts to benchmark agents doing complex tasks show that they aren’t typically reliable enough to function without close supervision. LiveBench 2.0 shows Claude Fable 5.2 and ChatGPT-6 Astra succeeding on 82.9 and 75.6 out of 100 tasks, respectively, and an effort by the AI infrastructure company EON to test agents in a simulated corporate environment found the most successful model tested, Claude Opus 4.8, performed tasks at 76.8% accuracy. Now, a startup known as Plurai wants to boost those numbers with the same techniques that put self-driving cars on the street: Simulations using synthetic data based on a company’s own digital systems, meant to prepare models to tackle difficult edge cases. Co-founders Ilan Kadar and Elad Levi previously worked for Nexar, which develops autonomous driving technology. Kadar worked with Waymo to simulate and evaluate its end-to-end deep learning driving software. “The moment that we saw the wave of AI agents, we saw the same pattern: That it is very easy to build a demo, but [hard] to get something that will be reliable and cost effective,” Kadar told TechCrunch. “Since we saw the same pattern, the same pitch was that we want to build this simulation layer.” On Wednesday, the startup said it had raised $13 million in seed funding to make that happen. The round was led by Team8, with participation from U&I, Velocity, and Mercer. Like the end-to-end models trained to drive cars, AI agents are probabilistic systems operating in unpredictable environments. When pressed by customers, agents tasked with booking travel can ignore spending policies. Or, when tasked with querying one database, agents can reliably provide an answer, but combining information from multiple datasets tends to gum up the works. A long conversation with a customer service bot can overwhelm an agent with too much context and lead to wrong turns. To fix that, Plurai creates a digital twin of the company’s electronic systems, including the knowledge base and tools that an agent will have access to in production. It then maps all the possible flows of the agents and uses that graph to prepare the model with evaluations and fixes for possible edge cases. The platform works alongside existing agentic tools like Claude Code, Codex, Copilot, and Cursor. However, Kadar says the company’s real promise is using the data it gathers to post-train small, open-weight models tailored to individual customer needs. Tests performed in cooperation with Nvidia and Nebius showed the company’s models outperforming midtier frontier models at lower costs. “We can take a large language model, we can take the task, decompose it into a smaller task using the simulation, train [an open-weight] model, and using the simulation, verify that the quality is higher or comparable to the frontier model, and an order or two orders of magnitude cost reduction,” he said. Reah Miyara, a Google DeepMind researcher who backed Plurai as an angel investor, said the company’s edge comes from understanding failure modes in production, and generating synthetic data to tune models. As businesses try to optimize their AI expense, Plurai’s approach could prove a real advantage, since IT leaders are seeing that “frontier-capable models are out of distribution with my specific data, and the cost of these things isn’t sustainable in the long term,” Miyara said. Plurai hopes analogies between AI agents in physical and digital environments can prove predictive: While powerful general AI models are imbuing robots with fascinating capabilities, they aren’t yet reliable enough to be deployed widely. Meanwhile, robots powered by AI models built for specific tasks are in the field right now, working for customers and gathering valuable real-world data. “My view is that no matter how smart OpenAI and Anthropic model will be — and they will be much smarter — they will not know your business and your policy,” Kadar said. events.title: Dubai's public parking fines overtake fees
events.summary: It’s been inching in that direction for years, and now it’s official: Dubai’s public parking monopoly earns more from fines than public parking fees. Parkin reported record third-quarter revenue , up 21% to 415 million dirhams ($113 million), driven by enforcement, expanding business with private developers, and longer-term permits. The latter may have skewed the results: Sales of discounted “seasonal cards” were up 37%, the company said, and those permits aren’t counted in public parking utilization and revenue, even though their holders occupy spaces. Parkin also expanded its portfolio to 272,500 spaces, nearly tripling the number managed for private developers over the past year. Still, for anyone parking in Dubai, it feels like enforcement is stricter, aided by the deployment of advanced cameras and AI-powered monitoring. — Mohammed Sergie

events.title: Company that owns Nvidia-linked Megaspeed lists Singapore address occupied by interior design firm
events.summary: Swiftdata, the parent company of Megaspeed International, changed its registered address from an office building in Jurong East to Midview City in April. Swiftdata, the parent company of Nvidia customer Megaspeed, changed its registered address to Midview City in April. ST found no sign it was using the unit and was unable to contact Swiftdata . Megaspeed is under probe in Singapore for “suspected breaches of our domestic laws” and in the US over possible chip export breaches. SINGAPORE – A little-known Singapore company that owns Megaspeed International, the firm at the centre of US investigations into the possible diversion of advanced Nvidia chips to China, has a registered business address that an interior design firm says it has occupied for over four years. Swiftdata, the parent company of Megaspeed – which saw a seemingly meteoric rise to become a massive buyer of Nvidia chips – did not appear to be occupying the unit at an integrated business hub when The Straits Times visited on Nov 11. ST was unable to get in touch with Swiftdata. The company, incorporated in 2023, is the sole shareholder in Megaspeed, owning all of its 10 million shares, according to Accounting and Corporate Regulatory Authority (ACRA) records. The sole director of the company is Tan Yong Pong, who is also the sole director of Megaspeed, while Khloe Ng Wei Shi is listed as the corporate secretary for both firms. ACRA records show that Ng is also the company secretary of the interior design firm and a holding company using the same Midview City address. Swiftdata changed its registered address from an office building in Jurong East to Midview City in April. No one answered when The Straits Times rang the doorbell of the unit , which had the greeting “hello” emblazoned at its entrance, alongside a shoe rack with four pairs of slippers . Tenants in the building told ST the unit is occupied by an interior design firm. When contacted, the co-founder of the firm said he leased the space directly from Midview City, and has been operating there for more than four years. “I do not know Swiftdata, Megaspeed or any of their affiliates,” he said. He said his company is the “sole occupier of the address, someone somewhere must have used our address as a virtual address without our knowledge”. Tenants on the same floor also said they had not encountered anyone associated with Swiftdata. Asked about Swiftdata’s tenancy, Philip Chang, complex manager for Midview City, said he was “unable to provide any information due to PDPA regulations”. The PDPA, or Personal Data Protection Act, governs the collection, use, disclosure and care of personal data in Singapore. Megaspeed, which describes itself as a specialised cloud provider, is being probed in Singapore and the US. The US authorities began investigating Megaspeed over suspicions that it breached US chip export restrictions in late 2024. Singapore police confirmed in October 2025 that they were investigating Megaspeed over “suspected breaches of our domestic laws”. The Straits Times was unable to reach Swiftdata at its registered address at Midview City on Nov 11. The unit is occupied by an interior design firm. The company returned to the spotlight in late October this year when news broke that the US was concerned about Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang’s close ties to Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive. On Nov 8, Jensen Huang admitted to having an affair with her. Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, was the director and managing director of Megaspeed from March to November 2023. Previously known as 7Road International, Megaspeed’s ownership was transferred to Huang Le Limited when it was renamed in March 2023. The company became wholly-owned by the newly incorporated Swiftdata in November that year. According to Bloomberg, Megaspeed, through its affiliates, imported at least US$4.6 billion (S$5.9 billion) worth of Nvidia hardware since its founding in 2023 to November 2025. The news agency later reported that the “once-obscure spinoff of a Chinese gaming enterprise has evolved into the single largest South-east Asian buyer of Nvidia chips”. According to ACRA records, Megaspeed’s total assets surged from US$32.9 million in 2023 to almost US$3 billion in 2024, in an almost 90-fold increase. Its revenue rose from almost zero in 2023 to US$294.3 million in 2024, and its total liabilities jumped from US$22.9 million to almost US$3 billion over the same period. Megaspeed has received unqualified audit opinions in recent years, which is the most favourable conclusion an auditor can issue after reviewing a company’s financial statements. It has not publicly disclosed its financial statements for 2025. The company’s primary business activity is listed on ACRA as hosting services by non-data centres as a cloud service provider, while its secondary business activity is data analytics, processing, hosting and related activities.

events.title: US futures climb and Nvidia shares stabilize in a brutal week for the chipmaker
events.summary: U.S. futures are rising as Nvidia’s shares look to rebound and Brent crude remains below $100 a barrel U.S. futures are rising with crude still below $100 a barrel as shares of Nvidia stabilize in a brutal week for the chipmaker. Futures for the S & P 500 gained 0.9% on Wednesday, while those for the Dow Jones Industrial Average edged up 0.2%. Nasdaq futures climbed 1.9%. Nvidia was the single heaviest weight on the S & P 500 on Tuesday, but shares are up 3.7% in early trading Wednesday. They are still down almost 10% this week. The company that is central to the artificial intelligence boom has been under pressure since the company’s board announced an investigation into its CEO, Jensen Huang, following revelations of his affair with a purported Chinese spy. President Donald Trump said the FBI is investigating the affair , which Huang has acknowledged and apologized for. Among other technology stocks, CoreWeave jumped more than 15% before the market opened after posting better-than-expected third-quarter revenue and a boost in its 2026 revenue outlook. The U.S. bond market is closed Wednesday for Veterans Day, but the stock markets remain open. The price of Brent crude, the international standard, rose 1.9% to $93.22 a barrel. U.S. benchmark crude oil gained 1.2% to $87.05 per barrel. events.title: Spain’s workers hold a general strike over housing costs ahead of a national election
events.summary: Millions of Spanish workers have shut down businesses and disrupted transport in a massive protest over housing costs BARCELONA, Spain -- Millions of Spanish workers shut down businesses and snarled transport in a massive protest Wednesday over housing costs that the government hopes to leverage ahead of a national election later this month. The walkout — under the slogan “Salaries. Housing. Prices.” — was the first general strike in Spain in 14 years. In Barcelona, the country’s second-largest city, most storefronts on a main shopping boulevard were boarded up in anticipation of violence during protests later in the day. Some retail chains were open to business while public transport was at a standstill or facing long delays. The subway opened only for the rush hour. Carlos Ferrer, a 45-year-old customer service worker who was trying to get back home to Alicante by train from Barcelona, said sometimes only “radical measures, such as a general strike” can force a change of course. “Authorities need to feel pressure from the citizens so they can do something," he said. Rain pelted the capital, Madrid, as strikers marched down main streets and blocked off Gran Vía, the city’s main thoroughfare, where big brand stores remained open although some were also boarded up. Unions have called for workers to march through the city center later Wednesday, and protests are also planned in more than 50 cities and towns. Manuel Gómez, a 19-year-old student in Madrid, welcomed the protests, which he said marked a change for the country. “In Spain, we have a serious problem, which is that when we don’t like something, we never go out to protest,” he said. About 5% of flights for Wednesday were canceled at airports across the country, according to the country’s airport operator, AENA. “The strike has exceeded the labor unions’ expectations,” said Unai Sordo, secretary general of CCOO, one of the two unions calling the strike. “It has been a success in terms of turnout.” Earlier, the two unions — CCOO and UGT — reported significant work stoppages in strategic sectors. They said the stoppages amounted to 90% in the automotive and port sectors, 85% in the meat industry, 82% in waste collection, and 75% in the energy sector. Minor incidents were reported in the first hours of the strike. Tires were set on fire at roadblocks in Barcelona, and scuffles with police were reported near the main wholesale market on Madrid’s outskirts. Police also used pepper spray against the strikers in some places. Many schools and universities reportedly closed or are working at minimal capacity. In Madrid, this added to an ongoing strike started by teachers nearly a month ago demanding better working conditions. In southwestern Spain, classes were suspended due to bad weather. “It’s extremely important to remind people that we, the workers — who are also renters or who also pay mortgages — are the ones with the power to halt production and bring the economy to a standstill,” Sandra Mora, spokesperson for the Tenants Union, told national radio, RNE. The strike brought workers, activists, politicians and ordinary Spaniards around the same interests — accessible housing. The average rent in Spain has almost doubled in the last 10 years, eating into household budgets and angering voters. The subsequent death of Maricarmen , as the woman became known, caused even more indignation and solidified her as a symbol of Spaniards who feel they pay too much in rent and can’t even dream of homeownership. Housing activists leveraged the uproar over Maricarmen's eviction to call for the general strike, and soon won the backing of the UGT and CCOO unions. The housing activists are seeking the elimination of pricey tourist apartments, a crackdown on real estate speculation and the automatic renewals of leases as a way to protect renters. Unions demand more government intervention in the housing market and a new minimum wage agreement through talks with the business owners' association. The nationwide protests over Maricarmen's eviction propelled Spain’s government to push through emergency measures to limit evictions and help tenants, but right-wing parties in the Parliament refused to ratify them , claiming they would provoke a flight of properties from the rental market. Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez then doubled down and called an early election , hoping to earn four more years in power for his left-wing coalition. The vote is set for Nov. 29. Then, in late October came a brutal high-speed train collision — Spain's second deadly rail disaster of the year — that killed 69 people.

events.title: Duolingo, Strava, and Ticketmaster Are All Caught Up in EU’s New Digital Fairness Rules
events.summary: The European Commission announced a sweeping set of updates to consumer law on Wednesday to protect European Union citizens from “harmful digital practices”—whether while online shopping, browsing social media , or doing their Duolingo lesson. Within the package, the Commission unveiled its Digital Fairness Act to address harmful practices online. Proposed rules include banning dark patterns —practices that manipulate consumers into making decisions they would not otherwise make, such as falsely claiming a product is running low. They will also curb dynamic pricing by ticket retailers, like Ticketmaster ; force influencers to disclose when they are being paid to promote a product; outrule personalized advertising and pricing targeting minors or taking advantage of sensitive data; make digital subscriptions easier to cancel; and give consumers a right to interact with human customer service. The package “represents the most significant reform of EU consumer protection rules in more than 20 years” according to Michael McGrath, the EC Consumer Protection Commissioner, noting that existing consumer rules were developed before ecommerce, the attention economy, and use of personal data for marketing took off. “The digital fairness act will make sure the digital economy works for consumers and not against them,” he said at a press conference. The bill will also enable all consumers to turn off addictive design features on digital services, such as autoplay of videos and streaks—including on apps like Strava and Duolingo. Some of these patterns the EU has already restricted for children through its Kids Act , which in addition to banning under-13s from accessing social media and chatbots, targets addictive designs in those services. Some European rights groups have called for those protections to be extended to all consumers and, teasing the Digital Fairness Act in September’s State of the Union address, President Ursula von der Leyen said: “But it is not only minors who are at risk. Addictive design, for example, is harming everyone. That is why we need a wider framework.” Some of the risks are also already regulated by the EU Digital Services Act. On Friday, the European Commission said ByteDance’s TikTok had breached those rules with the “rabbit hole effect” of its “For You” feed algorithm which personalizes content recommended to users. The tech regulator had previously found TikTok’s “addictive design” broke the rules by including features such as infinite scroll, autoplay, and push notifications, in addition to the algorithm. In July, it found Meta to be in breach of the act due to similar features on Instagram and Facebook . If confirmed, both companies may now face fines of up to 6 percent of worldwide annual turnover. The new regulation is designed to fill the gaps between this, the Digital Markets Act, and August’s AI Act , says executive vice president Henna Virkkunen, “not duplicate this.” The package should simplify consumer protection rules across the bloc’s 27 members and be a “strong safety net in the digital world,” she adds. The Commission aims to accelerate cross-border cooperation through strengthened enforcement rules. These would also give the regulator direct powers to investigate large-scale impact and fine firms up to 6 percent of their worldwide annual turnover. Non-EU companies would be required to appoint a local legal representative to cooperate with authorities. events.title: Air traffic control boss says he was ‘most disliked person in the UK’ after flight chaos
events.summary: Nats chief says he ‘quite enjoyed’ ignoring calls from Ryanair CEO to quit over system outages in September The boss of Nats has said he was “the most disliked person in the UK” after air traffic control systems failed twice in September, disrupting flights for hundreds of thousands of passengers. He told an aviation industry conference: “My name is Martin Rolfe, I’m the CEO of Nats – or as I like to think of myself, the most disliked person in the UK in September.” Airlines led by Ryanair called for Rolfe’s resignation after two technical failures in a fortnight at the two control centres run by Nats (National Air Traffic Control Services) stopped flights taking off and landing. However, Rolfe said he was “quite enjoying” ignoring the repeated calls from the Ryanair chief executive, Michael O’Leary, to quit. Airlines have said the outage on 8 September alone cost them tens of millions of pounds. The chaos that day stemmed from a problem in Nats’s flight control systems and is now the subject of a government-commissioned inquiry. Rolfe told the Airlines 2026 conference in London on Wednesday that Nats had expected to handle about 8,000 flights that day and 6,000 had flown, although he did not put a number on the long delays that many of those experienced. On 21 September, a further glitch at Nats’s second control centre at Prestwick in Scotland led to more than 200 flight cancellations. Rolfe said the causes for both events were unprecedented but had been fixed, although he could not promise there would be no more outages. He said he understood the disruption for people planning holidays and travel, adding: “If I am the cause of that disruption, I would expect to come in for a lot of flak. “We do these jobs knowing that they come with that level of personal responsibility and accountability and that’s where I think we’re most tested. “So yeah, I was definitely unpopular. There hasn’t been a poll, so I can’t say for sure.” He said he had not considered resigning, despite repeated calls by airlines, particularly Ryanair’s O’Leary , who has demanded his sacking for several years since flights were grounded on the August bank holiday in 2023. In fact, I quite enjoy not doing that.” He said that the particular faults experienced in September “will never recur” but added: “Nobody standing on a stage like this can credibly promise that a complex technical system will never experience another fault.” Speaking on stage later, Neal McMahon, the chief operating officer of Ryanair, criticised Rolfe for pointing out the usual reliability of Nats’s operations: “It’s like listening to the captain of the Titanic saying that 99% of the journey went just grand … We’re still left with two shitshows in September as a result of the system.” According to Nats’s early report, the software problem in September was not immediately believed to be serious. The Civil Aviation Authority is reviewing the findings and will report to the transport secretary, Heidi Alexander, early in 2027. In a potentially ominous warning for Rolfe, Alexander subsequently told the conference: “Like you, I expect that system to be resilient. And like you, I was angry when it fell short … [it] was simply unacceptable. She said she would not “jump the gun” before the CAA findings but added: “I can assure you that I will do whatever it takes to ensure that lessons are learned.”

events.title: Diesel still costing close to a ‘dismal’ £2 a litre despite oil price falls
events.summary: Pump prices stay stubbornly high as leading bank official warns energy costs are likely to remain ‘elevated’ The price of diesel on UK forecourts remains stubbornly close to October’s record high of £2 despite a sharp fall in oil prices. A litre costs an average of 197p, according to the AA, which described the situation as “dismal”. By contrast, petrol has fallen 6p to 168p from the peak of 174.7p in early October. That was the highest level since August 2022. High fuel prices are putting huge financial strain on households and businesses and Christopher Waller, a US Federal Reserve governor, told a conference in London this week that energy prices could remain “elevated”. He said a rise in tanker traffic through the strait of Hormuz came at a price: “The insurance now needed for ships making this passage, and the ship-to-ship transfer of oil necessary to guard against Iranian attacks, are reportedly boosting oil prices by $20 to $30 a barrel.” Diesel production is also being affected by limited refining capacity and other constraints, Waller said, adding: “As a consequence, elevated prices for diesel in the United States are not expected to moderate as readily as crude oil prices would in a more peaceful Middle East.” In the UK, the AA said that another 10p reduction could be on the cards for petrol because wholesale costs were falling. The wholesale cost of unleaded fell from 77p a litre to 68p in the second half of October, and now sits below 62p. As a rule of thumb, each 5p reduction at the pump knocks £2.75 off the cost of filling a typical car’s 55-litre tank. Luke Bosdet, the AA’s spokesperson on pump prices, said it was “hit and miss” but already possible to find petrol below 160p in certain areas, based on the government’s fuel finder data. “London and the south-east stand out for not showing any fuel stations with the bargain petrol prices of northern England, Wales and even Scotland,” he said. “Some forecourts are still charging close to the peak prices of early October and, given how much wholesale costs have fallen since the middle of last month, that is unforgivable.” The average diesel price is down only 2p a litre, from the all-time record of £2. With the wholesale cost down around 4p a litre since mid-October a further small reduction at the pump was possible, Bosdet said.

Hackers, apparently, after toilet paper maker's customer data exposed 2 days ago DigiCert admits 16-month security lapse exposed customer information 5 days ago October crypto-tracker hack: Access cracked, law enforcement tokens packed 6 days ago China's spaceplane bears striking resemblance to America's X-37B 14 days ago A 2013 breach of Russian-language cybercrime forum YouHack exposed its members' login details – and millions of credentials they had posted about other victims, according to newly cataloged data. Have I Been Pwned (HIBP) added the breach on Wednesday, recording 7.2 million unique email addresses. Around 107,000 belonged to forum members, whose exposed data included usernames, IP addresses, and mostly unsalted MD5 password hashes. Unsalted MD5 is a poor choice for protecting passwords. It's fast to compute, allowing attackers to test guesses at speed, and identical passwords produce identical hashes. Hardly good hygiene for a hacking forum. You might expect members of a cybercrime forum to know better than to reuse passwords or register with an email address tied to their real identity. Expectations and reality are not always on speaking terms, as AlphaBay founder Alexandre Cazes demonstrated. YouHack, a longtime cybercrime forum, moved to a different domain after the 2013 breach and remains active, giving cybercrims a place to trade stolen credentials and financial data. The data collated from that digital burglary was eventually bundled into 2024's so-called Mother of all Breaches – a 12TB, 26 billion-record mega-dump of files taken from myriad data security lapses. HIBP separately published its findings concerning another Russian data breach today. It said the 2023 breach of Russian bank Sberbank's loyalty program (SberSpasibo) contained records belonging to 48 million users. The dataset included 3.3 million unique email addresses, alongside phone numbers and dates of birth. Bank card numbers were stored as unsalted SHA-1 hashes, which could let attackers test possible numbers against the leaked hashes for a match. Reporting on the SberSpasibo breach at the time suggested the records were dated between April 2017 and February 2022, and the attack was claimed by the pro-Ukraine hacktivist outfit NLB. events.title: The Download: preserving minds and weighing open AI risks
events.summary: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. Six wild ideas for perpetuating your mind As we age, we forget most of what we’ve experienced, yet there’s still undeniable continuity: At 30, or 50, or 70, you will still be you.  To preserve that elusive continuity of self, some far-thinking technologists are exploring ways to keep the brain going, even beyond death. Their ideas range from freezing brains in liquid nitrogen to augmenting living ones and uploading our memories to the cloud. Here are six possible paths for keeping your mind going, and how feasible they might be . —Antonio Regalado This story is from the Impossible edition of our print magazine. Subscribe now to get every issue as soon as it lands. MIT Technology Review Narrated: Open models have real benefits. Do they outweigh the risks? Anthropic recently released a report arguing that a powerful new model released by the Chinese company Z.ai, poses a major cyberattack risk. Its core concern was that it is freely available for anyone to download and modify. The warning was the latest flashpoint in the debate over open frontier AI models. Critics warn that bad actors can misuse them, while supporters argue they prevent a handful of companies from controlling the technology. The debate, however, is more complicated than it seems . This is our latest story to become an MIT Technology Review Narrated podcast, which we publish each week on Spotify and Apple Podcasts . Just navigate to MIT Technology Review Narrated on either platform, and follow us to get all our new content as it’s released. The must-reads I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology. 1 COP31’s flagship pledge to electrify 35% of energy use is sinking Only around a dozen nations are reportedly ready to sign it. ( Politico ) + It requires quadrupling the pace of electrification. ( New Scientist $) + John Kerry says the US must follow China on clean energy. ( Guardian ) + But the US skipped the talks entirely for a second year. ( NYT $) + What’s the future of electricity? ( MIT Technology Review ) 2 The Nvidia spy scandal reportedly involves $7.5 billion of chips Alice Huang allegedly obtained 240,000 restricted chips. ( Information $) + Trump was told of Huang’s spy link on Air Force One . ( NYT $) + Experts warn the scandal could erode America’s AI lead. ( Verge ) + Nvidia’s slide has let Microsoft overtake it in value. ( Reuters $) 3 Studies found AI agents go rogue because they’re “incorrigible” Their training rewards them for finishing tasks at any cost. ( NYT $) + This is why AI agents lie and cheat to reach their goals. ( MIT Technology Review ) 4 Anthropic has scaled back its IPO valuation to $1.4 trillion It aimed for $2 trillion before the recent AI jitters. ( Guardian ) 5 Drone strikes have wiped out 3% of Yandex’s cloud customer data Ukraine hit three of its data centers in October. ( Reuters $) + Ukraine’s drones are fighting data centers for fiber. ( Ars Technica ) 6 Moderna says its new vaccine could prevent cancer in high-risk people The company’s CEO calls it the “holy grail” of cancer prevention. ( FT $) + Hong Kong is testing a next-gen ultrasound cancer treatment. ( SCMP ) 7 Scientists have slowly reversed human cells’ ages by decades One age marker was set back as far as 60 years. ( Wired $) + “Reprogramming” is the buzziest de-aging idea. ( MIT Technology Review ) 8 Robot vessels are hunting for mines in the Strait of Hormuz AI helps them spot mines camouflaged on the seabed. ( BBC ) 9 Life may have started inside a tiny bubble That’s the idea behind the “lipid first” origin theory. ( Quanta ) 10 As Voyager 1 reaches a light day from Earth, here’s what it’s taught us Its discoveries rewrote textbooks in real time. ( New Scientist $) Quote of the day “What a dereliction of duty. He’s supposed to protect America, not China, not his friends.” —Chuck Schumer, the Senate minority leader, accuses President Donald Trump of ignoring warnings about the alleged relationship between Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and a Chinese spy. One more thing How refrigeration ruined fresh food Bananas may not be chilled in the grocery store, but they’re the ultimate refrigerated fruit. It’s only thanks to a network of thermal control that they’ve become a global commodity. And that salad bag on the shelf? It’s not just a bag but a highly engineered respiratory apparatus. According to Nicola Twilley—a contributor to The New Yorker and cohost of the podcast Gastropod—refrigeration has wrecked our food system. Thankfully, there are promising alternative preservation methods.  Read the full story on her research . —Allison Arieff We can still have nice things A place for comfort, fun, and distraction to brighten up your day. Drop me a line .) + A whisky made like wine is wowing the spirits world. + Britain lost in the fog makes for hauntingly beautiful photos . + Chronophoto is a fiendishly addictive game that challenges you to date old photos to the year. + Dozens of saxophonists met up in New York to play the gloriously cheesy riff from George Michael’s “Careless Whisper.”

events.title: A Newborn Died in a Faith-Healing Sect. The State — and One Ex-Believer — Stepped in to Save Her Twin.
events.summary: Evelyn at the grave of her twin, Ginnifer The deputy medical examiner thought the family was being evasive. Eric Tonsfeldt had been dispatched to the pistachio-green house in Oregon City on the night of March 5, 2017. Inside he found Sarah Mitchell in bed, her dead newborn in her arms. Mitchell is a member of the Followers of Christ, a sect known for refusing medical treatment. She had received no prenatal care. Three women without medical training guided her delivery that afternoon. Tonsfeldt listened as the family insisted that the baby, whom they had named Ginnifer, had seemed healthy for most of the afternoon, then suddenly stopped breathing. They couldn’t explain why the baby appeared so underweight. Their answers to many of Tonsfeldt’s questions were vague. Nobody would make eye contact with him. Later, investigators would discover that 13 minutes after Ginnifer’s birth, Followers began exchanging a series of worried texts. “Not good breathing,” one wrote in a group chat. Another requested prayers: “She’s really bad.” (One person in the chat would later advise deleting the messages.) No one had called 911 as the gaps between each breath increased. When asked why not, Ginnifer’s father later said, “Because it’s in God’s hands.” He anointed his daughter with olive oil and wept as he prayed that she would be OK. Ginnifer died in his arms at 7 p.m., four hours after she was born. Tonsfeldt gently collected the newborn and examined her in another room. She weighed 3½ pounds, roughly half that of an average full-term infant. He found no signs of injury or trauma. The living room in the house where Ginnifer was born and died. Dozens of Followers of Christ members filled the home that day, but none called 911. Clackamas County District Attorney’s Office Followers anoint the ailing with olive oil. Clackamas County District Attorney’s Office The medical examiner still felt that something was awry. To play for time, he asked if someone would make him a cup of coffee and headed to the kitchen. As Tonsfeldt waited, one of the baby’s grandfathers approached him and blurted out an unexpected question: Would it make a difference if Ginnifer had a twin? There was another baby, a girl named Evelyn. She was alive. In the dim light of a bathroom, Tonsfeldt found women huddled over a tiny newborn, who was barely making a sound. They were feeding her from an eyedropper. He told the family to get her to a hospital. After Evelyn’s grandfather made it clear they weren’t going anywhere, Tonsfeldt summoned the police, who delivered an ultimatum: Take Evelyn to the hospital or they’d do it themselves. Evelyn, at 14 days old, was still so small she could fit into dolls’ clothes. Courtesy of the Phillips family Evelyn’s family relented. A patrol car followed to make sure they got there. She was admitted to a neonatal intensive care unit in Portland with respiratory distress syndrome. With the help of a breathing machine and a feeding tube, Evelyn began to stabilize. An autopsy would later conclude the same condition, common in premature babies, had caused her sister’s death. The Mitchells were charged with murder by neglect, as well as criminal mistreatment for failing to get Evelyn medical care. That left authorities with another challenge: Who would care for Evelyn? Her family assumed any custody arrangement would be temporary and suggested Marshall and Jennifer Phillips, a couple born and raised in the Followers. But Marshall was no ordinary Follower. Once, when his young son became gravely ill, he brought him to a hospital. In the eyes of the state, that made Marshall and his wife suitable candidates to look after Evelyn. Evelyn’s family didn’t know then that Marshall’s choice to save his son had set him on a yearslong journey, one that would eventually lead him away from the only life he’d ever known. And that he would take Evelyn with him. Jennifer and Marshall Phillips For more than a century, states have wrestled with how to address the deaths of children whose parents refuse them medical care for religious reasons. As early as 1901, a father in New York who believed in the “power of God to heal the sick through prayer” was prosecuted for failing to call a doctor for his young daughter who died from pneumonia. Since then, courts have repeatedly held — in cases where Christian Scientists refused treatment or Jehovah’s Witnesses declined blood transfusions — that adults are free to reject medical care for themselves. Whether they can be compelled to provide medical care for their children is another matter, one that’s been left to states to decide. Courts have generally deferred to legislatures on this question. Video: This Secretive Religious Sect Doesn’t Believe in Medical Care Marshall Phillips was raised in the Followers of Christ, which forbids medical care. When his son fell gravely ill, he took him to the hospital. That choice set him on a yearslong journey, one that would eventually lead him away from the only life he’d ever known. Teresa Mahoney, Noelle Crombie, Beth Nakamura and Samantha Swindler/The Oregonian For decades, Oregon’s law gave latitude to faith healing and authorities did little to intervene. Between 1989 and 1999, 18 children of the Oregon City-based Followers died. (The sect numbered between 1,500 and 2,000 at its peak.) Most or all of those deaths were preventable, according to the state medical examiner at the time, who estimated that the child death rate in the sect was 26 times that of the general population. The revelation of those deaths, in The Oregonian and other news outlets, prompted state lawmakers to act. In 1999, they removed spiritual treatment as a defense for second-degree manslaughter and criminal mistreatment. In 2008, prosecutors filed their first case against Followers parents after a 15-month-old died from untreated bronchial pneumonia and a blood infection. A jury convicted the girl’s father of a single count of criminal mistreatment, a misdemeanor, and acquitted her mother. Two more children in the sect died without medical attention during this period, prompting the Legislature in 2011 to do away with the spiritual defense for any crime. Among those supporting the change: the Christian Science church, which by then had softened its stance amid a steep decline in membership. In a letter to lawmakers that year, a church official wrote: “Spiritual care should never be practiced at the expense of a child’s life.” Evelyn in her room Changes in Oregon law — and prosecutors’ willingness to pursue parents who watched their children die — spurred a slow but perceptible shift: Deaths of children in the Followers have become an anomaly. Ginnifer Mitchell’s death in 2017 came amid that yearslong decline. Since then, one child has died due to lack of medical care. events.title: Prophecy, Scorn and a Rejection of This World: The Forbidding Vision of a Faith-Healing Preacher
events.summary: Walter White baptizes a Followers of Christ member in 1951. He led an Oregon City, Oregon, offshoot of the sect. Courtesy of the Phillips family It was a stark and forbidding vision for those who followed the righteous path. Scorn, the preacher told his congregation, was a person’s lot if they led an “honest, clean, pure, godly life.” The world hated “people that live like that,” he said. “They want you to be just as ungodly and filthy as they are,” he said in a rare audio recording, obtained by The Oregonian/OregonLive, of a 1958 sermon. The preacher was Walter White, who led an Oregon City offshoot of the Followers of Christ, an Idaho sect that spurns medical treatment as a show of faith. White was a grocer, originally from Picabo, Idaho, whose congregants came to view as a prophet. He rambled at times during his sermon but always returned to simple and severe messages about choosing righteousness rather than the ways of the world. A trim figure in wire-rim glasses and dark combed-back hair, he spoke in a voice that evoked the stentorian tones of an old newsreel announcer. In the scratchy recording, people cough and babies cry as he preaches. White was uneasy about being taped, according to a note by the congregant who made the recording. White didn’t want his message to fall into what he thought were undesirable hands. He viewed disbelievers with disgust. They put their trust in human experts, such as doctors, rather than in God. People like that, he told the faithful, “want to be somebody.” They want “the wisdom of the world and admiration.” Today, nearly 60 years after White’s death, his pronouncements continue to influence the faithful. For many Followers, White remained “the highest authority,” said Mark Shaw, who left the sect in 2019 and keeps in touch with some Followers. Members invoked his teachings to settle disagreements. “It was used as the trump card,” he said. “It was the discussion-ender.” White’s grave in the Followers’ cemetery outside of Oregon City Beth Nakamura/The Oregonian To understand the modern-day Oregon City congregation, it’s essential to examine White’s role. No pastor ever succeeded him, leaving the sect all the more reliant on his teachings. The Oregonian/OregonLive and ProPublica have published a series of articles in recent months about the Followers of Christ in Oregon and Idaho , focusing on the long history of parents in Followers congregations declining to seek medical care for their critically ill children and the sometimes fatal consequences . Little has been publicly known about White, likely due to the Followers’ culture of isolation and secrecy. The Oregonian/OregonLive was able to piece together details through documents we obtained, including biographical sketches, a transcript and the recording of the sermon, along with written accounts of dreams White purported to have and records of baptisms he performed. Among the documents was a list of his prophecies and even a sex guide he disseminated. White was born into the Followers, whose members migrated to Idaho from the Midwest around the turn of the 20th century. Men in White’s family preached, and he joined them in his 20s, the story goes, after he dreamed that worms would devour him if he didn’t. In the early 1930s, White joined two church elders on a journey from Idaho to Oregon City to minister to a dying man. After talking with them, the man readily discarded his medications and was relieved to see White, an avid smoker, roll a cigarette because the man didn’t want to kick the habit. For the next five years, White traveled between Idaho and Oregon to preach and by 1938, he had moved to Oregon to lead a fledgling congregation. Followers at the time were led by a constellation of preachers and elders, all men. Notes from one of their meetings in 1937 revealed that Followers believed White possessed the “gift of prophecy.” It also recorded the debates that simmered among them — whether women should be allowed to cut their hair, for instance. They talked about the value of dictionaries, which some classified as “worldly” items to be avoided, and determined that women assisting with home births should not “look under the cover” as women labored. One account written years later by a Follower suggested that White split with a prominent Idaho preacher after revelations that the man had sexual contact with a 15-year-old girl. Some of those values still shape the Followers today. Congregants tend to stay out of what they view as the worldly affairs of politics and civic life, and they generally don’t pursue education beyond high school or vocational training. The Followers remain patriarchal; men are expected to lead their households. White, second from left in the back (in suspenders), with Followers leaders in Oregon City in 1937. By 1938, he had moved to Oregon to lead a fledgling congregation. Courtesy of the Phillips family White was known among Followers as “brother Walter.” An undated black-and-white photograph shows him baptizing a child in what appears to be a baptismal pool, his arm raised in prayer. In another image dated 1951, he wears a suit jacket and tie, a mug in one hand and a cigarette in the other. As much a ruler as a spiritual leader, White enjoyed near-absolute authority. Followers believed he possessed such divine power that he knew their thoughts and secrets. They turned to him for approval on matters both consequential and mundane, from marital advice to appliance purchases. (White even weighed in on where to shop: He owned a local market and made it clear he expected to see Followers there.) White’s earthly teachings extended to a perhaps unexpected realm: Couples on the cusp of marriage received a sex guide, which continued to be distributed as recently as 2018. Complete with explicit detail and anatomical diagrams, the 15-page manual includes chapters titled “the ideal love act” and “the control of climax.” And, in a seeming exception to the prohibition on medical treatment, it goes so far as to recommend that women who feel inhibited should consider seeing a doctor “who has given the sex problems sincere study.” White preached the Oregon City sect’s singularity: His flock was spiritually superior to other Follower congregations, he contended, including ones in Idaho and Grants Pass, Oregon. By the 1950s, he had cut off ties to those groups. In 1965, White told his congregation of his prophecy that the end times were near. He recounted a dream, which he said was set against the backdrop of the Kennedy Space Center in Florida, that involved walking with Jesus Christ, according to one account. He dreamed they climbed a launchpad, and White noted he was impressed with Christ’s physical agility. Days before White shared his vision, NASA launched Gemini 3, the first U.S. mission to send multiple astronauts into space. events.title: From blood group ID to cycle racks: I asked for little ways to fix broken Britain and the public’s ideas give me hope | Martin Lewis
events.summary: From blood group ID to cycle racks: I asked for little ways to fix broken Britain and the public’s ideas give me hope There are thousands of small tips to make our country better. People know what is wrong, and it’s clear they have solutions H ave you ever come across an annoying little problem and thought, “why don’t they just fix that?” If so, I want to hear from you. I’m looking for your ideas for practical, low-cost, non-controversial ways to improve the UK – whether that’s health, schools, transport, business, housing, policing, justice, tech, shopping, money – or owt else entirely. The spark for this happened just over a year ago, when I spoke at Politico’s fringe event at Labour’s conference. The key discussion was about Keir Starmer’s unpopularity. I was asked what I’d have advised the government when it took power, so I said : “Come up with 100 small things that piss people off and that you can fix, and they can see that you have fixed them.” Then I reeled off a list of small fixes for my subject area: the counterproductive way council tax debt is escalated; renaming “tax-free childcare”; and so on. As I walked off stage, I emailed myself: “Set up an Institute for Small Ideas.” I started straight away, did some work, brought some people together, put it out to tender for charities to run it, and then a month ago it launched – albeit with a slight name change. Think of it as a sort of apolitical national suggestion box. And in those few weeks since launch, we’ve already had 42,000 suggestions. At a time when public debate can feel dominated by division, outrage and disagreement, there’s something quietly encouraging about tens of thousands of people taking the time to offer constructive ideas. Clearly the timing was fortuitous, as small ideas are now all the rage. We haven’t started the filtering process yet, but here are just a few of the ideas that have been suggested: Tell people their blood group at their first adult blood test. Knowing you’ve a common or rare type may make you more inclined to donate. It’s a brilliantly simple nudge that could widen the donor pool and save lives. A mandatory “AI-edited” label on property photos on estate agency sites. A “no wrong door” rule for councils and public bodies: report a problem anywhere, and they must pass it to the right place, rather than bouncing you from department to department, or from council to contractor to agency. Cinema seating plans that clearly show aisles and walkways for disability access. A voluntary wheelie-bin sharing scheme, so neighbours with spare capacity can help stop bins overflowing. The idea is that if someone could fix enough of these frustrations and make lives easier, save time and let everyone get on with work or the things they enjoy, the combined effect – and the feelgood factor – would help shift the national mood. To make this happen, I’ve funded the Small Ideas Initiative , with two charities – Nesta and Involve – running a project in the background. (I’m telling you this because I believe funding transparency is crucial in any policy charity.) They will filter the suggestions and hopefully select and publish at least 1,000 of the best to provide a bank of ideas others may look at in future. They’ll pick 200 of these to turn into fully researched policy proposals. Then, having got public feedback on those, we’ve brought together a cross-party panel – with representatives from Green to Reform and every party in between – who will need to unanimously agree the final 50-ish. These are meant to be useful and doable, not party political or controversial. And if that broad a church can agree on them, we’ve likely succeeded. These 50 will form the first Small Ideas manifesto we will campaign to get implemented. Since that Labour party conference a year ago, the prime minister has changed of course, and Andy Burnham seems to have taken small ideas to heart . Which means I hope the door may be open for many of these suggestions. Of course, I’m not suggesting that Britain needs only small ideas. These quick fixes are there to work alongside, not instead of, the longer-term big structural changes that society and the economy need. Yet if you focus only on legacy and not on legwork, it can leave the public feeling detached and with an impression that politics is futile, achieves nothing and is just talk without delivering. Small fixes are still fixes – fix a lot of them and it adds up. Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more So, if you have a solution for a broken part of the way things work, you have until 5pm on Thursday 12 November to put it forward at Small-Ideas.org. Martin Lewis is the founder of MoneySavingExpert.com and the Money and Mental Health Policy Institute charity. He has just set up the Small Ideas Initiative

events.title: What are cold weather payments and who can get them?
events.summary: As temperatures drop, heating costs rise, but there is some help for many households through cold weather payments. This financial help is triggered across hundreds of postcodes in England, Wales and Northern Ireland when there is a prolonged period of below-zero temperatures. In Scotland, those on low incomes and benefits may receive a separate winter heating payment, which does not depend on how cold it gets. The cold weather payment is a government benefit top-up to help with fuel bills , external . The average temperature in a local area must be recorded as, or forecast to be, 0C or below for seven days in a row. The temperature is recorded by the relevant weather station for your postcode. England and Wales: Enter your postcode here to check eligibility , external Northern Ireland: Enter your postcode here to check eligibility , external More than 1.4 million cold weather payments were made during winter 2025-26. Check the UK weather warnings in place Who can get cold weather payments and how much are they worth? To qualify, you must live in England, Wales or Northern Ireland. Payments are not age-related but you must already be receiving certain benefits, including: income-based job seekers' allowance income-related employment and support allowance universal credit - although there are certain exceptions Each cold weather payment is for a seven-day period and is worth £25. More than one payment will be made during the course of the winter if there are enough periods of cold weather. The scheme runs between 1 November and 31 March each year. Hospital stays can affect your entitlement to the payment so you should tell the Pension Service , external or Jobcentre Plus , external if you become an inpatient. You should also update the relevant service if you have a baby, or if a child under five comes to live with you. In Scotland, the winter heating payment is worth £62 , external , and is paid automatically between December and February. Heating tips to keep your home warm when budgets are squeezed Published 2 January How to keep babies warm in cold weather and other winter tips Published 2 January How to drive in snow and icy weather Published 2 January How do cold weather health alerts work? Published 22 June How do I get cold weather payments and how long does it take? You do not have to do anything in order to receive cold weather payments. The money should be paid automatically into the same bank or building society account as your benefits, within two weeks of the qualifying period of cold weather. If you do not receive a payment, you can contact the Pension Service , external or Jobcentre Plus , external . Cold weather payments do not affect other benefits. They are separate to the winter fuel payment , which is worth £100 or £300 depending on your individual circumstances. About nine million pensioners get the Winter Fuel Payment, after a government u-turn over changes to the eligibility rules. events.title: Tracking how Jensen Huang changed his stance on China
events.summary: Jensen Huang’s public rhetoric on China became more admiring, and his stance on export controls more critical, after the US restricted Nvidia’s made-for-China chip in 2025 — and as he had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy. A Semafor analysis of 42 podcast interviews with Huang since early 2022 shows how Huang’s argument around global chip policy evolved in a series of long-form, unscripted, and often friendly settings: Huang talked up China’s strengths and cast Beijing as a formidable competitor as he argued more forcefully for a careful balance between protecting US interests and making US technology the backbone of global AI development. Whether the Nvidia CEO’s position was shaped by his affair with an executive at a Singapore-based data center firm with alleged ties to Beijing is now a matter for the company’s board, which hired Wall Street law firm Wachtell Lipton to investigate, and for Congress, who plan hearings on the matter. But his stance on China and chip controls is freshly in the spotlight. Semafor identified dozens of exchanges about China across the interviews and used a pair of AI models from Anthropic and OpenAI to score each one on Huang’s stance on export restrictions and how he regarded China. Before China’s DeepSeek burst onto the global stage and Washington put new limits on Nvidia’s sales to the country in early 2025, Huang spoke on podcasts about export restrictions in a largely neutral tenor, framing them as a matter of compliance, according to our review. Mentions of China in Huang’s interviews rose roughly sixfold after those 2025 curbs, as the chip CEO argued that the restrictions hurt the US more than China. “If we leave a market altogether, there’s no question somebody else would step in ,” he told Michael Milken in May 2025. In 14 interviews since the 2025 curbs, he talked up China’s AI researchers, open-source models, and manufacturing, often as reasons the US can’t afford to cut the country off, or rejected the idea of treating it as an enemy. He invoked the “American tech stack” 34 times across eight interviews since July 2025, arguing that the world’s developers should build on US technology. In eight interviews he said that 50% of the world’s AI researchers are Chinese or in China, suggesting the country’s tech talent can’t be ignored. — J.D. Capelouto

events.title: A top lobbyist returns to the White House
events.summary: The News A conservative firebrand who helped craft the Trump administration’s campaign against Ivy League universities has returned to the White House to help chief of staff Stephen Miller build his team, a move that will test the administration’s efforts to contain the influence of lobbyists within the White House. May Mailman, who left her post as Trump policy adviser in 2026 to launch her own lobbying firm, will join the White House on a temporary basis as a special government employee, Axios first reported and Semafor confirmed. In recent months, Mailman had built a healthy stable of corporate clients with active matters before the Trump administration, including Vestis, a uniform supplier which has pushed the FTC to block a rival’s acquisition, people familiar with the matter said. The FTC is poised to block that deal , Semafor earlier reported. Other companies she’s worked for include Netflix, Meta, HPE, Comcast, and KKR, according to the people. Mailman, as well as the firms, either declined to provide a comment for this story or did not return a request for comment. Mailman served as a policy adviser early in Trump’s tenure, helping Miller go after Harvard and Columbia for what the administration called indifference to antisemitism on college campuses. She decided to return to the administration in recent days after Miller was named chief of staff, with Miller asking her to help him staff up his team and find ways to optimize relationships between government entities. Mailman ruled out a policy role when discussing her return to public service, though, in part over concerns that it would fuel a perception of impropriety, one person with knowledge of her thinking said. Still, the revolving door between the White House and lobbying work raises questions around how much Mailman stands to benefit personally from her new role and about the level of influence that corporations have held over this White House. The White House didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment. Mailman informed clients of her new role within recent days, and has instructed her firm — which she has taken a leave of absence from — to not engage with the White House while she is serving there for the next few weeks, some of the people said. Rohan’s view Americans on both sides of the aisle have grown frustrated with the level of influence big corporations have over this administration — with a CNBC survey of voters finding that corruption was the number one issue going into the midterms. That perception has only been fueled by the list of Trump-connected lobbyists who have gone in and out of the White House, perhaps the only bipartisan move left in DC. Mailman, perhaps uniquely, has shied away from the kind of publicity that some lobbyists have courted. And her efforts to create a firewall between her clients and her firm, as she returns to government service, stand in contrast to other administration power brokers, who openly tout their relationships with administration officials.

events.title: Mini record player on track for No 1 in Christmas toy parade
events.summary: Industry experts pick out tiny turntable as one of their ‘15 hottest toys’ for the festive season A record player so small it belongs at a party in a Barbie Dreamhouse is one of this year’s must-have Christmas gifts as the vinyl revival takes an unexpected turn. The £19.99 micro music set plays dinky 1.5in records and comes with an exclusive “mini vinyl” of the school disco favourite APT by Rosé and Bruno Mars. The toy makes the Toy Retailers Association’s annual DreamToys list of the 15 “hottest toys” this festive season. The Mini Brands record player taps into the huge market for collectible toys. Part of the appeal is the 45 mini records to collect, ranging from Billie Eilish’s Birds of a Feather to Neil Diamond’s Sweet Caroline. The discs are sold separately in £8 “blind balls” with part of the attraction being the mystery of which songs are inside. The trend for miniature products comes because making something smaller “makes it feel cuter”, suggests Melissa Symonds, executive director of UK toys at market research company Circana. While adults enjoyed the novelty, she suggested that children would relish acting out playing records in the same way that their parents did. The record player is unlikely to satisfy high-end audiophiles, however, because the “vinyl” isn’t real. Instead, the discs contain a chip that activates a 30-second clip from the player’s internal memory. The rundown of must-have toys comes as retailers brace for their most important trading period: the final three months of the year typically account for 45% of annual toy sales. Hopes are high after sales jumped 13% to £2.6bn in the first nine months, according to Circana, which it said was the “fastest growth in a decade”. During that period, 257m toys were sold – 38m more than in the same period last year. The buoyant picture is partly due to the “squishies” craze. Retailers are racing to keep up with demand for the sensory toys with NeeDoh the most popular official brand. Paul Reader, chair of the DreamToys selection panel at the Toy Retailers Association, said 2026 had been “incredible for the UK toy market”. He added: “We haven’t seen anything like squishies since the days of fidget spinners and before that POGs [a milk cap game].” Children loved the tactile toys, he said, because once you’ve “got it in your hands … you just can’t put it down”. After a period when “kidults” (aged 12 and over) buying expensive Lego sets and collectible figurines propped up toy sales, Reader said demand for toys like squishies was pulling children back into toy shops. “We’re seeing more children coming into stores, that after-school time is busier.” The 15 toys on the Dreamtoys list range in price from £13.99 for a NeeDoh squishy to £129.99 for a dinosaur-themed Hot Wheels garage. The furReal Gabby the Grow & Roar Tiger – an interactive cuddly toy that transforms from a cub into a tiger – may thrill an animal lover. For the legions of K-pop Demon Hunter fans there is a singing doll that belts out their hit Golden. The near-£50 Pokémon 30th Celebration Elite Trainer Box also makes the list, but as fans queue up outside stores to buy the latest card releases parents are advised not to leave tracking this gift down until the last minute. events.title: UK’s Cheval Collection launches new Dubai project in expansion push
events.summary: Cheval Collection , the UK-based luxury hospitality firm, has launched a new development in Dubai, with plans to expand in the UAE and the region as property demand increases. The project in Dubai South will have 98 serviced hotel apartments ranging from studios to three-bedroom units, and 95 one, two and three-bedroom branded residences. It is scheduled to open in 2030. Cheval South Bay is the fourth development for the company in Dubai and its sixth in the Middle East. It has two more under-construction properties being built in Saudi Arabia. Sales for Cheval South Bay are expected to start next year. Prices and the total value of the project have yet to be disclosed. “Announcing this project today shows what our confidence is like in Dubai, our confidence in the UAE, and our confidence in the wider GCC [Gulf Co-operation Council],” Nick Pilbeam, Cheval Collection’s chief commercial officer, told The National. “Cheval already operates two properties in Dubai, Cheval Maison The Palm, Cheval Maison Expo City Dubai … in the last six months, in the current situation, they've [performed] well. They've outperformed the market, certainly in occupancy because of this long-stay angle.” Cheval Maison The Palm and Cheval Maison Expo City, opened in 2023 and 2025, offer serviced apartments. The company also launched a branded residence development in Dubai Island in April. Cheval's latest announcement comes as property developers continue to launch projects in the UAE despite concerns about the slowing of the market as the Iran war continues. This week, Dubai’s Nakheel unveiled a 3.8 million-square-metre residential development next to Palm Jebel Ali, with a mix of villas, townhouses and apartments. It will also have education, health care, sport and leisure facilities across 15 neighbourhoods in southern Dubai, with two schools, a hospital and six mosques. In September, Aldar, Abu Dhabi’s biggest listed developer, and Sharjah-based Arada revealed plans to build new housing projects on Yas Island and at Seih Sdeirah in Abu Dhabi, representing a combined value of about Dh15 billion ($4 billion). Cheval is also exploring opportunities to start a new project in Abu Dhabi as the emirate’s property market has been performing strongly this year, with real estate transactions surging. A total of 38,483 transactions worth Dh171.26 billion were registered in Abu Dhabi in the first nine months of 2026, marking a 76.1 per cent increase in value and a 32.8 per cent rise in volume on an annual basis. “There's a lot going on in the Abu Dhabi real estate market,” Mr Pilbeam said. “I can't talk anything concrete just yet, but it is certainly a city and an area that we're looking at and interested in.” The privately owned company is also looking to expand in other parts of the Middle East and North Africa region, with a new property launch being planned “in a few weeks time” expected to take its portfolio to about 1,000 units. “We're clearly on a growth journey. However, we're still very selective about the projects that we go in for. We want to be in prime locations, in tier-one locations, tier-one destinations. We are negotiating multiple projects,” he added.

events.title: UAE's Landmark Group probes data breach in Shukran loyalty programme
events.summary: The UAE's Landmark Group is investigating a cyber incident involving “unauthorised access” to its Shukran loyalty programme, it said on Wednesday. The customer information involved includes names, contact details and dates of birth, the Dubai-based retail and hospitality conglomerate said. However, debit and credit card details were not compromised, as those are not stored on its system, Landmark Group said. Shukran points, which are redeemed for perks and discounts, are also unaffected. Landmark did not specify the severity of the breach, but it said any customers receiving text messages from the company about the incident could be affected. “We recently identified an incident involving unauthorised access to one of our systems. We acted immediately to contain it,” Landmark said. “We have also informed the relevant statutory and law enforcement authorities and are actively investigating the matter.” Landmark Group is one of the biggest retail corporates in the UAE, with more than 20 brands including fashion retailers Max, Splash and Centrepoint, electronics store Emax, Home Centre, Fitness First and Viva supermarket. It operates in all the Gulf countries, plus Egypt, Jordan, India, Malaysia and Indonesia. Cyber breaches are increasing as bad actors try to make financial gains or steal user data, prompting companies to strengthen their network defences. As well as financial damage, attacks on systems can have reputational consequences. Artificial intelligence has made cyber attacks more complex and agile. IBM said lost business remained the largest cost category in the region, averaging $3.57 million per breach. The UAE has put in place advanced cyber defence systems to fend off any attacks to protect the economy and society. On one Tuesday in September, the Emirates faced 640,000 attacks, national cyber security chief Mohamed Al Kuwaiti said.

events.title: ‘I’d steal 10-15 times a day’: ex-offenders on the addictions driving prolific shoplifting
events.summary: Former shoplifters say treatment and drug rehabilitation are essential to ending cycle of theft and imprisonment Police to target 500 chronic shoplifters in retail crime crackdown in England When Rhys, 34, stole goods from shops across Birmingham , he would often leave notes for the staff apologising for his actions. “I’d feel that guilty about it. I’d pass them notes, saying I’m so sorry about this,” he said. “But in the end, I was just that numb to it, and fearless as well. I’d walk in with a suitcase and ram everything into it, and not think twice about it.” Rhys was in the grips of drug addiction and turned to shoplifting to fund his habit. He had struggled with drug use since he was a teenager and then, in 2019, he took crack cocaine for the first time. “Within a week, I was going into shops and shoplifting for it, because you just can’t get enough,” he said. Over the next few years, he shoplifted 10-15 times a day and was sent to prison several times. However, without help to tackle his addiction, Rhys struggled to change his behaviour. “I’d spend hours shoplifting but, at the end of the day, I still wouldn’t have anything to eat. I’d be jumping back over the fence to go through the bins to get myself a sandwich. I wouldn’t even get myself a bottle of water,” he said. “My priority was always getting the stuff to sell for drugs.” On Wednesday, the home secretary announced plans to target 500 of the most prolific shoplifters across the country with police crackdowns in 17 areas. Measures include banning repeat offenders from high streets and town centres, closer monitoring of offenders with regular hearings before a judge and the use of electronic tagging. But former shoplifters say many prolific thieves are in the grip of drug addiction or experiencing mental health crises, and without more funding for support services, the problem will not go away. Keeley, 44, was once labelled Birmingham’s most prolific shoplifter, stealing between £5,000 and £9,000 worth of goods a day. She was sent to prison 28 times. Keeley had been addicted to drugs since the age of 13, after being groomed by an older man, and stole items such as designer handbags, which she could sell quickly to fund her habit. Her biggest fear was withdrawal, which had previously left her in hospital for 10 days. She said shoplifting was an exhausting necessity – one that often led to her walking 30,000 steps a day. “Shoplifting, to a lot of us, is the closest to a victimless crime as you can get. You’re not violating anyone’s house or privacy, or robbing food out of their mouth. “I know it’s not right, but it’s what we tell ourselves to justify it at the time – that you’re not hurting anyone – because none of us want to be doing what we’re doing.” Keeley said she “didn’t get caught much for the amount of stuff that I stole”. Yet she spent three decades in and out of prison, never receiving the help she needed. She eventually turned her life around when an off-duty security guard referred her to a drug support service, which led to her receiving buprenorphine injections to treat her opioid dependence. “We’re crying that we’ve got a shoplifting crisis, and we’re crying that we’ve got a drug crisis, but no one’s doing anything about the two together,” Keeley said. “If you treat the root cause and take the addiction away, we’ve got no reason to go out and commit crime.” For Rhys, help came in the form of an outreach navigator – a professional who connects vulnerable people to social services, housing and healthcare. He has been in recovery for 18 months, spends his time volunteering and has left shoplifting behind. “I went into Aldi the other day, and I asked for a carrier bag and scanned it straight away. It’s such a weird comparison – now I’m scanning these 30p bags. But before, I was going in there and filling a suitcase to steal,” he said. The social justice charity Revolving Doors said addiction, poor mental health and homelessness – often all three at once – were substantial drivers of Britain’s shoplifting epidemic . Pavan Dhaliwal, the charity’s chief executive, said: “The anger of retailers and shop workers is justified. Theft is not victimless, and abuse of staff is intolerable. “But if we want fewer thefts, rather than just more arrests, we have to ask a harder question: why does the same small group of people keep cycling through crisis and custody repeatedly?” Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters She said services that can direct people away from addiction and into stable housing were essential. “The people we work with show that recovery and rebuilding lives are possible with the right support.” Sean, 44, has been to prison 42 times since 2000. For decades, he had not spent more than six months out of custody and felt “powerless to addiction” that drove him to crime after a traumatic childhood.

Moller-Maersk says it is investigating "an IT security incident" involving the potential theft of data from a legacy system. In a statement issued on Wednesday, the Denmark-based shipping, cargo, and logistics giant confirmed it immediately launched an investigation into the attack and the affected system was secured. "Our findings so far strongly suggest no sensitive data has been disclosed," the company said . "The incident is isolated to a local system, and we have found no indication that there has been any impact on other Maersk systems or customer and partner systems that connect to Maersk through integrations such as APIs and EDI." Maersk described the legacy local system as one "from a previous acquisition," and said it does not expect the attack to have an effect on operations. Customers were reassured that they can continue to use Maersk platforms to manage their shipments as usual, and to expect updates from the company as and when they're available. "Cybersecurity remains a constant, ongoing priority for Maersk," it added. "We have rigorous processes in place to identify and prevent incidents and minimize customer impact. Mimicking the Petya ransomware strain, NotPetya was an infamous destructive wiper malware strain that wormed its way across the global economy. Western intelligence agencies attributed the malware to Russia's Sandworm group, an outfit believed to be part of the country's military intelligence service (GRU).
