events.title: House Democrats lobby against China committee
events.summary: Some Democrats on the House Foreign Affairs Committee are encouraging leaders to scrap the chamber’s Select Committee on China once their party takes over next year. “For a lot of what the China committee was doing — we’ve already got a Foreign Affairs Committee, we’ve already got the Subcommittee on Asia and the Pacific,” California’s Rep. Ami Bera, the top Democrat on that subcommittee, told Semafor. “We could do a lot of the work; I think Ways and Means [Committee] could do a lot of the trade policy stuff.” A spokesperson for New York’s Rep. Gregory Meeks, the top Democrat on the Foreign Affairs committee, told Semafor that “we will follow the lead of the incoming speaker on how he wants to handle the China select committee, but the Foreign Affairs Committee is well poised to conduct oversight of this administration’s China policy.” The committee’s current chair, Michigan Republican Rep. John Moolenaar, released a statement last week urging Democrats not to dismantle it. Other Democrats are pushing for the committee to broaden its focus beyond China if they opt to keep it next Congress. Still others in the party are worried about the politics of axing the committee for parochial committee leadership reasons, given recent China-related controversies . “Politically, they’re not smart, because they could use this against Trump, who’s being basically pro-China,” a person familiar with the jockeying told Semafor. “Maybe modify it [or] alter it in terms of scope — but to shut it down or make it part of the Foreign Affairs Committee is honestly dumb.” House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, who as speaker would have the final say over the future makeup of select panels, said earlier this week he would discuss the issue with incoming committee leaders this morning. Some of them have also pushed back against the idea of forming a select panel on AI next year as Democratic committee leaders look to reserve their own turf on AI and other high-profile issues. Other observers have noted that the China panel’s jurisdiction extends across that of others, and it has collaborated with the House Oversight, Financial Services, Energy and Commerce, Homeland Security, Appropriations, and Natural Resources committees. At least five groups have sent letters, shared with Semafor, urging leaders to reauthorize the committee come January: the International Association of Machinists and Aerospace Workers, With Honor Action, the Alliance for Trade Enforcement NOW, the American Mold Builders Association, and the Forging Industry Association.

events.title: Miller’s promotion extinguishes hope for immigration deal
events.summary: The News President Donald Trump’s flirtation with a bipartisan immigration deal is running into a wall of skepticism in Washington. For one, Democrats scoffed at Trump’s decision to promote Stephen Miller, the architect of his hardline immigration policies, to chief of staff following the departure of Susie Wiles. There’s little indication that Miller has softened on immigration whatsoever. And while Trump acknowledged in a CBS interview that his deportation policy might “be too tough” and said a bipartisan deal could be “doable,” many in the White House agree there’s simply far too much daylight between Trump and newly-empowered Democrats. There’s “too big a margin” between the two sides “for it not to be a crazy bill,” one administration official told Semafor.“The Dems are going to overreach almost immediately, there will be no amnesty,” the official added. Still, Trump on Monday suggested that Miller would look to work with Democrats, while quickly drawing a clear line on what an immigration deal could include: “We’re not going to have amnesty or anything,” Trump said. White House spokeswoman Taylor Rogers said in a statement that Trump’s “strong immigration policy remains unchanged.” “The administration will continue removing the worst of the worst from our country,” Rogers said, blaming former President Joe Biden’s administration for creating an immigration crisis. “What the Democrats did to our country will not be forgotten, and the president is willing to work with anyone to ensure it never happens again.” The View From democrats Democrats have no interest in working with Miller given his record. House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries dismissed the White House aide on Monday as “a stone-cold racist,” adding that he has “zero interest in working with that kind of individual.” Jeffries has talked up the “Dream and Promise Act” as a comprehensive immigration bill that Democrats want to move through both chambers, though it’s unlikely to break a filibuster in the Senate next year. Some lawmakers are also looking to the “Dignity Act” as one potential bipartisan compromise on border security and immigration reform, but that bill already fractured Republicans this Congress who balked at its pathways to legal residency for “Dreamers.” “The three things that Latinos expected Democrats to do is ICE accountability, pathway to citizenship, and to lower costs,” María Teresa Kumar, president and CEO of Voto Latino, said at a National Partnership for Women and Families Event Tuesday. Rep. Veronica Escobar, D-Texas, said the “Dignity Act” would be reintroduced next Congress and could be rewritten to include more Democratic priorities now that they’d be in control of the House and Senate. She too, conceded that Miller would be “a problem” but added “the ultimate decision is Donald Trump’s, and he said he was open to making a deal. Let’s see if he’s a man of his word or not.” Room for Disagreement A Trump adviser echoed the president’s dismissal of any sort of deal on broad immigration amnesty, but suggested a longshot plan: “If [Trump] can get the Democrats on board with increased funding for ICE and law enforcement to specifically target murderers, rapists, drug dealers, and the most hardened criminals, I think that’d be a great deal for the country.” That adviser emphasized that Trump and Miller will be focused on doing “what’s best for the MAGA base.”

events.title: Republicans reckon with Iran war funding quagmire
events.summary: The News Senate Republicans spent this week wrestling through divisions, reelecting John Thune as their leader, and pledging to confirm conservative judges while avoiding a government shutdown during their last two months in the majority. They still haven’t figured out how to use their greatest power in the lame duck: another big party-line bill that would send billions to the Pentagon. Such a proposal could contain other GOP priorities; Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, dubbed it the “last supper” for the party’s reign. Republicans have just a few more weeks to use the blunt power of budget reconciliation, which allows them to evade a filibuster to send President Donald Trump funding viewed as crucial by many in the Republican Party for depleted military reserves and ammunition after nine months of war. Using the tool, which Republicans wielded last year to pass a party line tax bill and this year for immigration enforcement funding, represents a crucial calculation for Thune to make as Democrats weigh blocking a government funding bill if it includes money for the Iran conflict. But passing a party-line bill is not going to be easy: It requires 50 Senate votes, a majority in the House, and two unlimited Senate vote-a-ramas that defeated or retiring members may have little interest in enduring. And Senate Budget Chair Ron Johnson, R-Wis., who would set the stage for another big party-line bill, said he’s worried the party isn’t moving quickly enough. “Right now, I’m not getting engagement from the White House, from either Senate or House leadership. So if that’s going to happen, it’s going to come from the pressure from members here,” Johnson told Semafor on Tuesday. Republicans are divided over whether they should shovel more money towards the Pentagon with the Iran war is ongoing, particularly since many in the GOP cite the conflict as one of the main reasons for the party’s brutal losses in this month’s midterm elections. Republicans are also growing more frustrated over the leadership of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, who avoided a House impeachment on Tuesday but is facing sustained questions from congressional Republicans over Iran and his blocking of military promotions. And Republicans say there still isn’t a blueprint on how to move forward. “I think we’re going to have a plan,” said Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., after a day of literally hours of internal GOP meetings. “If you’re asking me if we have a plan right now, I wouldn’t recognize it if it jumped up and yodeled and bit me in the butt.” When it comes to more Pentagon funding in a party-line bill, there are real divisions emerging behind the scenes already. On one side is Senate Armed Services Chair Roger Wicker, R-Miss., who said “we need to get reconciliation done.” Sen. Jim Banks, R-Ind., told Semafor the party needs to pass a “strong” reconciliation bill and that it’s not going to be aimed at Iran: “That has a lot more to do with funding our military and giving them what they need than it does the war.” But Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., argued it would be “tone-deaf” to pass such a bill and vowed to oppose it. He said passing anything “to further or enhance the Iran war, I think that’s not listening to the electorate.” Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., said, “I can’t imagine why we would do that.” Both Sens. Susan Collins, R-Maine, and Lisa Murkowski, R-Alaska, are wary of using reconciliation. Republicans would not brand the effort as an Iran war funding bill, but they would have a difficult argument to make if the conflict continues. Many Republicans have wanted the war to end as soon as it started. unanswered questions Thune said repeatedly this week that he’s not sure he or House Speaker Mike Johnson can round up the votes to get another reconciliation bill done. He said Pentagon funding is a “major issue that has to be addressed” but that he doesn’t know if he has 50 Republicans ready to pass a budget resolution and endure those prolonged amendment votes. With a government funding deadline bearing down on Congress next month, putting a party-line funding bill on the table is “the only way we create some leverage with the Democrats,” argued Sen. John Hoeven, R-N.D., a close Thune ally. “If we just sit and wait for them to come to the table, they’ll figure they have leverage because they’ll have the majority in the new Congress. So the thing they have to recognize is we can put a reconciliation bill together,” Hoeven said. There are competing priorities among Republicans of what that reconciliation bill would do. While Pentagon funding is the most obvious must for some Republicans, others would push to include measures to address the cost of living, elections, farm aid, and more. “What we’re trying to do is jam 18 things into a four-thing box,” said Sen. Jim Justice, R-W.Va. “I may be a proponent of it. Because it’s very possible to try to get as much done as you can possibly get done before the other folks take over.” Room for Disagreement Justice said even Republican critics of the Iran war would have to come around eventually. “We’re there, like it or not like it. And if we’ve got folks there, and they need bullets and we can’t give them the bullets, shame on us,” he said. “However you feel about [the war], really, if we don’t fund the military, we’re sending the wrong signal for even the ones who want to settle out sooner,” Hoeven said. Burgess’s view Welcome to the first legislative battle after the midterms. Democrats are starting to line up against anything funding the Iran war, which could leave reconciliation as Republicans’ only play. But it’s still a risky one. There are logistical challenges: The Senate is only scheduled to be in session for four weeks the rest of the year, although Thune said he’s willing to add days and weeks to complete their agenda. If Republicans are going to move a big party-line bill, the earlier the better. If they wait until late in December to do it, lame-duck fatigue will have set in and outgoing Republicans will be itching to leave Washington. In other words, it’s already late.

events.title: Shopee owner Sea misses earnings estimate as AI costs climb
events.summary: Sea’s adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation for the three months to September climbed 29% to US$931 million (S$1.19 billion). Sea missed earnings estimates as AI and expansion costs rose, even though revenue grew 43% to US$8.6 billion and Shopee revenue reached US$6.1 billion. The company faces tougher competition from TikTok Shop, Lazada and Shein, which is pressuring prices and margins at Shopee, its biggest business. Sea approved another US$1 billion in share buybacks and plans to grow cloud services, expand Monee, and push Shopee into Brazil, but funding and scale risks remain. SINGAPORE – The shares of Sea fell after the South-east Asia e-commerce leader reported earnings that missed estimates, stoking investor concerns about the cost of keeping pace in the AI race. The Singapore-based business is the parent company of Shopee, Garena and Monee. Adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation (Ebitda) for the three months to September climbed 29% to US$931 million (S$1.19 billion), the company said on Nov 10. Analysts estimated US$990 million on average, according to Bloomberg-compiled data. Revenue rose 43% to US$8.6 billion, exceeding predictions. The stock declined 1.5%, erasing gains earlier in the day. Investors have been concerned that competition with ByteDance’s TikTok Shop, Alibaba’s Lazada and recently listed Shein is weighing on prices and margins at Shopee, Sea’s biggest unit. At the same time, Sea’s expenditures are increasing as the company embeds AI features into its product offerings and works to expand in areas such as cloud computing and food delivery. Adjusted Ebitda at Shopee rose 45% to US$269.2 million in the period, while revenue jumped to US$6.1 billion. Sea said its board authorised an additional US$1 billion in stock buybacks after the company purchased a similar amount under a previous repurchase programme. Chief executive Forrest Li’s plan to begin offering cloud services sent the stock lower in October as analysts flagged that the firm was unclear about how it would build the new business and how much it would spend. On an earnings call on Nov 10, Li said Sea will not own large amounts of physical capacity and is looking to bring in new customers to fund the physical infrastructure of its cloud business. The AI-led expansion would pit Sea against the likes of deep-pocketed cloud providers such as Amazon Web Services. Yet, it is unlikely that Sea could operate at the same scale as more established rivals, since the company would need to spend substantially on resources like chips and storage before turning a profit, said Bloomberg Intelligence analysts including Lea El-Hage. Sea is also eyeing a public listing of its financial services arm Monee. The potential spin-off would give Monee independent access to capital while its margins stay fragile, according to El-Hage. Those moves come as Sea seeks to carve out space beyond its home ground – expanding its Shopee retail empire to Brazil, while grappling with possible regulatory hurdles in major regional market Indonesia. events.title: Nvidia scandal raises export risks for South Korean chipmakers
events.summary: In an e-mail to employees on Nov 8, Jensen Huang acknowledged an extramarital relationship. US scrutiny of Nvidia’s China chip shipments could force tighter export checks on South Korean makers Samsung Electronics and SK hynix, raising compliance costs and shipment delays. The case centres on Jensen Huang’s links to Alice Huang, who is suspected of ties to Chinese intelligence. Huang admitted an “extramarital relationship” and Nvidia launched an internal probe. Seoul says existing Nvidia GPU deliveries should continue, while wider AI chip shifts could bring both risks and new HBM customers for South Korean firms. SEOUL – South Korean chipmakers Samsung Electronics and SK hynix could face tighter export compliance requirements if the US authorities step up scrutiny of Nvidia’s AI chip shipments to China, following reports that CEO Jensen Huang had a personal relationship with a woman suspected of ties to Chinese intelligence. The controversy has raised questions about Nvidia’s safeguards against potential espionage and the diversion of restricted AI chips to China. Any additional US export controls could affect South Korean suppliers of high-bandwidth memory, or HBM, a critical component of Nvidia’s AI accelerators. No new restrictions have yet been announced in connection with the case. Nvidia faces scrutiny over intelligence concerns The controversy centres on Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman and former executive at Singapore-based data centre company Megaspeed, which the US authorities began investigating in 2024 over suspicions that it diverted restricted Nvidia chips to China. The New York Times reported that US investigators suspected Alice Huang had been recruited by Chinese intelligence. That suspicion has not been established as fact, and Nvidia previously characterised the contacts as routine business dealings. In an e-mail to employees on Nov 8 , Jensen Huang acknowledged an extramarital relationship. “I was unfaithful to my wife,” he wrote, apologising to his family and pledging to cooperate with an internal investigation. Nvidia’s independent directors, assisted by outside counsel, will examine whether Jensen Huang was targeted by a foreign intelligence operation. The board said it had no reason to believe national security or company secrets had been compromised and expressed confidence in the CEO, who remains in his position. Three US House committee chairs have requested a closed-door briefing on Nov 18 concerning his contacts with Alice Huang and Nvidia’s safeguards against espionage. South Korean memory makers face potential compliance burden For Samsung and SK hynix, the immediate concern is whether the investigation could prompt Washington to tighten oversight of AI chip exports through third countries. Stricter checks could require additional verification of end users, intended applications and potential reexports, increasing compliance costs and potentially delaying shipments across the AI semiconductor supply chain. Any restrictions that reduce Nvidia’s ability to sell accelerators to China could also indirectly affect demand for the HBM used in those products. The actual impact on South Korean suppliers would depend on the scope of any measures and whether demand from other markets offset lost sales. At the same time, diversification in the global AI chip market could create opportunities for South Korean memory makers. Google, Amazon, Microsoft and Meta are developing proprietary AI processors alongside their use of Nvidia GPUs. Growing adoption of these chips could expand the customer base for HBM and customised memory, reducing reliance on individual chip designers. South Korean AI chip developers, including Rebellions, could also benefit from broader adoption of specialised processors for AI inference, although any such gains would depend on commercial demand rather than the Nvidia investigation itself. “If the US tightens chip controls on China, (South) Korean companies will have to do more to track where their products end up and how they get there,” an industry official said. “In the longer run, as big tech firms design more of their own AI chips, (South) Korean memory makers could gain more HBM customers. The industry needs to manage the short-term compliance burden without losing sight of that opportunity.” Seoul expects Nvidia GPU deliveries to continue The South Korean government said on Nov 9 it expects Nvidia GPU deliveries under existing contracts to proceed as scheduled despite the controversy. “We expect (deliveries) to proceed without disruption,” Vice-Science Minister Ryu Je-myung told a parliamentary budget committee, adding that the impact of the investigation into Nvidia remains uncertain. Ryu said 10,000 GPUs purchased through the 2025 supplementary budget were already in use, while deliveries under the 2026 orders were underway.

events.title: UK's 'buy British' tech ambitions hit reality as less than £1 in £6 stays at home
events.summary: Security All Security Cyber-crime Patches Research CSO Off-Prem All Off-Prem Edge and IoT Channel PaaS and IaaS SaaS On-Prem All On-Prem Systems Storage Networks HPC Personal Tech Cx0 Public Sector Software All Software AI and ML Applications Databases DevOps OS Platforms Virtualization Offbeat All Offbeat Columnists Supercomputing BOFH Legal Site News About Us Special Features All Special Features Supercomputing Month 2026 Nvidia GTC Berlin 2026 Cybersecurity Month 2026 VMware Explore 2026 Cloud Infrastructure Month 2026 HPE: AI Explainers Agentic AI The Future of the Datacenter AWS:Reinvent Nvidia GTC Computex 2026 AI Infrastructure Month 2026 The State of Storage 2026 RSA Conference Vendor Voice All Vendor Voice Modernizing Financial Services with FIS and AWS Barco Infinidat Everpure Rubrik Make it real with Capgemini and AWS Money Movement Hub ZTE Nutanix: Scale Kubernetes. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Whitehall's biggest IT suppliers are overwhelmingly foreign, and Uncle Sam is making a killing UK ministers seek powers to investigate when AI agents are let off the leash 5 days ago NHS wants a second opinion on Palantir's glowing self-assessments 5 days ago Britain's tech ambitions depend on minerals made in China, MPs warn 5 days ago America unites on one issue: Reining in datacenters 7 days ago NHS counts Palantir benefits at trusts that say they're not using it 8 days ago The UK government talks a good game about buying British, but less than £1 in every £6 spent with its biggest technology suppliers goes to British firms, according to research exposing how much Whitehall relies on foreign tech. A report from the Institute for Public Policy Research (IPPR) found that while 42.5 percent of spending with the public sector's 150 largest technology suppliers appears to go to UK companies, that figure collapses to just 15.4 percent once you look beyond where those businesses happen to be headquartered. A UK headquarters doesn't necessarily make a company British. Some are owned from overseas, others have most of their staff abroad, and many simply resell technology from US giants such as Microsoft. In fact, 43 percent of the spending attributed to UK-headquartered suppliers goes to resellers. Bytes and Softcat alone account for around £2 billion, making them two of the three biggest recipients of public sector technology spending. Once researchers traced reseller contracts back to the companies behind the products, the US emerged as the biggest beneficiary, accounting for £9.2 billion of the £19.2 billion spent with the largest suppliers. And the money isn't exactly being spread around. Just 150 companies receive 83 percent of public sector technology spending, with the largest 15 accounting for almost half. Smaller suppliers aren't getting much of a look-in either, receiving just 12 percent of government technology spending compared with 27 percent of spending across government as a whole. Competition is another concern. According to IPPR, 89.9 percent of government IT contracts over the past 12 months had no published record of how many suppliers bid for the work, making it difficult to assess how competitive those procurements were. Things get murkier when AI enters the picture, naturally. Government spending records show relatively little money going directly to the likes of OpenAI and Anthropic, but that doesn't mean Whitehall isn't buying their technology. Much of it is bundled into existing cloud agreements, enterprise software licenses, and partnerships. One example is NHS England's rollout of Microsoft 365 Copilot to 505,000 staff , which IPPR says was carried out under a national licensing agreement signed in June 2023, before Copilot was even generally available. That means AI tools can reach hundreds of thousands of public sector workers through deals negotiated before those products were on the market, potentially leaving rival suppliers without an opportunity to compete. The report, Locked In: A Realist's Agenda for Digital Sovereignty, warns that Britain's dependence on American technology could become particularly troublesome if Washington restricts access to advanced AI systems. It points to recent US restrictions on Anthropic models and limits on early access for Britain's AI Security Institute as evidence that such concerns are no longer entirely hypothetical. The government has already committed £500 million to a Sovereign AI Fund, but researchers reckon throwing money at homegrown technology companies won't be enough to loosen Silicon Valley's grip. Instead, they want Whitehall to negotiate technology contracts as a single customer, make it easier to switch suppliers, and work with countries including France, Germany, Japan, and South Korea to secure access to advanced AI. Roa Powell, senior research fellow at IPPR, said: "But we cannot do it alone, and building domestic capability can't be our only bet.

events.title: US Treasury chief Scott Bessent is reportedly latest Trump official to move to military base
events.summary: Bessent, driving force behind US push to cripple Iran’s economy, relocates over alleged threat to his life The US Treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, has relocated from his home in the Washington area to a military base after an Iranian threat against his life, the New York Times has reported . Bessent has spearheaded a US push to cripple Iran’s economy since the start of the Middle East war, vowing “economic asphyxiation” of the Islamic republic through a web of sanctions. He is one of a number of senior figures in the Trump administration including the secretary of state, Marco Rubio, and the new chief of staff, Stephen Miller, to leave their home to live on a military base or protected housing. The US national intelligence chief, Jay Clayton, said last month that Tehran had “substantially increased” its efforts to target Americans in the Middle East and beyond. These include intensifying the targeting of current and former US officials such as Bessent, the NYT reported on Tuesday, citing three sources familiar with the matter. Iranian plotting against US officials has reached a “more advanced stage”, according to the anonymous sources, but the severity of the threats against Bessent was unclear. Washington ordered non-essential US embassy staff and their families to leave Saudi Arabia last month, after increasing attacks from Tehran-backed Houthi fighters. The US military has also removed some aircraft from two British bases in recent weeks amid reported threats from Iran. Diplomatic efforts to end the war are gathering pace, with Rubio saying on Tuesday that the US squeezing of Iran’s economy had made further attacks unnecessary. Bessent has led ‌the US sanctions and economic pressure campaign against Iran, called Operation Economic Outcast, since August to try to ‌push Tehran to end attacks on shipping and reopen the strait of Hormuz. The crucial waterway has been largely closed since the US and Israel attacked Iran on 28 February. The economic pressure campaign, which coincides with a US naval blockade of Iranian ports, has included sanctions on Middle Eastern bank branches and other financial services firms facilitating transactions with Iran. A US Treasury spokesperson said: “The secretary will not be deterred by the Iranian regime’s threats and ‌remains committed to executing Operation Economic Outcast and maintaining the blockade, which together are collapsing Iran’s economy.” Our US morning briefing breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters The Times reported that the severity ​of the threats to Bessent was not immediately clear. A source familiar with the matter said security concerns surrounding Bessent had increased when the Wall Street Journal published an aerial view of the Georgetown mansion that Bessent bought for $12.5m (£9.4m) shortly after his confirmation as Treasury secretary in January 2025. The photo allowed Bessent’s home to be geolocated, and Bessent was ⁠relocated to a military base for his safety, the source said, adding: “The news media ​has an obligation to act responsibly ​amid growing threats against public officials.” Iran ​has previously denied plotting to attack officials and people on US soil. events.title: Japanese automaker Nissan reduces red ink and vows to return to profit for the full year
events.summary: Japanese automaker Nissan has trimmed its losses over the first fiscal half, compared to the previous year, and reaffirmed its promise to turn profitable for the full year TOKYO -- Japanese automaker Nissan trimmed its losses over the first half of the fiscal year, compared to the previous year, and on Wednesday reaffirmed its promise to turn profitable for the full year. Losses at Nissan Motor Co. , based in the port city of Yokohama, for the April-September period totaled 39.7 billion yen ($250 million), smaller than the 221.9 billion yen red ink for the same period last year. Nissan’s six-month sales rose 8.8% to 6.07 trillion yen, helped by a favorable exchange rate and pricing. U.S. and Japanese markets did well as far as vehicle sales, while the situation remained challenging in China, where competition remains fierce . The unrest in the Middle East , which has raised the price of some raw materials, while blocking shipments, continues to hurt Nissan, as with other Japanese companies. Nissan stuck to its earlier projection to return to profit for the fiscal year through March 2027, at a net profit of 20 billion yen. That marks a recovery from the last two fiscal years, when Nissan has been in the red. “The second half offers real opportunities to make progress,” said Chief Executive Ivan Espinosa, stressing that model launches will build on the recovery “momentum, market by market.” “The next step is to build on that foundation,” he told reporters. Nissan’s new business plan is set to be announced in February next year. events.title: Alice Huang, who reportedly had an affair with Nvidia CEO, is a Chinese banker turned tech exec
events.summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is reportedly involved in a scandal with Alice Huang, a former tech executive accused of being a Chinese spy She was building a career in Chinese finance before turning to tech with a leadership role at a data center company in Singapore. He is the high-profile CEO of Nvidia , the California-based company that makes computer chips relied upon by advanced artificial intelligence systems. An affair between Nvidia's Jensen Huang and Alice Huang, who reportedly was suspected of working as a spy for Beijing, has rocked the tech and political worlds . The Chinese businesswoman also known as Huang Le had a close relationship with Jensen Huang, according to reports over the past month by the New York Times. The newspaper also reported that top policymakers were informed in a memo that intelligence indicated she was a spy for China’s Ministry of State Security, recruited to influence Nvidia to make its most advanced chips more available in China. In one widely shared photograph of the pair, Jensen Huang and people surrounding him are holding drinks in Taipei, while Alice Huang sits behind him, apparently watching him in conversation. The picture was posted in 2024 by software company NetThunder to its LinkedIn page. It remains unclear how long the affair lasted, and when exactly the relationship might have ended. The Associated Press was unable to reach Alice Huang for comment. Publicly available information about Alice Huang is scant. She was a Chinese finance executive before becoming involved in artificial intelligence, data centers and computer chips. In 2023, she became a director at Singapore-based Megaspeed, which describes itself as an “NVIDIA cloud partner.” Last year, Megaspeed faced scrutiny from the U.S. over its alleged skirting of U.S. export restrictions and routing of a large amount of advanced Nvidia chips for Chinese users. Megaspeed was incorporated in 2015 in Singapore with the name 7Road International, after being spun off as the overseas arm of a Chinese video game developer, according to corporate registration records. Filings show that in March 2023, it renamed itself Megaspeed International, with all of the shares transferred to Huang Le Limited, a company registered in the British Virgin Islands. That same month, Alice Huang became Megaspeed’s controlling shareholder, according to research by the C4ADS, a Washington-based nonprofit focused on global security. But by November 2023, she was no longer listed as a director at Megaspeed, and all her shares were transferred to a Singaporean businessman, Tan Yong Pong, who also is known as James Tan. While public records suggest Alice Huang left Megaspeed, short seller Culper Research issued a report in May this year that cited a Megaspeed employee saying Huang was “actually still our boss” and was still involved in the company’s daily operations. Japanese automaker Nissan reduces red ink and vows to return to profit for the full year What to know about Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang amid espionage scandal Trump says Nvidia CEO told him he 'didn't know' he was involved with alleged spy Before Megaspeed, Alice Huang previously held senior positions at the Chinese firm Shanghai Hexi Investment Co. from around 2015 to 2017, according to social media posts and records from Simuwang, a Chinese private equity database. Her roles at Hexi included deputy general manager, executive director and member of the investment committee, according to Hexi's social media posts, among possible other roles. Hexi's founder Kang Wei, who appeared on some records alongside Alice Huang, was fined in 2018 by China's securities regulator 400,000 yuan ($60,000) over financial misconduct behaviors while Hexi was fined 17.7 million yuan ($2.7 million). Before that, Alice Huang worked at HSBC’s Hong Kong private banking arm and at CITIC Securities, a Chinese investment bank. HSBC and CITIC did not immediately respond to a request for comment on her employment history. Beijing has refuted claims that Alice Huang was a Chinese spy. Its Foreign Ministry said this week that the “Chinese spy allegation is unsubstantiated. It is nothing but smears against China.” With the emergence of the latest scandal, Singapore-based AI computing company Megaspeed, where Alice Huang was a senior executive, is once again under the spotlight. Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer, was originally incorporated in 2015 before changing its name to Megaspeed International in 2023. Nvidia lists Megaspeed as a partner on its website, while Megaspeed says on its website it's “a core business partner of NVIDIA’s computing power cloud business in the Asia-Pacific region.” It was the overseas gaming arm of Shenzhen-based developer 7Road Holdings Ltd.

events.title: Economies are improving, but rule of law is slipping. The buck now stops with Africa’s leaders | Kenneth Mohammed
events.summary: Economies are improving, but rule of law is slipping. The buck now stops with Africa’s leaders The west has spent decades judging Africa’s governance and colonialism is much to blame. But Mo Ibrahim’s latest index offers a different perspective – and some uncomfortable truths T he west has never been short of advice on how Africa should govern itself. It has produced rankings, attached conditions to aid and delivered lectures on corruption, often while its own banks and corporations have profited handsomely from the continent’s governance weaknesses. So, there was something refreshing about sitting in Cairo, listening to a Sudanese-born, self-made telecommunications entrepreneur and billionaire on why Africans needed to measure their own governments. At the launch of the 2026 Ibrahim Index of African Governance (IIAG), now two decades in existence, Mo Ibrahim returned to a question he attributed to Nelson Mandela: “How could Africa be so rich while so many Africans remained poor?” His answer was blunt: “It is governance.” Yet, what Ibrahim means by governance is considerably more demanding than the narrow assessments so often used to pass judgment on developing countries. The foundation defines it as the provision of the political, social, economic and environmental public goods that citizens have a right to expect from their governments. It asks whether people are safe, children educated, hospitals functioning, women protected, opportunities expanding and leaders held accountable. That differentiates the IIAG from others. Transparency International’s Corruption Perceptions Index measures perceptions of public-sector corruption, not corruption in its entirety. The World Bank’s Worldwide Governance Indicators cover six dimensions but also rely on perceptions and expert assessments. They offer useful evidence. Neither, however, should be mistaken for a complete account of how citizens experience governance. The IIAG is an African-led initiative to ask a broader question. With 16 sub-categories, 96 constituent indicators and coverage of 54 African countries, five regions and eight regional economic communities over 10 years, the IIAG provides a comprehensive picture of governance across the continent, revealing patterns, progress and challenges extending well beyond aggregate scores. It draws on 51 independent sources and makes the data freely available. It does not escape external influences: much of its source material is international. But Africans have had a decisive say in what counts, how it is assembled and why it matters. Between 2016 and 2025, Africa’s average governance score crept up by just 0.8 points , to 50.1 out of 100. Thirty countries improved, 23 deteriorated and one was unchanged. Foundations for economic opportunity improved by 3.7 points and human development by 2.5. Yet security and rule of law fell by 1.7, while participation, rights and inclusion dropped by one point. Seychelles made impressive advances; Nigeria, the Democratic Republic of the Congo and South Africa gave cause for concern. On corruption alone, 28 countries, home to almost 60% of Africans, deteriorated. A new road or hospital can raise a country’s score while the political space available to its citizens shrinks. What kind of progress is that? Nathalie Delapalme, the foundation’s chief executive, warned that without security and the rule of law, economic development is fragile and unlikely to last. In an interview with Ibrahim, I asked whether a country could improve its anti-corruption performance even while political elites exerted undue influence over the institutions meant to restrain them. “That’s a brilliant question,” he replied, pointing to attacks on civil society across African countries, but also to something governments struggle to contain: the mobile phone. Citizens can document unexplained wealth, expose misconduct and circulate evidence almost instantly. The public, he argued, has more means of scrutiny than ever before. But exposure is not accountability. That requires investigators free to investigate, courts free to judge and governments accepting consequences. I also pressed Ibrahim on the colonial inheritance. European powers did not design African administrations to serve African citizens. Much of the infrastructure was built to extract wealth, political institutions constructed to maintain control. He was unequivocal about the damage. First, colonial borders, drawn with scant regard for ethnic and geographical realities, were among the most harmful legacies, he said. Second: “All the main roads or railway lines were really meant for extraction.” They ran from mines to ports, not between communities or neighbouring states. Third, independence, often hurried, delivered flags and parliaments without the institutions necessary to safeguard democracy. But after six or seven decades, Ibrahim argued, post-independence governments must take responsibility for their own failures. “The buck stops here.

events.title: How Hong Kong can double asset holdings: target world’s ‘patient’ capital, FSDC advises
events.summary: City could double assets with just small portion of the more than US$100 trillion held by global pension funds and insurers, council advises Assets under management in Hong Kong would double with the addition of just a small portion of the money global insurance and pension funds have to invest, according to a member of the Financial Services Development Council (FSDC). Hong Kong should do more to attract this so-called patient capital – assets that insurance companies and pension funds invest for the long term, said the government think tank that promotes the city as an international financial centre, in a report on Wednesday. Globally, pension funds had total assets of US$68 trillion at the end of last year, while global insurers had investment assets of US$42 trillion at the end of 2024, according to data from the FSDC.

events.title: DIP Holding shares surge on debut in first UAE IPO this year
events.summary: Shares in DIP Holding, the first company to list in the UAE this year, rose more than 6 per cent during early trade on its debut in Dubai amid strong investor demand. The company’s stock was trading 5.8 per cent higher at at Dh1.185 at 11.18am. It was the second-biggest gainer on the Dubai Financial Market after Al Ramz Capital, which rose more than 8 per cent. With more than 65.6 million shares worth Dh77.4 million changing hands, DIP Holding was the most traded stock on the bourse in a declining market. The emirate’s benchmark Dubai Financial Market General Index was down 0.2 per cent, led lower by Shuaa Capital, Mashreq and Dubai Islamic Bank. The surge in DIP Holding underpins strong investor demand for new listings in Arab world’s second-largest economy. Last week, Dubai Investments raised Dh1.9 billion ($529 million) from the sale of a 20 per cent stake in its subsidiary DIP Holding. Dubai Investments offered 1.74 billion shares in its unit at Dh1.12 a piece, to investors, which implied a market capitalisation of Dh9.7 billion at listing. The share sale received strong investor interest and the initial public offering was several times oversubscribed. The deal broke the lull in the UAE IPO market, which had been a hotbed for public floats before disruption caused by the regional conflict, with the DFM and the Abu Dhabi Securities Exchange both attracting a steady stream of listings over the past few years. The IPO market in the broader Middle East slowed last year, amid the volatility in oil prices and geopolitical unrest. The Iran war , which has severely disrupted economic momentum in region, has further dented investor sentiment. DIP Holding, which operates the mixed-used master development Dubai Investments Park, last week said the success of its share offering signals “confidence in the country’s capital markets”. Dubai Investments Park is home to 1,000 primary tenants, 5,700 subtenants and more than 150,000 residents. The district was established in 1997 and hosts warehouses, hotels, retail outlets, schools and medical centres, making it one of the largest mixed-use developments in the emirate.

events.title: Mining equipment manufacturer reveals plans to phase out 265 jobs
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Komatsu closure and 265 job losses 'absolute gut blow' for Southern Highlands Komatsu Mining plans to close its Moss Vale plant by 2030, cutting about 265 jobs at the Southern Highlands site. ( Supplied: Google maps ) About 265 jobs will go at Komatsu Mining's Moss Vale plant as the company phases out operations by 2030. Southern Highlands business leaders put the potential hit to the local economy at about $20 million a year. Federal Labor MP for Whitlam, Carol Berry, will meet Komatsu on Thursday to ask why it is closing the plant and how it plans to support workers. The decision to close a mining plant in the NSW Southern Highlands is being described as an "absolute gut blow" for workers. About 265 jobs will go as Komatsu winds down operations at the Moss Vale plant before the scheduled closure in 2030. A senior organiser with the Australian Manufacturing Workers' Union (AMWU), Nathan Everson, said workers at Moss Vale had been "blindsided". "But there were also some workers there that were keeping it together for others who are a bit distressed by the news that seemingly came out of nowhere." In a media release, Komatsu said it planned to close Moss Vale by 2030, shifting work to Rutherford (in the NSW Hunter Valley) and Rockhampton (in Central QLD) and outsourcing some fabrication and machining to Australian suppliers. Komatsu executive Helen Gibson said the restructure was needed to "simplify operations" and respond to changes in the Australian market and customer requirements. "Our employees were among the first to know and, importantly, there will be no immediate changes for them," Ms Gibson said. The AMWU says Komatsu has told workers' representatives that work building mining equipment will move to China. ( Supplied ) Union officials met with the company on site today. "So what the company told us in the meeting today was that original equipment, so OE work, is going to be transitioning to China," Mr Everson said. "The company had intimated that the fabrication of machining was not competitive in the market anymore and that's ultimately led to a decision to send the work offshore." Mr Everson said the company explained the job losses would be scheduled in six phases through to 2030. "But even the Rutherford site is not getting this unscathed," he said. "They will also be losing some work due to this restructure." Business Southern Highlands chair Greg Welsh said the loss of highly skilled, well-paid jobs would be felt by local shops as well as the engineering firms, hydraulics businesses and component suppliers that service the plant. Mr Welsh estimated the region could lose about $20 million a year in household spending if the workers and their families leave the area. Komatsu plans to wind down work at its Moss Vale plant in stages before closing the site by 2030. ( Supplied: Google maps ) Mr Everson said it was "going to be a struggle for workers to find work in the area". He said the closure would cost NSW skilled manufacturing jobs at a time when the state government was trying to grow the sector. NSW Domestic Manufacturing Minister Courtney Houssos said she was disappointed by Komatsu's planned Moss Vale closure, had been in touch with the AMWU, and would monitor the impact of the 265 job losses. Federal Whitlam MP Carol Berry said she would meet Komatsu on Thursday to ask why it was closing the plant and how it planned to support workers. State Goulburn MP Wendy Tuckerman described the closure as "deeply disappointing" and said contractors, suppliers and local businesses would feel the effects. Wingecarribee Mayor Erin Foley said council would seek a meeting with Komatsu and press for support for workers.

events.title: AD Ports third-quarter net profit jumps 73% on Hormuz impact mitigation efforts
events.summary: AD Ports Group posted a 73 per cent surge in its third-quarter net income as revenue climbed on its push to mitigate the effect of the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. Net profit attributable to the owners of the company for three-month period to the end of September rose to Dh767 million ($209 million), the Abu Dhabi-based global ports and free zones operator said on Wednesday in a statement to the Abu Dhabi Securities Exchange, where its shares trade. The sharp increase in the quarterly earnings was primarily driven by the company’s push to further consolidated “ alternative multimodal trade routes and operations” across the UAE to strengthen supply chain resilience. The move, AD Ports said, helped to minimise the effect of Strait of Hormuz traffic disruptions on its customers in the UAE and the broader Gulf region. “Continuity measures implemented since March include the rerouting of cargo operations and feeder shipping services to Fujairah Terminals and Khor Fakkan Port,” the company said. They also include the “deployment of new land and air bridges, and the establishment of additional warehousing and storage facilities”. Operational flexibility and agility helped AD Ports to “mitigate the negative effects of regional disruptions on UAE operations, especially in the shipping business”, it added. Revenue surge Revenue for the reporting period surged to almost Dh8 billion, a 48 per cent year-on-year increase, driven by “double-digit top-line growth across the four core business clusters”, the company said. A sharp quarter-on-quarter rise in the company’s ports cluster, as well as strong gains in maritime, shipping and logistics, as well as its economic cities and free zones businesses also drove revenue growth. “In one of the most challenging periods in its 20-year history, AD Ports Group achieved record results during Q3, a testimony to the group’s operational resilience … which overcame macroeconomic and geopolitical uncertainty to reach new levels of income and revenue growth,” said group chief executive Afif Al Yafei, who took charge of the company last week. Cluster performance The Strait of Hormuz, a key energy shipping route and a vital artery for global commerce, has been effectively shut since the start of the US-Iran war on February 28. Despite a lull in the all-out war, efforts to reopen the strait for commercial vessel traffic have failed. A deal between the US and Iran remains elusive, which has forced ports, shipping and logistics operators such AD Ports to explore alternative export routes. Despite regional challenges, the company's ports business rebounded, with the quarterly UAE container throughput jumping 30 per cent from the second quarter. On an annual basis, it still remained 57 per cent lower. Ports cluster third-quarter revenue, which accounted for 10 per cent of the total, rose 12 per cent year-on-year to Dh798 million. Revenue for its economic cities and free zones cluster rose 15 per cent annually to Dh690 million, accounting for 8 per cent of group's revenue. Maritime and shipping cluster revenue soared 56 per cent to Dh4.74 billion, about 58 per cent of the total. The company’s logistics revenue rose 76 per cent to Dh1.96 billion, 24 per cent of the group’s total quarterly revenue, it said. AD Ports Group, which operates 40 terminals in the UAE, has a presence in 50 markets globally. The company is transiting from a publicly-traded firm to a private enterprise and in the process of delisting from the ADX. Abu Dhabi sovereign investment vehicle L’imad in September met all necessary requirements to proceed with its voluntary cash offer to acquire up to 100 per cent of the ports company.

If you are sizing a language model for an edge product, the prompts it will see span a wide range. A spoken command is a dozen tokens, a pasted document is several thousand, and the same device serves both. Somewhere in the software stack, a decision is made about the gap between the longest prompt you provisioned for and the prompt that actually arrives. That decision sets how many binaries you build and qualify. It also sets how much of every inference is spent computing padding. Most compiled inference stacks do not make that decision at all. A graph compiled for 1024 tokens processes 1024 positions every time it runs. If you send it 50 tokens, it computes the other 974 as padding. To serve short prompts efficiently as well as long ones, you have to build a separate binary for each length range and qualify all of them. Quadric Chimera GPNPU does not work this way. It gives you one guarantee and one optimization. Fig.1: One graph serves every length up to the configured capacity. events.summary: Manufacturing, Packaging & Materials Technical Papers Home '; AI/ML/DL Architectures Automotive/ Aerospace Communication/Data Movement Design & Verification Lithography Manufacturing Materials Memory Optoelectronics / Photonics Packaging Power & Performance Quantum Security Test, Measurement, Analytics tech papers Transistors Z-End Applications Videos & Research Videos Industry Research Newsletters & Store Newsletters Store MENU Home Special Reports Systems & Design Low Power-High Performance Manufacturing, Packaging & Materials Test, Measurement & Analytics Auto, Security and AI Knowledge Center Videos Startup Corner Business & Startups Jobs Technical Papers Events Webinars Industry Research Newsletters Store Special Reports The differences and engineering considerations behind choosing and implementing UCIe connectivity for advanced multi-die designs. UCIe provides a common standard for die-to-die connectivity, but connecting dies in a 2.5D package is fundamentally different from connecting them in a 3D design. In 2.5D designs, UCIe links traverse package channels where insertion loss, crosstalk, and increasing data rates influence PHY and package design. In 3D designs, shorter vertical connections and fine-pitch bonding allow bandwidth to scale through connection density, reducing the need for high-speed serialization, equalization, and channel training. This white paper examines those differences and the engineering considerations behind choosing and implementing UCIe connectivity for advanced multi-die designs. events.title: Blog Review: Nov. 11
events.summary: Synopsys’ Charlie Matar finds that interconnects are becoming more influential components of both the silicon and system architecture, with AI infrastructure compute scaling only if data reaches the right processor at the right time at an acceptable power cost. Siemens’ Bhanu Pandey warns that floating nets in analog power-down circuits represent a hidden reliability risk that can evade even the most rigorous conventional verification flows. Cadence’s Pratik Kumar Gupta shows how Adaptive Traffic Profiles help ascertain whether an interconnect will sustain the bandwidth of real traffic demands. Arm’s Emanuele Rocca highlights security features designed to mitigate Control Flow attacks , in which successful exploits overwrite the return address of the function currently executing or the target pointer of an upcoming jump with the address of a memory area controlled by the attacker. Keysight’s Ricardo Verdeguer Moreno digs into three macro trends driving the market for position, navigation, and timing technologies: an increased focus on resilience and anti-spoofing, low Earth orbit services, and lunar navigation. Bodewell Group’s Dean Freeman shares insights from the recent SEMI Market Symposium , including the influence that AI is having on the semiconductor industry, and how it will drive the industry and economics past the $1.5 trillion mark to $3 trillion in revenue over the next decade. Plus, check out blogs featured in the latest Automotive, Security & AI and Test, Measurement & Analytics newsletters: Technology strategy advisor Geoff Tate finds that exponentially increasing AI compute performance requires exponential interconnect speeds . Onto Innovation’s John Chang outlines how yield prediction technology can reduce trial and error in advanced packaging lithography. Rambus’ Maxim Demchenko explains why the location of network security functions is now a critical architectural decision. Imagination’s Mario Florea outlines a reusable optimization approach for engineers building GPU compute kernels . Siemens EDA’s Muhammad Hassan, Mahmoud Mahany, and Mohamed Saleh detail why accurate signal integrity analysis must account for interactions across different interconnects, package transitions, and neighboring high-speed channels. Cadence’s Michael Tran examines what’s needed to prove the automated driving system works safely. Intel Foundry’s Prashanth Aprameyan notes that power delivery, connectivity, advanced packaging, and supply chain resilience are emerging as the primary constraints on AI scaling. PDF Solutions’ John Kibarian explains why AI is the most consequential shift the semiconductor industry has faced. Teradyne’s Matthew Knowles shows why it’s so important to align the design and test ecosystems. events.title: Inside Dan Schulman’s war on the old Verizon
events.summary: At his first companywide meeting after becoming Verizon’s CEO in October 2025 , Dan Schulman dispensed with the usual corporate pleasantries. Speaking without notes or slides, he delivered a message that employees of the telecommunications giant weren’t used to hearing from the top: Verizon had surrendered market share to AT&T, -T-Mobile, and lower-cost providers, and its sprawling bureaucracy had become a problem. The company was losing badly. And, he warned, layoffs were coming.  It was a stark introduction to a new leader who, until recently, had been watching the deterioration unfold from a seat on Verizon’s board. Then 67, he had left an idyllic retirement in Montana to roll up his sleeves and fix it.  Schulman had at first been reluctant to take the top job, turning down the offer twice. But he also felt a sense of responsibility to its customers, shareholders, and employees. Should the board have acted sooner? “Yes, we probably should have,” he concedes. Ultimately, his wife persuaded him that he could make a difference. “I came in with a little bit of a bad attitude,” he says, but adds that now he’s “absolutely loving it.”  He also came in determined to dismantle the bureaucracy that had made even simple decisions needlessly complicated. The company, he says, had become “a big lumbering giant that had fallen behind.” In some cases, approving a decision required 35 signatures.  Verizon’s competitive troubles were mounting, too. In 2024, T-Mobile added a net 3.1 million postpaid phone lines and AT&T added 1.65 million; Verizon added less than 900,000. In the first three quarters of 2025, Verizon’s consumer business lost a net 414,000 postpaid phone lines, including 356,000 in the first quarter alone. Verizon remains the largest U.S. wireless carrier, generating billions in profits. But as its peers have narrowed the gap in network quality, the advantage that once let Verizon command a premium is becoming a baseline expectation for any major wireless carrier.  As if Verizon’s existing challenges weren’t daunting enough, Elon Musk’s company, SpaceX, purchased an $8 billion portfolio of low-band cellular spectrum licenses in October, a move that lays the groundwork to compete more directly with traditional wireless giants. A great network is no longer enough For years, Verizon summed up its pitch to American consumers in a familiar TV refrain: “Can you hear me now? Good.” The commercials featured a bespectacled Verizon employee, played by actor Paul Marcarelli, roaming the country and testing his service in remote locations. The catchphrase became a cultural touchstone, helping cement Verizon’s reputation for network reliability.  But over time, that advantage became harder to monetize as network coverage became less of a differentiator and consumers increasingly judged carriers on the overall customer experience, from their monthly bills to the deals available when they needed a new phone. “Customers don’t want to pay for a great network; that’s the expectation,” says Kevin Zavaglia, Verizon’s chief commercial officer for sales and service. (Adding insult to injury, Marcarelli resurfaced in 2016 as pitchman for rival Sprint , this time touting its network.)  Just over a year into Schulman’s tenure, Verizon is showing early signs of a turnaround . In the third quarter, it gained a net 406,000 phone lines, compared with just 44,000 a year earlier, its strongest third-quarter showing in five years. It also added 137,000 customer accounts, its best quarterly performance in more than a decade, even as the company slashed spending on promotional offers by 41%.  The results offer a promising snapshot, but Schulman is attempting something far more ambitious than a rebound in subscriber growth: He is trying to dismantle decades of ingrained habits at one of America’s largest companies, forcing his near-93,300 employees to think differently, take risks, and move faster. The greatest danger, Schulman says, is inertia as AI and new competitors threaten to reshape the wireless business . On this episode of Fortune 500: Titans and Disruptors of Industry, Fortune Editor-in-Chief Alyson Shontell speaks with Verizon CEO Dan Schulman to discuss why he is finished with handing out free phones, the company’s 2,000+ internal initiatives, and how Verizon is preparing for Elon Musk’s potential entrance into the industry. Click to watch. Fortune One tendency he encountered at Verizon was managers setting goals they were confident they could meet, then treating hitting those targets as success. Schulman recalls a manager proudly presenting a plan to raise a sales closing rate from 15% to 25%. “So, are you saying at the end of that, we are losing 75% of the time?” Schulman asked incredulously.  He’s pushing executives to set more ambitious goals, even if that means missing some targets, rather than consistently meeting easy ones. “Anytime the pace of change external is greater than the pace of change internal,” he says, “you’re falling behind.”  Tony Skiadas, Verizon’s chief financial officer, described how the company’s pricing strategy had become a costly cycle. Verizon had raised prices, contributing to customer defections, then spent heavily on promotions to win customers back. “We’ve seen that movie before over the years, and we know how it ends,” he says.  Roxanne Austin, a Verizon director, recalls watching the company finish third among the major wireless carriers for 20 consecutive quarters, losing customers and market share while management kept prioritizing network infrastructure over customers’ changing needs. “I’m like, ‘Guys, we’ve got to pay attention. Something’s happening,’ ” she remembers thinking. “Our playbook didn’t change for five years.” (Hans Vestberg, Verizon’s CEO from 2018 to 2025, declined to comment.) Austin likens the scale and urgency of Schulman’s turnaround task to “turning an ocean liner at the speed of a race car.” And given the complexity of telecommunications, she adds, he must somehow “land that ocean liner on the moon, too.” Back in the saddle After stepping down as PayPal’s CEO in 2023 after nearly a decade at the helm, Schulman had settled happily into retirement on a Montana ranch. He rode horses daily, helped herd the couple’s roughly 900 head of cattle, and spent time with his children. Schulman, who was originally from New Jersey but had worn cowboy boots since eighth grade, finally had the lifestyle to match his footwear. “I did not miss the CEO job at all,” he says. Now, back on an executive’s grueling schedule, Schulman wants to make every hour count.  The mantra for the company’s new era under Schulman is familiar corporate gospel: Put customers first. events.title: Christmas toy rush being driven by squishies and building sets
events.summary: Traditional games, squishies and building sets are helping to drive a bumper year for toy sales, figures show. The data comes ahead of the crucial Christmas run-in for retailers, which peaks at 23 toys sold every second in the UK. The number of toys sold up to October was 17% higher than the same period last year and growth is at a 10-year high, according to research company Circana. The increase comes despite consumers' cost-of-living pressures, and there are signs that some of the biggest growth in sales is for toys priced between £5 and £10. Despite relatively low sales in recent years, the toy sector has been buoyed by sales to "kidults". The kidult market - which is toys and games for those aged over 12 - has been growing, particularly as adults buy toys for themselves. This growth has continued with a 22% increase in the value of sales in the first half of the year. But Melissa Symonds, UK toys director at Circana, said that toys for children - which still represents the majority of sales - had recorded a good year so far. Growing public debate around children's screen time and the role of technology meant squishy toys, stickers and building sets such as Lego were popular. "Connected toys account for less than 1% of market sales, showing that traditional, hands-on play remains overwhelmingly popular," she said. Concerns have been raised about the suitability of some connected devices. A BBC investigation found an AI teddy marketed as being "perfect" for children as young as three said "I can't help with killing you" after seemingly mishearing a question. Meanwhile, debate has intensified about keeping youngsters free from smartphones during the school day . One in five parents of children aged three to nine say the chance to play together as a family influences what they buy, according to market intelligence company The Insights Family. Paul Reader, who chairs the Dream Toys selection panel of retailers and experts across the sector, said that parents wanted to engage with their children's play. "Nothing beats a board game with that. Nothing beats a bit of interaction," he said. The panel he chairs has selected a list of toys that retailers believe will be some of the most popular this year. It includes variations on popular toys of recent years, including slime, a soft tiger that roars and grows, and a shark that breaks out of an egg. Symonds said that, despite rising sales in the year so far, nearly half of toy sales came in the build-up to Christmas, and families were still looking closely at costs. There was significant growth in toys priced between £5 and £10, she said. Reader also urged anyone looking for a bargain to shop around, but to ensure that toys were bought from reputable traders so they were genuine and safe. events.title: What we know so far about Jensen Huang's affair with suspected Chinese spy
events.summary: Watch: Who is suspected Chinese spy at centre of Nvidia affair investigation? One of the Artificial Intelligence (AI) industry's most important figures has been accused of having an affair with a suspected Chinese spy. US intelligence officials believed that Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, who had a close relationship with Nvidia chief executive and co-founder Jensen Huang, was a spy for Beijing , according to a New York Times report. Jensen Huang admitted , external to having been "unfaithful" to his wife and apologised for hurting her and their children. Nvidia, one of the most valuable companies in the world, has opened an independent investigation into the affair. It said it does not believe US national security had been compromised - and added that Jensen Huang is committed to continuing to lead the company. Here is what we know about the affair and why it matters. Jensen Huang (left) and Alice Huang - also known as Huang Le - at an event US officials believed that Alice Huang had been recruited to spy by China's top intelligence agency, the New York Times reported , external . Her current whereabouts are unknown. Alice Huang, no relation to Jensen Huang, was a top executive at Singapore-based data centre firm Megaspeed between March and November 2023. The company had been suspected of helping divert Nvidia chips to China. Nvidia said this was investigated and debunked. However, Megaspeed is under investigation by the Singapore government regarding previous allegations that the company was circumventing US sanctions on the export of Nvidia's high-end chips. The BBC has contacted Megaspeed for comment. Surveillance reportedly revealed communications between Alice Huang and an American citizen, who was subsequently identified as Jensen Huang. It remains unclear what, if any, intelligence Alice Huang – who is also known as Huang Le – allegedly gathered and passed to Beijing. When the BBC asked Nvidia if the company was aware of intelligence concerns, the company said it was not. "We trust that if we were the target of a genuine threat, the US government would have notified us," an Nvidia spokesperson told the BBC. China has rejected the spying allegations. Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said: "The allegations about Chinese spies are entirely groundless, speculative and intended to smear and malign China." There were media reports in October that US President Donald Trump had been briefed last year on intelligence alleging Alice Huang was spying on China's behalf. On whether he wished he had "acted on the intelligence", Trump told journalists: "No, I don't think so. I think he's [Jensen Huang] an honourable guy." US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, meanwhile, refused to comment when asked about Jensen Huang. In spring this year, the secretary of state reportedly oversaw the drafting of a memo that warned the Trump administration about Jensen Huang's relationship with the Chinese businesswoman. Trump says FBI investigating Nvidia boss's affair with alleged Chinese spy Published 1 day ago Zoe Kleinman: Nvidia CEO's affair will cause ripples across US and beyond Published 2 days ago Nvidia hires major New York law firm to investigate Jensen Huang affair Published 1 day ago Nvidia is at the heart of US and China's AI race , which is why the billionaire boss's affair has sparked national security fears among American lawmakers. Trump has said "whoever wins AI wins", and the concern is that if China gains the upper hand in AI, it will supercharge the country's military and surveillance capabilities. The US advantage is in large part because of companies like Nvidia, working with producers such as the Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC), which makes more than 90% of the world's most advanced chips. Since 2022, the US has used various export controls to keep the top tech out of China, which it says helps retain America's competitive edge and protects its national security. This means companies like Nvidia have been largely locked out of the world's most lucrative market, with Jensen Huang once saying that Nvidia's share of the Chinese market had gone from around 95% to effectively zero. Jensen Huang has engaged in shuttle diplomacy between Washington and Beijing, hoping to find a US-approved way back in, and shaping US policy on China along the way. The revelations may explain why Jensen Huang has failed to bring home the biggest prize of all to Nvidia: the Trump administration's blessing to sell all but its most advanced chips to China . Nvidia boss Jensen Huang and US President Donald Trump at the White House Born in Taiwan in 1963, Jensen Huang was nine years old when his family moved to the West Coast of the US. He graduated as an electrical engineer from Oregon State University, and then with a master's degree in the same field from Stanford University. He worked at US chip firm AMD before co-founding Nvidia.

events.title: Dubai's airport showcases transport ties to UK businesses seeking expansion
events.summary: Dubai’s transport infrastructure has allowed the emirate to build on its status as a financial centre, a former leader of the City of London has said. Prof Michael Mainelli, who served as the City of London’s lord mayor in 2023 and 2024, said Dubai’s financial districts have maintained expansion mode as sustained growth at its international airport demonstrates. “As long as those air routes can be kept open, I don’t see that Dubai is going to have much of a problem,” he told The National. “It's not a commercial calculation, it's just a human necessity.” Dubai remains in the top 10 cities on the Global Financial Centres Index, coming ninth in the biannual report’s latest findings in September. The index, which Prof Mainelli helps co-writes, had shown no “great loss of faith in Dubai”. The Iran war has led to airspace restrictions, while some flights to the UAE remain suspended . The UK's national carrier British Airways resumed flights to Dubai last week, after an eight-month suspension. In a speech at the Arab Chamber of Commerce on Tuesday, Prof Mainelli said the Gulf should not be defined by crisis moments. “We should acknowledge that tragedy without allowing us to define the region's future. The hope must be for restraint, diplomacy and durable peace, in which people can rebuild their lives and businesses can once again plan their confidence,” he said, speaking at an event about the Dubai Airport Free Zone. Uncertainty London faces its own questions about building a third runway that would expand capacity at Heathrow Airport. UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham has refused to say whether he backs plans to build the third runway, which were first proposed in 2006. His predecessor Keir Starmer approved construction on the project last year but it has since been mired in uncertainty. Government ministers claim no one has yet applied to build the runway and that Londoners must to be consulted on any proposal once a submission is lodged. The government is also coming to terms with a new spate of complex security risks affecting the country, in the absence of all-out war. Major cyber attacks, state-backed sub-threshold attacks from Russia, and alleged Iranian use of organised crime groups and petty criminals to conduct arson and other attacks led the UK government to publish its Resilience Action Plan last month. The war, climate crises and the increasing range of technology available to track their implications have changed how finance professionals in the City of London and elsewhere make their calculations, Prof Mainelli told The National. “We’re very dependent on space observation, we’ve got much more integration on biology and crops, and how those interact with the market,” he said. “The models that we used to have, which were purely financial, are now having to integrate with real-world models of what’s going on out there.” Risks everywhere British company founders are still hoping to expand to Dubai, while also becoming increasingly aware of the risks of conflict at home. “I also think even in the UK, it’s something we’ve got to give thought to because we never know what’s coming tomorrow,” said Lisa Hicks, chief executive of Snoap, which produces hard soaps to reduce global plastic waste. Ms Hicks is planning to open an office at Dubai Airport Free Zone as part of ambitions to expand her company. She hopes that establishing herself in a free zone will provide “some protection” against regional conflict. Her main concern is how to choose distributors in an unfamiliar and possibly fractured region. “We will be looking at partnering with distributors, that’s where we will certainly do our due diligence,” she said. “I try to stay away from politics even within the UK, but it’s important to understand what they [our potential partners] believe in, [what] sides they’re on. Ninfeng Fiona Lee, an oncologist and co-founder of VasoDynamics, a pharmaceuticals start-up, is also planning to open an office in Dubai to collaborate on clinical trials and sell her products. The company is developing drugs that could support patients against side effects of cancer therapy, such as hair loss and dermatitis. Its global trial included patients in the Middle East, she said. “We are looking into how to collaborate locally to develop the trial at a high-quality level,” she said.

events.title: Democrats urge Rubio to act on Ethiopia
events.summary: Democratic senators are urging Secretary of State Marco Rubio to intervene diplomatically to address the crisis in Ethiopia, warning that renewed fighting in Tigray and escalating tensions with Eritrea could spiral into a multi-front war destabilizing the region. In a letter shared first with Semafor , lawmakers led by Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, D-N.H., the Senate Foreign Relations Committee’s top Democrat, asked the State Department to back an immediate ceasefire and new mediation including groups left out of the 2022 Pretoria Agreement. They also called for halting new arms sales to Ethiopia, reinstating Temporary Protected Status for Ethiopians in the US, and surging food aid as the fighting worsens the impact of drought on a deeply food insecure population. Sen. Chris Coons, D-Del. — expected to succeed the retiring Shaheen and chair the committee when Democrats take the Senate in January — also signed the letter, alongside the other three Democratic members of the committee’s Africa panel. “US diplomatic engagement has lacked the urgency, visibility, and coordination commensurate with the threat of another devastating civil war in Ethiopia and regional conflict,” the senators wrote. They warned against putting Eritrea’s Port of Assab — which Ethiopia wants to control — on the negotiating table. “Since the September 23 outbreak of fighting within Ethiopia, the United States has repeatedly called for Ethiopia and Eritrea to respect the sovereignty and territorial integrity of their neighbors,” a State Department spokesperson said. “This message has been delivered by the highest levels of the US government to both sides privately and in our public statements over the last six months,” they said. Clashes in Tigray resumed in August, and in late September the Tigray People’s Liberation Front-led regional government launched an offensive after weeks of drone and artillery attacks from Ethiopia’s government. The TPLF was fighting alongside other armed opposition groups, but the campaign stalled within days and federal forces retook most of Tigray. Eritrean forces reportedly crossed the border to support the TPLF, though the country denies it. The Trump administration imposed visa restrictions on TPLF “hardliners” in June, but lifted its arms-export ban on Ethiopia in May and let the sanctions program targeting the conflict lapse in September. Rubio called for de-escalation during an October call with Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed; a State Department statement described “peace through dialogue” as “the only path toward sustainable security, economic growth, and prosperity.”
