events.title: Nvidia’s crisis has corporate governance experts reaching for the popcorn
events.summary: Nvidia’s stock sank 5.47% on Tuesday, following a 4% drop on Monday, a loss of about 9.5% in two days, even though there wasn’t much news out of the company. CEO Jensen Huang has reportedly been trying to conduct business as usual after admitting to an extramarital affair with Alice Huang, whom U.S. intelligence agencies believe was spying for China. The biggest development: the board hired the law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to conduct an internal investigation. What comes next is mostly a guessing game, even for the people who study how boards are supposed to handle crises. Two corporate governance professors, Ann Lipton of the University of Colorado and Todd Henderson of the University of Chicago, say there is no real precedent for a CEO caught up in a suspected honeypot. And while they have views on what the investigation should ask, like everyone else, they’re watching to see how it plays out. “There have actually been affair cases and sexual harassment cases,” Lipton said, but she was quick to add that she doesn’t know of previous cases that also involve potential national security compromises. Henderson, whose research interests include corporations, securities regulation, and law and economics, said much depends on facts few people have yet, including, most importantly, what, if anything, Alice Huang got out of Jensen Huang. (Secrets about Nvidia’s fabs or chip designs would matter to the Justice Department. Ordinary corporate information probably would not.) Lipton described the investigation led by Nvidia’s independent board members, with their own outside counsel, as perhaps the most “standard” aspect of the whole affair so far. She also observed that an investigation will be “exactly as thorough” as the directors running it want it to be, which is also standard. Henderson made a related point about incentives, saying that Washington law firms that conduct internal investigations “know who pays their bills.” He didn’t suggest that’s happening here. Lipton said she sees three lines of inquiry, including whether the law was broken, whether Huang violated Nvidia’s internal policies, and whether the board was misled, including how forthcoming he was and when he was on notice. It’s notable, as Wired reported Monday , that Huang hired a PR crisis firm known for handling sex scandals a full year ago. Of course, the driver could have been about the affair alone. It’s unclear when Huang learned Alice Huang was a suspected spy. The board said in a Sunday statement about the matter that Nvidia “has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised.” Henderson similarly stressed the importance of what Huang knew and when. He described two scenarios. In one, Huang hires a PR firm because an extramarital affair is embarrassing, without knowing who the woman is. In the other, he knows she is a suspected Chinese spy. “I think that’s very different,” he said. “If I were a board member and the CEO of a company with very sensitive technology was in that situation, I would be furious if they didn’t tell me.” Not telling the board that you have cancer “or that you’ve been sleeping with a Chinese spy,” said Henderson, “seems to me to be a fireable offense.” Either way, Lipton expects shareholder suits, and she said two kinds are possible. Securities fraud, which she said is “only about lying,” is the most obvious, and as we reported yesterday, Nvidia is already facing a proposed class action lawsuit that alleges Nvidia and Huang misled investors by concealing Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang while describing dealings with her former employer as routine. “You can have as many affairs with Chinese spies as you like,” Lipton said. “You just can’t lie about it under the federal securities laws.” A mismanagement claim under Delaware law, where Nvidia is incorporated, is much harder. Employees do “stupid or reckless or damaging things all the time,” she said, and courts don’t let shareholders sue each time. Shareholders bringing such a claim on the company’s behalf, known as a derivative suit, must first show the board is incapable of handling the problem, usually by proving directors are implicated or so beholden to the CEO that they can’t act independently. Nvidia’s 10-member board has a track record of loyalty and deference to Huang, as outlined by a New York Times piece Tuesday morning. Still, the investigation those “independent” directors have announced with outside counsel makes that very hard. Lipton cited, for example, a shareholder suit over alleged mismanagement at McDonald’s several years ago, after its chief people officer was accused of harassment and its CEO had a relationship with a subordinate. Ultimately, the court found no reason the board couldn’t deal with the misconduct on its own. Even if none of this ends up threatening Huang’s job, the episode raises other governance questions that don’t look great in retrospect.

events.title: Aldi cuts hundreds of UK head office roles as part of global cost trimming
events.summary: Supermarket’s move labelled ‘shortsighted’ by worker who calls upper management ‘woefully out of touch with reality’ Aldi’s UK business is cutting hundreds of head office roles as part of a global effort to trim costs at the budget grocer. The retailer is consulting with its technology team on the loss of up to 150 roles after 103 redundancies in its finance and administration team earlier this year and almost 20 more redundancies among buying directors. One affected worker described the cuts as “shortsighted” and said they showed that “upper management [are] woefully out of touch with the reality”. Jobs in stores have not been affected, although Aldi said it had reduced the number of regional managers slightly, affecting a handful of high-paying roles. The German-owned group is reducing the number of people in local country operations as it centralises more work. Aldi is outsourcing finance, procurement and administration roles to India, among other countries, as part of a deal with Genpact, a company that helps businesses develop the use of AI technology. Sources said consultation was set to begin on redundancies in payroll in the coming months. The company has also recently reduced the number of cleaning hours for the agency workers at its head office in Atherstone, Warwickshire. A spokesperson for Aldi said: “At Aldi, our promise to customers is that we will always offer great quality products at unbeatable prices. Across our international business, we continuously review all aspects of our operations to ensure we operate simply, efficiently and use our global scale to deliver on that promise. “We are therefore making some adjustments to the way parts of our UK business are structured. Any changes are being introduced gradually and following a consultation period. We recognise that this is difficult for those involved, so we are giving colleagues as much notice as possible, with full support available to everyone affected.” The company said it had invested £300m in lowering prices on 900 products in the UK this year. The cuts in the UK come as Aldi struggles to keep up the pace of growth. UK sales at the chain rose only 0.4% in the 12 weeks to 1 November, according to the latest industry data from Worldpanel by Numerator, with Aldi’s market share falling back by 0.1 percentage point year on year. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning The fall came as the average unit price at Aldi fell by 0.1%, making Aldi the only retailer reducing overall prices during the period. The retailer has faced tougher competition from the traditional supermarkets, several of which now match it on price on key items alongside their much wider range of other products. Morrisons cut hundreds of head office roles this spring shortly after Sainsbury’s eliminated 300 head office jobs as it restructured its technology team and Argos delivery network, and Tesco laid off a similar number of people as it changed the way it operated bakeries. This summer, Asda said up to 1,000 jobs were at risk as it introduced more automation into its logistics operation.

events.title: Tories would have to raise state pension age above 70 to keep triple lock, says minister
events.summary: Kemi Badenoch attacked reforms but is not being clear about how party would meet costs, Torsten Bell claims Kemi Badenoch’s Conservatives would have to raise the state pension age above 70 to meet the cost of keeping the triple lock, Treasury minister Torsten Bell has claimed. Labour has announced reforms to the triple-lock promise to come into force in the next parliament – with the initial proceeds earmarked for Andy Burnham’s national care service. The Conservatives have attacked the move, and insisted they would stick with the triple lock, which increases the state pension each year in line with the largest of inflation, 2.5% or earnings growth. However, Bell argued that with the costs of an unreformed triple lock increasing over time – to £50bn by 2050, according to government estimates – a Tory government would end up repeating the approach they took in the 2010s and speeding up planned increases to the state pension age. “If you don’t want to have an adjustment to the triple lock, then you will need to do other things to make the state pension remotely sustainable,” he said. “We don’t need to guess what they would do because they’ve literally just done it, which is they repeatedly and at very short notice accelerated the increases in the state pension age. “They did that in the in 2011 and in 2014. Some people had as little as five years’ notice.” In 2013, the then chancellor, George Osborne, described increasing the pension age as, “one of the less controversial things we have done,” which had nevertheless delivered “absolutely enormous savings”. The state pension age, now under review, is already expected to increase to 68 between 2044 and 2046; but Bell claimed the Conservatives would end up going further. “All I’m saying is, Conservatives do raise the state pension age aggressively, and they have,” he said. “And even though they know that the triple lock should change, they are opposing it – and the consequence of that is they would end up making people wait into their 70s.” The triple lock had previously been seen as too politically risky to reform, particularly in the light of the backlash against Labour’s plan to remove the winter fuel allowance from the vast majority of pensioners – which was subsequently abandoned . But Bell said the public would prefer Burnham’s willingness to make an argument to what he claimed was the Conservatives’ failure to be honest. “I think this is a bigger problem for Kemi Badenoch than she thinks. She thinks that her brand is principled, know what you think, tell it straight. And on this, she has done the opposite – we know that she knows it needs to change,” he said. He cited the Conservative leader’s own suggestion, as recently as last year, that the triple lock should be means tested , and former Conservative chancellor Jeremy Hunt’s claim that the policy was an “anchor drag” on the public finances. “The triple lock kind of is the final nail in the coffin of the idea that there’s anything fiscally responsible about modern Conservatism,” Bell said. Under Labour’s planned reforms , the state pension will rise each year by the highest of inflation, or 2.5%. It will only rise in line with earnings growth if its value has slipped behind recent wage growth. Bell, the MP for Swansea West since 2024, was previously director of the Resolution Foundation thinktank. He retained his role as pensions minister – working between the Treasury and the Department for Work and Pensions – when Burnham came to power in July. He said the prime minister’s 10-year plan, which may now be delayed until the new year, will include a promise of a better deal for future pensioners. “It’s just really important to be able to say to people, ‘the comfortable retirement that your parents had: we’re going to make sure that today’s private sector workers have got those’,” he added.

events.title: For Trump, Musk and Farage, the message is the same: voters don’t want to be hijacked by billionaires | Rafael Behr
events.summary: For Trump, Musk and Farage, the message is the same: voters don’t want to be hijacked by billionaires A lesson from the US midterms is that electorates are repelled by the arrogant mega-rich buying democracy. This is a fight Labour can afford to pick For most people, $224m (£168m) is a lot of money, especially if you spend it and get nothing in return. But Elon Musk is richer than most people. In fact, there is no one richer. As the wealthiest of the US’s tech oligarchs Musk could afford to blow huge sums on a failed bid to prop up Republican candidates in Texas, his adoptive home state, in last week’s midterm congressional elections. He is reported to have spent a further $250m failing to engineer results in other races. His riches plausibly swung voters the other way in Texas. James Talarico, who last week became the first Democrat to win a Senate seat in the state since 1988 , made defiance of Musk’s meddling a rallying cry in his campaign. In political campaigns, as in other forms of marketing, it isn’t always easy to know what kind of spending moves the dial or how far. But donors wouldn’t donate if they thought the result was beyond their powers of procurement. In the US, that market is out of control and the sums involved are bonkers. British politics is cheap by comparison. According to the Electoral Commission, the total combined expenditure of all parties and campaign organisations in the year running up to the last general election was £94.5m . A shot at becoming mayor of a mid-sized US city might cost twice as much. That is significant context for the kind of money Reform UK and its leader have taken from just two individuals, dipping into fortunes earned in the cryptocurrency trade. A verdict will soon be delivered by the parliamentary standards commissioner in the case of a £5m gift that Christopher Harborne , a Thailand-based billionaire, bestowed on Nigel Farage shortly before he ran for parliament in 2024, and that he did not register once elected. Farage denies any wrongdoing. Harborne gave Reform UK another £9m in 2025 and then £36m earlier this year. That number was chosen in a competitive flourish to equal the £36m that Ben Delo, another crypto billionaire , had given Farage’s party days before. This is unprecedented, gamechanging spending. But it skews the game in unpredictable ways. Farage’s political fortunes have not been boosted along with his personal finances. When the scandal of the first £5m infusion broke, he tried to pre-empt the standards commissioner’s investigation by putting his case before the “court of public opinion” in a quixotic byelection , which he ended up fighting against a novelty candidate dressed as a space-travelling dustbin. When the report finally lands, a damning verdict could lead to a suspension from the Commons and a recall petition, forcing Farage into another byelection. He may not bother contesting it. He doesn’t attend the Commons much anyway and doesn’t appear to be enjoying himself as much as he was before his financial affairs came under scrutiny. His newly sullen mood has coincided with Reform UK losing its lead in opinion polls. The party has fallen behind Labour in all surveys and dipped to third place, behind the Tories, in some. Farage is personally disliked by a majority of voters ; deeply so by enough that they form tactical-voting blocs to obstruct Reform UK candidates in byelections. That would probably form a formidable barrier to the party’s leader ever becoming prime minister. Most of the aversion has accrued over the long years of Farage’s nationalist posturing. Brexit-induced animus and liberal outrage at demagogic immigrant-bashing antedates the conspicuous influx of crypto money and other high-profile scandals. But there is polling evidence that even voters who count as the target demographic for Reform UK, and who might once have accepted the party’s pleas of victimisation at the hands of establishment conspiracy, are put off by the smell of seemingly dodgy deals . Research conducted over the summer by More in Common found that perceptions of Farage as being seen as “sleazy or corrupt” were emerging as an obstacle to support even among “dissenting disruptors” – the polling company’s label for the electoral segment, roughly one in five, who most mistrust institutions and would gladly see the system torn down by a strongman leader. A lot of those people were habitual non-voters, stirred out of apathy by the leave campaign in the Brexit referendum. Farage used to have a near monopoly on their allegiance but now faces competition from Rupert Lowe’s even more aggressively far-right Restore Britain party. Lowe, elected to parliament as a Reform candidate, broke with Farage and has since been elevated from relative obscurity by Musk. The X proprietor’s enthusiastic reposting and deployment of algorithmic privileges have given the Restore Britain leader a profile and audience that rivals the reach of world leaders.

events.title: Developing countries in limbo as rich nations delay new climate finance plans
events.summary: Many governments are yet to set targets, leaving recipient countries struggling to plan and attract private investment Developing countries have been left in limbo by the failure of some of the world’s biggest economies to flesh out their plans for new climate finance. Poor countries are supposed to receive $300bn a year from the governments of industrialised nations by 2035, along with about $1tn from other sources, to help them cope with the effects of extreme weather and shift to a low-carbon future. But many rich governments have not yet set out their targets and plans for providing climate finance beyond the end of this year or next. This gap is damaging because it means recipient countries cannot plan and makes it harder for them to attract private sector investment to supplement the public sector money. Analysis by the NRDC and E3G thinktanks seen by the Guardian shows that the developed world is broadly on track to meet the $300bn a year goal – known as the NCQG, or national collective quantitative goal – set at the Cop29 conference two years ago. By 2030 they should be providing about $229bn a year. The multilateral development banks should provide about $185bn of that. Joe Thwaites, international climate finance director at the National Resources Defence Council, co-wrote the original analysis along with the E3G thinktank and told the Guardian that unless development banks and national governments made sharp cuts in the next round of financing, which is unlikely, then the level of finance needed by 2030 would be almost met. “Most countries look in quite good shape on climate finance,” he said. “The problem is that they’re not being very public about it.” If the EU continues its current provision of about $36bn a year (which is likely) then – taking into account the pledges already made by the UK, Canada and some other smaller countries – there would remain a gap of about $7bn to fill. If a different president is in the White House, the US could make up some of the shortfall, along with Japan and Australia, which have yet to set out climate finance goals, according to Thwaites. Further analysis by Carbon Brief suggested that if countries failed to implement any new climate finance after their current targets expire, the developing world would face cuts of 70% in bilateral finance (which excludes the development banks) from the rich world. But Thwaites said this was highly unlikely. “It’s unfortunate that they have been quite silent on this, however. If they would talk about it more, it would reassure the G77 [group of developing countries],” he said. Climate finance is a vexed topic at the Cop31 talks, which began on Monday in Antalya, Turkey, but are being presided over by Australia in a compromise deal struck after the two countries vied for the presidency. Some developing countries wanted to reopen previous resolutions on climate finance, as they were concerned that there could be cuts to provision. The planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essential The World Bank retired its official climate finance target this summer, under pressure from Donald Trump’s White House, but will still provide tens of billions a year in finance towards climate-related projects. Other development banks are likely to continue with their climate finance plans, according to Thwaites. France, Germany and Australia are among the major countries yet to publicly state their new climate finance goals. It is highly unusual for a developed Cop host country such as Australia to fail to set out new plans on climate finance ahead of its hosting. The UK cut its climate finance earlier this year. Australia was contacted for comment, as was Germany. A spokesperson for France’s AFD aid agency said: “Our Climate and Biodiversity Strategy maintains AFD’s level of ambition and sets out the following targets for the 2025–2027 period: €6 billion in climate finance per year and €800 million per year for biodiversity.” A spokesperson for Japan said the country was “fully committed to fulfil the obligation under the Paris Agreement, actively providing support to developing countries in climate action. This support is channelled through the Japan International Cooperation Agency, international organisations and climate funds including the Green Climate Fund (GCF) and the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage. While Japan does not plan to announce any new financial pledges at present, this does not indicate any shift in our policy explained above. For example, Japan has committed up to 165 billion yen to the GCF’s second replenishment for the 2024–2027 period (GCF-2) and is steadily implementing this commitment.”

events.title: How Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's extramarital affair could cause collateral damage in Washington
events.summary: Jensen Huang, CEO of Nvidia, is under scrutiny after revelations of an affair with a Chinese businesswoman, Alice Huang, who is suspected of spying WASHINGTON -- Extramarital affairs are usually private matters. Jensen Huang’s has global implications. The 63-year-old is the leading face of the artificial intelligence revolution with his black leather jackets and fluff of grey hair. He runs the company Nvidia, which produces highly coveted computer chips. That's landed him on a late-night-phone-call basis with President Donald Trump, a promoter of the industry. But Huang was also liaising with a Chinese businesswoman who has allegedly fed intelligence — as well as advanced chips — to China. The woman, Alice Huang, is a former executive at the Singapore-based cloud computing company Megaspeed. It's a saga of personal betrayal, corporate espionage and high-tech development, and the fallout is spreading across Washington. There are bipartisan calls for investigations on Capitol Hill. The U.S. Department of Justice has opened its own probe. Nvidia, one of the most valuable companies in the world, is conducting an internal review. Some expect the technology to reshape human civilization by imbuing computers with the vast powers of creation and analysis, and Trump has repeated that “whoever wins AI, wins." Nvidia is the backbone of America's plans for dominating the field. When asked about Huang's affair, Trump said this week that he had spoken to the tech executive as the scandal grew. “I think he’ll be in good shape," Trump said, adding that "he said he had absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy.” As for when the president first learned about the concerns involving Alice Huang, Trump brushed off the question. “They could have been mentioned," he said. "Certainly it didn’t make much of an impact on me.” With the AI race between the U.S. and China often framed as a fierce and consequential rivalry, the Justice Department has persistently warned of the espionage threat posed by Beijing. That includes efforts to cultivate well-placed relationships in government and private industry, as well as to acquire sensitive technology such as AI chips developed in the U.S. Last year, Megaspeed faced scrutiny from the U.S. Commerce Department over its alleged skirting of U.S. export laws and routing of a large amount of advanced Nvidia chips to Chinese users. The company denied those allegations. U.S. intelligence officials eventually concluded that Alice Huang had spied for China, according to The New York Times. The Commerce Department's probe was handed off to the Justice Department, and its National Security Division is investigating whether Megaspeed violated export control laws in an inquiry that will also include scrutiny of Alice Huang, according to a person familiar with the matter who insisted on anonymity to discuss an ongoing law enforcement probe. Megaspeed did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Tuesday, and The Associated Press was unable to reach Alice Huang. Jensen Huang has apologized to his company about the affair, saying he hurt his wife and their children, but he didn’t address reports that Alice Huang was a suspected spy. Nvidia’s board said that it had “no reason to believe” that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, and that Huang would remain in charge while cooperating with the investigation. Beijing has said the “Chinese spy allegation is unsubstantiated" and called it “nothing but smears.” Baby buried alive for 24 hours released from the hospital; father charged House tables Hegseth impeachment, effectively killing it in current Congress Wisconsin state trooper detained by ICE After their first dinner together at Mar-a-Lago in early 2025, Trump latched onto Huang as a tech titan positioned to deliver on the president’s own promises of an economic renaissance. The computer chips produced by Nvidia would essentially turn data centers into factories that made raw intelligence, which could then be applied across the economy to produce cars, new pharmaceutical drugs, advanced weapons and seemingly unparalleled wealth. Trump would regularly phone Huang to discuss this future. “From the moment that I met him, the only thing that he’s ever talked to me about is creating more jobs, re-industrializing the United States, of protection, of national security,” Huang told AP in an interview this summer. "He knows that if America is wealthy, we have a lot of tax revenues. We can fund the military, we can fund our economy, we fund our communities, create more jobs.” Trump saw his political fortunes — and that of the country — in Huang's Nvidia. Huang joined Trump on Air Force One for a state visit to Beijing earlier this year. Just last month, Trump awarded Huang with a National Medal of Science.

events.title: Hellyer Metals liquidator lashed for 'serious lack of judgement'
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Hellyer Metals liquidator removed after federal judge lashes 'serious lack of judgement' Hellyer Metals is one of six companies that owned the Hellyer gold mine. ( Supplied: Hellyer ) The liquidator of a company that part-owned a Tasmanian gold mine has been removed from the role by a federal judge, who said the man had failed to properly investigate the company's transactions. Liam Bailey was removed as Hellyer Metals' liquidator on Tuesday. Hellyer Metals is being pursued in court for damages totalling more than $36 million over a failed business deal. A federal judge has fired the liquidator of Hellyer Metals, which part-owned a north-west Tasmanian gold mine, saying he failed in his duties and behaved in "objectively concerning" ways. The decision comes 12 months after the Tasmanian government ordered the Hellyer Gold Mine be shut down temporarily over unpaid debts, which occurred at about the time a "highly questionable" transaction was made from Hellyer Metals to an associated company, Celestial Group. At the same time, Hellyer Metals was being pursued in court by resources company Goshawk Mining and investment firm Saxby Capital for damages totalling more than $36 million over a failed business deal. The Hellyer mine and tailings dam in Tasmania's north-west. ( Google Earth ) On Tuesday, federal court Justice Shaun McElwaine removed Hellyer Metals liquidator Liam Bailey and ordered him to hand over all relevant records to Adam Johnston, who he appointed in Mr Bailey’s stead. Justice McElwaine said "very real" questions on Mr Bailey's impartiality had been raised, and that along with his lack of action since his appointment in January, it was clear "a new liquidator with a laser-like focus" was required. Plaintiffs lose confidence in liquidator In a lengthy decision, Justice McElwaine detailed a complex timeline over recent years that resulted in Hellyer Metals entering voluntary administration in January this year and appointing Mr Bailey as liquidator. Justice McElwaine said at that time Hellyer Metals had recently conducted the transaction in question, after which Goshawk Mining obtained a Supreme Court order freezing $36.4 million worth of assets in Hellyer's associated companies. He said, in the following months, Mr Bailey failed to properly investigate the company he was liquidating and the circumstances of the transaction, despite having access to voluminous records and financial resources. Mine's ex-bosses forced into bankruptcy The former bosses of Hellyer mine, in Tasmania's north-west, have been ordered to repay a combined $8.5 million in allegedly misappropriated funds after failing to set aside a bankruptcy ruling. Justice McElwaine said the plaintiffs, Goshawk Mining and Saxby Capital, sought the federal court's intervention and Mr Bailey's removal as they had lost confidence in him and his impartiality. Mr Bailey submitted to the court that no proper cause for his removal had been shown, but Justice McElwaine disagreed. "He was spurred into action because of it." He also said Mr Bailey provided a draft of his statutory report of the liquidation to Hellyer's directors. "These are the very people intimately involved in the transaction," the judge said. The state government issued Hellyer gold mine a three-week stop-work order in October 2025, over alleged compliance failures and unpaid mining royalties. ( Supplied: www.hellyermetals.com.au ) Sacking 'required' for proper liquidation Justice McElwaine said a "reasonable liquidator … would have acted with more haste". "For more than eight months Liam Bailey has had the benefit of a detailed analysis of the transaction … which manifestly warranted urgent investigation," he said. events.title: Prada’s new Milan exhibition turns a century of fashion into fresh discoveries
events.summary: Prada has launched a new permanent exhibition in Milan called “Pradasphere,” showcasing over a century of fashion history MILAN -- MILAN (AP) — Iconic A-line skirts twirl overhead, silver-covered handbags gleam in a secret underground passage and a spacesuit prototype brings more than a century of fashion history into the future at Prada’s new permanent exhibition in Milan, called “Pradasphere.” The highly visual journey through the Italian luxury brand’s evolution is connecting Prada aficionados with the fashion house’s heritage in ways that go beyond nostalgia, and already is promising a commercial payoff. “The exhibition is a multiplier,” said Lorenzo Bertelli , Prada Group's chief group marketing officer. Prada projects that the Pradasphere exhibition anchoring the brand's expansion in the Galleria Vittorio Emanuele shopping arcade will add 100 million euros ($111 million) in annual revenues, and Bertelli said that target could be surpassed. Pradasphere is fully booked into the new year and Bertelli said visitors have shown a tendency to spend more after immersing themselves in the brand’s history, sometimes going back to make an additional purchase after walking through the eight Pradasphere spaces. “We see that the customers who go through the museum have a completely different perspective of the brand and also they browse the store with completely different minds,” said Bertelli, who has been identified as the future leader of the Prada Group. The 38-year-old, whose roles include executive chairman of Versace, is the son of creative director Miuccia Prada and Prada Group chairman Patrizio Bertelli. Longtime Prada lovers will know that Mario and Martino Prada founded Fratelli Prada in 1913 in the historic Galleria. But they may never have seen in person the luxury bags and accessories, including a pleated evening bag with a devilish head-shaped clasp, its tongue sticking out, a detail that appeared on the Spring-Summer 2024 runway. And it may be news that the brothers designed the brand’s signature inverted triangle logo. Miuccia Prada’s third-generation entrance into the family business is announced with trademark nylon bags that she began designing in the 1970s, embodying the Prada high-low, industrial-luxury paradox, and a chocolate brown opera coat from her first runway collection presented in 1988. The exhibition contains many runway hits, including the 2012 Flame heels and the Formica tile prints that gave birth to Prada’s “ugly chic” reputation, while also highlighting Miuccia Prada’s and the senior Bertelli’s reach into art, architecture, film and sport. “Curiosity and having fun is what drives my parents,” the younger Bertelli said, adding that experimentation doesn't always bring immediate financial success, “but for sure it drives the enrichment of our story, and our culture and our knowledge.” Baby buried alive for 24 hours released from the hospital; father charged House tables Hegseth impeachment, effectively killing it in current Congress Wisconsin state trooper detained by ICE He cited as an example investments in sports and engineering made with the formation of the Luna Rossa America’s Cup sailing team in the 1990s, which helped develop the kind of materials expertise that led Prada to collaborate with Axiom Space on a space suit, a prototype of which is displayed at the end of the exhibition. Prada helped design the suit’s outer layer, which is engineered to withstand extreme thermal conditions, as well as the high-performance inner layer, with a focus on thermal regulation and comfort. It is intended for astronauts walking on the moon on NASA’s Artemis IV mission , targeted for 2028. Just 20 visitors are admitted to Pradasphere by appointment each hour to explore the compact eight rooms of the exhibition, which Bertelli promises will be in constant evolution. Prada’s presence in the Galleria now spans eight floors, encompassing the existing Marchesi 1824 pastry shop and Osservatorio Fondazione Prada contemporary art space, alongside the new exhibition, private salon and apartment. Most visitors end their journey in a secret underground passage connecting the menswear and womenswear boutiques, the latter occupying the original Fratelli Prada premises. The passage contains “lesser-known” chapters from the brand’s history, including a chandelier dress created for Baz Luhrmann’s “The Great Gatsby.” “It was a great experience,” said Luca Missio, an architect from the northeastern Italian city of Udine. “I recognized the stores I’ve visited around the world, in Tokyo and New York, in the models and displays. events.title: Prime property, slow sales: why London’s stock of empty high-end flats is piling up
events.summary: Homes in the West End, Mayfair and Marylebone are going unsold – and developers are counting the cost L ondon has no shortage of luxury flats. There are ultra-modern blocks in the most upmarket neighbourhoods – including Chelsea, Kensington and Mayfair – that offer marble lobbies, concierge services and views across the city’s skyline. The problem for property developers is finding wealthy residents to fill them , leaving brand-new properties in London’s most desirable postcodes standing empty. In the capital’s zone 1 – which includes the City financial district, the West End and central areas such as Mayfair and Marylebone – there were 1,400 completed but unsold homes at the end of September, three times the number recorded in 2016, according to figures from the market researcher Molior. Just 1,600 homes started construction in the area in the past 12 months, 75% fewer than a decade ago, it found. As a result, building these high-end homes is becoming increasingly hard to justify commercially for developers. Construction costs are rising and volatile, borrowing is now more expensive and financing a project can mean sitting on a fast-growing debt pile before a single flat is sold. The multimillion-pound homes developers are building remain way out of reach for the average Londoner, while a range of factors have put a squeeze on some wealthy buyers . A rise in borrowing costs has become the latest headache in the high-end property market, which was hit hard by Brexit, the Covid pandemic and higher property taxes after a period of rapid price growth post-financial crisis. The sector is starting to crack. London Richmond, which marketed itself as a specialist developer in the capital’s “finer areas”, had boasted a portfolio of 20 properties worth more than £30m, spanning affluent neighbourhoods including South Kensington, Wimbledon and West Hampstead. It appointed administrators in August, after its owners ran out of funding. More than 300 creditors are still waiting for payment of £39m in remaining debt, according to its administrator BTG. The developer Ardmore Construction – which was building 10 major projects across the capital including two residential towers in King’s Cross and luxury hotel developments in Mayfair and Kensington – also fell into administration, in 2025. While its parent company Ardmore Group continues to trade – after its creditors accepted a company voluntary arrangement – the construction arm of the business still owed more than £29m to its creditors and subcontractors as of September. Jon Neale of the property consultancy Montagu Evans said high-end developers were being squeezed by a double whammy of rising costs and weaker demand. “The fundamental problem is that construction costs have gone through the roof,” he said. “On the other side, demand for these properties has gone down … A lot of those homes are being sold to overseas buyers and they are not in the market as much as they were,” he added, pointing to tax changes around stamp duty and the abolition of the non-dom regime . Overseas buyers can face stamp duty of up to 19% on additional properties – which means, for example, the purchase of a £10m home could trigger a £1.9m stamp duty bill. Marcus Dixon of the real estate company JLL said developers needed more certainty that there will be a market for their homes once they finish building them. “Uncertainty over taxation, buying and holding costs has deterred more discretionary purchasers from committing to buy,” he said. “This hits the prime markets, both new and existing homes, harder, as we see fewer needs-based buyers in this sector of the market.” The slowdown has hit bigger developers, too; in October, British Land announced it would not go ahead with the second phase of its Canada Water development on the south side of the River Thames, amid soaring costs and weak sales. The city’s biggest residential developer, Berkeley Group, said this year that it would stop buying new land, and the rival builder Taylor Wimpey has said it plans to pull out of the city entirely. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning The difficulties are particularly pronounced in the market for flats. The average flat price was about £431,000 in June, down £2,000 from the same month in 2016, according to Land Registry figures published in August. If flat prices had kept pace with inflation, the average would be £180,000 higher now. House prices, by contrast, have risen by about a fifth over the same period. Even on the most expensive roads in the country, the market is slow. No 1 Palace Street, a luxury residential development a stone’s throw away from Buckingham Palace, entered administration in 2023. By 2025, only 20% of the project’s flats had sold, according to its administrator FRP Advisory. The shaky market is starting to hit jobs.

These changes will align local currency pricing with global levels and apply to the Australian Dollar (AUD), Chinese Yuan (CNY), Indian Rupee (INR), Norwegian Krone (NOK), and New Zealand Dollar (NZD). events.title: Sharpest home loan drop on record as property investors exit market
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Plummeting demand from property investors drives record fall in new home loans Topic: Construction and Real Estate Industry Both the number of new loans and value of homes have dropped, according to new data. ( ABC News: Declan Bowring ) New figures show a record drop in new home loans, falling 15 per cent overall in the September quarter. Investor loans fell much faster at 31 per cent, compared to 5 per cent for owner-occupiers. Housing Minister Clare O'Neil welcomed the fact that home owners were faring better than investors. The number of new home loans plummeted through the middle of this year, especially for property investors, as rate hikes and tax changes cooled the housing market. The total number of loans fell 15 per cent, and their total value dropped 16 per cent from June to September, according to figures from the Australian Bureau of Statistics. New loans for investors fell by 31 per cent and by 5 per cent for those buying for themselves. Both the overall and investor drop broke official records. Mish Tan, the head of finance statistics at the bureau, said the data suggested investors were being deterred not just by high rates but by "tax changes and expectations of lower house prices". Conditions in the housing market were weak before the May budget, when the federal government unveiled plans to curb property investor tax breaks, but have deteriorated markedly since that time and spread beyond Melbourne and Sydney to other capitals. Nationwide, house prices have fallen 6.7 per cent from their peak in March, the fastest decline in the past 40 years according to property data company Cotality. The rate of auction clearances has also fallen. Liberal housing spokesperson Andrew Bragg argues that confidence in the market has tanked. ( ABC News: Matt Roberts ) The opposition and property groups have blamed the figures on the negative gearing and capital gains tax changes. Liberal housing spokesperson Andrew Bragg said the deterioration showed confidence in the market had tanked and argued, "Loans to everyone are down. No-one wins from these crazy taxes." But Housing Minister Clare O'Neil welcomed the fact that homebuyers fared better than investors in the data, saying this was what the tax changes were meant to achieve. "Volumes are down, as you would expect in a period where prices are softening. But these figures also clearly show a strong shift away from investors and towards Australians buying a home to live in," she said. Reserve Bank says tax changes playing a role Economists say five rate hikes this year, which have taken rates to their highest level since 2008, have contributed to the fall. But Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock said investor demand had fallen "so much further" than in previous rate-hiking cycles. Mortgage borrowers are likely to feel the sting of the RBA's latest cash rate rise, but savers and overseas travellers will also see the effects. "[That] suggests that there's something else going here, and the something else going on is the tax changes," she said. Her comments did not mention owner-occupiers, suggesting only that the tax changes were affecting investor demand. Treasury analysis, which underpinned the government's changes, predicted a modest decline of two percentage points in house price growth. Treasury has described this figure as a "structural" forecast, not a short-term one factoring in rate hikes. But while Treasury and the government have stuck by the forecast in public, there is private recognition within government that the scale of the fall is deeper than was expected. Housing minister says 'balance is shifting' While government ministers have been eager to emphasise they do not want prices to fall as such, and are not targeting a given price with their policy, they have framed their tax changes as a deliberate strategy to advantage homebuyers over investors. "We've had a housing market geared towards investors for a generation, and where did it get us? Plummeting home ownership, out-of-control house price increases, and a generation losing hope," Ms O'Neil told the ABC. "These numbers show the balance is shifting back towards Australians who are buying a home to live in, and especially to our first home buyers." Housing Minister Clare O'Neil says the balance is shifting towards first home buyers. ( ABC News: Callum Flinn ) First homebuyers fared worse than non-first homebuyers, with an 8 per cent fall compared to a 3.5 per cent fall, but much better than investors. Mr Bragg said the results reflected poorly on the government.

Asking cos that’s how long it might take to shut one down Shipping giant Maersk probes 'IT security incident,' data theft 11 hours ago November Patch Tuesday boasts over 1,000 bugs, one already under attack 1 day ago Ring robots ready to patrol paranoids’ pads 1 day ago Barracuda’s email security gateways bitten by make-me-root vulns 1 day ago Trump taps Palantir security chief to run battered US cyber defense agency 1 day ago In 2019, OpenAI decided not to publicly release a new model because its research uncovered “concerns about malicious applications of the technology.” And on Tuesday, the company announced it has built a kill switch for the models deployed in its research labs, months after some of them displayed disturbing behavior. “As our models get more powerful and the associated safety and security risks become bigger, it becomes more and more critical that we can detect potential issues, and quickly stop models in their tracks when needed,” OpenAI explains in a Tuesday post . The company named the kill switch “Control Room” and described it as “a central system to track model workloads across our research infrastructure and stop them quickly when safety or security concerns arise.” The facility can apparently stop models from producing any output 35 seconds after a decision to pull the plug – and can go faster. “The 35-second lag comes from a caching layer for inference authorization, to support the required volume of traffic. We are working to drive this number down to zero so that we can end jobs instantly,” the company promises. A rookie mistake in critical infrastructure design is to build both production and resilience tools on shared resources that could be taken offline by a single incident. OpenAI seems conscious of that risk, because it says the tool “has been built to keep working even when other systems fail, and to stop model output if Control Room itself goes down.” OpenAI hasn’t explained why it took so long to build a kill switch or why it decided now is the moment when it needs one. The Register fancies recent examples of agents exceeding their brief in worrying ways – like attacking Hugging Face , causing trouble at the Wikimedia Foundation , or going a little too deep when researching Australian healthcare data – may have influenced the timing of this development. “Control Room is already deployed across our research infrastructure, where the need is greatest,” the company’s announcement states. “Our external model-serving stack is already much more centralized by nature, with a well-developed operational capability to quickly take down model deployments if needed.” OpenAI says it plans to “strengthen and expand the system over the coming months, alongside our investments in monitoring for misaligned behavior and security breaches.” That’s a variant of Big Tech’s usual “We’re sorry and we promise to do better in future” proclamation that follows the latest SNAFU. events.title: Poland’s Orlen becomes first buyer to cancel QatarEnergy LNG contract
events.summary: Poland’s Orlen has terminated a long-term liquefied natural gas supply contract with QatarEnergy, blaming the Qatari company’s inability to deliver cargoes as the Iran war continues to disrupt shipments through the Strait of Hormuz. Orlen exercised its right to end the agreement because of an “ongoing force majeure” that had left QatarEnergy unable to meet its delivery obligations, it said in a regulatory filing late on Tuesday. The contract, for 1 million tonnes of LNG a year priced against crude oil, had an estimated value of €570 million ($637 million) this year. It was signed in 2009, with deliveries starting in 2016, and was due to run until 2034. The agreement will remain in force for 60 days following the notice of termination. Orlen will keep a second contract with QatarEnergy, linked to gas prices, for up to 1 million tonnes a year until 2034. The company said the decision “does not affect the security of gas supplies” to Poland, which has its own gasfields and other long-term supply agreements. It is the first cancellation by a customer of QatarEnergy, which supplied about a fifth of the world’s LNG before the war, Bloomberg reported. Missile strikes in March badly damaged two of the 14 production units at Qatar’s main LNG export plant, forcing QatarEnergy to declare force majeure on shipments for the first time . Force majeure is a legal clause that allows suppliers to miss deliveries because of events beyond their control. Prolonged use of the clause typically gives buyers the right to walk away from a contract. QatarEnergy has extended the measure every month , with its latest notice covering shipments until the end of the year, forcing buyers in Europe and Asia to turn to spot cargoes at prices that are at their highest in years. Orlen has since signed deals to buy LNG from projects in Texas and Louisiana, including Port Arthur and Plaquemines.

events.title: Asian stocks fluctuate as US rate worries temper tech bounce
events.summary: Tokyo, Seoul and Taipei – where most of Asia’s leading AI-linked firms are listed – enjoyed big gains, with Shanghai, Sydney, Singapore, Wellington, Mumbai and Bangkok also up. But there were losses in Hong Kong, Jakarta and Manila. Asian shares were mixed as AI stocks bounced, helped by CoreWeave and Anthropic updates, but gains were limited by US inflation worries and a possible bigger Fed rate hike. US consumer prices rose 0.4% in October, above forecasts, and Fed officials warned on inflation. Traders now fear a stronger December rate rise. Markets also watched Nvidia, now under FBI investigation, while SoftBank fell after a more than US$7 billion quarterly loss. Oil prices edged up despite recent falls. HONG KONG – Most Asian stocks rose on Nov 11 on renewed optimism over the AI trade, while traders appeared to take in stride forecast-topping US inflation data and the prospect of a bumper interest rate hike in December . After last week’s rout fuelled by fears that Democrats would ramp up regulation of artificial intelligence , beaten-down tech stocks have bounced this week on bargain buying and a feeling their fears may have been overdone. Sentiment was also given a boost by earnings from data centre operator CoreWeave, which said sales would come in at US$13 billion ( S$16.7 billion ) to US$13.3 billion in 2026 , beating estimates. The news soothed worries about the company’s health after suffering heavy selling in October amid speculation that it could struggle to finance its vast debt pile as borrowing costs continued to rise. That sparked a period of panic over the tech sector as firms rely heavily on debt to fund their eye-watering AI investments. Also lifting confidence was Anthropic’s filing showing it planned to raise up to US$64 billion in its upcoming initial public offering , valuing it at as much as US$1.4 trillion. The maker of AI agent Claude had been expected to raise up to US$100 billion in its IPO, which would have made it the largest IPO on record. The stock market debut is being seen as a gauge of how long the AI spending boom can last. Its filing also revealed that revenue soared to US$17 billion in the third quarter, up from just US$1.4 billion in 2025 . And in another sign of the sector’s health, Bloomberg reported that ChatGPT-maker OpenAI had earned US$10 billion in quarterly revenue for the first time in July-September, thanks to demand for its software. The figure marked an increase of nearly 50% from the previous three months and a near threefold jump year-on-year. However, chip giant Nvidia was still in focus following the bombshell revelation of an affair between chief executive officer Jensen Huang and a woman reportedly suspected of being a Chinese spy. The firm is now the subject of a Federal Bureau of Investigation probe . All three main indexes on Wall Street ended in the red on Nov 10 , snapping a two-day rally, but Asia fared a little better. Tokyo, Seoul and Taipei – where most of Asia’s leading AI-linked firms are listed – enjoyed big gains, with Shanghai, Sydney, Singapore, Wellington, Mumbai and Bangkok also up. But there were losses in Hong Kong, Jakarta and Manila. Traders are also now fretting over the possibility of a bigger-than-expected rate hike by the Federal Reserve when it next meets in December. US consumer prices rose 0.4% on-month in October, a slowdown from September’s 0.6% but more than the 0.3% forecast. While the reading reflected a significant moderation in energy price increases, food prices shot higher with medical care, household furnishings and several other categories. Chicago Fed boss Austan Goolsbee told PBS Newshour the reading was “another distressing report, borderline disturbing”. The report came hours after Fed governor Christopher Waller called for a swift response to inflation, suggesting he could even support a 50-basis-point hike in December. A second Fed official, Dallas Fed president Lorie Logan, also signalled strong support for swift action to address inflation. “Market participants continue to navigate the political implications of the Democratic swee p a nd the economics of AI infrastructure,” said Chris Weston at Pepperstone . He said investors were “forced to reassess assumptions around future revenues, cash flows and funding conditions”. “Add a hotter-than-expected US (consumer price) print, a heightened focus on Anthropic’s IP O and a major buyers’ strike on Nvidia, and there’s no shortage of catalysts driving market price action,” he added. Oil prices edged up after sinking again on Nov 10 in the hope of a US-Iran agreement to end their war and reopen the crucial Strait of Hormuz. International benchmark Brent was hovering around US$92 a barrel, after dropping below US$90 for the first time since August. Both contracts are down around 20% since the start of the month.

events.title: Singapore’s accountancy sector adds jobs, raises pay as firms prepare workers for AI
events.summary: As routine tasks are automated, employers must consider how young accountants will develop the judgment traditionally gained through such work, said Acting Minister for Manpower Jasmin Lau. PHOTO: INSTITUTE OF SINGAPORE CHARTERED ACCOUNTANTS Singapore’s accountancy sector grew in 2025, adding 579 jobs and lifting median pay across all seniority levels, while revenue rose 5.1% to about $3.7 billion. AI is changing accountancy work, so firms must train juniors to use judgement, review AI output, and take responsibility for decisions, Acting Minister Jasmin Lau said. ACRA, ISCA and schools are boosting skills through AI training, internships and FlexConnect, while EY and Nexia won awards for using automation to free staff for higher-value work. SINGAPORE – Singapore’s accountancy sector added jobs and raised median salaries across all surveyed seniority levels in 2025, even as AI changes the work accountants do and the skills they need. The sector’s workforce grew by 579 positions, or 2.7%, from 21,783 in 2024 to 22,362 in 2025, while revenue increased 5.1% to about $3.7 billion over the same period, according to the Accounting and Corporate Regulatory Authority’s (ACRA) Accounting Entities Survey 2026. Accounting entities reported more than 1,200 job opportunities, around 80% of them in audit and assurance, and business advisory services. The growth comes as firms face the challenge of preparing employees for work that increasingly involves reviewing AI-generated analyses and making decisions based on them. As routine tasks are automated, employers must consider how young accountants will develop the judgment traditionally gained through such work, said Acting Minister for Manpower Jasmin Lau in her speech at the Institute of Singapore Chartered Accountants (ISCA) Conference at Sands Expo and Convention Centre on Nov 11. Reconciliations and first drafts are among the tasks AI is starting to handle, but they have also helped juniors traditionally learn their craft, she added. Reconciliation involves comparing financial records and investigating any differences, while first drafts are initial versions of documents, such as reports, that require review. “As firms automate these tasks, I hope they will think about how juniors can still develop a feel for when something does not look right,” Lau said. Done well, automation could make entry-level roles more interesting, with graduates spending more time evaluating what tools produce, working with senior colleagues on difficult decisions and meeting clients earlier. “This will take deliberate effort from employers in training young staff and in giving them real responsibility,” Lau said. The annual ACRA survey drew responses from 238 accounting entities, representing 92% of the sector’s estimated revenue. Business advisory services led revenue growth, while audit and assurance remained the largest service category, contributing to nearly half of total revenue. Residents accounted for 522 of the 579 positions added, taking the resident workforce to 17,027. Median monthly salaries for first-year audit assistants rose from $3,000 to $3,400, while those for first-year associates increased from $4,200 to $4,600. For first-year senior associates, the figure rose from $5,400 to $5,800. First-year managers’ median salaries increased from $7,750 to $8,250, and first-year directors’ from $13,500 to $14,500. Alongside hiring, firms are prioritising new skills. AI application, ethics and governance topped workforce development priorities for the next three years, cited by 67% of respondents, followed by advanced data analytics and visualisation at 45%. To help prepare future entrants, ISCA signed a five-year memorandum of understanding with all five polytechnics and the Institute of Technical Education (ITE). The partnership will create opportunities for practical AI learning, industry projects, mentorship and internships. More than 3,000 polytechnic and ITE students have enrolled in ISCA’s AI Fluency Programme. Lau said accountants’ responsibility for assessing information would remain essential. “AI tools can churn out analyses very quickly. But someone still has to decide whether that analysis makes sense and take responsibility for it.” Retaining experienced professionals is another priority, particularly as more workers care for both young children and elderly parents, she added. ISCA is piloting FlexConnect to connect experienced accountancy professionals seeking flexible arrangements with businesses needing temporary or specialist finance talent. The initiative covers part-time, contract and project-based roles, including assignments to cover employees who are on extended leave. More than 100 professionals have registered their interest since the pilot began in September. Lau said smaller practices could particularly benefit from help covering prolonged absences. “This effort, FlexConnect, is still at the pilot stage, but I think it is a good idea and I hope it grows.

events.title: Aussie filmmakers left scrambling amid David Walliams allegations
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts David Walliams movie shot in Australia by local director drops association with writer A movie based off a David Walliams book has dropped all association with him. ( Supplied: King Bert Productions/Story Bridge Films ) A new Australian movie based on a book by David Walliams will scrub the writer and actor from the movie and publicity materials. Fing! has also been dropped by streaming platform Stan, which was set to release the movie after its cinematic release in January. It follows allegations of grooming and sexual assault against the Little Britain star and children's author. The Australian producers of Fing!, an upcoming children's movie based on a book by David Walliams, have confirmed his cameo has been removed from the film following allegations against the comedian. Its distributor, Transmission Films, has also confirmed that Walliams, a co-writer on the movie, will also be removed from its publicity, and its streaming distributor Stan has confirmed it will no longer release the movie. In an investigation published by The Guardian and ITV, Walliams is alleged to have groomed teenage fans and sexually assaulted a 15-year-old girl, and to have harassed young female colleagues. Walliams, who lost a High Court battle to avoid being identified in the UK media and did not appeal the decision, denied targeting teenagers and using his fame to manipulate them to have sex, his lawyers said. A UK/Australia co-production, Fing! stars Taika Waititi, Mia Wasikowska, Iona Bell and Blake Harrison, with a screenplay written by Walliams and Kevin Cecil. It is directed by Australian filmmaker Jeffery Walker ( Apple Cider Vinegar ). It is based on Walliams's 2019 book Fing. Williams has sold more than 60 million copies of his kids' books worldwide. Fing! will retain its January 14 Australian release date, as confirmed by local distributor Transmission Films. The cast of Fing!, director Jeffery Walker (far left) and co-writer Kevin Cecil (far right) at the film's Sundance premiere in January 2026. ( Getty Images: Dia Dipasupil ) "Walliams will not be participating in the Australian publicity campaign," a Transmission Films spokesperson told ABC Arts. "The campaign will focus on the film's Australian production, director and lead cast." The fantasy family film follows parents tracking down a mythical beast to appease their unruly child. In addition to co-writing the screenplay, Walliams was set to feature in the film as a character called Headmaster. "The film's producers have advised that they have removed Walliams's cameo appearance from Fing!" the Transmission spokesperson said. Stan was slated to make Fing! available on its streaming platform following the movie's theatrical run, but has confirmed to ABC Arts it has been dropped. "In light of the recent and serious allegations against David Walliams, Stan has removed Fing! from its content slate," a Stan spokesperson said. The film's US distributor, Angel Studios, has also confirmed that it will be removing Walliams from the film. "We take the allegations reported regarding David Walliams seriously," it said in a statement to Variety . "Our thoughts are with anyone who has been affected ... and [Walliams] will have no involvement in the film's release or promotion." UK distributor Sky has removed the film from its upcoming slate altogether. "The allegations made against David Walliams are extremely serious," a spokesperson said. "We have notified the producers of the film of our intention to exit our position as the UK and Ireland licensee of Fing." While Fing! has lost its streaming distributor Stan, it will be released in cinemas in January. ( Supplied: King Bert Productions/Story Bridge Films. ) Fing! was filmed in Queensland in 2025, with support from Screen Queensland. "David Walliams's FING! is beloved by children around the world, and it's incredible to see our Production Attraction Strategy supporting renowned Queensland creatives as they bring it to life on the big screen," Queensland Arts Minister John-Paul Langbroek said in a press release at the time . Screen Queensland said it was aware of media reports about Walliams. "During production in early 2025, FING! generated more than $24 million in local expenditure and employed approximately 210 Queensland crew, as well as utilising small businesses to supply goods and services," a Screen Queensland spokesperson said. "Screen Queensland assesses all applications for the Production Attraction Strategy incentive against a range of eligibility criteria including local expenditure and employment opportunities.

events.title: UOB’s strategy to match Asean growth in the digital age
events.summary: The Singapore-headquartered bank stays true to its founding mission by evolving with the markets it serves UOB got its start in Singapore 90 years ago, when it was first known as the United Chinese Bank. From the beginning, the bank’s aim has been to serve its communities while also growing alongside them. UOB branched out to Malaysia in 1951 and then to Hong Kong in 1965. By the 1980s, the bank had opened a representative office in mainland China and installed its first ATM machines in Singapore. As technology evolved and the world transitioned into the digital age, UOB adapted its offerings to suit customers’ changing banking needs, such as the UOB TMRW (pronounced “tomorrow”) mobile banking app that provides a personalised digital banking experience through the use of data and artificial intelligence (AI). The app offers retail deals and rewards, customised insights and support to help customers manage their personal finances, such as spending alerts, security checks for duplicated transactions and new big-ticket transactions, and digital investment capabilities to make investing a more accessible activity. The bank also offers UOB Infinity, a digital banking platform for business clients that provides cash management and trade services for them to improve their business cash flow and working capital. Clients can also use the platform to exchange and validate documents with their suppliers, buyers and distributors. The bank entered its next phase of growth with the formation of the Innovation Group, a department tasked with developing new capabilities for the bank by harnessing advanced technologies such as generative AI and agentic AI to deliver an enhanced customer experience. The Innovation Group aims to drive innovative initiatives across the Asean region while being mindful of the distinct needs of each market. To support this goal, UOB is partnering with universities and research institutes located across the Association of Southeast Asian Nations to help build an innovation ecosystem in the region and nurture future talent for the workforce. As part of this effort, the bank recently launched the UOB Innovation Hub at Singapore’s Nanyang Technological University, which provides a space for aspiring start-up founders and entrepreneurs to develop and test ideas. These initiatives reflect UOB’s broad approach to innovation from its position as a bank focused on the Asean region. By developing advanced technologies, building partnerships and investing in talent, UOB is working to deliver smarter banking solutions for consumers and businesses while also improving connectivity across its key markets – all part of its long-standing mission of serving the local communities in which it operates while creating value for its customers and employees. events.title: How AI Helps Recyclers Turn Mixed Waste Into Reusable Material
events.summary: As world leaders gather for COP31 in Türkiye, the event’s emphasis on zero waste puts a practical challenge in focus: how to keep products and materials in use for longer. Globally, less than 7% of the materials entering the economy come from recycled or reused sources. Municipal solid waste generation accounts for over 2 billion tons of trash per year — a figure that could nearly double by 2050 . AI and robotics are helping change this trajectory, as innovators around the globe improve sorting to recover resources that would otherwise end up in landfills. “A more circular economy relies on making better use of what we already have,” said Josh Parker, head of sustainability at NVIDIA. “AI can help us understand what’s in a waste stream, identify what can be recovered and automate the work of sorting it. We’re giving innovators the computing tools to make those processes more effective and bring them to more places.” See how four members of the NVIDIA Inception program for startups are applying AI to keep valuable materials in circulation. AIRECO Gives Plastic Waste New Life Recycled plastic is only used if its cost and quality can compete with new material. Too often it can’t: Incoming waste is of inconsistent quality, sorting depends on hard-to-find manual labor and mixed scrap ends up downcycled into low-grade products. The founders of AIRECO, a Taiwan-based startup, believe that AI sorting can cut down the cost and improve the quality of recycling to make these materials more commercially useful. The company uses vision AI to sort plastics more finely, enabling materials to be plucked out of mixed scrap piles for closed-loop recycling, where used items are reprocessed into new versions of the same product. “The finer you sort, the more you can recycle,” said Chun-Feng Liu, founder and CEO of AIRECO. “With finely sorted material, it’s more likely that an item can stay in the loop — a plastic bottle recycled back into a bottle again and again, rather than ending up in other products that are hard to recycle further.” The company uses NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX modules to run inference across its pilot line at a recycling plant in Tainan, including to drive robotic arms that pick targets off a conveyor belt. Recognition accuracy on the test line tops 95%. In a full production line planned for next year, the team aims to nearly triple annual waste processing capacity from 18,000 to 48,000 tons while cutting operating costs by 85%. EverestLabs AI Puts Robotics on the Recycling Line At material recovery facilities, the plants that separate household recyclables, sorting must be done in real time at fast-moving conveyor belts — requiring rapid analysis to identify and sort items. EverestLabs AI, a U.S. startup, deploys computer vision-guided robots on those sorting lines. About 150 robots are currently deployed in facilities across North America and Australia. “Other robots have infinite time to finish their tasks,” said R. Paul Singh, CEO of EverestLabs AI. “We don’t have that luxury because our conveyor belts are going to come in at a certain speed, and we have to act at a fast clip before the material moves. It’s a real-time game.” EverestLabs runs AI inference on NVIDIA RTX GPUs at the edge and trains its models on NVIDIA data center GPUs , optimized using NVIDIA CUDA. The company estimates its deployed systems have so far identified about 40 billion objects, recycled roughly 25,000 tons of material and avoided about 30,000 metric tons of carbon dioxide emissions. Their team is constantly working to improve its models to correctly classify and pick every kind of object while capturing metadata about the material type, brand and packaging of each. They’re also shipping agentic AI tools to provide actionable data to recycling facility staff, from floor managers to executives responsible for multiple facilities — and are looking to extend that capability to adjacent industries. Greyparrot Gives Recyclers a Clear View of the Waste Stream Recycling plants can process tens of thousands of tons of waste a day, yet operators have long judged what’s on the belt by manually sampling less than 1% of it. U.K. startup Greyparrot built its Analyzer platform to change that. Mounted above conveyor belts, it uses computer vision to identify each passing object by material and brand, even in dusty environments or poor lighting on belts moving up to 4 meters a second. “Waste changes all the time. It shifts by hour, by season, by supplier,” said Ambarish Mitra, cofounder of Greyparrot. “Before, operators guessed based on a tiny sample, and now they can see exactly what’s on the belt.” Greyparrot uses NVIDIA GPUs to train AI models on billions of objects, while NVIDIA Jetson modules run rapid detection at the edge. More than 300 Analyzer systems, operating in over 20 countries, have made over a trillion bounding box detections to date — reducing the time needed to check 15 tons of waste from 375 hours to just six. Facilities using the real-time data from Analyzer report efficiency gains of 10% to 30%. At global packaging company Amcor, the solution helped increase the yield of food-grade plastics by 12% . Brands including Coca-Cola, Colgate-Palmolive and Kenvue also use Greyparrot technology to measure how their packaging is recycled in real sorting plants. reverse.fashion Gives Discarded Garments a Second Look Europe generates nearly 7 million tons of used textiles a year. About a quarter of these textiles are collected separately and sorted by hand into hundreds of categories, destined for uses ranging from vintage resale to downcycling as furniture filling or cleaning cloths. The work is slow, costly and hard to staff, which keeps the value of reusable garments buried. reverse.fashion, a Berlin-based startup, is helping automate the job with high-resolution computer vision. Its system identifies product type, defects, color, size, brand, fabric construction, season and style and assigns each garment to its most valuable category. “Compared to classical waste sorting, our AI models have to run at very high resolution because humans are picky with textiles,” said Karsten Pufahl, cofounder and chief technology officer of reverse.fashion. “The computer vision pipeline needs to spot small defects to determine the quality and potential value of each garment.” As it moves across a conveyor belt at 3 meters a second, each textile analyzed by Reverse Fashion passes through over a dozen vision AI models optimized with NVIDIA TensorRT software and running on NVIDIA Jetson modules at the edge. The models are trained on NVIDIA GPUs in workstations and the cloud. The system sorts in an hour what would’ve previously taken a week to sort, Pufahl estimates, and is currently rolling out to facilities in Europe. events.title: The Democratic leadership revolt has a glaring problem
events.summary: The Republican leadership fights are over. For Democrats, the pain has only just begun. Why it matters: All the talk about changing party leadership is empty if no one steps up to run. Senate Republicans demanded more time and deeper conversations about their leadership, but no one stepped forward to challenge John Thune, who won by acclamation. Democrats are demanding their own conversations about the party's future and the leadership of Chuck Schumer and Hakeem Jeffries. Neither has a challenger. ‼️ The intrigue: Where there was a contested leadership fight, the challenger won. Rep. Jim Jordan, the Freedom Caucus founding member who spent years tormenting Republican leaders, will now lead the battered House GOP after defeating 12-year leadership veteran Rep. Steve Scalise by 33 votes. Jordan is the kind of fighter House Republicans want to take on Democrats as they enter the minority, lawmakers told Axios. "We're gearing up for war. And you're talking to a guy who's known as a hammer. You know we need someone who can punch hard, and I think that he'll do that," Rep. Randy Fine (R-Fla.) told Axios. 🤺 Zoom in: No such fighter has emerged to challenge Democratic leaders from within their ranks, and Schumer said he is "confident I will be elected majority leader." The closest thing to a challenge is Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.), who's listening to calls to run for Democratic leader while also considering a presidential campaign. It's hard to do both. Meanwhile, opposition to Schumer is building: " [T]he time is now for change," Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) said Tuesday. He appeared with Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.), who said she's not "actively seeking the job" but demanded a plan for change. 🏛️ Over in the House, Jeffries is dismissive of the idea that anyone would challenge him after the midterms gave him a massive majority. "You think I don't have the vote nailed down? I guess we'll find out next Wednesday," he told reporters on Monday. Some of his new members are signaling that they're not afraid to defy their new leaders. Rep.-elect Don Leonard (D-Ohio) said it "aches" his heart to potentially oppose the first Black speaker, "but Rome is burning." But other new members are on Jeffries' side, like Reps.-elect Marni von Wilpert (D-Calif.), Denise Powell (D-Neb.) and Cait Conley (D-N.Y.). 🤝 Jeffries also has high-profile progressive incumbents on board, such as Rep. Greg Casar (D-Texas), Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.), Pramila Jayapal (D-Wash.) and Ro Khanna (D-Calif.). "There is one candidate in this race , Hakeem Jeffries, and I think that everyone is far more concerned about what that leadership means, what is it promising?" Ocasio-Cortez told reporters on Tuesday. Between the lines: Thune and Jordan don't have much of a relationship; Thune had left the House for the Senate two years before Jordan arrived. What's next: Senators say they plan to be in the Capitol working on Veterans Day. Thune committed to working more days during the lame-duck session to ensure they leave no judge appointments behind, senators said.
