events.summary: Security All Security Cyber-crime Patches Research CSO Off-Prem All Off-Prem Edge and IoT Channel PaaS and IaaS SaaS On-Prem All On-Prem Systems Storage Networks HPC Personal Tech Cx0 Public Sector Software All Software AI and ML Applications Databases DevOps OS Platforms Virtualization Offbeat All Offbeat Columnists Supercomputing BOFH Legal Site News About Us Special Features All Special Features Supercomputing Month 2026 Nvidia GTC Berlin 2026 Cybersecurity Month 2026 VMware Explore 2026 Cloud Infrastructure Month 2026 HPE: AI Explainers Agentic AI The Future of the Datacenter AWS:Reinvent Nvidia GTC Computex 2026 AI Infrastructure Month 2026 The State of Storage 2026 RSA Conference Vendor Voice All Vendor Voice Modernizing Financial Services with FIS and AWS Barco Infinidat Everpure Rubrik Make it real with Capgemini and AWS Money Movement Hub ZTE Nutanix: Scale Kubernetes. Not Chaos. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters New regulator will require modelmakers to test and allow inspection, but not much more US bit barn boom sees energy needs grow 10x as fast as grid capacity 7 hours ago OpenAI builds a kill switch for its research models 19 hours ago Anthropic tiptoes into MS Office territory 1 day ago To thwart reverse engineering by agents, dev proposes blinding them 1 day ago 14-year-old creates tool for AI agents to band together like a team 1 day ago Australia’s government will consider creating a new criminal offense to punish AI companies which knowingly release harmful models. Canberra dangled that possibility yesterday when releasing the results of an investigation into OpenAI’s admission that its agents accessed non-public medical records – and that it didn’t disclose the incident for weeks. Security at the agency which held those records fell short of contemporary best practice but Canberra nonetheless ordered a rapid review into Australia’s ability to handle infosec incidents involving AI. That review landed yesterday, complete with 18 recommendations including one that would make it mandatory for AI companies to report misaligned behavior or security incidents involving their models, and perhaps impose criminal penalties for “egregious regulatory non-compliance.” Another recommendation calls for consideration of “A standalone ‘failure to prevent’ offence which would criminalize instances where the company is responsible for developing an AI model that engages in harmful conduct, and the company fails to take reasonable steps to prevent that harm.” The review suggests two ministries and Australia’s Federal Police consider those reforms, meaning this is not something that will happen in a hurry, if at all, for a couple of reasons. One is that Australia yesterday proposed a new regulator which will require AI players to do six things: Maintain security controls across all stages of development and deployment Identify and manage serious risks associated with their models Allow independent evaluation of their models Provide mandatory notification of incidents to the Australian Government rapidly Maintain and publish safety and security frameworks to ensure good governance, risk management and transparency Respond to updated standards and rules as technologies change. If AI companies straighten up and fly right, Canberra might not need to do more. The other reason Australia might not criminalize AI is economic pragmatism. Canberra wants to ensure leading AI companies invest in local datacenters, especially facilities where they train and run frontier models. Such investments would mean Australia scores some of the AI boom cash sloshing around the world, while also giving the government the ability to at least point to leading-edge AI running on local shores and therefore theoretically remaining accessible even if war or a diplomatic rupture makes it hard to access advanced AI hosted offshore. Other nations in Asia, such as South Korea and India, are addressing those risks by building substantial sovereign infrastructure and working to develop sovereign frontier-class models trained on local data and especially data in their local languages. Canberra can’t match that investment without pouring petrol on its raging inflation problem. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese is therefore instead trying to regulate AI without scaring away investment. Threatening to lock up AI executives is not likely to make them enthusiastic when asked to approve building datacenters down under. Some sections of Australia’s population won’t mind it if big tech doesn’t show up: Protests against datacenters are already widespread. Your correspondent recently spoke to the organizer of a protest group opposed to development of a new datacenter which is just three kilometers from four existing bit barns, one of which abuts a sizable apartment complex and has operated without incident or opposition for years.

events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts David Jones's receiver set to close 19 stores A retail analyst says David Jones has too many stores. ( ABC News: Fletcher Yeung ) Department store David Jones's receiver is set to close half of its 38 stores. The retailer was placed into voluntary administration less than a week ago, with McGrathNicol appointed as administrator. The affected stores are expected to close later in the year, with stock being discounted or sent to other locations. David Jones's receiver has confirmed it will close 19 of the retailer's 38 stores. ABC News has also seen correspondence sent to staff and suppliers confirming the store closures. The sites affected include a store in Sydney's Parramatta, three in Victoria and sites on the Gold Coast and Sunshine Coast in Queensland. New South Wales (7): Macquarie Centre, Macarthur Square, Parramatta, Wollongong Central, Hornsby, Green Hills and Warringah Mall Victoria (3): Malvern Central, Highpoint and Glen Waverley Western Australia (3): Hay Street Mall, Garden City and Carousel Queensland (2): Robina Town Centre and Sunshine Plaza South Australia (2): West Lakes and Marion Australian Capital Territory (1): Woden David Jones staff were sent a message this afternoon from chief executive Erica Berchtold about the "difficult news", which said a consultation period was about to begin for affected employees. "I know how much our stores and the people in them mean to all of us, and this is difficult news for our whole business," Ms Berchtold wrote. "We all know that the business could not continue operating as it was. In a letter to suppliers, David Jones said: "We expect the affected stores to continue trading through the peak seasonal period, with closure dates anticipated to occur later in the year." Stock at closing stores will be discounted or sent to other locations. Do you know more? Email our journalist on terzon.emilia@abc.net.au or em.terzon@proton.me Consumer experts have advised shoppers to be cautious about how they purchase items from David Jones amid the uncertainty . They said to prioritise going in-store to avoid the chance of something going wrong. There has been a surge in online orders since the receivership was announced and the David Jones website warns that "deliveries may take longer than usual". Common delivery options such as express, same day, Saturday delivery, and click and collect are unavailable. There are delays in the delivery of online orders. ( Supplied: David Jones ) The change-of-mind policy now says items purchased from November 7 must be exchanged within 14 days. Online purchases have an extra five days. Items purchased before November 7 have 30 days for an exchange. David Jones was placed in voluntary administration less than a week ago. McGrathNicol was appointed as the voluntary administrator, acting on behalf of all the entities owed cash from its creditors. Separately, FTI Consulting has been appointed as the receiver acting on behalf of David Jones's main secured lender, Hilco. The collapse of the 188-year-old department store comes after negations with major landlord Westfield broke down, with the retailer's owner, Scentre Group, confirming David Jones had not paid rent since September in breach of its contracts. Five outlets in Westfield shopping centres have already been flagged for closure due to them running at a loss, including Parramatta, Hornsby, Woden in Canberra, Carousel in Perth and Southland in Melbourne. Retail analyst Tom Kierath told ABC Business Daily that David Jones had "some wonderful sites", but it had too many. He said parties interested in buying the business would likely be eyeing a smaller store footprint. "I think the interest will be in a handful of sites rather than, necessarily the broader business," Mr Kierath, head of consumer research at Barrenjoey, said. "Obviously some of the restructuring that's going on at the moment … if it does come back, it will come back in a much smaller, slimline version of it current self." Analysts expect David Jones will focus on flagship stores such as Elizabeth Street in Sydney. ( ABC News: Fletcher Yeung ) Mr Kierath said there was a place for a new-look version of David Jones, potentially with a focus on flagship stores with an enhanced offering. "I think there's definitely a place for that, and with an enhanced food and beverage offering," he said. "People are spending more and more out, and if you can make your stores a desirable place to hang out and spend time and eat and drink, that's another part of the offer that they can have. "It probably needs to be reshaped a little bit.

events.title: Nvidia-backed CoreWeave targets 2028 profitability as AI demand surges
events.summary: CoreWeave, backed by chips giant Nvidia, has emerged as a focal point of growing AI bubble fears. CoreWeave said it expects adjusted profitability in the first half of 2028, backed by strong AI demand, US$132.5 billion (S$165.75 billion) backlog, and US$9 billion in prepayments. The Nvidia-backed firm has US$46.9 billion debt, plans under US$5 billion extra capital through 2027, and says customer contracts will help fund and repay borrowing. CoreWeave sees no major risk from US election changes to its data centre build-out, but expects more scrutiny, slower pacing, and continued high spending to meet demand. CoreWeave said on Nov 10 it would become profitable on an adjusted basis in the first half of 2028, as the AI cloud company sought to reassure investors that strong demand and customer commitments will support its debt-fuelled expansion. CoreWeave shares have crashed more than 40% in the past month after the firm emerged as the focal point of growing AI bubble fears , with investors worried about heavy borrowing for setting up data centres against the backdrop of rising interest rates and the pace of returns on the massive investments. The steep sell-off also triggered a broader crisis of confidence in the AI trade. Earlier in the day, AI juggernaut Anthropic kicked off a roadshow for its share sale at a lower target valuation than earlier estimates. Easing some jitters, CoreWeave said it would not tap unsecured debt markets at current yields and that it had enough cash flow from existing customer commitments to repay current debt and any additional borrowing needed to fulfil those contracts. CoreWeave had about US$46.9 billion ( S$60.09 billion ) in total debt as of the end of September. It expects to raise less than US$5 billion in additional capital through 2027. Chief executive officer Mike Intrator said the company had US$9 billion in customer prepayments and deposits that will flow in over the next three months. “Customer contracts come first, and investment follows. Because CoreWeave’s investments are tied to committed demand, lenders have something concrete to lend against and customers typically help fund the build-out,” he said in a statement. CoreWeave’s revenue backlog stood at US$132.5 billion at September-end, rising from US$104 billion at the end of June. At the same time, its quarterly capital spending jumped to US$14.5 billion from US$9.4 billion in the prior quarter. That spending is necessary to bring capacity online to meet the surging demand, CoreWeave said, as it is largely sold out of capacity through the next year , with about 10 times as much demand as available capacity. No impact expected from changes in political landscape Investors have been worried about tech companies’ data centre expansion plans as they prepare for a tougher regulatory environment after the Democratic win in the midterm elections. Public backlash has already been growing in the US around data centres’ impact on local resources including water and power . “There is going to be a lot more scrutiny on how you build, how you use resources... But I don’t think it’s going to require a material change in how we go about building our infrastructure. I don’t think it’s going to materially distort the costs of the build-out,” Intrator told Reuters in an interview. “I do think that there is going to be a pacing issue, as people need to be more transparent and work through the process with the communities and that’s going to be prevalent across the industry. But that’s how we’ve done it historically and it has been a hallmark of how we’ve built our data centres.” Intrator said that CoreWeave will not ramp up international expansion plans because of the election results. “This is not a new strategy that you’ve got us building into as a reaction to the elections. This is something that we have been working at diligently for a year and a half already,” he said. CoreWeave now expects 2026 revenue to be between US$13 billion and US$13.3 billion, from US$12.4 billion to US$13.2 billion earlier. It also lifted the lower end of its annual spending target by US$2 billion, now projecting spending of US$37 billion to US$39 billion. CoreWeave’s third-quarter revenue surged nearly 170% to US$3.66 billion, beating estimates of US$3.55 billion, while a per-share loss of 95 US cents came in smaller than estimates for a US$1.16 loss, according to data from LSEG. events.title: Sony bets on home-grown anime to fuel decades of future growth
events.summary: The first instalment of Demon Slayer’s Infinity Castle trilogy grossed about US$800 million worldwide in 2025. Sony is investing heavily in anime to drive long-term growth and shift from hardware to valuable IP, using hits like Demon Slayer to build lasting franchises. The company is expanding through Crunchyroll, Aniplex, Kadokawa and new studio Hayate, while also exploring more M&A and wider uses such as games, music, live events and theme parks. Sony faces a shortage of skilled animators and slower production, so it is training talent and using technology carefully, with Iwakami saying AI should support creators, not replace them. TOKYO – From the Walkman and PlayStation to Spider-Man’s box office records, Sony Group has shown a knack for shaping global pop culture hits. Now in the midst of a strategic transition, the company is pouring time and money into a home-grown genre with the potential to power growth for decades to come: anime. After turning Demon Slayer: Kimetsu No Yaiba into a global phenomenon, the company is working to seed or acquire the next anime blockbuster. Some 80 years into its history, Sony is determined to create franchises that will last about as long. The US$28 billion (S$35 billion) anime industry is one of the fastest-growing genres of entertainment globally. For Sony, it is a key part of a broader shift away from relying on physical hardware like the PlayStation console and towards intellectual property (IP) and content. Much as with beloved game characters transcending their original format, hit anime franchises become gold mines not only for viewership but also for merchandise, music and live experiences. “With Demon Slayer, it is our intent to make this last 10 or 20, if not 50 to 100 years,” Atsuhiro Iwakami, president of Sony Music Entertainment Japan and chairman of Aniplex, Sony’s anime production company, said in an interview. He points to Dragon Ball and One Piece, stories that have survived long enough to pass from parents to children and which Sony has rights to stream internationally. “We want to make sure we’re part of creating the type of franchise that can withstand decades.” Tokyo-based Sony has turned anime into a scalable business in recent years, with acquisitions of services like Crunchyroll, now the world’s largest streaming platform dedicated to the genre. It has become a go-to destination for fans, who have grown from a niche group to a much larger contingent with the help of various celebrities and music artistes embracing the genre. The proof of the concept for Sony came with the Demon Slayer saga, depicting the adventures of a young swordsman battling demons while trying to restore his cursed sister to human form. Its 2020 movie, Mugen Train, became Japan’s highest-grossing film, dethroning Studio Ghibli’s 2001 classic Spirited Away. Five years later, the first instalment of Demon Slayer’s Infinity Castle trilogy grossed about US$800 million worldwide, demonstrating that a franchise born from Japanese manga could become a global theatrical blockbuster. The distinctly Japanese aesthetic and storytelling style, far from hampering international appeal, was a big part of the attraction. At the centre of Sony’s push to do more with anime is Iwakami, who has been with Aniplex since its inception and has helped shape its trajectory over almost three decades. He is part of the strategic collaboration inside Sony to turn Aniplex and Crunchyroll into a complementary duo, where one produces and the other distributes original content. Iwakami’s defining bet was to combine the visual craftsmanship of ufotable, a studio known for spectacular anime aimed at what he calls “geeks or nerds”, with the mass appeal of manga from Weekly Shonen Jump. That experiment delivered Demon Slayer. The underlying Demon Slayer IP still belongs to Japan’s century-old manga publisher Shueisha, whose titles also include One Piece, Dragon Ball and Naruto. Asked whether Sony might invest in closely held Shueisha to gain greater access to its rich IP, Iwakami left the possibility open. “Perhaps, if the opportunity presents itself,” he said. Japanese entertainment companies are often competitors and collaborators at the same time, making takeover deals complicated. “So it’s not necessarily the case that just because we want to buy something, we can actually make that happen,” Iwakami said. “But if timing and chance align, we would certainly be open to entertaining different types of M&A.” Sony is taking steps toward becoming an IP powerhouse. In 2025, it became the largest shareholder in Kadokawa, owner of a vast library of manga, novels and games. It is also trying to create more IP from scratch. Securing the franchises and storylines that build enduring appeal is becoming increasingly competitive as streaming giants such as Netflix and Walt Disney also compete for anime licensing deals.

events.title: See which incomes are hit hardest by tax bracket creep
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Bracket creep worst for minimum wage earners and those entering top bracket New analysis reveals the taxpayers hit hardest by bracket creep. ( ABC ) New analysis shows people who earn about $45,000 or $190,000 are penalised the most by bracket creep. The federal opposition has promised to index income tax brackets and end bracket creep. Economist Saul Eslake said he supported the idea in principle but was doubtful spending could be cut to offset it. Workers who earn the minimum wage and those who are on the cusp of the top tax bracket are the hardest hit by bracket creep, according to new research. The federal opposition wants to stamp out the longstanding feature of Australia's tax system, where people see larger proportions of their incomes taxed over time. It occurs because tax brackets do not move with inflation, so people "creep" into higher brackets. Analysis by the e61 Institute and economist Richard Holden has found that workers earning about $45,000 and those earning about $190,000 are penalised the most by bracket creep, largely because their incomes are on the cusp of higher brackets. Over a decade from 2028, someone who currently earns $45,000 would face an increase of more than five percentage points in their average tax rate. This level is close to the full-time minimum wage, although many part-timers also earn in this range. Over the same period, someone who currently earns $190,000 would face an increase of more than four percentage points. In both of these cases, more than half of a person's real income growth would be taxed. While those two groups are the worst affected, the vast majority of taxpayers would face a hike of at least two percentage points and see at least a quarter of their real income growth taxed. "Taxing workers more without explicit policy change is neither an equitable nor a credible mechanism for [raising revenue]," e61 chief executive Michael Brennan said. "The tax increase falls unevenly across the income distribution." Budget claims of 'return to surplus' rely on bracket creep In practice, the scenario e61 uses is unlikely to play out because it assumes there are no income tax cuts for a full decade. As history shows, governments almost always cut taxes every few years, often close to elections, "handing back" some or all of the bracket creep. Over several decades, these tax cuts have served to keep average tax rates broadly stable, albeit in an irregular and uneven way. But the authors note that this same unlikely assumption is used in the government's own budget projections, helping successive treasurers to claim that the budget is on track to return to surplus, when this would not be true without bracket creep. Analysis by the independent Parliamentary Budget Office shows the budget would have a deficit equivalent to 0.7 per cent of GDP (the size of the economy) by the end of the decade without bracket creep, contrary to the official projection of a 1 per cent surplus. "Bracket creep should not be treated as a serious long-run funding strategy," the authors wrote. "Fiscal projections that implicitly assume it will repair the budget are not credible." Coalition bid to index tax brackets Opposition Leader Angus Taylor has pledged to index tax brackets to inflation if elected, phased in over two years from 2028. The proposal would result in bracket creep being paid back to taxpayers as a lump sum at the end of each tax year, based on the level of inflation. The opposition said the budgetary cost of the tax cuts could be met in the first three years by its proposed cuts to Labor's climate and housing policies and industry subsidies, and by scrapping Labor's $250 tax offset for wage earners. Over the longer term, Mr Taylor has suggested the cost to the budget would be met by limiting government spending, prompting accusations from Labor that the Coalition would be forced into unspecified and damaging spending cuts to fund its plans. Economist Saul Eslake told the ABC that, while he supported indexing tax brackets in principle and that doing so would impose greater honesty on governments, he was doubtful governments could find the spending cuts to balance it out. "I don't believe what the Coalition says about how much they're going to save over time. It's been evident since Josh Frydenberg's last budget that government spending was set to be higher than the average which had prevailed for decades," he said. "That's for three reasons. The public clearly wants more aged, disability and health care … and there's a bipartisan consensus that whether the public wants it or not, they're going to get more spending on defence.

events.title: "Rome is burning": Incoming House Democrats prove unusually willing to defy leaders
events.summary: House Democrats' incoming freshman class is barely a week old and already threatening to defy party leaders in ways most of their incumbent colleagues wouldn't dare. Why it matters: It's a dynamic House leaders may have to learn to live with as they integrate a massive group of new members who were swept into office on a wave of populist, anti-establishment anger. "My class is huge not because of ... the Democratic Party and its brand but despite it," said Rep.-elect Don Leonard (D-Ohio). "Many of us are outsiders who didn't come up through the machine, don't buy into the conventions." Congressional Progressive Caucus chair Greg Casar (D-Texas) told Axios: "Any members that are new and have just run their elections are going to be very close to where the voters are, and we know the voters are very upset." State of play: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) is on track to become speaker, in part thanks to his rock-solid support among sitting House Democrats. His supporters include high-profile progressives such as Casar and Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.), Pramila Jayapal (D-Wash.) and Ro Khanna (D-Calif.). "There is one candidate in this race, Hakeem Jeffries, and I think that everyone is far more concerned about what that leadership means, what is it promising," Ocasio-Cortez told reporters on Tuesday. Things get more spotty when gauging Jeffries' support among incoming freshmen, some of whom have openly declined to commit to supporting his leadership. That includes members of the informal progressive "Bloc," including Reps.-elect Darializa Avila Chevalier (D-N.Y.), Melat Kiros (D-Colo.), Claire Valdez (D-N.Y.), Adam Hamawy (D-N.J.) and Chris Rabb (D-Pa.). "As far as I've heard, Jeffries is the only one running," said progressive Rep.-elect Randy Villegas (D-Calif.). "But ... I think we need to see some prioritization of some legislation, particularly around health care, foreign policy and immigration." Some incoming and sitting House Democrats have been flooded with calls and emails urging them not to elect Jeffries speaker, Axios previously reported . The intrigue: It's not just progressives hesitating to throw their full-throated support behind Jeffries. The list also includes some moderates in districts President Trump carried by double digits in 2024. Said Rep.-elect Teresa Benitez-Thompson (D-Nev.), a member of the center-left New Democrat Coalition: "I just won a district that went for Trump two years ago by 14%. … I've got to turn around and show that we're making change." "For anyone running for speaker, that's my message back to them," she added. "It's much more about, like, what can you do for Nevada?" "I'd like to see who's on the ballot," said Rep.-elect Jake Johnson (D-Minn.), a member of both the New Dems and the centrist Blue Dogs. "Until I've had an opportunity to chat, until I've had an opportunity to see who's out there, I'm not making any decisions." Yes, but: Plenty of freshmen are supporting Jeffries as well. Well-represented in that contingent are incoming members who ran in marquee races with substantial backing from House Democrats' campaign apparatus, including Reps.-elect Marni von Wilpert (D-Calif.), Manny Rutinel (D-Colo.), Denise Powell (D-Neb.), Cait Conley (D-N.Y.) and Rebecca Bennett (D-N.J.). Rep.-elect Zack Mullock (D-N.J.), who didn't have support from the national party, told Axios he is "not making many big splashes" as a new member: "You're going to have pretty strong support for Hakeem, and I'll be part of that support." Zoom in: Several members, such as Leonard and Rep.-elect Richard Ojeda (D-N.C.), have said they want to see Jeffries commit to a ban on corporate PACs as a prerequisite for voting for him. "We need a 28th Amendment in the year 2028 or before to shut down Elon Musk and corporate money and Israeli lobby money, for that matter," Leonard said. Said Ojeda: "I have hard lines: I want to make sure that we are making sure we are getting big money out of politics. It's time for us to stop allowing the billionaire class to buy our elections." The bottom line: Leonard said it "aches" his heart to potentially oppose the first Black speaker of the House, but that "Rome is burning." The Ohio Democrat said he needs to be able to tell his districts "the leader shares our sense of urgency for transformational change and is willing to take the size of his caucus and take it for a spin."

events.title: X launches its own clipping feature to spur influencer engagement
events.summary: Over the past few years, X has released a number of features to make itself a friendlier hub for influencers. The latest effort to attract social media talent? Its own clipping tool. Clipping is the pivotal social media technique by which longer videos are spliced into TikTok-attention-span length “clips” and then strategically posted to engage as many eyeballs (and thus derive as much ad revenue) as possible. On Monday, X announced the tool, which, from what we can tell, appears to be little more than a straightforward video-trimming feature that lets users edit videos and post them to X. The site says that every clip includes a “Clip from” label that links back to the original video from which it was derived, allowing X users to see more about the creator and the creator’s content. “Grab your favorite moment from any video, add your take, and post it without leaving X,” the company posted . The platform added that both creators and clippers can “earn from views on the clip through Original Content Rewards,” X’s rewards program . The program is only available for eligible creators and pays out based on specific levels of audience engagement. In many cases, influencers pay special firms to handle clipping for them. More and more large companies are also turning to such services to run marketing campaigns, and the technique has been used in political campaigns as well . Over the last several years, X has tried to compete with other social sites by expanding the kind of content it supports. To take on sites like YouTube, X introduced long-form videos in 2022 (when the site was still known as Twitter), and they have since taken off on the platform. To be more like Substack, it long ago dispensed with the site’s traditional character limits and introduced long-form blog posts , which are available to premium subscribers. X has kept at it this year. In March, it added a feature called “ exclusive threads ” that lets creators put parts of a thread behind a paywall so only subscribers can read them, and in July it launched a livestreaming studio and set aside $1 million for creators who go live. events.title: Singaporeans want to invest more, but life’s financial demands hold them back: Survey
events.summary: When it comes to investing, Singaporeans take a more measured approach, with stability as their top priority. More than half prefer to put their money in fixed deposits. SINGAPORE – Singaporeans are more likely to ramp up investing after they get their first full-time job than their peers in Hong Kong and Australia, but major life expenses, such as buying a first home, can slow their investing momentum as they shift their focus towards financial security. A new survey found that 65% of Singaporeans who cited their first job as their biggest financial milestone invested more later, compared with 49% in Hong Kong and 42% in Australia. The survey was commissioned by digital wealth management platform Syfe and conducted by YouGov among 1,212 adults in Singapore, as part of a wider study of 3,315 respondents across Singapore, Hong Kong and Australia in late September and early October 2026. The survey showed a desire to invest: About 50% of respondents in Singapore and Hong Kong want to invest more than they do now, while the number is higher in Australia at 61%. As Singaporeans enter their 30s, 40s and 50s, their financial priorities become more complicated as buying a home or raising children can add considerable pressure on household finances. Across the three markets surveyed, 54% reduced their investments after purchasing their first home, while 50% did so after having their first child. In Singapore and Hong Kong, supporting ageing parents adds another financial responsibility. All respondents cited the fear of losing money as their biggest hurdle to investing, followed by insufficient funds and a lack of investment knowledge. For Singaporeans, stability is their top investment priority, and they place less weight on growth than investors in Hong Kong or Australia. That preference has shaped how Singaporeans plan to invest. Among those who put stability first, 54% are likely to put their money in fixed deposits, while 40% prefer equities. For those who prioritise growth, 61% are likely to invest in equities. Singaporeans in the 25 to 34 age group are more likely to prioritise growth over stability, but only 13% of those aged 55 and over put growth first. Singaporean women are less likely than men to rank growth as their first investment priority. One of the more striking findings is the decline in investment confidence among older Singaporeans. Unlike Hong Kong, where confidence is highest among those aged above 55, Singapore and Australia show the opposite pattern. In Singapore, 40% of those aged 18 to 24 said they were extremely or very confident about making investment decisions. The proportion fell to just 12% among those aged above 55. The gender divide is also pronounced. Singapore recorded the widest investment confidence gap among the three markets. While 35% of men said they were extremely or very confident about investment decisions, only 13% of women felt the same. Women were also twice as likely as men not to invest, at 32% against 15%. They tend to worry about losing money and fear a lack of investing knowledge. Among Singaporeans who already invest, men are also more confident than women. As retirement approaches, the focus shifts from accumulating wealth to ensuring that savings can support a longer period of financial independence. Yet many Singaporeans appear uncertain about how much they actually need. The survey found that 76% of respondents here believed their retirement savings were below what they expected to need. More concerningly, a third had never calculated their retirement savings target, while 40% have a retirement plan or simply picked a round number that felt right. How people set their target matters, the Syfe report said. Those who picked a round number aim lower than those who worked it out. In Singapore, those who picked a round number have a median target of $700,000 to $999,999. This compares to $1 million to $1.99 million for those who based their target on their expenses. Hong Kong and Australia show the same pattern. The average retirement savings across all sources, including CPF, rise with age. Gen Z – or those 14 to 29 years old – have an average of $61,000 in savings, compared with $192,000 among millennials (aged 30-45), and $455,000 among baby boomers (62 to 80 years old) and older. Only 15 per cent of Singaporeans were working towards a traditional full retirement. The most popular aspiration was semi-retirement, at 27 per cent, while 13 per cent said they did not plan to retire at all. This reflects changing attitudes towards retirement, with many expecting to continue working in some capacity rather than stop earning altogether. Having a financial plan appears to make a difference to confidence. Singaporeans with a retirement plan were nearly twice as likely to feel confident about investing as those without one, at 32% versus 17%.

events.summary: OpenAI has regained momentum with competitive new AI models, aggressive price cuts and a greater focus on AI agents to help customers automate work. OpenAI’s Q3 revenue hit US$10 billion for the first time, up nearly 50% from the previous quarter and almost three times a year earlier, driven by demand for new AI software. The ChatGPT maker has regained momentum with new models, lower prices and AI agents that help customers automate work, while Anthropic’s growth has slowed. OpenAI is raising funds at a US$1.25 trillion valuation and has delayed any public listing until 2027, as rival Anthropic targets a US$1.4 trillion debut. NEW YORK – OpenAI’s quarterly revenue hit US$10 billion (S$12.8 billion) for the first time in the three months ending in September, according to a person familiar with the matter, driven by strong demand for its latest artificial intelligence software. The ChatGPT maker’s revenue increased nearly 50% from the prior quarter and nearly threefold from the same period a year earlier, said the person, who spoke on condition of anonymity as the information is not public. The financial details were shared with investors during a call on Nov 10. After slipping behind long-time rival Anthropic in 2026 by some measures, OpenAI has regained momentum with competitive new AI models, aggressive price cuts and a greater focus on AI agents to help customers automate work. OpenAI’s business has shown signs of accelerating at a moment when Anthropic’s revenue growth has begun to slow somewhat. Anthropic, which is nearing a landmark Wall Street debut, reported third-quarter revenue of about US$17 billion. The rate of growth from the second quarter slowed to around 47%, compared with a more than 140% increase in the previous quarter. (OpenAI and Anthropic have historically calculated revenue figures differently.) OpenAI is in the process of completing a new round of funding at a US$1.25 trillion valuation after delaying plans to go public until 2027. OpenAI recently completed an initial US$11 billion part of that round, Bloomberg News previously reported. Anthropic is targeting a US$1.4 trillion valuation for its public listing later in November. events.title: Robot vessels take on the dangerous work of mine hunting
events.summary: This South Korean vessel is among the ships damaged in the Strait of Hormuz Traversing the Strait of Hormuz remains one of the most dangerous trips a vessel can take. Despite assistance from the US Navy, ships are still being attacked . "To transit the Strait of Hormuz you need agreement between the captain and the crew to take the risk. You need war risk insurance. And the captain has to make the final decision," says Steve Cameron, a former merchant navy officer and maritime consultant. Missiles and drones are a threat from the air, but under the surface mines may also be lurking. "If you're a captain, you'd like to see evidence mines aren't present," Cameron adds. Modern mines rest on the seabed and detonate when they detect an acoustic or magnetic signal, triggering a pressure wave that will break the keel of a passing vessel. Others can rise through shallow waters or float, or be powered towards a target. The technology itself is not difficult or costly, but the mere threat can stop a tanker fleet from sailing. Ian McFarlane of French defence group Thales is a naval architect who knows mine warfare well. "Mines are a very cheap way of waging a naval war, as the Royal Navy is acutely aware," he says. Finding sea mines has traditionally been the job of specialist mine-hunting vessels, with crews of around 80 sailors. To keep humans out of harm's way, an increasing amount of the work is done by systems that are autonomous and monitored from the shore. They might only need 20 personnel, working in shifts on land. With the recruitment and retention challenges facing Nato navies these highly-portable robot systems are very attractive. Such tech has been under development for 20 years. During the 2003 Iraq war the US Navy poked around the seabed looking for mines with a torpedo-shaped robot called the Remus 100. Pinging around with sonar these little machines operated down to around 100ft depth and spared divers a difficult and dangerous task. Iran's military published this picture of a US submersible captured in the Gulf The latest conflict in the Gulf is testing much more capable systems. The US military is sparing with details about their mine-hunting craft, but we have seen glimpses of them. Iranian forces hauled an uncrewed US autonomous sub , external out of the waters of the Strait of Hormuz in early September. The Pentagon claimed this robot, an Extra Large Uncrewed Underwater Vehicle (XLUUV) from US autonomous defence tech venture Anduril, was a malfunctioning older device with no classified equipment on-board. Whatever its mission, no sailors were imperilled. That, says William Lupton, a naval analyst with Shephard Group, "was a drop in the ocean compared to having prisoners taken", and part of the point of uncrewed vessels. What if an uncrewed vessel is captured? Nato navies are reluctant to go into details, but computer drives can be wiped or destroyed remotely by various means. This may have taken place inside the humming circuit boards of the XLUUV seized by Iran. The Thales Uncrewed Surface Vehicle is packed with sensors Such autonomous tech is being embraced by forces around the world. Cooperation between Thales, the Royal Navy, and France's Marine Nationale has produced a robot motor launch. The Thales Uncrewed Surface Vehicle (USV) is packed with sensors programmed to detect mines via sonar that was developed for the oil and gas industries. It tows a 5m long rectangular box, similar to a large torpedo, that takes a hi-resolution look at the seabed and creates a 3D picture refined by AI. The latest mines are designed to blend into their surroundings and the software spots anything that looks like a mine. Autonomous systems are cheaper than conventional minehunters, plus they can be deployed, along with containerised control centres, by air. Steve Prest, associate fellow at the RUSI defence think tank, introduced uncrewed mine hunting into the Royal Navy and was its first fleet robotics officer, a title he acquired in 2014. "There is a bunch of ways to look for a mine using robot boats or robot subs, and while you can't prove the negative, that no mines are there, you can reduce the risk." He says US robot minehunters can either blow up a mine or just mark the spot as somewhere to avoid. "We'll see more use of autonomy but also the missions and capability will expand. And AI will be analysing data from those vessels on the spot as opposed to data being analysed when a drone returns." The Royal Navy recently announced its concept of a hybrid navy - mixing drones with conventional warships. But Prest thinks for this vision to succeed the fleet must operate as one distributed force, sharing data in what he terms a cognitive architecture. The robot only makes a real difference as part of this scheme and it's a mistake to focus on individual uncrewed assets. "Uncrewed or autonomous vessels are not the operating system. They are applications running on it.

events.title: Scoop: Commerce Department received national security warning on Nvidia CEO affair
events.summary: Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick was sent a highly classified memo warning about Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's relationship with suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang, multiple sources familiar told Axios. Why it matters: Lutnick oversees the agency charged with keeping sensitive U.S. technology out of the hands of American adversaries. The warning raises questions about how the department weighed potential security risks as it cleared advanced Nvidia chip sales to China-affiliated entities. Driving the news : Secretary of State Marco Rubio oversaw the drafting of the memo detailing Huang's relationship with Alice Huang, who U.S. intelligence officials believe is a Chinese intelligence agent, according to The New York Times. The memo, which drew on surveillance of Alice Huang and a chip-smuggling investigation into her company, Megaspeed, circulated before President Trump's trip to May 13–15 trip to China. Rubio also warned Trump directly aboard Air Force One before a refueling stop in Anchorage where Jensen Huang joined the delegation. He hadn't initially been invited to participate, the Times reported Tuesday . On May 14, Reuters reported that the Commerce Department had cleared around 10 Chinese companies to purchase Nvidia's H200 chips. Some export approvals predated the warning. Nvidia disclosed in February it had received an H200 export license, and Huang told Axios' Ina Fried in March the company had licenses covering Chinese customers. Yes, but : It's unclear how those approvals ultimately translated into sales, as China's government has halted some chip-buying activity in spite of U.S. approvals. Megaspeed purchased billions of dollars' worth of Nvidia chips, according to multiple media outlets. What they're saying : Trump said on Monday that it was possible intelligence officials had shown it to him, but he didn't recall: "Certainly, it didn't make much of an impact on me." The Commerce Department did not comment. Catch up quick : Nvidia has been rocked by the scandal , losing about $1 trillion in market value since the Times' first reported the relationship, although some of that decline also came after an overwhelming number of Democrats promising to slow an AI data-center buildout were elected in the midterms. Huang acknowledged an affair Sunday , and Nvidia's board announced an independent investigation. The board expressed confidence in his leadership and said it had no reason to believe national security secrets were compromised. What to watch : New revelations continue to drop almost daily about the administration's handling of the Nvidia CEO's relationship. Lawmakers in both parties have promised investigations and demanded more information, including closed-door testimony from Jensen Huang next week. Top Democrats on the House Foreign Affairs committee have also demanded answers from Lutnick about the administration's chip approvals, "including to companies with concerning links to China and amid alarming reports of potential Chinese intelligence ties to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang."

AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Sheets, Whiteboards, and Data artifact types bring Claude closer to a productivity suite US bit barn boom sees energy needs grow 10x as fast as grid capacity 5 hours ago Microsoft's Patch Tuesday can't break stuff if it won't install 8 hours ago Google gooses Python AI performance by... removing Python 11 hours ago OpenAI builds a kill switch for its research models 17 hours ago Australia may make knowingly selling unsafe AI a crime 20 hours ago Anthropic has introduced three new types of artifacts that show the company tiptoeing into the office productivity market long dominated by Microsoft and Google. On Tuesday, the Claudefather announced Claude Sheets, Claude Whiteboards, and Claude Data, and promised the imminent arrival of Claude Meetings. These artifact types join existing ones – Docs, Slides, Design, and Motion – to form a nascent Claude-dependent productivity suite. Anthropic initially used the term artifacts to refer to shareable AI-based interactive tools, like dynamic charts. But the scope of the term has been stretched to cover specific artifact types, which refer to what traditionalists might take to mean files associated with specific hosted applications. "An artifact is anything Claude makes for you that you'd put in front of someone: a design, a deck, a document, a dashboard, or a small interactive tool," the company explains. The key thing that distinguishes an artifact from a file is that users are meant to interact with artifacts through Claude, rather than storing and transferring them independently. Think of it more as a container or managed object that opens in Claude (via a sharing URL), because artifacts in fact consist of various content types – .txt, .md, .html, .jsx, .svg, .pptx, .docx, .zip, .pdf, and .mp4, among others. Anthropic's vision of Claude as a container for other applications goes beyond artifacts. The AI biz has also expanded its interactive connectors , which turn Claude into a landlord for other software applications. Its own promotional video for the feature hammers that point home in its title: " Your apps have moved into Claude ." "Starting today, partners can embed their apps directly in Claude, so you can work in Adobe, Atlassian, and others without switching tabs," Anthropic said. "Plugins from Salesforce (beta), NetSuite, and Workday (beta) come with built-in skills, so sellers can prep for a call, accountants can analyze financial data, and HR teams can handle time off and expenses." In a prior era, those would be fighting words. Tech companies like Apple, Google, and Microsoft have worked for years to maintain their positions as platform landlords. Anthropic's invitation to become a Claude tenant ought to set off competition alarm bells. But perhaps with LLMs being able to re-create other people's apps on demand, there's less interest in defending app boundaries as if they were moats to keep out rivals. With AI, the call is coming from inside the house. Alongside the rollout of Claude Sheets, Whiteboards, and Data, Anthropic is pushing the notion that Claude is useful for people working outside of computation and mathematics, the occupational category that, according to the company's own data , accounts for a larger share of Claude usage than any other. "Inside Anthropic, non-technical teams are starting to get as much out of Claude as our engineers," the biz insists, hauling out canned testimonials from the likes of Accenture and Datadog. If Anthropic can demonstrate that there's an untapped market of non-coders who would welcome a Claude subscription, investors in the company's pending IPO will be glad to see it.

events.title: Trump swung between war and diplomacy — then chose a third way
events.summary: When Secretary of State Marco Rubio met with his G7 counterparts in Paris on Tuesday, he told them that President Trump had considered resuming the war with Iran or cutting a deal — but chose a third option: strangling the Iranian regime, three people who attended the meeting told Axios. Why it matters: The Iran war has become a political albatross in Trump's second term, costing Republicans dearly in the midterms. For months, the president has alternated between threatening to obliterate Iran and predicting it will capitulate and give him the deal he wants. "He's been searching for the solution, but he wasn't sure what's the best way to go," a U.S. official close to Trump said. This debate over which course to follow has led to strife between several factions within the top echelon of the administration. Each faction had the support of U.S. allies in the Middle East — namely Israel favoring renewed strikes and most Gulf countries opposing them. Driving the news: After meeting with the Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani on Monday, Trump said that a new round of strikes against Iran is "quite unlikely" and "doesn't seem to be necessary." Trump said he instead favors continuing the economic crackdown and naval blockade against Iran, in addition to a new operation dubbed "Iron Gate" to cut off land routes that Iran uses to move advanced weaponry and other technology. Behind the scenes: Rubio explained the U.S. Iran policy in a closed meeting on Tuesday with the foreign ministers of the G7 countries in Paris. "The President doesn't just have two options. It's not just return to war or sign a ridiculous peace deal. We won't do a stupid deal. The third option we have is to continue to do what we do now," Rubio said, according to three people in the room. Rubio went on to say that the U.S. is imposing devastating costs on Iran's economy, making it harder for it to fund terrorist organizations or rebuild its military. And there's no end date. "The President is not under false time pressure, the Iranians are inflicting major damage on their own economy," Rubio said. The intrigue: U.S. officials say that Rubio was among the members of Trump's national security team who pushed for the strangulation strategy, along with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, CIA Director John Ratcliffe and Jared Kushner, Trump's adviser and son-in-law. That group opposed the resumption of war, didn't believe Iran's current positions could lead to a deal that serves U.S. interests and lobbied for the third option. State of play: Rubio is deeply skeptical of a diplomatic breakthrough. " Iran would love a deal. The problem is the conditions they continue to place are absurd. Like, they're not even serious right now," he told reporters after the G7 meeting. That could change if the Iranians feel more economic pain, he said. "Eventually you have to eat," he said. "Eventually the economic realities penetrate the skull of even the most radical lunatic. So I think as time goes on that will have an impact." Yes, but: Several U.S. allies — such as Turkey, Iraq and Pakistan — are concerned about Trump's intention to prolong the economic squeeze, a U.S. official said. The person said those allies worry that U.S. pressure on them to stop doing business with Iran — including by stopping flights and closing their borders — will create instability in their own countries. The other side: The course Trump has chosen is completely at odds with the directive Iran's Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei gave his government and the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. Khamenei ordered an end to the "no war, no deal" status quo, demanding a clear conclusion to the war. Iran's civilian leadership interpreted this as a green light to negotiate a deal. But if the current stalemate continues and pressure on Iran intensifies, the IRGC could see it as a green light for more aggressive attacks in the region in an attempt to break the status quo. "Iran has no intention of simply accepting this situation indefinitely," said Danny Citrinowicz, an expert on Iran at the Atlantic Council. "Tehran may conclude that increasing the economic and security costs for Washington and its regional partners is the only way to force a change in American policy." He added: "The danger is obvious: Iran escalates, Washington responds, and both sides find themselves in another military confrontation that neither necessarily wanted." What to watch: Qatar's prime minister briefed the G7 meeting on mediation efforts and his conversation with Trump the previous day. Al Thani said he came away from his meeting with Trump believing there's more breathing room for diplomatic efforts. The sticking points remain which side will take the first step toward de-escalating and which confidence-building measures the parties will agree to take. The Qatari prime minister said he wants to bring in China and European countries as guarantors, to help ease deep Iranian suspicions that Trump will break the agreement and resume the war in a few months.

AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Newer server processors pack more cores into fewer boxes, creating a need for network speed AMD: Where we're going we don't need (as much) DRAM 15 hours ago VMware floats new standard to make sure apps don’t break in hybrid K8s environments 1 day ago AMD winds up Zen 6 cores for faster clock speeds 1 day ago AMD's Epyc X-chips are back after a three-year hiatus 1 day ago A closer look at Verano, AMD's first step toward a Zen-based superchip to rival Nvidia's Vera Rubin 1 day ago Server consolidation has led Cisco to boost the speed of top-of-rack switches to 100G. The networking giant last week announced the catchily named N9348C8D-H2, a 1U device packing 48 100G SFP-DD ports and eight 400G QSFP-DD uplinks. At the Cisco Live event in Melbourne, Australia, this week, Cisco’s senior veep for datacenter and internet infrastructure, Kevin Wollenweber, said one reason the company created the device is that modern servers often feature a pair of fast network interface cards. The twin cards are needed because sixth-gen server processors from Intel and AMD offer dozens, or even hundreds, of physical processor cores and therefore generate a lot of traffic. The density of computing power those processors provide has led chipmakers and server manufacturers to suggest replacing handfuls of machines running older, power-guzzling Xeons and Epycs with boxes running more efficient sixth-gen chips. The Register hears it’s not uncommon to achieve 6:1 server consolidation ratios when moving from third- or fourth-generation Xeons or Epycs to current models. Users who make that move can pack many more server cores into the same rack. Power bills go down, but the quantity of data leaving a rack goes up. Wollenweber said Cisco realized it had “tons” of switches that offer 25G ports but felt it had a gap in its range for non-AI scenarios like server consolidation that produced increased data flows. The exec admitted that the 100G ports may be overkill for a modest collection of new servers, but argued users recognize it won’t be long before they grow into the excess capacity – perhaps as they use more agentic AI applications. Cisco sees traffic from AI agents stressing the north-south connections that link organizations to the cloud and also driving much more east-west traffic across internal networks. At Cisco Live, the company’s execs suggested that network upgrades are therefore an inevitable necessity. That’s not entirely self-serving, because agents will vastly outnumber humans and constantly create traffic, compared to the flurries of network activity that happen when humans use generative AI or chatbots. Cisco argues that deploying agents at scale will therefore only be possible on highly automated networks. “Humans can no longer comprehend the amount of data that we actually have in a network,” Wollenweber told The Register . Cisco’s Canvas agentic operations platform aims to at least make humans aware when their attention is needed, by detecting problems and offering to make repairs. Joe Vaccaro, Cisco’s senior vice president and general manager for Network Platform and Assurance, told The Register he believes network administrators don’t feel threatened by suggestions from AI agents when they concern familiar, routine, low-risk tasks that IT pros are confident the agents can handle. Over time, he said, networking pros will learn to trust agents with more complex work.

events.title: GOP House rejects Hegseth impeachment effort
events.summary: House Republicans voted Tuesday evening to block an effort to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth , shielding a top Trump administration official from a politically embarrassing rebuke. Why it matters: The vote marks a victory for Hegseth, the Trump administration and Republican leaders, who were bracing for the prospect of a rebellion within their own ranks. But the reprieve is probably short-lived: Democrats are all but guaranteed to force the issue again when they retake majorities in the House and Senate in January. The vote to refer the impeachment measure back to committee passed 211-204, with Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.), the measure's sponsor, the lone GOP "no" vote. Driving the news: Massie forced a procedural vote on his resolution to impeach Hegseth, alleging he has defied Congress and illegally continued the U.S. war in Iran. The Trump administration has been vehemently defending Hegseth , including through a statement opposing the impeachment effort issued shortly before the vote. "Has Pete Hegseth committed impeachable crimes? The question is absurd and the answer is: obviously not," Vance said Tuesday on X . "Like so much of Congress , impeachment has become a ridiculous show that stands in for actual policymaking. Congress has so many tools for registering its policy disagreements," Vance added. Axios' Marc Caputo and Alex Isenstadt previously reported that Hegseth is on " thin ice " with Trump officials. Between the lines : Republican leaders protected their members from having to go on record on the politically difficult issue before Election Day after Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) sent lawmakers home early to campaign. What's next: Tuesday's vote effectively kills any effort to impeach Hegseth this Congress.

AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Virtzilla also taking on KubeVirt by sharing VM API with the CNCF AI agents are a 'bane' for some website operators, says Cloudflare 5 days ago VMware quietly offers European users extended sales and support for low-end vSphere 6 days ago VMware returns to low-end server virtualization with 'vSphere Express' 7 days ago Broadcom denied names of cloud providers backing VMware merger challenge 8 days ago Architect creates open source replacement for VM migration tool VMware has hidden 8 days ago Advocates for cloud-native software have long argued that their approach to development makes applications portable across different Kubernetes environments. But VMware argues that’s not happening across hybrid clouds, and has taken the lead in an effort to improve matters. That effort, the new Workload Conformance Working Group in the Kubernetes community, aims to establish a shared standard for how workloads run on Kubernetes. The group’s web page points out, “Certified Kubernetes tests the cluster, and Kubernetes AI Conformance tests whether a cluster can run AI and ML workloads. Nothing comparable exists for the workloads themselves, so cluster operators still check each application by hand before routine maintenance or a Kubernetes upgrade. Every cluster operator ends up repeating the same assessment, and application maintainers get the same questions from each environment they support,” the group asserts. The proposed solution? “A common specification with repeatable tests would give both groups the same baseline to start from.” Prashanth Shenoy, VP of product marketing in Broadcom's VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF) division, told The Register that standard is needed in part because applications packaged to run in public clouds don’t always run well in hybrid clouds. That’s challenging for VMware, and other vendors of hybrid clouds like Nutanix and Red Hat, because they all sell tools to create and run a stack that users can deploy to both on-prem infrastructure and public clouds. VMware therefore thinks it will find support for an effort to ensure that cloud-native apps run predictably and efficiently in any Kubernetes environment. The effort to create this standard is in its very early days. “The first step is deciding which workloads and behaviors the specification covers,” states the announcement of the working group’s formation. “The scope includes security, resilience during disruptions, resource use, networking, storage, API usage, and observability, but the group hasn’t yet agreed on specific requirements or on how to test them. “However, one rule is already set: every requirement needs an objective test that a test binary can run, so nothing subjective goes into the specification.” Shenoy thinks application vendors will likely support this effort because they want to package their wares once and have them run anywhere. VMware this week announced another contribution to Kubernetes by moving its VM API to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) Sandbox. The CNCF, which maintains Kubernetes, is already home to KubeVirt, a tool that allows users to create and manage VMs inside a Kubernetes cluster. The VM API lets Kubernetes users create VMs that run under other hypervisors – including VMware’s own ESXi. VMware previously integrated Kubernetes into vSphere with Kubernetes, introduced as part of vSphere 7 in 2020. Chronicling Virtzilla’s long and convoluted attempts to package and sell the container tech it acquired along with Pivotal Software would be a tedious exercise. Suffice to say past efforts didn’t catch on, and VMware is now trying a different approach to making VMs a first class citizen of Kubernetes. The CNCF’s interest shows this is not a vanity project for VMware, because while developers generally prefer to write for containers, operations folk often decide to run those abstractions within lightweight VMs.

events.title: Nvidia hires major US law firm to investigate alleged Chinese spy affair
events.summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has become the face of the US AI boom Nvidia has hired one of the largest law firms in the US to investigate the affair between its own chief executive and an alleged Chinese spy. Jensen Huang, who co-founded the tech company, has admitted to having a romantic relationship outside of his marriage. The woman, Alice Huang, is alleged to be a spy for Beijing. Nvidia said on Tuesday that it had hired New York law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz, and that its attorney Joon Kim would lead "a thorough and independent investigation". The FBI is also conducting its own probe . The company's share price has fallen almost to a yearly low, with $500bn (£375bn) wiped of its stock market value since Friday. Nvidia is widely considered one of the most important companies behind the artificial intelligence (AI) boom, given it is the sole manufacturer of a computer chip used in AI tools. It is the world's second most valuable company after Apple and its chips have become a matter of national security for US officials who are keen to win the AI race. Alice Huang, who is also known as Huang Le, and is not related to Jensen Huang, was an executive at Singaporean company Megaspeed, which has been a customer of Nvidia. Megaspeed had been suspected of helping divert Nvidia chips to China, a concern that Nvidia has said was investigated and debunked. Nvidia has also maintained that the US government did not inform it that Megaspeed posed an intelligence concern. What we know so far about Jensen Huang's affair with suspected Chinese spy Published 18 hours ago Zoe Kleinman: Nvidia CEO's affair will cause ripples across US and beyond Published 2 days ago According to the New York Times, Secretary of State Marco Rubio sent a memo to top officials in Washington earlier this year warning that Jensen Huang was in a close relationship with a Chinese spy. Beijing has rejected claims that the Nvidia chief has been targeted, with its foreign ministry saying the allegations were "intended to smear and malign China". US President Donald Trump said on Monday that he had spoken to Jensen Huang, who had said he had "no idea she was a spy." Trump said he believed him. However, the relationship has drawn more political attention. Congressional leaders of the House Committee on Foreign Affairs have asked Huang to appear next week for a closed door briefing. The Nvidia boss has yet to say whether he will attend, a person familiar with the committee's demand told the BBC. The committee has the authority to subpoena Huang, effectively forcing him to appear before it, if deemed necessary. When announcing on Sunday that it would investigate the affair, Nvidia's board said it had no reason to believe the company's secrets or national security were compromised. It added that a committee of independent directors would oversee the probe. Watch: Who is suspected Chinese spy at centre of Nvidia affair investigation? Wachtell is one of the largest law firms in the US and has several notable clients in the tech industry. Among them are OpenAI and Salesforce. Joon Kim is a former US Attorney for New York's Southern District and spent several years working as a government attorney focusing on fraud and other criminal acts. The Nvidia investigation will likely be treated as urgent, according to sources familiar with the matter, as Jensen Huang's public image is tightly intertwined with the company. He has become a key public figure in the development on AI, arguing the technology is a "new industrial revolution" and is on par with the advent of electricity. It is unclear, however, if Wachtell will be able to interview Alice Huang. A spokesperson for Nvidia declined to comment on Tuesday when asked if Jensen Huang had retained any of his own legal representation amid the company investigation and the separate one launched by the FBI. events.title: He took down Andrew Cuomo. Now Jensen Huang is in his crosshairs
events.summary: The Scene Joon Kim has taken down mobsters, pursued a congressman, and investigated sexual harassment claims that toppled a New York governor. His latest assignment will decide the fate of a $4 trillion dollar company the global economy depends on. The former acting US Attorney for the Southern District of New York was tapped to investigate whether Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was the target of a Chinese espionage campaign, following Huang’s bombshell admission Sunday that the chief executive had an extramarital affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy. Kim, a 55-year-old prosecutor who joined Wachtell Lipton last month, will lead an internal probe overseen by a committee of independent directors, into whether Nvidia’s Huang compromised trade secrets — or, more pressingly, the US’ national security interests. The company has said it has confidence in its CEO and has “no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised.” A spokesperson for Wachtell declined to comment on the firm’s and Kim’s behalf. Shares in Nvidia have dropped 10% since Huang’s admission, knocking $500 billion off the company’s market value and stoking worries about the future of a company that underpins an AI financing buildout that has ensnared most of the global financial system. It comes against a fraught national security backdrop in which US officials have been warning for months of foreign influence campaigns and corporate espionage. A tangled web Huang, a close confidant of US President Donald Trump, has pushed Nvidia to take stakes in hundreds of companies across the AI boom it supplies. The company has also entered into billions of dollars worth of financing deals up and down Wall Street. Even Kim’s own employer, Wachtell Lipton, is not immune: OpenAI is one of Wachtell’s highest-profile clients, and the law firm’s M&A advisors are working on the company’s pending IPO, according to people familiar with the matter. Nvidia is a major OpenAI investor and the primary supplier of the chips that underpin the data centers (which Nvidia also finances) that power OpenAI’s models. Corporate probes can range from window dressing to essentially prosecutorial in nature, and Nvidia has 4 trillion reasons to limit its damage. It’s unclear how far Nvidia’s board will let Kim roam, but the board has already drummed up corporate governance concerns: The unusually long-tenured board lacks the experience and stature typically found at companies as large as Nvidia’s and has let Huang run the company with no clear successor and more than 50 direct reports. Mob bosses Kim began his career at New York’s Southern District more than two decades ago, working in the organized crime unit before leaving for Cleary Gottlieb in 2006. The son of a South Korean diplomat, Kim traveled around the world, including in Jordan and the UK. In his first stint as a federal prosecutor, Kim took on mob boss John “Junior” Gotti in a federal racketeering trial, trying him for the kidnapping of future New York mayoral candidate Curtis Sliwa. “His entire adult life, John Jr. has thought himself special, entitled to everything, accountable for nothing,” Kim said at the time. His former colleagues describe Kim as dogged, citing his time at the Southern District in 2013, under Attorney Preet Bharara, where Kim pursued a successful case against disgraced former Congressman Anthony Weiner and briefly ran the Southern District after Trump fired Bharara. Kim returned to Cleary in 2018, where he led a number of internal investigations into allegations of executive wrongdoing at large corporations, including Nissan Motors’ probe into former CEO Carlos Ghosn. But among his most defining cases was New York Attorney General Letitia James’ investigation into sexual harassment allegations against then-Governor Andrew Cuomo, which led to his 2021 resignation. Cuomo’s office was “rife with bullying, fear and intimidation,” Kim said when announcing his findings. A sensitive assignment Before Sunday, Huang and spokespeople for the company had publicly denied that the Nvidia CEO had an affair with Alice Huang. The company abruptly changed tack on Sunday, when Huang wrote a letter to employees admitting to the affair and announcing a plan to initiate an independent probe. The company had assembled an independent committee to oversee the investigation and was on Sunday leaning toward tapping former Cooley CEO Stephen Neal, the Financial Times reported and Semafor can confirm. Some Nvidia directors also suggested tapping Cooley to run the independent probe, other people familiar with the matter said. Cooley is Nvidia’s longtime outside counsel and would have exposed the company to criticism that the probe wasn’t independent, especially since Cooley is best known for its tech and IP practices, and isn’t considered by white-shoe lawyers to have a top-tier white-collar investigations practice. Nvidia declined to comment on either the nature of the independent committee or on whether directors considered tapping Cooley. Notable Neal has been involved in other high-profile misconduct cases , including representing disgraced Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes.

events.title: November Patch Tuesday boasts over 1,000 bugs, one already under attack
events.summary: It’s another doozy of a Patch Tuesday, with Microsoft fixing 1,094 bugs in its products, including one that attackers exploited before Redmond released a patch. Jake Knott, head of threat intelligence at exposure management firm watchTowr, succinctly said in an email to The Register : “Maybe we should just go home.” “Most security teams haven’t quite recovered from the last month of bumper-to-bumper critical vulnerabilities, emergency patches, and ‘2shell’-branded everything, and we’re yet again at another Patch Tuesday,” Knott told us. Starting with the zero-day: It’s an Outlook spoofing vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-124194 , and it only garnered a 6.5 out of 10 CVSS rating. But as Dustin Childs, head of threat awareness at TrendAI’s Zero Day Initiative, warns, don’t let the score or the name lull you into thinking it’s OK to put off patching this one. “It’s labeled spoofing, but the impact is bigger than the name suggests,” Childs said in his monthly Patch Tuesday review . “An attacker sends a specially crafted message file and convinces a user to open it,” he wrote. “Outlook then connects to an attacker-controlled network location without showing the usual external-content warning, which discloses the user’s NTLMv2 hash. The attacker can use that hash to authenticate as the user.” Microsoft marked CVE-2026-124194 as exploited, but per usual didn’t say when the attacks started, who is battering this bug, and what they are doing with the access post exploitation. These details will likely start trickling out soon. Plus, now that there’s a public fix, other miscreants are undoubtedly already scanning for vulnerable versions and reverse engineering the patch for their own attack purposes. So prioritize this fix, and keep an eye on your inbox for any suspicious files. Back-to-back months of 1K+ CVEs Despite the second month of more than 1,000 CVEs (October had 1,474 ), CVE-2026-124194 is the only one under active exploitation, and none of the 1,094 are listed as publicly known. Childs says this shouldn’t give organizations “false comfort.” “Logging back-to-back months above 1,000 CVEs proves automated bug-hunting has permanently reset patch volume,” he told The Register . “With AI making patch-diffing and exploit generation near-instant, the threat window opens the minute these updates drop.” For defenders, this means two things, Childs added. “What defenders need to know and do right now is abandon broad triage and take immediate defensive action: patch Exchange and Domain Controllers (LDAP/Kerberos) first to stop zero-click compromise, ring-fence exposed network services like DNS and DHCP to prevent wormable spread, and verify manual administrative fixes on your cloud services,” he said. Zero-click threats There are two zero-click threats in this month’s batch of fixes: CVE-2026-116928 and CVE-2026-119958 . Both are critical, carrying 9.8 CVSS ratings, in part because they don’t require any user interaction to exploit. CVE-2026-116928 is an out-of-bounds write in Microsoft Windows Search Component that could lead to remote code execution. An unauthenticated attacker could abuse this search feature in Exchange “by sending an email containing a specially crafted attachment,” Redmond warned. “Exchange automatically processes the attachment for indexing, so the recipient does not need to open the email or attachment. Successful exploitation could allow the attacker to execute code with the permissions of the affected processing service.” CVE-2026-119958 is an out-of-bounds write vulnerability in Windows' implementation of the Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) that could allow unauthenticated attackers to execute code remotely without user interaction. This one can be exploited by sending specially crafted LDAP requests to vulnerable systems, potentially compromising domain controllers. Childs also counts 30 CVEs that pose a “wormable risk,” requiring zero authentication and zero user interaction over a network. All of those are listed in his blog, so prioritize fixing those as well. And…Xbox remote code execution And finally, for funsies, a critical flaw in the Windows Xbox Live Networking Service, CVE-2026-112967 , that could allow remote code execution also made this month's roundup. It's a heap-overflow vulnerability with a 9.8 CVSS rating that doesn't require authentication or user interaction to exploit. So don't take a gaming break between testing November's updates. Or, if you do, at least make sure vulnerable Windows systems running the Xbox Live Networking Service are on your patching list, too. ®

events.title: Milei plots data center buildout in Patagonia
events.summary: Argentine President Javier Milei is pitching his country as a regulation-free “AI hub,” as US tech firms weigh building data centers abroad in the face of overwhelming domestic pushback. Milei, a self-described anarcho-capitalist , has pushed for a tax break for the facilities and touted Argentina’s “abundant energy” and “extensive, inhospitable land” as ideal for the rapid AI buildout. An energy executive planning a facility to power AI in rural Argentina told the Financial Times he was flooded with calls from potential US investors and clients, following midterm elections in which American voters resoundingly rejected data center construction: “[Argentina’s] coming late to the party, but it has huge potential to catch up .” — Mary Lawrence Ware
