events.title: Anthropic revenue could top $600B: Goldman
events.summary: Anthropic could generate $685 billion in revenue by 2030, placing it among the largest companies in the world, as the AI lab gears up for a $1.4 trillion IPO as soon as next week. The Goldman Sachs projection points to total sales of more than 130 times Anthropic’s 2025 figure, as the company gears up to spend about $900 billion on its AI buildout . The blockbuster sums will make CEO Dario Amodei one of the world’s most influential executives and, in turn, empower institutions sympathetic to his beliefs about effective altruism and existential risk, intensifying a debate over AI safety: The Trump administration has condemned effective altruism , and Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg and Nvidia’s Jensen Huang have criticized Amodei as a “doomer.” — Brendan Ruberry

events.title: US inflation slows less than expected in October
events.summary: Hotter-than-expected US inflation data sparked a Treasury selloff Tuesday, heightening expectations of a rate increase at the Federal Reserve’s December meeting. Food prices saw a broad spike while a diesel crunch pushed up freight costs, widening out the number of affected goods categories. The price pressures are unlikely to be a one-month phenomenon, Santander’s chief US economist told The New York Times, as a simmering Iran war drives up the price of numerous commodities: “We run the risk that the floodgates open .” A Mizuho economist said the central bank could hike by half a point in response: “The Fed skipped October and now will probably need to do some make up .” — Brendan Ruberry

events.title: Huang scandal puts Nvidia chip loopholes in focus
events.summary: The unfolding Nvidia saga has intensified scrutiny of the legal means by which top Chinese firms are able to access advanced American compute. While Megaspeed, the Singaporean firm at the center of the scandal, is suspected of smuggling Nvidia chips to China, Washington’s export controls have spawned lucrative opportunities for Asian cloud operators that get their hands on the most advanced Nvidia chips, offering a legal loophole to Chinese hyperscalers. Singapore-based DayOne is worth roughly $15 billion and counts ByteDance as its top customer, while Moonshot has looked to tap Nvidia chips hosted in Europe , highlighting “the nonsensical nature of our export control regime ,” a Carnegie Endowment expert said. “No administration has had the cojones to do something about it.” — Brendan Ruberry

events.title: Microsoft Fixes Nearly 1,100 Security Vulnerabilities
events.summary: Microsoft did another four-digit patch drop today, releasing updates to fix almost 1,100 security vulnerabilities in its Windows operating systems and supported software. This month’s Patch Tuesday addresses 63 critical flaws — including a zero-day in Microsoft Outlook — and comes amid important security updates from other software makers, including Adobe , Apple , Google and Mozilla . Image: Shutterstock.com. Diorama by @zepp1969. November’s patch release from Redmond tackles 1,093 vulnerabilities, fixing 63 “critical” flaws that can be exploited to seize control over a Windows system with little or no help from users. Nearly half of those critical bugs are remote code execution vulnerabilities. Overall, 535 of the flaws addressed this month allow an attacker to elevate their privileges on a vulnerable device. This latest round of updates means Microsoft has shipped more than 5,100 security patches so far this year, a staggering number considering that a year ago Microsoft was averaging around 100 patches per month. Microsoft credits advances in artificial intelligence for helping to find (and fix) such a large volume of security bugs in recent months. Last month, Microsoft pushed more than 1,400 fixes. According to Redmond, just one of the flaws is already seeing active exploitation: CVE-2026-124194 , a spoofing bug in Outlook. The advisory for CVE-2026-124194 says it affects Microsoft 365 Apps for Enterprise and editions of Microsoft Office . Several other major software makers pushed security updates this week to fix critical weaknesses in their products. Apple on Monday released out-of-cycle security updates to fix at least nine vulnerabilities in iOS/iPadOS , macOS , watchOS and visionOS . Among the weaknesses reportedly fixed in Apple’s release include an iMessage flaw that could let a remote attacker join a group chat and receive its messages; the updates also fix a separate iMessage flaw that could let someone added to a group access messages sent before they joined. Lee Neely , an instructor at the SANS Institute , noted that Apple backported the fix to iOS 18. “I take notice when Apple releases fixes to more than two versions,” Neely wrote in a SANS newsletter today. “You really need to get to version 27.2.1 of their OSes and push folks who are holding onto devices which cannot run the current version. The best plan often involves setting an upgrade date for old hardware. Run through all your Apple devices and make sure everything is up to date, don’t assume the fixes went out automatically.” Google this week released Chrome version 157.0.8103.50 , which resolves nine security holes, including CVE-2026-125350 , the sixth zero-day vulnerability this year for Chrome (this bug also is being patched in Chromium-based browsers like Edge). The latest Chrome version follows its November 3 release, which fixed 213 vulnerabilities. A new version of Mozilla Firefox out today ( Firefox 160 ) resolves almost 100 CVEs, about half of them high severity. Adobe today released patches for at least 110 vulnerabilities across a range of products, with nearly half of the flaws rated high severity. Adobe said there is no evidence any of the security holes it addressed this month are being actively exploited. Chris Goettl , vice president of product management at Ivanti , said it’s easy for security teams at large enterprises to feel overwhelmed by the volume and criticality of patches from Microsoft lately. But he notes that while some 95,000 vulnerabilities have been assigned CVEs this year across all vendors, only 217 have so far this year been added to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) list maintained by the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA). “Roughly four in ten of this year’s exploited vulnerabilities sit in operating systems, endpoint software, browsers, and server platforms, which a continuous patch strategy can close quickly,” Goettl said.”The rest calls for exposure management alongside patching, especially the 44% that sit in edge devices and IT management or remote access tools, the internet-facing systems that hold privileged access. Teams that can quickly identify those assets, confirm exposure and act on confirmed exploitation can focus on the small slice of vulnerabilities attackers are actively using, while the rest stays on the normal patch cadence.” Please don’t neglect to back up any important data if you haven’t recently; generally speaking, this is a task best accomplished before applying operating system updates. As ever, if you experience any issues installing this month’s bundle of love from Microsoft, please drop a comment about it in the space below.

events.title: Wall St retreats as hot inflation data, Fed comments fuel rate worries
events.summary: Traders working on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange in New York City on Nov 10. US stocks fell after inflation rose 0.4% in October, above forecasts, which pushed markets to fully price in a December Fed rate hike. Fed comments from Christopher Waller, Lorie Logan and Jeff Schmid added rate fears, with some warning that higher or faster hikes may still be needed. Tech shares led losses, with Nvidia down more than 5%, while investors also watched Anthropic’s planned IPO and wider worries about the AI boom. NEW YORK - US stocks stumbled on Nov 10, as a hotter-than-expected inflation reading cemented expectations for a rate hike from the Federal Reserve in December and fuelled concerns the central bank may be more aggressive in raising rates. The Labour Department said the Consumer Price Index increased 0.4% in October, its third straight gain of 0.4% or more and above the 0.3% estimate of economists polled by Reuters, after advancing 0.6% in September. The data came after Fed governor Christopher Waller said the central bank should raise short-term borrowing costs in December even if data shows inflation cooled in October, and should consider an upsized half-point rate hike if the inflation picture worsens. Markets are now completely pricing in a rate hike of at least 25 basis points at the Fed’s December meeting, according to CME FedWatch, up from 84% on Nov 9. The two-year US Treasury yield, which typically moves in step with interest rate expectations for the Fed, surged 19.1 basis points to 4.738% and was on track for its biggest daily gain since April 9, 2025, after US President Donald Trump launched his sweeping global tariffs. The jump has come even as oil prices have eased to two-month lows as US officials have downplayed any imminent military actions against Iran. “What kind of has the market spooked a little bit is this idea of, ‘Well, we were already pricing in a December hike... but maybe it’s not 25, maybe it’s 50, and maybe the Fed’s more worried about inflation than I am, so let’s sell some stocks,’” said Jason Ware, chief investment officer at Albion Financial Group in Salt Lake City, Utah. “From our perch, that is irrational. The thing that has pushed CPI up over the last six months and has the Fed a little bit more concerned and therefore has restarted hiking rates is because we’ve seen oil, energy and diesel push through in terms of inflation. If we have oil now going the other way... this is all going to settle down.” The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 223.12 points, or 0.43%, to 52,166.63, the S&P 500 lost 48.06 points, or 0.64%, to 7,501.88 and the Nasdaq Composite lost 290.69 points, or 1.15%, to 24,962.44. The S&P 500 and Nasdaq had risen for two straight days, bouncing back from sharp losses last week sparked by concerns about the potential for government regulations slowing the AI buildout. The S&P 500 technology sector dropped more than 1% as the worst-performing of the 11 major sectors, weighed down by another drop in Nvidia, which fell more than 5% and has tumbled about 10% over the past two sessions. The company’s stock reflects mounting concerns over CEO Jensen Huang’s future at the chip company after it initiated an internal probe into spy claims involving Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang. The CEO’s relationship with Alice Huang facilitated the shipment of at least US$7.5 billion worth of the company’s chips through Chinese firms, the Information reported on Nov 10. But declines for the broader Philadelphia semiconductor index were more muted, off roughly 1% after two consecutive sessions of gains, as volatility in the AI trade increased. Aside from Waller, other Fed officials speaking on Nov 10 also took a hawkish tone. Dallas Federal Reserve president Lorie Logan said that the Fed needs to deliver at least two more quarter-percentage-point interest rate increases to bring down inflation, and may need to do so promptly, while Kansas City Federal Reserve president Jeff Schmid said he believes the current policy rate is “fairly accommodative.” Investors are also bracing for Anthropic’s expected public listing later this month. The AI lab revealed that its initial public offering is expected to raise as much as US$64.4 billion, giving the company a fully diluted valuation of up to US$1.4 trillion. A listing by Anthropic could also force other AI heavyweights to compete harder for investor dollars. Neocloud firm CoreWeave is expected to report quarterly earnings after the market close on Nov 10. Questions about the sustainability of the AI boom and the company’s debt burden have pressured the stock recently, which was now down about 33% on the year. CoreWeave shares were off 2.3% on the session, while those of its peer Nebius tumbled more than 6%. Declining issues outnumbered advancers by a 2.53-to-1 ratio on the New York Stock Exchange, and by a 2.49-to-1 ratio on the Nasdaq.

events.title: Ring robots ready to patrol paranoids’ pads
events.summary: If you didn't have any privacy concerns about slapping a Ring doorbell on your front door or putting Ring cameras inside, you'll love Amazon's newest offerings, which move around homes and businesses to capture views stationary cameras might miss. The house of Bezos announced the launch of Ring Robotics on Tuesday along with its first two products: a drone designed for indoor home security, and a wheeled robot with a telescoping camera mast for automated after-hours business patrols. Both are designed to proactively patrol spaces as well as respond to alerts from connected alarm systems and Ring-connected devices. According to Ring founder Jamie Siminoff, this is something customers actually want, as those stationary cameras just can’t quite see everywhere. “It’s not just a new category of security; it’s the beginning of a future where proactive, autonomous protection is something every home and every business can have,” Siminoff said. The consumer-focused Ring Drone Cam launches from its own charging dock that Amazon says keeps the thing “out of sight” when not in use, and when in flight is able to patrol a home by flying around pre-programmed routes to take in the sights with its 148-degree FOV, 2K camera that includes LED illumination for night patrols. Amazon says it can also respond to alerts from cameras, sensors, and alarm systems. The Ring Rover Cam, designed with businesses in mind, is sort of like a security Roomba that sports a camera on a telescoping mast that Amazon says can be programmed to certain heights to let it see over counters, shelves, and other workplace obstacles. The Rover can also perform 360-degree scans and includes a siren, lights, and two-way audio so you can yell at intruders who aren't dissuaded by its presence. The Rover streams and records video in up to 4K while moving or patrolling and is designed to make regular patrols of businesses during off hours. It can also detect people and respond to alerts from connected Ring devices. Of course, given that this is Ring we're talking about, these flying and free-wheeling cameras use Amazon's cloud for some processing, likely inviting privacy concerns about what footage and mapping data the company can access and retain. The Amazon-owned security tech firm has faced a number of privacy complaints over the years, some of which have resulted in multimillion-dollar settlements. Ring agreed to pay $5.8 million in a 2023 settlement with the FTC over allegations that employees and contractors improperly accessed customers' private videos and that the company failed to adequately protect accounts against unauthorized access – just imagine the privacy concerns raised by flying robots. More recently, the company took heat for partnering with surveillance outfit Flock Safety, a relationship which it has since canceled . Amazon/Ring also invited criticism for a Super Bowl ad earlier this year promoting a new feature called Search Party, which would remotely activate Ring cameras to search for lost pets, suggesting that Amazon had the ability, in theory, to use Ring cameras like a dystopian neighborhood surveillance network. Another Ring feature, Familiar Faces, which uses AI-powered facial recognition to identify people captured by compatible cameras, prompted a proposed class-action lawsuit filed in June. The complaint alleges that the feature collected biometric information from visitors and passersby without their consent. If we can’t have iRobot, we’ll do it with Ring Amazon abandoned its efforts to buy Roomba robot-vacuum maker iRobot in 2024, blaming regulatory scrutiny for the move. The FTC, under then-chair Lina Khan, examined the deal's potential effects on competition and consumer privacy, including concerns about the information Roombas collect while mapping customers' homes. European regulators, meanwhile, raised concerns that Amazon could use its marketplace to disadvantage rival robot vacuum makers. With this Ring move, Amazon is once again putting robots capable of mapping interior spaces into customers' hands, reviving some of the privacy questions raised during its failed iRobot acquisition. As Amazon explains in Tuesday’s press release, both new Ring robots are powered by AI Pilot, “a custom-built system that uses the devices’ cameras, specialized vision models, on-device sensors, and cloud processing to see, think, and navigate autonomously.” To help the Ring robots understand where they're operating, the devices generate floor plans of interior spaces, according to Amazon. “Carry Ring Drone through your space or let Ring Rover autonomously explore, and it turns what it sees into a floor plan,” the company explains of the setup process. AI Pilot takes the reins in identifying the types of rooms it sees and suggests key patrol areas it should focus on, which users can add to in the Ring app. Amazon claims that videos captured by these new flying and free-wheeling cameras will be protected by an encryption scheme it calls Throw Away the Key Encryption (TAKE). The system temporarily allows Ring's cloud services to access recordings for enabled features before the relevant encryption keys are deleted. Ring announced the scheme in August, presenting it as a way to limit access to customer recordings without sacrificing cloud-powered features. “With TAKE, your Ring videos are protected with unique, rotating encryption keys,” Amazon explained. “A copy of the keys is temporarily held inside a secure enclave within the cloud; think of it as a sealed vault that can only provide Ring access to the key under strict, limited conditions.” The keys, Amazon claims, are later deleted so that only users and those they allow access to can see videos, with Ring only retaining them “to power the intelligent features that you have active on your account.” “We take privacy concerns seriously, and we believe privacy and customer control are fundamental to building products people trust,” a Ring spokesperson told The Register when asked about prior privacy concerns. “That is why customers decide where these devices go and when.” We asked about floor plan security, but didn’t get an answer about that. As for when those devices will be available, the Rover Cam will start shipping on December 16 at a price of about $1,000, but the Drone Cam might not ever actually make it to homes. Amazon’s announcement mentions a release date of January 27, 2027, but that’s subject to the FCC giving its blessing. “Ring Drone Cam has not been authorized as required by the rules of the FCC,” Amazon’s release states. “This device is not, and may not be, offered for sale or lease, or sold or leased, until authorization is obtained.” Amazon told us that the Drone Cam would still start shipping in January, luckily giving everyone a few months to figure out how to deal with this new, more mobile, invasion of privacy. ®

events.title: A tabloid scandal bankrolled a Long Island Democrat, mostly with out-of-district money. A Hollywood-linked tycoon backed a Republican who beat him.
events.summary: Leaked photos were supposed to end Chris Gallant’s campaign. Instead, they bankrolled it. After the New York Post published archived images of the Democrat modeling bondage gear for a San Francisco leather retailer, his fundraising took off. In the quarter the photos surfaced, Gallant raised more than the incumbent. His October quarterly FEC report shows $929,825 in receipts for July through September. Rep. Nick LaLota reported about $609,000 for the same period. The money bought a close loss, not a win. LaLota won a third term in New York’s 1st Congressional District last Tuesday, 51.1% to 48.9%, a margin of nearly 7,000 votes with 560 of 561 election districts reporting . Gallant first held out for absentee ballots, then conceded Wednesday . LaLota’s margin shrank from about 11 points in 2024 to about two, in a year Democrats swept to control of Congress . Nor was the money especially local. A Fortune review of both campaigns’ raw 2026 FEC filings through Oct. 14 found that in-district donors accounted for about 16% of LaLota’s money from named individuals and just over a third of Gallant’s. The post-leak surge followed the same pattern. In the 32 days after the Post story ran on Sept. 13, Gallant reported $276,055 in itemized contributions. Only $65,997 of it, about 24%, came from individuals inside NY-1, and almost half of that came from 62 donors in the Hamptons. Donors in Manhattan and California gave $73,606 combined, more than every donor inside NY-1 put together. In NY-1, the people who funded the race and the people who voted in it were often different. Both campaigns were bankrolled mostly by donors outside the district, including major Wall Street, Hollywood and tech names. Even the men on the ballot live beyond its lines: both reside near Amityville, on Long Island’s South Shore, which means neither could vote for himself. A district with a summer address NY-1 runs from Suffolk County’s North Shore villages to the East End, with vineyards and farms on the North Fork and the Hamptons on the South Fork. In between lie Smithtown and Brookhaven, where suburban neighborhoods give way to woods and residents are largely commuters, law enforcement and small-business owners. Each summer, the South Fork fills with the people who run Wall Street and corporate America. That makes the district one of the country’s busiest political ATMs, where financiers and industry titans host fundraisers for both parties . Suffolk County donors gave more than $45 million to campaigns in the 2020 cycle alone, according to OpenSecrets data CNBC cited. In August, Vice President JD Vance raised more than $5 million from young Republican donors at the Southampton home of Omeed Malik , president of 1789 Capital and a prominent Trump donor. Two candidates, one shrinking margin LaLota, a Navy veteran and former Suffolk County elections commissioner, was first elected in 2022 to succeed Lee Zeldin and was re-elected in 2024, defeating former CNN anchor John Avlon by about 11 points. In that race, LaLota criticized Avlon for his dual residency in both Sag Harbor and Manhattan. Gallant, 37, is an Army National Guard Black Hawk pilot, a former FAA air traffic controller at JFK, a former union leader and a volunteer firefighter. He won the June primary with about 63% of the vote, defeating Lukas Ventouras , a 25-year-old law student and district resident who had raised about $124,000, mostly in unitemized small-dollar donations. Gallant later picked up endorsements from Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg. After the Post story, Gallant’s attorney, Sara Azari, who previously represented former Rep. Eric Swalwell after misconduct allegations, confirmed the photos were authentic and consensual. Gallant told the New York Times he hoped it could be his “Kim Kardashian moment,” and the campaign began selling “Make Politics Sexy Again” merchandise . LaLota stuck to calling Gallant “weak and woke” and needling him for declining to debate . Asked by Fortune about the surge, Gallant answered through Slingshot Strategies , a consulting firm that promises “a proven track record of shifting the conversation” for candidates facing “overwhelming odds” and “difficult fights.” He said the Post story “backfired on them” and that the Times interview let voters see “a proud gay man who refused to be ashamed of his identity, and it resonated.” On LaLota’s outside money, he said, “I never had to rely on outside interests to try and buy this seat.” About a third of his own money from named donors came from inside the district. LaLota cast the surge as a product of the controversy itself. “On the same days my opponent was backing out of debates, he was monetizing his BDSM and pornographic modeling past,” he said in a statement to Fortune . “Instead of boasting how kinky he is, as he did to the Times , he owes Long Islanders an explanation for choosing vanity and fundraising over debates and accountability.” Where the money came from Fortune analyzed itemized contributions dated in 2026 in both campaigns’ raw FEC filings through Oct. 14, so the comparison covers the same stretch of the race for both candidates. Repeat donors were counted once, refunds subtracted and conduit entries adjusted so no gift was counted twice. The FEC does not require campaigns to name individuals who give $200 or less in a cycle, so those donors are excluded. Fortune placed donors inside or outside NY-1 based on the mailing city they listed, which may differ from where they vote. Individuals may give $3,500 per election this cycle, or $7,000 for the primary and general combined. Fortune tallied the filings by hand, then used Claude, Anthropic’s AI model, to clean the raw files and check the calculations. LaLota had the bigger war chest. Through Oct. 14, he had raised $4.5 million and had $2.31 million in cash on hand. Gallant had raised $1.7 million and had $426,000 on hand. The sharper contrast was where the money came from. Of the 785 named donors in LaLota’s 2026 filings, 29% listed mailing addresses in the district. Together they gave $207,161, only 16% of what he raised from named individuals. PACs and other committees supplied $1.18 million, about a quarter of his total for the cycle. Gallant’s support was more local, but not by much. Of his 1,031 named donors in the 2026 raw file, 390 (38%) listed addresses in NY-1 and nearly $300,000, about a third of the roughly $876,000 he raised from named individuals this year. Counting gifts from 2025, his itemized individual total for the cycle is $1.15 million . events.title: Nvidia faces deepening scrutiny over China chip ties, CEO affair
events.summary: Nvidia chief Jensen Huang allegedly had an affair with a Chinese businesswoman who is said to be a spy for Beijing. Nvidia lost about US$430 billion in value as reports linked CEO Jensen Huang to a Chinese businesswoman alleged to be a spy, raising fresh fears over governance and chip sales. US officials and lawmakers are pressing for answers. Chuck Schumer wants tighter China chip export rules, while Nvidia’s board has hired outside counsel to investigate. Reports say Alice Huang helped move about 240,000 Nvidia chips into China through firms in China and Singapore. Nvidia says there is no reason to believe national security or company secrets were compromised. NEW YORK – Nvidia shed about US$430 billion (S$551 billion) in market value over two sessions as new reports deepened questions about chief executive Jensen Huang’s relationship with a Chinese businesswoman alleged to be a spy for Beijing. The controversy escalated on several fronts on Nov 10 as allegations emerged that Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang aided at least US$7.5 billion in Nvidia chip shipments to China and that US Secretary of State Marco Rubio had previously briefed President Donald Trump on the affair. Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer demanded answers from the administration and tighter curbs on chip exports to China, while the company’s independent directors hired outside counsel to investigate. US Republican Senator Kevin Cramer from the Senate Banking Committee called on Jensen Huang to step down as CEO. “The potential for extortion is so tremendous that something as sensitive as Nvidia chips, I just think he’s got to go,” Cramer told Politico late on Nov 10. The allegations have turned Huang’s personal conduct into a broader risk for Nvidia, raising questions about the company’s governance and its dependence on the CEO who has led it for more than three decades and built it into the dominant supplier of AI chips. He owns about 3.6% of the company – but does not have majority voting control – and runs an unusually flat organisation in which dozens of executives report directly to him. The Federal Bureau of Investigation is separately examining whether the 63-year-old Huang was targeted by a foreign intelligence operation. Huang has told employees he was unfaithful to his wife, but provided no details about the relationship. Huang apologised to top executives at a closed-door meeting on Nov 9 before pivoting to business and was back holding meetings at Nvidia’s headquarters on Nov 10, CNBC reported. Nvidia has said its board has no reason to believe US national security or company secrets were compromised and that Huang has committed to cooperating with the internal review. The board has retained Joon Kim, a Wachtell Lipton partner and former acting US Attorney for the Southern District of New York, whose practice includes internal investigations and white-collar defence , to lead the probe. Nvidia’s stock, which had been nearly flat in 2026 before news of the affair broke, has fallen 9.5% since then. The shares have lagged the broader market on investor unease over whether massive spending on AI will deliver adequate returns. The New York Times reported on Nov 10 that Rubio had briefed Trump aboard Air Force One en route to China about US intelligence indicating Huang was involved with a woman believed to be a Chinese spy. The briefing marked at least the second time in seven months that Trump had been told about the intelligence, the Times reported, citing people with knowledge of the matter. Trump said on Nov 9 he had spoken with Huang and asked whether he knew the woman was a spy. Trump said Huang told him he had “absolutely no idea” and that he believed the Nvidia CEO. Trump also said he had not known about the alleged ties when Huang accompanied him to China in May. A White House official disputed the report and referred Reuters to Trump’s comments on Nov 9. Schumer said on Nov 10 that Congress must have a full accounting of Trump’s defence of Huang and called on lawmakers to quickly approve new restrictions on US chip exports to China. “He’s supposed to protect America, not China, not his friends,” Schumer said, accusing Trump of failing to address foreign espionage in the American technology industry. US news publication Axios, citing sources, reported on Nov 10 that Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick was sent a highly classified memo warning about the Nvidia CEO’s relationship with Alice Huang. Reuters could not immediately verify that report. The Commerce Department and Nvidia did not immediately respond to requests for comment outside regular business hours. Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, along with her husband and sister, built a network of companies across China and Singapore to acquire Nvidia chips, The Information reported.

events.title: Grok Build coding agent leaks oodles of confidential info, some belonging to SpaceXSI
events.summary: Grok Build, the vibe-coding agent from SpaceXSI, is leaking data—some of it proprietary business information and other sensitive secrets—from thousands of its users, including the very same Elon Musk-owned company that offers the platform, new research shows. The information is revealed through links allowing Grok Build users to share their apps with others. Grok takes steps to randomize the URLs so only people who know the exact URL can access the data stored there. A design decision by developers of the platform, however, completely torpedoes that objective and makes it possible for anyone to enumerate thousands of live Grok Build projects. Except in rare cases, clicking those links opens the app and reveals all data associated with it. You had one job Research from security firm Claroc shows that the exposed data includes things like internal business plans, ad proposals, medical exam results, galley checklists from a celebrity cruise line, and employee names and ID numbers. Ironically, some of the sensitive data comes from two-dozen apps built by SpaceXSI (the name of the now-merged SpaceX and xAI) itself. A small sampling of the documents revealed in the SpaceXSI apps—Claroc found 24 of them—include an onboarding plan, marked confidential, for a new member of SpaceXSI’s enterprise sales team, a sales territory map of 594 accounts, internal system addresses for sales team tools, and advertising proposals. events.title: OpenAI acquires Odessia, travel startup created by Sonder founder
events.summary: OpenAI has acquired an AI travel agent called Odessia, according to Odessia’s founder, Francis Davidson. Davidson says in a post announcing the deal that he’s now working for OpenAI, helping the AI lab with the future of travel. Terms of the deal were not disclosed, but this looks like an acqui-hire. Davidson’s announcement focused largely on how he built his AI travel agent Odessia by directing teams of AI agents. The year-old Odessia raised a $6 million pre-seed round led by Sequoia and launched its AI travel agent around five months ago. Davidson says that it had helped early adopters plan millions of dollars’ worth of travel, but the tool has already been shut down. An OpenAI spokesperson confirmed the hire to TechCrunch. “We’re thrilled to welcome Francis to OpenAI. Francis is a proven founder who has built multiple businesses to help people travel, and we’re excited he’s chosen to build with us.” However the AI lab has not announced new travel-specific products or plans. It does, however, count such companies as Bookings.com, Expedia, and KAYAK as customers or partners. Travel is also one of the main areas that people are using personal AI assistants to help with. And, back in July 2025, when OpenAI launched its ChatGPT agent , it mentioned travel as one of its potential uses. OpenAI’s spokesperson didn’t have more to share on its plans for travel-related products, except to say that travel is one of the areas that chatbot users frequently ask about. “1.2 billion people turn to ChatGPT each week for help with everyday tasks — from understanding their health, figuring out what to make for dinner, building a budget, and even planning a trip. We see a real opportunity to make these experiences even more useful,” the spokesperson said. Acquiring Odessia is interesting for another reason. Davidson is well known in the travel industry after he founded a travel startup called Sonder as a college student in 2014. It was sort of like Airbnb, but it focused on short-term leasing of upscale apartments in major cities worldwide. The pandemic badly hurt it, and as it climbed out of that rut, it went public via a SPAC but didn’t raise as much money as it needed, Davidson later said in a post announcing his resignation as CEO in June 2025. When a key partnership with Marriott fell through , the company went into bankruptcy and wound down. The bankruptcy trustee sold Sonder’s name, trademarks, and website domain in 2026 to TravelAI, and that website operates as a curated guide to the kind of travel rental properties that Sonder was once known for. Prior to its downfall, Davidson had built Sonder into a unicorn with over $600 million in revenues. While Sonder was not, ultimately, a success story, Davidson is the kind of battle-scarred founder that Silicon Valley often values. So we’ll have to wait and see what OpenAI has in store with travel now that he’s joined the company. Note: This story was updated with OpenAI’s comments and updated revenue for Sonder. events.title: Credit card debt hits record high as Americans struggle with cost-of-living
events.summary: Federal Reserve Bank of New York ; Note: Not adjusted for inflation; Chart: Axios Visuals Americans' credit card balances hit a record $1.29 trillion in the third quarter, according to a new report released by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. Why it matters: Falling behind on credit card payments can trap struggling households in a cycle of fees, damaged credit and increasingly expensive borrowing. The latest figures show that financial pain is concentrated in lower-income communities, even as delinquency rates improve nationally. By the numbers: Consumer credit card balances rose by $22 billion in the third quarter, an increase of 1.7%. That's $52 billion higher than a year earlier. The figures aren't adjusted for inflation, meaning some of the increase reflects higher prices rather than greater borrowing in real terms. Total household debt, including mortgages and student and auto loans, rose $334 billion, reaching a record $19.1 trillion in the third quarter. The total is up $5 trillion since 2019, just before the pandemic. Yes, but: Fewer credit card balances are becoming seriously delinquent, a sign of some improvement in Americans' ability to keep up with payments. The rate at which credit card debt becomes seriously overdue edged down to 6.9% in the third quarter, though it remains notably above the 5.2% recorded before the pandemic. Between the lines: A separate report from the New York Fed on Tuesday showed Americans in lower-income neighborhoods are having a harder time keeping up with credit card payments relative to their wealthier counterparts. Delinquency rates remain above pre-pandemic levels across all neighborhood-income groups, with the gap between the richest and poorest areas increasing since 2022. In the lowest-income neighborhoods, 10.3% of credit card balances became seriously delinquent over the past year — more than double the 4.4% rate in the wealthiest neighborhoods. The big picture: Average credit card balance per borrower is now $6,678, according to TransUnion's Q3 insights report. Borrowers under 30 had the highest rate of credit card debt newly becoming at least 90 days overdue, the Fed's report found. What we're watching: Democrats won the midterms promising to lower prices — but delivering relief that voters can actually feel in their household budgets will be difficult to fulfill.

events.title: Jim Jordan wins House GOP minority leader race
events.summary: House Republicans elected Judiciary Chair Jim Jordan (R-Ohio) as their new leader Tuesday, handing the reins of the battered GOP conference to one of its most prominent conservative firebrands. Why it matters: Jordan's victory marks a major shake-up in House Republican leadership, elevating a founding member of the hardline Freedom Caucus who campaigned as an alternative to the leaders who presided over the GOP's crushing midterm defeat . Jordan bested Majority Leader Steve Scalise (R-La.), who had served as the No. 2 House Republican since 2014, in the conference-wide secret ballot for minority leader. Scalise trailed Jordan by 33 votes. Jordan's victory signals an appetite among House Republicans for a more confrontational approach as they prepare to enter the minority. State of play: Jordan and Scalise entered Tuesday's election locked in a tight race, with both camps expressing confidence in their chances of winning. Jordan drew public support from some of the conference's most conservative members, who argued Republicans needed a change in direction after their devastating midterm losses. Scalise leaned on his longstanding relationships across the conference and his decade-plus of experience in leadership. The big picture: Jordan's ascent represents a remarkable turnaround for a conservative agitator who spent much of his career challenging the Republican establishment before becoming one of President Trump's most vocal allies. He'll be tasked with uniting a fractured Republican conference and leading the party's efforts to reclaim the House majority in 2028. Zoom out: Beyond the top job, current whip Tom Emmer (Minn.) beat back a challenge from Rep. August Pfluger (Texas) to stay on as minority whip. Conference Chair: Lisa McClain (Mich.) won a three-way race with Reps. Erin Houchin (Ind.) and Greg Steube (Fla.). NRCC Chair: Brian Jack (Ga.) beat out Rudy Yakym (Ind.) to lead House Republicans' campaign arm. Current NRCC Chairman Richard Hudson (N.C.) lost his own reelection bid last week. events.title: OpenAI, Anthropic face new oversight as New York’s AI safety law takes effect
events.summary: New York is gearing up to enforce one of the country’s most significant AI safety laws. The state opened a registration portal Tuesday, with which large frontier AI developers like Anthropic and OpenAI will be required to register by January 1, 2027. The RAISE Act , New York’s safety and transparency bill, kicks in at the start of the year. It mandates that large frontier developers — companies with more than $500 million in annual revenue — have to publish safety frameworks on their websites, report critical safety incidents within 72 hours, and issue public model transparency reports. The newly formed Office of Digital Innovation, Governance, Integrity, and Trust (DIGIT) will implement the RAISE Act and oversee large frontier AI labs. Penalties can be as high as $1 million for one violation and $3 million for subsequent violations. The state also can bring enforcement actions against companies that fail to register with the new portal, though a spokesperson declined to provide specifics. “Tech moguls tell us that their vision for AI is inevitable,” Governor Kathy Hochul said Tuesday during a press briefing. “They tell us get on board or get left behind… That any collateral damage is worth it as long as we win the race to the AI cliff.” On Tuesday, Hochul also launched the New York Center for AI Responsibility and Research based at State University of New York’s Binghamton University. The center will independently evaluate the safety, security, and operation of advanced AI systems and work with DIGIT to review companies’ safety frameworks. Hochul first announced the center in January with $55 million in donations and capital. “We’re building a national model for smart, sensible AI regulation, a model that puts communities above corporations and people above powerful technology,” Hochul said. The RAISE Act isn’t the only safety law New York has passed. Last year, the state began enforcing a law that requires AI companion operators to regularly let users know they’re talking to a bot, and to make reasonable efforts to detect suicidal ideation and self-harm. In October, Hochul signed a separate chatbot safety law for minors, restricting behaviors like deceptive human-like interactions, emotionally manipulative or sycophantic responses, and encouragement of behaviors like suicide or disordered eating. That law takes effect June 1, 2027. Other states have also passed similar AI safety and transparency bills to the RAISE Act. California’s SB 53, which took effect in January, mandates that frontier AI labs have in place and publish safety frameworks, enact whistleblower protections, and report critical safety incidents within 15 days. Illinois’ SB 315, which will go into effect at the start of 2027, has similar requirements, plus includes independent safety compliance audits. events.title: Proximal Ventures raises debut fund to back startups bringing AI to drug development
events.summary: While established venture firms continue to attract capital, first-time fund managers are facing one of the toughest fundraising environments in years. But that didn’t stop Sahir Raoof, a former SignalFire investor and executive at two healthcare startups, from raising $27.5 million for his first solo VC fund. Raoof’s firm, Proximal Ventures , is betting that AI can transform the tools, infrastructure, and services that support drug development. Pharmaceutical companies have historically outsourced various stages of drug development to specialized service providers, from synthesizing thousands of molecular compounds and figuring out how to manufacture drugs at scale to analyzing clinical trial data. “For a long time, the assumption was that pharma is not a great buyer of software, but a really good buyer of services,” Raoof told TechCrunch. Raoof believes AI could automate much of that work, creating an opportunity for startups to capture billions of dollars in pharmaceutical industry spending. By using AI, these companies could deliver the same services at a lower cost and in significantly less time, he said. Some of the most valuable applications of AI so far have been in service-oriented industries like law and finance, Raoof said. He sees similar opportunities in pharmaceutical services. Proximal plans to invest in pre-seed and seed-stage startups, writing checks from $500,000 to $1.5 million. The firm has already backed seven startups, including ChronicleBio, co-founded by former OpenAI executive Fidji Simo, which uses AI to analyze biological and medical data to better understand chronic diseases and identify potential treatments. Before spending two years as a principal at SignalFire, Raoof led business development at clinical trial recruitment startup Iterative Health and previously oversaw partnerships at Flatiron Health, an oncology data company acquired by Roche for $1.9 billion in 2018. “If you’re building a company that’s selling into the life sciences, one of the hardest things to do is starting that initial commercial flywheel,” Raoof said. His sales chops, deep understanding of the healthcare ecosystem, and extensive industry relationships gave limited partners, the investors in VC funds, the confidence that he could spot strong startups and help them land customers. Proximal’s backers include VC firms SignalFire and Kleiner Perkins, Bertelsmann Healthcare Investments, and individual investors such as Dimension Capital co-founders Nan Li and Zavain Dar. Amy Abernethy, co-founder of Highlander Health and former principal deputy commissioner of the FDA, is also an investor. She first met Raoof when they worked together at Flatiron Health, where she served as chief medical officer. She told TechCrunch that his ability to build relationships and spot industry bottlenecks made a lasting impression. Abernethy is convinced that his abilities, along with the understanding of what the healthcare market needs, will make him a successful investor. It is these qualities that have helped Proximal invest in startups alongside some of the better-known, much larger funds, she added. events.title: 3 charged with plotting terror attacks in U.S., Europe
events.summary: Three individuals were charged in connection with alleged Iranian-linked terror plots, including a September scheme against a British Royal Air Force Base that housed U.S. military personnel and aircraft, per an indictment unsealed Tuesday. The big picture: The indictment alleges that a leader of an Islamic terrorist group attempted to coordinate with his fellow defendants from jail by passing coded messages through third parties. The charges include conspiracy to provide material support to a Foreign Terrorist Organization, conspiracy to provide material support for acts of terrorism, attempted acts of terrorism across national boundaries and conspiracy to bomb a place of public use, among others. Driving the news: Since early in the year, the three men named in the indictment worked to commit terror attacks on behalf of an Iran-aligned terrorist network, the indictment alleges. The eight-count superseding indictment names Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood al-Saadi, a dual Iranian-Iraqi national; Mohsen Mohajeri, an Iranian national; and Mohammad Ali al-Hassani, an Iraqi national. It highlights nearly 20 attacks and attempted attacks, which included plots against Jewish institutions in Europe and the U.S. Al-Saadi was charged in May for working with the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and Kata'ib Hizballah, both of which the U.S. has designated as Foreign Terrorist Organizations. What's inside: Even after al-Saadi was arrested and transferred to U.S. custody, he allegedly passed coded messages to his fellow defendants in the days leading up to an attempted plot targeting the RAF Fairford base in England. The U.K. earlier this year allowed the U.S. to use RAF Fairford for limited defensive strikes against Iranian missile capabilities, elevating the base's position on the IRGC's radar . Al-Hassani and Mohajeri were in Iran at the time, but relied on a network of contacts in the U.K. whom Al-Hassani allegedly paid to prepare by acquiring vans and barrels of fuel and researching chemical accelerants in preparation for the Fairford attack, the indictment says. Catch up quick: British police arrested five men on suspicion of terrorism near the base back in September. Iran denied any involvement in the suspected plot at the time, Axios previously reported. What they're saying: "Today marks a major disruption of an alleged global terrorism conspiracy," Acting Principal Deputy Assistant Attorney General for National Security M. Scott Proctor said in a statement. Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional information.

events.title: X-energy gets green light to build its first small modular nuclear reactors
events.summary: Nuclear startup X-energy announced Monday that it had been given the go-ahead from federal officials to build its first four commercial reactors. The Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) approved the construction permit application for four of X-energy’s Xe-100 reactors at a Dow chemical plant in Texas. Each reactor will be capable of generating 80 megawatts of electricity and 200 megawatts of heat. X-energy says the approval is the first for an advanced nuclear reactor at an industrial site in the United States. The U.S. nuclear industry has pinned its hopes on small modular reactors — or SMRs — like those being developed by X-energy. By shrinking the reactor, proponents say it will speed construction and reduce costs, though those advantages have yet to be proven. No SMR is currently in operation in the U.S., and X-energy says Dow’s reactors won’t be operational until the early 2030s. X-energy claims that its reactor design, which flows helium gas over uranium-containing fuel pellets, is safer than many existing reactors, but the Union of Concerned Scientists questioned the claim and the speed with which X-energy received the permit. “The NRC only accomplished this feat by pushing consideration of critical safety questions to a later date—issues the NRC should’ve fully resolved before green lighting construction,” Edwin Lyman, director of nuclear power safety for the organization, said in a statement. The nuclear industry has benefited from strong interest from hyperscalers and data center developers, who are desperate for any and all sources of electricity. Amazon’s Climate Pledge Fund led X-energy’s $500 million Series C-1 , and the big tech company has also committed to buying 5 gigawatts of capacity from the nuclear startup. X-energy rode that wave of excitement earlier this year when its April initial public offering raised $1 billion. But since then, investors’ optimism has tempered. The hesitancy isn’t surprising: Nuclear power plants are expensive to build and can take years to complete. Eventually, X-energy hopes to rein in both time and cost, but its first reactors are likely to be pricey. The new permit approval gave X-energy a small jolt yesterday, though it was only enough to recover last week’s losses. The company’s shares are trading at less than half their initial offering price. events.title: Jensen Huang scheduled for Nvidia's GTC event as criticism and scrutiny increase
events.summary: Embattled Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang has cancelled plans to attend several technology summits, but he remains listed as the main speaker for his company's GTC event in Washington next month. He is scheduled to deliver the keynote address on the first day of Nvidia's flagship exhibition , running from December 1 to 3. That is assuming that Mr Huang, who admitted to having an affair with a woman who US investigators say is a Chinese spy, does not resign under intense public scrutiny. On Monday, his daughter, who also works for the company, scrapped plans to take part in a South Korean technology event because of the controversy surrounding her father. That led to awkward moments as reporters in South Korea pushed Nvidia employees for answers. 🚨 NVIDIA AI Day Seoul turns chaotic as reporters shout and scuffle while grilling executives on Madison Huang (Jensen Huang’s daughter) canceling her Korea trip. Officials dodge the questions and abruptly shut the event, slipping out the back door amid “family reasons” talk.… — nini (@ninimeili) November 9, 2026 Videos of reporters and photographers pursuing Nvidia officials with questions spread on social media. "Can you give us a statement?" at least one reporter shouted, shortly before a photographer appeared to bump into a wall as Nvidia staff members were leaving the venue in South Korea. Scrutiny of Nvidia's chief executive has only increased since Sunday, when he admitted to cheating on his wife. Over recent years, Mr Huang has irked officials in Washington by lobbying hard to change US technology export laws aimed at preventing countries such as China from obtaining some of the world's most powerful processors. Supporters of those laws say they protect the country's lead in the increasingly important AI race, and keep countries the US views as adversaries at a distance. Mr Huang, however, felt differently, and insisted that it hurt the US if the country's products were not used in certain markets such as China. His admission of a relationship with a technology executive, Alice Huang, whom the US has accused of being a spy for China, confirmed the worst fears of the Nvidia chief executive's critics. Reports in The New York Times , The Washington Post and Bloomberg have suggested that Nvidia exerted influence to try to end US government investigations into whether or not certain US technology was being smuggled into China. Democrats and Republicans in Congress, meanwhile, have increased calls for investigations into Mr Huang's affair and his company's actions in recent years. "If Jensen Huang was giving information to this individual that turns out was a Chinese spy, then yes, absolutely he put national security at risk," Republican Representative Brian Mast told reporters on Tuesday. On Monday, US President Donald Trump said he spoke with Mr Huang, and told reporters that Nvidia's chief executive insisted he did not know that Alice Huang was a spy. Critics of Mr Huang and Nvidia, however, say whether or not he knew she was a spy misses the point. Huang's 2025 Washington GTC revisited Almost a year ago, when he took the stage in Washington at the company's GPU Technology Conference exhibition, the atmosphere was remarkably different. The mood surrounding AI had yet to sour to the extent that it has among many in the US, and Mr Trump was encouraging US companies and technology executives to invest, build and not worry about regulations. At the same time, however, some White House officials and members of Congress were concerned about US technology potentially being obtained by China. “It’s hard not to be sentimental and proud of America …” For the first time ever Nvidia’s GTC took place in Washington, and the company’s CEO Jensen Huang made sure to drive that point home several times pic.twitter.com/PAzeqe5gMx — Cody Sigel Combs (@CodyCombsNEWS) October 28, 2025 Mr Huang never changed his tune, however, and kept pushing to be able to sell his company's powerful CPUs and GPUs to China. After speaking for almost two hours at the GTC exhibition, he later joined US Energy Secretary Chris Wright to talk about partnerships and take questions from reporters. "The benefit to the United States when it comes to American technology being available in China comes down to winning the hearts and minds of their developers," he said, insisting that more sales and the US "technology stack" becoming the global standard would offset any security risk. Mr Huang then boasted of Nvidia's history of working with China. "Nvidia has been in China for 30 years. They have been accommodating and they've been welcoming," he said. "Half of the world's AI researchers are in China." Mr Huang insisted that the US needed to work hard to provide technology to those customers. "That's to the benefit of the US." He was asked several times about concerns raised from some about the danger of selling US technology to China, which could hypothetically be used against the US. Mr Huang repeatedly disagreed with the premise of the questions. "America's Pentagon would never use some other technology from an adversarial country, neither will theirs. It's very sensible," he said. A few weeks later, Mr Trump said he agreed with Mr Huang and would change export policy to allow for China to buy some of Nvidia's H200 chips. Fast-forward to the current scandal and reports surrounding Nvidia, and it seems that Mr Huang's infidelity might be the least of anyone's worries. Instead, critics who accuse Nvidia of disregarding US national security might now insist that Mr Huang's liaison with an alleged spy is a symptom of poor governance at the company.

events.title: To thwart reverse engineering by agents, dev proposes blinding them
events.summary: Now that LLMs can help analyze commercial software binaries and recreate their functionality, one software developer and student has created a project designed to make this process more difficult. Timo Zhang's project is called Blind LLM Agents (BLA), and as its name suggests, it attempts to interfere with efforts by AI agents to scrutinize app code. "Coding agents can reverse-engineer shipped packages, CLIs, and WASM in minutes," Zhang told The Register in an email. "Classic obfuscation was built for humans and static tools, not LLMs that reason about meaning. Blind LLM Agents is a protection layer for that threat model." Such agents can also help developers build alternatives to existing commercial software. Last month, Artcraft , a two-person development shop, released seven open-source apps that aim to be replacements for Adobe's commercial apps Photoshop, Illustrator, Premiere Pro, Lightroom, After Effects, InDesign, and Acrobat Pro. Artcraft claims these apps are "clean-room reimplementations" written from scratch in Rust using Anthropic Opus 5.5. Setting aside the question of whether enlisting an AI model to reimplement an app really immunizes the creator from legal risk, those making apps face the possibility that someone will have an LLM probe published app binaries and reconstruct them through reverse engineering. There's in fact a framework for this, Reverse Engineer Anything (REA). Zhang has faced some criticism on social media for creating a limited barrier to copying other people's work (which at this point might simply be the work of another LLM). But not everyone accepts that all publicly accessible binaries should be easily available for review and reuse. BLA cannot prevent committed reverse engineering efforts, but it may add a bit of friction to the process when LLMs are involved. "It doesn't write app code — it hardens what you've already built," Zhang said. "A transform pipeline (plus MCP tools / an agent Skill) applies renaming, lane splitting, seed-derived string encryption, build polymorphism, WASM export renaming, decoys, self-seal integrity checks, and a coverage matrix that won't claim protection it can't prove. Behavior stays equivalent; recovery cost goes up." Zhang said various evaluations like red teaming and CrackMe challenges to recover keys or flags from hardened artifacts show that BLA is effective. "We also drive REA (a reverse-engineering agent) against those builds," he said. "Fail-to-break is the pass. CI tracks defense score, self-verifies integrity coverage, and checks functional equivalence. We raise the cost — we don't claim it is unbreakable." The project website says as much, noting that it raises the effort for analysis and adds decoy code, but doesn't promise protection against traditional interactive reverse engineering tools like Ghidra or Frida. Zhang said he's aware of other software projects that aim to interfere with AI, such as Poison Fountain for poisoning training data and Anubis for deterring bots and scraping. BLA, he said, is different. It's for hardening shipping code against reverse engineering and LLM-aided analysis. ®

events.title: Hot US inflation report seals Federal Reserve rate increase
events.summary: A hotter-than-expected inflation report has put new pressure on the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates at its December meeting, and a top policymaker said he expects the Iran war to have a lingering effect on energy costs. US government data on Tuesday showed Consumer Price Index inflation accelerated at a 0.4 per cent monthly pace in October, slower than its 0.6 pace in September but still above estimates. Core inflation, which excludes the volatile food and energy indices, rose at a 0.3 per cent monthly pace last month, also higher than forecasts. The Bureau of Labour Statistics did not submit a year-on-year measure due to the October 2025 government shutdown. Traders have virtually locked in odds for the Fed to raise rates in its final policy meeting of the year. About 90 per cent expect the Fed to raise interest rates by 25 basis points, while about 10 per cent expect a larger increase of 50 basis points, according to data from the CME Group. Driving these odds was Fed governor Christopher Waller , an influential member on the central bank's rate-setting committee, who said before the report's release thaat he would support raising rates by 50 basis points next month if October inflation held firm. It would be the Fed's largest rate increase since 2022. “Hiking only 25 basis points would put our credibility at risk; a risk I am not eager to take," Mr Waller told an event in the UK. Karl Schamotta, chief market strategist at Korpay, wrote in a note: “The last consumer inflation update before the Fed’s early December meeting took on added significance this morning when Governor Christopher Waller indicated he would vote for a rate hike." Dallas Fed president Lorie Logan, another voting member on the Federal Open Market Committee, also added to expectations of a December rate increase when she told an audience in Houston that she supports raising it at least two more times. “It may be possible to move more rapidly this winter than the FOMC has moved so far this fall,” Ms Logan said. The US central bank left interest rates unchanged in October after raising them by a quarter percentage point in September . Fed chairman Kevin Warsh at the time said the central bank remained committed to reining in inflation, which has remained above the Fed's 2 per cent target for more than five years. Last month's increases were driven by rising energy and food costs, which remain high due to Iran war. The Bureau of Labour Statistics said four of the six major grocery shop food group indexes increased last month, while one decreased. The energy index moderated from a 5.2 per cent increase in September to 0.7 per cent in October. “Grocery-store inflation accelerated notably after a string of quiescent readings, underscoring the lags between energy price shocks and non-energy consumer prices,” wrote Bernard Yaros, deputy chief US economist at Oxford Economics. US central bankers typically look through energy price shocks because they fade quickly, although the nine-month conflict in the Middle East has – for now – reset that perspective. “And there are reasons to also expect elevated energy prices to persist,” Mr Waller said. “First, even as there is increased tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, that traffic is moving at great expense." Mr Waller said maritime insurance to pass through the waterway, and the ship-to-ship transfer of oil to guard against Iranian attacks, are reportedly raising oil prices by between $20 and $30 a barrel. Mr Waller, who was a finalist for the Fed chairman job last year, said diesel oil production is affected by limited refining capacity and other restraints. “As a consequence, elevated prices for diesel in the United States are not expected to moderate as readily as crude oil prices would in a more peaceful Middle East,” he said. The yield on the 10-year Treasury, a benchmark for borrowing costs, climbed back to 5 per cent after the CPI inflation report, while the yield on the 30-year Treasury rose more than 10 basis points to 5.36 per cent. The yield on the two-year Treasury, which is sensitive to short-term Fed rate moves, climbed 19 basis points to 4.736 per cent. Major indexes on Wall Street were all trading in the red, continuing a period of volatility spurred by Democrats' sweeping midterms victory last week. The dollar gained against a basket of currencies. Prices for spot gold and silver fell. Current projections from the Fed show they expect rates to remain steady at 4.1 per cent in 2027 before slowly easing in 2028. The Fed's preferred inflation metric is forecast to end the year at 3.7 per cent before moderating to 2.3 per cent in 2027 and 2.1 per cent in 2028. Central bankers are set to update those forecasts next month.

events.title: Progressives confront their limited leverage as they take on Democratic leaders
events.summary: The News By Corbin Trent’s estimate, he’s spending 15 hours a day on a cause that has animated the left ever since Democrats won huge majorities in the House and Senate: urging them to dump their leaders. Trent, a former spokesman for Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, has some well-known allies in his long-shot campaign to oust Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries. They include actor Mark Ruffalo, former Ocasio-Cortez chief of staff Saikat Chakrabarti, and countless progressive influencers. But they don’t include Ocasio-Cortez, who underscored on Tuesday that she’s backing Jeffries. Even Trent acknowledged that what legions of online progressives are asking for — the rejection of leaders who just presided over Democratic landslides — is unlikely to happen. “I reckon it’s about a 10% chance on Schumer and a 3% chance on Jeffries,” Trent told Semafor. “What matters, and matters a lot, is making it loud and clear that voters asked for something else. That it is being denied to them. If you’ve ever got a chance to beat these folks, you need votes.” Theoretically, the votes to shake up leadership are at least within reach. Informal whip counts and hallway interviews confirm that dozens of newly elected Democrats are interested in challengers to the two New Yorkers who occasionally break from the left. But realistically, the battle to replace Jeffries and Schumer was built for a disappointing election , not a landslide. And the obstacles of the anti-leadership campaign are revealing the limited reach of a progressive movement that wants to pick the next presidential nominee. Critics of Schumer haven’t given up on enlisting Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen to challenge him, but no Democrat has stepped up to take on Jeffries. Even if Van Hollen mounts a campaign, it will be a massive uphill climb for progressives to deny Schumer the votes in next month’s closed-door vote. The left’s chances of defeating Jeffries are even lower. But by forcing the question, progressives hope to either pull off a miracle — or at least, keep an argument going. Activists believe that they, not Schumer and Jeffries, put in the work to win the biggest Democratic victories in decades. The progressive media outlets that exploded after the party’s 2024 loss to Trump are now watching the leaders take credit for what they think their movement built. Their message is consistent: That voters who want “change” and support progressive ideas will stay engaged only if the leadership changes and President Donald Trump is forced to veto big progressive bills. At last week’s post-election Crooked Con, a gathering of progressive activists, strategists, influencers, and podcast addicts, the demand for new leaders hung in the air. Attendees walking up to the Washington Convention Center on Saturday were offered leaflets about stopping bipartisan permitting reform moving through the Senate, warning that it would speed up the building of “immigrant detention centers.” (The bill advanced two days later.) Inside, there were excited murmurs whenever a Democrat was asked about replacing Schumer or Jeffries. Pressed by Pod Save America co-host Jon Lovett on whether she would challenge Schumer, Michigan Sen. Elissa Slotkin gave a winding answer that didn’t rule it out — but suggested that Schumer could win her over. “Look, if he wants to be majority leader, what is your plan for the first 100 days?” she said. “How are you going to do things differently so that Democrats get their sh*t together?” That got muted applause from an audience ready to join an insurgency. There was much more excitement when Rep.-elect Milat Kiros of Colorado said there had been a “mandate” for change, not for current leadership; Kiros unseated Rep. Diana DeGette in one of the left’s biggest primary wins. Everywhere he went, Van Hollen was asked if he would challenge Schumer. In a short interview with Semafor, he disputed the idea that the leader had earned the job already by electing between seven and nine new Democratic senators. “I’m glad that the DSCC and Senate Majority PAC raised a lot of money,” Van Hollen told Semafor. “I mean, their Republican counterparts raised even more money. I think the lesson from this election was, this was people power over money.” The scale of the Democratic wins has made the entire push trickier. “Look, we had a wonderful, wonderful outcome,” said Maurice Mitchell, the president of the Working Families Party, which clashed with DC Democrats over primaries in the Midwest and California. “It’s almost like it would be greedy of me to want better outcomes. But I know there were elections that could have been won if we were able to move as a united front.” David’s view The modern left is at its most powerful inside the Democratic Party after the party screws things up. Hillary Clinton’s defeat convinced many Democrats, even his Senate colleagues, that Sanders would have won the presidency, and his populist ideas were more popular than whatever it was she ran on. Kamala Harris’ defeat was even more empowering for Sanders, whose “Fight Oligarchy” rallies brought out hundreds of thousands of people. After victory, the left’s challenge is twofold. One: Schumer and Jeffries didn’t blow it. They are no longer the brittle wimps who were protesting outside of federal buildings last year and insisting they’d “fight” Trump. They beat him. Two: Democrats really did listen to them. Last year’s government shutdown fight, while it did not end as progressives wanted it to, was about healthcare funding — the sort of life-or-death economic issue the left wanted to focus on. The eventual Democratic themes of the election were “costs, chaos, and corruption” and “fighting for an affordable America.” What’s worth watching most closely right now is how upstart progressive media — Hasan Piker, Drop Site, Lever, Majority Report, and other influencers — approach all this. Left-leaning media has a much larger reach than it did eight years ago, when Democrats last assembled for an open presidential primary. They have willed a “leadership challenge” story into existence when most of DC thinks they’re bound to fail. They aren’t done. Room for Disagreement The challenge of actually replacing leaders who just won is already weighing on progressives, who are already asking themselves whether they’re undercutting their own allies. “People are doing what they should be doing, which is swing for the fences. Go after leadership, if that’s what people want to do. But if we don’t get that, we can’t just let it destroy us emotionally,” former New York Rep. Jamaal Bowman told Don Lemon on Monday. events.title: Speech Processing Pioneer Bishnu Saroop Atal Dies at 93
events.summary: Bishnu Saroop Atal Acoustics and signal processing pioneer Life Fellow, 93; died 19 August Atal was an acoustics and signal processing researcher at Bell Labs in Murray Hill, N.J., and later at AT&T ’s Shannon Laboratory, in Florham Park, N.J. His pioneering work on voice-coding techniques became the foundation for efficient, high-quality voice transmission over cellular networks. He received the 2013 IEEE Jack S. Kilby Signal Processing Medal for “fundamental and pioneering contributions to speech coding.” He joined Bell Labs in 1961 as a communications researcher, and his early work there focused on speaker identification technology. During the 1960s he helped develop linear predictive coding , a powerful method for analyzing and compressing speech. LPC is now the most widely used method for encoding speech at a low bit rate. Atal developed increasingly sophisticated low-bit-rate speech-coding techniques. They included multipulse LPC , which improved the quality of compressed speech. Bishnu Saroop Atal Nokia Bell Labs He also worked with his colleague Manfred R. Schroeder to develop code-excited linear prediction , a method for producing high-quality speech at very low bit rates. CELP became a foundational technique in modern speech coding, letting digital communications systems carry voice using less bandwidth. The extra efficiency expanded cellular capacity, allowing wireless networks to handle more simultaneous calls. Later in his career, he led the acoustics and speech research departments at Bell. The company named him a Fellow in 1994. When AT&T Bell Laboratories split into separate research organizations in 1996, Atal continued his career at the AT&T Florham Park headquarters, and he was named a Fellow the following year. He retired in 2002 and became an affiliate professor of electrical engineering at the University of Washington , in Seattle. There he continued his research in speech processing, speech recognition, and high-dimensional computing. Atal was elected to the National Academy of Engineering in 1987 and the National Academy of Sciences in 1993. He received numerous awards including the 2018 International Speech Communication Association Medal for Scientific Achievement and a 2003 medal from the Franklin Institute . He received a bachelor’s degree in physics in 1952 from the University of Lucknow , in India, and a master’s degree in 1955 in electrical engineering from the Indian Institute of Science , in Bengaluru. While working full time at Bell he earned a Ph.D. in EE in 1968 from the Polytechnic Institute of Brooklyn (now New York University’s Tandon engineering school ), in New York City. Darryl Palmer Jr. Chair of the IEEE Central Illinois Section Senior member, 55; died 30 August Palmer was a dedicated IEEE volunteer, serving as chair of the Central Illinois Section and as the government relations chair of Region 4 . He was a member of the IEEE Industrial Electronics Society and its industrial activity committee. He also served as associate editor of the IEEE Transactions on Industrial Informatics . In 1986, at age 16, Palmer completed a summer internship at NASA’s Glenn Research Center , in Cleveland. He helped develop FoilSim , an interactive educational software program that introduces aerodynamic engineering to preuniversity students. While studying computer science at Cleveland State University in 1996, he joined the university’s Allen-Bradley PLC lab as a research assistant. He designed hardware and software systems for the Glenn Research Center to collect and process thermal wave imaging data. He also designed software for General Motors ’ North American robotic and welding division. In 1999 he completed a second internship at the research center and helped develop EngineSim , an educational software program that models jet engine design and testing. For his work, NASA recognized him with a Space Act Award . In 2000 he earned his bachelor’s degree in computer science and became a software engineer at the Danfoss Drives manufacturing facility in Loves Park, Ill. He worked on embedded control systems for variable-frequency drives and high-power equipment. He also developed sensorless control technology for beam pumps used in the oil and gas industry. In 2014 Palmer and his wife, Alexandra “Sasha” Goodwin , founded Janus Choice, a health technology platform that matches hospital patients with post-acute care facilities. He served as its CEO until the company closed in 2020. From 2018 to 2023, he was a lead software engineer at Adept Coalescence , a startup in Rockford, Ill., focused on developing front-end software for control systems. He then worked in Peoria, Ill., as a control systems team lead at Caterpillar , a manufacturer of construction and mining equipment. Henry Leopold Richter Telecommunications engineer Life senior member, 99; died 12 August Richter was a spacecraft engineer at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory , in Pasadena, Calif., before starting his own public safety communications consultancy. He earned a bachelor’s degree and a Ph.D. at Caltech in 1952 and 1956, respectively. In 1955 he joined JPL as an engineer and supervisor of its new circuit elements group. Later, he was assigned to NASA’s Explorer program as project manager for satellite design, serving as a liaison between the organization’s satellite instrumentation group and its operations and data groups. Since 1958 the program has launched more than 90 missions for physics, geophysics, and astrophysics research. As NASA prepared to launch Explorer 1 in January 1958, Richter worked with the San Gabriel Valley Radio Club in Los Angeles to set up stations across the United States to track the satellite. He eventually was named JPL section chief and was responsible for scientific instruments on the lunar Ranger, Surveyor , and Mariner programs. He also helped develop NASA’s Deep Space Network , an international tracking and communications system. Richter left NASA to become vice president and technical director of Xerox Electro-Optical Systems , in Pasadena, Calif. In the mid-1970s, he joined the Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department as a communications engineer, overseeing the department’s microwave and mobile radio networks. He later ran a telecommunications consulting practice for more than 20 years. His clients included federal, state, and local government agencies, school districts, universities, and organizations. His work covered strategic technology planning and the design and implementation of public safety radio, microwave, CCTV, and paging systems. He wrote several books including America’s Leap Into Space: My Time at JPL and the First Explorer Satellites (2015), a personal account of his experience working on the Explorer 1 and America’s space program. In 2019 the Radio Club of America presented him with its Lifetime Achievement Award for “significant achievements and a major body of work that has advanced the art and science of wireless technology.” R
