Nancy Pelosi’s replacement is ready to regulate AI —Grace Huckins As a California state senator, Scott Wiener authored legislation aimed at curbing the risks of advanced AI. Now, after winning a tight congressional race for Nancy Pelosi’s open San Francisco seat, he could play a key role in setting federal AI policy. I spoke with Wiener only a few hours after he had been declared the victor. But he was already thinking about AI risk: during our 20-minute conversation, he used the phrase “recursive self-improvement” half a dozen times.  “We need to slow this down,” he told me. “Because it’s moving very quickly, and we could sleepwalk into a disaster.” Still, he describes himself as only “cautiously optimistic” about Congress’s ability to rein in AI. Here’s what he plans to do about it . The backlash about data centers might really just be about electricity  —James O’Donnell As voters went to the polls across the US last week, I was in Ashburn, Virginia, part of what’s known as Data Center Alley—the world’s largest data center hub. But a few days in Ashburn convinced me the real fault line may be electricity: drawing it from the grid or generating it onsite provokes different forms of blowback. events.title: Wall Street bonuses set to grow after banner year for IPOs and AI
events.summary: A word of caution for Wall Streeters planning how to spend their year-end bonuses: This may be as good as it gets for a while. Bonuses at big banks and investment houses are set to grow again thanks to a blockbuster year of historic IPOs, AI financings, and zippy markets, according to pay consultancy Johnson Associates, whose annual bonus report is required reading across the financial industry. But the AI trade is now starting to sour, interest rates are rising, and last week’s Democratic gains may darken the backdrop for 2027. Even this year’s bumper crop will be shared unevenly, tilted more heavily toward the best performers rather than spread “peanut-butter-like” across and within divisions, Alan Johnson told Semafor. “Firms now value the best people more than they ever have, and value the average person less,” he said. “Nobody is going to wring their hands if an average performer is complaining — ‘don’t let the door hit you on the way out.’” Financial executives are keen to avoid the trap of 2021, when their efforts to gift-wrap the fruits of a banner year as special, one-time bonuses got baked into expectations anyway, with predictable howling in 2022 . — Liz Hoffman

events.title: Wall Street is unbothered by Nvidia's Jensen Huang scandal
events.summary: Wall Street giants have hundreds of billions of dollars riding on Jensen Huang, but sound remarkably unfazed by the trouble the company is in. Goldman Sachs CEO David Solomon said on CNBC that the key-man concerns around Huang are overblown. “I don’t think the ecosystem is centered around one individual,” Solomon said. “I think no matter how this plays out, Nvidia will continue to be a great and important American company.” Goldman is part of the Wall Street consortium that has committed to raising $500 billion to help Nvidia finance the AI buildout, an alliance that will allow the company’s ambitions to outrun even its own healthy balance sheet. The other five finance heavyweights in the group — BlackRock, Brookfield, Blackstone, KKR, and Apollo — either didn’t provide a comment when asked about Nvidia’s troubles, or pointed to Solomon’s remarks. Meanwhile, the tech-heavy Nasdaq closed up nearly 3% Monday and shares of hyperscalers and neoclouds like CoreWeave soared, perhaps on the theory that the scandal could bring tougher export controls on chips, leaving more supply for US buyers. — Ellen DiMauro

events.title: Evolving metal extraction processes
events.summary: The metals industry has experienced transformational moments before: the Bessemer process, flash smelting, electric arc furnaces, and modern continuous casting all changed what was possible. Yet, for more than a century, most extraction processes rely on techniques and pathways that would be familiar to metallurgists from generations ago. Processes have become larger and control systems smarter, but the fundamental science behind separating metals from ores has changed less than many realize. Today’s materials challenges are different from those of the 20th century, but why are critical metals still produced using largely the same scientific foundations? EvoMaterials, a technology platform developed by Outokumpu—the global leader in sustainable stainless steel and the producer of ferrochrome with 67% lower carbon footprint than the industry average—is exploring that question by rethinking how metals can be extracted: “We decided to go beyond the current constraints and look fundamentally at what’s the best way to do this with the benefit of the scientific engineering knowledge and hindsight that we have today,” says Caspar Stinn, technical director for extractive metallurgy at Outokumpu. “We’re looking at how we can reimagine metals production.” A supply chain problem disguised as a materials problem As economies expand and the world becomes increasingly electrified, data and scientific models point to rising demand for many minerals, driven by technologies ranging from data centers to aerospace, water treatment, energy systems, and defence. According to Antoine Allanore, professor of metallurgy at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) this coincides with many Western economies having reduced their domestic processing capacity for the very metals those industries depend on. Metallurgy is now strategically important, shaped not only by cost and availability but also by carbon footprint, geographic origin and supply-chain resilience. That reality is particularly relevant for chromium and other specialty metals used in high-temperature and extreme environments. Chromium-based materials play a critical role in aerospace systems, power generation, corrosion-resistant infrastructure and defense technologies, where materials must perform under demanding conditions. Beyond optimization For decades, metallurgical innovation largely focused on improving yields, energy efficiency and process control. EvoMaterials is based on the idea that some metallurgical processes may benefit from entirely different chemical pathways. The platform originates from research into sulfidation-based processing technologies, initially pursued to reduce carbon emissions associated with ferrochrome production. Laboratory work revealed broader potential. Lab-scale trials demonstrated that these alternative process chemistries could potentially do more than lower emissions. They could recover valuable metals from lower grade resources and industrial side streams while fundamentally altering how separation processes are performed. The opportunity is to rethink how mineral resources are used and how much value can be extracted from them, bringing in greater resource efficiency and stronger industrial competitiveness. Understanding traditional smelting vs. new proprietary technology Source : Outokumpu Development of the technology began in the United States in 2021 for chromite from Outokumpu’s Kemi mine in Finland, the only chrome mine in the European Union and one of the few such operations across the Western world. Since then, Outokumpu has evolved the technology through extensive research and development, combining new process chemistries with proprietary metallurgical expertise, supported in part by a non-exclusive patent license agreement from MIT. “The technology is a new application for separating metallic elements from materials,” explains Allanore. Historically, that separation has been achieved using carbon- and energy-intensive approaches. The new method creates a different chemical environment that enables more efficient extraction with fewer losses and fewer unwanted by-products, recovering critical materials from resources considered waste. Innovation happens at the boundaries EvoMaterials sits at the intersection of several scientific disciplines, a combination that strongly resonates with Stinn, who completed his PhD in Materials Science and Engineering at MIT, where his research focused on low-carbon metals processing and recycling technologies. Modern materials innovation draws on a growing mix of chemistry, materials science, physics, computational modeling, and engineering. With advanced simulation tools and AI helping researchers identify promising directions, scientific discovery still depends on experimentation and testing in the lab—on getting your hands dirty and doing the hard work. “Science today is much more interdisciplinary than it was, and the collaboration across disciplines reveals new scientific opportunities,” says Stinn. Engineering can translate those opportunities into more efficient and cost-competitive metals production. Building a technology platform A technically significant aspect of EvoMaterials is that it’s not a single process, but a technology platform. Allanore compares EvoMaterials to platform technologies in other industries, where a single scientific breakthrough can enable multiple downstream applications. Once a new extraction pathway has been mastered for one material system, the same scientific principles may be adapted to entirely different metals and mineral resources. The initial application becomes only the starting point. “The future and the potential impact might be much broader than the original and current developments that are happening,” Allanore explains. That possibility is increasingly important as industries seek secure supplies of nickel, chromium, molybdenum, and other strategic materials needed for advanced manufacturing. The future of materials companies The broader implication extends beyond metallurgy. Companies that develop proprietary process technologies may create value through production but also through intellectual property and scientific expertise. Based on Outokumpu’s technology leadership, that transition could create entirely new categories of value, enabling the production of high-value critical materials from ores and resource streams that previously appeared uneconomical or inaccessible. The result would be a fundamental shift in how metals are manufactured, where sustainability, resource efficiency, supply security, and economic value become outcomes of the same technological architecture rather than separate objectives. The next step for EvoMaterials is pilot-scale validation, with a pilot plant in New Hampshire to begin operations in the first half of 2027. The facility will scale the proprietary technology from laboratory to one-ton production, providing a step toward industrial-scale deployment targete

events.title: Ransomware threat blares from Vanderbilt University computers during cyberattack
events.summary: Classes at Vanderbilt University are proceeding as scheduled today, although access to most university systems remains restricted following a cyberattack claimed by ransomware group BYOD. Vanderbilt announced on Monday morning that it was dealing with "an active cybersecurity incident," and that the fallout may affect university devices, systems, and cloud-based services. The Nashville-based university initially told students and staff to shut down university devices and disconnect from campus Wi-Fi. It warned them to watch for unexpected prompts, altered files or permissions, unfamiliar applications, and unsolicited authentication requests. Campus computers reportedly began playing an audio threat attributed to BYOD. Student newspaper The Vanderbilt Hustler cited posts on campus social network Fizz showing the message. "You have been compromised by BYOD," the recording said. "We suggest you reach out to us as soon as possible. Instructions have been placed on your desktop. Failure to communicate will result in this estate being brought to the ground completely. Make the right choice or rot with the wrong one." By Monday evening, Vanderbilt had restored access to campus Wi-Fi, but warned that access to most systems remains restricted. "We know this has disrupted important work and caused frustration across the university," it said . "Vanderbilt Information Technology is working with government agencies and other partners to manage this situation." Students were told to attend classes as scheduled on Tuesday and contact instructors about flexibility on coursework deadlines. Staff were instructed to report to work normally. Vanderbilt's Athletics department said that its ticketing system was unavailable, and that students were unable to claim tickets for the college's football game against Alabama on Saturday. BYOD claimed responsibility for the attack on Vanderbilt on Monday, along with extensive data theft. "If you could not tell already, your databases are locked [and] we have your entire estate and research data," it said via its leak site. "Over 1 million SSNs, full names, email addresses, phone numbers, student and employee records, full takeover of your DC, whatever was on your network, we possess." Vanderbilt has not confirmed BYOD's claims about the extent of its access or the data allegedly stolen. BYOD may be a familiar name to some. The group previously claimed attacks on the University of New Mexico and Trump Mobile's customer database . BYOD also claimed responsibility on Monday for an attack on Texas Health and Human Services. The agency has not publicly confirmed an incident and did not immediately respond to our questions. ®

The telecoms company is pushing for AI-led growth, with the launch of a strategic project to develop and expand digital infrastructure capacity within the UAE and abroad. Etisalat has also announced a commercial service that increases upload speeds to smartphones threefold, boosting the UAE's push towards the next-generation 6G standard for mobile communications.

events.title: COP should put itself out of business
events.summary: Tim’s view In the decade since the Paris Agreement, the annual round of UN climate summits has seemed like a parallel universe, increasingly out of touch with geopolitics and the real economy. Between the idealism-bordering-on-naivete, and the impenetrable thicket of acronyms, jargon, and obscure treaty provisions, “sometimes I come into negotiation rooms and the contrast with the real world cannot be any bigger,” Ali Mohamed, Kenya’s special climate envoy, told me here. There are still many people here at COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye, this week who would love to see the oil and gas industry shuttered tomorrow, energy access and prices be damned. Fossil fuel companies’ record-breaking profits this year are proof that, like it or not, the world still needs a lot of this stuff. While the Iran war certainly did drive some countries to accelerate their adoption of renewables, the global reprioritization of energy security means “there is no doubt we’re backsliding” on the goal adopted at COP28, in Dubai, to transition away from fossil fuels, Mohamed said. And needless to say, nothing that happens at COP has any real legally binding force on any country. So what’s it all for? I’ve asked myself this question a lot in the past 48 hours, while navigating Antalya’s maddeningly overwhelmed transit system (although I will say the COP venue itself, if you can manage to get inside, is the nicest one we’ve had in years). One answer is that pragmatism was never the point. Idealism is a feature of UN summits, not a bug, Eurasia Group analyst María José Valverde said: “COP goals aren’t designed to be achieved. It’s about where we want to take humanity.” Another answer is that, while it may not get headlines, “there’s still all kinds of shit happening behind the scenes,” as one diplomat put it to me this morning, from deals on clean cooking stoves in Africa to negotiations among European countries to remove bureaucratic barriers between their rail networks that force more commercial traffic onto dirtier highways. And while it may not be happening at activists’ preferred pace, clean energy adoption already driving a tangible transition away from fossil fuels. That’s in spite of a surge in overall energy demand that has made it harder to displace any one source. In the absence of all renewables that have been built since 2010, the International Energy Agency reported last week , global fossil fuel demand in 2025 would have been 8% higher, “an amount equivalent to India’s total energy consumption.” The big goal for this particular COP is to drive this trend forward by getting countries to agree on a target to raise the share of total global energy demand served by electricity from 23% today to 35% by 2035. That’s basically another version of the fossil fuel transition goal, viewed through the opposite end of the kaleidoscope, which could be more palatable to the oil-producing countries that are usually the spoilers here. Whatever is negotiated here will, again, be nonbinding. And it’s impossible to say precisely what role COP, per se, has had in the pace of the clean energy rollout up to now. But to the extent that these meetings mainly serve to send long-term political signals that buttress — if not dictate — the economic signals companies use to make energy investment decisions, the best outcome for COP is to put itself out of business, as clean energy projects increasingly beat fossil fuels on merits unrelated to environmental ideology. “In the real world, things are happening and not waiting for the negotiations,” Mohamed said. “The transition is going to happen whether you want it to or not.” Notable In December, new US Commerce Department rules will make it costlier to import Chinese manufacturing components for solar panels, as part of an effort to make it harder for US solar firms to rely on China.

events.title: Smart meters to cost the UK billions: 2G switch-off means replacing 12-13 million
events.summary: Between 12 and 13 million UK smart meters could stop working properly when 2G and 3G networks are switched off by 2033, and replacing them all is likely to cost around £4 billion ($5.3 billion). Smart meters have long been a controversial topic thanks to the British government's botched rollout of the technology; they were supposed to be fitted into 80 percent of households by 2020. But numerous delays and technical hitches, such as consumers finding their meter stopped being smart if they switched energy supplier , hindered progress. Now, a report from connectivity biz Wirepas, "The European Connectivity Trilemma," shows that it isn't just Brits who have problems, but that other European countries also have their share of smart meter issues and that no two countries have adopted the same approach. The UK's issues center on the fact that early meters used 2G or 3G cellular connections to transmit energy usage back to the supplier. These continued to be fitted until 4G versions began arriving at the end of 2024, the report says. This issue was covered by The Register back in 2023 , and again in 2024 . However, the government had already announced measures to phase out 2G and 3G networks by 2033 several years earlier, back in 2021, so it was known that any meters being fitted would have a limited lifespan. In fact, 3G services have now already been withdrawn by the networks , and they all plan to phase out 2G ahead of the 2033 deadline . BT/EE will begin closing its network from May 2029, VMO2 will start the same summer, and Vodafone aims to switch off in spring 2030. The report claims the UK now faces two substantial areas of expenditure as a result. The first covers newer, second generation (SMETS2) meters, where only the communications module needs swapping out, but even this is likely to cost £1.3 to £1.4 billion (c $1.7 to $1.9 billion) before the hardware cost of each new hub is even factored in. The other is for an estimated 7 million older, first-generation (SMETS1) meter installations, which have the cellular comms hard-wired in, so the whole meter typically needs replacing. The report authors estimate this will cost another £2.1 billion to £2.45 billion ($2.8 billion to $3.3 billion), at an indicative replacement cost of £300 to £350 per installation. This results in the estimated £4 billion in gross replacement costs, which will ultimately feed into household energy bills, adding to the very costs the government is currently trying to reduce. We asked the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero (DESNZ), which oversees smart meters, for comment. A spokesperson said: "Smart meters are already helping millions of consumers manage their energy and save money on bills," they told The Reg . "The transition to 4G is a planned upgrade that will continue to deliver the benefits that smart meters already provide to households and industry." While some of these older meters would naturally have been due for replacement as part of normal asset renewal cycles, the cell network shutdown makes the replacement program unavoidable and dictates when much of the expenditure must occur. According to the report, the SMETS2 replacement largely applies to central and southern Britain, as second-gen meters in the north use a long-range radio network and are not subject to the 2G/3G cut-off. However, the issue of older SMETS1 meters applies nationwide. Wirepas' interest in all of this is that it specializes in IoT connectivity and is pushing NR+ as a solution to the issue. Based on the DECT-2020 New Radio standard developed by the European Telecommunication Standards Institute (ETSI), this is designed to be scalable and operates in the license-exempt and globally available 1.9GHz part of the spectrum. When 4G technology reaches the end of its life, (which isn't likely to happen until the 2040s, and there is no planned date) the UK's smart meters will need to be replaced once again, the report asserts. However, this is sufficiently far in the future that it is unlikely to trouble policymakers anytime soon. ®

events.title: China’s trade surplus soars past $1T
events.summary: China’s trade surplus passed $1 trillion for the first 10 months of the year, as the country’s exports grew at record speed despite several countries putting up trade barriers. Flatlining consumption at home has pushed Chinese manufacturers to find customers abroad, fueling anger in foreign markets over their domestic industries being hollowed out. Soaring fuel prices caused by the Iran war have also helped drive demand: China’s EV and plug-in hybrid exports for October surged 145% year-on-year. AI-related exports have also jumped. Beijing, meanwhile, is unlikely to accede to US and European calls to bolster its domestic demand, with one asset manager telling the South China Morning Post he did not think the country’s “macro policy stance will change significantly .” — Jeronimo Gonzalez

events.title: ExxonMobil eyes Venezuela return after two decades
events.summary: ExxonMobil signalled it would resume operations in Venezuela almost two decades after leaving the country, a boost for Washington’s campaign to increase oil and gas output in its de facto protectorate. While crude production has risen moderately since the US ousted Venezuela’s president in January, it remains far below its 1990s peak, held back by outdated infrastructure and a lack of experienced workers: Exxon’s boss called the country “ uninvestable ” just a few months ago. Oil majors fear that Venezuela — which has the world’s largest stated reserves — is still too politically unstable to commit billions of dollars to its economy, though the recent return of opposition leader María Corina Machado and her push for elections may help assuage those concerns . — Jeronimo Gonzalez

events.title: Honda reports robust results on the back of healthy motorcycle sales
events.summary: Honda has reported a 66% rise in net profit for the first half of its fiscal year, driven by strong motorcycle sales TOKYO -- Honda’s net profit rose 66% in the first half of its fiscal year, the Japanese automaker reported Tuesday, driven by strong motorcycle sales. Tokyo-based Honda Motor Co. reported a profit of 516.76 billion yen ($3.3 billion) for the six months through September, up from 311.83 billion yen a year earlier. First half sales rose 13% to 12 trillion yen from 10.6 trillion yen. The robust results came despite costs in its electric vehicle program, where it dropped some models. Honda said EV-related losses erased 484.8 billion yen from its operating profits. But officials stressed that Honda expects battery EVs might eventually become more popular and it will remain flexible enough to switch to EV production in the future. Honda raised its full-year operating profit forecast to 780 billion yen from 650 billion yen. Honda attributed the more optimistic forecast to favorable exchange rates and efforts to reduce the impact of U.S. tariffs, including shifting production to the United States. The maker of the Super Cub motorcycle and Accord sedan also announced major production investments in North America and Brazil. Honda plans to build a new auto production plant in Ohio, increasing production capacity in North America to 1.91 million vehicles by 2029 from 1.67 million. The company expects U.S. demand to grow, especially for its hybrid models. events.title: Grand Theft Auto VI is almost here. What to know about the characters, music and billions at stake
events.summary: Grand Theft Auto VI is set to release on Nov. 19, marking a return to the neon-lit streets of Vice City LOS ANGELES -- LOS ANGELES (AP) — Grand Theft Auto has never been much for following the rules. Nearly three decades after a video game built around stealing cars, outrunning police and embracing criminal mayhem first arrived, the franchise has survived controversy, transformed open-world gaming and become one of the biggest sellers in entertainment. Now, after a 13-year wait since its last main installment, Grand Theft Auto VI is preparing for another big score. The latest chapter arrives Nov. 19 with a return to the neon-soaked streets of Vice City with two protagonists. For longtime fans, GTA VI is a highly anticipated return. For everyone else, here’s what to know about the blockbuster video game, its characters and the enormous business riding on its release: The franchise began in 1997 as a relatively simple, top-down game that allowed players to roam fictional cities, steal vehicles, evade police and commit crimes. The release of Grand Theft Auto III in 2001 helped redefine open-world gaming. It gave players greater freedom to explore a sprawling three-dimensional city, pursue missions and interact with their surroundings. Later installments expanded that freedom with larger environments, cinematic storytelling, social satire and detailed worlds. The influence reached far beyond games about stealing cars. Ubisoft’s Assassin’s Creed series brought open-world exploration to historical settings, while Bethesda’s The Elder Scrolls games expanded their own longstanding tradition of open-ended fantasy role-playing. Nintendo’s The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild later emphasized experimentation and discovery, allowing players to use the environment itself to solve problems. For Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas and Grand Theft Auto V, Rockstar Games recruited real-life gang members to help bring authenticity to background characters and dialogue. Former writer and audio director Lazlow Jones has said some performers challenged scripted lines, prompting developers to let them use language drawn from their own experiences. That attention to detail helped create the sense of a living world that became a hallmark of the franchise, even as the series drew criticism for its depictions of violence, crime and women. But controversy did not stop the franchise’s commercial rise. According to publisher Take-Two Interactive, the franchise has sold more than 470 million units worldwide. Grand Theft Auto V, released in 2013, accounts for more than 230 million of those units and reached $1 billion in retail sales in just three days. Its online multiplayer component, Grand Theft Auto Online, has helped keep players engaged through years of updates, new activities and in-game purchases. This time, the action returns to Vice City, Rockstar’s fictional version of Miami, and expands across the surrounding state of Leonida, a Florida-inspired setting filled with beaches, highways, nightlife and criminal enterprises. At the center are Lucia Caminos and Jason Duval, a couple trying to improve their circumstances through a life of crime. Lucia has recently been released from prison while Jason, a former soldier who became involved with drug runners in the Leonida Keys, is looking for a different path. Their plans become more complicated when a seemingly straightforward criminal job goes wrong, drawing them into a conspiracy that stretches across Leonida. Baby buried alive for 24 hours released from the hospital; father charged House tables Hegseth impeachment, effectively killing it in current Congress Wisconsin state trooper detained by ICE The trailers suggest a story mixing romance, robberies, betrayals and the series’ familiar satirical take on American culture. Rockstar has revealed several supporting characters, including bank robber Raul Bautista, aspiring music executive Dre’Quan Priest and nightclub owner Boobie Ike. Rockstar has kept much of the voice cast under wraps, including the performers behind Lucia and Jason. One familiar actor has confirmed his involvement: Stephen Root , known for his work in “Office Space,” “King of the Hill” and “Barry.” He told The Associated Press in September that he appears in the game, adding that fans had already recognized his distinctive voice in promotional footage. Root has been identified in reports as the voice of Brian Heder, an aging drug runner operating out of the Leonida Keys. Rockstar has introduced the character but has not publicly confirmed Root’s casting in that specific role. Beyond the return to Vice City, one of the biggest changes is the focus on two protagonists whose relationship drives the story. Grand Theft Auto V featured three playable main characters. The new installment centers on Lucia and Jason as partners navigating the criminal underworld together.

events.title: Google DeepMind melds humans and AI agents to vet Signal's secure messaging techniques
events.summary: Google DeepMind researchers have completed a formal verification of Signal's messaging security, marking what they claim is the first time AI has helped devise a proof that links protocol-level security guarantees to a widely used cryptographic implementation. They did so using AlphaProof Code, a multi-agent framework for formal software specification and verification. AlphaProof Code relies on a human-guided agent that writes a Lean specification, assesses machine code semantics, and crafts an agent-authored proof that the Lean kernel checks against the specification. In this instance, AlphaProof Code verified Signal’s post-quantum PQXDH handshake and Triple Ratchet , thereby validating the design of libsignal 's forward secrecy, authentication, post-compromise security, and handshake secrecy. In so doing, the Google/DeepMind team – Swarat Chaudhuri, Andrew Ferraiuolo, Anton Kovsharov, Tej Chajed, Sam Schlesinger, Karn Seth, Jonathan Katz, Charles Sutton, and Pushmeet Kohli – has taken a step toward a challenge the Beneficial AI Foundation issued in April to formally verify the Signal protocol and Signal app with Lean. The AlphaProof Code process involves working with various models to turn Signal's security goals into a human-reviewed mathematical specification. Based on this spec, the researchers assigned Gemini Carbon agents to generate Lean code proving the correctness of the libsignal implementation. After the agents generated 6.5 million lines of Lean code, they undertook an auditing pass and flagged bits that required human review. The result is theoretical in that it assumes perfect cryptography and doesn't guarantee the computational secrecy of bytes. But it's still a meaningful assertion of correctness. "It's a system that is fundamentally built for human AI collaboration," said Swarat Chaudhuri, research scientist at Google DeepMind and a professor at the University of Texas at Austin, in an interview with The Register . Traditionally, said Chaudhuri, you start proving theorems with well-defined problems formulated by a mathematician that get submitted to an AI agent for proof. In this case, the researchers had to figure out what to prove. "In formal methods, we always had this belief that verification is the hard bit," he said. "There's thirty or forty years of work on how to scale up verification. Now we are able to do that. So now the question is what are we verifying? … That process is fundamentally human-in-the-loop, but we devised a process of trying to scale it up to the extent possible with AI." As Chaudhuri and his colleagues note in their research paper, "AlphaProof Code: Verifying Signal’s Security at the Machine-Code Level," formal verification used to require heroic efforts. Formally verifying the seL4 microkernel took 20 person-years, while developing the verified CompCert C compiler took six years. AlphaProof Code, they believe, can drastically reduce the cost of formal verification, though their Signal work still took four weeks for a team of five people and "quite a few tokens." "The dream is definitely to scale this up," said Chaudhuri. "So you know there's been this rise in offensive AI capabilities, right? There are a lot of insecure systems around the world, and they're going to be exploited. "So what we really need to do is to apply this kind of technology to code at large all over the world and figure out what is it that you want to guard against? How do you write those properties, how do we specify those properties? That's going to be super important, but we have to figure that out." Pointing to a related DeepMind project, AlphaProof Nexus , which is focused on mathematics, Chaudhuri said the next step is to apply this technology during the software design process – not just to cryptographic protocols but code in general. "We really believe that the next frontier is not going to be proof but specification in this kind of research," he said. "And so that's why we took on this domain where that was actually a hard problem. And I think that we have some really good insights now about how to go about this, although not the last word by any means." ®

events.title: Jensen Huang has lost the debate on China chip sales
events.summary: Andy’s view Nobody outside the Oval Office has been more influential on US policy toward chip sales to China — and, by extension, the superpower race for AI supremacy — than Jensen Huang. The Nvidia CEO had Donald Trump’s ear. And he used his privileged access to make the case that keeping China hooked on Nvidia hardware and software was critical to maintaining the US technological lead. Cutting off sales to America’s chief strategic rival, he cautioned, only encouraged Beijing to speed up development of its own AI technologies that would, over time, become the global default. Whatever the merits of that argument, the events of the past 48 hours have almost certainly doomed his central contention. Huang’s admission of an affair with a woman who, according to US intelligence, is a Chinese spy plays directly into the hands of hawks in Washington pressing to clamp down on tech transfers to China. This camp has insisted all along that Huang’s advocacy was not only self-serving — a thin justification for his pursuit of profits — but, on its face, absurd. Under Chinese leader Xi Jinping, China is going all out for tech self-sufficiency precisely to escape the kind of dependencies that Huang envisages. Indeed, Xi has been cool on Huang’s marketing pitch. Although Trump greenlit sales of Nvidia’s H200 chips to China (taking a cut of revenues for the US government), Beijing is strictly limiting imports. Huang’s defenders insist he’s been arguing in good faith. Ben Thompson, the author of the influential Stratechery newsletter, argues that “it is entirely rational — and defensible — for Nvidia to want to sell chips to China.” By doing what he thinks is right, Thompson contends, Huang and Nvidia have “achieved unimaginable success.” It also needs pointing out that Huang stands by his patriotism. In a letter to staff, he insisted, “I love our country and our company.” But having allegedly been compromised in a Chinese “honeytrap,” one of the central figures in US technology and co-founder of one of the world’s most valuable companies, will be hard pressed to convince US congressional investigators he’s always put US national interests first. They’ll want to know whether Alice Huang extracted any Nvidia secrets in the course of their affair. Did she have access to his unguarded laptop? Or his cellphone? Did she garner any insights into White House strategy during their assignations? Of special interest to lawmakers looking at potential conflicts of interest: The Nvidia CEO’s relationship with the Singapore company Megaspeed, where Alice Huang was an executive and that was under investigation by the US Commerce Department over suspicions it formed part of a clandestine supply chain shipping Nvidia chips to China and Southeast Asia data centers. The issue is whether the romance influenced his business decisions. (The New York Times reported on Monday that the Commerce Department’s inquiry was suspended following outreach from an Nvidia executive. The department denied wrongdoing, and Nvidia said the company regularly consults with officials.) This drama will run and run. For the new Democrat-controlled Congress, the scandal offers multiple lines of attack against Trump. I’ve been predicting a backlash to the president’s China policies, widely criticized by politicians in both parties as weak and feckless — particularly his relaxed approach to tech transfers, but also on Taiwan, human rights, and military readiness in the Asia Pacific. The onslaught has now been brought forward. Chris Coons, the incoming chair of the Senate Committee on Foreign Relations, signaled the start of hostilities in a post on X. “The more I learn about the insane relationship between the Trump Administration, Chinese spies, and AI billionaires,” he wrote “the more I’m convinced there is nothing this administration does that isn’t corrupt .” Whether Huang will keep his job or not is an open question. Those who claim that he’s irreplaceable may be underestimating the political storm that’s about to break. In any event, he’s lost the debate on chip sales to China, with significant commercial consequences for Nvidia, and even larger implications for superpower rivalry. He may well feel wronged, but as Thompson, the Stratechery analyst, put it, “he has only himself to blame.” Notable WIRED reported that in October 2025, around the same time he was first linked to Alice Huang, Jensen Huang hired consultants from the crisis communications firm Heller, which is known for managing sex scandals.

events.title: 60 million children got Trump Accounts. Fewer than 1% were claimed in the first week
events.summary: Every finance team member has some experience with a suspense account, the place where money/transaction remains parked when nobody can match it to an owner. Controllers watch it closely, because a balance you can’t trace to a person isn’t really an asset yet. America has just opened tens of millions of children’s accounts that will need the same kind of matching. On Oct. 1 the Treasury said it had finished automatically creating investment accounts for more than 60 million children; with those opened earlier, the total is about 70 million. Babies born from 2025 through 2028 qualify for a $1,000 federal deposit. Michael and Susan Dell say they have now put $250 into the accounts of almost 25 million children. Unlike the federal seed, which arrives only after a parent claims the account, the Dell money was deposited without any claim. The money sits in low-cost U.S. stock index funds. BNY runs the initial accounts as the Treasury’s financial agent, with Robinhood as broker and initial trustee. A week later, according to Bloomberg Law , Helen Morrison, Treasury benefits tax counsel, speaking in her personal capacity at an American Bar Association tax meeting, said roughly 164,000 of the 60 million new accounts had been claimed. That’s less than 1%. It’s early. The program will succeed or fail at the claim, not the deposit. Two failures are already built into the design. The first is an account a parent never claims. Under the Treasury’s rules, a parent has to claim the account in an app, verifying identity and relationship, before the $1,000 federal seed arrives or relatives and employers can contribute. Without that claim, the federal money never arrives. An unclaimed account that received Dell’s $250 holds that deposit; one that got neither the federal seed nor Dell money is an empty shell opened automatically. The second is an account that was funded but lost at 18, when a young adult has to find it and prove it’s theirs. Both depend on paperwork families often lose. Britain’s Child Trust Fund shows how the second failure plays out. Children born between 2002 and early 2011 got a fund seeded with at least £250; the state opened one when parents didn’t. In September, HM Revenue & Customs said that of roughly 3.8 million accounts matured since 2020, around 827,000, more than one in five, were still unclaimed, averaging £2,310 each. That’s roughly £1.9 billion still waiting to be handed back. Britain has set up a government-and-industry taskforce to find the owners. In the U.S., the National Association of Unclaimed Property Administrators estimates that about one in seven Americans has property sitting unclaimed with a state. The firms holding these accounts should care for two reasons. One is compounding. A $1,000 seed earning 7% a year would be worth about $3,400 at 18 if left invested. What happens to a Trump Account that loses touch with its owner is still an open question. These are federally created IRAs for minors, and state unclaimed-property clocks typically don’t start until an account is payable or distributable, often not before adulthood, so the money probably stays invested. Growth is worthless, though, to an owner who never receives it. If America does no better than Britain, where more than a fifth of matured accounts sit unclaimed, millions of young adults will start out without the stake they were given. The other is commercial. A custodian holding millions of tiny, unclaimed accounts carries the servicing cost and regulatory risk without the client relationship. A reachable owner is a future customer. A lost one is a liability. The money abroad was stranded by a design that left tracking to the people least able to do it. Families move and lose letters; phone numbers change. Every institution knew whose money it was on day one, and over the years that link broke. On a software go-live across seven entities across three continents, my team agreed with each stakeholder on who owned which activity, and major issues still arose months later. A sign-off before launch did not give us an owner for each balance; only a monthly check did. For a program that runs across the Treasury, the IRS and the custodian, bodies that do not always talk to each other, that monthly check matters even more. The same discipline applies here. Each account should stay tied to the Social Security number, and whoever holds the account should check contact details against official records every year, as brokers already screen customers for identity and sanctions. The rule I would change is the one that makes core money wait on a form. Israel’s savings plan for every child , running since 2017, deposits a monthly sum for every child receiving child allowance and pays the management fees until age 21. For about a third of children born in 2023, the National Insurance Institute reported, parents never chose a fund, so the money was placed by default, and still arrived. The handover at 18 deserves the care a brokerage gives a product launch, not a letter in the mail. Well before that birthday, the young owner should be able to see the account on a phone, with a plain statement of what it holds and what it has earned. Israel adds a grant of 582 shekels at 21 for savers who leave the money invested. Done well, this could be a powerful investor-education tool. A statement showing $1,000 growing over 18 years teaches compounding better than any lecture. A forgotten account teaches nothing, and on a custodian’s books it is just another balance in suspense. events.title: Louis Rossmann Wants More People to Care About the Right to Repair
events.summary: I love my old iPhone 14 , but I’m starting to face the facts: It’s going to die. The battery is about to go; apps take longer to load than they used to. Some of it I can fix. I can go to the Genius Bar and swap the battery. Maybe I could even do it myself; that’d buy me some time. But eventually, Apple won’t support this wildly expensive device at all, and there’s not much I can do about it. Apple did start offering self-repair services a few years ago, but it involves renting nearly 80 pounds of equipment and requires you to use official parts. When all is said and done, it doesn’t save you that much money versus just going to the Apple Store . But if I buy a screen or a camera component from a third party, there's a chance my iPhone is gonna lock me out of certain features because it doesn't recognize it. This problem goes far beyond iPhones. Manufacturers have put similar locks on all kinds of gadgets, from video game consoles to cars to smart home devices, making them hard to modify and even harder to restore after some firmware update renders a certain feature unusable. Not surprisingly, a lot of people think this isn't fair, that there should be a better way to do it. I think at this point it's safe to say it qualifies as a movement, one that unites under the banner of “right to repair.” Built around the radical idea that when you buy something you should be able to truly own it, right-to-repair advocates believe consumers have the right to maintain, fix, or modify any piece of hardware they’ve purchased. The movement has gained even more traction now that AI makes it even easier to hack the software powering consumers’ devices. To find out what’s next for the right-to-repair movement, I went straight to the source: Louis Rossmann, a YouTuber and consumer rights advocate who recently organized the Own Your Shit tour , which went around the US earlier this year to call for the death of Section 1201 of the Digital Millennium Copyright Act, which prohibits users from bypassing digital restrictions put on devices by manufacturers. Rossmann and I talked about more than just Section 1201. We also discussed the US midterm elections , putting out bounties to find product fixes, and what will happen as the right-to-repair movement collides with the rise of AI. This interview has been edited for length and clarity. BRIAN BARRETT: Louis, thank you so much for being here. You're someone who spends a lot of time not just evangelizing over “right to repair,’ but I would imagine introducing it to people who don't know what it is. How do you do that? LOUIS ROSSMANN: I try to avoid talking about it, and I try to show people. So instead of telling people, “Here’s why you should care about this issue,” which sounds like lecturing, what I’ll do is if I’m done fixing something for a customer and they say, “The Apple Store told me $2,000," and we could do it for $200, when they’re giving me the hug and saying, “Thank you for getting back all of our baby pictures” or something, I’ll say, “Here’s how close you were to this never happening.” I like to tell them, “This is the document that I used to fix your device.” When they ask me what was wrong with it, I’ll tell them, “By the way, you should know that Apple tells the company that makes this chip not to sell it to me, and if everybody in that chain listened, I would not be able to fix this, and you wouldn’t have any of your data back.” So I always try to show people and get them excited about what it is I’m doing. I have over 1,000 repair videos on YouTube where I show people how to do what I do, and there are people that say, “I was working at Walmart for seven bucks an hour, and I picked up a soldering iron and started fixing boards on eBay, and now I make triple what I did before.” There are people that fix their own things, so not just making careers for people, but maybe somebody saved themselves some money by doing a repair themself. Or when I fix something for somebody that otherwise wouldn't have been fixed or that they were told couldn’t be fixed. I always try to get people personally invested because lecturing people about it just doesn’t make it very fun. Your organization has a wall of shame, almost, of examples of things that companies have done to take away the ownership of a product. Because that’s really what it is, right? It's like you buy something, you expect to be able to own it and do what you want with it, but that's not always how it plays out. To your mind, what are some of the more egregious instances of companies not letting you know what you want? Some of my favorites are some of these thermostat companies. One of them sent out a firmware update after the company went bankrupt that required that you pay $117 a year to get some of the functionality that you had beforehand. So it’s not even necessarily when a company has a device that has a specific date when it’s gonna turn off.

events.title: Microsoft is giving Claude the keys to UK Copilot tenants by default
events.summary: Microsoft will enable access to Anthropic's Claude models by default for UK Copilot tenants next month, giving administrators a deadline to decide whether US-based processing fits their compliance requirements. From December 9, UK tenants whose administrators have not already chosen a setting will have Claude access enabled. Administrators can disable it, but leaving the setting untouched means opting in. In this instance, Anthropic operates as a Microsoft subprocessor , and Claude models are already on by default for most customers in the Windows giant's commercial cloud. The exceptions, notably, include the European Union, the European Free Trade Association, and the UK. However, UK tenants aren't in scope for Microsoft's EU Data Boundary - launched at the start of 2023 - and so Redmond is flipping the switch for the country. Anthropic processes the relevant data in the United States, Microsoft's documentation states . Administrators therefore have until December 9 to review whether that meets their organization's data-handling requirements and set access accordingly. Microsoft is also retiring the setting that restricts Claude access to Microsoft 365 alone. "This affirms Microsoft's commitment to offering choice between leading AI models while maintaining enterprise-grade security and compliance," the Redmond-based biz said. So long as you don't mind processing happening in the US. ®

events.title: Trump plans imperial final act to his presidency
events.summary: President Trump, with the clock ticking and congressional investigators closing in, plans to govern even more imperially , hell-bent on stretching executive power, targeting those on his enemies list, pardoning allies, and daring the courts and Congress to slow him down. Why it matters: Trump and his allies are exploring executive action on new tariffs and immigration restrictions, and asserting greater control over spending. On X over the weekend, Trump discussed targeting and perhaps jailing Democrats who investigate administration officials. He claimed politically motivated harassment . Trump is retooling his White House by elevating the one official who's synonymous with his all-gas-no-brakes style: Stephen Miller, who took over for Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff on Monday. Watch Miller and Russ Vought , the White House budget director, to understand how this approach will unfold. Both are architects and advocates of vastly expanding presidential power, believing there are virtually no restraints on what Trump can do as president. The Swamp can expect tougher sledding: Miller, unlike most of his predecessors, is driven more by ideology than by meetings with lobbyists or industry groups. "Stephen gives zero f*cks what K Street thinks," a Trump confidant told us. Between the lines: Midterm losses pushed Presidents Clinton and Obama to the center. Trump's instincts are the opposite: Assert maximal power. The playbook: Restore MAGA. Two years ago, MAGA — mostly its network of podcasts , YouTubers and online activists — was a powerful, united force in media and politics. Today it's a hot, divided mess. Trump's attention to his base drifted. Now Vice President Vance and Miller desperately want to rebuild and rev up MAGA. That's why ending the Iran war , curtailing aid to Israel and pushing harder on RFK Jr.'s MAHA agenda are suddenly top-tier topics. Rule by pen. Miller, Vought and White House lawyers have been drafting executive actions to govern without Congress, with Justice Department opinions ready to defend them, Reuters reported just before the election. Remember: Vought was an architect of the Heritage Foundation's Project 2025 blueprint for maximizing executive power in Trump II. Target enemies. Before, it was pure payback. Now, it's also a preemptive warning that the Trump administration will target anyone, including elected members of Congress who target them. Trump ally Roger Stone told us: "Many Democrat lawmakers are going to find themselves under indictment and fighting conviction. Watch." Purge the "deep state." The Supreme Court's ruling in a case about independent agencies, Trump v. Slaughter , widened the president's power to remove officials. "The Slaughter case gives the president tremendous powers," Trump said in an Election Day phone interview with CBS News' Robert Costa. The June ruling handed Trump the power to fire the heads of the FTC and other independent regulators ( like FERC ) for any reason or no reason. More monuments. Trump's pharaonic need to gild the White House, build a ballroom, erect a triumphal arch and slap his name on buildings is also an exercise in raw power. He told New York Magazine's Ben Terris why he's honoring himself: "Nobody will do it once I'm gone. When I leave here, nobody will." No one can stop him. The Republican resistance: Expect very little inside the new Congress. The reason: Most of Trump's Capitol Hill critics are gone. What's left is a much smaller, but more Trumpian, band of middle-aged and older white Republicans with margins too small to matter much. The Trump bet: Congressional Republicans will quickly feel Democrats are overreaching and unify in solidarity with Trump, even if it's forced or begrudging. Yes, but: One of Trump's most predictable attributes is his unpredictability. He said on election night that he'll " work together " with Democrats. What that may look like (with a heavy emphasis on "may"), based on reporting by Axios' Marc Caputo: Soften aspects of immigration enforcement, particularly regarding masked agents harassing U.S. citizens. Find common ground with MAHA's healthy food agenda, which has become the subject of vicious post-election infighting among Trump insiders. Sign legislation from the new Congress that would undo massive Medicaid cuts in his "One Big Beautiful Bill." The bottom line: Trump is still Trump. He's 80 and it shows. But he meets force with force and he'll go down swinging the more Democrats attack him. "Trump and his team are at our best when our backs are against the wall," one adviser told Caputo. "Trump comes out fighting. We're full-throated and full-throttle." Go deeper : Texas, Texas, Texas.

events.title: EU's €212M border IT project lands IBM and Atos in legal water
events.summary: The European Union has dragged IBM, Atos, and Leonardo into court over years of delays to its troubled €212 million smart border system, which finally went live after missing a string of deadlines and leaving travelers stuck in airport queues. The lawsuit dates back to December 22, 2025, when eu-LISA, the agency behind the EU's fingerprint-and-facial-image border checks for non-EU travelers, filed its claim in an Estonian court. The lawsuit was buried in eu-LISA's 2025 financial accounts , published in July, with no mention of who was being sued. The Financial Times has since named the three companies after obtaining letters exchanged with the agency. In a statement to The Register , eu-LISA confirmed it had initiated proceedings "in line with the Agency’s responsibility to protect the EU’s financial interests." "The proceedings concern the system’s development phase and have no impact on its current operation. EES (entry exit system) is fully operational," the agency said, declining to discuss the ongoing case. The EES was supposed to be ready in 2022 yet wasn't live until October 2025 and was only fully operational from April. Travelers have since had to contend with hours-long airport queues and fingerprint scanners that reportedly struggle with sweaty fingers. Behind the scenes, things weren't going much better, with the consortium and eu-LISA spending years arguing over missed deadlines, financial penalties and who was to blame. IBM Belgium and Atos Belgium were already arguing over penalties back in October 2021, when they disputed a fine from eu-LISA and pointed to the COVID-19 pandemic and other factors beyond their control as reasons for the delays. By February 2022, the consortium was pushing back against another set of deadlines, warning that the agency's timetable was unrealistic. "Ignoring reality is not prudent and will not help to achieve the plan," the companies wrote, according to the FT. "On the contrary, working with an unrealistic plan will cause frustration for all stakeholders." The consortium also criticized eu-LISA's "overall governance," suggesting relations between the two sides had become rather frosty. The fallout wasn't cheap. The contract had already grown from €142 million to €212 million in 2021, and the delays kept adding to the bill. In its 2022 accounts [PDF], eu-LISA acknowledged difficulties with the consortium and warned of additional costs, with the setbacks also holding up other EU IT projects. By 2023, it had nearly doubled its annual EES budget to €40 million by diverting funds from elsewhere, partly to cover rising hardware and software maintenance costs. The FT also reported that IBM agreed in March 2022 to let eu-LISA withhold certain payments while the dispute over damages was resolved. The original contract expired last year, with a new consortium taking over implementation, although IBM, Atos, and Leonardo remained responsible until August. The project has attracted scrutiny for more than its ballooning budget. Last year, Atos reportedly used its Moscow office to procure software for the system, raising questions about Russian involvement in sensitive European border infrastructure. The EU's anti-fraud office, OLAF, found sufficient grounds for further investigation, according to an internal report seen by the FT. However, it referred the matter back to eu-LISA despite describing the agency's initial assessment as insufficient. Estonia's Harju County Court confirmed that the civil case had been filed, although no hearings have taken place or been scheduled. IBM and Atos did not respond to The Register 's questions. The EES may finally be up and running, but the argument over who should foot the bill for getting it there looks far from settled. ®

events.title: The AI Safety Debate Has Lost the Plot. We Asked 10 Experts What the Real Nightmares Are
events.summary: In early fall, I felt my anxiety rising from its usual baseline. Was it September’s back-to-school energy? The looming midterm elections? Nope, I realized with annoyance: It was AI—again. Only this time, instead of its purveyors warning of massive job displacement, they were foretelling mass extinction. Who needs jobs when we’re all dead? Curiosity soon replaced my knee-jerk irritation. The summer of 2026 was a clear turning point in the AI narrative. Less than four years after ChatGPT launched, OpenAI software broke out of a supposedly safe test environment and hacked into a major open-source platform, Hugging Face . These bits of software— AI agents —were assigned human attributes: They had “gone rogue,” displayed “bad behavior,” “cheated.” Soon after, former and current Anthropic researchers suggested that advanced AI might kill us all in the next decade. Is any of this real ? On the one hand, from my desk as a Silicon Valley correspondent, I often hear that workers in the AI labs are stunned by the advancements they’re seeing. On the other, the end of humanity seems extremely far-fetched. Amid the hyperbolic discourse, whose views can we trust? So WIRED set out to compile a guide to AI safety—a set of ideas that rewire our collective thinking around what safety really means and how it should work. I spoke with a panel of experts across disciplines, asking each of them: Is the world going to end? Once that was covered, I grilled them on the biggest risks they think we’re facing. Almost no one, it turned out, was Pollyannish. Nearly everyone I spoke to expressed genuine concerns about the threat of cyber and biological attacks. One expert who studies the risks of AI in nuclear operations said she’s stunned by how quickly error-prone AI systems are being adopted in defense. AI-enabled attacks in these areas could be catastrophic, if not fully apocalyptic. Is AI safe? For our ongoing series , WIRED assesses the real threats of artificial intelligence. Most members of the panel were skeptical about any pause in development: They nearly all agreed that, with big AI companies so tightly cuffed to the trains of capitalism, a pause wouldn’t last long. “Democracy” and “governance” came up often—or anti-democracy, as more than one person suggested that AI’s current trajectory is tyrannical. Lawmakers have a big role to play, but many of my sources think governments will be too slow; one prominent technologist said it’s almost absurd to view the US courts as arbiters of global AI safety. Still, the famed computer scientist Yoshua Bengio urged the public to apply pressure to politicians, adding to me, “That’s your job too.” So, what—or who—will keep us safe from AI? Looking to regain some faith in humanity, I called a theologian who often meets with the AI labs. If there’s even a slim chance that we’re losing control of the essential institutions that undergird society, he said, then we should focus on foiling that. But AI raises other questions too. What does it mean to be conscious? To create? To commune with other people? The answers are “entirely up for grabs,” he said. My anxiety’s still kicking around, but I took some comfort in knowing that corporations don’t get to call all the shots on the future. The bigger questions facing humanity are in all our hands. BIGGEST CONCERN: Nuclear catastrophe I’ve been working hard to educate the nuclear community on the risks and lack of reliability of AI systems, and I’m concerned by the willingness of many people in the sector to integrate these models into their workflows, into nuclear operations. I think this is incredibly urgent. I’m not a doomer, but to me, if these AI models make it into the operations of nuclear systems, we’ll be introducing an incredibly faulty, unreliable system that could lead to catastrophic failures. MOST OVERBLOWN RISK: Extinction As true safety engineers, we don’t engage with that because there are no numbers to back it. This is a very cold way to say it, but when we are talking about how safe is “safe enough,” we’re examining how many people might die. There’s an entire science behind it. Our claims have to be falsifiable and verifiable. You can’t just say, “Humans are going to go extinct in 10 years. Believe me. It might be a 10 percent chance; it might be a 25 percent chance.” How should people think about AI safety? Some of the comparisons that people draw between AI and nuclear are quite frustrating. Despite constantly comparing AI to nuclear, they’re denying standard risk assessment techniques as being sufficient to control AI. I wrote an entire paper on this. Part of this field of risk assessment was born out of the Manhattan Project. Scientists were very concerned, and they developed rigorous standards around systems to limit harm to human life, the environment, and even financial and national security assets.

events.title: How a MAHA leader turned and torched the White House
events.summary: Calley Means quickly rose from wellness entrepreneur to senior Trump health adviser — and now he's attacking the White House and suggesting top aides undermined the president's health agenda. Why it matters: His scorched-earth campaign — which continued Monday in comments to Axios — marks a stunning turn for a figure who was the administration's most vocal advocate of the "Make America Healthy Again" agenda. It also raises questions about what the escalating fight between Means and former White House officials will accomplish for the movement. Driving the news: Means told Axios he's going public with his allegations of corruption — especially by former White House chief of staff Susie Wiles — because of the high stakes. "It is existential to the survival [of] America that we rid DC of Susie's brand of politics," Means said in a text exchange. Means' initial comments on Friday's episode of "The Joe Rogan Experience" went viral , and he continued the campaign with an appearance on CBS' "Face the Nation" Sunday. Asked if he's worried about lawsuits after comments from a Wiles spokesperson and former White House deputy chief of staff James Blair — who Means has also accused of wrongdoing — Means pointed to his X post warning them and other parties to "immediately preserve all potentially relevant records and communications." Means has kept up a steady stream of X posts about his allegations and the way he claims the officials have responded to them. "Susie - I'm not intimidated and you will not scare me. Again, please stop sending me emotional texts. This is not personal - this is civilizational," Means posted Monday . White House spokesperson Allison Schuster said in a statement the Trump administration has won "extensive victories for the MAHA Agenda." The Department of Health and Human Services and a Wiles spokesperson didn't respond to requests for comment. The big picture: After hitching their wagon to President Trump ahead of the 2024 election, MAHA leaders have been complaining for months of a lack of progress on issues around healthy foods and pesticide use. But whether the public feud Means has initiated will have any impact on the policy agenda he's championed — or whether it's more of a personal grievance tour — remains to be seen. A former HHS official said that after Republicans' midterm wipeout, Means is "highlighting that one of the more popular aspects of Trump's domestic agenda should be something [the administration] spends more time on to prepare the party for 2028." The intrigue: The MAHA base sees incoming chief of staff Stephen Miller as an ally, even though he hasn't said much about movement priorities like cleaning up the food supply, curbing food additives or scrutinizing vaccines. Miller's wife, Katie, hosted Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. on her podcast and has posted photos of dishes with ingredients like raw milk, per the Washington Sun . Means told "Face the Nation" that Miller understands corporate influence over health care and that he represents a break from Wiles. "Stephen Miller has been nothing short of a champion in Making America Healthy Again. As a father of four, Miller is acutely aware of the importance of transforming our food, health, and scientific systems for the next generation of Americans," Schuster said. Zoom in: Means, who resigned from his senior adviser post late last month, grew up in Washington and interned in George W. Bush's White House and at the Heritage Foundation before going on to work as a consultant to beverage and drug industries. He told Axios in 2024 that his mother's preventable death from a chronic disease in 2021 prompted him and his sister, "functional medicine" physician and health influencer Casey Means, to advocate and work to reverse the chronic disease crisis. The siblings wrote a best-selling book called "Good Energy." Calley Means also co-founded Truemed, a company that helps people buy wellness equipment using money in health savings accounts, retaining an interest while advising Kennedy, per the New York Times . Means is widely credited with facilitating the alliance between Kennedy and President Trump in the summer of 2024 and became a special government employee in the new Trump administration. He made frequent, at times flamboyant appearances in public forums, railing against a "crisis of trust" in health care institutions and claiming at one 2025 Axios event that Kennedy "has a spiritual mandate" from voters to reform broken government institutions. Means' sister was tapped by Trump to be surgeon general, only to see the nomination withdrawn in April amid questions over whether she could win over enough Republican senators to be confirmed. Calley Means at the time blamed Senate health committee Chair Bill Cassidy (R-La.) for delay tactics. What we're watching: It's not clear what role Means will play outside the administration — or whether his turnabout has helped or hurt the MAHA cause. Key initiatives like developing a definition for ultra-processed foods remain unfinished, and the Food and Drug Administration appears to be taking a more conciliatory stance toward drug developers and other industries it regulates.

events.title: Trump diplomatic nominee shaped a pro-Russia Balkans policy
events.summary: The Scoop President Donald Trump’s nominee for US ambassador to Azerbaijan has played a leading role in his administration’s headline-grabbing alignment with a pro-Russian government in the Balkans, more than half a dozen people familiar with his involvement told Semafor. Senators had eyed a hearing as soon as Tuesday on whether to confirm Alexander Alden, currently a senior adviser to Secretary of State Marco Rubio, to the high-stakes diplomatic job . With Democrats readying to take control of the chamber next year, Republicans are under growing pressure to advance Trump’s nominees in the lame-duck session. It’s not clear why Alden didn’t make the cut this time — but whenever he does appear, he’s likely to face questions about his behind-the-scenes advocacy for Republika Srpska, a Russia-linked territory in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The territory’s Serb-controlled government gained national attention last month when two of Trump’s top advisers , James Blair and Chris LaCivita, traveled there ahead of its elections. The ruling party in Republika Srpska is helmed by Milorad Dodik, a Bosnian Serb who was under US sanctions for undermining peace in the region until Trump lifted them last year. Lawmakers in both parties have urged Trump to reimpose the sanctions as Dodik continues his calls for Republika Srpska to secede. Inside the administration, however, Alden is seen as a Dodik champion, according to the people who spoke with Semafor: “Some have referred to him as the ‘Serb in the State Department,’” one person said, adding that “a lot of the lines he was using are exactly the same things that we hear Dodik saying.” A second person described Alden as “the principal driver behind Bosnia policy as it relates to Dodik and Republika Srpska” whose “fingerprints are all over” Trump’s second-term moves. A third person expressed concern that “over the next two years, we’re going to see Dodik move for secession … as a consequence of some of the policy decisions that Mr. Alden has been involved in.” Azerbaijan, where Alden is nominated to serve, is an Eastern European ally of Serbia whose president also maintains a good relationship with Dodik. The US is also seeking to keep Russian influence at bay there, a mission that could prove complicated for Alden to execute if he’s confirmed. “If these allegations are true, it shows incredibly poor judgment,” which “would be of concern for anyone becoming a US ambassador,” said Jim O’Brien, who served as assistant secretary of state for European and Eurasian affairs during the Biden administration. Alden previously changed his name from the common Bosniak surname Mulabdic, two of the people said. He currently advises Rubio as a special government employee, which allows him to remain a senior counselor for Palantir. His first Senate-confirmed job never materialized amid allegations of workplace misconduct . “Alden is a seasoned national security official who provides valuable policy advice drawing upon his extensive experience and expertise,” a State Department spokesperson said, adding that he “enjoys the full trust and confidence of senior leadership at the Department of State.” As for his name change, the spokesperson said “Alden is first and foremost an American working to advance American foreign policy around the world.” ‘Pretty Aggressive’ The people who spoke with Semafor said an understaffed State Department had allowed Alden the opportunity to intervene on behalf of Russia’s allies in Bosnia before senators confirmed Brendan Hanrahan as assistant secretary of State for European and Eurasian affairs three months ago. Five of the people said that Alden traveled to Bosnia in June for meetings of the region’s Peace Implementation Council, where he threatened European officials in attendance to approve the US’ choice to lead the region’s Office of the High Representative. Deputy Assistant Secretary of State for Western Central Europe and Southern Europe Dan Lawton led the delegation, but “it was clear [Alden] was the guy in charge [and] he wanted to force this guy through,” a fourth person said. “So the dynamic was pretty aggressive and oppressive; he was kind of looming over everybody.” The High Representative is an international body that enforces the Dayton Peace Accords, which ended Bosnia’s gruesome civil war three decades ago. Its previous leader, Christian Schmidt, quit, citing US pressure to leave the role. Dodik had long raged against Schmidt, whom he views as an impediment to Republika Srpska’s secession from Bosnia. He told a Serbian media outlet last month that he’d asked the Trump administration to “get rid” of the high representative in exchange for repealing certain laws. Alden personally selected the US pick to replace Schmidt, Italian diplomat Antonio Zanardi Landi, according to two of the people Semafor interviewed. Five of the people told Semafor that Alden warned the US might defund the office if European officials didn’t accept Landi, whom the European officials ultimately rejected. Landi was seen as likely to “do Dodik’s bidding,” as House Democrats laid out in a September report . Transparency International’s Srdjan Blagovcanin called the fallout the most “visible” evidence of a “wider divergence between EU and US” when it comes to Bosnia. The State Department spokesperson pushed back on the characterization of Alden’s behavior the meeting, saying Lawton was “the only one who spoke at the meeting” and “any assertion that he was looming over” attendees “pointed political nonsense.” A senior State Department official, who confirmed that Alden accompanied Lawton to the meetings, called Lawton “responsible for day-to-day US foreign policy in the Western Balkans.” They described the Trump administration’s approach as “led by Rubio,” with support from Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau, Hanrahan, “and other senior officials and advisers.” ‘Boot-On-The-Neck-Type Feeling’ The enduring stalemate over choosing a new high representative threatens to hurt US-backed plans for a gas pipeline that could counter Balkan dependence on Russian gas. Alden’s role in weakening the office, which was created to promote regional stability after the bloody civil war in the 1990s, is a potential red flag for senators in both parties. Yet senators may also not advance his nomination out of broader concern about Republika Srpska’s influence on the Trump administration. The territory’s government has spent more than $11 million lobbying the administration since 2025, according to Justice Department filings, and even more on informal efforts, like Dodik’s visit to Mar-a-Lago last week. That’s about four times what it spent between 2022 and 2024 . “Officials involved in corrupting US policy to Bosnia and Herzegovina and obstructing this committee’s oversight of the region should be held accountable for their complicity in advancing lobbying interests at the expense of peace in Bosnia,” Senate Foreign Relations Committee ranking membe

events.title: House Republicans to pick new leaders
events.summary: House Republicans will vote on Tuesday on whether to overhaul their leadership. Rep. Jim Jordan, R-Ohio, and current Majority Leader Steve Scalise, R-La., are competing for minority leader, after Speaker Mike Johnson opted against running for minority leadership (he might not even serve his full term next Congress). House Republicans will hold their candidate forum Tuesday morning and vote on their picks in the afternoon. Some in the party are hungry for new blood. Jordan, who rose up the ranks as a pugnacious Freedom Caucus and Judiciary Committee leader, would be the one to best demonstrate the “divergence in values between the two parties,” said Rep. Brian Mast, R-Fla. Others want to stay the course. “This election was not the fault of our leadership,” said Rep. Mike Simpson, R-Idaho. Current Majority Whip Tom Emmer, R-Minn., and Rep. August Pfluger, R-Texas, are running for minority whip. There’s competitive races downballot, too. Current Conference Chair Lisa McClain, R-Mich., faces challenges from Reps. Erin Houchin, R-Ind., and Greg Steube, R-Fla. And Reps. Brian Jack, R-Ga., and Rudy Yakym, R-Ind., are running for NRCC chair. Rep.
