events.title: The blue wave's tough-on-crime surprise
events.summary: Democrats swept into power last week as voters also embraced tougher criminal penalties and restrictions on bail. Why it matters: Six years after the George Floyd protests, Democrats won big without promising a return to sweeping 2020-era reforms. Some even adopted border-security rhetoric associated with Republicans. Democrats gained at least 12 state legislative chambers and won governorships in Georgia, Iowa, Nevada, Ohio and Texas. By the numbers: Voters approved all six statewide ballot measures Ballotpedia tracked that proposed tougher sentences, criminal penalties or bail restrictions in 2026. Five passed Nov. 3 in Indiana, Louisiana, Tennessee and Colorado. Alabama approved the sixth in May. Four expanded when courts could deny or restrict bail. Two increased penalties, including for fentanyl offenses and child sex trafficking. The shift: Some Democratic winners embraced tougher border-security language while opposing Trump's immigration crackdown. Texas Sen.-elect James Talarico called himself a "border security Democrat ," criticized former President Biden for failing to secure the border and said there needs to be comprehensive immigration reform. Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed , a progressive, said days before the election : "We needed tougher border security." He also criticized Trump's use of ICE. Zoom in: Colorado voters backed Democrats, tougher penalties and limits on federal immigration enforcement. That included electing Phil Weiser (D) as governor and approving tougher fentanyl penalties and life without parole for child sex trafficking. They rejected a measure requiring police to notify federal immigration authorities in certain cases involving violent crime suspects or people with prior felony convictions whose immigration status was unlawful or uncertain. Weiser and state Democrats are now weighing changes to the fentanyl measure, arguing it falls short on promised addiction treatment. Yes, but: Virginia voters approved automatically restoring voting rights to people convicted of felonies upon release from incarceration. Zoom out: Ballotpedia's historical analysis found more punitive sentencing and bail proposals dominated from 2022 through 2026, reversing 2012–2020, when less punitive measures appeared more often. Meanwhile, the nation's violent-crime rate plunged 9.7% in 2025 , its steepest annual decline in 90 years. The murder rate fell 18.5%, according to the FBI.

events.title: Scoop: El Salvador blasts U.S. State Dept. over Haiti gang war
events.summary: State Department officials have quietly raised objections to El Salvador's gang-fighting efforts in Haiti — even as President Trump has offered his full support, according to diplomatic notes and informed sources. On Monday, El Salvador issued a formal rebuke that questioned the "credibility" of the top U.S. diplomat in Haiti. Why it matters: The controversy exposes the tension between Trump's MAGA foreign policy objectives and the professional diplomatic establishment in the State Department. "There is a class of bureaucrats who don't want to see the change in the Western Hemisphere that POTUS wants," a U.S. official told Axios. Zoom in: Haiti is a failed state racked by extreme corruption and gang violence despite years of international efforts, including the UN-backed Gang Suppression Force (GSF) that El Salvador and other nations have backed. Four Salvadoran aviation technicians supporting medical evacuations were captured Oct. 18 by gangs that refused to heed the entreaties of El Salvador's President Nayib Bukele to return the men or their bodies. Bukele responded by surging special forces units to Haiti after receiving the blessing of Trump, an ally, on Oct. 27, Axios first reported . "You have to do what you have to do," Trump told Bukele, who proceeded to launch military operations that resulted in firefights with gangs in the streets of Port-Au-Prince. Friction point: Tensions between State Department officials and El Salvador erupted after an Oct. 31 gang attack on a Salvadoran convoy of five armored personnel carriers near the U.S. embassy, which was struck by gunfire. On Nov. 3, Salvadoran attack helicopters repelled gangs attacking GSF soldiers from Chad, Bukele posted on X . The next day, U.S. Chargé d'Affaires David Howell complained in a text message to Haitian Prime Minister Alix Didier Fils-Aimé that El Salvador wasn't "coordinating" with the GSF. "They took at least three casualties. They don't have a medical plan. They nearly killed GSF troops as I understand it," according to a copy of the text message shared with Axios. Howell asked the prime minister to tell El Salvador's defense ministry to stop operations "as soon as possible ... until they coordinate. They are going to kill [GSF] troops or civilians and or get themselves killed." El Salvador later accused Howell of spreading misinformation. On Nov. 5, the U.S. embassy in San Salvador sent a formal protest in a diplomatic note to Bukele's government, saying that the U.S. "strongly opposes this lack of coordination by Salvadoran military personnel," the document shown to Axios says. The note said El Salvador's "failure to coordinate" endangered the GSF and that "Salvadoran small arms fire" struck the U.S. embassy, "nearly hitting U.S. personnel." Behind the scenes: Bukele was infuriated by the so-called "dipnote," a source said. "His attitude was, 'What the f*ck? I checked with Trump. He said do what we have to do, and some bureaucrat is fighting this?' " said a source who spoke with Bukele. State Department officials said it was unclear who authorized the diplomatic note and didn't comment about Howell's correspondence to Haiti's prime minister. On Monday, Bukele's government fired back at Howell and the State Department officials. El Salvador's diplomatic note provided a point-by-point rebuttal with 4 "clarifications:" Regarding the gunfire that hit the embassy, El Salvador's ministry of foreign affairs wrote that its troops essentially had their backs to the building and were firing away from it. "It is ruled out that the fire from the Salvadoran personnel struck the facilities of the American Embassy," El Salvador wrote. 2. During the attack on troops from Chad, El Salvador wrote, "Salvadoran personnel repelled the attack. It is ruled out that the fire of the Salvadoran elements was directed toward the position of Chad." 3. El Salvador also said that since Oct. 26, its armed forces repeatedly have coordinated "air assets" with the GSF and Haitian officials. 4. In its most caustic reply, El Salvador said it "categorically denies" Howell's claim that three of its soldiers were casualties. "The fact that false information has been disseminated on a matter of such gravity, without providing any evidence to support it, generates serious doubts about the credibility of the rest of the assertions contained in the aforementioned report, which likewise lack any type of evidence that would allow their accuracy to be verified," the note said. What they're saying: An official spokesperson for El Salvador couldn't be reached. Haiti's prime minister didn't return messages seeking comment. A State Department official insisted that "three Salvadorans were injured ... one of which was serious enough to have been medevaced outside the country for additional treatment." A source close to El Salvador's government showed Axios a picture of the smiling soldier with a leg brace on and said he was flown out of Haiti because there were no adequate medical facilities, not because the injury was serious. The State Department, echoing comments from U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Sunday, said it appreciates El Salvador's efforts, "but the Trump administration has also been clear on the need to deconflict anti-gang operations to ensure seamless implementation of President Trump's policy to support efforts to free Haiti from gangs."

events.title: How Nvidia's crisis and politics could deliver the pause AI leaders want
events.summary: A political backlash against AI and data centers — now compounded by a crisis facing the technology's most influential champion — could help force a slowdown that industry leaders have struggled to achieve voluntarily. Why it matters: Tapping the brakes on AI development — which frontier AI developers claim to want but have so far failed to do given the risk of offering an advantage to a competitor — could give society more time to prepare for economic upheaval and the risks of superintelligent systems. A wave of Democratic victories and data center moratoriums is now joined by a potentially weakened Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who admitted to having a relationship with an alleged Chinese spy. Huang, who has led the industry in barreling through past resistance to AI acceleration, may be less able to do so while under a microscope. While both factors could stymie data center expansion in the U.S., it's far from clear that would slow AI's advance. Between the lines: Huang has been a powerful counterweight to calls for AI restraint, dismissing fears of an AI bubble or purported catastrophic risks to humanity from the technology. An investigation — by the board, an ascendant Democratic Congress or federal authorities — could curb his ability to make the case for continued expansion, leaving an opening for those calling for more restrictions. Nvidia says Huang will remain CEO and the news won't slow the company, but the potential impact on his political influence is hard to measure. The fallout extends beyond that. Nvidia is both the dominant supplier of AI chips and an investor in companies building AI infrastructure. A crisis that raises questions about its leadership, business practices or financial relationships could ripple through the industry's expansion plans. The intrigue: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk have all warned about the potentially catastrophic risks of advanced AI, with all expressing, at times, the need to slow or pace the development of advanced AI. But the competitive race has made it difficult for any one company to hit the brakes without risking falling behind rivals or China in a high-stakes race for supremacy. What they're saying: Anthony Aguirre, CEO of the Future of Life Institute, says a slowdown in data center construction would be welcome, even if it wouldn't accomplish nearly as much as more direct restrictions on frontier AI development. "I'll take whatever I can get," Aguirre told Axios in an interview. Aguirre and a number of other researchers have long seen the development of increasingly powerful AI as an existential threat. But he is skeptical that slowing data center construction alone would buy society an additional year or two, given the vast computing resources companies already possess and the growing ability of AI systems to help improve themselves. Aguirre said the bigger opportunity may be political: Resistance to data centers could help generate momentum for legislation and regulation that more directly limits the development of potentially dangerous AI systems. The big picture: Aguirre argues that the goal shouldn't simply be to delay superintelligence by a year or two, but to reconsider whether humanity should build it at all. He favors a "pause and pivot" toward AI systems designed to augment human abilities rather than replace them. Other researchers and executives favor continued development with stronger safeguards, reflecting a broader debate over how much restraint is necessary and what form it should take. Yes, but: Slowing data center construction in the U.S. doesn't necessarily mean slowing AI progress globally. Meta and other companies are exploring data center construction outside the U.S. Google announced a plan last week to invest $15 billion over two years in Malaysia. And Chinese AI developers wouldn't face the same U.S. restrictions, potentially allowing them to narrow the gap with American competitors. The other side: The threat from China isn't as straightforward as it appears. Chinese AI companies benefit in part from distillation of leading American models and technical knowledge developed in the U.S., Aguirre said. Slowing the American frontier could therefore have some effect on China's pace as well. A U.S. decision to slow frontier development could open the door to direct conversations with China about mutually pacing the technology, rather than treating superintelligence as an unavoidable arms race. The bottom line: The AI industry is hoping to overcome political resistance and keep building. Advocates of slowing frontier AI see an opportunity to turn that resistance into something bigger: a chance to reconsider not just how fast AI should advance, but how far it should go.

events.title: Royal Navy stands up first autonomous boat squadron
events.summary: Britain’s Royal Navy has formally commissioned its first uncrewed boat squadron, operating seaborne drones on front-line operations as part of its “Hybrid Navy” strategy. The force says the 1 st Autonomous Squadron officially entered active service on November 5 at a ceremony in Portsmouth Naval Base. It comprises around 180 personnel, about the same as a Type 23 frigate, split into two watches to enable operations around the clock. This active squadron replaces Project Beehive, the navy’s experimental program to build a fleet of autonomous and remotely operated vessels, through which it obtained 20 uncrewed boats from UK-based Kraken Technology Group. The force is understood to be using both Kraken’s K3 Scout, and the SM400 from SYOS Aerospace, known by the Royal Navy as the Rattler. The K3 Scout is an 8.4 m boat capable of 55 knots and can carry a payload of up to 600 kg. It has a range of up to 650 nautical miles and endurance of up to 7 days. The maker describes it as capable of a range of missions, including anti-ship and anti-submarine to detecting and countering other drones and even casualty evacuation. The Rattler boat is 7.2 m and has a 500 kg modular bay, with a range of up to 950 nautical miles. It was used last year in a demonstration during which 5 of the uncrewed boats were remotely-piloted to escort patrol ship HMS Tyne and mine countermeasures mothership HMS Stirling Castle Part of the new squadron’s mission will be to act as pathfinder for drone operations, working on bringing additional types of uncrewed surface vessel (USVs) into fleet service and conducting a range of operations alongside other organizations – both as single vessels and as part of a task group. The “Hybrid Navy” concept was outlined by First Sea Lord General Sir Gwyn Jenkins earlier this year, who made the case that uncrewed vessels would be vital in filling the gaps left by the Royal Navy’s much depleted surface fleet. Speaking at the launch of the autonomous squadron, Fleet Commander Vice-Admiral Steve Moorhouse hailed it as an historic occasion, but warned that the seas are becoming more contested, more dangerous and harder to operate in. “A hybrid navy is about giving our people better tools. It means more reach, more striking power and more options,” he stated. Last week, the force also launched strike drones from one of its aircraft carriers for the first time. Nyan one-way drones made by BAE Systems were launched from the deck, as well as a Tekever AR5 fixed-wing uncrewed aircraft, the same kind the British Army has selected to replace its troublesome Watchkeeper fleet. Elsewhere, the Ministry of Defence (MoD) says it has launched a British-built satellite called Titania into orbit, claiming it “gives the Armed Forces a new pair of eyes in space.” However, the original purpose of the orbiter was understood to be to test high-speed optical communications from low Earth orbit directly to Earth, using laser beams that are harder to intercept than radio links. Titania is the second satellite in the UK’s growing constellation of military satellites in orbit, following the launch of Tyche in October, and will be operated by UK Space Command as part of the ISTARI* program. The latter aims to deliver satellites and supporting ground systems to expand space-based intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance, the MoD said. However, while the satellite is British-made, it got into space via an American rocket, riding on SpaceX’s Transporter-18 mission. ® * What is it with the tech industry and Tolkien references?

events.title: The new battle for Congress: Trump's veto
events.summary: Democrats will charge into January with a sweeping mandate — but as President Trump has repeatedly noted, his veto power can deliver a robust roadblock to his opponents' agenda. Why it matters: Democrats may be forced to compromise to get legislative priorities through. Trump will have to decide how frequently he'll use the power — and whether he'll strike down bills popular among Americans. State of play: Democrats have secured 54 seats in the upcoming Senate, per the AP's projections , and are leading in two tight races in Mississippi and Alaska that have yet to be called. In the House, they've won 254, per AP , with several race calls still to come. Neither majority will be large enough to cross the two-thirds threshold Democrats would need to override a presidential veto on their own. Friction point: Trump knows that — and has teased his plans to impede Democrats' progress by using the power liberally. On Tuesday night, as election results rolled in, Trump posted an image of a red MAGA-esque hat that read "VETO" in all caps. A similar hat was displayed on the Resolute Desk during a Thursday signing ceremony. Asked on Fox News how he'd work with a Democratic Congress, Trump pointed to the veto: "They're in control, but they're really not in control because they can send over, you know, 50 different great bills that they're all excited about and I send them back with a nice stamp, veto." White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis said in a statement provided to Axios that Trump is "willing to work with anyone to continue delivering victories for hardworking Americans." She added, "If Democrats choose to pursue radical left policies, they are choosing to work against the American people." Worth noting: Lawmakers secured enough support to override a Trump veto across party lines during his first term on the National Defense Authorization Act in 2021. Yes, but: While Trump could use veto threats to force lawmakers to negotiate or to halt legislation altogether, vetoing popular measures could benefit Democrats' messaging for 2028, when a potential trifecta in all three branches of government would let them enact their agenda with little interference. Responding to an image of Trump's "VETO" hat Thursday, Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) wrote , "If Donald Trump wants to be Mr. Veto, let's test that out. The new Democratic majority in Congress should pass bills to make life more affordable and our government less corrupt." But doing so will still require coalition-building on the Hill, says Jonathan Lewallen, an associate professor at the University of Tampa who has studied policy agenda-setting and veto threats. He highlights two key issue areas where Trump has already threatened vetoes in the first half of his administration that Democrats have pledged to tackle: defense policy and consumer protection . Yes, but: "There may come a point in the next two years where Trump is still issuing lots of veto threats and potentially even vetoing the occasional bill, and it just becomes less effective as a strategy," Lewallen says. That means the administration might instead use another tactic with legislation they disagree with: quietly letting them become law automatically after 10 days without Trump's signature. The bottom line: Reversing Trump's agenda from Capitol Hill isn't expected to be smooth sailing. But winning back control of both chambers isn't just about passing bills, with Dem-led investigations, hearings and subpoenas expected on the horizon . events.title: AI stocks bounce back — with one notable exception
events.summary: Data: FactSet; Chart: Matt Phillips/Axios The AI trade has regained momentum despite — or maybe because of — Nvidia's struggles following the weekend revelations from CEO Jensen Huang. The big picture: Monday's sudden burst of exuberance for AI was the latest wide swing for a market upended by last week's "blue tsunami" in the midterm elections and the threat they could pose to the data center boom. By the numbers: The Nasdaq 100 index of large-cap technology shares soared 3.4%, its biggest daily jump since late March and its second-best showing of the year. Zoom in: Stocks romped across the AI ecosystem — well, with one important exception. Pick-and-shovel plays such as engineering and construction companies, and makers of data center inputs like fiberoptic cables, servers and data storage devices soared. The companies that build and lease out data center computing power, known as neoclouds, also jumped. (Those companies had been at the epicenter of recent jitters about financing for the AI boom.) Hyperscalers rose, paced by Meta, which notched a gain of 5.1%. Semiconductors roared, with the SOX index posting its best gain — 6.9% — since late July. Yes, but: The glaring exception to the AI-palooza was its best-known player, Nvidia. Weekend revelations from CEO Jensen Huang — who acknowledged having an affair with a woman suspected of connections to Chinese intelligence — left investors grappling with uncertainty about the CEO's future. The intrigue: Some investors may see Nvidia's pain as potential gain for rivals. Broadcom jumped 8.8%, its best day in nearly a year. Advanced Micro Devices soared 13.3%, benefiting also from an upgrade to "Outperform" — effectively, a "buy" recommendation — from Oppenheimer analysts on Sunday. Context: Bullish commentary from Wall Street established the background music for Monday's big bounce, as analysts urged investors to buy into the market's recent soft patch. "We believe stocks are now clearly in oversold territory," Goldman Sachs analysts wrote in a note Monday. "We believe the market's reaction to the midterms is overdone," wrote Morgan Stanley tech analysts in a note entitled "Buy the Drop: AI Investment Opportunities Post the U.S. Midterms," which it published Sunday night. "We do not think AI is a continued sell here. In fact, tech drawdown is offering certain opportunities. The selloff was very sharp," JPMorgan equity strategists wrote Monday. These analysts could be right. The recent slump has been deep in certain sectors such as chips. And buying the dip has been a solid strategy in recent years, especially for retail investors . The other side: On the other hand, there may be good reasons such stocks sold off. For example, even before the news about the Nvidia CEO or the anti-data center vote at the polls, Wall Street expectations for capital expenditures from hyperscalers had been looking a bit flat. Given that a large percentage of that AI investment is spent on the semiconductors needed to make these computing centers, well, compute, that would seem to be important for tech investors. What's next: Will the stock market's rally be the start of a new phase of AI exuberance? Or is it just an example of Wall Street's proverbial dead cat bounce ?

events.title: Support for death penalty reaches 50-year low, poll finds
events.summary: Support for the death penalty in the US has dropped to a more than 50-year low following a botched execution in Tennessee. Forty-nine percent of American adults approve of the death penalty for convicted murderers, according to Gallup , the first time the figure has dropped below 50% since 1971. Support for the death penalty is sliding among all political groups but most among Democrats, only 28% of whom are currently in favor. Seventy-three percent of Republicans are in favor of it, as well as half of independents. The poll was taken after the botched killing by lethal injection of Christa Pike, which caused Tennessee to pause executions for the remainder of the year. Outgoing California Gov. Gavin Newsom, a possible 2028 Democratic presidential contender, also recently spared the lives of hundreds of prisoners on the state’s death row. — Morgan Chalfant

events.title: The Garbage Man: Bill Gates Has Earned Billions Investing in Climate-Polluting Landfills
events.summary: Mark Harris for ProPublica. Source images: Getty Images, RMI. In November 2015, world leaders descended on Paris to negotiate a historic agreement to limit global warming. But on the summit’s opening day, attention turned to a private citizen slouched awkwardly in a chair on stage: Bill Gates. Gates, with his characteristic flop of sandy hair, grinned impishly as President Barack Obama called him a “visionary” and a “driving force” behind a pair of pledges that both saw as key to the larger agreement. First the world’s largest economies would double their spending on research into clean-energy technologies. Then investors like Gates would back the startups that emerged. The Microsoft cofounder had already enlisted two dozen other billionaires to join the effort. For Gates, who’d become increasingly consumed by this unprecedented threat to human well-being, the moment marked his arrival as a leading figure in the fight against climate change. “If we back over 50 different breakthrough approaches, we know that several of those will give us the solution that we need,” Gates said during his own speech. He would invest at least $2 billion of his own money in companies developing geothermal wells, new kinds of nuclear reactors and machines that pull carbon from the air , to name just a few. With much less fanfare, however, Gates has put more than double that amount into a very dirty, old-school industry. At the time of the Paris summit, he was already the dominant shareholder of America’s No. 2 landfill operator, Republic Services. He has since increased his stake to 38% of the company, a position worth $29 billion. Bill Gates’ Stake in Republic Services, a Landfill Operator, Now Exceeds a Fifth of His Net Worth Note: “Other” includes stakes in other publicly traded companies and accumulated dividends and investment returns. Sources: Forbes’ The World’s Billionaires, Bloomberg’s Billionaires Index, SEC filings, StockAnalysis.com Chris Alcantara/ProPublica While fossil fuels get most of the attention, scientists increasingly see landfills as a crucial climate issue. They’re responsible for as much as a fifth of the country’s emissions of methane , a highly potent greenhouse gas, studies show. Republic alone generates as much climate pollution as 3 million gasoline-burning cars each year, according to its own reports. One might imagine that a landfill operator with Gates as its largest shareholder — and with three people closely linked to Gates on its board — would lead the way in tackling those emissions. Even after seemingly softening his stance on global warming in a controversial blog post last year, Gates remains one of the world’s most prominent voices on the issue. As he did in his bestselling 2021 book “How to Avoid a Climate Disaster,” he continues to advocate for cutting emissions , and he has called on his fellow business leaders to do their part.  Gates, though, has failed to make Republic live up to his own climate principles, a ProPublica investigation has found. Federal inspectors have repeatedly found methane escaping from Republic landfills at levels above federal limits. The company has refrained from adopting the ambitious emissions-reduction goal embraced by its main competitor. Republic has even lobbied against policies that could make the wider industry cleaner, including by keeping organic waste out of landfills in the first place. “It seems very likely that Bill Gates has the power to influence Republic’s behavior to make it more climate-friendly, even if that costs the company profits,” said Ann Lipton, a legal scholar who studies corporate governance at the University of Colorado, Boulder.  As for whether he should, in her words, “put his money where his mouth is,” Lipton said, “you can leave it to the reader to make the moral judgment.” Gates’ Climate Awakening Gates didn’t respond to repeated requests to discuss his landfill investments, and ProPublica couldn’t find any public comments he’s made about them. But the bet has proven wildly lucrative. Since November 1999, when he emerged as the owner of 5% of Republic’s shares — “ It’s ‘Garbage In’ for Gates ,” the New York Post headline read — the company’s stock price has soared thirtyfold. And Gates has personally received $2.6 billion in dividends, a ProPublica analysis of securities filings shows. In those early days, Gates hadn’t yet awakened to the threat of global warming. It was a different time. Microsoft Windows ran on more than 80% of personal computers. Gates was the world’s richest person, and his bespectacled face graced the cover of Time magazine twice that year . He was simultaneously criticized for what a federal judge determined to be Microsoft’s monopolistic practices and admired for establishing what was soon to become the world’s largest charitable foundation.  A rare clue to why Gates made his foray into landfills can be found in an interview he gave to Fortune that year. To fund his plan to give away virtually his entire fortune, he said he’d given his personal money manager, Michael Larson, a simple remit: Sell Microsoft shares, buy safe, boring assets.  Republic’s then-chairman, billionaire Wayne Huizenga , had flown Larson by helicopter to his private golf course in Florida, according to the article. It’s unclear if Huizenga pitched Republic there, but it fit the remit. America would always produce trash, ensuring a steady stream of revenue. After that initial investment, Larson progressively increased Gates’ stake in Republic over the years that followed. Larson would also acquire a small chunk of Republic’s main competitor, Waste Management — which Huizenga also once led — on behalf of the Gates Foundation. It was only in 2006, when he asked two climate scientists to educate him, that Gates started to grasp the potentially “catastrophic” effects of greenhouse gases , he later wrote. events.title: Brent falls below $90 a barrel for first time since August
events.summary: Brent fell below $90 a barrel for the first time since August after US President Donald Trump said further military action against Iran was no longer necessary and that the war could end soon. Brent, the benchmark for two thirds of the world's oil, slid briefly below $90 per barrel before trading at $90.32 at 1.33pm UAE time. West Texas Intermediate, the gauge that tracks US crude, was trading 2.27 per cent lower at $84.77. “At this point, taking the military action doesn’t seem to be a very necessary thing … I think it’s going to be ending fairly soon,” Mr Trump said at the White House on Monday, after a meeting with Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman. Brent crude extended Monday’s near 6 per cent plunge after Mr Trump's remarks that he would delay launching more military strikes against Iran following appeals from regional leaders, said Axel Rudolph, chief technical analyst at IG. “However, the US naval blockade in the Strait of Hormuz remains in place, meaning the market still faces a significant supply risk if tensions escalate or shipping through the world’s most important oil chokepoint is disrupted,” he added. The Strait of Hormuz, an important chokepoint for global crude supplies, remains disrupted. Oil flows through the waterway averaged 7.82 million barrels per day over the week to November 8, about 46 per cent of the prewar level of 17.14 million bpd, according to the latest data from Kpler. This data excludes Iranian exports travelling through the channel. Investors are also keeping a close eye on Ukraine-Russia peace talks in Abu Dhabi. Any signs of de-escalation between the two countries, which have been at war since February 2022, could put further downward pressure on oil prices if sanctions are eased on Russia, a major producer. The sanctions, aimed at curtailing the country's revenue from oil, have disrupted Russian shipments.

events.title: Russia's top independent newspaper closes after decades, citing official pressure
events.summary: Russia’s most celebrated independent newspaper, Novaya Gazeta, has closed its Moscow offices, citing relentless pressure from the government MOSCOW -- MOSCOW (AP) — Novaya Gazeta , Russia's most celebrated independent newspaper, closed its Moscow offices Monday, citing relentless pressure from government officials. It was the last major independent media outlet critical of the Kremlin that remained active in Russia. Others closed or moved their operations abroad after President Vladimir Putin sent troops into Ukraine in February 2022. In a statement published Oct. 30, the newspaper said the Russian authorities and the security services had "forced our editorial team to cease operations.” “Human rights and freedoms have been abolished in this country, and defending them is now treated as a crime,” the newspaper said. "Elections and elected governing bodies have been effectively dismantled, civil society institutions have been wiped out, freedom of conscience and human dignity have been trampled underfoot.” Launched in 1993, Novaya Gazeta quickly became known for its fierce reporting and dedication to uncovering Russian human rights abuses and corruption. Six of its journalists have been killed, including Anna Politkovskaya, who reported on atrocities during the second Chechen War at the start of Putin’s first term as president. She was fatally shot in her apartment building in 2006. On the newspaper's final day in its office Monday, journalists slowly removed the portraits of their slain colleagues from the newsroom where reporters and editors planned their work. Tatiana Britskaya, the editor of Novaya Gazeta's investigations desk, said she had expected the outlet's closure almost every day for the past 4 1/2 years. “It is an incredibly difficult decision, because this is more than a workplace, more than an office — this is our home, and we're losing it,” she said. Novaya Gazeta had faced growing government pressure as the Kremlin cracked down on critics, with repression sharply intensifying after the start of the conflict in Ukraine. Baby buried alive for 24 hours released from the hospital; father charged House tables Hegseth impeachment, effectively killing it in current Congress Wisconsin state trooper detained by ICE Longtime editor-in-chief Dmitry Muratov, who shared the 2021 Nobel Peace Prize with Philippine journalist Maria Ressa, was attacked on a train in 2022 by an assailant who poured red paint over him, causing severe irritation in his eyes. Muratov stepped down as editor in 2023 after being named a “foreign agent” by Russian authorities. The designation carries strong pejorative connotations in the country and can bring additional government scrutiny. The newspaper was fined after it was accused of discrediting Russia’s armed forces, and it also was declared a foreign agent. Authorities blocked all of its online platforms, seized its printing house, revoked its media registration and shut down the donation system that allowed it to receive support from readers. In a final blow, the newspaper was ordered to clear out its Moscow offices. As reporters left the building and gathered in the street, a new sign was affixed atop the nameplate that once announced the newspaper's office. It read, “Here lived Novaya Gazeta.” Sergei Sokolov, Novaya Gazeta's editor-in-chief, said he believed the newspaper would return one day “with renewed strength.” “We will live, and I am sure that this country, caught in such a terrible era, will eventually stir. As soon as those first signs appear, Novaya Gazeta will return, to our readers and to our colleagues.” Some of Novaya Gazeta’s staff left Russia in 2022 and opened a separate project, Novaya Gazeta Europe . The new outlet has been sharply critical of the Kremlin and its military action in Ukraine. events.title: Microsoft teaches schools that free email was just a phase
events.summary: Microsoft is retiring its free education email service, leaving schools, colleges, and universities facing new licensing bills if they want to keep students' mailboxes. The company announced plans last week to retire Office 365 A1, the Student Use Benefit program, and free Exchange Online for Alumni. The changes generally take effect at institutions' first renewal or extension on or after January 1, 2028. Office 365 A1 provides eligible institutions with web-based Office applications, Teams, and email at no charge. Its replacement, Microsoft 365 Education A0, excludes Exchange Online, SharePoint Online, and Teams. Eligibility also depends on paid faculty licensing and students actively using Windows devices for education. A spokesperson for the UK's Department for Education told The Register : "We are disappointed that Microsoft has made this decision. However, we are pleased to have successfully negotiated some additional concessions for the UK, giving schools, colleges and universities the time they need to be able to successfully transition to new licensing agreements." An industry insider said the loss of free Microsoft-hosted email could add thousands to institutions' bills. Another organization noted "significant concerns… around affordability, equitable treatment across the sector, and the longer-term implications of the changes." A spokesperson for UK education technology body Jisc told The Register that its "focus has been on ensuring that UK education providers are well supported and have sufficient time to assess their options." "We continue working closely with Microsoft and sector partners to support those discussions and help institutions make informed decisions about their future requirements." Also being retired are free Exchange Online for Alumni – which lets graduates retain their mailboxes – and the Student Use Benefit, providing student licenses at no additional charge when institutions purchase qualifying faculty licenses. Microsoft plans a paid alumni replacement. The Windows giant is also changing storage entitlements and introducing Microsoft 365 Education A7, its "most advanced education offering," which adds AI, security, governance, and device-management features. Asked why it was removing those services from the free tier, Microsoft framed the overhaul as a response to institutions' changing needs. A spokesperson told The Register : "Education institutions are evaluating AI, security, privacy, governance, and teaching and learning as connected priorities rather than separate technology decisions. "Microsoft is updating the portfolio now to provide a clearer path from foundational access to advanced capabilities, while enabling institutions to adopt technology according to their needs and readiness. This evolution reflects both the value Microsoft 365 Education has gained since the last pricing change nearly a decade ago and the structure of the new portfolio. "Microsoft's broader goal is not technology adoption for its own sake. It is to support AI and digital experiences that strengthen learning, preserve educator judgment and give institutions the controls they need to manage data, privacy, and responsible use." Office 365 A1 stopped accepting new web-direct orders on November 5, 2026, with partner-channel sales ending on May 1, 2027. Retirement is scheduled for January 1, 2028, but existing agreements remain valid through their current terms. Institutions that need continued service must move to replacement licenses at the applicable renewal or contract expiry. ®

events.title: Nakheel unveils mega development for 50,000 residents in Dubai
events.summary: Dubai’s Nakheel has unveiled a new master development next to Palm Jebel Ali as property developers continue to launch housing projects despite Iran war-driven uncertainty. Palm Springs, a 3.8 million-square-metre residential masterplan, will have a mix of villas, townhouses and apartments, Nakheel said on Tuesday. It will also have education, health care, sport and leisure facilities across 15 neighbourhoods in southern Dubai, with two schools, a hospital and six mosques. Leisure facilities include a dedicated Country Club and Sports Club, alongside recreational, fitness and sports facilities. Nakheel, part of Dubai Holding Real Estate, did not reveal the total value of the development or its time frame. The new development is being planned for about 50,000 residents. “Palm Springs reflects our long-term confidence in southern Dubai and its role in the city’s future,” said Khalid Al Malik, chief executive of Dubai Holding Real Estate. “With Palm Jebel Ali nearby, our focus is on creating a community that brings homes and supporting infrastructure together from the outset.” The masterplan also includes about 593,000 sq m of open space, including a central park and landscaped areas, Nakheel said. More than 35 kilometres of cycling, running and walking routes are planned to link the neighbourhoods with parks, retail and leisure destinations. Property developers are continuing to launch projects in Dubai despite concerns about the slowing of the market as the Iran war continues. Abu Dhabi’s Aldar said last month it plans to launch a major development of villas and townhouses in Dubai by the end of this year as part of the company’s expansion across the UAE. Work is also progressing on Nakheel's other flagship development, Palm Jebel Ali, after the developer awarded contracts in April worth more than Dh3.5 billion ($950 million) for the construction of 544 villas. Ginco General Contracting is set to build 354 villas across Fronds A to D, while United Engineering Construction will construct 190 on Fronds E and F. Nakheel has also started handing over 892 villas and townhouses at the redeveloped Jebel Ali Village near Ibn Battuta Mall, more than four years after the community’s original 290 homes were demolished.

events.title: Reducing Lithography Learning Cycles To Accelerate FOPLP Ramps
events.summary: For manufacturers scaling advanced AI packages, pressure is mounting from every direction. On one side, demand continues to rise. While on another, AI packages are growing larger and integrating more high-bandwidth memory (HBM) and high-performance chips. And that’s to say nothing of the production teams who face increasing pressure to ramp new processes quickly. While achieving high yield remains a critical goal, success increasingly depends on how quickly manufacturers can establish stable process conditions and transition from development to high-volume manufacturing (HVM). Fan-out panel-level packaging (FOPLP) has emerged as an attractive path forward for manufacturers looking to scale advanced packaging production. Compared with traditional wafer-based approaches, FOPLP can significantly improve substrate utilization while increasing the number of packages produced per substrate. In one study comparison, a 300mm wafer achieved approximately 55% substrate utilization with six packages per wafer, while a 300mm panel achieved 86% utilization with 12 packages per panel and a 510 × 515mm panel achieved 74% utilization with 30 packages per panel. This enables manufacturers to improve manufacturing efficiency and reduce costs per package. However, realizing those benefits requires overcoming significant lithography challenges. As panel sizes increase, manufacturers must contend with pattern distortion, die shift, and resulting overlay errors across the substrate. These effects directly impact yield and make process optimization substantially more difficult. Unlike traditional wafer-based processes, panel-scale variation does not behave uniformly. Instead, distortion patterns can vary significantly across the panel, creating localized challenges that are difficult to correct using conventional approaches. The sweet spot Ultimately, process engineers must identify the “sweet spot” between overlay yield and throughput. To compensate for panel-level distortion, manufacturers typically rely on a range of correction strategies. Global correction maintains throughput but often leaves localized overlay errors uncorrected. Zone correction can improve yield, with field data in our study indicating yields between 40% and 80%, but at reduced throughput. Die-by-die correction can further improve yield but introduces a significant throughput penalty. Site-by-site correction offers a compromise, balancing yield improvement with higher throughput. However, finding that balance is rarely straightforward. Identifying the optimal operating window often requires repeated experimentation across variables, such as exposure field configurations, die layouts, panel layouts, and overlay thresholds. Each adjustment can require another trial run and another round of data analysis. The result is increased engineering effort, additional material consumption, longer development cycles, and delayed production ramps. For manufacturers under pressure to bring capacity online quickly, every additional iteration delays the path to production. Moving beyond trial-and-error By combining offline metrology data with yield prediction algorithms, manufacturers can evaluate process performance before committing to extensive physical trials. Instead of repeatedly testing possible operating conditions on production hardware, engineering teams can assess likely yield outcomes in advance and identify promising process windows earlier in the development cycle. The process begins with detailed metrology measurements that capture panel-scale variation, including pattern errors and die shifts. Yield prediction algorithms then evaluate this information alongside process variables, such as exposure field configuration, panel layout, die layout, and overlay thresholds. Using these inputs, manufacturers can estimate expected yield performance and compare alternative process strategies without executing full production experiments. The value extends beyond simple prediction. Visualization tools such as heat maps, vector plots, histograms, and yield dashboards help engineers understand process sensitivities, isolate sources of variation, and identify root causes more quickly (Figure 1). This enables more targeted process optimization and faster decision making. Fig. 1: Yield prediction analysis tools showing 1) parameters for analysis, 2) X-axis overlay error and 3) Y-axis overlay error. A comparison of these maps reveals that the Y-axis exhibits the most significant overlay errors, which directly contribute to yield loss. This insight enables users to pinpoint the root cause of the issue and take corrective actions effectively, thereby improving overall process performance. Yield prediction technology has also been evaluated using production substrates in an HVM process. In the initial assessment, differences between predicted and measured yield ranged from 1.2% to 2.7%. Further analysis showed that variability in manual inspection judgments was the primary source of the discrepancies. After the inspection process was standardized, prediction errors were reduced to 0.2% to 0.8%. Accelerating qualification During process development, manufacturers can use yield prediction technology to evaluate process conditions through simulation before running qualification substrates (Figure 2). Rather than relying exclusively on physical experimentation, engineers can evaluate multiple parameter combinations, identify promising operating conditions, and then use qualification substrates to validate the predictions. This approach can reduce trial-and-error iterations while accelerating process refinement and shortening development timelines. Fig. 2: Residual overlay error vector maps generated under various process conditions help accelerate process refinement, reduce trial-and-error iterations and improve efficiency during R&D. Just as important, it helps engineering teams focus their efforts on optimization rather than repetitive trial-and-error experimentation. Extending yield prediction to mass production The benefits of yield prediction technology can also extend beyond process development. In mass production, the technology can be integrated into the lithography workflow for real-time, in-line process monitoring and earlier defect detection. A standard lithography workflow includes multiple process steps before final inspection determines overlay yield. Errors introduced along the way can result in rework or permanent yield loss. By integrating yield prediction earlier in the workflow, manufacturers can identify potential problems before final inspection, enabling earlier intervention while reducing the manpower, time and costs associated with rework (Figure 3). Fig. 3: Yield prediction technology can be integrated into the production workflow to support real-time, in-line process monitoring and earlier defect detection. events.title: Test Struggles To Keep Pace With AI
events.summary: Key Takeaways: AI workloads are changing faster than chips can be designed, manufactured, and tested, forcing chipmakers to rethink test strategies. More complex packaging and additional test insertions are generating vast amounts of data, much of it siloed across companies and facilities. Chipmakers need better ways to monitor aging and reliability as customers push to extend the life of increasingly expensive AI hardware. The rapid pace of change in AI models and approaches is creating confusion over what to test, when to test it, and what to monitor once chips are in the field. Until recently, test targets and the timing for test insertions generally were determined by fab processes and the laws of physics, and the results of those tests were deterministic and quantifiable. But starting with the rollout of generative AI and the ensuing explosion of data centers, the gap has widened between the rollout of new algorithms and use models and the time it takes to deploy a chip in the field. An increasing number of high-performance processors used in data centers, and many at the edge, are multi-die assemblies. The chips are more complex and take longer to design, manufacture, package, and assemble, and the workloads for which they are designed often change by the time those chips leave final test. Along the way, there are more test insertions along the way, each of which generates more data. The tests are more complex and varied, as well. In addition to electrical tests, these chips need to be analyzed for mechanical integrity. AI workloads can stress one part of a multi-die assembly more than others, and they can change quickly as algorithms and use cases evolve. That, in turn, requires increasingly complex multiphysics simulations and more real-time monitoring of processor and memory utilization, thermal gradients, and datapath throughput, along with accelerated aging that can affect signal integrity. “It’s a huge challenge,” said Scott Segura, vice president of sales at Advantest . “People are starting to put more active components into the substrate, and moving things closer to each other, as well, so it’s turning into more test insertions. What shifts left? What shifts right? There are substrate testers today that are just trying to make sure you have contact, but now we’re seeing functional testing moving into substrate testing. And at the die level, we’re probing performance. We’ve got to control thermal. For known good dies, they have to be able to handle 3 kilowatts at the die level, so now we’re testing singulated dies. There’s going to be a shift in how you slice up where things go, and packaging is the key. As you’re putting more and more stuff in the package, into the substrates, whatever you’re stacking this stuff on, you’re going to have to start testing those different steps. Silicon photonics has five insertions right now.” It only gets more challenging from here with the transition from wafers to panels, which will require entirely new equipment and processes. At the same time, packaging and assembly, which used to be done in one location, is now being split between fabs and OSATs. That creates ongoing challenges around who sees what data, when they see it, and how much of it can be shared with other companies. “Test insertions typically are done at different locations,” said Jeorge Hurtarte, senior director of product marketing in the Semiconductor Test group at Teradyne . “For example, from wafer sort to singulated die probe could be done at a fab. They have their data collection workflows. They have their own test programs. And they gather failure mechanisms as a result of the testing done at wafer sort and singulated die probing. When it comes to the next step, which is where we put together a compute die plus a stack of HBMs, plus perhaps other chiplets into an interposer — and it’s going to panels today from round wafers to optimize the utilization of equipment and putting as many dies as possible on a 310 × 310mm panel — this wafer/panel interposer substrate test will likely be done by the OSAT. That’s a different location with a different test program and a different data collection environment or workflow. They don’t necessarily talk to the previous test insertion data. And unfortunately in the fabless world, people don’t share data unless the customer owns everything.” Fig. 1: Evolving test strategies and emerging test insertions. Source: Teradyne Testing gets more complicated It took slightly more than two years from the introduction of ChatGPT in November 2022 to widespread commercial adoption of agentic AI systems. That’s roughly the time it takes to design, verify, and validate a chip, get that design onto a shuttle in a fab, package it, and integrate that chip into a functional system. But during that time, the industry shifted from arrays of GPUs for massively parallel multiply-accumulate operations to a combination of GPUs, CPUs, and customized and programmable accelerators for orchestrating how agents work and interact. Those involve very different optimization and prioritization schemes — hierarchies that are constantly being re-evaluated as workloads shift. Hyperscalers and large chipmakers have been pushing EDA vendors to reduce the time it takes to design these mini-systems. But even if the chip design cycle could be shrunk from today’s 18 to 24 months to as little as 6 months — a stated goal by some large chipmakers — there would still be a significant gap between the time it takes to get to working silicon and the time it takes to roll out new training and inference models. And that could change again if recurrent self-improvement lives up to its promise. “We have customers now that will tape out chips, run their models on them, or look at what the end application is, and they’ll end up not going to market with them,” said Advantest’s Segura. “They’ll do a derivative of it, or they’ll do a different version of it. That could change how much memory they’re stacking on it, how many cores it has, how much cache it has, and the overall architecture. It totally changes depending on whether you’re training a frontier model or whether it’s a CPU hosting something. Even our customers sometimes guess wrong. They go through a chip development cycle, get the silicon out, start to run models on it, and they find out the use model has shifted, or they didn’t put enough memory in, or it’s too expensive. They’ve got to be pretty nimble about what they develop, as well. You see a lot of chiplet designs because it lets them scale a different number of cores, for example. If they originally planned for 256 cores, they may only need 192.” Breaking down data silos The reasons underlying the gap between hardware and software

events.title: Which Passing Chips Need More Testing?
events.summary: Key Takeaways: Chips that pass identical tests can carry very different reliability risks, because marginal behavior often hides inside specification limits. Device-level models, cross-insertion data, and physical inspection can flag suspicious passing parts, but an anomaly isn’t proof of a defect. Extra screening pays off only when the added test can expose the suspected weakness at a lower cost than the failures it may prevent. A chip passes wafer sort, moves through assembly, and passes final test. Nothing in its results gives anyone a reason to hold it. Yet another chip with nearly identical results could fail in the field because of a weakness neither test exposed, whether that’s a thin timing margin, a slight resistance shift, or a combination of measurements that looks harmless when each is viewed alone. The challenge for manufacturers is figuring out which of those passing chips deserve another look without retesting everything. Test engineers have always known that a passing result doesn’t guarantee lifetime reliability. What’s changed is how much they can learn about each device. Internal parametric measurements, manufacturing history, and predictive models can now reveal unusual behavior inside a population of passing parts, but spotting a suspicious device is just the beginning. “The cost of test and the amount of test is exploding, and the ability to test before system-level test is a challenge,” said Kimon Michaels, executive vice president of products and solutions, director, and co-founder of PDF Solutions . “But of course, one of the big challenges is how much of your supply chain is at risk at that point, or the amount of product that you’re throwing away if it fails at that point.” The longer a marginal device goes undetected, the more value gets invested in it. But testing every device more thoroughly isn’t free. Extra patterns eat tester time, burn-in ties up equipment, a packaged device may need another mechanical insertion, and rejecting every statistical outlier throws away some good silicon. On the other side of the ledger is the part that escapes into a customer’s system. “Nothing is more expensive than a field failure,” said Michaels. “The challenge is that the advanced technologies, in some respects, are even more sensitive to reliability failures.” Manufacturing tests can only approximate the conditions a chip will see in operation. Voltage, temperature, timing, and workload are controllable during test, but the interactions inside a fully assembled system are much harder to reproduce. “Individual dies can pass wafer sort and final test, and then behave differently once the dies, memory devices, interconnects, firmware, and software are all working together,” said Eli Roth, smart manufacturing product manager at Teradyne . “We’re very good at finding hard failures. What’s much harder is finding devices that meet spec but are operating close to a reliability boundary.” Testing every combination of operating conditions is impractical, and even extensive system-level tests cannot guarantee that every weakness will surface. Manufacturers need a way to identify high-risk devices and decide whether a targeted test can expose the problem before shipment. Device-level models are exposing hidden outliers Conventional production testing relies on defined limits, with guard bands for measurement uncertainty and operating variation. Statistical analysis can flag devices near those limits or behaving differently from their neighbors on the same wafer or lot. Nevertheless, a chip can still pass every test while showing an unusual relationship among its measurements. Device-specific models offer another way to identify those differences. By comparing internal parametric measurements with the behavior expected from a particular device, engineers can detect inconsistencies that population-based statistics might overlook. Process and timing signatures can provide the basis for predicting how a chip should behave, allowing engineers to investigate discrepancies between predicted and measured performance. The pattern of those discrepancies matters. Design-related margin limits tend to show up consistently across a product population, but material problems don’t. “Material-induced variability behaves differently. It is often localized, asymmetric, or statistically scattered,” said Nir Sever, senior director of business development at proteanTecs . “Only a subset of devices, wafers, or regions on a die may show accelerated drift. The degradation slope may diverge from the population over time.” Localized or accelerating changes can suggest an emerging physical weakness. The difficulty is determining whether that variation represents a reliability risk worth investigating, and whether another test can reveal anything useful about it. The models making those calls also have a shelf life. “Data is not static,” said Michaels. “It drifts. It’s physics-based. There are changes to the process, and you have to be cognizant of that in how you retrain, how you monitor, etc.” Process adjustments, equipment changes, and product revisions can alter the relationships a model learned. That means engineers need to validate the models as carefully as the measurements feeding them, especially when an outlier flag can trigger extra screening or reject a part. Inspection explains marginal electrical behavior Some latent defects don’t produce a consistent electrical failure. A weakened interconnect may conduct well enough at room temperature, then become unstable under thermal or mechanical stress. That’s particularly hard to catch in advanced packages. Partial non-wetting, micro-bump voids, delamination, and warpage may not cause an immediate failure. “Voiding and non-wetting may weaken an interconnect without causing an immediate open,” said Chris Rand, principal technical engineer at Nordson Test & Inspection . “Variation in bump height, solder volume, or interconnect geometry can shift resistance or create continuity that changes under load, temperature, or handling.” X-ray or acoustic inspection can provide physical evidence of a suspected interconnect problem, while electrical measurements help establish whether an observed irregularity affects device behavior. Neither technique necessarily provides a complete diagnosis on its own. Correlating the results can narrow the possible failure mechanisms and help engineers select a stress condition more likely to expose the weakness. Comparing measurements across test insertions offers another clue. A chip may pass at every stage while its electrical characteristics slowly shift, a trend that individual pass/fail decisions would miss. “An unexplained drift is not a healthy sign,” said Greg Prewitt, director of Exensio Solutions at PDF Solutions. “If a device just changes, and you don’t think it’s a problem with the test setup, it requires more scrutiny.” Flagging that device and carrying the flag to later insertions lets manufac

events.title: China's trade surplus surpasses $1 trillion for a 2nd straight year, as exports surge 35%
events.summary: China says its trade surplus exceeded $1 trillion for a 2nd straight year HONG KONG -- China’s trade surplus exceeded $1 trillion for a second straight year , according to official data released Tuesday, as pressure mounts for greater balance in trade with Beijing. Exports in October surged 35.2% from a year earlier, the customs agency said. Exports have grown rapidly this year supported by high-tech goods like semiconductors and autos. Imports rose 41.6% year-on-year. Between January and October, China logged a $1.04 trillion trade surplus, even as the trade surplus narrowed last month to $105.3 billion from $133.5bn in September as imports picked up pace. That puts China on track for surpassing last year’s record $1.2 trillion trade surplus. “We expect Chinese exports to stay strong for the rest of this year, led by electronics and autos,” said Dave Chia, an economist at Moody’s Analytics. Overcapacity in many industries, excess domestic savings and weakened domestic demand are still forcing China to ship its goods abroad as some countries move to protect their own industries, said Alicia García-Herrero, chief economist for Asia Pacific at French bank Natixis. The situation is not sustainable, she said. Businesses are feeling the pressure of ferocious competition as China’s economy has slowed , said Cinders Zhou, who sells eyewear for a manufacturer in Linhai city in eastern China’s Zhejiang province. “It comes down to product quality, or rather the increasingly the lack of it across the industry, since there’s significant homogenization,” said Zhou, whose company makes frames and lenses sold both in and outside China. “That has forced everyone to compete on price,” she said. Trade curbs by the European Union pose an important risk at a time of heightened U.S. trade barriers and tariffs , Chia said. Top Chinese officials insist Beijing is not seeking to expand the trade surplus but wants more balanced global trade. China says its trade surplus exceeded $1 trillion for a 2nd straight year, as exports in October surged 35% Dozens injured in South Korea after bus crashes into 32 vehicles House Republicans consider issuing subpoena to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang China’s exports could be vulnerable to setbacks for the artificial intelligence industry, a concern that deepened with the Democratic victories in the U.S. midterm elections given the public backlash against expansion of data centers. “If the AI boom slows or turns into a correction, lower chip and electronics prices and smaller shipping volumes would hit China’s exports hard,” Chia said. Trade is among the top issues likely to be on the agenda in planned meetings between U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation leaders summit later this month in China’s technology hub Shenzhen. A two-month extension of a trade truce until January has provided some relief to exporters, though it’s unclear how long that may last. U.S. and European trade policies have added “a lot of difficulties” for Chinese businesses to expand in the markets, said Wang Xin, head of the Shenzhen Cross-Border E-Commerce Association, an industry group. Strong exports have helped offset sluggish domestic demand in China, where the economy is forecast to meet Beijing’s official target of a 4.5% to 5% annual growth this year, slightly slower than last year’s 5% expansion. events.title: Adnoc Gas studying potential new export routes to bypass Hormuz
events.summary: Adnoc Gas is to study potential new routes to supply gas amid the disruption to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, as the company raised its 2026 full-year net income forecast to at least $4 billion. “We’ve been evaluating in the past months and studying different means and ways of really delivering or finding alternative routes to deliver to our customers,” Adnoc Gas chief executive Fatema Al Nuaimi said during an earnings call. "At this stage, none of these plans are beyond the phase of study. While we were really busy managing the situation on the ground, it is only natural that we review how we serve our customers better." The company is also to undertake a "feasibility study" on an LNG project in Fujairah, chief financial officer Peter van Driel said. “It is work in progress and anything you ask is part of that assessment – size, amount of gas going in, markets, volumes that we want to sell to our customers. We will come back once a decision is made,” he added. Adnoc is building the Ruwais LNG project, which is expected to start commercial operations in 2028 and more than double the company's LNG production capacity to about 15 million tonnes a year. “We have seen, month on month, an increase in the number of ships that have reached the customers. Asia is our key market. We're very well positioned, in particular, to serve the countries close to Abu Dhabi … India, west coast China,” Mr van Driel said, without providing further details. Third-quarter earnings improved on the previous quarter despite the disruption caused by the Iran war. Net income for the three months to the end of September reached $1.33 billion, flat on an annual basis and roughly double the $664.6 million in the second quarter, Adnoc Gas said on Tuesday in a statement to the Abu Dhabi Securities Exchange, where its shares are traded. Revenue for the period fell by nearly 10 per cent annually to $4.38 billion. "Although market conditions improved during the third quarter, ongoing disruption to maritime movements through the Strait of Hormuz continued to create a challenging operating environment," the company said. Prolonged maritime disruption in the strait continued to curtail exports of liquefied petroleum gas, naphtha and liquefied natural gas. "Our operational strength and commercial agility enabled us to safely and reliably meet domestic and international demand and drive strong financial results despite continued challenging external conditions," Ms Al Nuaimi said. Adnoc Gas raised its full-year 2026 net income guidance to at least $4 billion, compared with its previous guidance of $3.5 billion to $4 billion. "Our outlook remains subject to developments in regional maritime conditions, which we continue to monitor closely," it said. Domestic gas sales volumes during the quarter declined by 19 per cent annually to 513 trillion British thermal units (Tbtu), "reflecting reduced reinjection gas and ethane offtake", the statement said. Sales gas volumes remained broadly flat year-on-year. Adnoc Gas supplies about 60 per cent of the UAE’s gas needs as well as customers in more than 20 countries. While the sales volumes of export and traded liquids were down 28 per cent annually, they were up 69 per cent on a quarterly basis, mainly driven by improved shipping activities, Adnoc Gas said. Despite higher gas and naphtha prices, the "continued disruption constrained the company's ability to lift and export its liquids and LNG cargoes, limiting its capacity to fully capture these higher market prices during the quarter", it added. Oil and gas prices surged globally after the Iran war began on February 28, with the Strait of Hormuz effectively closed. The waterway accounted for about 20 per cent of all oil and gas flows before the conflict erupted. Iran also launched attacks on energy infrastructure across the Middle East in response to US-Israeli strikes. Operations at Habshan, one of the world’s largest gas processing sites operated by Adnoc Gas in the UAE, were suspended in early April after it was damaged . One person was killed and four injured after falling shrapnel from intercepted Iranian strikes caused two fires at the complex on April 3. The company reported "significant damage" at the time. The site in Abu Dhabi had another incident on April 8. In the third quarter, restoration works at the damaged Habshan complex "progressed in line with plan", Adnoc Gas said. The company said it "remains on track" to restore full capacity by the second quarter of 2027. Long-term strategy Adnoc Gas has continued to execute its long-term growth strategy this year, despite operational constraints. The company awarded $8.2 billion in engineering, procurement and construction contracts, part of its largest capital investment, for the second and third phases of the Rich Gas Development project, the company said in August. These contracts build on Phase 1, announced in June 2025. The Rich Gas Development is a multi-phase, $13.2 billion capital investment programme by Adnoc Gas to expand gas processing and liquid recovery infrastructure across the UAE. It is also working on other key projects including Ruwais LNG, Maximising ethane recovery and monetisation (Meram) and Estidama – which together are expected to generate $13.4 billion in in-country value. Its expansion programme is aimed at delivering 60 per cent growth in Ebitda (earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation) by 2030 compared with 2023, with about $28 billion of investment planned between 2026 and 2030. Adnoc Gas also signed an agreement last week with Etihad Water and Electricity to explore supplying natural gas for new power generation capacity across the Northern Emirates. Also last week, the company signed a five-year agreement to supply up to 1.6 million tonnes of LNG to France's TotalEnergies.

events.title: Abu Dhabi's Adnoc Drilling wins contracts worth $314m from Kuwait Oil Company
events.summary: Kuwait Oil Company has awarded two contracts to Adnoc Drilling with an aggregate value of up to 96.5 million Kuwaiti dinars ($314 million), with the UAE company to provide and operate offshore jack-up rigs. The award marks Adnoc Drilling's entry into offshore Kuwait and will be its first offshore rig operations outside the UAE, the company said in a statement on Tuesday. Approved by Kuwait Petroleum Corporation’s Higher Procurement Committee, the contracts run for a four-year firm term, including mobilisation, with an option to extend by one year. The aggregate value of almost $314 million does not include the optional year, the company added. Adnoc Drilling expects to use one of its own jack-up rigs and to bareboat charter a second. Operations are expected to begin in the fourth quarter of 2027. “This award marks Adnoc Drilling’s entry into offshore Kuwait and an important step forward in our international growth journey,” said chief executive Abdulla Al Messabi. Adnoc Drilling is looking to expand to markets in the Middle East, including Syria, and is also exploring deals to boost its gas drilling business. The company acquired an 80 per cent stake in Oman’s MB Petroleum Services and a 70 per cent stake in global oilfield services company SLB's land drilling rigs business in Kuwait and Oman as part of its regional expansion plans last year. The company – with a rig count of 170, including 140 rigs in Abu Dhabi – said the contracts in Kuwait were expected to make their first full-year financial contribution in 2028. The company said the contracts built on its experience in complex offshore operations and were part of its “Drill-to-Operate” strategy, which focuses on strategic partnerships and new revenue streams to drive long-term growth. Kuwait is inviting international oil companies to help develop its offshore discoveries as it aims to raise production capacity to four million barrels per day by 2035. Last month, Adnoc Drilling reported nine-month net profit of $1.07 billion, driven by record revenue. The company expects its unconventional drilling business to recover and hit record levels next year, after a lull, chief financial officer Youssef Salem told The National . “By next year is when we expect to have that significant ramp-up, and then unconventional [will] go back to become even higher than what it was until Q2,” Mr Salem said at the time.

events.title: Cisco to link all future products to its SaaS-y Cloud Control management tool
events.summary: Cisco will no longer create products that don’t integrate with Cloud Control, its SaaS-y management platform that offers netadmins a single tool to manage all of the networking giant’s devices and much of its software portfolio. The networking giant announced Cloud Control in June 2025 and only made it available to customers in the USA. Cisco has previously told The Register that slow rollout reflects the fact that Cisco needs to nail privacy and other regulatory niceties, and deploy infrastructure, before introducing the service to other markets. It appears Cisco is now satisfied it has sorted out those issues. Jeff Schultz, Cisco’s senior vice president for portfolio strategy and marketing, today told the company’s Live conference in Australia that Cloud Control will come online in the European Union, UK, and Down Under in February 2027. Japan, India, and Canada will get their turn in May. Schultz said Cisco is “working tirelessly” to deploy Cloud Control across the world as soon as possible. He also revealed that, starting next year, Cisco will no longer ship products that don’t integrate with Cloud Control. That doesn’t mean those products will be manageable only if they can connect to Cloud Control. Instead, the decision reflects Cisco’s belief that the main thing stopping its customers buying more of its products is the complexity of operating them in concert. Schultz also feels that Cloud Control represents “platform advantage” for Cisco, because when users integrate networking, security, and observability the result is better manageability and resilience. Schultz also told the conference that Cisco will bundle its Thousand Eyes observability and security tool with the “Essentials” and “Advantage” licenses. “We admit it was hard to license and deploy,” he said during his keynote speech, adding that the tool will be deployed automatically with Wi‑Fi 6E and Wi‑Fi 7 hardware. Another product Cisco plans to bring to more customers is Live Protect, a tool that implements compensating controls for flaws that organizations can’t immediately patch. The product has become particularly useful since Anthropic's Mythos model, and similar AI offerings, made it possible to quickly find more software bugs and flaws and overwhelmed tech teams whose patching apparatus was not set up to handle hundreds of montly CVEs. Live Protect currently works on some of Cisco's datacenter switches, plus SD-WAN and WLAN controllers. From December, Cisco will extend it to 8000 series routers, secure firewalls, campus gateway, and to Cloud Control itself. From May 2027, Live Protect will work with Cisco’s ASR 9000 series service aggregation routers and Network Convergence System. "Expect this to be a major investment area," Schultz added. ®
