events.title: White House cautiously upbeat about Russia-Ukraine peace talks this week
events.summary: The White House is "cautiously optimistic" as peace talks between Russia and Ukraine resume in Abu Dhabi this week, U.S. officials said on Monday. Why it matters: The talks on Tuesday and Wednesday will be the first time the parties have met with U.S. mediators present since February, when they were suspended due to the war in Iran. White House envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner have worked for weeks to convince Russian President Vladimir Putin to restart negotiations. President Trump and his team hope Putin will be more willing to compromise after the U.S. lifted sanctions on Russian diesel sales and took other steps welcomed by Moscow. "The relations we have built with Putin will be instrumental in these negotiations," a U.S. official said. After the meetings in Abu Dhabi, Witkoff and Kushner may travel to Moscow and Kyiv to speak directly with Putin and Zelensky, a U.S. official said. Yes, but: The parties remain far apart, particularly over potential territorial concessions by Ukraine. Russia's escalating attacks on Ukrainian cities and Putin's refusal to agree to a ceasefire have cast doubt on prospects for meaningful progress. Behind the scenes: Over the last two weeks, Witkoff and Kushner had daily phone calls — sometimes multiple times a day — with Russian and Ukrainian officials to prepare for the upcoming talks, U.S. officials said. What they're saying: U.S. officials who briefed reporters on Monday struck a positive tone despite skepticism in Europe and Ukraine about Putin's willingness to end the war. "There is a shot to make significant progress towards a deal and to try and bridge the gaps," a U.S. official said. "Getting the parties back to the table wasn't easy to do and we see promising signs as mediators." The official added that Witkoff and Kushner want to use the talks to "crystallize" the decisions Putin and Zelensky will have to make. Driving the news: The talks in Abu Dhabi will focus on two tracks: A military working group led by the commander of U.S. European command, Gen. Alexus Grynkewich, will discuss post-war ceasefire monitoring and security arrangements. The working group made significant progress on this front during the last round of talks in February. A political working group that focuses on the most sensitive topic: territorial demands. There was no progress on this issue in February. State of play: The two sides haven't budged publicly. Russia is demanding control over the entire region of Donbas, while Ukraine insists that territory be divided based on current front lines. In private, though, U.S. officials say that both sides "have shown a little bit of flexibility" on the territorial issue in recent weeks. They say an agreement on territory won't be possible until security guarantees are reached. The big picture: Witkoff and Kushner invited senior officials from NATO, the EU and four major European powers — the UK, France, Germany and Italy — to Abu Dhabi to hold separate discussions on the sidelines of the Russia-Ukraine negotiations. Ukraine's European allies will play a key role in any post-war security arrangements. The U.S. also wants to start a third track of negotiations between European countries and Russia to create new ways of easing tensions and avoiding conflict. But many European countries are highly suspicious of the idea. They believe it endorses a Russian narrative that Europe is a security threat to Moscow and worry it will result in weakening NATO. U.S. officials stress that the proposed Europe-Russia security initiative would not replace or diminish NATO and the central role it plays in protecting Europe. But a new security agreement between Europe and Russia would help end the war in Ukraine, they say. A U.S. official said Witkoff and Kushner hope Russians will agree to include European representatives in the next round of peace talks after Abu Dhabi. What to watch: Ukrainian officials say they have three priorities for the talks: Clinching a deal to de-escalate tensions on the Black Sea and allow grain exports. Reaching an agreement to stop attacks on Ukrainian power plants and Russian oil refineries before the winter. Organizing a trilateral summit between Trump, Putin and Zelensky, possibly during the G20 summit in Miami next month.

events.title: Nvidia's Jensen Huang should have been on lookout for China 'honeytrap', expert says
events.summary: Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang has admitted to having an affair with a Chinese businesswoman who investigators believe is a spy. Experts say the tech titan should have known he was a vulnerable target. Political science experts and former government officials say that is especially true given the unprecedented levels of investment in artificial intelligence , and amid intense competition between the US and China to lead in the field. "Of course adversary actors are going to come after AI leaders in the US to get as much information and access to the what they think is classified information ," said Craig Albert, director of national defence studies at Augusta University in Georgia. Prof Albert, who also specialises in cyber security, said it's clear that Mr Huang fell into the "honeytrap that these leaders are likely to fall into". "This is one of the go-to operations that China prefers to execute, especially with the US, and it happens both in person and online," he said, noting how coveted US AI tech intelligence is, especially by China. Prof Albert says it is possible Mr Huang had been warned by US intelligence officials or private security staff to be on the lookout for this sort of tactic, as it has become relatively standard operating procedure. Even students travelling abroad are often briefed on the possibility of becoming subject to flirtation, he said. "You should probably pay attention to that type of thing," Prof Albert said. He said that despite Nvidia's initial insistence that no US national security or crucial technology information was compromised, China probably emerged with at least something. "I'm pretty sure Jensen doesn't have security clearance of any kind, but this is still a pretty successful operation depending on how long those two have been acquaintances," he said, referring to Mr Huang and alleged spy Alice Huang, an executive for Megaspeed, which has been accused of transferring technology to China. China's Ministry of Foreign Affairs has thus far denied accusations about the entire ordeal. "It is nothing but smears against China," an official with the country's Foreign Ministry said during a video address on Monday. But Prof Albert said China has perfected the "honeytrap" over hundreds of years. "This is their bread and butter," he said. "It's much easier for authoritarian regimes to do it." The confession from Mr Huang on Sunday comes after a series of recent concerns raised about Nvidia. Last week, the House of Representatives select committee on the Chinese Communist Party sent Mr Huang a letter requesting that he appear at a closed-door briefing. The letter, dated Wednesday and signed by the chairmen of the House foreign affairs committee, Brian Mast, and the permanent select committee on intelligence, Eric Crawford, says Congress is seeking to learn more about “Nvidia's security protocols against foreign adversary espionage” and his reported interactions with Ms Huang. That letter was sent before Mr Huang admitted to having an extramarital affair. Mr Mast, Mr Crawford and their fellow Republican representative John Moolenaar, told the Nvidia boss in the letter that they have long been concerned about alleged Chinese espionage and the possibility that it could result in the country gaining access to “cutting-edge US technology”. “Congress determines the extent to which US national security has been placed at risk,” the letter read. The authors asked Mr Huang to appear and discuss his interactions with the alleged Chinese agent on November 18. ICYMI: Chairman @RepMoolenaar , Chairman @RepBrianMast , and Chairman @RepRickCrawford have sent a letter to NVIDIA CEO @JensenHuang asking him to appear before their three committees this month. The letter expresses concerns over NVIDIA’s security protocols against foreign… pic.twitter.com/eSZBnw3pkE — Select Committee on China (@ChinaSelect) November 9, 2026 On Monday, the US select committee on the CCP posted on X: "In case you missed it," along with a copy of the letter in which Mr Huang's appearance was requested last week. Trump reacts US President Donald Trump, who has not been shy about occasionally meeting with Mr Huang throughout his second term in the White House, said that he had a brief discussion with Nvidia's embattled chief executive on Monday. President Trump told reporters that he still believes that Mr Huang is an "honourable guy", and that he respected what Nvidia's chief executive has built over the years. Mr Trump also told reporters that Mr Huang said that he had no idea that Alice Huang was a spy. "I believe him," President Trump continued, adding that the FBI is leading some sort of investigation into the matter but that he felt that Mr Huang "will be in good shape." Those seemingly vague and lackadaisical comments will likely add fuel to the ongoing scrutiny. President Trump has found himself caught up in the controversy in recent months due to his frequent interactions with Nvidia's chief executive where some said that Mr Trump was too quick to weaken US chip export policies at the request of Mr Huang, whose company stood to benefit. Critics of the decision strongly believe that those chip export policies protect the US lead in AI, particularly against China, which has struggled in obtaining the necessary semiconductors for the technology. Nvidia fallout On Sunday, shortly after Mr Huang admitted to his staff that he had been unfaithful to his wife, the company's board of directors announced it was launching an independent investigation with the help of an outside company to determine what transpired and if there should be any repercussions. "The board prioritises US national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of Nvidia and its shareholders," a statement read. It was alluding to concerns raised by elected officials for several years that Nvidia's push to relax certain technology export policies for China could harm the US. On Sunday, Nvidia's board said that while it had "no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, the board's inquiry will examine all available information". The actions of Mr Huang, who has been one of the most powerful and wealthy tech executives speaking out against strict US technology export policies, have prompted calls for him to face consequences. Chris McGuire, a senior fellow for emerging technologies at the Council on Foreign Relations think tank in Washington, was straighforward. "You have the CEO of one of the biggest companies in America, that is potentially compromised by the Chinese and they have some information on him – it really needs to be looked into," he told Bloomberg. Earlier on X, Mr McGuire said some members of the administration of US President Donald Trump had tried to convey that Mr Huang had been compromised, while other Trump appointees seemed to disregard it. events.title: Attackers backdoor trusted AWS integrations to steal secrets
events.summary: Unknown attackers used compromised identity and access management (IAM) credentials associated with Qubole's AWS account to access customer AWS environments, stealing secrets and other sensitive data from S3 buckets. Qubole is a cloud data processing platform that uses cross-account IAM roles to manage compute and access storage in customers' AWS environments without requiring customers to provide long-lived AWS access keys. The supply-chain attack abused this third-party, cross-account trust relationship. Google’s cloud-security shop Wiz declined to tell us how many organizations were affected, but called it a “broad, opportunistic supply chain campaign” that hit “multiple” customer environments. “Because many organizations left trust policies active even after deprecating the platform, the attacker was able to successfully assume integration roles, enumerate cloud resources, harvest secrets, and siphon data,” the researchers told The Register in an emailed response to questions. Qubole did not respond to The Register 's inquiries. Wiz, working with Google's Mandiant incident responders after AI data security company Sentra flagged suspicious activity, traced the malicious activity back to October 14, when credentials associated with Qubole's AWS account were used to call the sts:AssumeRole API to obtain temporary credentials for customer-managed integration roles. The calls originated from Qubole AWS account 805246085872 , and used IAM user ID AIDA3W7DIFLYOLTK63SFS , Wiz analysts Zack Morrow, Sean Johnstone, and Benjamin Read said in a Monday blog about the supply chain attack. “Across the affected environments, Wiz CIRT has not observed this IAM user in any activity other than that associated with this threat actor,” the trio wrote. This activity continued on October 15, and on October 18, the digital intruders began using a second IAM user from the same account. Once inside customers’ environments, the crooks began probing a ton of AWS services and stealing credentials, keys, and other secrets stored across Lambda, Secrets Manager, and SSM Parameter Store. The miscreants also used TruffleHog to test AWS credentials belonging to victim organizations, discover their Microsoft Entra ID secrets, and request OAuth tokens using Okta client credentials also uncovered while snooping around the AWS environments. Abusing the integration roles also allowed the criminals to steal data from customers’ S3 storage, although it seems they were largely opportunistic attackers, in some cases downloading entire buckets, as opposed to state-sponsored spies looking for specific data. The threat hunters haven’t attributed the supply chain attack to any particular group, and say they don’t have any insight into how the miscreants are using the stolen data. While investigating this incident, Wiz spotted a separate campaign between October 8 and October 11 that also used customer-owned AWS access keys for Qubole integrations. While a “small number” of these also resulted in the intruders compromising victim organizations’ AWS environments, Wiz said it can’t definitively connect the two sets of malicious activity. Organizations that have integrated with Qubole should rotate credentials - although rotating a credential does not end temporary sessions that were already issued. Customers should also review CloudTrail from October 1 onward, looking for AssumeRole events where userIdentity.accountId matches Qubole's AWS account ID, 805246085872, particularly those originating from non-AWS IP addresses. “For every role session you find, review all subsequent activity from that session, especially Secrets Manager, SSM Parameter Store, Lambda and S3,” the researchers wrote. “If the threat actor assumed an integration role, rotate every secret, parameter and Lambda environment variable the role could read, and revoke active sessions for the role.” “AWS services were not compromised by this issue and operated as designed," an AWS spokesperson wrote to use after we first published this article. "The activity describes how threat actors used credentials associated with a third-party provider to access some AWS customers’ accounts by assuming IAM roles those customers had configured to trust that provider. As always, we recommend all customers follow security, identity, and compliance best practices, including regularly reviewing cross-account IAM roles, removing access for integrations no longer in use, granting least-privilege permissions, and adding conditions such as source IP restrictions to role trust policies. AWS customers who suspect or become aware of unauthorized activity in their accounts should follow guidance for remediating potentially compromised credentials or contact AWS Support with any questions or concerns about the security of their account.” ® Updated on November 10 with statement from AWS.

events.title: Vulnerability that lets hackers SSH into Linux devices is under active exploitation
events.summary: Hackers are actively exploiting a recently discovered critical vulnerability that allows them to log in to privileged accounts on many Linux systems, multiple researchers are reporting. The vulnerability, tracked under the name *sshole, arises from the interaction between OpenSSH and a code library known as musl. Linux systems that use both of these packages and meet certain other requirements can be hacked to give unauthenticated access to high-privilege accounts in a matter of seconds. *sshole became publicly known last Thursday and quickly stoked concerns it could lead to widespread compromise of Linux machines. Four days later, the prediction shows signs of becoming real. Attackers conducting "mature intrusions" Security firm Greynoise said Monday that honeypots it maintains in Southeast Asia have come under attack by a group it’s tracking as GT10. The group conducted “mature intrusions" into the systems, which Greynoise uses to detect attempted or successful attacks in real time. Greynoise subsequently gained access to a GT10 server that revealed potential other victims and some of the tools used in the campaign. A backdoor the group is using in the attacks contains Chinese language comments and appears to be generated with the use of AI. Read full article Comments

events.title: Republicans' final weeks in power may be consumed by fights they don't want
events.summary: Republicans are returning to work this week, facing the prospect of an especially lame lame-duck session after a bruising midterm election that set off a countdown clock on their control of Congress. Why it matters: Democrats have little incentive to help Republicans advance their agenda before January, while departing GOP lawmakers could complicate matters further by skipping votes or defying party leaders. As a result, most of the items on their to-do list could get kicked to the new Congress. That's aside from a few items House GOP leaders would rather avoid altogether: another Jeffrey Epstein bill and an impeachment vote . Lawmakers also have just over a month before another potential government funding lapse. Driving the news: Rep. Thomas Massie — who GOP voters kicked to the curb in favor of a more Trump-aligned Republican — is pushing another Epstein-related vote, an additional headache for the administration and GOP leaders. He also plans to try to force a vote this week on his impeachment resolution against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Republicans lose their House and Senate majorities Jan. 3, ending their ability to set both chambers' legislative agendas. Reality check: Trump still wields the presidential veto power. Rodell Mollineau, a Democratic strategist and former communications director for the late Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid, said Democrats may postpone some legislative fights until January, when they'll have more negotiating leverage. "I think there's some things that Democrats would be happy to kick down the road," he said. Yes, but: Congress still faces major legislative hurdles. Lawmakers need to pass the annual National Defense Authorization Act, potentially setting up a fight over the Iran war as some Republicans grow more willing to criticize the conflict. A bipartisan permitting bill could overhaul how energy and infrastructure projects are approved. Senate Republicans are also racing to confirm more Trump administration officials and judicial nominees before Democrats take over. What they're saying: "What has to get done is appropriations and the NDAA bill," Nadeam Elshami, former chief of staff to Nancy Pelosi, told Axios. Democrats "feel emboldened in both of those discussions" and "have both the momentum and the leverage," he said, making them unlikely to support provisions advancing Trump's priorities. Permitting reform would be nice, Elshami said, but it faces "real hurdles." And as for Republicans' hopes of passing another reconciliation package? "I just don't see that getting done," he said. Between the lines: Dozens of House lawmakers and at least 17 senators are leaving Congress, raising questions about attendance, cooperation and how much work departing members actually want to do — consider it a professional case of congressional senioritis. Some, like Massie, have decided to shake the table and make their party feel their wrath. "If it's a critical vote, then I believe members would return," Elshami said. But on less consequential votes: "I highly doubt that they'll be in town." Mollineau sees competing incentives. "[O]bviously as a Democrat, I want as few of these people to come back as possible. Like if they're grumpy, stay away," he told Axios. But, he added, "You're still getting paid. This is still your job." Outgoing lawmakers eyeing lobbying jobs or future campaigns also have reason to show up: "members have very long, very long memories," he said. Even so, he warned: "I don't think they're going to be able to get the enthusiasm out of all these retiring members." What we're watching: Whether Congress manages to finish its major legislative priorities, or whether lawmakers leave those fights to the new Democratic majorities. events.title: The backlash about data centers might really just be about electricity
events.summary: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here . As voters went to the polls across the US last week, I was in Ashburn, Virginia, part of what’s known as Data Center Alley—the world’s largest data center hub. It’s also where the backlash now sweeping the country arguably first began taking shape. Driving through it is surreal. Concrete monolithic buildings loom along every major road, with names like Skybox and CloudHQ. It’s accepted wisdom in Big Tech that the war against data centers must be about something bigger than just data centers themselves. Two days after the midterms, OpenAI’s chief global affairs officer, Chris Lehane, wrote that data centers “have become a proxy for public unease about affordability, corporate power, and people losing control over their futures.” It’s a culture war, in other words. But spending a few days in Data Center Alley left me wondering if it’s really the proxy that Lehane describes. I came away convinced that the data center backlash is more about electricity than Big Tech admits. The industry can improve its image, but it can’t escape the physical consequences of its enormous appetite for electricity. Here’s why. There are two ways to power the sort of data center that AI companies want: connecting to the grid, or generating electricity onsite. In Virginia’s Loudoun County, where data centers are ubiquitous but have been built at a steadier pace than the breakneck expansion now underway elsewhere in the country, most are connected to the existing grid.  One facility I went inside, operated by Equinix, has massive diesel generators onsite for backup but gets its power from the local utility, Dominion Energy. Much of Dominion’s electricity is generated by natural gas (which is cleaner than coal or oil, but worse than renewables). The average data center operating in this part of Virginia today has a power capacity of 54 megawatts. That’s more than the power draw of the Denver International Airport .  Elena Schlossberg, a prominent activist against data centers in Virginia, told me she’s “always banging my head against the wall” when the industry paints the fight as a culture war. “It was always about power,” she says—that is, electricity. Some Virginia protesters appear more animated by a broader anti-tech populism than Schlossberg, to be fair. But it’s the particular consequences of drawing so much power from the grid that have done the most to shape how the backlash has played out.  Recent protests have led to new rules from the state that data centers must pay fully for the cost of new transmission lines to the grid and make sure they’re not spread among everyone else. Data center developers told me they’re preparing for new rules that would cut them off from grid power during peak demand. Schlossberg also worries about the downstream effects of a strained grid—for example, that data centers will run more diesel generators or that Dominion Energy will expand fossil fuel inputs rather than renewables to meet demand. The overwhelming majority of AI data centers being built elsewhere in the country are not designed this way. The scale desired is so massive that companies are setting up in rural areas where there is virtually no grid infrastructure to connect to. Building there means bringing your own power (so-called “behind the meter” power), in the form of natural-gas-powered turbines. Companies also build diesel generators for backup. Anthropic, for example, has reportedly agreed to pay $3.4 billion for gas turbines in what’s described as the largest power generation purchase by an AI company. Even if grids were nearby, they’d be unlikely to serve the amount of power demanded. The smallest data centers attractive for AI training are 300 megawatts. It’s a lot of power for one industrial site, but not unprecedented: One data center developer told me he’s eyeing a former steel mill already equipped to draw that much electricity from the grid. But the ideal facilities are more like 6,000 megawatts. That’s the estimated draw of the city of Chicago, which is powered by more than 20 power plants within the city alone (and dozens farther out). The notion of data center companies’ bringing their own power might seem attractive at first, because they wouldn’t be straining the grid. But generating electricity at this scale inevitably affects surrounding communities, and when public utilities build infrastructure of this magnitude, communities have traditionally expected a say in where it goes. Now, private companies are undertaking projects on a similar scale. Natural-gas turbines of any scale release air pollutants. When diesel generators are used, it’s even worse. And in the unprecedented rush to get these facilities operating, companies have become horrible neighbors (recall that Elon Musk violated air quality laws when he set up dozens of turbines to power a data center in Memphis, according to the Environmental Protection Agency). Big Tech’s tendency to chalk the backlash up to a culture war obfuscates one simple fact: There’s only so pleasant you can make a small city of computers to live around. Sure, companies can pursue better deals that raise tax revenues, hire local workers, and get more community involvement, as the protests are leading them to do . But if a small town is asked to welcome a Walt Disney World, an international airport, a steel plant, and the power plants to run them all, should we be surprised by its trepidation? Again, that’s not to say this is the sole reason for opposition to data centers. Fears of job losses, existential risks, and concentrated corporate power all fuel the backlash, as does misinformation (most facilities use far less water than many people think). Nor is consuming enormous amounts of electricity inherently bad: Many of the advances that have improved modern life have required just that. But as one developer recently told me, industry insiders see their ambitions as constrained less by public opposition than by a lack of electricity. That should tell us something. So what happens next? It’s possible that newly elected politicians’ actual stances on data centers won’t be as negative as the ones they campaigned on. But what seems true regardless is that if new data centers need their own power generated onsite, they’ll go where there are the fewest people able to resist them. That might mean the Permian Basin , where a network of natural-gas lines can be easy for developers to connect to and populations are sparse. Companies might also try their chances abroad; Google, in fact, announced the day after the elections that it will spend $15 billion on data center projects in Malaysia. But there’s one place where Big Tech may find virtually no limits at all, as Elon Musk posted just hours after the midterms results came rolling in: “Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now.”

events.title: Iraq sets ambitious target to more than double oil production by 2032
events.summary: Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Al Zaidi has set out an ambitious vision for Iraq's oil future, saying the country aims to lift production to ⁠seven million barrels per ⁠day ​by ⁠2030. Mr Al Zaidi said Iraq intended to increase production to ​10 million bpd by 2032, including about one million bpd from the Kurdistan region. Iraqi oil exports hit about 3.4 million bpd in October. Speaking to Kurdistan Region Prime Minister Masrour Barzani in Baghdad, Mr Al Zaidi said the “increase would positively reflect on development and the economy across the whole country”. Iraq has been ​pushing ⁠for ‌higher production by Opec countries as the economic fallout from the Iran war , and investment by major oil producers, increase pressure on Baghdad to boost output. The conflict ‌has ⁠hit Iraq ​particularly hard, forcing ​major export ‌cuts and depriving ⁠the state of oil ⁠revenue, which usually accounts for about 90 per cent of government income. Oil Minister Basim Mohammed Khudair told state news agency INA ⁠on Saturday that Iraq “is in talks with Opec to raise exports”. “There is ongoing dialogue with Opec to raise the export quota, given Iraq's unique circumstances and the conditions it has faced over the past five decades,” Mr Khudair said. He said Iraq “deserves to increase its production rates” to generate revenue for infrastructure and government plans. The production quota set by Opec allocates 4.431 million barrels per day to Iraq. Before the outbreak of the Iran war, Iraq produced around 4.4 million bpd. Production and exports then fell sharply after disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz, with exports down from 3.36 million barrels per day in February to 131,000 bpd in April. The result was a sharp drop in monthly oil revenue that previously hovered at about $7 billion, although Iraqi oil exports rebounded in October. To support the new target, Baghdad has been pushing to finalise oil and gas deals worth billions of dollars mainly with US companies, including Chevron, HKN Energy and Halliburton. It is also pursuing new export routes to reduce dependence on the Strait of Hormuz, including pipelines to Syria's Baniyas port on the Mediterranean and to Jordan's Aqaba port, as well as the Iraq-Turkey pipeline to Ceyhan.

events.title: Researchers pwn automakers’ Android apps to remotely unlock cars, honk horns
events.summary: Security researchers exploited flaws in Android apps to gain remote access to connected cars from two major automakers, allowing them to start engines, flash headlights, and sound horns. Shubham Shah, co-founder at Assetnote, and researcher Sam Curry worked together on the exploits earlier this year. By tinkering with the cars’ Android apps, they devised exploit paths to issue remote commands to vehicles in Australia and the US . The pair published separate blogs covering different aspects of the research; Shah said the US attack "required a lot more work" because the automaker "spent much more time securing the US, Canadian, and European OpenIDM environments." Both exploit chains centered around weaknesses in the ForgeRock identity platform relied upon by both automakers, the identities of which were kept anonymous by the researchers, who have previously highlighted flaws in the likes of Hyundai , Kia , Subaru , and many others . In the Australian version of the app, the researchers first found a vehicle identification number (VIN) using public licence plate checkers, and used those in queries to internal APIs, which provided personal information and owner email addresses. They also found hardcoded admin credentials for the ForgeRock OpenIDM that were meant for the staging environment but also worked in production. After bypassing the heavy WAF filtering by exploiting path traversal flaws, they were able to invoke the internal admin APIs and take over target accounts using only their email addresses. This let them mint authentication tokens, which they could issue to send arbitrary commands to affected vehicles through the mobile app. Issuing commands on the US version also required bypassing WAF filtering through a path traversal, though with a more involved technique: exploiting path confusion to reach the Apache Felix admin console. The researchers used factory default credentials in Felix’s OSGi Web Console to gain admin privileges. They then used Felix configuration manager to schedule a task that executed an inline Groovy script, giving them shell access to the identity servers. The researchers then queried local admin API endpoints, allowing them to view or modify user account data. From there, they logged into car owners’ accounts, and gained the ability to issue the same commands as demonstrated in the Australian version. According to Curry’s disclosure timeline, he and Shah approached the affected automakers in "early 2026," and the exploits were patched within two hours of receiving the report. Although the automakers wished to remain anonymous, it didn’t take long for some petrolheads to speculate that the partially blurred car in Shah’s demo video was a Toyota, citing the shape of the wing mirror and the unlock sound it made. Onlookers claimed that the two automakers in question were likely Toyota and its luxury brand Lexus. Asked wether the claims were accurate, a spokesperson for Toyota Motor Corporation neither confirmed nor denied them. Curry said he and Shah chose to uphold the manufacturers’ requests to remain anonymous out of concern for infoseccers’ current workloads. He said: "Obviously, they have asked not to be named, and while normally we would fight to actually include the company names, it's a busy time in the security world and I don't like the idea of them diverting resources because they are worried about something with this disclosure." ®

events.title: Nancy Pelosi’s replacement is ready to regulate AI
events.summary: As a California state senator, Scott Wiener authored legislation aimed at curbing the risks of advanced AI. Now, after winning a tight congressional race for former Speaker of the House Nancy Pelosi’s open San Francisco seat, he could play a key role in setting federal AI policy.  I spoke with Wiener on Friday, only a few hours after he had been declared the victor. But he was already thinking about AI risk. The previous day, the AI nonprofit METR had released a report that had been widely interpreted as evidence that Anthropic had achieved recursive self-improvement, a phenomenon in which AI meaningfully contributes to its own advancement and AI progress potentially spins out of control. “It’s very concerning,” Wiener said, citing the report as evidence that we are quickly running out of time to regulate AI. “It was my hope that Congress would take decisive action before [the end of] this year,” he said. “That does not appear to be happening.” Wiener has been increasingly focused on AI in recent years, and he’s made many of the AI safety movement’s concerns his own: During our 20-minute conversation, he used the phrase “recursive self-improvement” half a dozen times, for example.“We need to slow this down,” he says. “Because it’s moving very quickly, and we could sleepwalk into a disaster.” Wiener has already had real influence on AI policy. SB 1047, a bill that he authored in 2024, was set to become the first real piece of frontier AI legislation in the country before it was vetoed by California governor Gavin Newsom; he then sponsored SB 53, a lighter-touch bill that Newsom signed. Both bills have inspired proposed federal legislation.  Wiener’s congressional campaign received over $3 million from Public First Action, a nonprofit in favor of AI regulation that receives substantial funding from Anthropic. That contribution led opponents to criticize him for being too close to the AI industry , but Wiener says that couldn’t be further from the truth.  “Public First supported me because I was the first lawmaker in the country to introduce AI regulation and the first to pass it and get it implemented,” he wrote in a message after our interview. “The attacks on me for [Public First’s] support were shockingly cynical—literally attacking a candidate who actually regulated AI over Big Tech’s objection and falsely claiming the candidate is somehow too close to Big Tech.” Wiener says that if Congress forms a select committee on artificial intelligence—something that Democrats have discussed since September—he’d be eager to serve. And he’s enthusiastic about many of the policy ideas floating around Congress. “I think it’s really important to have a strong, empowered, nimble federal regulator,” he says, noting that Representative Ro Khanna, a fellow Democrat from California, has proposed legislation to establish such a regulator.  He also highlights the importance of whistleblower protections, testing and auditing requirements, and a kill switch requirement, and he wants to see Congress leverage its oversight powers to hold the AI labs to account. “This is about the future of humanity, and we want to make sure that the public has a say and that the public knows what’s going on,” he says. And as a longtime state legislator, he is opposed to broad federal preemption of state AI laws, which some of the proposed federal legislation would require. “States are, as Brandeis says , laboratories,” he notes. “You want the states to be able to continue to be nimble in ways that Congress sometimes is not.” Above all, Wiener says, he wants Congress to pass policies with real teeth. “It’s critically important that when Congress acts, that we do so in a way that is truly meaningful and that meets the moment,” he says. That means taking seriously the possibility of AI catastrophe, something he discusses in the sort of language typically used by AI safety experts. “We’re in a moment that is very dangerous in terms of the risk of loss of control over AI,” he told me. “We need to deal with recursive self-improvement. Once you’re in that realm, that really is potentially a recipe for total loss of control.” He’ll have some allies in the fight against catastrophic AI risk. Senator Bernie Sanders, for instance, has met with many of the AI safety movement’s most influential figures and has spoken repeatedly about AI and existential risk. But there’s still a large gap between Wiener’s Bay Area, AGI-pilled perspective and the national mood on AI, which is anchored by opposition to data centers. The fact that voters approved 40 out of 41 anti-data-center ballot measures on Tuesday might seem to be a good sign for Wiener and others who support AI regulation, but Wiener says he sees this movement as far more tied to local concerns than to bigger questions about AI risk. “Peoople who are really opposed to where AI is going—this is an area where they can actually do something about it,” he says. “But the data center revolt—to me, I think it’s more so that people are upset that there could be something like this in their community, with all the impacts near people’s homes, driving up electric bills and using water. I think that’s the bigger issue for most people, from what I can tell.” Wiener describes himself as only “cautiously optimistic” about Congress’s ability to rein in AI, given its poor track record on regulating the tech industry. He also has concerns about the ability to get legislation past President Donald Trump, who called concerns about catastrophic AI risk a “hoax” in September and has demonstrated a stark unwillingness to collaborate with China, something that Wiener sees as essential to preventing the worst consequences of AI. But he says Trump’s unpredictability provides  some measure of hope, though it’s a fraught kind of hope. “So far what we’ve seen are some problematic things, but not complete disasters,” Wiener says. “I hope that it doesn’t take a disaster to spur the president into acting. And I hope if that’s what it does take—which, like I said, I hope it doesn’t—but if it does, I hope it’s as small as possible.”

events.title: Low unemployment, but job worries persist
events.summary: Americans have conflicting views of the job market : They are more worried about unemployment rising nationwide, even as they are more confident that they could find another job if they lost their own. Driving the news: The perceived probability that unemployment will rise over the next year climbed to 45.3% in October, the highest since April 2020, according to the New York Fed's Survey of Consumer Expectations — an increase driven by those without a college degree. Yes, but: The perceived probability of finding another job if one lost their current position rose to 46.5%, the highest in about a year. Americans' perceived probability of losing their jobs over the next year also edged higher, rising 0.4 percentage point, to 13.9%. State of play: The mixed outlook underscores an unusual feature of today's labor market — hiring is picking up and unemployment remains historically low, but finding work can still be a prolonged struggle. The backdrop: The October jobs report showed that employers added a surprisingly robust 165,000 jobs last month. The unemployment rate has held in the narrow range of 4% to 4.2% for five consecutive months. But Friday's data also showed that 2 million Americans have been unemployed for at least six months, accounting for more than 25% of all unemployed workers. The average spell of unemployment climbed to 27.1 weeks in October, the longest since December 2021. (Excluding the pandemic, it's the highest reading since August 2016.) Of note: Ahead of the October Consumer Price Index report — out tomorrow — the New York Fed said that inflation expectations were unchanged last month at 3.9% over the next year, 3.3% over three years and 3% over five years.

events.title: Oil prices and bond yields no longer moving together
events.summary: Data: Axios analysis of FactSet data; Note: Correlation over preceding 30 trading sessions between daily change in West Texas Intermediate crude and change in 10-year U.S. Treasury yield; Chart: Neil Irwin/Axios For much of this year, on any given day, you could look at the price of oil and correctly guess what happened to bond yields. In the last few weeks, that correlation has evaporated. Why it matters: It's a sign that growth risks may be supplanting inflation worries as the dominant economic concern. State of play: It's not obvious whether an energy supply shock should affect inflation or growth more. On the one hand, more expensive fuel can ripple through prices for everything else. On the other, more expensive energy acts like a tax on consumers and businesses that consume it. Since the attack on Iran in late February , markets have treated the former concern as the central dynamic in the global economy. Zoom in: As such, on days when oil futures pointed to higher prices, bonds almost always sold off and their yields — which move in the opposite direction from their prices — rose. Traders were pricing in a world where inflation is higher for longer, and central banks react by raising rates more — and betting, implicitly, that growth would prove resilient despite the energy price headwind. For the 30 trading days ended Sept. 10, the correlation between the one-day move in West Texas Intermediate crude and 10-year U.S. Treasury yield reached a stunning 77%. The Financial Times noted in late September that the correlation was the highest it had been since the Persian Gulf War of the early 1990s. Yes, but: Now, that correlation has collapsed — and is about negative 10% over the last 30 trading days. In other words, on days when oil rises, it's more likely than not that bond yields fall. Between the lines: It's probably not a coincidence that this shift has occurred at the same time cracks have appeared in the debt market that's financing the AI buildout. As long as the AI and data center boom was powering ahead, seemingly impervious to energy price shocks or bubble fears, the inflationary impact of higher oil prices dominated the economic outlook. But with that sector wobbling, the economy may be more vulnerable to a growth slowdown as higher prices for gasoline, diesel fuel and other energy products weigh on activity. And that's giving the Federal Reserve more breathing room to avoid rate hikes. Of note: This inversion of the relationship is clearly on the mind of the Fed's leadership, even if they aren't ready to draw firm conclusions about its implications. In his news conference two weeks ago , chairman Kevin Warsh pointed to "a stable correlation" between oil prices and interest rates for much of this year, and while noting that he is not the author of a Wall Street newsletter, he nonetheless mused on the relationship at some length. What they're saying: "That correlation has been quite strong, until very recently where you've seen oil prices continue to move up, largely due to geopolitical events," he said. "But what's happened? Interest rates have rolled over to the downside." "To the extent that oil prices were to move lower, again, probably due to geopolitical events, that's something that we're going to have to interrogate. What are the effects on the Fed's dual mandate? What are the effects on financial market prices, and what are we going to do about it?" "But that's a hypothetical, and in fact, if we look at financial market prices, futures prices for oil, they've moved up over the course of the last several weeks, and I can't help but take note of that too." The bottom line: If this macro regime change persists, it suggests the Fed has more leeway to move with caution on further rate hikes, no matter what happens in the Strait of Hormuz.

events.title: Insight about how 'nature makes no leaps' promises better robot predictions
events.summary: Machine learning researchers have developed a technique that allows world models to make better predictions about how objects will behave. World models are used to train physical AI systems like robots how to navigate the real world. They predict the consequences of actions. But they do so based on observed data. These models could provide better direction to robots if they were able to make inferences about possible actions without being trained for all the possible outcomes. Randall Balestriero (Brown University, AMI Labs), Kerda Varaku, and Turing Award winner Yann LeCun (NYU, AMI Labs) describe an approach that might allow that to happen in a pre-print paper, "Counterfactual World Models: Natura Non Facit Saltus." The Latin refers to Gottfried Leibniz's axiom " nature makes no leaps ," which had a good run until it ran headlong into quantum mechanics. Yet for the authors, the saying explains how they have been able to devise a method for zero-shot physics inference. Counterfactual world models, said Balestriero in an email to The Register use "the mismatch between your prediction and the real world to figure out what did you get wrong, and from that you can better understand what happened for better future predictions, debugging, reasoning, all at test time." Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture ( JEPA ) models, developed by LeCun and colleagues back in 2023, have been proposed for robots because they can take an action as input and ask what the world would be like with that action. But a JEPA world model produces an average of outcomes and would not be able to anticipate counterfactual scenarios – events that didn't happen. The technique that the researchers developed is not specific to JEPAs – it can be applied to any world model that predicts the average next state under any action. But JEPA models are particularly well suited to being adapted. Balestriero said that the counterfactual world model experiments were done using off-the-shelf encoders (DINOv2 and MAE) without any fine-tuning and only a small predictor trained on top. Creating a counterfactual world model from that starting point would only require minor additions. Counterfactual world models predict alternative scenarios more effectively by inferring possibilities from what did occur. "In causal inference, answering 'What would have happened had I acted differently?' takes three steps," explained Balestriero. "You use what you observed to learn something about those hidden factors, you change the action, and you predict again with the hidden factors kept exactly as they were. "Our counterfactual world model does all three steps with one subtraction." Balestriero cited an example from the paper: a boat crossing a river with a hidden current and how the JEPA world model and counterfactual world model predicted the boat's movements. "The world model predicted where the boat would end up after steering left, and it actually ended up two meters further downstream," he explained. "Those two meters are the signature of the current that occurred. To answer 'where would the boat be had I steered right?', we take the world model's prediction for steering right and add the same two meters. In other words, the counterfactual is what actually happened, plus the difference between the model's predictions for the alternative action and for the action taken. "Physics enters to justify this rule, not as an equation the model fits. Over a short time, the effect of the action and the effect of the current each grow in proportion to the duration, while their interaction grows only with its square, so over short steps they simply add up, like forces. "We prove that the fraction of the disturbance's effect that this rule gets wrong shrinks with the square of the time step, and that no method using the same ordinary data can do better than this rate in the worst case." Counterfactual world models have three likely uses, according to Balestriero. The first is having a robot retry an action after a surprise event. "When an attempt fails because of something the robot could not see, such as an unexpected load, a current or a weak motor, the counterfactual world model lets it estimate which action would have worked in that same situation," he explained. "In our simulated tasks, choosing the action this way reaches the goal in 35 to 69 percent of events, against 14 to 23 percent for a planner that knows the true simulator but ignores the observed outcome. With two more attempts on the same event, success rises to 51 to 97 percent." He also sees these models being useful for adapting to persistent fault, like a miscalibrated motor, and helping people understand failures. "World models are trained to predict, and they are getting good at it," said Balestriero. "But a robot, a car or a drone acting in the real world is constantly surprised by things it could not see coming. After a surprise, the useful question is no longer what was expected, but what would have happened had it acted differently in that same situation. You need that answer to debug a failure, to tell a bad decision from bad luck, or to decide what to do on the next attempt, and prediction alone does not provide it." The researchers initial attempts to address the issue involved adding a learned component to the world model that infers whatever hidden disturbance (e.g. the current in the boat scenario) affected the anticipated outcome. But that approach was too fragile. "Trying to understand why led to the theory," explained Balestriero. "Learning the disturbance from ordinary data is not just hard, it is impossible in general: the hidden noise can be relabeled differently for each action without changing a single prediction, so the data cannot tell you which labeling is the right one. The missing piece has to come from outside the data. For physical systems, it comes from the fact that forces add and that their interaction builds up slowly in time. Once you accept that, the learned disturbance model becomes unnecessary: the gap between what happened and what was predicted already carries the information you need, and you carry it over to the other action." Balestriero said that control engineers have been implementing corrections of this sort for decades, to tune hand-built models. "What was missing was why the same correction is justified for learned world models that see the world through images, what can and cannot be recovered without paired data, and where it breaks," he said. "The paper answers these questions by connecting causal inference, control and world models. The title comes from Leibniz's law of continuity, natura non facit saltus, ' nature makes no leaps ,' which is precisely the property that makes all of this work." The researchers' paper was provided to The Register prior to its release on ArXiv . It is expected to be released this week. ®

events.title: Microsoft takes three decades to make Sticky Keys less sticky
events.summary: Windows testers are getting a new option in the Sticky Keys and Filter Keys dialogs – one to banish the pop-ups without needing to venture deep into Settings. It's only taken several decades for Microsoft to put the off switch where the interruption actually happens. The accessibility features themselves are useful, though triggering their activation prompts by accident is another matter. Once enabled, Sticky Keys let users press modifier keys (such as Control) one at a time instead of holding them down together. For example, rather than holding Control and pressing C to copy, a user can press and release Control, then press C. Filter Keys, meanwhile, ignores brief or repeated keystrokes and adjusts the keyboard's repeat behavior. However, the dialogs are of little use to people who don't need the features, and they can pop up at the most inconvenient moments. Tap Shift five times, and you'll see what we mean: Windows chimes and shows a dialog asking whether you'd like to turn on Sticky Keys. Dismiss it, hit Shift five times, and there it is again. Or hold down the right Shift key for eight seconds to be treated to the Filter Keys pop-up. You can stop this behavior elsewhere in the system, but it requires a trek through Windows settings. The change, introduced in the Experimental Windows Insider Build 26340.9882, adds an option to the Sticky Keys or Filter Keys dialogs to dismiss the prompts permanently. It's a small change, but one that should spare users an irritating interruption. Better late than never – even if "never ask me again" has taken roughly three decades to reach the dialog. Former Microsoft engineer Charles Opperman said he wrote the dialog in early 1995 "after @bradsilverberg kids kept activating StickeyKeys [sic] while playing Space Cadet pinball." Opperman added that a link to Settings was added in Windows 98 or what would become Windows 2000, and a checkbox was considered even then, but it wasn't deemed a priority. Users could turn off the prompt via settings. Now the option is front and center. The option is also rolling out in the Windows Insider Beta channel , although Microsoft has not announced a general release date. ®

events.title: AI Agents Are Testing the Limits of Zero-Trust Security
events.summary: This article is brought to you by Queen’s University Belfast . Several teams around the globe are leveraging AI by creating a task force of agents managed by an orchestrator and creating applications to support risk assessment, client profiling, match making, and information yield with a slight overview of decision making. One of the important components for these agents is to ensure that the logs are managed and historic relevance is not being used to avoid skewing towards same decision making. Thus, the system is expected to keep checkpoints in place where agents are prompted to delete such historic relevance. However, despite such methodology in place, a future prompt could make the agents bring forward the information that was supposed to be deleted and can be tricked into revealing more information, which is a classic case of context recovery attack. So, the question raised here is: How can we trust that our instructions have been followed? And where is the proof? There is an element of utilizing zero-trust architectures (ZTA) for orchestrating and managing agentic activity, which simply means all agentic interactions use the core principle of “never trust,” “always verify.” ZTA components include a policy enforcement point (PEP) that has to be trusted to maintain trust across the system, so the question that remains is where is the component of zero-trust, and shall we trust the policies enforced by PEP? Having a pro-agentic approach and utilizing agents could be helpful with the right guardrails in place. Opening our systems to random agents that are being trained on off-the-shelf models and blindly relying on them can pose significant cyber risks. For example, vibe coding by using an AI model to help develop software, giving away the entire codebase to an untrusted entity outside the organization can lead to vulnerability sweeping across multiple surfaces. Vibe coding by using an AI model to help develop software, giving away the entire codebase to an untrusted entity outside the organization can lead to vulnerability sweeping across multiple surfaces. This opens critical discussions towards how vibe coding could interfere with the positioning and implementation of trusted execution of the agentic queries. Consider an autonomous web of agents that relies on agents’ inputs to drive the operations. When the system is operating under low tolerance of failure and with non-tracking based agentic workflows, it could be computationally expensive to trust and verify each query in real-time that leads to the common trade-offs of memory vs execution. Another risk to consider is the zero-day attack. When it happens, how will the system react? Would such an event be manageable without a total infrastructure breakdown? The scale of impact can be observed from over reliance on agentic ecosystems with only one trusted layer. This could mean that when failure occurs, the entire ecosystem could be exposed, just like there will be no autonomy if the backbone network is not available, which essentially means no layer to place trust. How quickly can de-authentication attacks occur? An in-house experiment done at Queen’s University Belfast (QUB) provided an initial understanding of how the scale of agentic attacks could mean a lower window of vulnerability. The team focused on very popular de-authentication attacks and with agentic orchestration, the swift rate to do de-authentication attacks could go as low as 2 to 3 seconds. This gives little to no time to react and decide on patching the system. There is another aspect of the large-scale agentic system, which establishes trust under asynchronous autonomy. Trust serves as a critical foundation for traceability. How would you ensure that all the agents operating towards a common goal are aligned and understand the delays associated with their goals? Our team worked around this space, which at first involved demonstrating that the problem exists, and its impact and scale can be huge when you must prove trust under boundaries of asynchronous autonomy. Solutions towards such problems can be simplified by keeping things like AI-bill of material or leveraging distributed ledger technology that can provide underlying infrastructure of trust via traceability and immutability and keep the agentic activity and associated trust vectors agnostic to the platform. Within trust, another factor that is not well explored but needs a thorough investigation is the concept of horizontal anomalies. It defines how agents interact differently with various sources under different settings. As agents behave correctly and align themselves with the architectural expectations for one specific task or application, that does not necessarily mean these can be trusted for their operations across all associated components. How to identify such anomalies and what methods can be employed without complying with such agents remain open questions and topics for further exploration. The critical aspect is that utility of agents with semi to low trust governance offer short-term high benefits, but the cost of recovery when the system fails is yet to be explored, and this will not be a contained issue. We are looking into the system where agents are already sweeping into different entities and may not allow complete recovery. For example, a mere supply chain issue because an agent going rogue is now not a containable small task but needs sweeping across all the touch points of those affected agents. This essentially means despite the number of agents and their ability to trigger proxy-agents, which may not be directly linked to the wider ecosystem, there is a need to ensure that computationally expensive trackers are in place for all the agents. Other relevant PhD works carried out in our research group are towards sovereignty of AI, exploring aspects of trust and accountability. Our hypothesis is that sovereignty and trust need to be governed together as onus of provenance is high on the host of agents. Thus, it needs understanding of laws governing trust-based executions of AI. The important challenge here is that there is a vital difference between missed information and missed instructions, and both have different impacts when it comes to trusted accountability. Does true zero-trust architecture exist? The real-world issue with these systems lies in the failure to adopt approaches that historically have relied on state-based modeling when governing trust. In stateless systems where agentic autonomy is high, the convergence and reliability towards trust-provenance decreases significantly. Thus, it brings us back to the original question – does a true zero-trust even exist? Can policies be trusted? If so, how should these be managed without falling into the trap of policy-based accessibility and control issues? events.summary: Store Mac iPad iPhone Watch Vision AirPods TV & Home Entertainment Accessories Support Text of this article November 9, 2026 UPDATE Olivia Dean is Apple Music’s Artist of the Year for 2026 Olivia Dean was announced today as Apple Music’s Artist of the Year, recognizing her undeniable leap to stardom in what’s been the defining feel-good music story of 2026. She is the first UK artist to receive this honor. Olivia’s late 2025 album, The Art of Loving , truly broke through this year. Her hit “Man I Need” has charted on Apple Music’s Daily Top 100 every day since first appearing on August 29, 2025. In addition to selling out her global tour, she won a GRAMMY for Best New Artist and four BRIT Awards, including Artist of the Year. In fall 2025, Olivia opened for Sabrina Carpenter at Madison Square Garden, in New York City. Less than a year later, she returned for her own four-night residency and followed up with a six-night sold-out run at The O2 Arena, in London. Olivia has found and grown her audience with warm, vulnerable songs about love and friendship. Apple Music editors have highlighted the grace with which her music taps into the rich songwriting tradition of 1960s soul and pop, and is inspired by the sensuality of Sade, the brazenness of Prince, and the honesty of Lauryn Hill — all while fostering a community built on love. Olivia’s messages of affirmation and connection resonate deeply with her fans. Listeners have responded to her worldview that expressing love, in all its forms, is an active practice that takes conscious effort, an idea inspired by the 1999 book All About Love: New Visions , by bell hooks. “I love making music,” said Olivia. “It’s the best thing in the world. I think being Apple’s Artist of the Year feels really amazing. To be recognized as an artist that’s made an impact is really cool.” “What sets Olivia apart is that she speaks from the heart, every time,” said Rachel Newman, Apple Music’s co-head. “Her songs make you want to call a friend, dance in your kitchen, and tell someone you love them. She is open and genuine in everything she shares, and that connection is what turned a great year into a defining one.” As Apple Music’s Artist of the Year, Olivia will receive a physical award that represents the extraordinary artistry integral to creating music. Each Apple Music Award features Apple’s custom silicon wafer suspended between a polished sheet of glass, and a machined and anodized aluminum body. In a symbolic gesture, the same chip powering the devices that put over 100 million songs at listeners’ fingertips also sits at the very heart of the Apple Music Awards. Celebrate Olivia’s Artist of the Year appointment with a special selection of playlists dedicated to the songs and voices that have shaped the last 12 months. About Apple Music Apple loves music. Apple revolutionized the music experience with iPod and iTunes. Today, the award-winning Apple Music celebrates musicians, songwriters, producers, and fans with a catalog of over 100 million songs, expertly curated playlists, and the best artist interviews, conversations, and global premieres with Apple Music Radio. With original content from the most respected and beloved people in music, autoplay, time-synced lyrics, lossless audio, and immersive sound powered by Spatial Audio with Dolby Atmos, Apple Music offers the world’s best listening experience, helping listeners discover new music and enjoy their favorites while empowering the global artist community. Apple Music is available in over 167 countries and regions on iPhone, iPad, Mac, Apple Watch, Apple TV, HomePod, CarPlay, Apple Vision Pro, and online at music.apple.com , plus popular smart speakers, smart TVs, and Android and Windows devices. Apple Music is ad-free and never shares consumer data with third parties. More information is available at apple.com/apple-music . events.title: Northern Trust and Microsoft Frontier Company collaborate to transform client onboarding through AI
events.summary: November 9, 2026 Category: Company News Northern Trust and Microsoft Frontier Company collaborate to transform client onboarding through AI New c lient o nboarding a gent, built with Microsoft Frontier Company forward deployed engineer s , reduces onboarding data preparation time by 8 3 % , while enhancing efficiency and maintaining strong privacy, security and governance controls Microsoft Source | 6 minutes CHICAGO and REDMOND, Wash. — Nov. 9, 2026 — Northern Trust and Microsoft Corp. on Monday announced an expanded collaboration to accelerate AI transformation across Northern Trust, beginning with the deployment of a new AI-powered client onboarding agent for clients on Northern Trust Asset Servicing’s Front Office Solutions platform. Developed jointly by Northern Trust and Microsoft Frontier Company Forward Deployed Engineering (FDE) teams, the agent streamlines one of the most complex aspects of institutional client onboarding: transforming years of data and transaction history into a standardized format ready for use within Northern Trust’s reporting environment. The new capability combines advanced AI with enterprise-grade privacy, security and governance to help deliver a faster, more efficient onboarding experience for clients.   For Front Office Solutions clients, onboarding can be particularly complex given the breadth and depth of investment data involved. The platform provides performance and analytics for institutional investors, including foundations, endowments, pension schemes and large family offices. Onboarding can require Northern Trust to consolidate large volumes of investment and transaction data from multiple sources to reconstruct performance histories, particularly for alternative assets.  The challenge addressed by the new client onboarding agent reflects a broader industry trend: More than half of asset owners (57%) surveyed by Northern Trust cite consolidating data from multiple, disparate internal and external sources as their biggest challenge. The agent automates a key part of this process by converting clients’ historical transaction data into Northern Trust’s standardized format, cutting data preparation time by 83% — from two and a half weeks to three days i — while achieving a 96.5% F1 first-pass quality score, ii a standard AI evaluation metric that combines precision and recall into a single quality metric. The solution has been designed with human oversight embedded throughout the workflow, enabling analysts to review outputs, evaluate reasoning, resolve exceptions and continuously improve performance through expert feedback and governance. By using the agent during implementation, before the client goes live, analysts can identify and reconcile errors while validating the client’s starting data.  Built on Microsoft Azure, the agent uses Microsoft Foundry for enterprise AI and integrates with familiar Microsoft 365 tools, including Microsoft Excel and SharePoint, so Northern Trust analysts can review, refine and approve its work. A governed intelligence layer powered by Azure preserves approved onboarding knowledge, allowing the solution to build upon institutional expertise over time and continuously improve the onboarding process. The result is less manual work for analysts, a faster and more predictable experience for clients, and a more efficient onboarding experience.  Designed for the rigorous requirements of the financial services industry, the client onboarding agent incorporates robust privacy, security and governance controls. Taking an “eyes-off” approach, Microsoft hill-climbed on F1 first-pass quality scoring and other evaluation measurements using only anonymized data, ensuring Northern Trust client data remained securely governed under the firm’s control throughout the process. This model has enabled the organization to achieve production-scale performance while meeting the stringent data stewardship expectations of a highly regulated industry. Through this collaboration, Northern Trust and Microsoft have established a model for how highly regulated institutions can adopt frontier AI while retaining ownership and control of their data, expertise and institutional knowledge.  “At Northern Trust, our close relationships with our clients give us a unique perspective on how their needs are evolving and where we can create value,” said Pete Cherecwich, Chief Operating Officer, Northern Trust. “The client onboarding agent is an example of an approach that combines Northern Trust’s asset servicing expertise with Microsoft’s AI capabilities to help get clients up and running more quickly during onboarding. The solution reduces the time required to prepare and validate clients’ data while maintaining the oversight and controls our clients expect, creating capacity for both sides to focus on higher-value work.”   Northern Trust is applying AI to the qualities that have defined the firm for more than 135 years: service, expertise and integrity. At the center of this strategy is augmented intelligence: using AI as a force multiplier for human expertise, while keeping judgment and accountability with people. The firm’s collaboration with Microsoft Frontier Company brings that approach to life through AI-powered agents designed to transform critical business processes, enhance decision-making and deliver better client outcomes.  “Advanced AI can turn deep industry expertise into better client experiences and new capacity for growth,” said Bill Borden, Corporate Vice President, Worldwide Financial Services, Microsoft. “Through Microsoft Frontier Company, our collaboration with Northern Trust shows what next-generation enterprise operating models can look like: AI amplifying human expertise to accelerate service delivery and improve agility, with governance and human oversight built in. This approach points to a broader opportunity across regulated industries to transform complex workflows and deliver business value without compromising trust.”  About Northern Trust   Northern Trust Corporation (Nasdaq: NTRS) is a leading provider of wealth management, asset servicing, asset management and banking services to corporations, institutions, affluent families and individuals. Founded in Chicago in 1889, Northern Trust has a global presence with offices in 24 U.S. states and Washington, D.C., and across 22 locations in Canada, Europe, the Middle East and the Asia-Pacific region. As of September 30, 2026, Northern Trust had assets under custody/administration of US$19.9 trillion, and assets under management of US$2.0 trillion. For more than 135 years, Northern Trust has earned distinction as an industry leader for exceptional service, financial expertise, integrity and innovation. Visit us on northerntrust.com . Follow us on Instagram @northerntrustcompany or Northern Trust on LinkedIn .  Northern Trust Corporation, Head Office: 50 South La Salle Street, Chicago, Illinois 60603

events.title: Watch: Where Do Our Generic Drugs Come From? We Dug to Find Out.
events.summary: These days, we know where almost everything comes from. Everyday items like food, clothes and pens all carry labels listing where things are grown, manufactured or even designed.  So why is it so hard to find where prescription drugs are made? That question set off a 14-month investigation into where our medications are made, how the FDA polices drug manufacturers and what happens when inspectors report issues inside factories. The vast majority of prescriptions filled in the United States are for generic drugs, which are often far cheaper than brand-name alternatives.  For years, Congress, doctors and watchdog groups have questioned the quality of generic drugs made overseas. India produces about half of all generics used in the U.S., but the labels on pill bottles often don’t list where a drug is manufactured. Inspection reports describe unsafe manufacturing conditions at generic drug factories, but the Food and Drug Administration redacts the names of the medications made in those factories. That means if drugs made in errant factories wind up in your medicine cabinet, you’d have no way of knowing.  To better understand how the FDA regulates the generic drug industry, Debbie Cenziper and Megan Rose interviewed current and former factory inspectors, tested medications in a lab and sued the federal government for critical documents.  Here’s what they found: Birds defecated on boxes of sterile equipment. Inspectors reported finding dirty labs, mold and foul water at factories. Records referenced vials of medication that were “blackish” from contamination. Inspectors found what appeared to be metal shavings on equipment. Drug manufacturers manipulated and destroyed drug-testing records. At one factory, an analyst poured acid on records stuffed in a trash bin. At another, inspectors said in a report that records were “routinely manipulated” to cover up the presence of particulate matter —  which could include glass, fiber or other contaminants — in generic drugs. A lifesaving generic drug contained a lower amount of a key ingredient. We worked with an independent lab to test generic versions of tacrolimus , used to prevent organ rejection. We found some pills contained a lower amount of the key ingredient in the drug. Doctors and experts said that underdosing can leave patients vulnerable to organ rejection. The FDA allowed generic drug imports from banned factories — and didn’t inform the public. The agency gave some manufacturers a special pass to continue to ship drugs made in factories whose manufacturing practices were so bad they had been banned from the U.S. Over a dozen years, the FDA exempted at least 150 drugs or their ingredients from banned factories. A transplant patient’s lungs failed after she took generic versions of tacrolimus. Hannah Goetz had a double-lung transplant as a teenager and had to take tacrolimus twice a day. Her lungs failed in 2023, and she died at 21 years old, after years of relying on the generic drug made by two manufacturers with documented problems. Lawyers told Goetz’s mother that it was impossible to draw a straight line from Hannah’s death to a generic manufacturer, but her mother said she wonders if her daughter would still be alive if she took a different brand of tacrolimus. In a response to ProPublica, a spokesperson for the FDA said in a statement that the exemptions given to banned factories are “thoroughly evaluated through a multi-disciplinary approach” but declined to say exactly what those evaluations entailed. The agency also said it requires manufacturers to conduct additional quality checks with third-party oversight before sending drugs to the U.S. The agency did not respond to questions about how it can know that generics are safe without a more robust testing program.  In statements to ProPublica, drug companies said that they take patient safety seriously, adhere to quality standards and are committed to working with the FDA on any regulatory issues. ProPublica’s investigation , which went on to be a finalist for the Pulitzer Prize for investigative reporting , published in 2025.  Use our tool to find where your prescription drugs were made. ProPublica’s Brandon Roberts and a team of data journalists made a tool called Rx Inspector that will show you the facility that manufactured your generic prescription drugs and any inspection reports, warning letters and import bans we have from the FDA.  The data isn’t perfect; it’s possible the FDA hasn’t published everything it knows about a given facility, for example. Also, one company may have acquired another or moved the factory somewhere else. This tool also isn’t meant to provide you with medical advice: If you find something troubling, it doesn’t necessarily mean that your drug is compromised. Doctors and pharmacists advise that you not stop taking your medications. Instead, you should talk to your healthcare provider about any concerns. Step 1: Enter the name of your prescription drug, as well as the company name found on your pill bottle or drug label. Step 2: If there are multiple matches in our database, you can narrow your search using the markings found on a pill, for example. Step 3: When you click on a drug, we’ll show you any manufacturing facilities we’ve been able to connect to it. Click on a facility to see any information we have from the FDA. FDA inspections come with compliance outcomes, such as import alerts or warning letters. The best possible outcome of an inspection is “acceptable state,” which means the FDA took no compliance action and ProPublica found no issues documented by inspectors. Search your prescription here. ProPublica described Rx Inspector and the methodology used to build it to the FDA, which did not comment. The agency previously told ProPublica that it doesn’t reveal where drugs are made on inspection reports to protect what it deemed to be confidential commercial information. Read more of Cenziper, Rose and Roberts’ reporting from their series Rx Roulette or watch their video explainer . The post Watch: Where Do Our Generic Drugs Come From? We Dug to Find Out. appeared first on ProPublica .
