events.title: NASA keeps its PROMISE to raid Mars testbeds for parts
events.summary: NASA is moving ahead with its plan to repurpose a Mars rover engineering model as a lunar trundlebot for less than $400 million. The robot, dubbed PROMISE (Polar Rover for Observation, Mapping, and In-Situ Exploration), is a cut-and-shut of engineering test articles used for the Perseverance and Curiosity rovers, currently rolling around the Red Planet. During a weekend briefing , NASA outlined the plan for PROMISE: to land the robot on the lunar surface by late 2028 for an 18-month mission. PROMISE will be preceded by NASA's VIPER trundlebot, which is expected to survive only 100 days on the Moon's surface. PROMISE will carry copies of VIPER's science instruments, including a drill capable of boring 1 meter into the lunar regolith. Power will come from a Radioisotope Thermoelectric Generator (RTG) left over from the Cassini mission. NASA acknowledged the fuel was processed some time ago – the Cassini mission to Saturn was launched in 1997 – but anticipates there will be plenty of heat and power for PROMISE's components. Blue Origin is to deposit the rover on the Moon. NASA awarded the company a $94 million base contract, "with an option period worth an additional $140 million based on performance to deliver PROMISE to the lunar South Pole." The figures make it difficult to ascertain the exact cost of the PROMISE mission. However, during the briefing, NASA said it had "a pretty firm agreement with JPL to basically deliver the rover to the surface under $400 million." The $400 million includes the lander, which will be Blue Origin's Mark 1. Earlier this year, The Planetary Society's chief of space policy, Casey Drier, estimated that the mission (including repurposing the hardware developed for Mars and landing it on the Moon) would cost at least $723 million. At the time, NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said: "if PROMISE costs even 20 percent of your low-end estimate, we simply will not fly it." Assuming Isaacman was only talking about the rover, Drier's figure drops to $489 million without launch and landing costs. 20 percent of that is… not going to be enough. That also doesn't account for the impact of taking away the hardware built for the Mars program. During the briefing, NASA said it was "pretty comfortable" with how the Mars rovers were going and so was happy about repurposing the hardware or, as one speaker put it, "can we give it a new paint job?" A source told The Register that morale at the agency's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) was not high at present. Raiding successful programs to fulfill the administration's whims is unlikely to have improved the mood of engineers. Still. Another trundlebot on the Moon. Far better than using that spare RTG for yet another deep space mission, right? ®

events.title: Microsoft's Azure Linux gets 470-plus security fixes in one almighty patching session
events.summary: Microsoft has unleashed a whopper of an update for Azure Linux, packing more than 470 CVE fixes into a single release as the software industry's ever-growing pile of vulnerabilities shows little sign of shrinking. Over the weekend, Microsoft rolled out Azure Linux 3.0.2022 with fixes covering everything from the Linux kernel to open source packages and container software. The changelog runs to hundreds of entries, so anyone planning to read the whole thing might want to put the kettle on. Microsoft's release notes contain more than 470 CVE references, although some vulnerabilities appear multiple times because they affect different packages. So that's not necessarily 470 separate security holes, but it's still an impressive amount of patching for one release. The fixes span OpenSSL, curl, Kubernetes, Docker, QEMU, and a lengthy list of other packages that underpin modern Linux environments. The generic Linux kernel has been updated to version 6.6.161.1. There's also been some housekeeping following the eMudhra certificate incident , tracked as CVE-2026-114406. Microsoft has removed or distrusted root certificates that could validate compromised eMudhra intermediate certificates, while adding checks in Python and Go to reject the affected certificates. It has also preserved SSL.com TLS trust where required, presumably to avoid fixing one certificate headache by creating another. Container infrastructure gets plenty of attention, too, with fixes spanning KubeVirt, containerd, Docker Compose, and other components used to keep cloud workloads running. Several CVEs crop up repeatedly across these packages, helping explain the eye-watering number of entries in the changelog. The release includes less security-focused changes too, including new Dockerfiles, an OpenVMM patch for confidential computing support, fixes for systemd hangs, and adjustments to GRUB Secure Boot metadata. The hefty release comes amid an AI-fueled surge in vulnerability discovery that has left developers struggling to keep up with the resulting patch workload. As The Register reported e arlier today, Linux creator Linus Torvalds reckons there may finally be signs that the flood is easing, at least in some corners of the kernel. Torvalds said fixes are now arriving faster than new bug reports in the kernel's eBPF subsystem, although he noted that most other areas haven't reached that point. Whether the wider software industry is anywhere close to catching up is another matter, and Microsoft hasn't said if AI-assisted research contributed to the vulnerabilities addressed in this release. Azure Linux, formerly known as CBL-Mariner, is Microsoft's own Linux distribution, developed primarily for its cloud infrastructure and services. That makes keeping its many components patched rather more important than the modest version-number bump might suggest. And judging by the size of this latest changelog, Microsoft's patching teams aren't likely to be putting their feet up anytime soon. ®

events.title: Jensen Huang Hired a PR Firm Known for Handling Sex Scandals Last Year
events.summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang began working with a crisis communications firm known for handling public scandals a year before he admitted to having an extramarital affair with a woman suspected by US intelligence of being a Chinese spy. The firm, Heller, has handled Huang’s behind-the-scenes communications since at least October 2025, according to two sources familiar with the matter. Risa Heller, the firm’s founder, has built a reputation as a fixer for powerful men facing allegations of sexual misconduct and other personal controversies, according to a 2023 New York magazine profile . Her past clients and people who have sought her advice include former congressman Anthony Weiner, chef Mario Batali, and writer Jeffrey Toobin. Heller also handles corporate communications and issues unrelated to personal controversies for its clients. Heller’s public relations consultants were initially believed to be hired for matters related to Huang’s personal life, including his family’s philanthropic endeavors, according to people familiar with the arrangement. The firm frequently communicated with Huang and his daughter Madison, a product marketing director at Nvidia who has become an increasingly prominent figure within the company, sources tell WIRED. It’s not clear whether Heller’s early work with the Huang family involved Huang’s affair. In 2024, Huang began appearing in public with a woman who goes by Alice Huang, a former executive at the Singapore-based chip buyer Megaspeed, according to The New York Times. Megaspeed was created when it split off from a Chinese gaming and cloud computing firm in 2023, a few months after the US government began restricting exports of advanced semiconductors to China, including those developed by Nvidia. A subsidiary of Megaspeed later became a major buyer of Nvidia chips. In early October 2025, Jensen Huang’s business dealings with Megaspeed and his connection to Alice became public in a lengthy New York Times report , which alleged that the US Commerce Department was investigating whether the company was helping Chinese firms evade American export controls through its subsidiaries. The report caused tensions to rise within Nvidia’s top ranks, and Jensen was rankled by the story, according to sources. By the end of that month, Nvidia’s internal communications teams had been instructed to include Heller’s firm on any press inquiries about Huang, whether personal or professional, according to people familiar with the matter. When reached by email, a representative for Heller referred WIRED to Nvidia. John Rizzo, Nvidia’s head of public policy communications, declined to comment. US intelligence officials have determined that Alice (who has no known relation to Jensen) is a spy working for the Chinese government, according to the Times. Nvidia initially said that Jensen’s interactions with Alice were part of routine business with clients. But on Sunday, Huang acknowledged that his relationship with her was romantic in nature. In an email to Nvidia staff, he said he owed them and his family an apology. “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry,” Huang wrote. Nvidia’s board of directors announced it is opening an independent investigation into Jensen’s activities. It said it has no reason to believe that national security or confidential Nvidia information has been compromised. Before founding her firm, Risa Heller worked for Jane Harman, then a Democratic congresswoman from California, and later served as Democratic senator Chuck Schumer’s New York City press secretary. Rizzo, Nvidia’s head of public policy communications, also previously worked for Schumer, serving as his deputy communications director. Update 11/10/26 8:45am ET: This story has been updated to note that Nvidia declined to comment. events.title: Who Gives A Crap? Hackers, apparently, after toilet paper maker's customer data exposed
events.summary: Toilet paper purveyor Who Gives A Crap has found itself in a bit of a mess after an intruder accessed customer information through a third-party software provider, leaving the company scrambling to clean up a breach affecting shoppers in the UK, US, and Australia. In an email sent to affected customers over the weekend, seen by The Register , the loo roll seller warns that personal information was accessed without authorization after a security incident at an unnamed US-based marketing software provider. The email explains that the intruder gained access to the supplier's systems on October 30. The provider spotted the intrusion the following day and says it secured its systems by November 1, although Who Gives A Crap wasn't told until November 6. It's unclear why the supplier sat on the bad news for another five days before passing it on. The exposed information includes customers' names, email addresses, phone numbers, mailing addresses, and total spending with the company. In other words, someone may now know not only where you live, but just how much of your hard-earned cash you've flushed down the crapper. Payment information, order details, and passwords were not involved, and customers' accounts were not directly accessed. That's something of a relief, although whether the intruder actually made off with the data remains a pressing question. "We don't yet know whether the information was copied or downloaded," the company told customers, adding that it had found no evidence of misuse. In a separate public statement , Who Gives A Crap co-founder and CEO Simon Griffiths confirmed that the incident affected customers across the company's Australian, UK, and US stores. Canadian customers, meanwhile, appear to have escaped this particular toilet emergency, with the supplier reporting that no personal information belonging to shoppers in the country was accessed. Who Gives A Crap says it has since disconnected the provider from its systems, changed access credentials, and begun warning affected customers to watch out for suspicious emails, texts, calls, and other unsolicited communications. "The main concern is scam or phishing messages that use your real details to look convincing," the company warned in its customer email. While Who Gives A Crap has been busy cleaning up, the supplier at the center of this particular stink remains a mystery. The company hasn't identified the software provider or disclosed how many customers were affected, including those in the UK, and didn’t respond to our questions. Griffiths said the company is "engaging with the relevant regulatory authorities, as required." In the UK, the ICO told The Register : "We can confirm Who Gives A Crap Limited has reported an incident and we are assessing the information provided." Who Gives A Crap has plenty of toilet paper to hand, although cleaning up this particular situation might require more than a few rolls. ®

events.title: The AI bubble can wait, but your exit plan can't
events.summary: The AI bubble isn't about to burst, Forrester reckons, although businesses should prepare for a correction that could upend their suppliers, contracts, and prices. Spending on infrastructure has raced ahead of measurable returns, the analyst says, yet the financial strength of the companies funding the build-out is what keep Forrester from predicting an imminent crash. "Fears that an AI bubble is about to burst are premature," said Forrester emerging technology veep Brian Hopkins. "About nine-tenths of the money building today's AI computing infrastructure comes from large, healthy technology companies paying out of their own cash flow. The risk is concentrated in a few places: a small number of builders under real financial strain, and circular financing deals with the AI labs." Conveniently, Forrester has developed an AI Bubble Model to help technology leaders monitor the risks and prepare. Its latest report, " An AI Bubble Burst Is Not Imminent ," notes what many in the IT industry, including The Register , have been saying for a while: that the hyperscale operators are committing a record share of revenue into capital expenditure to bring online more infrastructure to support AI development and use. At the same time, the boost in productivity doesn't justify this supplier capacity build-out. Forrester calculates that the infrastructure investments break even only if AI raises US GDP by 5 percent by 2035. Published estimates suggest productivity improvements could provide about two percentage points of that uplift, leaving roughly $1.3 trillion to come from other sources of value. A recent report from management consultants Bain & Company came to similar conclusions, estimating the AI industry needs to generate $6 trillion in annual revenue by 2031 to keep funding all the infrastructure it needs, and this will require new uses beyond simply enhancing employee productivity. Forrester also claims that the forces making AI abundant also make parts of the market unstable, and says that enterprise users should take heed of how prices collapsed as major providers like Anthropic slashed token costs in response to competition from open source models. If demand disappoints as new capacity comes online, suppliers could cut investment, merge, change prices, or discontinue products. Customers could find themselves rebuilding AI plans around suppliers and services that no longer exist. Forrester advises businesses to track whether their AI projects deliver measurable value and limit their exposure to vulnerable suppliers – with its help, of course. Companies can judge how things are going by looking at the gap between suppliers' contracted business and revenue actually recognized, along with how they fund their build-outs. If a vendor leans more on outside investment and customer prepayments, as Oracle and CoreWeave have, this is a red flag to cut back dependencies on them, Forrester says. Enterprises should also stress-test AI plans against scenarios such as a key vendor announcing end of support in 12 months, and an AI model supplier defaulting on payments to its compute vendor and cutting back service-level agreements for enterprise workloads. Companies should know in advance which AI use cases to drop, what data and workloads need to be moved, and at what cost. But Hopkins sounded a further note of caution: "Oversupply on its own won't decide whether a correction comes. Demand will, and that's the biggest unknown, because it depends on enterprises finding lasting value in AI beyond simple productivity gains." Organizations shouldn't pull back, he insists. They should keep investing where AI delivers value that can be demonstrated, closely monitor the financial health of the companies building AI computing, and be ready for corrections. Recently, the International Monetary Fund started ringing alarm bells that financial markets are increasingly exposed to an AI-driven correction that could lead to widespread economic disruption. Earlier this year, the Bank for International Settlements also raised concerns that the current situation with the AI industry bore the hallmarks of historical economic bubbles and presented a risk to global economic stability. ®

events.title: Practice Makes Precise: At CoRL, NVIDIA and Partners Reveal How Robots Rehearse Delicate Work in Simulation
events.summary: Simulation, which has long been the proving ground for robots learning to walk, roll and hop, is now helping researchers teach robots tasks that require a finer touch: aligning gears, connecting cables and assembling small components. The shift from locomotion to manipulation is taking center stage at this week’s Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL) in Austin, Texas, alongside the rise of agentic robotics — a new paradigm that integrates frontier agents to create interpretable code for physical robotics systems. At CoRL, NVIDIA is introducing new open robotics technologies, including world action models , simulation tools, benchmarks and agentic workflows. Two NVIDIA papers are among six finalists out of thousands of submissions for the Best Paper Awards at CoRL: GRAIL (Generating Humanoid Loco-Manipulation from World Models), which presents a digital generation pipeline for 3D assets and simulator-ready scenes for robot learning. RoboTTT: Context Scaling for Robot Policies , which introduces a robot model and training recipe that scales visuomotor context three orders of magnitude beyond state-of-the-art policies without growing inference latency. These advancements help researchers train robots on complex tasks, evaluate their performance across changing conditions and use failures to guide further learning — building the precision, adaptability and autonomy needed to move from lab demonstrations to industrial deployment. NVIDIA is working with partners like Ambi Robotics , Bosch Research , Dexmate , Dyna Robotics , FieldAI , Flexion , Noitom Robotics , Siemens , Skild AI , RLWRLD , UC Berkeley , Walden Robotics and the University of Washington to bring these advancements to the broader robotics community. World Action Models Enable Next Level of Robot Autonomy The next level of robot autonomy requires robots to perceive their surroundings, anticipate how their actions will change the environment and execute complex, multistep tasks with a high degree of precision. World action models enable exactly that. At CoRL, NVIDIA is introducing GR00T 2 , an open frontier world action model built on NVIDIA Cosmos. Trained on diverse robot and human data, including 100,000 hours of NVIDIA open source human egocentric data , the model enables robots to learn dexterous manipulation skills. Key features include: Out-of-the-box performance: Completed 40 of 50 evaluated tasks at least once without task-specific demonstrations. Skill transfer: Learns from human demonstrations and transfers skills between different robot bodies without robot demonstrations Generalization with little data: Achieved 71% average success across 50 tasks with just one demonstration per task, increasing to 95% with five. Agent control: AI agents can use GR00T 2’s application programming interface and supporting tools to run skills in sequence and recover from errors. GR00T 2 currently ranks among the top three models across all vision language action and world action model categories for the RoboCasa365, RoboLab, RoboDojo and MolmoSpaces benchmarks, with multiple leaderboard wins. Nexuni is testing it for robotic laundry handling, Foxconn is applying GR00T 2 to factory automation for server manufacturing and Siemens is evaluating it across industrial use cases. MicroAGI is using GR00T 2, post-trained through reinforcement learning, to perform Ethernet cable swapping with a YAM robotic arm. Its agentic robotics approach automates the creation and calibration of simulation environments using Isaac Lab 3.0 and Newton, where the policy is trained. Training capable robots requires diverse data. Open NVIDIA workflows and models equip researchers with better tools for data collection and annotation: For researchers building robot-training datasets, NVIDIA’s new open Video to Data workflow turns human video into simulated robot demonstrations, with a challenge inviting researchers to advance it. The NVIDIA EgoHand open model — being demoed at CoRL and with over 40,000 Hugging Face downloads in the two weeks since launch — reconstructs 3D hand motion, trained with data from Noitom Robotics . Where the Training and Scaling Happens — in Simulation A pretrained model gives robots a core set of skills. Simulation lets researchers train, refine and evaluate skills at scale before deploying them on physical robots. NVIDIA Isaac Lab , an open source robot-learning framework, provides the foundation for that work. Its latest release, Isaac Lab 3.0 , allows researchers to use agents to quickly set up training environments with simulation-ready assets , switch between NVIDIA PhysX and Newton physics solvers , choose renderers for perception-based training and apply a new reinforcement post-training library to foundation models like GR00T. Accurate physics is critical to transferring learned skills from simulation to the real robot. Tighter integration with Newton , an open source physics engine, now allows Isaac Lab to model deformable objects such as cables and cloth, along with complex articulated systems such as robotic hands with many interacting joints. Integration with Newton simulates how a strawberry deforms under a robot’s grip. Together, Isaac Lab and Newton combine accurate physics with scale to enable researchers to train thousands of simulated robots in parallel. In a vision-based dexterous manipulation benchmark, Isaac Lab 3.0 with Newton achieved up to 2.5x the training throughput of Isaac Lab 2.3 with PhysX. Isaac Lab supports robot simulation with Newton and NVIDIA PhysX. Developers are extending Newton’s capabilities. At CoRL, Skild AI announced Scalable Throughput-optimized Engine for Embodied Learning, or STEEL, a new rigid-body physics solver built on Newton to accelerate robot training with Isaac Lab. Flexion showcased how Isaac Lab and Newton help train Reflect, its robot-intelligence model combining reasoning and whole-body manipulation. Flexion uses Newton for RL with Isaac Lab. FieldAI is using Newton — as well as Isaac Lab and Isaac Sim, built on NVIDIA Omniverse libraries — to train and validate robot policies for deployment in unstructured real-world environments. Dyna Robotics will demonstrate how parallel simulation in Isaac Lab helps train whole-body controllers for its semi-humanoid Taku robot for work in warehouses, hotels and food services. Walden Robotics is using Isaac Sim’s photorealistic rendering to train and evaluate its general-purpose robot in virtual environments for manufacturing and logistics, while Dexmate is exploring how coding agents can rehearse and refine manipulation strategies in Isaac Sim before executing them on its Vega robot. AlphaNIST , built in Isaac Lab, demonstrates how efficient practice can translate into precision. A single policy learns all 20 tasks on the NIST Assembly Task Board, manipulating millimeter-scale parts using only a yes-or-no success signal.

events.title: Nigeria election ruling may increase voter apathy
events.summary: Alexis’s view Nigeria’s Federal High Court invalidating the election candidacy of President Bola Tinubu’s leading challenger was unexpected — but not entirely surprising. Former Vice President Atiku Abubakar, runner-up in the last election, has fewer than 100 days to secure a reversal on appeal ahead of the January vote. But the broader danger is that last week’s legal curveball further erodes trust in Africa’s biggest democratic exercise. The ruling is consistent with a recent pattern of late interventions ahead of Nigerian elections. In 2019, the country’s then most senior judge was suspended weeks before the vote, prompting speculation that he was dismissed because he couldn’t be relied upon to back the incumbent if courts weighed in on a close result. And Nigeria’s central bank wreaked havoc four years ago when it issued new bank notes in a move widely seen as an attempt to disadvantage some politicians and favor others. Each intervention raised questions about the independence of key institutions. Tinubu was already the frontrunner, even before Atiku’s legal headache. Peter Obi, the other main opponent, should not be underestimated. But the failure of the opposition to unify behind a single candidate has weakened the challenge to Tinubu, despite widespread anger over the rising cost of living, which many blame on the president’s removal of the country’s fuel subsidy. The smart money is on the ruling against Atiku being overturned before the election. The danger for Tinubu is that suspicion that the judiciary undermined a rival — one who vowed to restore the fuel subsidy — turns Atiku into a lightning rod for public frustration. The more deep-rooted threat is apathy. Tinubu won in 2023 with just 27% voter turnout — the lowest since the return to civilian rule in 1999. Any sense that courts, rather than the ballot box, will sway the election could dampen interest further, handing the victor an even slimmer mandate to govern Africa’s most populous country. Under such circumstances, a Tinubu victory could soon feel Pyrrhic. Notable South Africa’s biggest party, the ANC, faced intense campaigns ahead of the local elections, which involved politicians spinning cars, watching grannies knit and wading through giant-sized potholes.

events.title: The cheap plastic drape saving mothers' lives in Nigeria
events.summary: An 80 cent “maternal drape” is saving women’s lives in Kano, Nigeria — the country where more women die in childbirth than anywhere else in the world. The drape measures blood loss during childbirth; once the level passes 300ml, midwives use massage, oxytocin, tranexamic acid, and IV fluids to encourage the uterus to contract. Hadiza Galadanci, an obstetrics and gynecology professor at Bayero University, was initially skeptical that anything could reduce the mortality rate from postpartum hemorrhage — experienced by 10% of women who give birth and the biggest risk to new mothers — when she was approached by researchers . But the drastic reduction in deaths since the drape’s implementation spurred her to persuade Nigeria’s health minister to introduce it as a national standard of care. Suppliers in Kano now produce them for Nigeria and neighboring countries. — Leah Quinn

events.title: Gabon outlines $2B mining project with Emirati and Chinese companies
events.summary: Gabon is planning a $2 billion project with Emirati and Chinese companies to mine and process rare earth elements and niobium, a metal used to strengthen steel, in a move aimed at exploiting the country’s undeveloped mineral wealth. The new investment would bring the long-stalled Mabounié deposit, southeast of Libreville, into production. Abu Dhabi-based mining group New Energy Metals is developing the deposit with engineering support from Beijing-based ENFI, with construction expected to begin in 2027, the presidency said. The development was announced during a visit by Gabon’s president to China last week, when the two countries agreed to strengthen ties. China already dominates the processing of many critical minerals, while the shift to cleaner energy and new technologies is driving US, European, and Gulf investors to court African governments for access to their resources. — Ruben Nyanguila

events.title: South Africa's Shoprite plans banking move with Investec
events.summary: Africa’s biggest grocer Shoprite plans to team up with upmarket lender Investec to offer customers a debit card and expanded financial services, as competition in South Africa’s banking sector heats up. Under the proposed tie-up, Shoprite, which built its retail empire by partly borrowing from Walmart’s mass market playbook, will use Investec’s banking backbone and regulatory framework to expand financial services to millions of its customers. The unusual pairing offers Investec, traditionally focused on wealthier clients, a way to “broaden our access to retail deposits,” said Investec CEO Fani Titi. The deal is subject to regulatory approval. The strategy takes Shoprite into an increasingly contested battle for South African wallets, where established banks are facing a growing crop of digital challengers. British fintech Revolut is targeting a 2028 launch in what would be its first African market. — Tiisetso Motsoeneng

events.title: Paraguay’s bank collapse brought down a president – and exposed as myth the nation’s status as a ‘Dubai of South America’
events.summary: Protesters on Nov. 5 burn a effigy depicting now ex-President Santiago Pena outside Congress in Asuncion, Paraguay, days after the beginning of a banking crisis to which he was linked. AP Photo/Jorge Saenz It started on Nov. 3, 2026, when millions of Paraguayans trying to access the Ueno banking app found they could no longer get their money . In a matter of days, the financial situation escalated into political crisis, in which the country’s president was ousted, placed under house arrest and charged with several corruption-related crimes. The political and financial crisis exposes a central contradiction in Paraguay’s recent economic development . Ueno, a bank celebrated for expanding financial access to ordinary Paraguayans, grew through unusually close relationships with political elites and public institutions. And while the Ueno crisis came as a shock, there were clear warning signs. As scholars with expertise in various aspects of Paraguay’s contemporary political , economic and environment development , we believe the collapse raises troubling questions about who benefits from financial modernization, who controls it and who bears the risks when it fails. The political relationships through which financial institutions grow, regulators exercise authority and public resources are entrusted to private companies are crucial national concerns, especially in a country that has presented itself internationally as a model of economic stability. A bank that grew faster than scrutiny Founded as a digital lender in 2021, Ueno attracted customers with mobile banking and cash-back offers. Its expansion brought useful services to people underserved by conventional banks, including rural customers. Ueno also expanded the credit card market to low-income customers , an unprecedented move compared to previously restricted banking practices. As Ueno expanded, Paraguay increasingly attracted investors drawn by its low taxes, economic stability and business-friendly policies. Promoted by some as a “ Dubai of South America ,” the country also became a magnet for conservative influencers , particularly from Brazil, who contrasted Paraguay’s economic model with the purported mismanagement of left-wing governments elsewhere in the region. Indeed, under President Santiago Peña, Paraguay has been one of Latin America’s most enthusiastic allies of the Trump administration and its expansive regional vision. But beneath the financial stability, Ueno stood at the precipice of a much deeper problem. Congress President Basilio Núñez places the presidential sash on Pedro Alliana as he takes office as Paraguay’s new president on Nov. 6, 2026. AP Photo/Jorge Saenz The central bank finally acted after accounting adjustments left Ueno’s solvency ratio below half the legal minimum. But problems had surfaced earlier. That included a supervisory report put out by the bank regulators in June 2026 that described roughly US$146 million in loans to three companies linked to Grupo Vázquez, Ueno’s controlling shareholder. Some companies had been transferred to group employees; supervisors questioned the collateral and ultimate use of the funds. That these warning signs went unheeded raises a related question of why regulators didn’t have a better handle on the situation and were not better able to contain the exposure. In any case, Ueno’s problems were exposed in dramatic fashion on Nov. 2, when the central bank placed Ueno into resolution, a process similar to bankruptcy but managed directly by Paraguay’s central bank. The lender, which says it has nearly 3 million customers – about half of the country’s population – halted transactions. The crisis quickly ensnared the governing party. Peña, an economist by training who was elected president in 2023 and had close ties to the bank, resigned on Nov. 5. The Senate then voted unanimously to remove him from office, thereby stripping Peña of his parliamentary immunity. He was swiftly put under house arrest, charged with corruption and succeeded by his Vice President Pedro Alliana, who was sworn in to serve until 2028. Meanwhile, the crisis has led to widespread protests, including outside Congress, with citizens accusing Peña and the ruling Colorado Party of “ stealing” their savings . When the regulator knows the regulated Part of the story of Ueno is a tale of the closeness between political and financial elites in Paraguay. Carlos Carvallo chaired Ueno’s predecessor bank before Peña appointed him Paraguay’s central bank president in 2023. Carvallo resigned on Nov. 3 and has since been charged with the same corruption crimes as Peña. For its part, the Paraguayan central bank says Carvallo recused himself from any Ueno decisions. Yet the potential conflicts of interest ran much deeper. Peña previously directed Banco Basa, linked to Colorado Party leader and former President Horacio Cartes, who retains considerable influence and was instrumental in helping push Peña out of office. Finance Minister Carlos Fernández Valdovinos also served on Basa’s board. Local reporters had documented these revolving-door relationships early in Peña’s term. Peña reportedly held a 1.58% stake in Ueno Holding , which shared its principal shareholder, Grupo Vázquez, with Ueno bank. His brother Francisco held shares in Luxembourg-based U Holdings , an indirect shareholder in the bank. Another shareholder was Juan Carlos López Moreira, Cartes’ former chief of staff. Both brothers exited in 2025. Peña has denied any wrongdoing , while prosecutors are examining allegations concerning his former business interests and his administration’s financial supervision. The inclusion of significant reserves of public funds made these connections especially consequential. Ueno held approximately $850 million in public funds , including $355 million from the country’s social security system , IPS, including health and retirement funds. It amounted to roughly 9% of IPS’s investment portfolio. Under Peña-appointed chairman Jorge Brítez, IPS relaxed eligibility requirements for bank deposits in 2023 and removed a capital-based exposure limit in 2024. Over the same period, its deposits at Ueno rose sharply. Grupo Vázquez’s technology firm ITTI won at least $2.3 million in state contracts after Peña took office, versus $675,000 before. ITTI attributed the increase to business expansion and denied a conflict of interest. Together these ties and regulatory changes raise important questions about regulatory capture and other potential conflicts of interest. What the growth figures leave out Paraguay’s economic gains are real. In August, the International Monetary Fund projected 4.4% growth in 2026 following 6.6% in 2025. Moody’s granted the country’s debt investment-grade status in 2024, and S&P followed in 2025. Hydroelectric power exports, agriculture and new infrastructure continue to underpin the economy. events.title: Africa returns to global debt market but prices stay high
events.summary: African sovereigns are flooding back into global debt markets, accepting some of the world’s highest borrowing costs and adding to the debate about how investors price risk just as the continent’s new credit agency begins operations. External debt owed by low- and middle-income countries climbed 5.5% to a record $9.4 trillion in 2025, the fastest pace since 2021 , according to the World Bank’s International Debt Report. Africa’s poorest borrowers, which are eligible for the World Bank’s cheapest financing, paid 9.8% interest on new bonds in 2025, nearly double the 5.5% paid by middle-income borrowers, whose rates fell. “Access to international finance has improved, but the price of that finance has not,” World Bank Chief Statistician Haishan Fu said. The report comes almost a month after the launch of the Africa Credit Rating Agency, the African Union’s most concrete answer yet to longstanding complaints that global rating agencies unfairly attach risk premiums that eat up an estimated $75 billion in additional annual interest fees . — Tiisetso Motsoeneng

events.title: Voters rejected data centers in dozens of communities, fueling the narrative that opposition to the AI infrastructure contributed to the 2026 blue wave
events.summary: A woman in New Port Richey, Fla., voices her opposition to the construction of AI data centers on July 18, 2026. Thomas Simonetti/AFP via Getty Images Data centers were on the ballot, both directly and indirectly, in the 2026 midterm elections. A total of 41 local ballot initiatives concerning data centers in 10 states were up for a vote. All but one resulted in measures to restrict or limit their development. The centers also may have played a role in several high-profile contests. In Ohio’s race for a U.S. Senate seat , Democratic challenger Sherrod Brown hammered incumbent Jon Husted for his past support of data centers. In Texas, Gina Hinojosa made Republican Gov. Greg Abbott’s track record of supporting tax breaks for data centers a focal point of her winning campaign. Her victory marked a historic break with decades of Republican control in the state. As governor-elect, she immediately reaffirmed her campaign pledge to pursue legislation protecting Texans from data centers. According to NBC exit poll data , 56% of voters felt that data centers were a major or even a crucial factor in influencing their congressional vote. For Black voters, the share was even higher, at 68%. Data centers are key components in artificial intelligence infrastructure , housing the computing resources used to train AI models. These massive facilities guzzle energy and water and are very noisy. Many Americans argue that their costs, in terms of land use , higher utility bills and environmental degradation , outweigh the benefits. I’m a professor of political science who studies political parties, electoral politics and technology. My forthcoming book, “Democratic Intelligence: Navigating Electoral Politics in an AI World,” examines how the adoption of this technology is reshaping established practices and power dynamics in campaigns. Before the midterms, it had already appeared to be disrupting some partisan alignments. Following those historic elections, which have thoroughly shaken up America’s political geography, the widespread pushback against data centers is now part of the narrative explaining the dramatic results of the 2026 midterms. Data centers, like these near Social Circle, Ga., require enormous amounts of electricity. AP Photo/Mike Stewart Disrupting political polarization In contrast to many other issues , concern about data centers is relatively bipartisan. The Annenberg Public Policy Center asked Americans in mid-2026 whether they support or oppose having data centers in their communities. Opposition was stronger among Democrats, at 69%, than Republicans, at 54%, but it crossed party lines. Local ballot measures restricting data centers also cut across traditional political alignments. Communities as disparate as deeply red Edgewater, Florida, and solidly blue Alhambra, California, voted to prohibit them. The margins for the restrictions were large, averaging 49 percentage points. The one restrictive local measure that failed to pass was in Harwood, North Dakota , population around 800. With a data center project already in progress, political and economic leaders prevailed in arguing that restrictions would cut into local revenue and stifle economic development more generally. Allies and adversaries Exit polls taken during the midterm elections also detected a degree of bipartisanship. Of the 56% of voters who said data centers played a “major” or “crucial” role in their vote , approximately two-thirds were Democrats and one-third Republicans. Exit polls, however, should be interpreted with care , given their methodological limitations. These responses hint at why the narrative that opposition to data centers helped fuel the Democrats’ historic midterm victory emerged right away. The seeds of this argument were in place before the election, picking up on unusual alliances that marked the data center opposition. In cities and counties, zoning fights are drawing a diverse kind of resistance : environmentalists, voters reeling under high electricity costs, local-control advocates and farmers concerned that data centers eat up land. They unite in opposition to projects backed by powerful corporate interests. William Lawrence, a Democrat who flipped a red House seat in Michigan in the 2026 midterm elections, speaks on the campaign trail. AP Photo/Paul Sancya Some of the bipartisanship around this issue has even seeped into Congress. Several weeks before Election Day, the House passed the Ratepayer Protection Act by a 417-3 vote. The bill would require states to consider adopting a policy that data centers pay for the upgrades necessary to meet their high electricity needs. The three nay House votes were from progressives who felt the bill’s measures, which would be voluntary, didn’t go far enough to protect consumers. Similar concerns killed the Senate version , a reminder that even allies sometimes follow different strategic paths. Some proponents of tighter regulation will accept incremental progress, while others push for more sweeping change. Brookings Institution scholars anticipate that the newly elected Congress will take up the issue again, this time with a directive to states to establish mandatory, not voluntary, requirements. Politics as usual As the midterm elections approached, candidates up and down the ballot blanketed the airwaves and digital platforms with ads against data centers . President Donald Trump pushed back, suggesting that data center opponents want their communities to be “backwards and poor.” Some Republican candidates walked a fine line between responding to voters’ concerns and not alienating the president. It matters little whether the data center electoral narrative is accurate, and so far, the reported evidence is limited. We need to know where losing candidates stood on data centers, not just the winners. That voters considered data centers important says nothing about which direction they leaned. And despite a 98% success rate across the 41 local ballot measures, it’s hard to gauge how much resistance there is to the more than 600 proposed data centers that are slated to be built. What does matter is that many people apparently are accepting the narrative because that alone will affect politics and the economy. Consider Elon Musk’s post on Nov. 4 on X, his social media platform : “Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now,” and the sell-off of data center-related stocks the next day. As the 2028 presidential primaries come into focus, I believe we should expect to see many Democratic and Republican hopefuls emphasizing their support for data center restrictions and bans as they throw their hats into the ring. Some parts of this article appeared in a previous article published on Oct. 26, 2026 Barbara A. Trish does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organization that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

events.title: South African voters punish ANC with worst-ever result
events.summary: The African National Congress suffered its worst-ever result in local elections, potentially shifting the balance of power in South Africa’s coalition government. The ANC, which led the country out of apartheid, won 31% of the vote nationwide, just over six percentage points ahead of the Democratic Alliance, a historically white-led movement. The performance extends the decline that cost the ANC its national parliamentary majority in 2024 and sets up a battle over the direction of economic policy as the once-dominant party prepares to choose a new leader next year. It also means the biggest cities, key drivers of growth in Africa’s largest economy, will mostly be governed by coalitions. The DA emerged as the largest party in three metropolitan municipalities in Gauteng, the economic heartland, including in the commercial hub of Johannesburg. That outcome is likely to boost its bargaining power nationally and in talks to form municipal governments where no party won a majority. But some warned the new political reality has drawbacks: “ Unstable coalitions with precarious leadership teams cannot deliver,” said Busi Mavuso, CEO of lobby group Business Leadership South Africa. — Tiisetso Motsoeneng

events.title: The unwinding of the AI trade will have bigger consequences than we think
events.summary: Liz’s view This feels like the beginning of the end of the AI trade. It’s going to have wider consequences than we think. The geyser of money is starting to sputter, affecting high-flying stocks and zapping debt deals. OpenAI set out to raise $30 billion, money it could have put together in its sleep a few months ago, and appears likely to fall far short . Lenders are treating SpaceX , an investment-grade giant, like a flier bet on a junk-rated startup. Those companies will likely find the money somewhere. But the can’t-lose trade powered by a combination of FOMO and the greater-fool theory of investing is evaporating, replaced by a tinder pile ready to ignite. The spark could come from almost anywhere. A data-center delay sets off a hyperscaler guarantee fight, a swarm of rogue agents hacking into a major city’s electric grid, Nvidia’s CEO admitting he slept with a Chinese spy , pick your poison. The market is sobering up and going back to doing its job of separating winners from losers. Some of those losers are likely to be household names with 12-figure valuations. And because the AI boom pulled in companies far outside Silicon Valley, the unwind will, too. Glassmaker Corning’s stock doubled in the first six months of the year after a $6 billion deal to outfit Meta’s data centers; it has now given up almost all of those gains. Modine, a maker of car radiators, is now trading lower than before it announced the spinoff of that business in January to become “a pure-play climate solutions company focused on the high-growth data center” market. Paint supplier Sherwin-Williams and HVAC-maker Carrier are in the middle of their own pivots to AI. The boom reached far beyond Silicon Valley. So will the hangover. Notable A Bloomberg analysis of corporate and regulatory filings and credit deals showed that markets’ dependency on tech — which, these days, is mostly AI — has grown to record levels. Technology also now makes up more than 50% of the S&P 500’s market cap.

The host has already called on countries to commit to ensuring that AI is designed, powered, and deployed in ways that support climate action. But so far, industries around the world aren’t doing nearly enough to harness the technology to actually drive down the greenhouse-gas emissions heating up the planet. AI companies like to make very optimistic claims about AI’s potential to help address climate change. The reality is far less promising. Read the full story . Meet the ecologist revealing the invisible networks that revive rainforests Tropical forests are our planet’s biggest terrestrial carbon sink, accounting for around 40% of carbon stored on land. events.title: AI chip financing hits a wall
events.summary: The AI bet is rapidly turning sideways. After rushing to lend gobs of money for the data-center buildout, now some investors can’t dump it fast enough. We’re hearing about whole portfolios of loans that are being shopped at steep discounts, with GPU financings in particular “getting smoked” over worries the life of those loans will outlive the useful life of the technology, one person told Semafor. On Friday, Bloomberg reported that Dutch bank ING was looking to dump $500 million of data-center loans, including a $25 million chunk backing Stargate, the OpenAI, SoftBank, and Oracle project. The next test for Wall Street will be whether Goldman Sachs and Apollo can convince enough investors to buy into a $40 billion chip financing deal for SpaceX, the largest of its kind, which the firms have started marketing. Some big players have already put a stake in the ground against financing as a whole: “Without casting aspersions on GPU financing,” Ares Management CEO Michael Arougheti said on a recent earnings call, the firm was going to pass on such deals. “I, for one, personally do not know how to underwrite the decline and depreciation curves on that type of technology,” he said. — Ellen DiMauro

events.title: Innovating with AI in the special chemicals industry
events.summary: Connected data, AI, and advanced modeling are helping scientists accelerate research and develop more sustainable materials. MIT Technology Review Insights archive page As companies look to accelerate innovation with artificial intelligence, cloud computing, and advanced modeling, the primary challenge is connecting new technologies to reliable data, scientific expertise, and the practical realities of bringing products to market. For specialty chemicals manufacturer Lubrizol, digital transformation is all about giving researchers the tools to test ideas faster, make better-informed decisions, and develop more sustainable materials without compromising performance. Girish Rao, vice president of information technology at Lubrizol, says the company is building a digital foundation that connects business processes, modern data platforms, and cloud infrastructure to support its research and development (R&D) teams. Their goal is to combine decades of accumulated technical data with the deep expertise of chemists and engineers who understand customer needs as well as the physical constraints of their work. Data scientists can help identify patterns, test new hypotheses, and model possibilities before researchers conduct physical experiments. But, Rao emphasizes, “it's not about replacing scientific judgment; it is about giving our scientists better tools.” Scientists, data scientists, and IT teams approach problems from different perspectives, prioritizing experimental validity, model performance, and platform security and scalability, respectively. By bringing these groups together in “fusion teams,” Lubrizol aligns them around shared objectives, starting with small pilots to build trust. "Once the trust is built between the team members and they know what value they're about to create," Rao says, "things go a lot better." Cloud infrastructure also gives the company flexibility to access computing resources and modern tools without making the substantial investments required to build and maintain its own data centers. These capabilities could prove especially valuable in advancing sustainability. Digital modeling can help researchers evaluate more formulations, explore materials such as starch and corn-based alternatives, and assess trade-offs across a product's life cycle. Promising a material in a laboratory is only the first step. Scaling production while meeting performance expectations, regulatory requirements, and financial constraints is still a tightrope walk, but AI's ability to model multiple variables could help teams navigate those competing demands. Looking to the future, Rao expects AI, automation, advanced modeling, digital twins, and connected data to converge as laboratories become more intelligent and manufacturing plants more efficient. The opportunity, he suggests, lies in bringing these capabilities together responsibly and at scale. “It's not just a single technology. I think it's the combination of all of these, and it'll be the ability to connect all these processes that are going to generate tremendous amounts of data." events.title: QatarEnergy agrees to buy 25% stake in Namibia's offshore oil block in expansion push
events.summary: QatarEnergy has entered into an agreement to buy a stake in an offshore oil block held by Chevron in Namibia, as part of the state-owned company’s expansion plans in the southern African nation. As part of the agreement, QatarEnergy is acquiring a 25 per cent interest in Petroleum Exploration License 0082 (PEL82), comprising blocks 2112B and 2212A, QatarEnergy said in a statement on Monday. Once the deal is complete, Chevron will hold a 55 per cent stake in the block, while Namibia’s Namcor and Custos Energy will each have a 10 per cent interest. The deal is subject to customary regulatory approvals. The PEL82 exploration licence covers an area of about 11,450 square kilometres off Namibia, at depths ranging from 350 to 2,300 metres. “We are pleased to further strengthen our relations with Chevron through this agreement, and to expand and diversify our footprint in Namibia,” said Saad Al Kaabi, Qatar’s Minister of State for Energy Affairs and chief executive of QatarEnergy. Namibia is emerging as one of Africa's oil and gas hotspots, with new discoveries made in the country’s offshore Orange Basin. The finds are estimated to hold about 11 billion barrels of light oil and 2.2 trillion cubic feet of natural gas reserves. If proven commercially viable, the discoveries could unlock an unprecedented revenue windfall for the Namibian government, potentially more than doubling the country’s gross domestic product by 2040, according to the US-based International Trade Administration. QatarEnergy is also working with other global oil majors, including Shell and France’s TotalEnergies, on exploration blocks in Namibia while expanding in the US and other countries. Last month, QatarEnergy signed a 20-year agreement to buy up to three million tonnes a year of liquefied natural gas from Woodside Energy’s Louisiana LNG project. The deal is expected to deepen Doha’s push into US supply, which it is using to hedge against disruption in the Strait of Hormuz . In April, QatarEnergy made a hydrocarbon discovery off the coast of the Republic of the Congo, adding to the Gulf producer’s international upstream portfolio.

events.title: What does the Blue Tsunami mean for inflation?
events.summary: The News The Democrats’ historic sweep in US elections has been setting markets askew, as investors guess at what it could mean for economic policy or the billions of dollars being poured into AI infrastructure. One thing seems clear: All signs point to disinflation, according to Thierry Wizman, global rates and FX strategist at Macquarie Group. For much of the last half of the year, the cost of capital has only been going up — yields on sovereign debt and corporate bonds alike have been rising, as hyperscalers loaded up on debt and the data center buildout faced pushback on the ground. The Fed raised rates. And the cost to buy insurance against hyperscalers defaulting on their debts has spiked . But if President Donald Trump retreats from the Iran war and oil prices fall, or tariffs are rolled back, Wizman said, yields will come down. “Ultimately the view on yields has to be linked to the view on inflation. So, most of what’s happened overnight as a result of the election feels disinflationary.” Q&A Ellen DiMauro: European sovereigns have been under pressure. At what point do those yields get interesting? Thierry Wizman: Well, they are interesting. Because they’ve been very volatile. If you’re thinking of jumping into France, I’d be somewhat cautious. It really depends on how the events are going to transpire over the next few months. But if you’re not the gambling sort, you would want to wait until there’s clarity on the election in France next year. And if there’s any clarity on any trajectory towards debt sustainability, the budget that’s going to have to be passed by the end of the year is a part of that, but it’s not going to be the thing that determines ultimately what France’s long-term debt trajectory is. That’ll be determined after the election. If there’s an austerity program that’s put in place, it’s not a question of what the yields are, it’s a question of, ‘what do I need to see happen?’ The yields are already very high and they’re already attractive. Are the hyperscalers crowding out Treasuries and competing with governments for cash? They’re definitely competing with governments for cash. It’s one reason why the US Treasury is considering reducing the issuance of 20- and 30-year bonds. It doesn’t want to crowd out the issuance of the bonds that are used to finance the expansion of the AI infrastructure economy. It’s one reason why bond yields have been higher all year. It’s evident in the data on how much issuance there’s been by corporations and it’s slated to continue potentially for another two years based on the CapEx intentions that the hyperscalers have divulged to investors already. So, there’s no doubt there. The answer is yes. Where are we seeing investors get scared? It’s not just that the hyperscalers may have over-invested, it’s also that the turn in the political atmosphere in the US is going to turn against the hyperscalers. Politically, not just economics. State and local legislatures [are turning] against data-center construction. Are prediction markets a better way to play at rates and foreign exchange markets? Are they a way to hedge? Not if you’re an institutional investor. Because there’s just not that much liquidity in these prediction markets. There are people who are trying to bring liquidity to the prediction markets by entering them and making markets. But the amount of capital that’s being devoted to them is not great enough yet for institutional-size bets. It’s difficult to look at the price of a prediction market and be assured that if you try to come into that market and buy or sell contracts that you won’t move the price. So, it’s not an easy way to hedge. It looked like the US Treasuries rallied on news of the Blue Tsunami. What’s your take on that? Well, there is the possibility that there’ll be less inflation in the US. So there’s three ways that could happen. One way is if the data-center construction slows down. That would depress the economy somewhat because the economy’s been very dependent on data-center construction. Bond yields could come down simply because the market thinks the economy will slow down a bit under a Democratic victory. Some of the tariffs might be rolled back and that would be disinflationary, something that helps bring down yields. And the final thing is the fact that oil prices are down on the premise that he’s not going to tempt the fates with an attack on Iran. It’s globally disinflationary. The unemployment rate has ticked up very slightly. How do you see that factoring into moves by the Fed and potential rate hikes? We’re still at a very low unemployment rate. The Fed is not really concerned about the labor market based on what they’ve said themselves. They’re much more concerned about inflation and inflation expectations right now. What else are you looking out for post-midterms? The Democratic agenda is going to be largely about reducing the cost of living. I don’t think they will succeed, but there may be people in the market who think that they will. So if there’s enough people who believe that and it’s in conjunction with maybe Trump reducing some tariffs here and there, the narrative around disinflation can continue.

events.title: Why Nvidia CEO's affair with alleged Chinese spy matters for AI race
events.summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has apologized for an affair with a woman the US believes was spying for China. The story could have profound implications for the world's most valuable company and the global AI race. Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang's admission to an affair with a woman whom US intelligence officials believe was working as a spy for China could have profound implications for the $5 trillion (€4.47 trillion) company. The Financial Times first reported on Huang's affair with Alice H., an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based customer of Nvidia, which has been suspected of trying to circumvent export controls to get advanced Nvidia chips into China. The newspaper reported that the US government and its intelligence community believe she was recruited as a spy by China's Ministry of State Security intelligence agency. Nvidia investigates CEO after reports of affair with Chinese spy US government officials drafted a memo about the allegations shortly before US President Donald Trump traveled to Beijing for a summit with Xi Jinping in May. What have Nvidia, US government said? Huang's relationship with the alleged Chinese spy has exposed him and the company to criticism that it may have allowed China to obtain valuable trade secrets as Beijing tries to gain an edge in the race to develop advanced AI models. Nvidia is initiating an investigation led by independent board members and an external law firm. It said in a statement that Huang "has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort." "The board prioritizes US national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of Nvidia and its shareholders," the company said Sunday. "While the board has no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, the board's inquiry will examine all available information." The company's shares fell in early trading on Monday. While US intelligence officials have not commented publicly on the claims, Trump — with whom Jensen Huang has a close relationship — has backed the Nvidia boss. "He's an honorable guy," said Trump. "I have not spoken to him ​about it. I just know he's a ​fine person, but you never know what is going on. I hope everything's fine." Tim Culpan, an Asia tech reporter who has covered Nvidia and Huang closely for years, told DW that while Nvidia's fundamental strengths as a company remain in place, Huang is hugely personally damaged by the story. "They're still going to make great chips and they're going to sell them to millions of customers around the world who want the best AI chips in the world," he said. "His opinion is going to carry a lot less weight now. And that, in the long term, will flow through to Nvidia and Nvidia's own corporate interests. So it won't be immediate. It's really a fact that he doesn't have the sway or the power that he might have had one week ago simply through this." Richard Windsor, a tech analyst and the founder of research company Radio Free Mobile, said the news could be very serious for Nvidia given how much the company has revolved around Huang for decades. "This problem is particularly acute because Jensen Huang is very hands-on, meaning that the key decisions that led to its success were ultimately taken by him and because there is no obvious successor," he said. "I suspect we are about to find out just how much the market thinks that the company is dependent on its iconic founder and CEO." Nvidia and Huang's attitude toward China and potential Chinese customers has been a bone of contention with US intelligence officials — despite Huang's close relationship with Trump. Huang has repeatedly lobbied Trump to ease restrictions on the sale of Nvidia chips to China . A 2025 export control deal heavily curbed sales, but Trump subsequently permitted the export of older H200 Nvidia chips to China in return for the US government receiving a cut of the sales. However, that deal has been complicated and bogged down by Washington's strict export-license review. China has also initiated import controls, despite strong demand from Chinese companies. China lacks access to the most advanced AI-capable chips. Beijing wants to develop its own alternatives but has struggled to catch up. Huang has argued that Chinese dependence on Nvidia's chips would prevent rivals such as Huawei from catching up and boosting China's ambitions to dominate AI supply chains. However, that argument has been dismissed by many US intelligence officials. They fear that unlimited Chinese access to the most advanced Nvidia chips would boost China's domestic AI sector, lead to its AI models catching up with the leading US models and see the chips being used in Chinese military applications. The US-China rivalry has become a central theme in the global AI story , with both countries seeking to gain an upper hand in the technology.

events.title: Firm Linked to Trump’s Sons Got Nearly $40 Million in Federal Contracts to Screen for Ebola and Other Diseases
events.summary: Donald Trump Jr., left, and Eric Trump, right, watch as their father, Donald Trump, center, speaks to members of the media in 2024. Justin Lane/EPA/Bloomberg via Getty Images The Trump administration awarded a small biosecurity company nearly $40 million to screen for Ebola and other infectious diseases just months after a firm linked to President Donald Trump’s elder sons invested in its parent company, according to records and interviews. The contracts, one to screen for Ebola in several U.S. airports and the other to respond to disease outbreaks in the Democratic Republic of Congo, are seven times the total value of government contracts the company had directly received before.  The company, XpresTest, has years of experience monitoring for COVID-19 and other diseases for the government at U.S. airports. That makes its parent, XWELL, an unusual hybrid, selling both spa treatments and biosecurity services. Last year, it made most of its money from waxing salons and airport spas that offer manicures, massages and “ chakra beds. ”  The contracts are the latest example of the president’s family benefiting financially from his administration’s actions. And the stakes for these deals are particularly high. In the Democratic Republic of Congo, an Ebola outbreak has killed more than 5,000 people this year, and the federal government is trying to stop the pathogen from coming to the U.S. XpresTest has never worked with Ebola or provided biosecurity services abroad, let alone in the kind of volatile locales it’s now expected to work in. The CEO of its parent company, Ezra Ernst, said XpresTest won both contracts in a competitive bidding process and pointed to its years of experience doing screening for COVID-19 and other pathogens at American airports. But even he acknowledged that working internationally is “a new thing for us” and expressed uncertainty about being able to complete the work in the Democratic Republic of Congo. “This is a risky contract. I’m not sure we can do it,” Ernst said in an interview.  Jeremy Konyndyk, who helped oversee the U.S. government’s response to a 2014 Ebola outbreak in West Africa, said there are some parallels between monitoring for COVID-19 and Ebola at airports, but he said it’s concerning that the government would award such a lucrative contract to a company that has no experience in Africa.  “There are countless organizations in the world that have decades of experience doing this work,” Konyndyk said. “I have to wonder why the hell they’re not going with someone who has actually done this before.” Under previous administrations, the U.S. government addressed international disease outbreaks in partnership with the World Health Organization. But Trump withdrew from the group last year, dismantled the U.S. Agency for International Development , which handled much of this work, and dramatically scaled back the global presence of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.  At the same time, the State Department launched the America First Global Health Strategy , which calls for the U.S. to use aid to foreign countries to “promote American companies and American innovations abroad.” This March, the State Department announced it would be giving up to $4.5 billion in funding for various purposes, including responding to infectious disease outbreaks.  Under that program, XPresTest was awarded $20 million. Other funding went to better-known global aid nonprofits, including International Medical Corps, Save the Children and the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies, whose awards ranged from $25 million to $35 million. The CDC also awarded XPresTest a contract, for $18.8 million. In response to questions from ProPublica about XPresTest and its parent company, XWELL, the State Department noted the firm’s previous work screening for diseases at airports under a contract with the CDC and said its own award was made “through a competitive process that builds on this successful model.” The CDC did not respond to a request for comment. A spokesperson for the president’s sons Donald Jr. and Eric Trump said that they are “merely passive, minority investors in a fund that invested in this company,” and that they had no “involvement in or knowledge regarding the negotiation or procurement of any of its contracts, including any government contracts.”  “Both are private citizens who hold no government positions, broken no laws and who have every right to pursue lawful business and investment opportunities,” the spokesperson said. The Trump sons’ connection to XWELL was established in February, when a fund called American Ventures invested in the company. The fund was launched by Dominari Holdings, a small financial firm with offices inside Trump Tower in New York. The leaders of Dominari hired the Trump sons as advisers after their father was elected to a second term and granted them a stake of more than 10% in Dominari. Anthony Hayes, the CEO of Dominari Holdings, told ProPublica, “We have never seen or even heard of Don or Eric using their family name to influence the granting of a government contract.” American Ventures has taken stakes in other companies that have benefited from Trump administration actions. The Florida-based drone company Powerus got a contract worth up to $90 million from the U.S. Air Force five months after the Trumps’ involvement was announced. Through American Ventures, Donald Jr. and Eric Trump also are acquiring a stake in a critical minerals group that has received U.S. government support to mine for tungsten in Kazakhstan. The Trumps have described themselves as passive investors who do not advocate for the companies they have stakes in before their father’s government.   XWELL was founded in 2006 as a line of airport-based spas that provided massages and facials. During the pandemic, the company, then known as XpresSpa Group, got $5.5 million from the CDC to offer travelers COVID-19 testing. It also collected waste from airplane toilets to check for new viral strains. It has done similar work for at least one other company that has received government contracts.  In January, XWELL announced that it was hiring a former senior adviser at the CDC who created and led the agency’s traveler surveillance program. The firm said the move was part of a plan to expand “its traveler-based pathogen surveillance capabilities to support international travel hubs and large-scale mass gathering events worldwide.” The following month, American Ventures invested about $30 million in XWELL. The company had lost money the previous year. “We were so cash-strapped, close to bankrupt,” its CEO said.  Its valuation before the cash infusion was just $3 million. events.title: Democrats face a tough sell with MAHA voters
events.summary: The potential for partnership between newly ascendant Democrats and the "Make America Healthy Again" movement is already threatened by their deep disagreements over Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. Why it matters: Democrats want to convince health-conscious voters that they're the party that can deliver on food and pesticide use, but many view an alliance with Kennedy as a nonstarter. They're already threatening to investigate Kennedy, and they're clashing bitterly with him over vaccines and other issues — so any common ground with MAHA over nutrition and pesticides could take a back seat to those fights. State of play: Most MAHA-backed candidates lost at the polls last week. Some of the movement's leaders blame low turnout for the GOP's terrible election night, saying MAHA faithful stayed home because they were disappointed with the Trump administration and a lack of progress on food and environmental issues. Whatever they may think of the White House and federal health officials, the base remains intensely loyal to Kennedy, who created the movement during his 2024 presidential bid. "The voters sent a clear message to this administration and to all political parties, that we are not motivated to vote for people who have a lack of integrity. Promises were made, and promises were broken," said Zen Honeycutt, founder of Moms Across America. While she's open to working with Democrats going forward, "We want them to work with Kennedy, not against him," she added. "That's the red line for almost all of us. You cross that line and you go after Kennedy, you are never getting our vote," she said. "I'm not interested in working with people who are trying to get rid of our champion." The big picture: Some Democrats were making overtures to MAHA voters on key issues ahead of the midterms. Lawmakers like Sen. Cory Booker (D-N.J.) have already said they're willing to work with Kennedy on issues like cleaning up the food supply, school lunches and banning the use of certain pesticides. Now, the movement's leaders are responding to those overtures. Driving the news: "There are good people across the political spectrum who want to be part of this, and we're going to find every last one of them and fight with them," MAHA Action president Tony Lyons said last week on the organization's weekly call. Lyons also rejected suggestions that the movement is dead, saying "we've won the hearts and minds of the American people." Yes, but: Democrats have drawn the line on vaccine issues, refusing to adopt Kennedy's medical freedom agenda or greater scrutiny of vaccine safety. Few seem willing to accommodate Kennedy, who's likely to be a top target for oversight and investigations once Democrats take power. And Kennedy remains committed to relitigating vaccine safety claims that mainstream scientists say have been thoroughly debunked. That's likely to kill any bridge-building before it starts. After Maryland Democratic Sen. Angela Alsobrooks called for Kennedy to resign or be fired, MAHA influencer Kelly Ryerson — known as "Glyphosate Girl" — said she didn't understand the strategy and warned it "will lose many future voters." "Food Babe" Vani Hari wrote to Democrats in response to the same post: "This is not how you win a coalition or work together. This is how you waste time while our children continue to get sicker than any developed nation." Honeycutt warned: "To get rid of him because you don't like the fact that he's trying to make vaccines safer is absolutely insane." The intrigue: Though MAHA hasn't secured major political wins or a raft of new laws, big portions of its platform remain popular with the electorate, with support cutting across party lines and including many independents. For the new Democratic majority, progress on certain MAHA-backed issues may be more important than the actual endorsement of MAHA leadership.
