events.title: Elon Musk's empire braces for Democratic crackdown
events.summary: Elon Musk's sprawling empire — from rockets to robots, electric cars to AI — is facing a political onslaught with few parallels in modern corporate history. Why it matters: The world's richest man confronts a constellation of risks spanning the halls of Congress, his Texas industrial empire, Wall Street and his vision for AI supremacy. 💰 Political: To Democrats, Musk embodies corrosive forces of the MAGA era — extreme wealth, billionaire influence over government, the gutting of federal institutions, the poisoning of social media and the unchecked power of AI. Musk spent at least $475 million on the midterms, becoming the election's largest individual donor — only to see more than 99% of his traceable spending go to losing candidates, according to WIRED . Musk's most humiliating defeat came in Texas, where a $160 million bet on Ken Paxton ended in a Democratic sweep of the Senate seat, governorship and attorney general's office. In a hint of a possible détente, Sen.-elect James Talarico praised the billionaire as a "great business leader and entrepreneur," and offered to work with him on technology and innovation. Musk, who said last month that Talarico "hates Texas," responded : "Nice of him to say that." ⚖️ Congressional: Armed with subpoena power, Democrats are preparing to investigate Musk's DOGE operation, its access to sensitive government data and whether his companies benefited from his extraordinary influence over the Trump administration. Musk is already downplaying his dependence on Washington, claiming government contracts will account for less than 5% of SpaceX revenue a year from now. "Happy to cancel any that the government doesn't want," he posted Friday . The scrutiny also extends to national security: Lawmakers are demanding answers about Musk's reported communications with Vladimir Putin and his role in the October slowdown of Starshield that disrupted Ukraine's drone operations. Elon Musk responds to reporting about his vulnerabilities in Texas. Screenshot via X 🏭 Regulatory: Musk moved his home and the headquarters of Tesla, SpaceX and X to Texas, betting on a safe haven for his expanding empire. Now, the Democratic takeover threatens to turn his political sanctuary into a regulatory minefield. Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa is suing to uncover 1,374 pages of largely redacted communications with Greg Abbott, while incoming Attorney General Nathan Johnson has pledged to scrutinize state broadband grants awarded to Starlink. Tesla's robotaxi ambitions also face new obstacles as Democrats threaten to derail federal legislation that eases state safety restrictions. Hinojosa herself urged Tesla last year to delay its Austin launch until stronger regulations took effect. 📉 Financial: Tesla and SpaceX shed roughly $460 billion in combined market value in the two days after the election, then rebounded Friday as investors raced to reassess the risks to Musk's business empire. Wall Street is especially concerned that Democratic scrutiny could complicate a potential Tesla-SpaceX merger , while new restrictions on AI data centers threaten a cornerstone of Musk's growth strategy. In a fitting coda to a brutal week, Musk announced Friday that Tesla will wind down Cybertruck production by mid-2027, pulling the plug on a pet project plagued by weak sales, recalls and quality problems. 🤖 Technological: The midterms have given the backlash against AI new political muscle, threatening both the massive data centers powering Musk's ambitions and the technology behind Grok itself. Democrats are preparing legislation that would require independent safety testing of advanced AI models and hold developers liable for harmful outputs. Lawmakers have already demanded SpaceX's AI safety records. Voters sided against data-center development in 44 of 45 local referendums , while incoming Democratic governors in Georgia and Ohio pledged tougher restrictions. Musk joked on X: "Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now." The bottom line: Democrats must find a way to separate Musk the political combatant from Musk the industrialist, whose companies are central to America's technological and military power.

events.title: Planet-sized problems collide in permitting debate
events.summary: Efforts to fight climate change, conserve nature and build clean energy have long unfolded on competing tracks. Now, they're colliding — and exposing tough trade-offs for environmentalists. Why it matters: Congress' sweeping permitting debate is forcing those competing priorities into the same conversation, with major consequences for climate action and conservation. Driving the news: The Senate is set to hold an initial procedural vote Monday on a sprawling bipartisan bill that would make it easier to build power lines and energy projects of all kinds, including clean energy and fossil fuels. At the heart of the debate is how much public scrutiny projects should face before they're approved — and how much protection those approvals should receive afterward. Supporters say the current system takes too long, delaying clean energy and other infrastructure. Opponents warn that speeding things up could come at the expense of wildlife, public lands and tribal rights. Between the lines: The dilemma reflects a fundamental tension within the environmental movement: Building the infrastructure needed to combat climate change can threaten nature, while protecting nature can complicate efforts to build that infrastructure. Wind and solar farms, for example, can require large expanses of land, potentially disrupting wildlife habitats even as they help reduce greenhouse gas emissions. "The part of my organization that cares about climate sees great opportunity and the part that cares about nature sees some dangers," said a leader of one organization that focuses on both causes, speaking anonymously to discuss the proposal candidly. The big picture: Both parties broadly agree Washington needs to overhaul federal permitting, a perennial goal that has eluded Congress for years. The question is what reforms can attract enough support to pass both chambers. The bill's bipartisan sponsors and the White House want action before year's end. But some Democrats, emboldened by their midterm victories, argue they should wait until next year, when they'll have more power and time to scrutinize the legislation. Even if the Senate passes the bill, the House would still need to approve it before it could reach President Trump's desk. Zoom out: The legislation is confined to the United States, but the tensions it exposes are global — and are playing out at two major international gatherings. Representatives from more than 190 countries are gathering in Antalya, Turkey, for annual United Nations climate talks beginning Monday. The host country is pushing to increase electricity's share of global final energy consumption from just over 20% today to 35% by 2035, which would require much of the same buildout under discussion in Washington. A separate, lower-profile UN gathering focused on protecting biodiversity concluded in Armenia late last month. Countries acknowledged they're falling short of their goal to halt and reverse nature loss by 2030, while agreeing on steps to accelerate progress. What they're saying: The fact that these two discussions take place separately is part of the problem, said Ani Dasgupta, head of the World Resources Institute. Within the U.S., the permitting debate is forcing these conversations to converge. "We want everyone to be more overt about this tension, rather than covert about it," said Dasgupta, a former World Bank official. "I don't think it helps to say we can't build anything today, and also that we need to take everyone's rights away to build stuff." Friction point: Three provisions of the Senate bill show what's at stake for conservationists. Public lands: Former Biden climate adviser John Podesta warned that an earlier version of the bill could make federal permits harder for agencies to reverse, potentially allowing the Trump administration to approve development on sensitive public lands that future administrations would struggle to undo. Federal reviews: The legislation would shorten and limit aspects of federal environmental reviews, including public input and opportunities to challenge project approvals in court. Conservationists and tribal organizations warn the changes could weaken protections for wildlife, public lands and culturally significant sites. Wildlife: The bill would allow states to take over certain federal responsibilities for assessing how projects affect endangered species. Environmental advocates warn the changes could weaken protections for vulnerable wildlife. Catch up quick: An updated version released Saturday revises rules on permit reversals and adds safeguards for wildlife and tribal consultation. But the changes haven't satisfied all conservationists. The Wilderness Society reaffirmed its opposition on Saturday, warning the bill still threatens public lands and weakens environmental protections. Zoom in: Carter Roberts, head of the World Wildlife Fund, which has not taken a public position on the bill, says environmentalists should seek solutions that address both climate change and nature loss. "The best solutions to climate change also conserve nature and prevent it from disappearing," Roberts said. The other side: Sponsors of the legislation and other proponents emphasize that no bill is perfect and trade-offs are inevitable. "There's no question that making the system more efficient diminishes certain aspects of access to project approval. That is the point of the legislation," said Jason Grumet, head of the American Clean Power Association. But he added: "We think the balance has been struck in a way that sustains meaningful access." What we're watching: Whether lawmakers can reconcile these competing priorities and pass the bill before the new Congress takes office remains uncertain. The bottom line: "The permitting bill debate is not a unique debate," said Dasgupta, who is in Turkey for the climate talks. "Everywhere in the world, we need to build stuff."

events.title: AI's "too big to fail" CEO is facing a crisis with no backup
events.summary: There is no Nvidia — nor an AI boom as we know it — without Jensen Huang. He has reassured jittery markets with his words, bankrolled a trillion-dollar buildout and put economies on his shoulders. Now, the world is wondering if he can save himself . Why it matters: Global markets must confront a terrifying reality: The AI ecosystem's first "too big to fail" executive is suddenly vulnerable, and there is no backup plan if he is forced to step down. Catch up quick: Huang apologized Sunday and Nvidia's board launched an independent probe after he admitted to having a relationship with a woman named Alice Huang, an alleged Chinese operative. Nvidia's board expressed confidence in his leadership and said it had no reason to believe national security or company secrets were compromised. President Trump stood by Huang, calling him "an honorable guy." The big picture: Keeping his job is one thing. Maintaining the ability to steady markets, finance customers and shape government policy is another. These are the five questions that now loom over the AI boom : 1. What happens to Nvidia? Forged 33 years ago (initially using a Denny's as an impromptu office), Nvidia is a uniquely founder-driven company, making any potential leadership transition incredibly perilous. Investors have little precedent for valuing the company without him. "It's very hard to envision Nvidia run by anybody else," said Dan Gallagher, an analyst with Washington Post Intelligence and long a keen observer of the chip titan. Huang has more than 60 direct reports, eschews traditional corporate layers and hasn't been publicly grooming a successor. "I don't know if anyone's going to know how to value Nvidia" without him, Gallagher told Axios. 2. What happens to the market? Huang has repeatedly rescued the AI trade from bearish sentiment. On multiple occasions, he has offered backstops to shore up growth plans for companies across the AI landscape, from CoreWeave to OpenAI. In July, he argued that cheaper open models would boost demand for Nvidia's chips, pushing back against a market scare. Last month, he toured Europe pitching national AI projects as debt investors signaled their appetite for some AI financing was limited. 3. What happens to the companies that depend on him? The risks vary across an industry that relies on Nvidia for chips, capital and credibility. The AI giants: Anthropic and OpenAI have options. Anthropic plans to barrel ahead with an IPO this month and already uses chips from Google and Amazon. OpenAI is developing its own chips in-house and with Broadcom. Diversification is underway, but replacing Nvidia is not in the cards near term. The "neoclouds": Companies such as CoreWeave that rent out computing power have less room to maneuver. CoreWeave suffered a prolonged stock-and-bond selloff last month as investors began to question how it would finance continued growth. Nvidia has provided crucial backstops to many neocloud companies. The "neolabs" and AI startups: Nvidia has supplied investment and offered access to computing for AI startups such as Thinking Machines Lab, as well as dozens of other startups providing a variety of services in the AI race. 4. Where does the investigation lead? Southeast Asia's data center boom puts the limits of U.S. chip restrictions in focus. The loophole: U.S. restrictions on shipping advanced chips to China generally haven't stopped Chinese companies from accessing them in overseas data centers, the New York Times reported . Nvidia told the Times that remote access is consistent with U.S. export controls because the chips remain outside restricted countries. That access is distinct from suspected smuggling. The Times reported that Megaspeed, the Nvidia customer where Alice Huang worked, was under investigation for steering advanced chips to China. 5. What happens to Huang's advocacy? His arguments for selling chips to China and embracing open AI models will face renewed scrutiny, with many of his comments potentially being seen in a new light due to the relationship. Huang has repeatedly, and stridently, pushed to loosen restrictions on sales to China , arguing that reliance on American technology serves U.S. interests. The bottom line: Huang has made himself the AI boom's indispensable man. The industry must now reckon with what happens when its fortunes depend so heavily on his.

events.title: Jensen Huang spy scandal rocks AI race
events.summary: The world's most powerful AI executive admitted Sunday to an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, sending shock waves through an industry built on his singular influence. Why it matters: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has fashioned himself as the indispensable leader of an indispensable company — a $4.5 trillion behemoth with unparalleled clout in Silicon Valley, on Wall Street and inside President Trump's White House. Trump stood by Huang on Sunday evening, telling reporters that the Nvidia CEO is "an honorable guy" and "probably has an excuse" for his infidelity. The big picture: Huang, who has led Nvidia since founding the chipmaker 33 years ago, has become the AI boom's chief evangelist and most authoritative voice. He has brushed aside fears of both a speculative bubble and technological catastrophe, joining forces with Trump to calm markets and the public as warnings of an AI apocalypse reached fever pitch. For almost any other CEO, an affair with a suspected foreign intelligence operative could be career-ending. Huang's grip on Nvidia — and the company's extraordinary importance to the AI economy — may insulate him from the same fate. Driving the news: Huang confessed to the affair in a letter to staff Sunday, apologizing to his family as Nvidia's board launched an independent probe into the suspected Chinese intelligence operation. U.S. officials believe Alice Huang, an executive at Nvidia customer Megaspeed, was recruited by Beijing's top spy agency to gather information and potentially influence Nvidia's campaign to expand advanced chip sales to China. Nvidia's board said it had no reason to believe national security or company secrets were compromised and expressed confidence in Jensen Huang, who intends to remain CEO during the investigation. Zoom in: The New York Times first exposed the suspected Chinese espionage operation on Oct. 29, reporting that a woman believed to be working for Beijing had developed a close relationship with Nvidia's CEO. The company portrayed their interactions as routine business dealings — an account now under scrutiny in the wake of Huang's admission that he was "unfaithful" to his wife. Trump defended Huang on Oct. 31 as a "great, brilliant person," but hedged when asked if he should remain a White House adviser: "I would like to say yes. I mean, unless we find out something to the contrary." The intrigue: The Trump administration reportedly knew about the suspected Chinese intelligence operation long before it became public. Trump was briefed in 2025, according to the Times, and Secretary of State Marco Rubio personally oversaw a classified intelligence memo warning senior officials this spring. Yet Trump continued to embrace Huang as a trusted adviser, welcoming him to the White House as the Nvidia chief pressed to loosen restrictions on advanced chip exports to China. Reality check: There's no public evidence that Huang's relationship influenced his advocacy for selling to China, a longstanding commercial priority for Nvidia. "Today's news will not slow NVIDIA. Jensen is committed to continuing to lead NVIDIA as CEO without interruption," John Rizzo, head of public policy communications, said in a statement. What to watch: Huang's scandal comes amid a dramatic reversal of political fortunes for the AI industry, as voters rejected data center expansion and handed control of Congress to Democrats promising tougher oversight. A post-election rout wiped trillions from U.S. stocks on Thursday, deepening uncertainty over an AI boom that has powered much of the market's growth. Huang's admission is now poised to open an explosive new line of inquiry : Did the White House disregard intelligence warnings while advancing policies championed by one of Trump's closest corporate allies?

events.title: The climate case for AI has not been made
events.summary: This week, as countries meet in Antalya, Turkey for the United Nations climate conference, one topic likely to dominate the conversation is artificial intelligence. The host has already called on countries to commit to ensuring that AI is designed, powered, and deployed in ways that support climate action. But so far, industries around the world aren’t doing nearly enough to harness the technology to actually drive down the greenhouse-gas emissions heating up the planet, despite some very optimistic claims from AI companies. In 2024, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman declared that AI would unleash “astounding triumphs,” including “fixing the climate.” The year before, in a 2023 op-ed , the head of sustainability at Google and her coauthor wrote that AI could reduce global emissions 5% to 10% by 2030.  Some academic researchers have examined these AI-related climate claims. A peer-reviewed study published last year, led by researchers at the London School of Economics’ Grantham Research Institute and the firm Systemiq, estimated that AI could help cut global emissions by the equivalent of 3.2 to 5.4 billion tons of carbon dioxide annually by 2035—roughly on par with the US’s annual energy-related emissions on the high end, even after subtracting AI’s own energy footprint. Those potential gains are mostly concentrated in three sectors: power, meat and dairy, and vehicles. But projections like these are only as good as our willingness to test them against present-day reality. So is there evidence that the largest companies in these three sectors are beginning to integrate AI in line with the study’s projections, and if so, do the results match expectations? Or is the 2035 number still mostly aspirational?  Companies across these sectors have announced plenty of initial efforts to incorporate AI into various business practices. But an AI-assisted review of public information from significant market actors in each sector, conducted and reviewed by the second author of this piece, found that few have announced they’re pursuing the specific emissions-reducing routes that informed the projections in the study—and fewer still claim they’ve used them to achieve meaningful climate progress. The power sector is where the earlier study’s underlying math is most concrete: AI-driven forecasting of supply and demand could increase the amount of renewable electricity that reaches the grid from already-built solar and wind facilities by up to 20%, which could prevent an estimated 1.8 billion tons of emissions a year.  Yet of the grid operators reviewed in China, the United States, and Europe, only one deployed a known meaningful, working AI program of this sort, according to the analysis. A partnership between the UK’s National Grid ESO and Open Climate Fix halved the grid operator’s solar-forecast error (the difference between the amount of incoming sunlight predicted and the amount that actually reaches solar panels), avoiding hundreds of thousands of tons of carbon dioxide a year. Beyond this example in the UK, though, many other grid operators in the EU, the US, and China had little to show in the public record in terms of the AI integration envisioned by the study. The meat and dairy sector offers the starkest contrast between technology readiness and market reality. To achieve the 2035 emission reductions anticipated in the earlier study, AI would need to close the taste and cost gap between traditional proteins and alternative ones, such as lab-grown or plant-based burgers and milk substitutes.  In one of the clearest efforts to achieve this, the AI and food tech company NotCo recently formed a joint venture with Kraft Heinz using its platform Giuseppe , which analyzes plant molecular data to pinpoint combinations replicating the taste, texture, and smell of animal products.  But few other alternative-protein companies had such a deeply integrated way of using AI in product development, the AI-assisted review suggests. Meanwhile, the sector seems to be facing more fundamental problems, including stubbornly slow mainstream consumer adoption and declining funding levels. Most notably, venture capital flowing into cultivated meat fell from a $989 million peak in 2021 to around $83 million last year.  The transportation sector offers some hopeful examples of the type of AI integration necessary to achieve the study’s projections, particularly among battery manufacturers and ride-sharing platforms. CATL—which controls roughly 40% of the global market for electric-vehicle batteries—launched an AI system trained on more than 100,000 battery design cases and 600 terabytes of test data. It cut the time needed to screen candidate materials by two orders of magnitude, according to the company. Independent researchers also found that the ride-sharing platform Didi Chuxing was able cut per-trip emissions 16% on average by using AI-optimized routing to minimize detours. There’s another big problem in the climate case for AI, though: Oil and gas companies are also interested in these tools for many reasons, including the potential to increase production of fossil fuels . Technology firms that committed to sustainability goals in the past should answer questions about how their tools could be used to boost old, dirty energy as well as clean, renewable energy. Finally, it’s also worth noting that integrating AI is just the first step, and it remains unclear to what degree the technology can accelerate the sorts of improvements and innovations envisioned. AI also does little to shorten the standard paths to certifying, permitting, building, packaging, marketing, and selling any resulting products, facilities, or services.  The findings of the analysis, carried out by Anthropic’s Claude Code, were reviewed against public documents and media accounts to ensure their accuracy. It is possible that some companies and utilities in these industries are pursuing AI-assisted applications that would fit into the initial study’s scenarios but haven’t yet been disclosed publicly.  Greater and better-targeted AI integration and efficiency gains in these three sectors may well materialize, bringing the 2035 projections closer to reality. But it won’t happen without deliberate and sustained efforts to ensure that AI delivers more environmental benefits than harms. Notably, so far the rapid adoption of AI models and buildout of data centers has driven a huge increase in energy consumption and emissions, and this has led major tech companies like Microsoft, Google, and others to fall well off track in their corporate climate goals. At this point it would be surprising if the sector even manages to zero out its climate pollution: Emissions associated with global data centers (which may handle AI as well as non-AI computing tasks) could exceed 300 million tons annually in 2035, according to the IEA’s base forecast . events.title: Lawyers in This State Are Allowed to Ghost Clients for Years. Why Don’t More Judges Stop Them?
events.summary: When a person challenging their conviction can’t afford a lawyer, a judge will appoint one. Last year, Philadelphia Common Pleas Court Judge Frank Palumbo advised a newly appointed lawyer that his case looked “like it’s going to be a … dismissal.” Illustration by Mark Harris for ProPublica. Source images: The First Judicial District of Pennsylvania; David Swanson/The Philadelphia Inquirer. One morning in July 2025, I was the lone spectator in Judge Frank Palumbo’s courtroom in Philadelphia, watching prosecutors and public defenders haggle over the fates of defendants. Palumbo paused the proceedings to talk to a lawyer he’d appointed to help a prisoner who had ineptly challenged his conviction. The lawyer profusely thanked the judge for the job. Then, Palumbo offered a bit of guidance: “I think I know where this is going to go. I don’t want to make it overly complicated. It’s real simple.”  The judge said he’d pass along a brief that a different lawyer had filed arguing that there was no merit to the man’s claims in a related case. “I’m not saying plagiarize,” the judge said. The attorney told the judge he got the message. “So it’s called a Finley letter,” he said, using the common legal term for that no-merit brief, in which an attorney can argue against the client’s claims and ask to withdraw from the case.  “It’s looking like it’s going to be a Finley dismissal,” the judge agreed after a bit more discussion, “but every option is open.”  I’ve spent years covering criminal justice in Pennsylvania, including the post-conviction system that allows people to argue that their lawyer had mishandled their case or to raise newly discovered evidence. That day, I left the courtroom wondering how what I’d observed squared with the state’s promise of effective legal representation in cases like this.  That question sent me on a yearlong reporting odyssey, during which I read hundreds of Finley letters, tracked down court financial records from all 67 Pennsylvania counties, interviewed dozens of lawyers and analyzed thousands of court dockets. What I wanted to know was: Why has it become the norm for Pennsylvania’s lawyers to argue against their own clients? And who is this system serving? I found that lax rules, low pay and heavy caseloads have compromised legal representation under the state’s Post Conviction Relief Act. Over the past year, I’ve reported on how lawyers, working under fee structures banned in other states, fell years behind on their cases. I spoke with prisoners who’d waited nearly a decade for their lawyers to file anything and others whose lawyers filed Finley letters despite compelling evidence of innocence . I also looked at three years’ worth of invoices and found that, three quarters of the time, Philly lawyers who wrote Finley letters had never spoken with their clients, contacted the trial lawyer or obtained available police files before deciding their claims had no merit.  None of those seemingly basic steps, I was surprised to learn, is required under the law. In fact, dozens of lawyers I spoke to expressed sharply divided opinions about the extent of their obligations to these clients.  But court-appointed lawyers are not working unsupervised. Judges are largely in charge of appointing them to cases, and those same judges are supposed to make sure they’re doing a timely and diligent job.  I noticed that judges continued to assign lawyers more cases even after appeals courts flagged serious issues with their work. And when it came to Finley letters, judges accepted almost all of them over the three years of cases I reviewed, despite the lawyers’ minimal investigative efforts. Some of the letters they approved contained obvious factual errors or even named the wrong client. Last fall, after Palumbo gave the lawyer a copy of a Finley letter, the lawyer followed the template. His no-merit brief said that his client’s claim could not be considered because he’d missed his filing deadline. The bulk of the document was, in fact, identical to the other lawyer’s brief.  Palumbo, who didn’t respond to my requests for comment, accepted the Finley letter anyway, let the lawyer drop the client and dismissed the claim. Who Judges Judges? I thought a fair way to evaluate judges would be to look at the rulings of the Pennsylvania’s Superior Court, the state’s appeals court that hears hundreds of challenges to judges’ rulings on post-conviction matters each year. And boy, did the Superior Court have thoughts on how judges are handling post-conviction cases.  In one withering opinion, a judge bemoaned an “embarrassing saga” of deficient lawyering that a Berks County judge had tolerated. Another derided a Philly judge and the five attorneys she’d appointed who all missed appeals deadlines, writing, “As Hall of Fame manager Casey Stengel said of the hapless 1962 New York Mets, ‘Can’t anybody here play this game?’” After logging hundreds of rebukes laid out in Superior Court opinions by hand, I asked some colleagues with data skills to help identify as many of these cases as possible across the last 14 years, the time frame for which opinions were reliably posted online. In an excerpt from a court opinion, a judge mentions that at least five attorneys had abandoned a client. Obtained by ProPublica We found that the appeals court flagged more than 250 cases in which judges didn’t intervene as lawyers provided what the court labeled ineffective representation: “sandbagging” a client at a hearing, stonewalling a petitioner who’d mailed two dozen letters to the lawyer’s office or filing boilerplate appeals so vague that they doomed their clients’ cases. In hundreds more cases, judges failed to appoint a lawyer at all, held hearings where petitioners went unrepresented or allowed a lawyer to drop a case, leaving the client stranded on appeal. More than 200 times, they oversaw lawyers who abandoned clients, tanking their appeals or stalling their cases for years. “Judges are in a terrific position to be able to prevent these kinds of injustices,” said Marissa Boyers Bluestine, a longtime post-conviction lawyer who now works at the University of Pennsylvania’s law school. The scathing reversals aside, the Superior Court affirms about 80% of lower-court rulings. That’s expected given the strict deadlines and complicated rules about how appeals must be filed. The appeals court is also required to defer to the lower court’s factual decisions. And when it reverses due to an error, the recourse is generally limited to ordering a do-over or, on rare occasions, instructing the lower court to explore sanctions. In one opinion, the court resorted to using boldface to call out an egregious failure: “The PCRA court did nothing in this case for 20 years.” Then, it told the lower court to try again. events.title: House GOP gears up for leadership reshuffling
events.summary: House Republicans will see a post-election reshuffling this week, with every senior rung of their leadership facing competition — and President Donald Trump is staying out of it. Reps. Jim Jordan of Ohio and current Majority Leader Steve Scalise of Louisiana are vying for minority leader. Current Majority Whip Tom Emmer of Minnesota and Rep. August Pfluger of Texas are competing for next Congress’ GOP minority whip spot, while current Conference Chair Lisa McClain of Michigan faces challenges from Reps. Erin Houchin of Indiana and Greg Steube of Florida. After their massive Election Day losses, some GOP lawmakers are inclined to fully overhaul their leadership. Rep. Marlin Stutzman, R-Ind., who’s backing Jordan, told Semafor: “I think we need to tell the American people, ‘We heard you loud and clear. You’re frustrated, and we need new leadership.’” As Republicans look for ways to claw their way out of the hole that the midterms left them in, they’ll also be deciding on a new campaign chief. Reps. Rudy Yakym of Indiana and Brian Jack of Georgia are running to chair the National Republican Congressional Committee. Notably, neither are seen as interested in carving out distance from Trump. Democrats will start their leadership elections next week, though Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries isn’t expected to face any serious challenges to becoming speaker. There’s not much legislative action yet in the lame-duck session, but Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth will be impeached by the House this week. Though his conviction in the Senate is unlikely, it will be a critical moment for House Democrats to show unity heading into their takeover of the chamber. Jeffries said he was a “hard yes” on Hegseth impeachment on ABC’s . With House Republicans looking for a scapegoat after their midterm losses, the impeachment vote could pick up votes on the right, too. Rep. French Hill, R-Ark., said on CBS’ that he would “want to hear the debate on it, to see if it merits impeachment or some other disciplinary action or some other action by the president,” adding that he was dissatisfied with how the Iran war has been handled. House Republican leaders will also face attendance problems post-midterms that are likely to complicate prospects for any other lame-duck legislative action. — Nicholas Wu

events.title: Senate’s post-election drama escalates quickly
events.summary: Congress’ lame-duck session starts with a bang on Monday, as Senate Republicans debate their future after last week’s shellacking and Democrats face their first vote on a permitting reform bill that is cleaving them. On the first front, Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., is expected to deliver Senate Republican Conference Chair Tom Cotton, R-Ark., a letter on Monday with the requisite five signatures needed to force a special conference meeting. That won’t delay Majority Leader John Thune’s leadership election, nor will it block Thune’s bid to helm the conference in the minority, but it will force a debate about party leadership — and there may eventually be a vote on whether to delay the leadership election. Meanwhile, the Senate will take a procedural vote on the permitting reform bill this evening, and it’s looking likely to advance despite opposition from some environmental groups. Democrats are seeking more changes to the bill, but many in the party think it’s the right time to move permitting legislation that has now stalled for multiple Congresses. Two climate hawks, Sens. Martin Heinrich, D-N.M., and Sheldon Whitehouse, D-R.I., are both publicly pushing to pass the bill in the lame duck, and Democrats often trust their ranking members to cut a good deal. The bill will take probably a couple weeks to pass in the Senate if it advances. Barring a delay, Senate Republican leadership elections are scheduled to take place at 9 am on Tuesday; in 2022, Republicans squashed a similar delay tactic. This time around, some Republicans, like Utah Sen. Mike Lee, say they need a plan on how the lame duck will play out before deciding on their leadership votes. Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., who has run twice for leader, wants a commitment to pass the GOP’s voter ID legislation. Even swing-state Sen. David McCormick, R-Pa., endorsed a pause to digest and debate what happened. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer’s day in the spotlight will come, but not for a few weeks: Democratic leadership elections will happen in early December.

events.title: NVIDIA Announces New Planned Investments in Korean Startups at the MSIT-NVIDIA AI Startup Partnership Forum
events.summary: Korea’s Ministry of Science and ICT and NVIDIA hosted the MSIT -NVIDIA AI Startup Partnership Forum at COEX. Representatives from the Ministry of Science and ICT and NVIDIA met with over 20 Korean startups across foundation models, physical AI, AI infrastructure and AI semiconductors. NVIDIA also announced an investment in Korean startup Point2 , with additional investments planned in Motif Technologies , RLWRLD and Upstage. Point2 Technology, an AI interconnect company, builds scalable, radio frequency-based interconnects that move data between chips and racks in AI factories, offering an innovative alternative to conventional copper and optical interconnect solutions for AI cluster scale-up, delivering the reach, performance and efficiency needed for next-generation AI infrastructure. Motif Technologies , a Seoul-based AI lab, develops foundation models for building AI agents that carry out complex tasks, including Motif-3, a large language model released with open weights. RLWRLD, a physical AI startup based in San Francisco, Seoul and Tokyo, develops robotics foundation models that enable humanoid and industrial robots to perform complex real-world tasks that require five-finger dexterity, such as precisely inserting components, threading nuts onto bolts and kitting parts from moving conveyors. Upstage , a Korean enterprise AI company, develops Solar language models and document AI tools that help businesses extract information from complex documents, streamline workflows and build AI applications for everyday operations. The companies represent work across the full AI stack , from infrastructure to models to robotics applications. The planned investments build on NVIDIA’s work with Korea’s startup and venture community, including more than 1,000 Korea-based members of NVIDIA Inception , a program that helps startups grow with access to preferred pricing, technical expertise and opportunities for investor introductions. events.title: Bikers and Bug-Lovers Join Forces to Fight a New Google Data Center
events.summary: On Wednesday afternoon, Jamie Robins strolled up to the entrance of Google’s UK headquarters in Kings Cross, London. He brandished a letter containing details of a petition signed by almost 55,000 people, calling for Google to abandon plans to build a large new data center in Thurrock, 15 miles to the east of London. Robins works for wildlife conservation trust Buglife, part of an unlikely alliance of special-interest groups trying to block the Thurrock development. Buglife and local wildlife groups fear for an endangered plant, rare bumblebee, and other invertebrates whose habitat they say will be destroyed. Nonprofit Foxglove says the data center will emit too much pollution. The Thurrock Hammers motorcycle club wants to return to racing on the site. Members of the various groups joined Robins outside Google’s office last Wednesday, holding placards demanding the company “search elsewhere” for somewhere to put its facility. Across the UK, companies like Google are preparing to build industrial-scale data centers, part of a scramble to meet the swelling demand for the compute needed to run artificial intelligence models and other digital services. The UK government is eager to encourage them , hoping to capture a share of the hundreds of billions of dollars flowing into the AI industry and minimize the country’s dependence on foreign partners for compute. But like in the US , people living near to the proposed developments are making their objections known and trying to gum up the works. Google says its plans for the Thurrock site prioritize biodiversity and the reduction of emissions. “We share the concerns that Buglife and others have—and their expectation that this site should be developed sustainably,” Adam Elman, director of sustainability EMEA at Google, tells WIRED. But the situation in Thurrock underscores the level and breadth of resistance that data center developers face as the public mood towards them appears to sour . Though small, the demonstration outside Google was one of a number of anti-data center protests that took place across Europe last week . In Amsterdam, protesters scaled a crane at a Microsoft data center site and unfurled a “fuck AI” banner. “There’s local campaign groups against data centers popping up every week,” says Robins. “People are angry about data centers turning up in their back gardens. They’re angry about data centers flouting local opinion—and about the impact it has on wildlife.” The Thurrock site is located next to a fuel stop, where an arterial road meets the highway that encircles London. On the plot, the remnants of Arena Essex, a disused motorcycle racing stadium, border grassland scribbled with old footpaths, and a lake. Google acquired the site through a subsidiary in 2023. In May last year, it applied for permission to build a data center campus there. When locals caught wind, they coordinated with national wildlife and environmental groups and began to kick up a fuss. Of the 1,000 responses submitted by members of the public to the planning authority, only one supported the project. (Thurrock Council says that many of the responses were submitted by people living outside the local area.) The protest group argues that Google’s proposal fails to properly account for the negative effects of the data center development: the loss of the raceway sporting facility, the destruction of habitat for rare flora and fauna, and the up to 570,000 tonnes of emissions it could produce each year—which Foxglove claims cannot be accommodated under the UK government’s carbon budget. “We’re an outlier. We object on different grounds. I think that’s why I think we’re quite useful to the whole campaign,” says Mark Sexton, director at the Thurrock Hammers motorcycle club. “The unlikely alliance has got some attention.” Google says the objections are grounded in misconceptions about its plans. The company claims it will achieve a net gain in biodiversity by retaining habitat and transplanting endangered plants to another location; and that it will offset the emissions by financing new sources of renewable energy generation, with a view to becoming carbon-neutral by 2030 . Google argues that razing the motorcycle stadium will not result in the loss of an invaluable community facility because the track has already been out of use for a number of years. “We want to be good neighbors,” says Elman. “We recognize the ecological value of these sites. Our goal is to minimize the impact as much as possible.” Unconvinced by Google’s reassurances, the protesters intend to continue to fight the development—one small act of protest at a time. “Do I think we’ve got much hope? Not right now,” says Rob Pownall, founder of nonprofit Protect The Wild, who attended Wednesday’s demonstration. “But this is another chip off that massive ice block.” There are some signs the grassroots anti-data center movement is starting to win concessions.

events.title: Welcome to Weed Island
events.summary: Steven Tan walks along a narrow concourse in the Northern Leaf greenhouse in St Lawrence, Jersey, reading aloud the strains of his cannabis plants: Pink Gasoline, Moon Beam Gelato, Carbon Fibre, Gorilla Kush. Rows of plants stretch off into the distance. To the untrained eye, they look largely the same, with their distinctive jagged-edged, multi-fingered leaf shape and sticky buds like tiny pinecones. But Tan, the CEO and director of medical cannabis manufacturer Northern Leaf, knows them intimately. “These plants are all different,” he says, stopping next to a mature Carbon Fibre specimen. “Just like humans.” Northern Leaf is one of the largest licensed medical marijuana producers in Europe. Its 100,000-square-foot growing facility is based in Jersey, the largest of the Channel Islands, located between England and France. Previously, this greenhouse was home to Jersey tomatoes, once a famed crop on the island that came close to extinction, thanks to growing fuel costs and cheaper competition from overseas. Now, it is fitted out with all of the technology required for cultivating cannabis that meets strict regulations for medical use, which include: automated irrigation, environmental monitoring, and air purification. Despite being just 45 square miles in size, with a population of 100,000, Jersey—which lies 14 miles off the coast of the French mainland but is a British Crown Dependency—has emerged as an unlikely player in the medical cannabis industry. Although its total exports (over 9,200 kilograms in 2025) are small compared to UK growers, this represents an enormous amount per capita, and cannabis is fast becoming one of the island’s important new industries. Jersey’s chief minister, Lyndon Farnham, has previously said that he wants Jersey to be a “centre of excellence” for medical cannabis, and for cannabis production to become a mainstay of the island’s economy. Jersey, a British Crown Dependency that sits between the UK and France, that has become an integral hub for the medical cannabis industry. Currently, 90 percent of Jersey’s cannabis production comes from Northern Leaf. In 2025, the company exported £8.4 million ($11.3 million) worth of medical marijuana to markets including the UK and Germany (regulations mean it is only permitted to grow for export and cannot sell to customers in Jersey). Tan has much greater ambitions. He points to another famous Jersey export, Jersey Royal potatoes. “Jersey’s potato industry did £40 million in 2025,” he said. “I am already doing a quarter of the potato industry on 5 percent of the land. On 20 percent of the land, I could create an industry worth more than the potato industry. That is where it will get interesting.” Born in Malaysia to a Chinese dad and Irish mother, Tan, 50, wanted to become a vet, but after graduating from university in 1998, ended up developing software for Citibank. He was making good money, but his heart wasn’t in finance. What really interested him was growing weed. “I loved the science of it, the genetics, the seeds, the smells,” Tan says. The early 2000s were the perfect time for an inquisitive young business grad to get into the cannabis business. Across the world, governments were legalizing medical marijuana and moving towards decriminalization over draconian sentencing. Tan began bouncing around jurisdictions that were relaxing laws on cannabis, working as a consultant in California, the Netherlands, and Canada. “I started to see these legal frameworks opening up. The minute they existed, I went there,” he says. Jersey has a somewhat unique regulatory environment. As a Crown Dependency, it has close ties to Britain, but is not a part of the UK. Crucially, it is self-governing: It can make its own laws. Jersey’s main reputation today is as a tax haven, attracting some of the world’s wealthiest individuals and companies, thanks to its lack of capital gains tax and 0 percent corporation tax for most companies. Along its coastline, next to twee beachside cafes and Nazi bunkers (the Channel Islands were the only part of the British Isles to be occupied by Hitler’s forces in World War II), you can find offices of international banks and wealth management firms catering to the super rich. Although traditionally culturally conservative, Jersey has become something of a trailblazer on cannabis. The island legalized medical cannabis in 2019. Today, five private clinics operate on the island. The latest figures suggest that 6 percent of the population is prescribed cannabis, compared to an estimated 0.4 percent in Germany and 0.1 percent in the UK. Upon legalization, the island’s chief minister, Lyndon Farnham, laid out ambitious plans for the island to become a hub of the medical cannabis trade, repurposing the horticultural facilities and know-how from its tomato-growing glory days for this new endeavor. Tan joined Northern Leaf as CEO in 2024, when the company was in dire straits after a failed IPO.

events.title: Korea Advances Physical AI Across Industries With NVIDIA
events.summary: Tapping into the country’s strengths in manufacturing and engineering, NVIDIA is helping advance Korea’s physical AI ecosystem. The country’s industry leaders are applying accelerated computing, AI and simulation to everything from semiconductor manufacturing to robotics and autonomous vehicles. These efforts are helping bring physical AI from development into real-world production. Samsung Advances Semiconductor Engineering With Accelerated Computing and AI Physics Samsung Electronics is expanding its collaboration with NVIDIA to advance semiconductor innovation through accelerated computing and AI physics. The work spans materials research, process development and device engineering. In technology computer-aided design, Samsung is working with NVIDIA cuISS and NVIDIA cuDSS to accelerate computations involving sparse linear systems. The collaboration also extends to GPU acceleration for process and optical simulations. In materials research, Samsung’s sMOL platform has run selected quantum chemical calculations up to 5x faster end to end with NVIDIA cuEST . Samsung is also exploring NVIDIA cuEquivariance to speed up tensor operations used in training and inference for atomistic AI models. Samsung is developing chip-scale thermal and mechanical analysis workflows with NVIDIA PhysicsNeMo . In one AI homogenization case, combining AI-predicted effective material properties, coarser grids and GPU acceleration resulted in a roughly 1,600x speedup. Simulation time fell from about 18 hours for a fine-grid solve on a 32-core CPU to 41 seconds for a GPU-accelerated coarse-grid solve. Looking ahead, NVIDIA Agent Toolkit could connect these simulation tools and AI models, helping future engineering agents run analyses and compare design options. Kakao Mobility Collaborates With NVIDIA to Advance Autonomous Driving Development Kakao Mobility plans to build on NVIDIA’s autonomous vehicle computing and safety technologies to advance development of a level 4 autonomous driving system. The work combines Kakao Mobility’s proprietary driving software and experience operating in Seoul’s Gangnam district with NVIDIA’s vehicle computing platform. Kakao Mobility plans to use NVIDIA Hyperion , a reference platform for vehicle sensors and compute, powered by NVIDIA DRIVE AGX Thor. It also plans to use NVIDIA Halos to support safety across the development and validation of its autonomous driving technology. Initial development is planned around Kia purpose-built vehicles, integrating Kakao Mobility’s autonomous driving software with NVIDIA technologies. The effort aims to support future level 4 mobility services in Korea. LG Electronics Advances Robot Learning and Factory Simulation NVIDIA and LG Electronics successfully demonstrated NVIDIA Isaac GR00T-powered robotic manipulation and manufacturing tasks using LG’s CLOiD robot in an actual manufacturing environment. The collaboration implemented a physical AI data flywheel connecting real-world data collection, NVIDIA Cosmos-based data augmentation, GR00T model training, NVIDIA Jetson AGX Thor onboard computing and simulation-based evaluation, establishing reusable workflows for continued development and validation of CLOiD’s robotic capabilities. The teams are using this work to refine a repeatable process for training, evaluating and improving robots for manufacturing. events.title: Korea’s AI Ecosystem Advances and Secures Agentic AI With NVIDIA
events.summary: As AI agents take on more work, they need capable open models and security that advances alongside them. Hyundai Motor Group is exploring NVIDIA NemoClaw blueprints and the NVIDIA OpenShell runtime, while AIM Intelligence is integrating its Starfort platform with NVIDIA OpenShell to support secure AI agents for employee productivity and enterprise workflows . A key component of the NVIDIA Open Agent Safety Platform, OpenShell provides a secure runtime with sandboxed execution and policy-based controls to safeguard sensitive data, manage access to enterprise tools and govern autonomous agent actions. AIM Intelligence , a Korean AI security company, is integrating its Starfort agent control platform with NVIDIA OpenShell. The goal is to combine OpenShell’s runtime access controls with Starfort’s detection of malicious instructions and data leakage. The company is also considering a preliminary proof of concept for the public energy sector, with potential applications across enterprise, industrial and robotics environments. On the model side, LG AI Research is opening application programming interface access for K-EXAONE-2.5, developed using NVIDIA Nemotron datasets, including Nemotron-Personas-Korea . Nemotron-Personas-Korea is an open dataset of 7 million fully synthetic Korean personas, grounded in official Korean statistics, that model builders use to ground training data and evaluation in Korean contexts. NVIDIA Nemotron is a family of open models, datasets and techniques that help developers build specialized, efficient AI agents. Learn more about NVIDIA Nemotron open models and get started building secure agents with NVIDIA OpenShell . events.title: NVIDIA Dynamo Recipes Bring Korea’s Leading Open Models to Production
events.summary: NVIDIA is releasing Dynamo-optimized deployment recipes for Korea’s leading open models: A.X K2 from SK Telecom , K-EXAONE 2.0 from LG AI Research , Solar Open 2 from Upstage and Motif-3 from Motif Technologies . As models grow beyond the capacity of a single GPU, they must be split across multiple GPUs, requiring careful coordination of request routing and communication to maintain performance. NVIDIA Dynamo is an open source, distributed inference-serving framework built to deploy models in multi-node environments at data center scale. It handles this routing and communication to maximize inference performance. Optimized for NVIDIA B200 GPUs, these recipes take the guesswork out of deployment, delivering up to 2x performance out of the box. They help developers bring Korea’s open models into production faster and turn them into broadly accessible AI for All services. events.title: NVIDIA, Rebellions and SK Telecom Announce Collaboration to Advance Sovereign AI Infrastructure With NVIDIA NVLink Fusion
events.summary: News Summary: Rebellions plans to adopt NVIDIA NVLink Fusion to connect its next-generation R200 neural processing units to NVIDIA’s open infrastructure platform for rack-scale inference. SK Telecom plans to deploy these systems in its AI data center to support its vision for full-stack sovereign AI spanning infrastructure, proprietary models and public-facing services, including those under Korea’s “AI for All” project. The collaboration, supported by Korea’s Ministry of Science and ICT, aims to connect domestic semiconductor innovation with infrastructure for sovereign AI.   NVIDIA, Rebellions and SK Telecom today announced a collaboration to advance Korea’s sovereign AI infrastructure — using NVIDIA NVLink Fusion™ to bring together NVIDIA’s open infrastructure platform, Rebellions’ Korean-designed AI processors and SK Telecom’s AI data center, model and service capabilities. As part of the agreement, Rebellions will use NVLink Fusion to connect its Rebel R200 neural processing units (NPUs) to the NVIDIA platform, and harness the NVIDIA MGX™ rack architecture for rack-scale system development. SK Telecom plans to deploy these systems, drawing on its AI data center operations expertise, proprietary models and services. Supported by Korea’s Ministry of Science and ICT (MSIT), the collaboration aims to support AI services tailored to Korea’s language, industries and priorities, connecting Korean semiconductor development with the systems and operational capabilities needed to deliver AI at scale. “Korea has the talent, technology and industrial ambition to become a world leader in AI,” said Jensen Huang, founder and CEO of NVIDIA. “Sovereign AI gives nations the power to turn their language, culture and expertise into intelligence. With NVLink Fusion, Korea’s chipmakers can connect their custom ASICs to NVIDIA’s AI factory platform, tightly coupling their processors with NVIDIA compute to run AI workloads. Together with MSIT, Rebellions and SK Telecom, we’re building the computing foundation for Korea to produce its own intelligence and power its next industrial revolution.” “Today’s announcement marks a turning point, opening a new chapter for sovereign AI by connecting Korea’s AI silicon and models with global systems technology,” said Sunghyun Park, cofounder and CEO of Rebellions. “By integrating Rebellions’ purpose-built silicon and system design with NVIDIA’s NVLink Fusion, high-speed interconnects and rack-scale design expertise, and SKT’s model and data center operations capabilities, we will deliver low-latency and energy-efficient inference for frontier models at scale. As a leading Korean AI silicon startup, we will lead the charge to establish Korean technology as a core pillar powering AI worldwide.” “This collaboration is meaningful in that it validates the potential of next-generation sovereign AI infrastructure by combining global AI infrastructure technology with Korean AI semiconductors,” said Jung Jai-hun, president and CEO of SK Telecom. “By linking SKT’s AI data centers, proprietary AI models including A.X K2, and public-facing AI services developed under the ‘AI for All’ project, we will strengthen our full-stack sovereign AI competitiveness and contribute to the growth of Korea’s AI ecosystem.” Scaling Silicon Innovation With NVIDIA’s Open Infrastructure Platform NVLink Fusion extends NVIDIA’s vertically integrated, horizontally open AI platform to custom XPUs. It enables chipmakers to combine specialized silicon with NVIDIA’s high-bandwidth, low-latency scale-up networking and established infrastructure ecosystem, helping improve performance, reduce deployment risk and accelerate time to market. Rebellions is developing its next-generation R200 NPU, optimized for low-latency and energy-efficient inference using frontier models, including multitrillion-parameter mixture-of-experts models. Through NVLink Fusion, Rebellions will connect its R200 NPUs within a rack through NVIDIA NVLink ™ scale-up networking. The NVIDIA MGX rack architecture and reference designs will support development of the systems, while the MGX ecosystem gives Rebellions access to an established supply chain of original design manufacturers and component suppliers. Connecting Infrastructure, Models and Services SK Telecom brings experience building and operating AI data centers, alongside its proprietary foundation models and public-facing AI services. Building on its long-standing collaboration with NVIDIA in AI development and sovereign infrastructure, SK Telecom plans to connect these capabilities and deploy them in its AI data center using the standardized MGX rack architecture to deliver full-stack sovereign AI. The MGX rack architecture provides a foundation for GPU and NPU systems to share data center design elements, including rack footprint, power delivery and cooling. This approach can support infrastructure planning alongside Rebellions’ processor and system development. The companies plan to develop an approach to disaggregated inference, assigning different stages of AI response generation to the processor architecture best suited to each task. Their planned work includes using NVIDIA GPUs for prefill and Rebellions NPUs for decode to improve inference throughput and power efficiency. SK Telecom plans to connect this infrastructure with its proprietary foundation models and public-facing services, including those under the government’s AI for All project, to advance its full-stack sovereign AI strategy. Supporting Sovereign AI Infrastructure With NVLink Fusion MSIT is supporting collaboration between NVIDIA and Korean NPU companies, beginning with Rebellions and SK Telecom, to strengthen Korea’s sovereign AI infrastructure. “This collaboration with NVIDIA marks a significant step forward, as it enables Korean-developed NPUs to enter the computing infrastructure market alongside NVIDIA, a global leader in AI computing, through NVLink Fusion,” said Bae Kyung-hoon, Korea Deputy Prime Minister, and Minister of Science and Information and Communication Technologies. “The government will actively support this collaboration to deliver tangible results and further advance cooperation with NVIDIA across a range of areas, including physical AI and securing GPU supply.” By connecting Korean-developed processors and models with NVIDIA infrastructure and SK Telecom’s data center expertise, the companies aim to establish a foundation for sovereign AI services across Korea’s public and private sectors. Availability Rebellions’ R200 systems are expected to be ready for deployment in 2028.   ]]>

events.title: Nvidia’s $4.5 trillion test of founder immunity
events.summary: There’s little precedent in US corporate history for the crisis facing Nvidia after reports that Jensen Huang was targeted by a Chinese “honeytrap” operation . The national security implications of the allegation, the chipmaker’s founder-CEO’s centrality to his company’s growth story, and Nvidia’s pivotal place in the AI ecosystem all mean the fallout is likely to stretch further than other cases of executive infidelity. Nvidia’s board on Sunday announced an independent investigation, but expressed confidence in Huang. In his own statement admitting that he had been unfaithful to his wife, Huang said he remained “fully committed” to the company. Nvidia is, at the time of writing, the world’s second-most valuable company after Apple, with a market capitalization of $4.5 trillion — almost 12% of the Nasdaq 100 index. And no public company has been more important to the AI revolution or its impact on stock markets: The ravenous appetite from hyperscalers such as Amazon and Google for Nvidia’s chips propelled its annual revenue from under $11 billion to more than $130 billion between 2020 and 2025. The most bullish analysts think its sales will hit $1 trillion in 2029. Huang’s personal indiscretions do not change Nvidia’s order book. But he has been inseparable from its commercial success story, helming its new product presentations, negotiating the loans to customers that have made Nvidia “the central bank of AI,” and dealing directly with President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping at a moment when access to the world’s most advanced AI chips has been called “the defining strategic question” facing the two superpowers. On Sunday, Sequoia’s Shaun Maguire, a Huang supporter, called him “irreplaceable for America’s AI leadership.” The nod to earlier US intelligence warnings that China is targeting US tech leaders will serve as a cautionary tale for many of Huang’s peers in Silicon Valley. Meanwhile, any challenge to investors’ confidence in Huang’s leadership, or any allegation that his personal relationship influenced Nvidia’s lobbying in Washington, could have serious implications for his position and his company’s valuation. Nvidia’s stock already took a beating from a wider reversal in chip stocks as US voters’ protests against data centers shook confidence in the market’s AI trade. Extramarital affairs and relationships that were not disclosed to board members have felled CEOs at companies as prominent as Boeing and McDonald’s in the past. In many cases, boards and investors focused on ethical breaches, such as executives using company funds inappropriately or advancing the careers of romantic partners who reported to them. The allegations about Huang are more serious, but the reaction to those past peccadilloes offers some clues to what Nvidia can now expect. Directors will now face questions about when it knew of the allegations, and whether the earlier investigation it reportedly conducted was thorough enough. That could test a board that is short on corporate heavy-hitters — there’s not one sitting CEO on the board other than Huang — or people with deep experience of national security or political crisis management. The company can also expect litigation from shareholders, and possible regulatory action, if Huang or the board held back material information from investors (Nvidia previously denied the allegations of an affair to media outlets). And Huang is unlikely to avoid high-profile investigations from Congress, whose incoming Democratic-led majority is suspicious of Big Tech CEOs and is already preparing a rash of subpoenas for Trump allies. Huang, unlike many other Silicon Valley founders, is not in control of his own fate: He has run Nvidia as if he fully controls it, but he lacks the dual-class stock that shields tech founders like Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg and Alphabet cofounders Larry Page and Sergey Brin. While his near-4% stake gave him a net worth of $155 billion at Friday’s close, it does not protect him should the board or investors try to oust him. For now, that outcome looks unlikely. There is no obvious successor waiting in the wings, lawmakers are fully aware of Nvidia’s strategic significance to the US, and Wall Street knows Huang as a brilliant founder who has made fortunes for his shareholders. Bill Ackman, the hedge fund manager, was among the investors urging support for Huang on Sunday. Huang has promised to cooperate with the investigation his board has launched. He has no choice. Investors who struggle to imagine Nvidia without him have $4.5 trillion reasons to hope and expect that he rides out this crisis. But his serious lapse in judgment will dent confidence in one of the world’s most consequential companies, at the very moment when investors have shown that their faith in the market’s AI growth story has limits.
